Raster the sample with steps matched to this narrowed probe, and combine with a saturation‑curve calibration (measure signal vs depletion intensity at a knife edge/test pattern) plus regularised deconvolution of the residual PSF.

Practical requirements: pulsed, tightly synchronised pump–probe timing shorter than the core‑hole/excited‑state lifetime (so the depletion is still "on" when the probe interacts), very high peak intensity — hence a diffraction‑limited undulator nanofocus, an XFEL/high‑repetition‑rate source, or a hybrid X‑ray‑probe/optical‑depletion scheme; precise nanometre‑level overlap and drift control of the two foci; per‑pulse intensity normalisation for both beams; and careful checks that the depletion channel is reversible (not simply ablating or permanently damaging the sample), with dose spread over many pulses and, if needed, cryogenic cooling. The payoff is a genuinely sub‑diffraction, element‑ and chemical‑state‑selective probe obtained without any improvement to the focusing optic, source emittance or detector pixel size.

Physically magnify the specimen instead of the image — i.e. apply an "expansion microscopy" style sample preparation before the X‑ray scan. Cross‑link the structures of interest to a swellable polyelectrolyte hydrogel (e.g. acrylate/acrylamide monomers polymerised through the sample after anchoring proteins/labels with a bifunctional linker), homogenise the mechanical resistance of the matrix by proteolytic/detergent digestion, and then dialyse in water so the gel swells isotropically by a factor of ~4–10× in each linear dimension. Stain the expanded gel with a heavy‑metal or nanoparticle contrast agent and image it by micro/nano‑tomography as usual.

Because every feature separation in the object is now physically 4–10× larger while the beamline's effective voxel size, detector MTF, source penumbra and scan protocol are unchanged, structures that were previously well below the instrument's point‑spread function are lifted above it: an instrument with, say, 100 nm resolution reports ~10–25 nm *effective* resolution referred back to the original specimen, and features that formerly occupied one voxel now span many voxels, so segmentation and quantification improve as well. The expansion also dilutes the material along the beam path, lowering absorption, beam hardening and — crucially — the radiation dose deposited per unit of original biological structure, so longer exposures and more projections can be used without damage‑induced deformation.

Practical requirements: verify that the expansion is truly isotropic and calibrated (image the same region before and after with a pre‑registered fiducial pattern or correlative light microscopy and measure the local distortion field, which should be <1–2 % over the field of view); keep the swollen gel mechanically stable during rotation (mount in a capillary, or partially re‑crosslink/re‑embed it so it does not creep or drift during the tomographic scan); use a contrast agent that binds the anchored targets and not the bulk gel, since the gel is mostly water and gives almost no signal; and account for the reduced density (contrast per voxel drops as 1/expansion³) by using phase contrast or high‑Z labels plus longer exposures. The trade‑off is that the method works only for soft, digestible/embeddable specimens and destroys the native density information, but for biological and soft‑matter samples it delivers a genuine order‑of‑magnitude gain in effective spatial resolution with no change whatsoever to the source, optics, detector or reconstruction pipeline.

For crystalline materials, stop trying to *image* the microstructure and instead reconstruct it from **diffraction data — i.e. use diffraction‑contrast tomography / 3DXRD (scanning‑3DXRD) with a forward‑modelling, Friedel‑pair reconstruction.**

Illuminate the sample with a monochromatic box (or line) beam while rotating it through 360°, and record with a near‑field (and, if available, simultaneously a far‑field) pixel detector the Bragg spots produced by every grain as it passes through diffraction condition. Rather than assigning material to voxels from an attenuation image, one indexes the spots, pairs each reflection with its Friedel mate (hkl and −hkl, which are geometrically symmetric about the beam) and then *forward‑models* the grain: the position, shape and orientation of each grain are the free parameters of a fit to the measured spot positions, shapes and intensities on the detector, refined iteratively (algebraic/6‑D reconstruction, or a per‑voxel orientation fit in scanning mode).

The gain in "resolution" comes because a diffraction spot's **centroid can be located to a small fraction of a detector pixel** (typically 1/10–1/20), and each grain contributes hundreds of independent reflections at many rotation angles; the redundancy averages out noise so grain boundaries, grain centres of mass and orientations are determined far more precisely than the nominal voxel size — sub‑micrometre boundary localisation and ~0.01–0.05° orientation (and ~10⁻⁴ strain) resolution from a detector whose pixels project to several micrometres. Attenuation‑contrast tomography could never separate two neighbouring grains of identical density at all, whereas here they are distinguished by *orientation*, an intrinsically sharp, discrete label, so the effective resolution is set by the angular/spot‑centroid precision rather than by the imaging optics, scintillator blur or source size.

Practical requirements: an undulator beam with fine monochromatisation (ΔE/E ≲10⁻⁴) so the spots stay sharp; fine, uniform rotation steps over the full 360° with an accurate, drift‑free rotation axis (Friedel pairing itself provides an internal calibration of the axis, detector distance and tilt); a low‑noise, high‑dynamic‑range detector placed close to the sample for the near‑field spots; a specimen with moderately low mosaicity and a grain size large enough that spots do not overlap excessively (spot‑overlap is the real limit — mitigated with a line/box beam, layer‑by‑layer scanning, or sparse‑indexing algorithms); and finally combination with a conventional absorption‑contrast scan of the same volume so that pores, cracks and second phases can be overlaid on the grain map. The result is a 3‑D, non‑destructive, time‑resolvable grain map whose geometric precision beats the voxel size of the same beamline by roughly an order of magnitude, with no change to the source, optics or camera.

Adopt an **edge‑illumination (apertured‑mask) imaging geometry with sub‑aperture sample dithering**, which makes the mask — not the detector or the source — define the resolution.

Place a highly absorbing "pre‑sample" mask (a laser‑cut/electroformed gold or tungsten foil with slits or a 2‑D aperture array, several absorption lengths thick) immediately upstream of the specimen so the beam is split into a set of narrow, well‑separated beamlets, each much narrower than a detector pixel (e.g. 1–2 µm beamlets on a 50 µm pixel array). A matched "detector" mask (or simply the pixel edge) is aligned so that each beamlet falls partly on an absorbing edge, i.e. the system works at the steep flank of the illumination‑curve. In this configuration each detected value samples the object only over the width of one beamlet, and any refraction/attenuation by the sample changes the fraction of that beamlet passing the edge, giving strong differential‑phase and dark‑field sensitivity as well as absorption. Then **step the sample (or the mask) transversely in increments much smaller than the beamlet width** and interleave the resulting frames onto a fine sampling grid, so the beamlet width — and ultimately the mask fabrication precision and the stage step — sets the point‑spread function.

Why this raises real resolution: the scintillator blur, pixel pitch and detector MTF drop out entirely (they only have to register how much of each beamlet got through), and because the technique is fully incoherent‑tolerant it does not require a small source or a narrow bandwidth — so one can run in pink/broadband beam with high flux and short exposures, which in turn suppresses drift‑ and motion‑blur. Refraction angles are measured with sub‑microradian sensitivity, so edges of weakly absorbing features are sharpened rather than smeared, and the beamlet geometry intrinsically rejects scattered radiation that would otherwise wash out high spatial frequencies.

Practical requirements: mask apertures fabricated with sub‑micrometre accuracy and rigidly mounted, thermally stabilised and pre‑aligned to the beamlet trajectory (the masks must be re‑aligned if the beam moves); a piezo/flexure translation stage with repeatability well below the dithering step and closed‑loop feedback; per‑frame I₀ normalisation; and a retrieval algorithm that converts the measured beamlet intensity shift/broadening into transmission, refraction and scattering channels before merging the dithered frames and reconstructing (for tomography, repeat the dithering sequence at each rotation angle, or use a continuous "skipped/rolling" dithering scheme to keep the scan time affordable). The result is projection and tomographic images whose resolution is an order of magnitude finer than the physical pixel size, obtained on an ordinary large‑pixel, high‑efficiency detector and with a low‑coherence, high‑flux beam.

**Fuse a low‑resolution channel with a high‑resolution one through structure‑coupled (joint) reconstruction.**

Rather than upgrading any hardware, acquire the *same* volume simultaneously (or sequentially, on the same rotation) in two complementary modalities that have very different resolution/sensitivity trade‑offs — for example a fast, full‑field absorption/propagation‑phase‑contrast tomogram with fine voxels (sharp edges, poor chemical specificity) together with a coarsely sampled scanning X‑ray‑fluorescence (or XANES/µ‑XRD) tomogram whose resolution is limited by the focal spot, step size and counting time. Register the two datasets to sub‑voxel precision (fiducials or mutual‑information/image‑correlation alignment, with refinement of relative magnification, rotation centre and drift), then reconstruct them *jointly* rather than independently: use an iterative, model‑based inversion in which the coarse‑channel reconstruction is regularised by a structural coupling term (parallel level sets, joint total variation, directional/structure‑tensor TV, or a "guided‑filter"/joint‑sparsity prior) that forces its gradients to be parallel to those of the sharp channel, while the data‑fidelity term keeps it quantitatively true to the measured fluorescence counts.

Because edge positions in the coarse map are then dictated by the high‑resolution channel and only the *amplitudes* are fitted to the sparse, noisy data, the elemental/chemical map inherits the fine channel's boundaries: interfaces are localised to a fraction of the scan step, partial‑volume mixing at boundaries is largely undone, and effective resolution improves by roughly 3–10× at no extra dose or beamtime. The same framework applies to fusing a fast dynamic (in‑situ) scan with a single high‑quality static scan of the same specimen, or a local high‑magnification volume with the global coarse volume.

Practical requirements: verify that the two modalities really share edges (a "structure mismatch" — e.g. a trace element distributed smoothly inside a dense phase — must be allowed for by weighting the coupling term and checking against an independently reconstructed control), tune the coupling strength by cross‑validation on a known test object so that features present only in the guide channel are not hallucinated into the other, normalise incident flux per point, and correct self‑absorption in the fluorescence channel using the attenuation map from the absorption reconstruction (which the fusion supplies for free). The result is genuinely sharper, quantitative chemical/structural 3‑D maps obtained with no change to the source, optics, detector or scan geometry.

Tune the **propagation (sample‑to‑detector) distance and the phase‑retrieval parameters** so that in‑line phase contrast sharpens rather than blurs the image. In practice, instead of leaving the distance at an arbitrary value, deliberately set it so the first Fresnel fringe width is comparable to (about one to two times) the detector's point‑spread function — i.e. work at a Fresnel number near unity for the feature size of interest — since too short a distance gives no edge signal, while too long a distance produces multiple overlapping fringes that alias into the pixels and smear fine structure. Then, when retrieving phase from that single‑distance data, do not simply apply Paganin's filter with a nominal δ/β: measure or fit the true δ/β for the material pair at the working energy (or deliberately use a slightly lower value than the physical one), because an over‑estimated δ/β acts as a strong low‑pass filter and is one of the most common, unrecognised causes of resolution loss in phase‑contrast tomography. Finish by applying a matched unsharp‑mask/Wiener deconvolution of the known Paganin kernel combined with the measured detector MTF, so the low‑frequency‑boosted, noise‑suppressed reconstruction retains its high spatial frequencies. This recovers a factor of ~2 in resolvable feature size with no change to the source, optics, detector or scan protocol — only the propagation distance and the reconstruction parameters are optimised.

Add a **stochastic single‑emitter localisation channel using X‑ray‑excited optical luminescence (an "X‑ray STORM/PALM" scheme)**: sparsely label the structures of interest with X‑ray‑excitable luminescent nanoprobes (e.g. Eu/Tb‑ or Ce‑doped oxide/garnet nanoparticles, quantum dots, or persistent‑luminescence phosphors) whose emission can be switched, bleached, blinked or resolved spectrally, and collect their visible light with a high‑NA optical objective/EMCCD looking at the sample from the side while the X‑ray beam scans or floods it. In each frame only a few, well‑separated emitters are "on", so each luminescent spot is an isolated point source whose centroid can be fitted to a few nanometres — far below the size of the X‑ray focus, the zone‑plate/KB point‑spread function, the scintillator blur or the detector pixel pitch. Accumulating tens of thousands of frames and plotting all fitted centroids builds a pointillist super‑resolved map, which is then overlaid on the conventional (attenuation/phase/fluorescence) X‑ray image of the same field to give molecular‑ or feature‑specific detail at nanometre precision within a micrometre‑resolution X‑ray volume; depth information comes from astigmatic/biplane fitting of the optical PSF or from stepping the X‑ray sheet/probe through the specimen.

Practical requirements: probes bright enough to emit ~10³–10⁴ detectable photons per activation cycle (localisation precision scales as PSF/√N), a labelling density sparse enough that only ~1 emitter per optical diffraction‑limited spot is active at a time, a transparent (or thin/side‑viewable) mount so the visible light escapes, drift correction with fixed fiducials or cross‑correlation between frame blocks, and control of the X‑ray dose so that photobleaching and radiation damage do not deform the structure before enough localisations are accumulated. The gain requires no change to the X‑ray source, optics, detector or scan protocol — the resolution limit is transferred from the X‑ray imaging chain to the photon statistics of individual labels.

**Choose the photon energy to maximise contrast‑per‑dose rather than simply using the hardest available beam — i.e. work at the lowest energy (longest wavelength) that the specimen still transmits, ideally on a resonance/absorption edge of the constituent of interest.**

The rationale is that in most high‑resolution X‑ray imaging the smallest resolvable feature is *dose‑limited*, not optics‑limited: the number of photons needed to detect a feature of size *d* scales roughly as 1/(Δµ or Δδ)²·d⁴, so any increase in the intrinsic contrast between the feature and its surroundings shifts the achievable resolution down steeply. Absorption and phase‑shift cross‑sections rise very rapidly as the energy falls (roughly E⁻³ for absorption), so a low‑Z or biological specimen a few micrometres thick imaged in the "water window" (284–543 eV, between the carbon and oxygen K‑edges), or a thin section imaged at 1–5 keV instead of 20–30 keV, delivers an order of magnitude or more contrast per absorbed photon; tuning to just above an element's K‑ or L‑edge (or taking an above‑/below‑edge difference pair) adds element‑specific contrast on top of that. Practical bonuses at low energy: Fresnel zone plates and multilayer Laue lenses are far more efficient and can be made with a higher numerical aperture (soft‑X‑ray zone plates routinely give 10–30 nm focal spots at 10–20 % efficiency, versus a few per cent for thick hard‑X‑ray optics), the depth of focus is more generous relative to the resolution, and the specimen scatters far more strongly to high angles, which is what actually sets the resolution in coherent‑diffraction/ptychographic reconstructions at a given dose.

Practical requirements: the sample must be thinned (to ≲1–10 µm for soft X‑rays) or prepared as a section/pillar so it is not opaque; the whole beam path, sample chamber and detector must be under vacuum, with the sample cryo‑cooled to tolerate the higher absorbed dose; and one should verify by calculation (transmission ≈ 1/e is close to the optimum) that the chosen energy gives maximum signal‑to‑noise rather than either too little absorption contrast (too high an energy) or too little transmitted flux (too low an energy). For thick or dense specimens the same logic is applied in reverse — go just high enough in energy to penetrate, and no higher — and combined with edge‑tuned or dual‑energy subtraction so that contrast, and hence the dose‑limited resolution, is optimised rather than discarded.

Beat the radiation‑damage limit in the *time* domain by adopting a "diffract‑before‑destroy" single‑pulse acquisition. Rather than accumulating dose slowly (where damage, mass loss and beam‑induced motion blur the finest detail long before enough photons have been collected), deliver the entire required dose in one, or a few, extremely short and intense X‑ray pulses — e.g. a single‑bunch/few‑bunch or short‑pulse (low‑alpha, crab‑cavity or laser‑slicing) mode of the storage ring, an X‑ray chopper gating one bunch train, or an XFEL‑class source — with the beam pre‑concentrated onto the specimen by a condenser or focusing optic so that the pulse contains ≳10⁶–10⁹ photons per resolution element.

Because the exposure (femtoseconds to sub‑microseconds) is shorter than the time needed for the photo‑ionised atoms to move, for heat to propagate, or for the specimen to expand/fragment, the recorded projection or diffraction pattern reflects the *undamaged* structure even though the absorbed dose is one to several orders of magnitude above the conventional (even cryogenic) damage tolerance. Since the achievable resolution scales steeply with the deliverable dose (dose ∝ 1/d³–1/d⁴), this directly converts into finer resolvable features, while simultaneously freezing out all vibration, stage drift and sample motion — the usual practical resolution killers in long scans.

Practically, one images a fresh, identical copy of the specimen for each shot (a stream of nanoparticles/cells injected across the beam, a raster of "single‑use" positions on a fixed target grid, or a serial‑delivery chip), records each shot on a fast, high‑dynamic‑range, single‑frame‑readout pixel detector, and then classifies, orients and merges the thousands of single‑shot patterns/images computationally (expand–maximise–compress orientation recovery, or averaging after alignment) to build one high‑statistics, high‑resolution 2‑D or 3‑D reconstruction. Requirements are pulse‑to‑pulse intensity normalisation, rejection of blank/multi‑hit shots, control of pulse energy so ablation does not occur *during* the pulse, and a sample‑delivery system reproducible enough that the merged copies are structurally identical.

Upgrade the nanofocusing optic itself by moving to a **wedged multilayer Laue lens (MLL) pair fabricated by atomic‑layer/magnetron‑sputter deposition**, i.e. push the numerical aperture up by nanofabrication rather than by clever illumination or post‑processing. Conventional zone plates are capped at ~20–30 nm resolution because their finest outer zones must be etched lithographically with a huge aspect ratio; an MLL instead grows the "zones" as a sputtered/ALD multilayer stack with thicknesses that can be laid down with sub‑nanometre precision (finest layers of only a few nm) and then sectioned to the correct thickness, so the aperture and hence the NA can be far larger. Crucially, the layers are deposited with a **wedged (tilted) geometry** so that every layer satisfies the local Bragg condition across the whole aperture — removing the volume‑diffraction efficiency loss and the aberrations that limit flat MLLs — and two such lenses are mounted in a crossed (KB‑like) arrangement, with a matched central stop and order‑sorting aperture, to focus in both directions. Together with laser‑interferometer‑referenced mounting to hold the relative tilt/roll of the two lenses to microradians, this delivers a hard X‑ray probe of <10 nm with high (tens of per cent) efficiency and works at high photon energies where zone plates become impractically thick, so scanning nanoprobe, ptychographic and full‑field measurements all gain roughly a factor of 2–5 in spatial resolution together with a higher flux density (shorter dwell times and therefore less drift blur). Practical requirements: verify the achieved focus at‑wavelength (Siemens‑star or ptychographic probe retrieval), maintain a monochromaticity better than 1/N for the number of layers, and use a short, stiff, thermally stabilised metrology loop between lens and sample because the focal length and depth of focus shrink with NA.

**Use harmonic (lock‑in) demodulation of a dithered probe in scanning experiments, so the effective point‑spread function is a high‑order derivative of the beam profile rather than the beam profile itself.**

In any scanning‑probe synchrotron measurement (µ/nano‑XRF, STXM, µ‑XRD, XANES mapping), the signal is the convolution of the object with the focal‑spot intensity profile, and the spot size is normally taken as the resolution limit. Instead of trying to shrink that spot with better optics, superimpose on the raster scan a small, fast, sinusoidal *dither* of the beam–sample relative position — amplitude of the order of (or somewhat below) the spot FWHM, at a few hundred Hz to a few kHz — produced by a piezo flexure on the sample stage, by a piezo‑driven tilt of the last KB mirror/zone‑plate stage, or by a fast beam‑steering element. Then detect the resulting signal not as a DC level but with a lock‑in amplifier (or by digitising continuously and Fourier‑demodulating in software) at the **second, third or higher harmonic** of the dither frequency.

The physical gain: expanding the measured signal in the dither amplitude shows that the *n*-th harmonic component is proportional to the object convolved with the *n*-th spatial derivative of the probe profile. Because each successive derivative of a smooth (approximately Gaussian) probe has a progressively narrower central lobe — and, crucially, strongly suppressed tails — demodulating at n = 2–3 narrows the effective PSF by roughly √n and largely removes the long halo/side‑lobe tails from zone‑plate higher orders, mirror slope errors or CRL aberrations that ordinarily smear elemental maps far more than the nominal FWHM suggests. Typical gains are a factor of ~1.5–3 in resolvable feature size and a dramatic improvement in edge sharpness and in the rejection of "background" signal from material just outside the nominal probe. The demodulated harmonic signals can afterwards be integrated (or jointly inverted with the calibrated derivative kernels) to recover a quantitative, sharpened map.

Two further benefits come free: (i) lock‑in detection at a kHz carrier sits far above the 1/f region, so beam‑intensity drift, storage‑ring current decay, detector dark drift and slow thermal drift of the optics are rejected automatically, which by itself preserves high‑frequency contrast in long maps; and (ii) the dither continuously averages over sub‑spot position jitter in a *known* way rather than blurring it randomly.

Practical requirements: the dither amplitude and phase must be calibrated interferometrically (or against a knife edge/Siemens star) and must be stable to a small fraction of the amplitude; the detector and electronics must be fast enough that many dither cycles fit within each dwell point (photon‑counting detectors with time stamping, or an energy‑dispersive detector read out in short time bins, work well); the incident flux must be monitored and the demodulated signal normalised per cycle so that beam fluctuations are not aliased into the harmonic; the dwell time must be increased modestly because the harmonic amplitudes are weaker than the DC signal (higher harmonics fall off quickly, so n = 2–3 is the practical optimum); and the probe profile should be measured in situ (knife‑edge or ptychographic probe retrieval) so the derivative kernels used in the final inversion are the true ones. The result is a genuine sub‑spot‑size, tail‑free chemical or structural map obtained with no change to the focusing optic, source or detector — only an added piezo dither and lock‑in/demodulation stage.

Deliberately place the rotation axis half a detector pixel off the optical centre and record a full 360° scan instead of 180°. Because each projection at angle θ+180° is the mirror image of the one at θ but is sampled on a grid displaced by exactly half a pixel, the two half-turns interleave: after flipping and merging them, every sinogram row is sampled on a grid of half the physical pixel pitch, i.e. at twice the detector's Nyquist frequency, and the volume can legitimately be reconstructed on a half-size voxel grid. This doubles the true sampling-limited resolution using the existing source, optics and camera, and costs only the extra angular views (cheap with continuous fly-scanning).

In practice: determine the axis offset to better than ~0.1 pixel by cross-correlating the 0° and 180° projections (or by reprojection-based self-calibration), keep the rotation stage wobble and drift well below half a pixel (air-bearing stage, short stiff metrology loop, drift correction between half-turns), use uniformly and finely spaced angles over the full 360° so the interlaced sinogram is consistent, and finally deconvolve the measured detector/scintillator PSF and MTF from the merged sinograms — since after interleaving the limit is set by the detector blur rather than by the sampling. The same off-axis 360° trick simultaneously doubles the usable field of view, so a wider specimen can be imaged at the highest magnification without truncation artefacts.

**Exploit prior knowledge of the specimen's composition in the reconstruction — i.e. use discrete/segmentation‑coupled tomography (DART‑type algorithms) with sub‑voxel boundary modelling.**

Many synchrotron specimens (metal–pore, catalyst–support, fibre–matrix, labelled–unlabelled tissue) consist of only a small number of materials with essentially known attenuation/phase values, which can be measured from large homogeneous regions of a first conventional reconstruction. Instead of solving for a continuous grey value in every voxel, run an iterative algebraic reconstruction (ART/SIRT) in which the interior of each identified phase is *fixed* to its known value and only the voxels near the phase boundaries are left free, alternating between projection-data updates of the boundary voxels and re-segmentation of the volume; the boundary voxels are additionally modelled as *partial-volume mixtures* (grey level = volume fraction of each phase), so the position of the interface within a voxel is estimated as a continuous quantity from its measured intensity.

This raises the effective spatial resolution for two reasons: (i) the unknown count is reduced by orders of magnitude, so the inverse problem becomes strongly over-determined and the reconstruction can be pushed to (and beyond) the sampling limit without the noise amplification, streaking and edge ringing that force one to low-pass filter a filtered-back-projection reconstruction; and (ii) the partial-volume/level-set treatment localises interfaces to a fraction (typically 1/5–1/10) of a voxel, so thin films, cracks, necks and small pores that are thinner than one voxel are still measured quantitatively rather than being blurred away by the point-spread function. The same over-determination means the required number of projections and hence the dose can be cut substantially, which in turn shortens the scan and reduces drift- and damage-induced blur — a further real gain in resolution.

Practical requirements: verify that the sample really is (locally) multi-phase discrete, and estimate the phase grey values and the detector/scintillator PSF beforehand so that the forward model includes the blur being inverted; include a smoothness/TV regularisation only on the free boundary voxels; use a "soft" segmentation with a hysteresis threshold so noisy voxels are not prematurely frozen into the wrong phase; validate the result against a conventional reconstruction of the same data and, ideally, against a higher-magnification scan of a sub-region, to make sure the sharp interfaces are data-driven and not artefacts of the discrete prior. The gain requires no change to the source, optics, detector or scan geometry — only the reconstruction algorithm and the added prior information.

**Use X‑ray structured‑illumination microscopy (moiré‑based SIM).** Instead of improving the objective or detector, illuminate the specimen with a fine sinusoidal interference fringe pattern whose period is *smaller* than the resolution limit of the imaging chain — produced, for example, by two‑beam interference from a beam splitter/crossed‑mirror pair, or by the Talbot self‑image of a phase grating placed just upstream of the sample. Object detail that is too fine to be transmitted by the optic then beats against the fringes and is down‑shifted (moiré) into spatial frequencies that the lens/scintillator/pixel array *can* record. Acquire a small set of images in which the fringe pattern is phase‑stepped through a full period (typically 3–5 steps) and repeated for two or three fringe orientations (azimuths), so that the high‑frequency information is encoded from several directions.

In processing, Fourier‑transform each frame and solve the resulting linear system to separate the superimposed frequency components; each component is then shifted back to its true position in reciprocal space by the known illumination wave‑vector, and the enlarged, stitched spectrum is inverse‑transformed (with a Wiener/apodisation filter) into the final image. The effective cut‑off becomes (k_optic + k_illumination), i.e. roughly a **two‑fold or better gain in resolution** over the same optic and camera — and, because the illumination is non‑uniform in a known way, the same data also give optical sectioning that removes out‑of‑focus haze in thick samples.

Practical requirements: the fringe period, orientation and phase must be calibrated (measure the empty‑beam pattern and refine the wave‑vector from the data itself); fringe contrast must be preserved, so a transversely coherent, sufficiently monochromatic beam and a vibration‑free, thermally stabilised grating/mirror mount with sub‑fringe‑period stepping precision are needed; per‑frame incident‑flux normalisation is essential since the unmixing is a difference operation; and the extra frames per view multiply the dose and scan time, which can be offset with a bright low‑emittance source and fly‑scanning. Extending the scheme to tomography simply means repeating the phase‑step sequence at each rotation angle, yielding 3‑D reconstructions whose resolution beats the detector's Nyquist/MTF limit without any new X‑ray optic, smaller pixels or sample modification.

Detect the X‑ray‑induced signal with a **sharp scanning‑probe tip instead of a far‑field detector — i.e. do synchrotron X‑ray scanning tunnelling microscopy (SX‑STM) / tip‑collected photoelectron nanoscopy.**

Bring an insulator‑coated, conductive STM/AFM tip (only the very apex exposed, apex radius of a few nanometres) into tunnelling/near‑contact proximity with the illuminated surface, and use the tip itself as the "pixel": the monochromatic synchrotron beam is tuned across an absorption edge of a chosen element, and the tip collects the locally photoejected/Auger and tunnelling‑modulated electron current from the few‑nanometre (down to atomic) volume directly beneath its apex, while the beam‑induced component is separated from the ordinary topographic tunnelling current by chopping the X‑ray beam and lock‑in demodulating at the chopper (or bunch‑clock) frequency. Rastering the tip then yields an image whose resolution is set by the **apex geometry and tip–sample gap**, not by the X‑ray focal spot, zone‑plate zone width, scintillator blur or detector pixel pitch — routinely ~1 nm and, in favourable cases, single‑atom/single‑molecule identification, with full elemental and chemical‑state (XANES) contrast obtained simply by scanning the photon energy at each point.

Practical requirements: UHV and a low‑vibration, thermally drift‑compensated STM head with a short, stiff metrology loop (drift must stay well below the apex size over the map); insulating coating of the tip shank so that photoelectrons from the surrounding illuminated area (which floods tens of micrometres) do not swamp the apex signal; grazing‑incidence illumination and a pre‑focused, high‑flux nanoprobe to raise the tiny photo‑induced current above the noise; careful bias/gap regulation so that the "smart‑tip" signal is not confused with topographic or field‑emission artefacts; and normalisation for beam decay plus a reference measurement on a known standard to calibrate the elemental contrast. The trade‑off is that the technique is surface‑sensitive and slow (probing only the top few nanometres, one point at a time), so it complements rather than replaces bulk transmission imaging — but it converts an X‑ray‑optics‑limited measurement into a tip‑limited one and gains one to two orders of magnitude in lateral resolution with no change to the source, beamline optics or camera.

In a scanning (nanoprobe/STXM) experiment, replace the single-element or segmented "bucket" detector with a fast pixel-array detector and reconstruct the image from the **centre-of-mass / differential-phase-contrast (iCOM) signal of the recorded bright-field disc at every scan point**, rather than from the integrated transmitted intensity.

Because the transmitted intensity image is simply the object convolved with the probe (resolution ≈ probe size, cut-off ≈ NA/λ), whereas the first-moment (COM) signal of the bright-field disc is formed by interference between overlapping regions of the probe's own pupil, its contrast-transfer function extends out to **2·NA/λ** — i.e. roughly a factor-of-two finer resolution from exactly the same focusing optic, scan step and source. Integrating the measured COM vector field then yields a quantitative phase map of the specimen with far higher signal-to-noise per unit dose than absorption contrast for weakly absorbing (low-Z, biological, polymer) samples, so the finer sampling actually converts into real detail rather than noise.

Practical steps: use scan steps of ~1/3–1/4 of the probe size (fly-scanning with a fast, low-noise pixel detector so the extra points cost little time); calibrate the detector's angular scale and the probe's pupil function in situ (e.g. from a ptychographic probe retrieval or a knife-edge/Siemens-star target); normalise every frame to the incident flux and subtract the descan/beam-drift contribution to the COM (a slow drift of the beam mimics a uniform phase gradient, so an I₀-monitored, thermally stabilised optic and periodic empty-beam reference frames are essential); and finally deconvolve the measured, aberration-including CTF from the integrated phase image with a regularised Wiener filter, which simultaneously removes the residual aberration tails of the KB/zone-plate focus. The same dataset also gives the incoherent bright-field, annular dark-field and (if desired) full ptychographic channels for free, so the acquisition can be pushed further to sub-probe resolution without any change to the source, optics or scan hardware.

**Close the loop on the instrument itself: co‑mount a calibrated resolution standard with the specimen and use an automated, real‑time image‑quality metric to continuously optimise the beamline during the scan.**

In practice, glue a nanofabricated test object (a Siemens star, a Fresnel‑zone or lithographic line/space pattern with features spanning the target resolution) and a scatter of sub‑resolution gold/tungsten nanoparticles onto the same holder, just outside — or at the edge of — the field of view containing the sample, so that both are imaged in every projection under identical conditions. Then run a software feedback loop that, for each frame, computes an objective sharpness metric (edge‑spread/MTF from the star spokes, the power‑spectrum cut‑off, the fitted width of the nanoparticle point images, or a Fourier‑ring‑correlation between split frames) and uses it as the error signal to drive the beamline actuators: autofocus of the visible‑light objective on the scintillator (or of the X‑ray optic), sample‑to‑detector distance and defocus, KB/zone‑plate alignment and astigmatism correctors, monochromator tuning, and the rotation‑axis position, tilt and wobble. Slow drifts of the optics under heat load, thermal expansion of the stage, and settling of the sample environment — the usual reasons a scan that started at the nominal resolution ends up several times blurrier — are then corrected while the data are being taken rather than discovered afterwards.

The same fiducials serve three further purposes: (i) their measured point‑spread function gives the actual, in‑situ PSF/MTF of that specific dataset, which can be deconvolved from the projections before reconstruction instead of using a nominal, catalogue value; (ii) the nanoparticle positions give sub‑pixel tracking of drift, vibration and axis runout for per‑projection rigid registration; and (iii) frames whose metric falls below a set threshold (a vibration transient, a beam trip, a focus excursion) can be automatically flagged and re‑acquired or discarded, so a few bad projections do not blur the whole reconstruction.

Finally, the standard provides an *honest, quantitative* resolution figure (smallest resolved spoke period, or the FRC/FSC threshold crossing) for the final volume, so acquisition parameters — exposure, number of angles, magnification, propagation distance — can be tuned empirically to the point where the measured resolution, not the nominal voxel size, stops improving. This requires no new optics, source or detector: it simply ensures that the instrument actually delivers, and demonstrably delivers, the resolution it is capable of throughout a long scan.

Replace the standard filtered‑back‑projection pipeline with an **interpolation‑free, Fourier‑space iterative reconstruction on a pseudopolar grid — i.e. equally‑sloped tomography (EST) / GENFIRE‑type reconstruction.**

The point is that a large, usually unrecognised part of the resolution loss in tomography happens *inside the reconstruction*: FBP (and most gridding codes) must interpolate the measured polar Fourier data onto a Cartesian grid, and that interpolation acts as a low‑pass filter that preferentially destroys the highest spatial frequencies (the ones sitting at the sparsely sampled outer rim of Fourier space), while the ramp filter simultaneously amplifies noise there and forces the user to apodise. Instead, acquire the projections at angles chosen so their slopes are **equally spaced rather than equally spaced in angle** (θₙ = arctan[(2n−N)/N]); each such projection then maps *exactly* onto one line of a pseudopolar grid, so its 1‑D fractional/pseudopolar Fourier transform can be inserted into the 3‑D Fourier volume with no interpolation at all. The volume is then completed by iterating between Fourier and real space: at each cycle the measured pseudopolar lines are re‑imposed exactly, while in real space physical constraints are enforced (positivity, a tight support/loose object boundary determined from a first coarse reconstruction, zero density outside the sample, and known‑phase or histogram/discreteness priors if available). The missing Fourier values between the measured lines — including those beyond the naive Crowther/Nyquist angular sampling limit and in a missing wedge — are thereby *filled in* self‑consistently rather than smeared over by interpolation.

The practical gains are (i) high spatial frequencies are transferred to the reconstruction with essentially unity weight, so edges are genuinely sharper and the resolvable feature size approaches the true detector/probe sampling limit rather than the FBP‑degraded value; (ii) the same resolution is reached with several times fewer projections (and hence several times less dose and scan time), which for beam‑sensitive or drifting specimens converts directly into further real resolution because damage and drift blur are reduced; and (iii) the iterative constraints suppress streaks and noise without the low‑pass apodisation normally needed.

Practical requirements: program the rotation stage to the equal‑slope angle list (it is a simple non‑uniform angle table, fully compatible with fly‑scanning); refine the rotation‑centre, tilt and per‑projection drift to better than 0.1 pixel before insertion, since the method's advantage relies on the lines lying exactly on the grid; use an oversampling ratio ≥2 (blank space around the object) so the real‑space support constraint is meaningful; monitor convergence with an R‑factor on withheld projections and quantify the achieved resolution objectively by Fourier shell correlation between two half‑datasets, to be sure the recovered high frequencies are data‑driven rather than constraint‑generated. No change to the source, optics, detector or sample is required — only the angle list and the reconstruction algorithm.

**Switch the detector from a 2‑D framing camera to a line‑scan/TDI (time‑delay‑integration) detector used with continuous sample translation, and set the translation speed so that the sample advances by only a *fraction* of a pixel per line readout.**

In a TDI detector the accumulated charge (or the counting register) is shifted from row to row in exact synchrony with the moving image of the sample, so each line of the object is integrated many times as it sweeps across the sensor. Two resolution benefits follow. (i) The sampling pitch along the scan direction is no longer the physical pixel pitch but is set by the ratio of stage velocity to line rate — driving the stage at, say, 1/4 pixel per line produces genuinely oversampled, non‑aliased projections on a grid several times finer than the pixel array, so after deconvolution of the (now sampling‑unlimited) detector PSF the true MTF limit rather than Nyquist sets the resolution. (ii) Because the signal is integrated over many stages while the image and the charge move together, one obtains the photon statistics of a long exposure *without* the motion blur of a long exposure, which lets you use a very thin, high‑resolution scintillator (or a fine‑pitch direct‑detection sensor) whose low quantum efficiency would otherwise be prohibitive, and lets you run the scan continuously with no stop‑start settling, vibration or dead time.

Practical requirements: the stage velocity, line rate and detector clock must be phase‑locked (encoder‑ or interferometer‑triggered line readout) so that the charge transfer matches the image motion to a small fraction of a pixel — any mismatch produces a shear/smear that directly degrades resolution; the magnification and the scan direction must be aligned to the TDI shift axis to within a fraction of a pixel over the full stage travel; flat‑field and per‑column gain must be calibrated (column defects become stripes along the whole scan); and for tomography one repeats the sub‑pixel‑pitch line scan at each rotation angle (or spirals the sample continuously through the line beam), which also matches naturally to a tall, narrow, high‑flux beam footprint and gives lower scatter than full‑field illumination. The result is finer sampling, better photon statistics and no motion blur, with no change to the source, optics or sample.

Optimise the **specimen mounting/embedding medium by refractive‑index (density) matching**, so that the sample's own boundaries stop limiting what can be resolved inside it.

Rather than imaging the specimen in air inside a thick container, immerse and immobilise it in a liquid, gel or resin whose real refractive‑index decrement δ (and attenuation) closely matches that of the specimen's outer surface and of the sample holder — e.g. ethanol/glycerol mixtures, agarose, low‑density resin, or a density‑graded solution — held in a thin‑walled, low‑Z, smooth capillary (polyimide, quartz) with no bubbles or menisci in the field of view.

The reason this improves *real* resolution is that in propagation‑based/phase‑contrast and high‑magnification tomography the outer sample–air interface produces an enormous phase step whose strong, high‑order Fresnel fringes and associated streak/halo artefacts extend deep into the reconstruction, and whose huge dynamic range forces one to use a short propagation distance, a small δ/β and heavy low‑pass filtering — all of which throw away the high spatial frequencies carrying the fine internal detail. Removing that dominant step lets you (i) push the propagation distance out to the optimum Fresnel number for the *internal* features, (ii) use the full detector dynamic range on the weak internal contrast instead of on the sample outline, (iii) avoid the cupping/beam‑hardening and streaking that otherwise blur interfaces, and (iv) mechanically damp the specimen so it cannot move, dry, shrink or creep during a long scan, eliminating drift/motion blur.

Practically: match δ to within a few per cent by titrating the medium and checking the residual edge fringe on a test scan; keep the container wall thin and concentric with the rotation axis (a smooth cylinder gives an easily corrected, slowly varying background); degas the medium to avoid bubbles that mimic pores; verify the medium does not swell/deform or chemically alter the sample, and take a medium‑only reference scan for background subtraction. No change to source, optics, detector or reconstruction is needed — the fine features simply become visible at the sampling limit instead of being buried under boundary artefacts.

Use the **scattering signal rather than the image itself as the resolution carrier — i.e. perform scanning SAXS/WAXS (small‑ and wide‑angle) tomography, including tensor tomography, so that nanometre‑scale structure is retrieved inside each micrometre‑sized voxel.**

Instead of trying to shrink the probe or the voxel until it matches the feature size, raster a focused (µm‑scale) monochromatic beam through the specimen at many translations and rotations and record, at every point, a full 2‑D small‑/wide‑angle scattering pattern on a fast, close‑coupled, photon‑counting pixel detector. Tomographic inversion of the *angle‑ and q‑resolved* intensities (with the reciprocal‑space tensor/spherical‑harmonic model that handles the orientation dependence of anisotropic scatterers) then yields, for every voxel, the local scattering curve I(q) and its orientation distribution.

The key point is that the structural information contained in each voxel is limited not by the beam size, the optics, the scintillator blur or the detector pixel pitch, but by the highest momentum transfer recorded: real‑space structure is characterised down to d ≈ 2π/q_max — a few nanometres or better with a WAXS detector — from a scan whose spatial sampling is a thousand times coarser. Lamellar periods, fibril diameters and orientations, pore/particle size distributions, crystallite size (from Scherrer broadening) and degree of alignment are therefore quantified three to four orders of magnitude below the nominal voxel size, so a µm‑stepped scan delivers nm‑scale structural "resolution" while keeping a millimetre‑scale field of view, modest dose per point and manageable scan times.

To exploit it: choose the sample–detector distance (and, if needed, run two detectors or two distances) so that the q‑range brackets the length scales of interest; use fine, continuous fly‑scanning with per‑point I₀ normalisation and a beamstop‑plus‑high‑dynamic‑range merge so the weak high‑q signal is not lost; keep the rotation axis and translation stages accurate to a fraction of the step so voxels from different angles register correctly; correct for absorption, air/window parasitic scattering and multiple scattering (thin the sample so it scatters only once); and provide enough angular coverage — several tilts as well as rotations — for the tensor reconstruction to be well posed. Combining the resulting nano‑structural map with a conventional absorption/phase tomogram of the same volume (registered to sub‑voxel precision) gives both the µm morphology and the nm‑scale internal architecture, without any change to the source, focusing optic or camera.

**Add a Talbot(-Lau) grating interferometer to the beamline and exploit its sub‑pixel phase‑stepping and dark‑field channels.**

Place a phase grating (π or π/2, period of a few µm) downstream of the sample and an analyser (absorption) grating of matched period at a fractional Talbot distance in front of the detector (adding a source grating if the source is extended). The self‑image of the phase grating carries a fringe pattern whose period is far finer than the detector pixel; the sample's local refraction shifts each fringe and its unresolved microstructure reduces the fringe visibility. By stepping one grating in many increments of a *fraction* of the grating period (and, better, additionally dithering the sample by sub‑pixel amounts and interleaving the resulting frames), one measures, for every pixel, the transmission, the differential phase (refraction angle, with nanoradian sensitivity) and the dark‑field (visibility‑loss) signal.

Why this improves resolution: (i) the differential‑phase channel is a derivative signal, so edges and interfaces are localised to a small fraction of a pixel — integrating it gives a phase image with much sharper, higher‑contrast boundaries than the absorption image at the same pixel size, and after deconvolution of the detector MTF the practical resolving power improves by roughly a factor of two; (ii) the sub‑period stepping/dithering data can be merged onto a sampling grid several times finer than the physical pixel pitch, since the fringe (not the pixel) is the ruler; and (iii) the dark‑field channel quantifies structure (pores, cracks, fibres, powders) *below* the resolution limit — sub‑micrometre features that are invisible in the image are still measured through their ultra‑small‑angle scattering, and the correlation length probed can be tuned by changing the inter‑grating distance or energy.

Practical requirements: gratings with high aspect ratio and sub‑micrometre period accuracy on rigid, thermally stabilised, piezo‑driven mounts with stepping repeatability well below the period; alignment of the grating lines to the detector rows and Moiré‑fringe minimisation; per‑frame I₀ normalisation because the retrieval is a fit to intensity oscillations; and, for tomography, repetition of the stepping sequence at each angle (or an interlaced/"sliding‑window" scheme, or single‑shot Moiré‑fringe analysis) to keep scan time and dose acceptable. Because the technique tolerates a modest source size and a broad bandwidth (a Lau source grating restores fringe visibility), it can be run in a high‑flux pink beam with short exposures, which further reduces drift and motion blur — so the gain in edge sharpness and sub‑pixel structural sensitivity is obtained without any new X‑ray objective, smaller pixels or brighter source.

For any evolving/in‑situ specimen, build the sample's **motion and deformation into the reconstruction itself (motion‑compensated, "4D" tomography)** instead of assuming a static object. Acquire a fast reference tomogram of the undeformed state, then, during the loading/heating/flow experiment, keep acquiring projections continuously while the sample changes; estimate the time‑dependent displacement field (rigid drift plus non‑rigid strain) by projection‑based digital volume/image correlation — tracking embedded high‑Z fiducial particles or natural speckle in the projections and refining the field so that projections from different times/angles become mutually consistent. Insert this deformation field as a warping operator in the forward model of an iterative (model‑based/algebraic) reconstruction, so every projection is effectively back‑warped to a common reference configuration before being combined.

This matters because in dynamic experiments the practical resolution limit is not the optics, pixel size or dose but the fact that the object moves/creeps by many voxels during the minutes needed for a full rotation, which smears interfaces and forces users to shorten scans (fewer angles, noisier data) or to coarsen the voxels. With the deformation explicitly modelled, all projections of the whole scan — even those spanning a large change of state — contribute coherently to a single sharp volume; motion blur is inverted rather than averaged in, the full angular sampling and the finest available voxel grid can be used, and the recovered displacement/strain field is a quantitative bonus output. Practical requirements: sufficient trackable texture or fiducials, sub‑voxel registration accuracy, regularisation (smoothness/incompressibility) of the deformation field, alternating updates of the volume and the motion field until convergence, and validation against a static high‑quality scan of the same region.

**Use an energy‑resolving (spectroscopic, multi‑bin photon‑counting) detector and reconstruct energy‑binned/K‑edge‑subtracted volumes instead of a single polychromatic grey‑value image.**

Replace the integrating scintillator‑camera with a hybrid CdTe/Si photon‑counting array (Medipix/Timepix‑type) that sorts every detected photon into several narrow energy bins, and run the experiment in a high‑flux pink/broad‑bandpass beam. Each reconstructed dataset is then effectively monochromatic, which removes three blur mechanisms that are usually mistaken for "detector resolution": (i) beam hardening — in a polychromatic reconstruction the effective attenuation coefficient varies with path length, producing cupping, dark streaks between dense features and edge "smearing" that force heavy filtering and hide thin, low‑contrast interfaces; (ii) the chromatic point‑spread function — the propagation/Fresnel fringes, and the focus of any diffractive optic, are wavelength‑dependent, so a broad spectrum washes out precisely the high‑frequency edge signal; and (iii) scatter and harmonic contamination, which are rejected simply by discarding photons outside the chosen energy window rather than by attenuating the beam.

Beyond de‑blurring, the spectral data give **sub‑voxel material discrimination**: by acquiring bins immediately below and above the K‑edge of a labelling or constituent element and subtracting them, a voxel's grey value is decomposed into physically meaningful material fractions (e.g. contrast agent vs. tissue, catalyst metal vs. support). Because the edge jump is a sharp, discrete, element‑specific signature, a feature that only partially fills a voxel is still quantified through its partial‑volume contribution, so interfaces and thin layers can be localised to a fraction of the voxel — i.e. the *effective* resolution of the material maps beats the sampling limit of the same scan. Every photon is also counted once with no read noise and with essentially unity DQE at the chosen energy, so exposures are shorter and drift/motion blur correspondingly smaller.

Practical requirements: per‑pixel energy calibration and charge‑sharing correction (charge shared between neighbouring pixels both blurs the image and mis‑assigns energies — use charge‑summing/"cluster" processing); keep the count rate below the pile‑up limit (pile‑up distorts the spectrum and hence the decomposition), attenuating or fly‑scanning faster rather than integrating longer; correct for flat‑field and threshold dispersion in every bin separately; choose bin widths as a compromise between spectral purity and photon statistics; and reconstruct with a joint/spectral algorithm (one‑step material‑decomposition or joint‑sparsity across bins) so that the noise in individual narrow bins does not degrade the final maps. No change to the source, X‑ray optics, sample preparation or scan geometry is needed — only the detector and the reconstruction turn a chromatically blurred, beam‑hardened image into a sharp, quantitative, element‑specific one.

**Acquire the tomogram as a helical (spiral) fly‑scan with a deliberately *sub‑voxel* vertical pitch, and reconstruct it on a finer axial grid.**

In most synchrotron parallel‑beam tomography the through‑slice (axial, z) resolution is the poor relation: it is set by the vertical sampling of the detector rows, by the vertical intensity profile/penumbra of the beam, by slight rotation‑axis tilt and wobble, and by the depth‑of‑field mismatch between a thick scintillator and the visible‑light objective — so reconstructions are often noticeably sharper in‑plane than along the rotation axis, and thin horizontal features (layers, cracks, membranes) are smeared. Instead of stopping the sample at fixed heights and stacking independent slabs, translate the specimen continuously along the rotation axis while it spins, choosing the pitch so that the sample advances by only a small fraction of a detector‑row height (e.g. 1/3–1/5 of a row) per turn. Every point in the object is then viewed by many *different* detector rows at many different angles and at many different sub‑row offsets, so the union of all projections samples the object in z on a grid several times finer than the physical row pitch, and the row‑to‑row response and vertical beam non‑uniformity are averaged out rather than imprinted as ring/stripe artefacts on each slab.

Reconstruct this dataset not by slice‑by‑slice filtered back‑projection but with a helical/iterative (model‑based algebraic) algorithm whose forward model includes the exact helical trajectory, the measured vertical PSF of the scintillator/optics, and the per‑projection encoder positions; the redundancy of the interlaced axial samples makes the inverse problem over‑determined, so the axial deconvolution is stable and the volume can legitimately be reconstructed on voxels smaller than a detector row. Typical gains are a 2–3× improvement in axial resolution and near‑isotropic voxels, plus the removal of the "slab boundary" discontinuities and ring artefacts that normally limit stacked scans.

Practical requirements: encoder‑ or interferometer‑triggered synchronisation of the vertical stage with the rotation and the camera readout, so that the z position of every frame is known to a small fraction of a row; a stiff, wobble‑free air‑bearing rotation/translation combination with the axis calibrated for tilt and runout; per‑frame I₀ normalisation and flat‑fielding (rows are used interchangeably, so gain non‑uniformity must be well calibrated); an in‑situ measurement of the vertical PSF from a horizontal knife edge or nanoparticle fiducials for the deconvolution; and a pitch chosen small enough for the desired oversampling but large enough that total scan time and dose stay acceptable — helped by continuous fly‑scanning, which makes the extra projections almost free. No change to the source, X‑ray optics, detector or sample preparation is needed: only the scan trajectory and the reconstruction geometry.

Optimise the **visible‑light relay of the indirect (scintillator‑based) detector for aberration‑free, index‑matched imaging of the luminescent screen**, rather than just increasing its magnification.

In most micro‑ and nano‑tomography detectors the measured point‑spread function is dominated not by the X‑ray physics but by the light‑optical chain: the scintillator emits a broad spectral band (e.g. YAG:Ce ~550 nm broad, LSO:Tb multiple lines), and a standard high‑NA objective focused *through* a high‑refractive‑index crystal suffers strong chromatic and spherical aberration plus spherical‑aberration‑induced defocus at the index step, which broadens the PSF far beyond the nominal effective pixel size.

Concrete measures: (i) insert a **narrow‑band emission filter** matched to the scintillator's strongest emission line so the objective works quasi‑monochromatically and its residual chromatic aberration vanishes; (ii) use an **apochromatic objective with a correction collar (or a purpose‑designed "scintillator‑corrected" objective) whose design cover‑glass thickness and refractive index match the actual crystal thickness and index**, or couple the objective to the crystal with an index‑matched immersion medium (oil/water) so that no refractive index step remains in the light path; (iii) focus precisely on the *X‑ray entrance face* of the crystal (where most of the absorption occurs) using a knife‑edge or Siemens‑star target and an automated sharpness metric, and keep the crystal's optical face flat, parallel and free of surface damage/back‑reflection (anti‑reflection coating or absorbing backing to suppress light back‑scattered from the far face, which produces a broad halo in the PSF tails); (iv) match the objective's depth of focus to the crystal thickness so that all emission depths remain in focus, and mount the whole objective–crystal–camera assembly in a thermally stabilised, vibration‑damped housing since a few micrometres of focus drift already doubles the blur; (v) finally, measure the resulting PSF/MTF in situ (edge‑spread from a sharp gold edge or sub‑resolution particles) and deconvolve it — including its long, low‑amplitude halo — from the projections before reconstruction.

Because these steps attack the halo and aberration tails rather than the sampling, they typically sharpen the detector PSF by a factor of ~2 and raise the contrast transfer near Nyquist substantially, converting the nominal effective pixel size into genuine spatial resolution — with no change to the source, X‑ray optics, sample or scan protocol.

**Record two (or more) propagation distances *simultaneously* with a stacked, semi‑transparent detector chain, and phase‑retrieve from the multi‑plane hologram set.**

Instead of moving the camera to several sample–detector distances one after another (which costs time, dose and, worse, introduces drift/registration errors between frames), build the detector as a "beam‑splitting" stack: put a very thin, weakly absorbing scintillator (a few µm of LSO/YAG, absorbing only ~5–20 % of the beam) with its own high‑NA objective/camera at a short propagation distance, let the transmitted beam continue downstream through a vacuum/He flight tube, and image it again on a second (and if desired a third) thin scintillator–camera unit at a much larger distance; alternatively use a 45° thin scintillator/pellicle so the visible light is split off without attenuating the X‑rays.

Why this raises real resolution: in single‑distance in‑line phase contrast the contrast‑transfer function has zeros whose positions depend on the Fresnel number, so whole bands of spatial frequencies — precisely the high ones that carry the finest detail — are lost or must be suppressed by a strongly low‑pass Paganin‑type filter. Recording several Fresnel numbers at once fills in each other's CTF zeros, so a joint (CTF/ Fresnel or iterative multi‑distance) phase retrieval recovers the full frequency band quantitatively, giving sharp, halo‑free edges and typically a ~2× gain in resolvable feature size. Because all planes are exposed by the *same* photons in the *same* instant, the datasets are intrinsically registered and immune to sample drift, vibration, beam decay and sample evolution — which is what normally spoils sequential multi‑distance holotomography and rules it out entirely for fast in‑situ or dynamic experiments. It also uses photons that would otherwise be wasted (a thin front screen would have transmitted them anyway), so no extra dose is incurred.

Practical requirements: keep the upstream scintillators thin and X‑ray‑transparent, with anti‑reflection/absorbing backing so their own light halo does not degrade the near‑plane image; calibrate the relative magnification, lateral offset, rotation and PSF/MTF of each detector unit to sub‑pixel precision using a common fiducial or Siemens‑star target (the effective pixel sizes will differ if the geometry is divergent); correct the slight beam hardening/attenuation imposed by the upstream screen on the downstream image via flat fields taken through the whole stack; choose the distances so their Fresnel numbers are complementary (zeros of one falling on maxima of the other) for the feature size of interest; and feed all planes into a single regularised multi‑distance phase‑retrieval and then into the tomographic reconstruction, repeating the whole stacked acquisition at each rotation angle in a continuous fly‑scan.

**Recover the resolution that geometric mis‑calibration is throwing away: perform a fiducial‑free, reconstruction‑driven "auto‑focus" self‑calibration of the full imaging geometry before/while reconstructing.**

Even a perfectly aligned beamline with a perfect detector will produce a volume several times blurrier than its voxel size if the assumed geometry is slightly wrong: an error of half a pixel in the centre of rotation, a few tenths of a degree of detector roll or rotation‑axis tilt, a small out‑of‑plane axis inclination, a slowly varying magnification (cone‑beam/divergent geometry), or the sub‑micrometre "sphere of confusion" and thermal drift of the rotation stage all smear every projection ray by a different amount, producing the familiar half‑moon/tuning‑fork artefacts, doubled edges and a systematically low‑pass reconstruction.

Instead of trusting nominal values (or gluing markers on the sample), treat *all* geometry parameters — centre of rotation, detector tilt/roll/skew, source‑to‑sample and sample‑to‑detector distances, axis inclination, and a per‑projection (x, y) shift and scale — as unknowns and optimise them by maximising a quantitative sharpness/consistency metric computed on the reconstructed volume itself: total variation or gradient energy, image entropy/negative kurtosis of the gradient histogram, the high‑frequency content of the power spectrum, or the residual between measured and re‑projected sinograms. Run this as a nested loop (coarse global search on the dominant parameters, then simultaneous gradient‑based/Nelder–Mead refinement, optionally on a down‑sampled sub‑volume containing sharp edges to keep it fast), so the algorithm converges to the geometry that makes the object as sharp and self‑consistent as physically possible. Sinogram‑consistency conditions (Helgason–Ludwig moment conditions, or 0°/180° mirror correlation) give excellent starting values and constrain the search; per‑projection shifts can then be refined last, which simultaneously absorbs stage runout, vibration and thermal drift without any markers on the specimen.

Practical points: use a region of the object rich in high‑contrast edges as the metric target; regularise or low‑order‑polynomial‑constrain the per‑projection shifts so noise is not fitted; verify by Fourier ring/shell correlation between two half‑datasets (the FRC cut‑off, not the artefact appearance, should improve); and re‑run the calibration for every dataset, since focus, magnification and axis position drift under heat load between scans.

Because the same measured photons are simply back‑projected along the *correct* rays, this typically recovers a factor of two or more in true resolvable feature size — and it costs nothing in dose, beamtime, hardware or sample preparation, requiring only the reconstruction software.

**Use photon‑energy (wavelength) diversity instead of geometric diversity for phase retrieval — i.e. record in‑line holograms of the same field of view at several photon energies with the geometry left untouched, and invert them jointly.**

In single‑distance propagation‑based imaging the contrast‑transfer function (CTF) has zeros at spatial frequencies where sin(πλz f²) = 0, so entire bands — including precisely the high frequencies that carry the finest detail — are not transmitted, and the usual Paganin‑type single‑image retrieval has to be strongly low‑pass filtered to stay stable. The standard remedy is to move the camera to several sample–detector distances, but that costs time and, worse, introduces stage drift, magnification changes and image registration errors between the frames. Instead, keep the sample, detector and optics rigidly fixed and simply retune the monochromator (a fast Si(111)/multilayer channel‑cut or pseudo‑channel‑cut scan takes seconds and, if the beamline is fixed‑exit and the undulator gap is tracked, leaves the beam position unchanged) to record holograms at, say, 4–8 energies spanning ±20–40 % in λ. Because the effective Fresnel number scales as 1/λ, the CTF zeros sit at different frequencies in every frame, so the zeros of one energy fall on the maxima of another and the *union* of the dataset covers the whole frequency band up to the detector's MTF limit.

The frames are then combined in a single regularised multi‑wavelength CTF/Fresnel or iterative (Tikhonov/TV‑regularised, or alternating‑projection) retrieval in which δ(E) and β(E) are propagated through the known dispersion of the material (tabulated away from edges, or fitted), so the reconstruction is quantitative and the high‑frequency band is recovered with near‑unity weight rather than being suppressed. Typical gain is a factor of ~2 in resolvable feature size and a large improvement in edge sharpness and halo/low‑frequency‑cupping artefacts, with the retrieved phase then fed into tomographic reconstruction (repeat the short energy sequence at each rotation angle, or interleave energies over the angular scan).

Practical requirements: a fixed‑exit monochromator with reproducible energy positioning and negligible beam‑position walk (monitor with a quadrant BPM and correct any residual sub‑pixel image shift/magnification change by cross‑correlating the empty‑beam frames); flat‑field, detector‑efficiency and scintillator‑absorption calibration at *every* energy separately, since both the quantum efficiency and the effective PSF of the scintillator are energy‑dependent; per‑frame I₀ normalisation; a choice of energies that avoids absorption edges of the specimen (or, if edge contrast is wanted, an explicit anomalous‑dispersion model); and short exposures so that the total dose is no higher than a conventional multi‑distance scan. Because nothing moves mechanically, the frames are intrinsically registered to sub‑pixel accuracy, making the method usable for in‑situ and dynamic experiments where sequential multi‑distance holotomography would fail — and it needs no new optics, no smaller pixels and no brighter source.

**Stabilise the illumination itself — run the beamline with active, closed‑loop beam‑position and intensity stabilisation so that the projections do not move or flicker during the scan.**

A large part of the "resolution" lost in a long micro/nano‑tomography scan is not optical at all: the photon beam wanders and fluctuates. Undulator‑gap changes and the varying heat load bend the first crystal of the monochromator and the mirrors, the electron‑beam orbit and current drift between injections, and slits/masks expand thermally. The consequences are (i) the illumination footprint translates by a fraction of a pixel to several pixels over minutes, so every projection is recorded under a slightly different beam and, when summed or back‑projected, high spatial frequencies are washed out; (ii) the flat field taken at the start no longer matches the frames taken later, leaving residual stripes → ring artefacts and reduced contrast transfer at high frequency, which forces low‑pass filtering; and (iii) intensity drift corrupts phase retrieval and any difference‑based (dithering, grating‑stepping, edge‑illumination) scheme.

The fix is instrumentation and control rather than optics: operate the ring in **top‑up mode** so the current and hence the heat load are constant; use a **cryogenically cooled, fixed‑exit monochromator** with feed‑forward correction of the crystal bending as the undulator gap/heat load changes; put **X‑ray beam‑position monitors (quadrant/blade XBPMs, or a diode array on the beam halo) upstream and immediately before the sample and close a fast (10–100 Hz) feedback loop onto the mirror/monochromator piezos and the electron‑beam orbit correctors**, holding the beam position to well under one effective pixel and the pointing to sub‑microradian; thermally shield, water‑stabilise and vibration‑isolate all slits, masks, filters and windows; and record an **I₀ monitor value for every single frame** together with interleaved flat fields (e.g. a flat every 50–100 projections, or a "moving‑sample" dynamic flat‑field/PCA flat‑field correction) so that any residual drift is normalised out rather than imprinted.

Because the same photons are then delivered from a stationary, constant wavefront throughout the acquisition, each projection is sharp, the flat‑field correction stays valid, ring/stripe artefacts collapse, and the reconstruction can be filtered right up to the sampling limit — typically recovering a factor of ~2 in genuine resolvable feature size in long scans, with no change to the source brilliance, imaging optics, detector or sample preparation.

**Push the resolution of the focusing optic itself by changing how the zone plate is *made*: use "zone‑doubled" (template + atomic‑layer‑deposition) Fresnel zone plates, and stack/align several of them.**

Instead of trying to lithographically write ever finer outermost zones — where electron‑beam writing accuracy and the achievable aspect ratio cap hard X‑ray zone plates at ~20–30 nm — pattern a coarse template with *twice* the final period (e.g. HSQ/Si lines at 2Δr), then conformally coat it by atomic‑layer deposition with a high‑Z material (Ir, Pt, W, HfO₂). Each template line acquires a dense sidewall on both edges, so the number of zones is doubled and the effective outermost zone width becomes the ALD film thickness, which can be controlled to sub‑nanometre precision (5–10 nm routinely). Since the diffraction‑limited resolution of a zone plate is δ ≈ 1.22 Δr_N, this alone buys a factor‑of‑two or better gain in probe size / point‑spread function for both scanning nanoprobe and full‑field TXM work — with no change to source, detector, scan protocol or reconstruction.

Because the ALD sidewalls are thin, the diffraction efficiency at hard X‑ray energies would normally be poor; recover it by **stacking two or more nominally identical zone plates** in series along the beam, aligned to a small fraction of the outer zone width (piezo x–y–θ stages with in‑situ alignment optimised on the measured focal intensity, and separations kept within the depth of focus so the stack behaves as one thicker optic). This raises the effective structure height to the optimal phase‑shifting thickness, boosting efficiency several‑fold, so the smaller focus also carries more flux — shorter dwell times, less drift and vibration blur, better photon statistics per voxel.

Practical requirements: match the monochromaticity to ΔE/E < 1/N for the (now much larger) number of zones; use a matched central stop and order‑sorting aperture, since the finer zones give a shorter focal length and tighter working distance; verify the achieved focus at‑wavelength with a Siemens‑star/knife‑edge scan or ptychographic probe retrieval, and correct any residual astigmatism from template line‑edge roughness or stack misalignment; and keep a short, stiff, thermally stabilised metrology loop between optic and sample because the depth of focus shrinks as Δr_N². The payoff is a genuine hardware‑level gain (sub‑10 nm probes) that propagates directly into every imaging mode that uses the optic.

Insert a **spiral (vortex) phase element into the imaging path to perform X‑ray spiral‑phase (Hilbert‑transform) contrast**, so the point‑spread function is converted from a broad Airy‑like blob into a sharp, isotropically differentiating "doughnut" kernel.

Practically, place a lithographically fabricated spiral phase plate (a helical‑ramp of low‑Z material, e.g. SU‑8/Si/diamond, whose thickness increases azimuthally to give a full 2π phase wrap at the working energy) — or a forked/spiral zone plate that imprints the vortex directly on the diffracted order — in the Fourier (pupil) plane of a full‑field transmission X‑ray microscope, or use it to shape the illuminating probe in a scanning nanoprobe. Because a vortex filter multiplies the object's spatial‑frequency spectrum by exp(iφ_q), it acts as a radially isotropic, first‑order derivative (2‑D Hilbert transform) operator: low spatial frequencies are strongly suppressed while high spatial frequencies are boosted, and the resulting image is dominated by edges and phase gradients rather than by the slowly varying bulk transmission. The consequences for resolution are (i) the effective PSF has a much narrower rising flank and a dark on‑axis null, so two closely spaced features that would merge under ordinary imaging are separated by a clear dip — an apparent gain of roughly 1.5–2× in resolvable feature spacing from the *same* optic and detector; (ii) the boosted high‑frequency transfer counteracts the roll‑off of the scintillator/objective MTF, so the contrast transfer near the detector Nyquist frequency is raised instead of being lost; and (iii) unlike differential‑phase or grating methods, the enhancement is isotropic — edges of all orientations are sharpened equally, with no preferred direction and no need for two orthogonal acquisitions.

Additional benefits: the huge dynamic range that normally forces one to expose for the sample outline is removed, since the vortex filter suppresses the DC/uniform background, so the full detector well depth is spent on the weak internal detail; and the same element can be used in "shifted‑vortex"/fractional‑charge mode to obtain quantitative phase by recording a small set of images with different vortex topological charge or off‑axis displacement, from which the true phase map is retrieved by a spiral‑filtered demodulation.
