Practical requirements: the phase plate must be accurately centred on the optical axis to a fraction of the diffraction‑limited spot (piezo x–y–θ mount with in‑situ optimisation on the depth of the on‑axis null of a test pattern), since decentring turns the isotropic filter into a directional one; the beam must be sufficiently monochromatic (ΔE/E small enough that the 2π wrap thickness stays correct, otherwise the vortex charge is smeared and the null fills in) and transversely coherent across the pupil; the measured vortex PSF should be calibrated on a Siemens‑star or sharp gold‑edge target and deconvolved (or the filter inverted) before tomographic reconstruction, so that the edge‑enhanced images are converted back into quantitative attenuation/phase maps rather than being interpreted directly; and the modest flux loss in the phase plate is compensated with slightly longer exposures. No change to the source, detector pixel size or scan geometry is needed — the gain comes purely from engineering the transfer function of the imaging system.

Get rid of the scintillator altogether and detect the X‑rays **directly in a thin, over‑depleted, small‑pixel semiconductor sensor**, engineering the charge transport so that the charge cloud — not a light spread — sets the point‑spread function.

Concretely: replace the indirect scintillator + visible‑light objective + camera chain with a back‑illuminated, fully depleted high‑resistivity silicon (or, for harder X‑rays, a thin GaAs/CdTe) monolithic active‑pixel/CCD sensor with a pixel pitch of only a few micrometres (1–5 µm is now achievable with MAPS/skipper‑CCD/DEPFET technology), and run it strongly over‑depleted (high bias, short drift path, thinned entrance window, cooled to suppress leakage and to allow long integration or single‑photon operation). Because each absorbed X‑ray is converted directly into electron–hole pairs that are swept along a high, uniform field to the collection nodes, the lateral spread is limited to the thermal‑diffusion width during a very short drift time (well below a micrometre for a thinned, strongly biased sensor), instead of the tens of micrometres of optical‑photon spread in a scintillator plus the aberrations, halo, depth‑of‑field mismatch and reflections of the relay objective. The conversion gain is also enormous (~3.6 eV per electron–hole pair versus hundreds of eV per detected optical photon in an indirect chain), so the detective quantum efficiency at high spatial frequencies rises dramatically: images are essentially read‑noise‑free at the same dose, which means shorter exposures and correspondingly less drift‑ and vibration‑induced blur.

Practical steps: choose the sensor thickness as a compromise between absorption efficiency at the working energy and diffusion blur (thin for resolution, or tilt/stack sensors to regain stopping power); calibrate and correct charge sharing between neighbouring pixels (measure the pixel response function with a sub‑pixel‑stepped pencil beam or a sharp edge, then deconvolve it, or apply cluster/charge‑summing logic); characterise and remove the peripheral field distortion at the pixel edges and any entrance‑window dead layer; keep the sensor cooled and thermally stable so gain and depletion depth do not drift during a long tomographic scan; and verify the achieved MTF in situ on a Siemens‑star or knife‑edge target before pushing the reconstruction filter to the new, finer Nyquist limit.

The result is a detector whose effective pixel size and MTF are set by nanofabrication and semiconductor physics rather than by light diffusion in a phosphor — a genuine several‑fold gain in projection sharpness and in dose efficiency, obtained with no change to the source, beamline optics, sample preparation or scan geometry.

**Replace the focusing element with an adiabatically focusing refractive lens (ADFL) stack — i.e. beat the aperture/absorption limit of compound refractive lenses so the probe NA, and hence the resolution, goes up.**

Ordinary nanofocusing CRLs are limited because every lenslet in the stack has the *same* small geometric aperture: the beam converges as it passes through the stack, so most of the material at the entrance simply absorbs photons while the effective numerical aperture stays low (≈100–200 nm foci for hard X‑rays). In an adiabatically focusing lens the aperture (and the parabola radius) of each successive lenslet is *tapered along the optical axis* to follow the shrinking beam envelope — a large aperture at the entrance where the beam is wide, progressively smaller radii and stronger curvature downstream where it is already converging. Because each element then works matched to the local beam size, the effective aperture accepted at the entrance can be increased several‑fold at essentially no extra absorption penalty, the NA grows accordingly, and diffraction‑limited hard X‑ray foci below ~20 nm (and, with silicon/diamond kinoform or 3D‑lithography‑written designs, ~10 nm) become achievable at 10–30 keV, where zone plates are impractically thick.

Practical implementation: fabricate the tapered lenslet series in low‑Z, radiation‑hard material (single‑crystal silicon or diamond by deep reactive‑ion etching, or polymer/SU‑8 by two‑photon 3D lithography) as a single monolithic block so that the lenslets are intrinsically aligned to nanometre accuracy — misalignment between elements, not the design, is the usual killer of CRL performance; use crossed (x and y) blocks or a rotationally parabolic profile for isotropic focusing; add a guard/beam‑defining aperture and a clean‑up pinhole to strip the un‑focused halo; and mount the block on a piezo hexapod with a short, stiff, thermally stabilised metrology loop, since the depth of focus shrinks as NA². Verify the achieved focus at‑wavelength by ptychographic probe retrieval or a Siemens‑star/knife‑edge scan, and correct residual figure errors by a matched corrective phase plate if needed. Because refractive optics are achromatic to first order (the focal length varies smoothly as 1/λ² and can be re‑set by simply translating the block), the same optic can be used over a wide energy range and for spectroscopic imaging.

The gain is immediate and applies to every downstream modality: a smaller, higher‑flux‑density probe means finer scanning XRF/XRD/XANES maps, a smaller diffraction‑limited spot for magnified projection/holotomography (the secondary source size sets the resolution there), higher‑resolution ptychography with shorter dwell times, and less drift/vibration blur because each point needs less exposure — all with no change to the source, detector, sample preparation or reconstruction pipeline.

Use a **monolithic Bonse–Hart crystal interferometer** for the imaging, so that the limiting factor becomes interferometric phase sensitivity rather than absorption contrast.

Cut a single, perfect silicon ingot into a monolithic block containing three (or four) parallel, equally spaced lamellae: the first acts as a beam splitter (Laue diffraction), the second as a mirror that redirects the two coherent arms, and the third recombines them. The specimen sits in one arm and a thin, tiltable phase shifter (a wedge of PMMA, Si or Al) in the other; recombination produces an interference field whose intensity depends on the *absolute* phase shift imposed by the sample. By phase-stepping the shifter through a full 2π in several increments at each rotation angle and fitting the sinusoidal intensity variation pixel-by-pixel, one obtains a quantitative, unwrapped phase-projection map — and, by tomographic inversion, a 3-D map of the refractive-index decrement δ.

Why this converts into better *effective* spatial resolution: in most high-resolution synchrotron imaging the smallest genuinely resolvable feature is set by whether it produces signal above the noise at a tolerable dose, not by the pixel or the optic. The phase cross-section of light elements is ~10³ times larger than the absorption cross-section at hard X-ray energies, and a Bonse–Hart interferometer measures the *total* phase directly (not its derivative, as in grating or analyser methods, and without the propagation distance and CTF zeros of in-line holography), with a density sensitivity of ~1 mg/cm³. Features one voxel across in soft tissue, polymers, hydrated cells or light-element composites, which sit far below the noise floor of an absorption or even a propagation-based scan, therefore appear with clear, sharp boundaries at the full sampling limit of the detector — and because the phase signal is obtained at very low absorbed dose, one can afford many more projections, finer angular sampling and finer voxels before radiation damage or beam-induced deformation intervenes. The same crystal geometry, run in analyser/rocking-curve (USAXS) mode, additionally quantifies structure well *below* the pixel size through ultra-small-angle scattering.

Practical requirements: the interferometer must be monolithic (all lamellae from one crystal) and held in a thermally isolated enclosure stabilised to the millikelvin level, since a temperature gradient of a few mK across the block, or a vibration of a fraction of a lattice plane spacing, destroys the fringe visibility; mount it on a vibration-isolated, actively damped granite bench in an evacuated or helium-filled path; use a highly monochromatic, well-collimated beam matched to the Darwin width; immerse the sample in a density-matched liquid cell so the phase excursion stays within one fringe and phase unwrapping remains unambiguous; and record the "sample-out" interferogram for background/aberration subtraction. The trade-offs are a small field of view (a few millimetres, set by the crystal aperture) and sensitivity to environmental noise — but where they can be met, the technique delivers quantitative 3-D density maps in which fine, low-contrast detail is resolved at the detector's sampling limit rather than being lost in noise.

**Numerically restore the coherence you actually have: use a mixed‑state (multi‑mode), instability‑aware reconstruction instead of assuming a single perfectly coherent probe.**

In coherent imaging (ptychography, near‑field ptychography, CDI, holography) the reconstruction is normally built on the assumption of one fully coherent illumination mode, one perfectly known scan position and a point‑like detector pixel. Reality violates all three: the beam has finite emittance and a finite bandwidth, the monochromator vibrates and the mirrors drift under heat load, the piezo stage has position errors and the sample creeps, the detector pixel integrates over a finite solid angle, and each exposure lasts long enough that the "instantaneous" wavefield changes during it. Every one of these effects reduces the *speckle contrast at large scattering angles* — exactly where the high‑spatial‑frequency information lives — so the reconstruction converges to a blurred object even though the data contain measurable signal out to high q. This "decoherence" blur, not the optic or the pixel size, is usually what caps real resolution in practice.

The fix is to put these degrees of freedom explicitly into the forward model and solve for them: decompose the illumination into a set of mutually incoherent probe modes (typically 3–10, obtained by orthogonalising the retrieved probe each iteration) whose intensities add on the detector; add, where appropriate, a small number of *object* modes to absorb sample motion, vibration or fast in‑situ dynamics within each exposure; refine every scan position (and a global affine/shear/drift model of the stage) as a free parameter; refine the propagation distance, detector tilt/distance and the effective pixel angular blur; and include an incoherent background term plus per‑frame incident‑flux normalisation for parasitic scatter and beam decay. Because the incoherent (mode‑summed) model reproduces the measured, partially washed‑out speckle correctly, the *coherent* part of the solution is no longer forced to blur itself to fit the data — the dominant mode carries the full high‑q information and the object is reconstructed at the true, detector‑limited diffraction resolution.

Practically: acquire with generous overlap (≳60–70 %) and enough diversity (varying defocus or a randomised, non‑periodic scan grid) so the extra unknowns are constrained; merge short and beam‑stopped long exposures into high‑dynamic‑range frames so weak high‑q speckle is above noise; start the mode refinement only after the single‑mode solution has roughly converged, and cap the number of modes by monitoring the error metric so noise is not fitted; quantify the achieved resolution objectively by Fourier ring/shell correlation between independent half‑datasets and by the phase‑retrieval transfer function, checking that the gain is data‑driven. The reward is typically a factor of ~1.5–3 in resolvable feature size, plus a direct measurement of the beam's coherent‑mode content and of the stage's error budget — with no change to the source, optics, detector or sample.

**Cascade two X‑ray optics in series ("relay"/compound X‑ray microscope) so the total magnification is the product of two stages, not one.**

In a conventional full‑field transmission X‑ray microscope the single objective (zone plate, MLL or CRL stack) typically gives only ~20–50×, so a 0.5–1 µm effective detector pixel projects back to 10–50 nm at the sample — comparable to the objective's own diffraction limit. The microscope is therefore *detector‑limited*, not NA‑limited, and any further improvement of the optic is wasted. The fix is to add a second imaging element: let the objective form a real intermediate image a metre or so downstream, and place a second, low‑NA relay optic (a large‑aperture zone plate, a CRL/kinoform stack, or a grazing‑incidence Wolter/Montel mirror pair) just after that intermediate image plane so that it re‑images it onto the camera with a further 10–30×. The net magnification of 500–1000× divides the scintillator blur, optical‑relay aberrations and pixel MTF by such a large factor that the detector drops completely out of the resolution budget, and the reconstructed resolution becomes the objective's true diffraction limit (δ ≈ 0.61λ/NA, i.e. sub‑10–20 nm) with comfortable Nyquist oversampling — while the camera itself can be a robust, high‑efficiency, large‑pixel device sitting far from the sample, leaving room for in‑situ environments.

Practical requirements: the relay must be aligned on the same optical axis and conjugated exactly to the intermediate image plane (piezo hexapods with in‑situ focus optimisation on a Siemens‑star target); each stage's aberrations and field curvature add, so use only the corrected on‑axis field or a relay designed as an aplanat, and measure the *system* PSF at‑wavelength and deconvolve its residual (a wavefront/ptychographic probe retrieval at the intermediate plane lets each element be characterised separately); order‑sorting apertures, central stops and clean‑up slits are needed after *both* diffractive elements to keep undiffracted and higher orders from fogging the final image; monochromaticity must satisfy ΔE/E < 1/N for the element with the most zones; and because the efficiencies multiply (perhaps ~1 % overall for two zone plates, much better if the relay is a reflective mirror pair), the lost flux must be recovered with a low‑emittance source, a matched condenser and longer/accumulated exposures with drift correction between frames. The payoff is that the microscope finally delivers the resolution its numerical aperture is capable of, with no change to the sample, the scan protocol or the camera.

**Eliminate the *temporal* blur of the detector chain in continuous ("fly‑scan") acquisitions by choosing a fast‑decay scintillator and a global‑shutter/lag‑free camera, and by deconvolving the measured temporal impulse response along the projection sequence.**

In continuous‑rotation tomography the sample never stops, so any memory in the detector smears each projection into the next: scintillators with long decay constants or afterglow (CsI:Tl, GGG:Eu, CdWO₄, and even "fast" crystals with slow phosphorescent tails), image‑intensifier persistence, CCD/CMOS charge lag and trapping, and rolling‑shutter readout all mean that a given frame contains a weighted admixture of the object as it appeared at earlier angles. The effect is an angle‑direction (azimuthal) convolution that mimics motion blur: edges tangential to the rotation are smeared, the sinogram is low‑pass filtered along its angular axis, and the reconstruction shows a characteristic "swirl"/comet asymmetry and a resolution several times worse than the nominal voxel size — and it gets worse the faster (i.e. the more dose‑ and drift‑efficiently) you scan, which is exactly why it is so often mistaken for a spatial‑optics limitation.

Practical measures: (i) select a scintillator whose decay time is far shorter than the frame period and whose afterglow at 1–10 ms is below ~10⁻⁴ (e.g. LSO/LYSO:Ce ~40 ns, YAP:Ce, ZnO:Ga, plastic/ceramic fast phosphors) rather than the brighter but slow alternatives, accepting slightly lower light yield in exchange for a clean temporal response; (ii) use a global‑shutter, lag‑free sCMOS/photon‑counting sensor and avoid intensifiers, so every pixel row samples the same angular interval; (iii) measure the actual temporal impulse response *in situ* — chop the beam with a fast shutter or use a single bunch/pulsed beam and record the decay of the detector signal, and independently measure the "angular ESF" by fly‑scanning a sharp high‑Z edge or a sub‑resolution wire and comparing it with a step‑and‑shoot scan of the same object; (iv) deconvolve that measured kernel from the sinogram along the angular coordinate (a regularised 1‑D Richardson–Lucy/Wiener step, or better, include the lag term in the forward model of an iterative reconstruction, since it is a simple linear, shift‑invariant operator in the angle direction); and (v) set the exposure/rotation speed so the sample rotates by less than half a resolution element per frame at the outer radius, using more frames rather than longer ones.

Because this attacks a blur that no optic, smaller pixel or brighter source can remove — and that is systematically absorbed into "measured resolution" without being noticed — correcting it typically restores a factor of ~1.5–3 in true resolvable feature size in fast and in‑situ scans, at zero cost in dose, beamtime or hardware beyond the choice of screen and camera.

**Make sure the focusing optic's full clear aperture is actually illuminated — i.e. insert an upstream beam expander / aperture‑matching stage so the probe is aperture‑limited, not illumination‑limited.**

The diffraction limit of a nanoprobe is δ ≈ 0.61 λ/NA, where the *effective* NA is set by the width of the beam that genuinely reaches the lens, not by the lens's nominal size. At most beamlines the coherent beam footprint at the optic (a KB pair, zone plate, MLL or CRL stack) is smaller than the optic's physical aperture — because the secondary‑source slits have been closed for coherence, because the undulator's natural divergence at high photon energy is small, or because the optic sits too close to the source — so only the central portion of the mirror/lens is used and the focus is correspondingly several times larger than the design value, with the "missing" outer aperture also producing broad PSF tails.

The fix is to expand and shape the beam before the optic rather than to buy a better optic: place an asymmetrically‑cut Bragg crystal (or a pair of them, expanding in each direction) or a weakly defocusing/diverging pre‑optic (a slightly de‑tuned CRL, a convex or bent mirror, or a "beam‑expanding" pre‑focus placed so its virtual source is close to the lens) upstream, so the beam is magnified transversely until it just overfills the optic's aperture in both directions; equivalently, move the optic further downstream, or open the secondary source slits in the direction where the source is already small enough to preserve coherence. Then trim the overfill with guard slits so no stray light bypasses the optic.

Practical steps: measure the actual beam profile at the optic plane (scan a knife edge or a fluorescence screen at the lens position) and compare it with the aperture; verify the achieved probe at‑wavelength by a Siemens‑star/knife‑edge scan or ptychographic probe retrieval and check that the FWHM has dropped toward 0.61 λ/NA and that the side‑lobe tails have shrunk; ensure the expanded beam still has transverse coherence across the *whole* aperture (otherwise the outer parts add incoherently and only fill in the tails — for a low‑emittance source this is usually satisfied, and mixed‑state/partial‑coherence modelling can be used if not); re‑check the mirror/lens figure over the newly used outer regions, since edge zones often have the worst slope errors and may need corrective figuring or a slightly reduced aperture; and account for the flux per unit area being lower after expansion by compensating with longer dwell times.

The payoff is a genuine factor of ~2–5 reduction in probe size (and in the PSF tails that blur scanning XRF/XRD/XANES maps and ptychographic probes) using the *same* optic, source, detector and scan protocol — simply by ensuring the numerical aperture that the lens was designed for is the one actually being used.

**Remove the oblique‑incidence ("parallax"/depth‑of‑interaction) blur in the detector, which dominates the point‑spread function away from the optical axis whenever a thick converter is used or the beam is divergent.**

In a thick scintillator or a thick high‑Z direct‑conversion sensor (CdTe/GaAs/Ge, often several hundred µm to a few mm thick so that 30–100 keV photons are actually stopped), a photon that arrives at an angle θ to the sensor normal — because the beam is divergent (magnified projection/cone‑beam geometry), because the detector is far off‑axis in a large field of view, or because the sensor is deliberately tilted — deposits its energy at a random depth *z* inside the converter and is therefore registered at a lateral position displaced by *z*·tanθ. Averaged over the absorption profile, this smears every event into an elongated, field‑position‑dependent, asymmetric streak of length ≈ *t*·tanθ (tens of micrometres or more at the edges of the field), which no upstream optic, smaller pixel, brighter source or better scan protocol can undo; it is also anisotropic, so it degrades resolution radially but not tangentially and is easily mistaken for "the detector MTF" or for misalignment.

Practical fixes, in increasing order of effort: (i) **make the converter normal to the local ray** — use a curved/tiled detector, or mount flat detector modules on a polygonal arc centred on the source (as is standard in astronomy and medical CT) so that θ ≈ 0 everywhere in the field, and keep the sample–detector distance long enough that the ray fan is narrow; (ii) **segment the converter along the beam** — use the light‑guiding/columnar or micro‑channel scintillator geometry with the columns *aligned along the local ray direction* (fan‑shaped columns), or stack several thin sensor layers and read them out separately, so the interaction depth is either confined or measured; (iii) **measure the depth of interaction event‑by‑event** — in a photon‑counting hybrid sensor, the drift time of the charge cloud (Timepix3‑style sub‑nanosecond time stamping relative to the bunch clock) and the degree of charge sharing/rise‑time both encode *z*, so each photon can be back‑projected to its true entrance position with a few‑tens‑of‑micrometre depth precision, collapsing the parallax streak; (iv) **calibrate and deconvolve what remains** — map the field‑dependent, anisotropic PSF by scanning a sharp gold edge or a sub‑resolution wire across the field at several radii and at the working energy (the absorption depth, and hence the blur, is strongly energy dependent, so do it per energy bin), then either deconvolve this spatially varying kernel from every projection or, better, include it explicitly as the field‑dependent detector response in the forward model of an iterative/model‑based tomographic reconstruction.

Because this attacks a blur that grows with field radius and with converter thickness — i.e. exactly the regime one is pushed into when trying to combine a large field of view with high stopping power at hard X‑ray energies — correcting it typically restores a factor of two or more in true resolvable feature size at the edges of the field and, crucially, makes the resolution *uniform* across the image, allowing the reconstruction filter to be pushed to the sampling limit everywhere instead of being set by the worst‑case corner of the detector. It requires no change to the source, beamline optics, sample preparation or scan geometry, and it simultaneously removes the systematic geometric distortion (each pixel's effective centre is shifted radially) that otherwise degrades the accuracy of centre‑of‑rotation and magnification calibration.

Shape the nanoprobe into a **non‑diffracting Bessel ("needle") beam with a refractive/kinoform axicon (or an annular/axicon‑zone‑plate pupil)** instead of using a conventional converging focus.

An axicon placed in the beam (or an axicon profile written into the zone plate/MLL) produces a probe whose central core can be made *narrower* than the Airy spot of an equivalent conical focus, and — crucially — that core stays essentially constant in width over a depth of field of hundreds of micrometres to millimetres rather than the few micrometres of a high‑NA focus. In scanning modalities (XRF, µ/nano‑XRD, XANES, STXM, scanning‑SAXS) this breaks the usual trade‑off in which pushing the lateral resolution down collapses the depth of focus, so that only a thin layer of a thick specimen is probed at full resolution while the rest contributes blurred signal: with a Bessel probe the *whole thickness* of the sample is scanned by the same narrow core, so projections and tomographic slices stay sharp throughout the volume, and the beam's self‑healing property means that an upstream inclusion, a window, a bubble or a dense grain that would destroy a normal focus only perturbs the core briefly before it reconstructs itself downstream. It also relaxes the sub‑micrometre axial positioning and focus‑drift tolerance that otherwise limits long scans and in‑situ cells (furnaces, load rigs, flow cells) where the sample cannot be kept exactly in the focal plane.

Practical implementation: fabricate the axicon in a low‑Z, radiation‑hard material (single‑crystal silicon/diamond by deep etching, or SU‑8 by two‑photon 3D lithography), or use a crossed pair of linear axicons/an annular apodized pupil with a matched central stop and order‑sorting aperture; choose the cone angle so that the core width matches the target resolution and the non‑diffracting length matches the sample thickness; measure the full 3‑D probe in situ (ptychographic probe retrieval, or knife‑edge/Siemens‑star scans at several axial positions) so that the concentric ring side lobes — which carry a large fraction of the power and would otherwise add a broad halo to every map — are known quantitatively; scan with steps of ~1/3 of the core width and finally invert the maps with a regularised, Poisson‑aware deconvolution using the measured ring‑structured kernel, which suppresses the side‑lobe contribution and sharpens the effective PSF further. Compensate the reduced fraction of flux in the core with a brighter low‑emittance source or longer dwell, and monitor I₀ per point.

The result is genuinely higher, *depth‑independent* lateral resolution in thick or awkwardly mounted specimens, obtained by re‑engineering the probe geometry alone — no new detector, source, sample thinning or reconstruction geometry required.

Abandon the full‑field, detector‑limited geometry for thick or highly scattering specimens and use a **collimated pencil‑beam, "first‑generation" translate–rotate scan with matched pre‑ and post‑sample apertures**.

Define the probe with a precision slit/pinhole assembly (crossed high‑Z slits or a laser‑drilled pinhole in a tungsten/tantalum block, several absorption lengths thick) placed just upstream of the sample, and put a *second*, aligned aperture/anti‑scatter collimator immediately in front of a single high‑efficiency, energy‑discriminating counting detector (Si/CdTe diode or a few pixels of a photon‑counting chip). Then raster the sample across the beam in steps that are a small fraction (~1/3–1/5) of the aperture width at each rotation angle, building the sinogram point by point.

Why this raises real resolution: the point‑spread function is now set purely by the aperture size, its lithographic/EDM fabrication accuracy and the translation‑stage step, not by scintillator light spread, visible‑optics aberrations, camera pixel pitch or detector MTF — all of which drop out because the detector only has to count how many photons passed the aperture. Just as importantly, the two collimators together accept only the direct ray, so Compton and small‑angle scatter from the sample, its container and any in‑situ cell — which in full‑field imaging superimposes a diffuse halo that flattens the contrast transfer at high spatial frequencies and is the dominant blur in thick, dense specimens — is physically rejected rather than corrected for. Because the finely over‑sampled scan measures the object convolved with a *known*, knife‑edge‑calibrated aperture transmission function, a regularised (Poisson‑aware Richardson–Lucy or model‑based) deconvolution then recovers a further factor of ~2 below the aperture width.

Practical requirements: interferometric or closed‑loop encoder feedback on the translation and rotation stages with repeatability well below the step size; accurate parallel alignment of the two apertures along the beam (re‑aligned if the beam moves), with a thermally stabilised, stiff mount; per‑point I₀ normalisation from a monitor upstream of the first aperture; energy‑window setting on the detector to reject harmonics and residual scatter; and continuous fly‑scanning of the translation axis with time‑stamped counting to keep the (inherently serial) acquisition affordable — with the flux lost to the tiny aperture recovered by pre‑focusing the undulator beam onto it with KB mirrors or a condenser. The trade‑off is scan time and a small field of view per pass, but the result is projection data whose sharpness and quantitative accuracy are limited only by nanofabrication and stage metrology, obtained with no imaging optic and no high‑resolution camera at all — and it works on thick, dense or awkwardly mounted samples where full‑field detectors are scatter‑limited.

Shorten the wavelength: run the experiment at a higher photon energy (e.g. move from ~8 keV to 20–30 keV or beyond) while keeping — or extending — the collected angular range. Because every diffraction‑limited resolution criterion scales linearly with λ (δ ≈ 0.61 λ/NA for a lens‑based microscope, δ ≈ λ/(2 sin θ_max) = 2π/q_max for coherent‑diffraction/ptychographic and Bragg‑CDI reconstructions), halving the wavelength halves the smallest resolvable feature for the *same* optic, detector and scan geometry. In practice this means pairing the harder beam with a large‑area, high‑stopping‑power (CdTe/GaAs) photon‑counting detector placed as close to the sample as possible — or tiled/translated — so that the higher‑q (wider‑angle) signal that the shorter wavelength makes accessible is actually recorded, and with high‑dynamic‑range merging of short and beam‑stopped exposures so the weak high‑angle speckle rises above noise. Hard X‑rays additionally penetrate thick, dense or in‑situ‑encased specimens without thinning, give a larger depth of focus for a given resolution (so thick objects stay within the depth‑of‑field limit), and suffer far less absorption‑induced dose per useful scattered photon, which is what ultimately caps resolution in beam‑sensitive samples. The trade‑off — weaker absorption/phase contrast and lower optic efficiency at high energy — is offset by using phase‑sensitive detection (propagation‑based or ptychographic phase retrieval, which is many orders of magnitude more sensitive than absorption at these energies), high‑efficiency optics designed for hard X‑rays (multilayer Laue lenses, multilayer KB mirrors, CRLs), longer counting times, and a low‑emittance source whose brilliance at high energy is now comparable to that at low energy.

Exploit **geometric foreshortening by illuminating the specimen at grazing incidence** (a "tilted‑sample" geometry), so that the *projected* probe footprint — not the probe itself — sets the resolution.

Instead of putting the flat specimen (thin film, membrane, device layer, polished section, layered stack) normal to the beam, mount it on a precision goniometer and tilt it to a small angle α (typically 0.1–10°, i.e. at or just below the critical angle for a total‑external‑reflection experiment) with respect to the incident micro‑ or nano‑beam. The footprint of the beam on the sample is stretched along the beam direction by 1/sin α, which means that, referred back to the *sample* coordinate, the probe is compressed in the perpendicular (depth/transverse) direction by a factor sin α: a 200 nm focus at α = 1° probes a layer only ~3–4 nm thick normal to the surface. Scanning the sample (or the incidence angle) therefore delivers depth or transverse profiles with a step size and resolution an order of magnitude — or two — finer than the focal spot, entirely independently of the optic's numerical aperture, the scintillator blur or the detector pixel pitch. The same trick simultaneously boosts the signal: the long path through the surface layer increases the interaction volume and hence the fluorescence/diffraction yield by 1/sin α, while the low incidence angle confines the illumination to the top few nanometres (evanescent field below the critical angle), suppressing background from the substrate and giving very high surface sensitivity per unit dose. Scanning α across the critical angle turns the penetration depth into a continuously tunable "virtual slice" selector for non‑destructive depth profiling (GIXRF/GISAXS/GIXRD).

Practical requirements: an extremely flat, low‑roughness specimen (roughness and waviness comparable to the compressed probe dimension are the real resolution limiter, and any long‑range curvature must be mapped and corrected); a goniometer with sub‑microradian angular resolution and a rotation centre held on the surface to sub‑micrometre precision, since the footprint position is hypersensitive to angle and height (do a height/angle "z–θ" alignment scan at every field position); an incident beam whose vertical divergence is much smaller than α so the angle is well defined across the footprint; correction of the anamorphic (highly anisotropic) sampling — the along‑beam resolution is *degraded* by 1/sin α, so either accept anisotropy, repeat the scan with the tilt applied along the orthogonal azimuth, or deconvolve the calibrated elongated footprint; and modelling of refraction and self‑absorption when converting the angle‑dependent yield into a true depth profile. The trade‑off is that the method is restricted to flat, surface‑ or layer‑type specimens and gives its enormous gain along only one axis — but where it applies, it converts an optics‑limited measurement into a geometry‑limited one and buys nanometre‑scale sectioning with no change to the source, focusing optic, detector or reconstruction software.

Acquire each projection not as one long exposure but as a **dose‑fractionated "movie" of many very short sub‑exposures, then align and merge them with an exposure‑dependent (dose‑weighted) Fourier filter** — the X‑ray analogue of the direct‑detector movie‑mode/dose‑weighting scheme that transformed cryo‑EM.

Practically: run a fast, low‑noise (photon‑counting or lag‑free sCMOS) camera so that the same total dose per angle is split into, say, 20–100 frames of a few milliseconds each; cross‑correlate the frames (using natural specimen texture or added high‑Z fiducials) to measure and remove the sub‑pixel beam‑induced motion, stage vibration, thermal drift and specimen creep that occur *during* the exposure — motion that in a single long frame is irreversibly baked in as blur; then, instead of simply summing the aligned frames, weight them in Fourier space according to the accumulated dose at which each was recorded. Because radiation damage destroys high spatial frequencies far earlier than low ones (the critical dose falls steeply with spatial frequency), the fine detail is taken almost entirely from the first, still‑undamaged frames while the low‑frequency, high‑SNR content is accumulated from the whole series. Frames showing a transient (a vibration, a beam trip, a bubble or a sudden sample shift) are simply discarded rather than contaminating the whole projection.

The same fractionated series also gives, for free, a per‑angle measurement of the actual drift/damage rate, which can be fed forward to optimise exposure time, and a natural half‑dataset split for an honest Fourier‑shell‑correlation estimate of the resolution really achieved. The gain — typically a factor of ~1.5–2 in resolvable feature size for beam‑sensitive or drifting specimens — costs no extra dose, beamtime, optics, source brightness or sample preparation: only a faster readout and a modified frame‑merging step in the reconstruction pipeline.

Insert a perfect‑crystal **analyser** between the sample and the camera and work in analyser‑based (diffraction‑enhanced) imaging mode: after monochromatising the beam, place a Si (or Ge) crystal in non‑dispersive (+,–) geometry behind the specimen and set it on the steep flank of its rocking curve, then record a series of images while stepping the analyser in sub‑microradian increments through the whole rocking curve ("multiple‑image radiography").

Two things sharpen the image, neither of which requires a better lens, smaller pixels, a brighter source or a different scan geometry:

1. **Angular (scatter) filtering.** The Darwin width of the analyser is only a few microradians, so it accepts essentially only the unscattered/ballistic ray direction. All the Compton, small‑angle and multiply scattered radiation from the sample, its container and any in‑situ cell — which in ordinary radiography superimposes a diffuse halo that flattens the contrast‑transfer function at high spatial frequencies and is often the true blur limit in thick or dense specimens — is physically rejected before it ever reaches the scintillator, so edges keep their full modulation right up to the detector's Nyquist frequency.

2. **Sub‑pixel edge localisation from refraction.** Because the transmitted intensity is a steep, calibrated function of the local ray deviation, each pixel measures the specimen's refraction angle with nanoradian sensitivity. Fitting the measured rocking curve pixel‑by‑pixel yields three separate channels — transmission, refraction (differential phase) and the rocking‑curve broadening (ultra‑small‑angle scattering / dark field). Integrating the refraction channel gives a phase image whose interfaces are localised to a fraction of a pixel (a derivative signal peaks exactly at the boundary), while the broadening channel quantifies sub‑pixel structure (pores, cracks, fibres) that is invisible in the image itself.

Practically: use a well‑collimated, highly monochromatic beam matched to the analyser's angular acceptance; mount the monochromator and analyser on a common, millikelvin‑stabilised, vibration‑isolated bench with sub‑microradian goniometry (a monolithic channel‑cut or a mechanically coupled pair minimises relative drift); normalise every frame to I₀ and to the measured empty‑beam rocking curve to remove crystal non‑uniformity; keep the beam path evacuated so no air scatter is re‑injected downstream of the analyser; and for tomography repeat a short rocking sequence (or use a two‑point "steep‑flank" scheme) at each angle, reconstructing the refraction channel with a Hilbert‑type filter instead of the usual ramp filter. The trade‑offs are flux loss, the anisotropy of the technique (sensitivity only in the diffraction plane, so rotate the sample or use a second, orthogonal analyser for isotropy) and a field of view limited by the crystal aperture — but where they can be met, the reconstruction becomes limited by the detector's sampling rather than by scatter‑induced haze and low soft‑tissue contrast, typically recovering a factor of about two in genuinely resolvable feature size.

**Deliberately mis‑align the detector's pixel grid with the rotation axis — i.e. roll the camera by a small, precisely calibrated angle (a few degrees) about the beam axis — and reconstruct the whole volume with a geometry‑aware (iterative/algebraic) algorithm that uses the true, irregular ray positions.**

In a standard scan the pixel columns are made exactly parallel to the rotation axis, so every projection samples each horizontal slice on *exactly the same* grid: the object is sampled only at the pixel pitch, aliasing is coherent from angle to angle, and the reconstruction can never exceed the detector's Nyquist limit. If the detector is rolled by a small angle α, each successive detector row crosses a given slice at a lateral offset of (row number)·pitch·sin α — i.e. a *different* sub‑pixel fraction — and, as the sample rotates (and, if a helical/vertical translation is added, as it moves in z), each object slice is sampled by many rows at many different, incommensurate sub‑pixel offsets. The union of all these measurements is an irregularly but densely interlaced sampling of the object on a grid several times finer than the physical pixel pitch, so the volume can legitimately be reconstructed on sub‑pixel voxels and the reconstruction becomes limited by the detector's MTF (which can then be deconvolved) rather than by its sampling. Aliasing is also randomised rather than coherent, so it appears as mild noise instead of structured moiré/streak artefacts.

Practical requirements: measure the roll angle (and detector tilt/skew) to better than ~0.01° by imaging a fine test grid or a tilted wire and refining it with a reconstruction‑sharpness/consistency metric; use an iterative, model‑based reconstruction whose forward projector places every ray at its true sub‑pixel position (filtered back‑projection on a slice‑by‑slice Cartesian grid throws the extra information away); keep the rotation‑axis wobble, drift and stage runout well below the sub‑pixel increment (air‑bearing stage, per‑projection drift tracking); use many finely spaced angles over 360° with continuous fly‑scanning so the interlacing is dense and cheap; and finally deconvolve the measured scintillator/optics PSF, since after interlacing the blur — not the sampling — is the limit. Choose α (and, if used, the helical pitch) so that the offsets are incommensurate with the pixel pitch over the field of view, maximising the diversity of sub‑pixel samples.

The gain — typically a factor of ~2 in genuinely resolvable feature size — costs nothing in dose, beamtime, optics, source brightness or sample preparation: only a rotated detector mount and a reconstruction code that knows about it.

Stop treating phase retrieval and tomographic inversion as two separate steps and instead perform a **single "one‑step" joint inversion of the whole raw dataset for the 3‑D object** (joint ptycho‑tomography / joint holo‑tomography).

Conventionally one first phase‑retrieves each rotation angle independently (per‑angle ptychographic or multi‑distance Fresnel reconstruction) and then feeds the resulting 2‑D projections into a filtered‑back‑projection or iterative tomographic code. Every angle is therefore solved from an under‑determined, noisy subset of the data on its own: low‑frequency phase ambiguities, ramps/offsets, unknown constant phase, probe errors and residual position errors must each be fixed by hand, and any mismatch between angles (a slightly different retrieved probe, an unresolved phase wrap, a sub‑pixel misregistration) is then back‑projected as blur, streaks and loss of the highest spatial frequencies.

In the joint approach the unknown is the 3‑D complex refractive‑index volume itself, and the forward model chains together: volume → line‑integral (or multi‑slice) projection at each angle → probe illumination → Fresnel/far‑field propagation → detector response. All measured diffraction patterns or holograms from all angles are then fitted simultaneously by gradient‑based optimisation, with the illumination function, per‑scan positions, rotation‑axis position/tilt, per‑angle drift and a background term refined as shared global parameters, and with a 3‑D regulariser (TV/sparsity/smoothness) applied directly to the volume.

Why this raises real resolution: (i) every diffraction pattern now constrains the *same* 3‑D unknown, so the massive redundancy across angles compensates for the data each individual angle lacks — high‑q speckle that is too weak to phase on its own becomes usable, and the reconstruction converges to the detector‑angle‑limited resolution rather than to the per‑angle limit; (ii) inter‑angle inconsistencies (phase offsets/ramps, unwrapping errors, registration errors) simply cannot occur, because there is only one object; (iii) because the problem is strongly over‑determined, the scan overlap, number of angles and dose per angle can be cut several‑fold at constant resolution — which shortens the scan and directly reduces drift‑ and damage‑induced blur; and (iv) refining the geometry and probe *inside* the same optimisation removes the alignment blur that normally caps 3‑D resolution well above the 2‑D projection resolution.

Practical requirements: a GPU/HPC implementation with automatic differentiation (the memory footprint of the full volume plus all frames is the main cost, handled by stochastic mini‑batching over angles and scan points); a good starting estimate from a conventional two‑step reconstruction; careful weighting of the Poisson likelihood and of the regulariser, validated by cross‑validation on withheld frames; and objective verification of the achieved resolution by Fourier shell correlation between two independently reconstructed half‑datasets, to confirm the recovered high frequencies are data‑driven rather than regulariser‑generated. No change to the source, optics, detector or sample is needed — only the reconstruction formulation.

**Form the image from high‑angle, incoherently scattered X‑rays in a scanning nanoprobe — i.e. adopt an annular dark‑field (ADF/HAADF‑style) detection geometry instead of bright‑field transmission.**

Focus the beam with a KB pair, zone plate or MLL, raster the specimen through it, and collect the signal not with an on‑axis "bucket" detector but with an annular (or annular segment of a pixel‑array) detector that accepts only scattering beyond the bright‑field disc, with an appropriately sized central beam stop/aperture defining the inner collection angle. Because photons scattered to high angles arrive from many independent, essentially uncorrelated scattering centres within the illuminated spot, the image is formed **incoherently**: the effective point‑spread function becomes |P(r)|² rather than P(r), which is roughly √2 narrower and — far more importantly — has drastically suppressed tails and no interference fringes, so the long halo produced by zone‑plate higher orders, mirror slope errors and CRL aberrations no longer smears the map. The contrast‑transfer function is positive‑definite and extends to ~2·NA/λ, i.e. a factor of about two beyond the bright‑field cut‑off, and it does not oscillate or change sign with defocus, so no phase‑retrieval or CTF‑zero problem limits the recoverable spatial frequencies. The signal also scales steeply with atomic number (Rutherford‑like Z‑contrast), so high‑Z inclusions, catalyst nanoparticles, labels or precipitates are localised as sharp, isolated peaks whose centroids can be fitted to a small fraction of the probe size.

Practical implementation: choose the inner collection angle a few times the probe's convergence angle so that the bright‑field disc and coherent Bragg/diffuse contributions are excluded (channelling/diffraction contrast is what breaks the simple incoherent picture in crystalline material — for crystals, use a larger inner angle or rock the sample slightly to average orientations); scan with steps of ~1/3–1/4 of the probe FWHM using continuous fly‑scanning so the extra points cost little time; normalise every point to the incident flux; measure the real probe in situ (ptychographic probe retrieval or knife‑edge/Siemens‑star scan), square it to obtain the true ADF kernel, and finish with a regularised, Poisson‑aware deconvolution of that kernel — which buys a further factor of ~2 because the incoherent PSF is smooth, positive and shift‑invariant, making the inversion far better conditioned than deconvolution of an oscillatory coherent PSF. If a pixel‑array detector is used, the bright‑field disc, differential‑phase and full ptychographic channels are recorded simultaneously for free and can be fused with the ADF map (which supplies the sharp, artefact‑free edges) in a joint reconstruction; the same detector geometry extends directly to tomography by repeating the raster at each rotation angle.

The gain — a roughly two‑fold improvement in resolvable feature size, with much cleaner edges and greatly reduced background from material just outside the nominal probe — comes purely from which photons are collected and how the data are inverted, with no change to the source, focusing optic, sample preparation or scan hardware.

**Use autonomous, adaptive (information‑driven) sampling instead of a uniform raster/angle grid, so the fine sampling is spent only where structure actually exists.**

In scanning modalities (nano‑XRF, STXM, µ‑XRD/XANES mapping, scanning‑SAXS) and in tomography, the step size — not the optic — often sets the practical resolution, because a uniform grid at the probe‑limited step over the whole field of view (or a full set of finely spaced angles) would take far too long and deliver far too much dose. Rather than coarsening the step everywhere, run the experiment in a closed loop: reconstruct/interpolate the map on the fly from the points already measured (Gaussian‑process regression, or a learned model such as SLADS/deep‑learning‑guided sampling), compute for every candidate position the expected information gain — posterior variance, predicted gradient magnitude, or the reduction in reconstruction uncertainty — and let the control software choose the next measurement points (and, in tomography, the next projection angle) accordingly. The result is that flat, homogeneous regions are sampled very sparsely, while interfaces, cracks, particle boundaries, hot spots and chemically changing regions are sampled at a step several times *finer* than the probe FWHM, giving genuine sub‑probe, deconvolvable oversampling exactly where resolution matters; the final map is obtained by a regularised inversion (with the measured probe PSF deconvolved) from the non‑uniform point set.

Practical requirements: a fast, low‑latency data pipeline (on‑line GPU reconstruction and detector streaming) so the decision for the next point is made within the dwell time; a stage that can move to arbitrary, non‑gridded positions with closed‑loop encoder/interferometric repeatability well below the fine step; per‑point I₀ normalisation; a "safety floor" of quasi‑random background points spread over the whole field so that features are not missed and the model cannot hallucinate structure in unsampled regions; and objective validation by re‑measuring a small held‑out set of points (or a densely scanned control region) and by Fourier ring correlation against a conventional full scan.

Because typically 70–90 % of the points of a uniform scan carry almost no information, the same beamtime and the same total dose can be re‑invested into a 3–10× finer step at the features of interest — a real gain in resolvable feature size and in edge localisation, with no change to the source, focusing optic, detector or sample preparation, and with the additional benefit of much less radiation damage to beam‑sensitive specimens.

Apply **"image‑scanning microscopy" (Sheppard pixel‑reassignment) to a scanning X‑ray microprobe/STXM**: replace the single bucket detector behind the focused probe with a fast pixel‑array (photon‑counting) detector, record the *full* bright‑field disc at every scan point, and then, instead of summing the disc into one number, treat each detector element as a separate confocal "detector pinhole" that forms its own complete scanned image. Each of these sub‑images is identical apart from a lateral shift equal to roughly **half** the detector element's angular offset from the optical axis (the product of the probe and detection point‑spread functions peaks midway between the two). Shift each sub‑image back by that amount ("pixel reassignment") and sum them.

Why it works: a confocal‑type image formed with an infinitely small detector pinhole would have a PSF equal to the *product* of the illumination and detection PSFs — about √2 narrower than either — but such a pinhole throws away nearly all the photons. Pixel reassignment recovers that same narrowed PSF while keeping **every** detected photon, so one gets a genuine ~1.4× (and up to 2× after deconvolution of the reassigned PSF) improvement in resolvable feature size at no cost in dose or dwell time, together with a large gain in signal‑to‑noise and strong rejection of signal from out‑of‑focus depths and from material outside the probe core (the long aberration tails of the KB/zone‑plate focus are suppressed because their contribution does not reassign coherently).

Practical steps: scan with steps of ~1/3 of the probe FWHM using continuous fly‑scanning so the extra sampling is cheap; calibrate the detector's angular scale and determine the optimal reassignment factor empirically (scan a Siemens star or knife edge and maximise the sharpness metric for each detector element, since the ideal factor deviates from 0.5 in the presence of defocus, aberrations or partial coherence); normalise each frame to the incident flux and subtract the slow beam‑drift‑induced descan (a wandering beam mimics a uniform reassignment shift); restrict the summed elements to the bright‑field disc, where the shift‑invariant reassignment model holds, and finish with a regularised Wiener/Richardson–Lucy deconvolution of the measured reassigned PSF. The same recorded frames simultaneously yield the integrated bright‑field, differential‑phase and dark‑field channels for free, and the scheme extends directly to tomography by repeating the raster at each rotation angle — all with no change to the focusing optic, source, sample preparation or scan hardware, only to the detector used and to how the per‑point frames are combined.

**Use a "coded‑exposure (flutter‑shutter) fly‑scan" so that rotation/motion blur becomes invertible instead of irreversible.**

In continuous‑rotation (fly‑scan) tomography and in most in‑situ experiments each projection is smeared because the object rotates or evolves during the exposure. A conventional open‑shutter exposure convolves the projection with a *box* temporal kernel, whose Fourier transform is a sinc with hard zeros: the spatial frequencies that fall on those zeros are annihilated and can never be recovered by any deconvolution, which is why users are forced to shorten exposures (photon starvation) or accept a blurred, low‑pass reconstruction. Instead, gate the beam during each frame with a fast chopper, piezo‑driven shutter, or by using the ring's bunch/pulse clock, switching it on and off according to a **pseudo‑random binary sequence** chosen so that the resulting temporal modulation has a nearly flat, zero‑free power spectrum (a "broadband" blur kernel). The sample keeps rotating, the total open time (and hence the photon budget and dose) is roughly half that of the continuous exposure, but now every spatial frequency survives with non‑zero amplitude, so the known coded kernel — expressed as a shift along the angular/motion direction — can be deconvolved from each projection (regularised Wiener/Richardson–Lucy, or better, built directly into the forward model of an iterative model‑based reconstruction, together with the object's angular trajectory).

Practical implementation: phase‑lock the chopper/shutter pattern to the rotation‑stage encoder and camera trigger so the exact on/off timing of every frame is known to microseconds; optimise the code sequence (MURA/random sequences searched for maximum minimum‑value of the DFT magnitude) for the expected number of resolution elements traversed per frame at the outer sample radius; record the true blur kernel in situ by fly‑scanning a sharp high‑Z edge or a sub‑resolution wire and comparing with a step‑and‑shoot reference; normalise each frame with an I₀ monitor gated by the same code; and vary the code from frame to frame so residual deconvolution artefacts are incoherent between projections and average out in the reconstruction rather than accumulating as streaks.

The payoff is that the rotation speed (or the process speed) no longer has to be traded against sharpness: one can spin several times faster — shortening the scan, reducing dose, drift and sample evolution — while still recovering projections whose resolution is set by the detector/optics PSF rather than by motion smear, typically restoring a factor of ~2–3 in genuinely resolvable feature size in fast and dynamic scans, with no change to the source, imaging optics, detector or sample preparation (only a synchronised fast chopper and a modified deconvolution/reconstruction step).

**Multiplex the probe: illuminate the sample with a dense array of nano‑focused beamlets (a Talbot array illuminator or a lithographic array of many small Fresnel/kinoform lenslets) and scan only over one array period, reading all beamlets in parallel on a pixel‑array detector.**

Instead of one focused probe that must be raster‑scanned over the whole field (slow, so drift, vibration and beam decay accumulate and blur the map) or a full‑field image whose resolution is capped by the scintillator/pixel PSF, place a periodic phase grating/lens array just upstream of the sample so the beam is split into hundreds or thousands of foci of a few hundred (or tens of) nanometres, spaced by several micrometres — far enough apart that each beamlet's transmitted/scattered/fluorescent signal falls on its own separate group of detector pixels and can be demultiplexed. The sample is then translated over only **one grating period** in fine sub‑beamlet steps; every beamlet simultaneously maps its own small sub‑field, and the sub‑maps are stitched into one image whose point‑spread function is the **beamlet size**, not the detector pixel pitch, scintillator blur or full‑field optic.

Why this raises real resolution: (i) the resolution is set by the array's nanofabricated focal spot size and the stage step, so an ordinary micrometre‑pixel camera (or an energy‑dispersive detector array) delivers sub‑micrometre/100‑nm imaging; (ii) the scan is shortened by the number of beamlets (N‑fold parallelisation), so drift, thermal excursions and sample evolution during acquisition — usually the real practical resolution limit in long nanoprobe scans — are reduced by the same factor, and the dose can be spread rather than concentrated; and (iii) because each beamlet is a small, well‑characterised probe, its measured profile can be deconvolved from the sub‑map for a further factor of ~2.

Practical requirements: choose the array period so beamlets are cleanly separated at the detector (and use a matched order‑sorting aperture/central stop to remove the un‑focused background); place the sample at the fractional Talbot plane where the foci are sharpest, holding this distance to within the (short) depth of focus with a stiff, thermally stabilised mount; calibrate each beamlet's position, intensity and profile in situ (empty‑beam frame plus a knife‑edge/Siemens‑star or ptychographic probe retrieval), since beamlet‑to‑beamlet intensity and shape variations otherwise imprint a periodic artefact; use closed‑loop piezo scanning with repeatability well below the step size, per‑frame I₀ normalisation, and sufficient monochromaticity for the diffractive array to form clean foci. Extended to tomography, the one‑period scan is simply repeated at each rotation angle, giving probe‑limited 3‑D resolution over a large field of view at a small fraction of the usual scan time.

**Image the emitted (fluorescence) photons through a coded‑aperture / pinhole camera instead of scanning a focused probe — i.e. do full‑field X‑ray fluorescence emission imaging in which a mask, not the beam spot, defines the resolution.**

Flood‑illuminate the specimen with a broad, unfocused (or line‑shaped) monochromatic beam tuned above the K/L edge of the element of interest, and place between the sample and an energy‑resolving pixel‑array detector (e.g. a Timepix/pnCCD‑type CdTe or SDD‑array camera) either a small high‑Z pinhole or, much better, a lithographed high‑Z coded aperture (MURA/uniformly‑redundant array, hole size well below the detector pixel pitch and thick enough to be opaque at the fluorescence energy). Each emitting point in the sample casts a shifted copy of the mask pattern on the detector; deconvolving the recorded, energy‑gated image with the known mask autocorrelation (or solving it as a regularised/compressed‑sensing inverse problem) reconstructs the elemental distribution.

Why this raises resolution: the point‑spread function is set by the **aperture size divided by the geometric magnification (mask–detector / sample–mask distance)**, i.e. by nanofabrication and mounting geometry — not by the focal‑spot size of the KB/zone‑plate optic, not by the scan step, and not by the detector pixel pitch (which is divided by the magnification). A 2–5 µm mask feature at 20–50× magnification therefore yields sub‑micrometre elemental resolution with a coarse‑pixel detector and no nanofocusing optic at all. The coded mask further transmits ~50 % of the emitted photons rather than the tiny fraction a single pinhole would, so the multiplex advantage buys orders of magnitude in signal over pinhole imaging, and because the whole field is recorded in parallel there is no serial raster: acquisition times drop from hours to seconds, which removes the stage drift, vibration and beam‑decay blur that usually degrade long scanning‑nanoprobe maps, and spreads the dose over the whole sample instead of concentrating it in a nanofocus. Energy gating on each fluorescence line gives simultaneous, intrinsically registered maps of several elements, and 3‑D information follows either from rotating the sample (emission tomography) or from depth‑dependent parallax between two masks/detector positions.

Practical requirements: the mask must be several absorption lengths thick at the fluorescence energy yet have low‑aspect‑ratio, accurately placed holes (electroformed Au/W or FIB‑milled Ta), rigidly and thermally stably mounted with its position calibrated to a fraction of a hole width; the detector must have good energy resolution and per‑pixel gain/charge‑sharing calibration so scattered elastic/Compton photons and neighbouring lines are rejected before decoding; the near‑field (rather than far‑field) decoding kernel must be used and the depth‑dependent magnification accounted for in thick samples; self‑absorption of the fluorescence inside the specimen must be corrected using an attenuation map from a companion transmission scan; and the incident flux and any parasitic background must be normalised per frame, since coded‑aperture decoding is a difference operation and is sensitive to non‑uniform background. The result is element‑specific imaging whose resolution is limited by mask fabrication and geometry rather than by the X‑ray focusing optic, obtained with no nanoprobe, no scanning stage and an ordinary large‑pixel detector.

**Close a laser‑interferometric metrology loop around the sample–optic pair and correct position errors in real time, so the instrument's mechanical stability — not just its optics — reaches the nanometre level.**

At the ~10–100 nm scale the resolution actually delivered by a nano‑tomography or nanoprobe instrument is usually set by the *relative* motion between the focusing optic (KB mirror, zone plate, MLL) or detector and the specimen during the scan: stage runout and "sphere of confusion" of the rotation axis, piezo hysteresis and creep, floor and cooling‑water vibration, acoustic pickup, and slow thermal expansion of the support structure. These add up to tens or hundreds of nanometres over the minutes to hours of a scan and blur every projection, so the nominal probe size or voxel size is never realised.

The fix is to build (or retrofit) the end‑station as a metrology instrument rather than a stack of stages: keep the **metrology loop short and stiff** — mount optic and sample on the same monolithic granite/Zerodur or Invar block, with the rotation and scanning stages as close together and as few in number as possible; use **air‑bearing or flexure stages with low runout**; and, crucially, add **multi‑axis heterodyne laser interferometers (or capacitive/fibre sensors) that measure the sample position directly against a reference mirror rigidly attached to the X‑ray optic**, in all relevant degrees of freedom including the rotation axis. Feed these signals into a **kHz‑bandwidth closed‑loop controller driving piezo actuators** on the sample stage (and/or fast steering of the beam), so that drift, vibration and axis wobble are actively cancelled *while* the data are being taken rather than being corrected — imperfectly — afterwards. Complement this with passive/active vibration isolation, temperature stabilisation of the hutch to ~0.01 K, removal of turbulent air and vibrating coolant lines from the loop, and logging of the interferometer readings so that any residual excursions can be used for exact per‑frame position assignment (and for rejecting frames taken during a transient).

Because every scan point or projection is then referenced to a position known and held to a few nanometres, the point‑spread function collapses to that of the optics/detector alone; scanning steps and voxel sizes far below the previous "practical" limit become meaningful, long high‑statistics scans and fine angular sampling no longer smear the data, and ptychographic/tomographic reconstructions converge to their true diffraction‑ or sampling‑limited resolution. This is precisely the change that took hard X‑ray nanoprobes from ~100 nm to sub‑20 nm performance, and it requires no new source, optic, detector or sample preparation — only instrument engineering and position feedback.

**Reconstruct the object as a continuous "implicit neural field" fitted directly to the raw projections, instead of as a discrete voxel grid.**

Rather than binning the data onto a fixed Cartesian voxel array (where every gridding/interpolation step in FBP or gridrec acts as an extra low‑pass filter and each voxel value is an average over a finite cube), represent the 3‑D refractive‑index/attenuation distribution as a smooth, coordinate‑based function f(x,y,z) encoded by a small neural network with Fourier/hash positional encodings. The network is optimised in a self‑supervised way (no training pairs, no external ground truth) by differentiable ray‑tracing: for every measured projection, rays are integrated analytically through the continuous field, blurred by the *measured* detector/scintillator PSF, source penumbra and — where relevant — Fresnel propagation, and compared with the recorded intensity under a Poisson likelihood; gradients update the network weights.

Why this yields genuinely finer resolution:

- **No discretisation or interpolation blur.** Rays are sampled at arbitrary, non‑grid positions, so information that falls between pixels/voxels (from off‑centre rotation axes, irregular angular spacing, drift, or continuous fly‑scans) is used exactly rather than being smeared onto the nearest grid point. The final volume can be *queried* on any grid, including one several times finer than the detector pixel projection, and the extra sampling is meaningful because the fit was never restricted to the coarse grid.
- **Self‑calibration of geometry and motion.** Centre of rotation, detector tilt/roll, magnification and a per‑projection rigid (or even non‑rigid) displacement are made free parameters of the same differentiable model and refined simultaneously with the object, so stage runout, thermal drift and sub‑pixel misregistration — which normally dominate the practical resolution limit in long scans — are absorbed instead of blurring the reconstruction.
- **A strong but generic continuity prior.** The network's smooth, multi‑scale parameterisation acts as an implicit regulariser that suppresses streaks and noise without the apodisation normally needed to tame the ramp filter, so the reconstruction can be pushed to (and, with the PSF deconvolution built into the forward model, slightly beyond) the sampling limit even from sparse‑angle, short‑exposure or missing‑wedge data — which in turn allows fewer projections and less dose, further reducing damage‑ and drift‑induced blur in beam‑sensitive or in‑situ specimens.

Practical requirements: a GPU implementation with automatic differentiation and mini‑batching over rays/angles; an accurate, independently measured PSF/MTF and noise model in the forward operator, so recovered high frequencies come from the data and not from the network prior; initialisation from a conventional FBP reconstruction to speed convergence; hold‑out projections for cross‑validation to set the encoding bandwidth/regularisation strength (an over‑expressive field can hallucinate detail); and objective verification of the resolution actually achieved by Fourier shell correlation between two independently fitted half‑datasets, plus comparison with a high‑magnification scan of a sub‑region.

The gain — typically a factor of about two in true resolvable feature size, plus near‑isotropic voxels and artefact‑free interiors — costs nothing in dose, beamtime, optics, source brightness or sample preparation: only the change of representation and reconstruction code.

**Put a wavefront‑coding (cubic‑phase) mask into the visible‑light relay of the indirect detector, so a high‑NA objective can be used with a thick, efficient scintillator without depth‑of‑field blur.**

In a scintillator‑based imaging detector the resolution/efficiency trade‑off is set by depth of field: a high‑numerical‑aperture objective (needed for a small effective pixel and a sharp PSF) has a depth of focus of only a micrometre or two, so light emitted at different depths in the crystal is defocused by different amounts. One is therefore forced to use a scintillator only a few micrometres thick, which absorbs a small fraction of the beam, giving noisy projections, long exposures and hence drift/motion blur — or to accept a badly broadened, depth‑averaged PSF.

Wavefront coding breaks this trade‑off. Insert a cubic (or logarithmic/free‑form) phase plate in the pupil of the microscope objective that images the scintillator. The resulting optical point‑spread function is deliberately blurred, but — crucially — it becomes **essentially invariant with defocus over a range ten to twenty times the natural depth of focus**, and its optical transfer function has no zeros. Every emission depth in the crystal is therefore encoded with the *same*, known kernel, which can be removed in a single, well‑conditioned deconvolution (measured in situ from a knife‑edge/Siemens‑star or sub‑resolution particle target, inverted with a regularised Wiener/Richardson–Lucy step, or included in the forward model of an iterative tomographic reconstruction).

The consequences are: (i) a scintillator ten or more times thicker (or a stack/tilted crystal) can be used with a high‑NA objective, so the detective quantum efficiency rises by an order of magnitude while the restored PSF stays at the diffraction limit of the objective rather than being set by the crystal thickness; (ii) the detector becomes insensitive to focus drift — thermal expansion of the objective mount, crystal bowing under heat load and small refocusing errors, which in a conventional high‑NA detector silently double the blur during a long scan, now leave the PSF unchanged and hence fully invertible; and (iii) because far fewer photons are wasted, exposures shorten and drift, vibration and radiation dose per projection drop, so the finer sampling actually converts into real resolution.

Practical requirements: fabricate/align the phase mask accurately in the objective's back focal plane (decentring makes the PSF asymmetric and depth‑dependent again); use a narrow emission filter matched to the scintillator line so the coded PSF is quasi‑monochromatic and stable; calibrate the coded PSF at several crystal depths to confirm depth invariance; and use a noise‑aware, regularised deconvolution (the coded transfer function is low but never zero, so noise amplification, not lost frequencies, is the only cost). No change to the source, X‑ray optics, sample preparation or scan protocol is needed — only the optical relay of the camera and one extra deconvolution step.

**Use "magnification diversity" super‑resolution: record the same object at several slightly different geometric magnifications and invert all of them jointly onto one fine grid.**

In a divergent (point‑projection/cone‑beam) geometry the effective pixel size projected back into the sample is p/M, with M = (source–detector)/(source–sample). Instead of picking one magnification and living with its Nyquist limit, acquire the tomogram (or projection series) at a small set of magnifications — e.g. move the sample a few per cent along the beam between scans, or step the detector, so that M changes by incommensurate amounts (M, 1.03M, 1.07M, 1.11M …). Each setting samples the object on a *differently scaled* pixel lattice, so a given object feature falls at a different sub‑pixel phase in every dataset; the aliased high‑frequency content folds back differently in each, and the union of the datasets contains information well beyond the Nyquist frequency of any single one.

Reconstruct them not separately (which would just average) but in a single model‑based/iterative inversion in which the forward model contains, for each dataset, its own exact magnification, the measured scintillator/optical PSF and source penumbral blur (which also scales with M), the geometry (centre of rotation, detector tilt) and Poisson noise statistics; the unknown is one continuous object sampled on a grid several times finer than p/M_max. Because the sampling grids are mutually incommensurate, the combined system is well conditioned and the de‑aliasing plus PSF deconvolution can be done stably, typically buying a factor of ~2–3 in genuinely resolvable feature size. The scheme is self‑calibrating: the relative magnifications, lateral shifts and drift are refined as free parameters by maximising the consistency/sharpness of the joint reconstruction, so they need not be known a priori to sub‑pixel accuracy.

Practical points: keep the total dose constant by splitting it over the magnification settings rather than adding scans; choose magnification steps that are *not* simple rational ratios (otherwise the lattices coincide and no new information is gained); ensure the sample is mechanically and radiation‑stable between settings (or use fiducials/digital volume correlation to register and, if needed, warp between them); re‑take flat fields at each position since the illumination footprint and penumbra change; and verify the gain objectively by Fourier shell correlation between two independently reconstructed half‑datasets rather than by appearance. The low‑magnification member of the set also provides the untruncated "outside" context that stabilises the interior problem if the high‑magnification scans are locally truncated. No new source, optic, detector or sample preparation is required — only a stage move between scans and a reconstruction code that knows the geometry of each dataset.

Adopt **near‑field (holographic) ptychography with a structured wavefront**: place a random phase modulator (a diffuser such as sandpaper, a nanoparticle/metal‑powder film, or a lithographed random phase plate) in the beam so the illumination reaching the sample is a fully known but highly structured, speckled wavefront with features finer than the detector's point‑spread function; then translate the sample laterally through this illumination in a set of overlapping (typically random, non‑periodic) positions at a short propagation distance, and record the resulting near‑field holograms.

Reconstruct with a **near‑field (Fresnel) ptychographic algorithm** that solves simultaneously for the complex object and the complex probe: because the structured probe imprints a fine, known carrier onto the object's information and each sample shift re‑encodes it differently, the high spatial frequencies that the detector could not sample directly are folded into the recorded intensity and can be recovered by the iterative inversion. The reconstruction is therefore limited by the speckle grain size, the probe knowledge and the scan‑position accuracy rather than by the pixel pitch or scintillator blur — typically a several‑fold gain in resolvable feature size — while, unlike far‑field ptychography, the whole illuminated field of view is imaged at once, so only a handful of positions (rather than thousands of fine scan points) are needed, giving short scans, low dose and full quantitative phase.

Practical requirements: choose the diffuser so its speckle size at the sample is of order the detector resolution and its phase excursion is ~1 rad; keep the propagation distance in the near‑field regime (Fresnel number ≫ 1 for the field of view but ≲ 1 for the speckle grains) so the modulation is well resolved; use ≥60 % overlap with random shifts to avoid raster‑grid artefacts; refine scan positions, propagation distance, magnification and drift as free parameters in the reconstruction, and include mixed (multi‑mode) probe states plus per‑frame flux normalisation to absorb partial coherence and beam instability; verify the achieved resolution by Fourier ring correlation of independently reconstructed half‑datasets. For tomography, simply repeat the small position set at each rotation angle. No new optic, smaller pixels or brighter source are needed — only a cheap diffuser and a near‑field phase‑retrieval code.

Bring in an independent, higher‑resolution imaging modality as a correlative "ruler and prior" for the synchrotron data: after (or before) the X‑ray scan, image the very same region of the same specimen destructively at much finer resolution — e.g. Xe‑plasma/Ga FIB‑SEM serial sectioning, SEM/TEM of ultramicrotome sections, or laboratory electron tomography — and use that ground truth to sharpen the X‑ray reconstruction.
