Practically: (i) mark the region of interest with fiducials (FIB‑milled marks, implanted nanoparticles) so the destructive dataset can be registered to the tomogram to sub‑voxel precision by 3‑D image correlation, refining relative scale, rotation and any non‑rigid distortion; (ii) forward‑simulate ("blur") the electron‑microscopy volume through the X‑ray forward model and compare it with the measured tomogram — the difference directly yields the *true, in‑situ* point‑spread/modulation transfer function of that particular dataset (including scintillator halo, source penumbra, drift and reconstruction filtering), which can then be deconvolved from the projections instead of relying on nominal catalogue values; (iii) use the fine data as a quantitative prior for a model‑based/learned restoration — it supplies realistic statistics of the sub‑voxel structure (wall thicknesses, pore/particle size distributions, interface sharpness, grey‑level histograms of the discrete phases) and paired low/high‑resolution training volumes registered to real, not simulated, data, so the restoration recovers frequencies beyond the nominal Nyquist limit without hallucinating; and (iv) crucially, it gives an *independent* validation of what resolution the enhanced reconstruction actually achieves, region by region, rather than only an FRC self‑estimate.

The pay‑off is that the non‑destructive, large‑volume, time‑resolvable synchrotron dataset inherits much of the resolving power of the destructive technique on the same material — typically a several‑fold gain in effective resolvable feature size and in segmentation accuracy — while the correlative sample is consumed only once, on a small sacrificial sub‑volume. Requirements: the specimen must survive both workflows (embed/stabilise it, do the X‑ray scan first since FIB milling is destructive), the sectioning must not introduce curtaining/shrinkage artefacts that would be mistaken for structure, and the prior must be applied with cross‑validation (withheld regions) so that detail is data‑driven rather than transferred from the electron images. No change to the source, optics, detector or scan protocol is needed.

Split the visible light from the scintillator with a beamsplitter (or a set of them) and image the *same* luminescent screen simultaneously with two or four identical cameras whose sensors are deliberately mounted with a lateral offset of half a pixel (and, for the four‑camera version, half a pixel in both x and y, plus a small relative roll). Every camera then samples the identical X‑ray projection on an interleaved sub‑pixel grid, so merging the frames yields a projection sampled at twice (or four times) the physical Nyquist rate, after which the measured scintillator/optics PSF can be deconvolved and the reconstruction filter pushed to the new, finer sampling limit.

The key advantage over moving the sample or detector between exposures is simultaneity: because all sensors see the same photons at the same instant, there is no drift, vibration, beam decay or sample evolution between the sub‑pixel samples, so the trick works for fast fly‑scans and dynamic in‑situ experiments where sequential dithering fails, and it costs no extra dose or exposure time. Practically, one calibrates the relative offsets, rotations and magnifications of the cameras to a small fraction of a pixel using a Siemens‑star or fiducial target and refines them from the data itself, flat‑fields and gain‑matches each sensor separately (the beamsplitter ratios differ), keeps the optical path lengths equal so all cameras stay focused on the same plane of the crystal, and merges the frames with a model‑based (rather than naïve interpolating) inversion that includes each camera's own PSF and noise. The result is roughly a factor‑of‑two gain in true resolvable feature size using the existing source, X‑ray optics, scintillator and scan protocol — only the light relay and the merging step change.

Build an **achromatic X‑ray objective by combining a diffractive and a refractive element into a "doublet"** — i.e. put a Fresnel zone plate (or MLL) in series with a refractive lens (CRL/kinoform) of opposite dispersion, so the strong chromatic aberration of the diffractive optic (f ∝ 1/λ) is cancelled by that of the refractive optic (f ∝ 1/λ²) over a chosen band.

Why this improves resolution: a zone plate only reaches its diffraction limit (δ ≈ 1.22 Δr_N) if ΔE/E < 1/N, so a high‑zone‑count, high‑NA lens forces you to a very narrow bandwidth and therefore to a photon‑starved beam — the practical resolution then collapses back to a dose/noise or drift limit rather than the design limit, and the focus is radially smeared whenever a wider bandwidth is used. With the chromatic focal shift corrected to first (and, with a third element, second) order, the same optic keeps a diffraction‑limited focal spot/PSF over a bandwidth of ΔE/E ~10⁻² instead of 10⁻⁴–10⁻⁵. One can then run with a multilayer or "pink" beam, gaining two to three orders of magnitude in flux: exposures and scan times shrink dramatically, so drift, vibration and beam‑instability blur — usually the real limiter in long nanoprobe/TXM/tomographic scans — largely disappear, the finer sampling actually converts into signal rather than noise, and spectroscopic (XANES) imaging can be done across an absorption edge without refocusing or losing resolution.

Practical points: match the refractive element's material (low‑Z, radiation‑hard Si, diamond, SU‑8 written by two‑photon lithography) and lenslet count so its dispersion exactly cancels the zone plate's over the working band; mount both on a common piezo hexapod with a short, stiff, thermally stabilised metrology loop and align their optical axes to a fraction of the outer zone width; keep a matched central stop, order‑sorting aperture and guard slits so undiffracted and higher orders don't fog the image; account for the residual absorption of the refractive element in the flux budget; and verify the achieved band‑integrated PSF at‑wavelength with a Siemens‑star/knife‑edge scan or ptychographic probe retrieval at several energies across the band, deconvolving any residual chromatic tail before reconstruction.

**Turn the high‑NA objective's shallow depth of focus from a liability into a resolution tool: acquire a through‑focus (focal‑series) image stack in a full‑field transmission X‑ray microscope and invert it with a measured three‑dimensional optical transfer function ("X‑ray optical‑sectioning / 3‑D deconvolution microscopy").**

Instead of recording one image at nominal focus (where everything outside the ±(λ/NA²) focal slab contributes an out‑of‑focus haze that flattens the contrast transfer and hides fine detail), step the sample — or the objective — axially in increments of about half the depth of focus through the whole specimen thickness, recording an image at each position. Each plane of the object appears sharp in one frame and progressively defocused in the others, so the stack is the object convolved with the *three‑dimensional* PSF of the microscope. Measuring that PSF at‑wavelength (image a sub‑resolution gold nanoparticle, or retrieve the objective's pupil/aberrations ptychographically, then propagate it numerically) and inverting the stack with a regularised, Poisson‑aware 3‑D deconvolution (Richardson–Lucy or a model‑based/TV‑regularised solver) simultaneously (i) removes the out‑of‑focus background, so lateral contrast at high spatial frequencies is restored right up to the objective's diffraction limit rather than being washed out by haze, and (ii) fills in part of the "missing cone" of the 3‑D OTF, delivering genuine optical‑sectioning depth resolution of the order of λ/NA² **without any sample rotation** — an enormous advantage for flat, laterally extended or truncated specimens (wafers, films, in‑situ cells, sections) that cannot be turned through 180°, and for fast in‑situ work where a full tomographic scan is impossible.

Because out‑of‑focus material is now modelled rather than tolerated, the microscope can be run at its *full* numerical aperture on specimens several times thicker than the depth of focus, instead of being forced to a lower NA (and hence coarser resolution) just to keep the whole object in focus.

Practical requirements: an axial stage with repeatability well below the focus step (closed‑loop piezo, with drift and lateral run‑out tracked by fiducials and corrected to sub‑pixel accuracy between frames, since a focal series is only as good as its registration); a defocus range extending beyond both faces of the object so the deconvolution is well posed; measurement of the true, possibly aberrated and slightly asymmetric 3‑D PSF (a nominal Gaussian/analytic kernel will generate artefacts); constant illumination between frames with per‑frame I₀ normalisation, since the inversion is difference‑based; dose fractionation over the stack so the total dose is no higher than a single long exposure; and objective validation of the achieved lateral and axial resolution by Fourier ring/shell correlation between two independently acquired half‑stacks, to confirm the recovered frequencies are data‑driven and not regulariser‑generated. If a few coarse rotation angles can be added, feeding the focal series from each into the same 3‑D forward model closes the missing cone almost completely and yields near‑isotropic resolution from a handful of views.

No new source, optic, detector or sample preparation is needed — only an axial scan and a 3‑D deconvolution step.

Use a **light‑sheet (selective‑plane) illumination geometry with orthogonal detection**: instead of flooding the whole specimen and relying on the imaging optics to give depth resolution, shape the synchrotron beam with a 1‑D focusing optic (a single KB/cylindrical mirror, a linear CRL stack, or crossed slits at a line focus) into a thin, wide "sheet" — sub‑micrometre thick in one direction but hundreds of micrometres wide — and view the excited plane at 90° to the sheet with a camera (an energy‑resolving pixel detector for X‑ray fluorescence, or a high‑NA visible objective + sCMOS for X‑ray‑excited optical luminescence from doped/labelled regions).

Because only the material lying inside the sheet emits, the depth (along the viewing axis) resolution is set by the *sheet thickness and its Rayleigh range*, not by the detector pixel size, scintillator blur, collection optic NA, or by any tomographic rotation — and the in‑plane resolution is set by the detection optics as usual. Stepping the sample through the sheet therefore builds a true 3‑D, optically sectioned volume with no rotation, so rotation‑axis wobble, missing‑wedge and self‑absorption‑along‑the‑projection‑path artefacts, which normally dominate the axial blur, disappear entirely. The whole illuminated plane is recorded in parallel rather than point‑by‑point, so acquisition is orders of magnitude faster than a scanning nanoprobe map: drift, vibration and beam‑decay blur during the scan are correspondingly reduced, and the dose is spread over a plane rather than concentrated in a focal spot, allowing more photons (and hence finer sampling) before radiation damage sets in.

Practically: choose the sheet's numerical aperture so that its confocal (Rayleigh) length matches the field of view — or use a "tiled"/axially‑swept sheet, or a Bessel‑beam sheet with deconvolution of its side lobes, to keep the sheet thin across the whole width; align the detection focal plane to the sheet plane to a fraction of the sheet thickness and re‑check it at every z step; calibrate the sheet's intensity profile in situ (scan a sharp edge or a thin fluorescent film through it) and deconvolve this measured axial PSF from the stack; correct for absorption of both the incident sheet and the emitted signal using a companion transmission scan; and use per‑frame I₀ normalisation plus fiducials for sub‑voxel registration of the z‑stack. The gain in axial resolution and in speed is obtained purely by re‑shaping the illumination and re‑arranging the detection geometry, with no new high‑resolution X‑ray optic, no smaller detector pixels and no change to the source.

**Eliminate beam‑induced thermal drift and deformation *inside the specimen itself* by engineering its heat (and charge) sink.**

At the 10–100 nm level, a very common — and usually unrecognised — resolution limiter is that the absorbed X‑ray power heats the sample: a micro‑pillar or thin section sitting on a poorly conducting glue blob, a plastic pin or an insulating capillary can rise by many kelvin within seconds of the shutter opening, and the resulting thermal expansion (plus insulator charging in vacuum, and creep of the adhesive) makes the specimen swell, bend and walk by tens or hundreds of nanometres over the minutes of a scan. Because the drift is *internal to the sample*, no rotation‑stage interferometry, beam‑position feedback or rigid‑body image registration can remove it — the object genuinely changes shape between projections, so edges are smeared and the reconstruction ends up several times blurrier than its voxel size.

The fix is thermal/electrical design of the mount: bond the specimen with a thin, high‑conductivity path (silver‑ or carbon‑loaded epoxy, indium, or FIB‑deposited Pt) directly onto a metal (Cu, Al, sapphire or diamond) pin/stub rather than onto polymer; keep the illuminated volume small and close to that heat sink (short pillars, thin sections); sputter a few‑nanometre conductive coat (C, Au, Pt) on insulating or biological/polymer samples to drain charge and to radiate/conduct heat; run the sample environment in flowing helium (or with a cold He jet/Peltier‑stabilised holder) instead of vacuum or still air, so convective/conductive cooling is orders of magnitude better; attenuate or spread the incident power to the minimum needed (or chop/duty‑cycle the beam and interleave angles) so the average heat load is low even though the per‑frame statistics stay high; and — crucially — let the sample come to *steady state* by pre‑illuminating it for a minute or two before starting the scan, so the fast thermal transient is over before data are recorded.

Practically, verify the improvement by imaging the same sub‑region at the start and end of a scan and measuring the residual expansion/displacement field with digital volume correlation (or by tracking a couple of high‑Z fiducials glued to the specimen); a well‑sunk, coated, He‑cooled mount should show sub‑voxel change, whereas a polymer‑mounted sample in vacuum will typically show many‑voxel creep. If a residual, reproducible expansion remains, it can be measured and included as a slow deformation field in a motion‑compensated reconstruction.

This costs nothing in dose, beamtime, source brightness, optics or detector — only in how the specimen is prepared and mounted — yet it routinely recovers a factor of two or more in genuinely resolvable feature size in long, high‑magnification scans.

Increase the number of independent resolution elements across the image by replacing the camera with a much larger‑format, higher‑pixel‑count sensor (or by tiling/butting several sensors into one seamless array), rather than by changing the X‑ray optics or the magnification.

The resolution of a projection or tomogram is ultimately the field of view divided by the number of usable sampling points, so a detector with, say, 8k×8k rather than 2k×2k pixels — or four 4k sensors abutted with a small overlap — quadruples the linear sampling of the same specimen at the same magnification and working distance. This decouples "how much of the sample I can see" from "how finely I can see it", which is normally the hardest compromise in synchrotron imaging: it avoids the need to cut the sample down, to stitch many high‑magnification tiles (with their registration and truncation problems), or to accept local/interior tomography artefacts, and it keeps the long working distance needed for furnaces, load frames and flow cells.

Practical implementation: use large fibre‑optic‑taper or lens‑coupled sCMOS arrays, or tiled photon‑counting modules mounted on a common, thermally stabilised, planar frame whose module positions, gaps, rotations and relative gains are calibrated to a fraction of a pixel with a Siemens‑star/grid target and refined from the data; interpolate or physically dither the array by one module gap between half‑scans so that inter‑module dead regions do not produce persistent ring/stripe artefacts; match the effective pixel size to the optical/scintillator point‑spread function so the new sampling is genuinely Nyquist‑matched rather than empty magnification (thin the scintillator and raise the relay NA accordingly); and provide the readout bandwidth, on‑the‑fly compression and GPU reconstruction capacity for the correspondingly larger datasets, plus a brighter beam or slightly longer exposures to keep photon statistics per (now smaller) pixel adequate.

The gain scales directly with the pixel count — typically a factor of two to four in resolvable feature size over the full specimen — and requires no new X‑ray optic, no change to source, sample preparation or scan geometry, only a bigger detector and its calibration.

**Turn the diffractive optic's chromatic aberration into a depth‑resolving tool ("chromatic/spectral focal sectioning").**

A Fresnel zone plate (or MLL/CRL) has a focal length that varies with photon energy (f ∝ E for a zone plate). Normally this is treated as a defect and suppressed with a very narrow bandwidth, which starves the microscope of flux. Instead, deliberately illuminate the zone‑plate objective (or nanoprobe) with a *broad‑bandpass* multilayer/"pink" beam chosen so that the focal length sweeps continuously across the full thickness of the specimen, and record the signal with an **energy‑resolving photon‑counting detector** (CdTe/Si Timepix‑ or pnCCD‑type, or an SDD in scanning mode) — or, equivalently, step the monochromator through the band without moving anything mechanically.

Because each photon energy is focused at a different, precisely known depth, sorting the detected photons into narrow energy bins directly yields a *stack of optical sections*: every bin is an image (or scanning map) in which one plane of the sample sits at the lens's true diffraction‑limited focus, while the rest is defocused in a fully calculable way. A single acquisition therefore delivers a depth‑resolved volume with the full lateral resolution of the optic and an axial sectioning set by the energy resolution and the numerical aperture (Δz ≈ f·ΔE/E, and ultimately λ/NA²) — **without any axial scanning, without sample rotation, and without the focus drift, vibration and registration errors that ruin a sequential through‑focus stack.** It simultaneously removes the flux penalty of high monochromaticity, so exposures are far shorter and drift/motion blur correspondingly smaller, and it is inherently immune to defocus drift of the stage because the depth coordinate is encoded in photon energy rather than in stage position.

Practical requirements: calibrate f(E) at‑wavelength (Siemens‑star or nanoparticle target at several energies) and measure the full 3‑D chromatic PSF, then invert the energy‑binned stack with a regularised 3‑D deconvolution that models the wavelength‑dependent PSF, the energy‑dependent contrast (δ, β vary across the band — avoid absorption edges of the specimen, or model the anomalous dispersion explicitly), and the detector's per‑pixel energy calibration and charge sharing; use a matched central stop and order‑sorting aperture sized for the whole band so that undiffracted and higher orders do not fog the sections; keep the count rate below pile‑up; and validate the achieved axial and lateral resolution by Fourier ring/shell correlation between two independently binned half‑datasets. Adding just a few coarse rotation angles closes the residual missing cone and yields near‑isotropic 3‑D resolution from a handful of views — all with the existing optic, detector and sample, changing only the bandwidth and the way the photons are sorted.

**Use a narrow ribbon ("section") beam together with dynamical‑diffraction (Borrmann‑fan) encoding — i.e. do X‑ray section topography — so that depth inside a crystal is mapped onto position on the detector instead of being limited by any optic.**

Instead of flooding the crystal (traverse topography), collimate the monochromatic beam with a slit into a ribbon only a few micrometres wide and let it enter the specimen at the Bragg condition. Inside a thick, near‑perfect crystal the incident ribbon fans out into the Borrmann triangle, and the wavefields that leave the exit surface at different lateral positions correspond one‑to‑one, through dynamical diffraction theory, to the depths at which they propagated. Every point of the recorded section topograph therefore carries a *known* depth label: a defect (dislocation, precipitate, growth striation, strain field) intersecting the ribbon shows up as a characteristic interference "direct/dynamical/intermediary" image whose position and fringe pattern fix its depth to a micrometre or better, even though the crystal is hundreds of micrometres thick and no image‑forming optic is used at all. Stepping the ribbon across the sample (and repeating for several reflections/azimuths) then builds a genuinely three‑dimensional defect map.

Why this beats the usual resolution budget: the limiting quantity is the slit width, the crystal's extinction length and the accuracy of the dynamical‑theory forward model — not the focal‑spot size, zone‑plate zone width, scintillator blur or camera pixel pitch — and the strain sensitivity of dynamical diffraction (Δd/d ~10⁻⁷–10⁻⁸) makes lattice distortions visible that are far too weak for attenuation or even phase contrast. Because only a thin slice is illuminated, sample‑generated scatter and the projection overlap that ruins traverse topographs are eliminated, so contrast transfer stays high right up to the detector's sampling limit.

Practical requirements: a highly monochromatic, well‑collimated beam matched to the Darwin width (ΔE/E ≲10⁻⁴, divergence ≪ the Darwin width, otherwise the fan is smeared and the depth encoding collapses); a slit with clean, sub‑micrometre edges mounted rigidly and thermally stabilised close to the sample; a high‑resolution detector (thin scintillator + high‑NA objective, or a nuclear emulsion/resist read out afterwards) with an effective pixel well below the fringe spacing; sub‑micrometre, drift‑free translation of the sample across the ribbon with encoder feedback; and simulation‑based analysis (Takagi–Taupin integration of the distorted‑crystal equations) to invert the measured fringe patterns into depths, defect types and strain fields rather than interpreting the topograph directly. The trade‑offs are that it applies only to near‑perfect single crystals and that a full 3‑D map requires many ribbon positions and reflections — but where it applies it converts an optics‑limited measurement into a diffraction‑physics‑limited one and delivers micrometre depth resolution with picometre‑level strain sensitivity using no high‑resolution X‑ray optic whatsoever.

Thin the specimen **along the beam direction** so that its thickness is smaller than the depth of focus of the imaging system, i.e. t < ~2δ²/λ for the target resolution δ (for example ~1 µm or less for 20 nm imaging at hard X‑ray energies). Prepare the sample as a FIB‑milled lamella/lift‑out, an ultramicrotome section, a cleaved thin flake or a laser‑machined slab mounted on a rigid low‑Z support, rather than imaging a bulk or needle‑shaped object.

The rationale is that at high numerical aperture (or high q in coherent imaging) the usable depth of focus shrinks quadratically with resolution, so in a thick object only one thin layer is ever in focus while everything above and below contributes defocused, out‑of‑plane signal; in addition, a thick object violates the projection (single‑scattering, weak‑object) approximation on which all standard phase retrieval and tomographic inversion rely, and it superimposes many overlapping features along each ray. All three effects — depth‑of‑field blur, multiple/dynamical scattering and feature superposition — degrade the measured contrast transfer at high spatial frequencies and are precisely what stops nano‑imaging from reaching the optic's or the detector's nominal limit. Making the object thinner also lowers absorption and self‑absorption (important for fluorescence), reduces small‑angle and Compton scatter haze, cuts the dose needed per resolution element, and allows a lower photon energy where contrast per absorbed photon is far higher.

Practically: choose the thickness from the target resolution and wavelength; use a low‑damage final FIB polish (low kV, or Xe‑plasma/Ar broad‑beam cleaning) so the surface amorphised/redeposited layer is much thinner than the target resolution; mount the lamella on a stiff, thermally conductive support (Cu/Si half‑grid or pillar) so it neither bends nor drifts during a long scan; if 3‑D information is needed, use laminography or a tilt series about an axis in the plane of the lamella and reconstruct with missing‑wedge‑aware iterative algorithms; and verify that the projection approximation now holds by checking that a multislice forward model gives no improvement over a single‑slice one. The gain requires no change to the source, optics, detector or reconstruction pipeline — only sample preparation matched to the depth of focus.

**Record the scintillator's emission as a light field (plenoptic detection) and refocus it computationally, so a thick, efficient screen can be used with a high‑NA objective without depth‑of‑field blur.**

Insert a precision microlens array at (or just before) the image plane of the visible‑light relay that views the luminescent screen, with the camera placed at the microlens focal plane. Each microlens then samples not only *where* the scintillation light originates but also *in which direction* it travels, i.e. the detector records the four‑dimensional light field rather than a single focal plane. Because the angular sub‑aperture images seen under each microlens shift laterally in proportion to the depth at which the X‑ray was absorbed in the crystal, the depth of interaction is encoded in the data and can be recovered in post‑processing: the sub‑aperture images are shifted and summed ("synthetic refocusing") to bring every depth plane of the scintillator into focus, and the correctly refocused contributions from all depths are then added coherently in the sense of intensity to form one sharp projection.

Why this raises real resolution: in an indirect detector one is normally forced to choose between a thin screen (sharp point‑spread function but poor stopping power, hence noisy frames, long exposures and drift/motion blur) and a thick screen (efficient but with the emission depth spread over many times the objective's depth of focus, which broadens the PSF and adds a wide halo). Light‑field detection removes this trade‑off — the blur from emission depth is *measured* and inverted instead of tolerated — so a screen ten or more times thicker can be used at full numerical aperture, raising the detective quantum efficiency by an order of magnitude while the restored PSF approaches the objective's diffraction limit. It simultaneously fixes two other systematic blurs: the depth‑of‑interaction parallax of obliquely incident rays away from the optical axis (each ray's true entrance position is recovered from its angular signature), and slow focus drift of the objective mount under heat load, since refocusing is now done numerically after the fact rather than mechanically before the scan.

Practical requirements: match the microlens pitch, f‑number and the objective's NA so that the sub‑aperture images just fill the space behind each lenslet without overlap (this sets the angular/spatial sampling trade‑off); calibrate the microlens grid position, rotation, pitch and the per‑lenslet vignetting to a fraction of a camera pixel using a Siemens‑star or fine grid target, and measure the depth‑dependent PSF by translating a thin fluorescent film or a sharp gold edge through the crystal; recover the final projection not by naive shift‑and‑add but by a regularised, Poisson‑aware 3‑D deconvolution of the calibrated light‑field forward model, which restores the lateral sampling that a plenoptic sensor nominally trades away; use a narrow emission filter matched to the scintillator's main line so the lenslet PSF is quasi‑monochromatic; and, if the raw angular sampling is too coarse, dither the microlens array (or the crystal) by sub‑lenslet steps between frames and interleave. Because it acts purely on the visible‑light relay, the gain — roughly a factor of two in sharpness together with a large gain in efficiency and hence in exposure time, drift and dose — requires no change to the source, X‑ray optics, sample preparation or scan protocol.

**Spectrally‑encode the spatial coordinate: use a dispersive optic to map photon energy onto lateral position on the sample, and read out the image with an energy‑resolving detector.**

Instead of defining resolution with a small focal spot or with fine detector pixels, illuminate the specimen with a broad‑band (pink/white) beam that has first been passed through a strongly dispersive element — a graded‑d‑spacing multilayer, an asymmetrically cut/bent crystal used in dispersive geometry, or a diffractive element whose diffraction angle varies steeply with wavelength. The optic focuses each photon energy to a *different* lateral position along a line on the sample, so the object coordinate x is encoded one‑to‑one in photon energy E(x). Every point of that line is then illuminated simultaneously, and a single energy‑dispersive detector (SDD, or an energy‑resolving photon‑counting/hyperspectral pixel sensor) records transmission, fluorescence or scattering as a function of E; sorting the counts by energy immediately decodes the whole line of the image in parallel.

The point‑spread function is now set by the *dispersion of the optic divided by the detector's energy resolution* (dx = (dx/dE)·ΔE), not by the focal‑spot size, the optic's numerical aperture, scintillator light spread or the camera pixel pitch — with a few‑eV‑resolution detector and a strongly dispersive element this corresponds to sub‑micrometre (and, with a microcalorimeter or a high‑dispersion crystal, potentially sub‑100 nm) sampling using no high‑resolution imaging optic at all. Because a whole line is measured at once rather than point‑by‑point, acquisition is orders of magnitude faster than a raster nanoprobe scan, so stage drift, vibration and beam decay — usually the real limit in long scans — contribute far less blur, and the dose is spread along the line instead of being concentrated in a nanofocus. Two‑dimensional and tomographic imaging follow by scanning the line perpendicular to the dispersion direction and rotating the sample.

Practical requirements: calibrate the energy‑to‑position map in situ (translate a sharp high‑Z edge or a fine test grid through the line and record which energies are attenuated) and re‑check it whenever the optic's temperature or alignment changes; choose the dispersion and the source bandwidth so the encoded line length matches the field of view while keeping the per‑point energy channel above the detector's resolution; correct for the strong energy dependence of the sample's attenuation/phase contrast and of the detector efficiency (measure an empty‑beam spectrum and normalise channel by channel, avoiding absorption edges of the specimen or modelling them explicitly); keep the count rate below pile‑up, since pile‑up mixes energies and therefore mixes *positions*; and finally deconvolve the measured spectral‑spatial kernel (the finite bandwidth of each channel convolved with the beam's local width) with a regularised, Poisson‑aware algorithm for a further factor of ~2. The trade‑off is that contrast becomes energy‑dependent along the encoded direction and the method needs a bright broadband source and a fast spectroscopic detector — but where these are available it converts an optics‑ and pixel‑limited measurement into one limited by spectral resolution and dispersion, with no nanofocusing optic, no fine scanning stage and no high‑resolution camera.

For crystalline specimens, use **Bragg ptychography (scanning coherent Bragg diffraction imaging) instead of a lens‑formed or single‑crystal‑illuminating measurement**: keep a chosen lattice reflection excited and raster a coherent, nano‑focused probe across the *extended* crystal in strongly overlapping steps (≳60 % overlap), recording at each position a full 3‑D reciprocal‑space volume by rocking the sample in fine angular steps through the Bragg peak with a photon‑counting pixel detector.

Because the redundant, overlapping far‑field data are inverted by iterative phase retrieval that simultaneously solves for the probe, the scan positions and the complex object, the resolution is no longer set by the focal‑spot size, the optic's aberrations, the scintillator blur or the pixel pitch — it is set only by the largest momentum transfer recorded around the Bragg peak (δ ≈ 2π/Δq_max) and by the positional stability of the scan. Improving it therefore reduces to well‑controlled steps: extend the angular/detector coverage around the reflection (move the detector closer, tile it, merge short and beam‑stopped exposures into high‑dynamic‑range frames so weak high‑q fringes rise above noise), increase the coherent flux, and refine positions/probe modes in the reconstruction. This routinely delivers sub‑10 nm 3‑D imaging with picometre‑scale lattice‑displacement sensitivity in *extended*, non‑isolated crystals (thin films, epitaxial layers, individual grains inside a polycrystal), where single‑shot Bragg CDI cannot be applied because the crystal is larger than the beam; measuring several non‑collinear reflections of the same region then yields the full strain tensor at that same nanometre resolution.

Practical requirements: a stiff, interferometrically referenced nanopositioning stage (position errors directly blur the reconstruction, though they can be refined as free parameters), fine monochromatisation and high transverse coherence so speckle contrast at high q survives, mixed‑state (multi‑mode) modelling to absorb partial coherence and vibration, and verification of the resolution actually reached by Fourier shell correlation between independently reconstructed half‑datasets.

**Proposed Experiment: "Reaction‑Coordinate Mapping" — Simultaneous laser‑pump/X‑ray‑probe XANES–XES–WAXS on a photocatalyst flowing through a turbulent micromixer**

**Idea.** Combine two normally separate time domains at one synchrotron beamline: (i) the *microsecond–second* chemistry of a bimolecular reaction, resolved by converting **position along a microfluidic channel into time** after rapid mixing, and (ii) the *picosecond–nanosecond* photo‑induced steps, resolved by conventional **laser‑pump/X‑ray‑probe** timing. Scanning the X‑ray microbeam along the channel while varying the pump–probe delay yields a two‑dimensional (t_mix, t_pump) movie of the same reacting system.

**System.** A molecular Co‑ or Fe‑based photocatalyst for CO₂ reduction (or H₂ evolution) mixed with a sacrificial donor/substrate solution in a chip‑based turbulent micromixer (mixing time < 100 µs), flowing at a controlled velocity so that 1 mm of channel ≈ 10 µs–1 ms of reaction time.

**Setup.**
- Undulator beamline in hybrid/single‑bunch mode; ~100 ps X‑ray pulses focused to ~5–20 µm and scanned along the channel.
- Synchronized high‑repetition‑rate (MHz) fs laser pump, with a mechanical chopper/pulse picker to isolate single X‑ray bunches; delay stage/electronic delay covering 100 ps → 1 ms.
- **Three detectors in parallel:** (1) energy‑dispersive or fast‑scanning **XANES/EXAFS** at the metal K‑edge (oxidation state, coordination geometry); (2) a von Hámos/Johann **X‑ray emission** spectrometer recording Kβ (spin state) and valence‑to‑core (ligand identity/protonation) lines; (3) a 2D detector for **wide‑ and small‑angle X‑ray scattering** (global structural/solvation changes). Optional simultaneous optical transient absorption for cross‑calibration.

**Measurement protocol.** For each channel position (i.e., each chemical "age" of the mixed reagents), record the full pump–probe delay series; repeat while titrating substrate concentration and pH. Flow continuously to refresh the sample and avoid photodamage/radiolysis; use a differential (laser‑on minus laser‑off) acquisition scheme.

**What it delivers.** A direct, element‑specific correlation between the transient electronic/spin state created by light (charge separation, metal‑to‑ligand charge transfer, ligand loss) and the *subsequent* catalytic intermediates formed on the mixing timescale (substrate binding, metal–hydride or metal–carboxylate formation, catalyst degradation). This resolves which short‑lived excited state actually feeds the productive catalytic cycle — information that neither pure ultrafast nor pure stopped‑flow experiments can supply.

**Novelty/impact.** Merges microfluidic space‑to‑time encoding with bunch‑resolved pump–probe X‑ray spectroscopy and scattering in a single, simultaneous multimodal acquisition, spanning ~10 decades of time (10⁻¹⁰–10⁻¹ s) on one sample. Analysis by machine‑learning/global‑fitting of the joint XANES–XES–WAXS dataset (validated against DFT/FEFF calculations) extracts intermediate spectra and kinetic pathways, providing structure–activity rules for rational photocatalyst design. The approach is directly transferable to enzyme turnover, nanoparticle nucleation, and battery electrolyte reactions, and is upgrade‑ready for MHz operation at diffraction‑limited storage rings.

**Proposed experiment: "Phase‑resolved surface movie" — kHz modulation‑excitation, ambient‑pressure XPS + NEXAFS with phase‑sensitive demodulation to film a heterogeneous catalytic cycle in operando.**

**Concept.** Instead of a single pump‑probe delay scan, drive a working catalyst with a periodic (square‑wave) perturbation of its *chemical* environment and use lock‑in (phase‑sensitive) detection of the synchrotron signal. Only species that respond at the excitation frequency survive demodulation, so short‑lived reactive intermediates are separated from the enormous background of spectator species — an X‑ray analogue of modulation‑excitation IR spectroscopy, but with element and oxidation‑state specificity.

**System.** CO oxidation (or NH₃/NO₃⁻ conversion) over Pd or Pt nanoparticles and a single‑crystal reference, at 1–10 mbar and 300–600 K.

**Setup.**
- Soft X‑ray undulator beamline (Al/O/C/N K‑edges, Pd 3d, Pt 4f) with a differentially pumped ambient‑pressure photoemission cell.
- Two fast piezo/solenoid gas valves alternate the CO:O₂ ratio (or isotope ¹⁶O₂/¹⁸O₂) as a square wave at 1 Hz–1 kHz, with jitter <10 µs, verified by a fast quadrupole mass spectrometer at the cell exit.
- Detection: a time‑stamping delay‑line/event‑mode electron analyser detector that records every photoelectron with (kinetic energy, arrival time) tags, so a full spectrum is reconstructed at any phase of the modulation cycle; simultaneous Auger‑yield NEXAFS and grazing‑incidence X‑ray fluorescence/diffraction from a second detector give adsorbate bonding and subsurface oxide formation.
- Data are Fourier‑demodulated at the fundamental and higher harmonics: amplitude gives the concentration of responding species, phase lag gives its position in the kinetic sequence.

**Measurement protocol.** Sweep modulation frequency over 3 decades (kinetic filtering: species with lifetimes ≫1/f are averaged out, so the "cut‑off frequency" of each demodulated peak directly yields its rate constant). Repeat versus temperature, pressure and particle size; use isotope switching to distinguish lattice from adsorbed oxygen; correlate the demodulated surface signals with the demodulated MS product signal to identify which species is truly on the productive path rather than a spectator.

**What it delivers.** Rate constants and a *phase ordering* (mechanistic sequence) for adsorbed CO, chemisorbed O, surface/subsurface oxide and carbonate, obtained under steady turnover — including the metal↔oxide switching that governs self‑sustained kinetic oscillations. It answers directly whether metallic or oxidized Pd is the active phase, a long‑standing controversy that steady‑state spectroscopy cannot settle.

**Novelty/impact.** First combination of chemical‑modulation lock‑in detection with event‑mode ambient‑pressure photoemission at a synchrotron; sensitivity to minority intermediates improves by 1–2 orders of magnitude because only the modulated component is retained. The scheme needs no laser, works at true operating pressures, and transfers straightforwardly to electrochemical potential modulation (fuel‑cell and CO₂‑reduction electrodes) and to hard X‑ray XAS/XRD at high‑brightness fourth‑generation storage rings.

**Proposed experiment: "Bond‑resolved movies of extreme‑condition chemistry" — stroboscopic, pulsed laser‑heated diamond‑anvil‑cell reactions filmed by time‑resolved X‑ray Raman scattering (XRS) with simultaneous XRD.**

**Concept.** X‑ray Raman scattering (non‑resonant inelastic scattering of ~10 keV photons) gives *bulk‑sensitive* K‑edge XANES of light elements (C, N, O, B, Li) through the diamond anvils, where soft X‑rays cannot penetrate. XRS has never been done time‑resolved because it is photon‑starved; the brightness of 4th‑generation rings (EBS/APS‑U) combined with large multi‑analyser arrays and event‑mode detectors now makes stroboscopic XRS feasible. The idea is to use it to watch *chemical bonding itself* (sp→sp²→sp³ rehybridisation, molecular→polymeric/extended‑solid transformations) rearrange in real time during a high‑pressure, high‑temperature reaction.

**System.** Molecular precursors compressed in a diamond‑anvil cell to 20–80 GPa: e.g. CO₂ → polymeric CO₂/“carbonia” and carbonates; CH₄ → diamond + hydrocarbons (planetary‑interior chemistry); N₂ → polymeric cg‑N; B–H or Li–N–H hydrogen‑storage mixtures.

**Setup.**
- High‑flux undulator XRS spectrometer (60–100 spherically bent Si analysers, von Hámos/Rowland geometry) recording the C, N or O K‑edge as an energy‑loss spectrum, with low‑ and high‑q analyser banks to separate dipole (bonding) from non‑dipole (local symmetry) contributions.
- Double‑sided fibre‑laser heating operated in **pulsed mode (1–100 µs pulses at 1–100 kHz)**, so each cycle drives the sample through the same heat‑up/react/quench trajectory; sample refreshes chemically only slightly per cycle, allowing millions of accumulations at each delay before conversion saturates.
- Every scattered photon is time‑stamped relative to the heating pulse (event‑mode pixel detectors); a fast pyrometer records T(t) shot‑by‑shot for thermometry.
- A second area detector collects **XRD simultaneously** (long‑range order, nucleation, phase fractions), and streak‑pyrometry/optical Raman provide cross‑checks. Multiple DAC positions/fresh sample spots are scanned to build up statistics and to work in the “few‑cycle” regime for irreversible reactions.

**Protocol.** Reconstruct, from the time‑stamped events, a full energy‑loss spectrum at each delay (µs–ms) after the heating pulse; repeat versus pressure, peak temperature, pulse length and duty cycle. Fit the delay‑dependent spectra with DFT/BSE‑calculated K‑edge signatures of candidate intermediates (e.g. CO₃ trigonal units, CO₄ tetrahedra, sp³ N chains) to obtain time‑dependent species fractions, then extract nucleation and growth rate constants and activation barriers by comparing XRS (short‑range bonding) with XRD (long‑range order) kinetics.

**What it delivers.** The first direct, element‑ and bond‑specific kinetics of extreme‑condition chemistry: whether polymerisation proceeds through a disordered/amorphous intermediate before crystallising, whether carbonate or tetrahedral carbon forms first, the lifetime of transient sp² carbon during diamond formation, and the true P–T–t path of synthesis of superhard/energetic materials — quantities currently inferred only from quenched, post‑mortem samples.

**Novelty/impact.** Converts XRS from a slow, static, brightness‑limited technique into a time‑resolved probe by exploiting cyclic laser heating and photon time‑stamping; provides light‑element XANES *inside* a pressure cell where no laser‑pump/soft‑X‑ray method can reach. Results constrain models of ice‑giant and deep‑Earth carbon/nitrogen chemistry and give kinetic (not just thermodynamic) rules for recovering novel extended solids to ambient conditions. The same stroboscopic, time‑stamped XRS scheme transfers to Li K‑edge studies of battery electrode reactions and to shock/T‑jump chemistry in liquids.

**Proposed experiment: “5‑D operando movies of a single catalyst nanocrystal” — stroboscopic, resonance‑contrast Bragg coherent diffraction imaging (BCDI) of one electrocatalyst particle under kHz potential pulsing.**

**Concept.** No existing method gives the *three‑dimensional*, atom‑resolved strain/defect field of an individual working nanocrystal *while* its chemistry changes on sub‑millisecond timescales. I propose to combine (i) Bragg coherent diffraction imaging, which retrieves the 3‑D lattice displacement field of a single ~100–300 nm crystal from a coherently illuminated Bragg peak, with (ii) stroboscopic, event‑mode accumulation over millions of identical, electrochemically triggered reaction cycles, and (iii) an incident‑energy scan across the metal K‑edge so that the *anomalous* (resonant) contribution to the same Bragg peak encodes oxidation state and site occupancy. The result is a five‑dimensional dataset: 3 spatial dimensions × time × photon energy (chemical state).

**System.** A single Cu (or Pd/Ni/Co‑oxide) nanocrystal on a transparent glassy‑carbon/SiN working electrode in a thin‑layer electrochemical flow cell: CO₂ reduction / hydrogen absorption (α↔β PdH) / oxide‑hydroxide redox in alkaline OER. The electrode potential is square‑wave pulsed at 0.1–10 kHz between an “off” and a “turnover” value, so the particle is repeatedly driven through the same reaction cycle and always returns to the same reference state.

**Setup.**
- Coherent hard‑X‑ray nanoprobe at a diffraction‑limited storage ring (EBS/APS‑U/SLS 2.0), ~9–15 keV, beam focused to ≈100–200 nm, illuminating one isolated crystal.
- Fast area detector operated in **event/time‑stamping mode**, every photon tagged relative to the potential‑pulse trigger; potentiostat, chopper and detector clocked to the ring RF (single‑bunch mode gives ~100 ps gating for the fastest, electric‑double‑layer‑driven response; µs–ms bins for the chemistry).
- Rocking curves at each of several Bragg reflections (111, 200, 220) are collected phase‑by‑phase; a multilayer‑monochromator energy scan across the Cu K‑edge repeats the whole sequence at 8–12 energies.
- Simultaneous fluorescence detector (element‑specific XANES of the same particle), product analysis by on‑line MS/electrochemical mass spectrometry, and an optional laser/IR pump for photo‑electrochemistry.

**Protocol.** Accumulate diffraction patterns sorted by phase within the potential cycle; phase‑retrieve one 3‑D image per time bin per energy. Cross‑correlate the reconstructed displacement/strain field with the resonant amplitude change to separate *mechanical* (lattice expansion, dislocation nucleation, faceting) from *chemical* (Cu⁰↔Cu⁺/Cu²⁺, H or O uptake) contributions, voxel by voxel. Sweep pulse frequency (kinetic filtering: features that cannot follow 1/f drop out, giving local rate constants), potential amplitude, temperature and electrolyte composition. Perform control cycles to detect irreversible restructuring, and use the “few‑cycle” regime plus many fresh particles for irreversible reactions.

**What it delivers.** A voxel‑resolved answer to where a catalytic reaction actually happens: whether reduction/oxidation nucleates at corners, edges, twin boundaries or subsurface defects; how fast a reaction front propagates into a single particle; whether dislocations are created *by* the chemistry and then act as reaction hot‑spots; the local activation volume and the time lag between charge transfer, lattice strain and product formation. It links single‑particle structural dynamics directly to measured current/product selectivity.

**Novelty/impact.** First implementation of *resonant, time‑resolved* BCDI with pulse‑synchronised photon time‑stamping — turning a slow, static imaging technique into a movie camera for single‑particle chemistry with ~10 nm spatial and µs (down to ns) temporal resolution, and adding chemical‑state contrast that conventional BCDI lacks. It closes the gap between ensemble‑averaged operando XAS/XRD and single‑particle electron microscopy (which cannot work in liquid at realistic potentials). The scheme transfers directly to battery cathode particles under pulsed cycling, to gas‑switching heterogeneous catalysis, and to phase‑change and photostriction studies with a laser pump.

**Proposed experiment: “Isomer‑resolved kinetic movies of radical chemistry” — time‑tagged, double‑imaging photoelectron–photoion coincidence (i²PEPICO) spectroscopy of a laser‑initiated gas‑phase reactor using tunable VUV synchrotron radiation.**

**Concept.** Multiplexed synchrotron photoionization mass spectrometry can follow transient species in real time, but it cannot cleanly distinguish *isomers* of the same m/z (e.g. QOOH vs. ketohydroperoxide vs. enol vs. Criegee intermediate), which is exactly where mechanisms diverge. I propose to make every ionization event a *coincidence* measurement — velocity‑map‑imaged photoelectron detected together with a position‑ and time‑resolved photoion — and to time‑stamp each coincidence relative to a photolysis laser pulse. Each event then carries four coordinates: mass, threshold‑photoelectron (vibrationally resolved) energy, ion recoil/kinetic energy, and reaction time. The result is a 4‑D dataset from which isomer‑ and even conformer‑specific concentration‑vs‑time traces are extracted without any chemical separation.

**System.** Low‑temperature autoxidation/combustion and atmospheric radical chemistry: pulsed 248/193 nm photolysis of a precursor (e.g. an alkyl iodide, oxalyl chloride, or diiodoalkane) in a slow‑flow quartz reactor at 1–100 Torr and 250–800 K, generating R•, which reacts with O₂ to give RO₂ → QOOH → ketohydroperoxide/OH, or CH₂I + O₂ → Criegee intermediates + their unimolecular decay.

**Setup.**
- VUV undulator beamline, 7.5–13.5 eV, ΔE ≈ 3–8 meV, rare‑gas harmonic filter, ~10¹² ph/s (continuous, quasi‑cw ionization = no pump–probe timing limitation on the X‑ray side).
- Reactor gas sampled through a pinhole into a skimmed molecular beam entering the i²PEPICO endstation: VMI electron optics + delay‑line anode for electrons, position‑sensitive ion TOF for ions.
- **Event mode:** every (e⁻, ion) coincidence is written with its arrival time relative to the photolysis trigger (µs resolution) and to the ring bunch clock; the laser fires at 1–10 kHz while the beam energy is slowly scanned, so mass‑selected threshold‑photoelectron spectra (ms‑TPES) are built up simultaneously at *all* reaction delays.
- Auxiliary: on‑axis pyrometry/thermocouples, a movable sampling pinhole (distance‑to‑time conversion for the slow chemistry), and isotopic labelling (¹⁸O₂, D) for mechanism tests.

**Protocol.** (i) Record the full 4‑D event stream; (ii) at each delay bin fit the ms‑TPES with reference/CBS‑QB3‑Franck–Condon‑simulated isomer fingerprints to obtain absolute isomer‑resolved concentration profiles; (iii) globally fit these profiles to a kinetic model to extract rate coefficients, branching ratios, and isomerization barriers; (iv) repeat versus T, P and O₂ concentration to obtain the pressure‑dependent falloff and to test master‑equation predictions; (v) use ion‑imaging (recoil energy) to separate parent ionization from dissociative ionization, removing the largest systematic error in conventional PIMS kinetics.

**What it delivers.** The first direct, time‑resolved observation and quantification of the key elusive intermediates of autoxidation — QOOH radicals, highly oxygenated organic molecules (HOMs), and specific Criegee conformers — including which isomer is formed first, how fast it interconverts, and what fraction leads to chain branching. These are precisely the numbers that combustion and atmospheric aerosol models currently guess.

**Novelty/impact.** Turns coincidence VUV spectroscopy (until now a static, thermochemistry technique) into a kinetics instrument by photon‑by‑photon time tagging synchronized to a photolysis laser, adding isomer selectivity that neither laser‑based transient absorption nor conventional synchrotron PIMS possesses. It requires no ultrashort X‑ray pulses, so it exploits the *continuous* nature of storage‑ring radiation rather than fighting it, and scales directly to higher repetition rates at diffraction‑limited rings. The same scheme transfers to catalytic microreactor effluents, plasma chemistry, pyrolysis of biomass surrogates, and prebiotic gas‑phase synthesis.

**Proposed experiment: “Reaction‑clock XPCS” — non‑equilibrium X‑ray Photon Correlation Spectroscopy with two‑time correlation analysis to watch the *dynamics* (not just the structure) of a chemical reaction as it happens, in a contactless acoustically‑levitated droplet.**

**Concept.** Every time‑resolved X‑ray method to date reports *average structure* versus time (XAS, SAXS/WAXS, diffraction). I propose instead to use the **coherence** of a 4th‑generation source to measure the *speckle fluctuation dynamics* of a reacting mixture, and to analyse it with **two‑time correlation functions g₂(t₁,t₂)** so that the relaxation time, dynamical heterogeneity and ageing of the nanoscale species are obtained *at every instant of the reaction*. Chemistry then becomes visible through its own fluctuation spectrum: monomer diffusion → cluster aggregation → dynamical arrest (gelation/crystallisation) each have a distinct, quantifiable dynamical fingerprint that structure‑only techniques cannot separate.

**System.** Solution‑phase nucleation and growth where the “classical vs. two‑step/prenucleation‑cluster” debate is unresolved: (i) ZIF‑8/MOF crystallisation from Zn²⁺ + 2‑methylimidazole; (ii) Pt or CdS nanoparticle nucleation from a molecular precursor; (iii) calcium carbonate/amorphous‑precursor biomineralisation.

**Setup.**
- Coherent hard X‑ray beamline (EBS/APS‑U/PETRA IV), 8–12 keV, ~5–10 µm coherent beam, ≥10¹² ph/s.
- **Acoustic (or electrostatic) levitation** of a 1–2 mm droplet in a temperature/humidity‑controlled chamber: no windows, no walls, no wall‑induced heterogeneous nucleation, no container scattering background, and the droplet can be rotated/refreshed.
- **Triggering:** the reaction is started either by (a) coalescence of two levitated droplets (reagent + reagent) with a piezo‑driven merge, or (b) an IR (1470 nm) laser **T‑jump** of 5–30 K in <10 µs applied to a pre‑mixed, kinetically frozen solution — the latter is repeatable, so the *same* reaction cycle can be run thousands of times.
- **Detection:** a Mpixel photon‑counting detector (EIGER2/AGIPD‑class) at 10–100 kHz frame rate in **event/time‑stamped mode**, recording speckle in the SAXS regime (q = 0.005–0.5 Å⁻¹) simultaneously with a WAXS bank (Bragg peak onset = crystallinity) and an energy‑dispersive **fluorescence detector for in‑situ XANES** at the metal edge (oxidation state/coordination of the precursor). Optional co‑mounted optical camera + Raman for droplet size and molecular speciation.
- **Dose control:** the beam is chopped and the droplet slowly rotated/translated so each illuminated volume receives a sub‑damage dose; ~10³ identical T‑jump cycles are averaged with dose fractionation, and “fresh‑droplet” single‑shot runs validate that radiolysis has not altered the kinetics.

**Protocol.** For each reaction cycle, compute g₂(q; t₁,t₂) in ~ms windows to obtain (i) the instantaneous relaxation rate Γ(q,t) and its q‑dependence (Γ∝q² diffusive vs Γ∝q¹ ballistic/stress‑driven, the latter being the signature of internal‑stress‑driven restructuring during gelation), (ii) the KWW stretching/compressing exponent (dynamical heterogeneity, jamming), and (iii) the four‑point susceptibility χ₄ for cooperative rearrangements. Overlay these dynamical observables on the simultaneously measured SAXS intensity/Guinier radius, WAXS Bragg onset and XANES speciation. Repeat versus supersaturation, temperature, ligand/modulator concentration and ionic strength.

**What it delivers.** A direct, model‑free answer to *when* and *how* the system passes from freely diffusing monomers/prenucleation clusters, through a dense amorphous liquid‑like intermediate, to an arrested/crystalline solid — including the lifetime of the amorphous precursor, whether nucleation occurs inside dense droplets (two‑step) or from solution (classical), whether growth is coalescence‑ or monomer‑attachment‑limited, and the moment at which metal‑centre coordination (from XANES) changes relative to the dynamical arrest (from XPCS). These correlation times are exactly the quantities missing from current nucleation theories.

**Novelty/impact.** First use of XPCS as a *chemical* kinetics probe under genuinely non‑equilibrium, single‑pass conditions, made possible by combining (a) repeatable IR T‑jump triggering with stroboscopic dose fractionation, (b) containerless levitation to eliminate wall nucleation and background, and (c) simultaneous multimodal SAXS/WAXS/XANES readout on one droplet. It adds an entirely new observable — reaction‑time‑resolved dynamics and dynamical heterogeneity — to time‑resolved synchrotron science, and transfers directly to polymer curing, sol‑gel and battery‑electrolyte SEI formation, protein liquid–liquid phase separation, and self‑assembly of colloidal catalysts.

**Proposed experiment: “Stereochemistry in motion” — time‑resolved X‑ray Natural Circular Dichroism (TR‑XNCD) with kHz helicity switching and lock‑in detection, applied to a working asymmetric (enantioselective) catalyst in a flow mixer.**

**Concept.** Every existing time‑resolved X‑ray method reports oxidation state, bond lengths, or long‑range order — none reports *handedness*. X‑ray natural circular dichroism (the E1·E2 interference term in the absorption of left‑ vs right‑circularly polarised X‑rays) is the only element‑specific probe of *absolute chirality at a single atomic site*, but it has only ever been measured statically on crystals because the signal is 10⁻³–10⁻⁴ of the edge jump. I propose to make XNCD a kinetic technique: modulate the photon helicity at kHz rates and phase‑sensitively detect the dichroism while a chiral catalytic reaction is running, so that the *transient chiral geometry* around the catalytic metal centre can be followed as the substrate binds, reacts, and the product leaves.

**System.** Enantioselective homogeneous catalysis where the stereo‑determining step is unknown: Cu(I/II)–bis(oxazoline) cyclopropanation/Diels–Alder, Rh–DuPhos asymmetric hydrogenation, or a Mn/Fe–salen epoxidation. Solutions of catalyst and prochiral substrate are mixed in a chip micromixer (mixing <100 µs); flow velocity converts *position along the channel into reaction time* (10 µs–1 s), and the same effluent is fed on‑line to a chiral UHPLC/CD detector that measures the enantiomeric excess produced by exactly the volume just probed.

**Setup.**
- APPLE‑II/Delta undulator (or a fast X‑ray phase‑retarder/diamond quarter‑wave plate) switching helicity at 0.1–5 kHz at the metal K‑ or L‑edge, on a high‑brightness DLSR beamline (10¹³–10¹⁴ ph/s).
- Solution flow cell/micro‑jet scanned by a 10–50 µm beam along the mixing channel; high‑count‑rate multi‑element fluorescence detector plus a partial‑fluorescence‑yield (HERFD) crystal analyser to sharpen the pre‑edge features that carry most of the XNCD.
- **Lock‑in/event‑mode detection:** each photon is tagged with the instantaneous helicity state; demodulation at the switching frequency retains only the dichroic component, rejecting flow, density and drift noise and pushing sensitivity to ΔI/I ≈ 10⁻⁵.
- Recorded simultaneously: helicity‑averaged XANES/EXAFS (coordination, oxidation state), Kβ/valence‑to‑core XES if flux allows, and optical CD/UV‑vis of the same channel; an optional ns laser or T‑jump can trigger photo‑initiated chiral steps and give sub‑µs access via bunch gating.
- Racemic and enantiopure catalyst runs, and mirror‑image ligands, provide the essential sign‑reversal control that proves the signal is genuinely natural dichroism and not instrumental artefact.

**Protocol.** For each channel position (reaction time), record the demodulated XNCD spectrum across the pre‑edge/edge; convert the sign and amplitude of the dichroic features into a transient chiral distortion (helical pitch, dihedral twist) of the metal coordination sphere by comparison with FDMR/DFT–multiple‑scattering XNCD simulations of candidate intermediates and transition‑state analogues. Repeat versus substrate concentration, temperature, additive/counter‑ion, and ligand backbone; then correlate, point by point, the *time‑resolved chiral amplitude at the metal* with the *enantiomeric excess measured downstream*.

**What it delivers.** A direct, atom‑specific answer to the central question of asymmetric catalysis: *when* in the cycle chirality is transferred, which intermediate carries the stereochemical information, whether the resting state or a short‑lived, weakly populated diastereomeric complex determines ee (Curtin–Hammett test), and how additives or solvent modulate the transient chiral distortion. It also detects racemisation/epimerisation of intermediates in real time, which no bulk optical method can assign to a specific metal site in an absorbing, coloured reaction mixture.

**Novelty/impact.** First conversion of XNCD from a static crystallographic curiosity into a *solution‑phase, time‑resolved kinetics probe*, enabled by kHz helicity modulation + photon‑tagged lock‑in detection + space‑to‑time microfluidic encoding at a diffraction‑limited storage ring. It adds an entirely new observable — element‑resolved handedness versus reaction time — to time‑resolved synchrotron science, gives experimental benchmarks for computational stereoselectivity models, and transfers directly to chiral‑induced spin selectivity (CISS) devices, chirality emergence during crystallisation of chiral solids, and photoinduced chirality switching in molecular machines.

**Proposed experiment: “Vibrational movies of a metalloenzyme’s iron core” — time‑resolved nuclear resonant vibrational spectroscopy (TR‑NRVS) combined with synchrotron Mössbauer spectroscopy on ⁵⁷Fe‑labelled catalysts, using a continuously refilled cryo‑quench “sample wheel”.**

**Concept.** Nuclear resonant scattering at the 14.4 keV ⁵⁷Fe resonance gives two unique observables that no other X‑ray method provides: (i) NRVS, an *isotope‑selective* vibrational density of states that shows every mode with Fe displacement (Fe=O, Fe–H, Fe–S, Fe–N–O stretches, exactly the bonds that define catalytic intermediates), and (ii) synchrotron Mössbauer spectroscopy (SMS) from the same nuclear forward‑scattering time spectrum, giving oxidation state, spin state and quadrupole splitting. Both are photon‑starved and have therefore only ever been done on static, cryogenically trapped samples. I propose to convert them into *kinetic* techniques, so that the vibrational fingerprint of a short‑lived intermediate — not just its electronic state — can be followed as a reaction proceeds.

**System.** ⁵⁷Fe‑enriched catalysts whose key intermediates are structurally contested: cytochrome P450/taurine dioxygenase Fe(IV)=O (Compound I / ferryl) species, [FeFe]‑hydrogenase terminal hydrides (H_hyd), nitrogenase Fe–H/Fe–N₂H_x states, and biomimetic Fe–oxo/Fe–peroxo model complexes.

**Setup.**
1. **Triggering, two complementary modes.**
 - *Reversible/photolytic chemistry:* a kHz ns laser photolyses a caged substrate (caged O₂, caged H⁺/NO, or photolabile Fe–CO), and the sample is stroboscopically cycled millions of times in a flow cuvette; every nuclear‑scattering photon is time‑stamped relative to the laser and to the storage‑ring bunch clock (single‑bunch/hybrid mode, ~100 ps gates).
 - *Irreversible chemistry:* a rapid‑mixing quench‑flow head sprays reacting solution, at a chosen post‑mixing age (50 µs–1 s set by mixer‑to‑nozzle distance and flow rate), onto the rim of a slowly rotating, liquid‑He‑cooled sapphire wheel that carries the freeze‑trapped droplets straight through the X‑ray beam and is then scraped clean and re‑coated. This gives a *continuously renewed* cryo sample of essentially unlimited volume — the only way to accumulate the ~10⁶ s⁻¹‑starved counts NRVS needs at a single reaction delay without radiation damage or sample exhaustion.
2. **Beamline.** High‑heat‑load undulator with a ~0.5–1 meV high‑resolution monochromator scanned ±120 meV about 14.4125 keV at a diffraction‑limited storage ring (10¹⁰–10¹¹ ph/s in the meV band); beam focused to ~20–50 µm onto the wheel rim or the flow cell.
3. **Detection.** Fast APD arrays for delayed nuclear fluorescence (NRVS) plus a forward‑scattering APD recording the nuclear‑decay quantum beats (SMS) simultaneously; a Si‑drift detector records Fe K‑edge XANES/EXAFS on the same spot for coordination‑number cross‑checks. All channels are recorded in event mode and sorted by reaction delay.

**Protocol.** Build a complete NRVS spectrum at each of ~6–10 reaction delays spanning µs–s (and, for the photolytic mode, ns–µs), together with the SMS spectrum from the identical volume. Subtract the (independently measured) resting‑state spectrum, weighted by the SMS‑determined population, to isolate the pure intermediate PVDOS. Assign the delay‑dependent Fe‑mode frequencies against DFT/normal‑mode simulations and against ⁵⁷Fe/⁵⁶Fe, D₂O/H₂O and ¹⁸O/¹⁶O isotope‑shift controls, which unambiguously identify Fe–H, Fe=O and Fe–OH modes. Repeat versus pH, temperature, substrate and mutant/ligand variants; globally fit species populations to a kinetic scheme.

**What it delivers.** The first *bond‑resolved, isotope‑selective vibrational kinetics* of an iron catalytic cycle: the actual Fe=O stretching frequency (and hence bond order/protonation state) of a ferryl intermediate while it is being consumed, direct detection and lifetime of terminal metal hydrides, the sequence of Fe–S cluster distortions coupled to electron transfer, and correlation of each vibrational signature with the simultaneously measured Mössbauer oxidation/spin state. These are the quantities that distinguish competing mechanisms (e.g. rebound vs. concerted O‑transfer; terminal vs. bridging hydride) and that current freeze‑trap studies can only obtain for artificially stabilised, possibly non‑catalytic species.

**Novelty/impact.** Turns nuclear resonant scattering — the most information‑rich but slowest synchrotron probe of iron — into a time‑resolved technique, by pairing photon time‑stamping with a continuously regenerated cryo‑quench sample wheel that decouples the required exposure time from the reaction timescale. It adds vibrational (force‑constant) information to time‑resolved X‑ray science, provides direct experimental benchmarks for computed transition states, and transfers immediately to other Mössbauer isotopes (¹¹⁹Sn, ¹⁵¹Eu, ¹²⁵Te, ¹⁶¹Dy) for battery, thermoelectric and magnetic‑switching chemistry.

**Proposed experiment: “Spin‑chemistry movies” — time‑resolved, element‑selective X‑ray magnetic circular dichroism (TR‑XMCD) plus X‑ray‑detected magnetic resonance of laser‑generated *radical pairs*, in a liquid microjet.**

**Concept.** All time‑resolved X‑ray methods so far track charge, structure or bonding; none tracks *electron spin on a specific atom during a reaction*. Radical‑pair chemistry (magnetic‑field effects, spin‑selective recombination, CIDNP/CIDEP, avian magnetoreception, triplet‑fusion photocatalysis) is governed by singlet↔triplet interconversion of two unpaired spins whose wavefunctions are distributed over different atoms of the donor and acceptor. Soft X‑ray circular dichroism at the C, N, O K‑edges (and metal L‑edges) is directly proportional to the local spin moment, so a *transient* XMCD signal measures, atom by atom, how much spin density sits on the donor versus the acceptor and how its polarization evolves. I propose to make XMCD a chemical‑kinetics probe by combining kHz laser photolysis, kHz helicity switching with photon‑tagged lock‑in detection, and a pulsed magnetic‑field/RF coil that lets the *reaction itself* be steered while it is being watched.

**System.** (i) A covalently linked donor–bridge–acceptor dyad (e.g. carotenoid–porphyrin–fullerene, or a flavin–tryptophan model) that forms a well‑defined radical pair on 100 ps–10 µs timescales; (ii) cryptochrome/photolyase protein, the proposed magnetoreceptor, with its FAD•⁻–TrpH•⁺ pair; (iii) a Ni‑ or Co‑photoredox catalyst where triplet/doublet spin state controls product selectivity.

**Setup.**
- Soft X‑ray undulator (APPLE‑II/Delta) at a diffraction‑limited ring, 280–860 eV (C, N, O K; Ni/Co L₃), helicity switched at 0.1–5 kHz; hybrid/single‑bunch mode gives ~70–100 ps probe pulses, extendable to µs by bunch summing.
- Liquid microjet or ultrathin SiN flow cell (transmission and total‑fluorescence/electron‑yield detection), continuously refreshed to avoid photo‑ and radiation damage; a jet‑integrated Helmholtz/stripline coil supplies static fields 0–200 mT and 10–500 MHz RF or ns field jumps.
- Synchronized 1–10 kHz fs/ns pump laser; every detected photon (or drain‑current sample) is tagged with helicity state, magnetic‑field state, and delay after the pump.

**Protocol.** Record ΔA_XMCD(E, t) = A_left − A_right at each edge as a function of pump–probe delay from 100 ps to 100 µs; demodulate at the helicity frequency (and at the laser on/off and B‑field on/off frequencies) to reach ΔI/I ≈ 10⁻⁵. Then (a) map the *spatial* distribution of the two spins by comparing N‑K (flavin/porphyrin) with C‑K (bridge/fullerene) dichroism; (b) sweep the static field to record an element‑resolved magnetic‑field effect curve at every reaction time; (c) apply resonant RF pulses (X‑ray‑detected magnetic resonance) to drive singlet–triplet mixing and read out the resulting change in each atom’s spin polarization, giving site‑specific hyperfine and exchange/dipolar couplings; (d) correlate with the simultaneously recorded helicity‑averaged XANES (oxidation state, protonation) and with optical transient absorption and product yields.

**What it delivers.** Site‑resolved singlet–triplet interconversion and spin‑relaxation rates; the actual spin‑density map of a transient radical pair and its distance/orientation (from the exchange coupling); direct proof of whether the magnetic‑field sensitivity of a reaction originates on the flavin, the tryptophan chain, or the metal centre; and the link between spin state and product branching in photoredox catalysis — quantities that bulk EPR/optical MFE experiments can only infer from ensemble averages.

**Novelty/impact.** First transfer of XMCD and of magnetic‑resonance pumping into the *time‑resolved chemistry* domain, on non‑magnetic, light‑element molecules in solution, using helicity‑modulated lock‑in detection of a 10⁻⁵ signal. It adds “spin” as a wholly new observable to time‑resolved synchrotron science, provides atom‑specific benchmarks for spin‑dynamics simulations of magnetoreception and spin‑controlled catalysis, and extends naturally to organic spintronics, singlet‑fission materials and chirality‑induced spin selectivity, where an element‑resolved spin clock is currently missing.

**Proposed experiment: “X‑ray‑pump / X‑ray‑probe site‑selective radiation chemistry” — using one storage‑ring bunch to *trigger* chemistry at a chosen atom and later bunches to *probe* it, with no laser involved.**

**Concept.** All conventional time‑resolved synchrotron work uses a laser (or mixing/T‑jump) as the trigger, which restricts the study to optically absorbing, optically accessible chromophores. I propose to use the X‑rays themselves as the pump: a hard‑X‑ray pulse tuned just above the K‑ (or L‑) edge of a heavy tag creates a *localized* core hole at one specific atom; the Auger–Meitner cascade leaves a multiply charged, highly localized “hot spot” that drives bond scission, charge transfer to the solvent and hydrated‑electron/OH• production. A second, independently tunable X‑ray pulse then probes the resulting chemistry by XAS/XES/scattering at a *different* element edge. Because the pump energy can be scanned across an absorption edge, energy deposition can be switched on and off at a chosen atom while total dose is essentially unchanged — an “element‑selective trigger” that is impossible with a laser.

**System.** (i) Halogen‑ or metal‑tagged biomolecules and radiosensitizers (5‑bromo/iodo‑uracil in DNA, Gd‑ or Au‑nanoparticle–labelled peptides) in aqueous solution, to follow Auger‑initiated strand/bond cleavage and the subsequent radical chemistry relevant to radiotherapy; (ii) actinide/lanthanide‑ or Fe‑containing solutions relevant to nuclear‑waste and geological radiolysis; (iii) ice/astro‑chemical ice films (CO, CH₃OH, H₂O with a heavy dopant) to test radiation‑driven prebiotic synthesis.

**Setup.**
- A canted‑undulator (or two‑branch) hard‑X‑ray beamline at a 4th‑generation ring in hybrid/camshaft mode: the intense **camshaft bunch is used as the pump** (focused to ~1–5 µm, ~10⁹–10¹⁰ ph/pulse after multilayer monochromatization to ΔE/E ≈ 10⁻², enough to make ~10⁻³–10⁻² core holes per tagged atom per shot), while the **probe** is taken from selected bunches in the following train, giving natural delays of ~2 ns to ~1 µs; a Si/Ge **split‑and‑delay line** on the same branch extends the range down to ~10 ps, and pulse‑picking chopper + slow bunch selection extend it to ms.
- Independent monochromators on pump and probe branches so pump energy (e.g. 13.5 keV, Br K‑edge; 33.2 keV, I K‑edge; 50 keV, Gd K‑edge) and probe energy (e.g. Fe/S/Br edge, or a metal reporter) are set separately; spatial and temporal overlap established with a fast diamond/YAG diagnostic and streak camera.
- Sample: rapidly flowing liquid microjet or thin‑film cell refreshed between pump shots so each pumped volume is measured once (single‑pass, dose‑controlled); accumulate over 10⁷–10⁹ shots.
- Detection in **event mode**: multi‑element fluorescence detector for probe XANES/EXAFS and Kβ/valence‑to‑core XES (oxidation state, protonation, ligand identity of fragments), a 2D detector for simultaneous SAXS/WAXS (fragmentation, bubble/solvent‑cage dynamics), and optical transient absorption at 700 nm for the hydrated electron as a cross‑calibration. Data are demodulated with the pump‑on/pump‑off pattern (lock‑in on the camshaft trigger) to isolate the pump‑induced difference signal at the 10⁻⁴–10⁻⁵ level.

**Protocol.** (1) Record ΔXAS/ΔXES/ΔSAXS versus pump–probe delay from 10 ps to 1 ms. (2) Repeat with the pump energy scanned across the tag’s edge (below‑edge = control, above‑edge = Auger cascade) — the difference isolates the strictly site‑specific channel from generic Compton/photoelectric radiolysis. (3) Vary pump dose per shot to separate single‑ionization from multi‑hit/track‑overlap chemistry. (4) Vary scavenger concentration (N₂O, formate, D₂O/H₂O, ¹⁸O) to identify e⁻_aq, OH• and H• channels and to obtain diffusion/reaction radii. (5) Globally fit species populations to a spur‑diffusion–kinetics model.

**What it delivers.** The first direct, atom‑selective view of *how energy deposited at one atom becomes chemistry*: the ps–ns charge redistribution and bond breaking after an Auger cascade, the time and radius over which the resulting hole/electron reach the solvent, the yield and fate of secondary radicals, and the point at which nominally “collateral” radiolysis, rather than the direct core‑hole event, dominates damage. For radiosensitizers it quantifies the true multiplication factor of a high‑Z label; for nuclear and astro‑chemistry it gives rate constants for reactions that simply cannot be triggered by light.

**Novelty/impact.** Turns the storage ring’s own bunch structure into a pump–probe pair and converts radiation damage — usually the experimenter’s enemy — into a controlled, element‑selective initiation mechanism with penetration depth and site specificity no laser can match. It requires no chromophore, works inside optically opaque or high‑pressure environments, and transfers directly to studies of beam‑induced chemistry in batteries and MOFs, to X‑ray‑driven photocatalysis, and to quantitative dose–damage models for macromolecular crystallography and radiotherapy.

**Proposed experiment: “Chemical‑movie tomography” — stroboscopic, 5‑D operando X‑ray total‑scattering / pair‑distribution‑function computed tomography (PDF‑CT) of a whole working reactor under periodic feed modulation.**

**Concept.** Time‑resolved synchrotron studies of reactions are almost always done on a single point of a thin, idealized sample, so they average over the enormous chemical gradients that exist inside real reactors, and they are blind to *amorphous/short‑range‑ordered* species (the very intermediates that matter: amorphous precursors, sub‑nm clusters, disordered oxides/carbonates, glassy SEI). I propose to turn PDF analysis — normally a slow, static, bulk method — into a spatially and temporally resolved one: acquire high‑energy total‑scattering patterns in continuous‑rotation, event‑mode tomographic geometry, and use a *periodic chemical perturbation* of the reactor so that data can be sorted by phase within the cycle and accumulated stroboscopically. The result is a 5‑D dataset: local G(r) (short‑range structure) at every voxel in 3‑D, as a function of time within the reaction cycle.

**System.** A real, mm‑scale packed‑bed or membrane microreactor: (i) Cu/ZnO/Al₂O₃ during CO₂‑to‑methanol under H₂/CO₂ pulsing; (ii) a Li‑ or Na‑ion pouch/coin‑cell electrode under square‑wave current pulsing; (iii) continuous‑flow crystallization of a MOF/zeolite where an amorphous precursor precedes the crystal.

**Setup.**
- High‑energy undulator beamline (60–100 keV, q_max ≈ 25–30 Å⁻¹) at a diffraction‑limited ring; pencil beam 5–20 µm, or a “multi‑beam/ line” illumination with a coded aperture to parallelize the sinogram.
- Sample on a continuously rotating/translating stage with **golden‑ratio (non‑repeating) angular sampling**, so any time window contains a well‑distributed, invertible angular set — no need to complete a conventional 0–180° scan per time point.
- Fast large‑area CdTe photon‑counting detector (kHz frame rate) in **event/time‑stamped mode**; every frame is tagged with rotation angle, translation position and phase within the modulation cycle.
- **Triggering/modulation:** fast gas valves (or the potentiostat/current source) impose a square‑wave perturbation of the feed composition, temperature or current at 0.01–10 Hz, with a mass spectrometer measuring the demodulated product response at the outlet.
- Simultaneous channels: XRF‑CT (element maps from a side detector), SAXS from the same frames (particle size/porosity), and an on‑line MS/IR for product analysis; a thermocouple/IR camera for the local T field.
