**Protocol.** (1) Bin all events by cycle phase; reconstruct each phase with **dynamic, temporally regularized tomography** (compressed sensing / total‑variation in space + smoothness in phase, or a neural implicit representation), yielding one 3‑D scattering‑pattern volume per phase bin. (2) Correct each voxel’s pattern for absorption/Compton and Fourier‑transform it into a local G(r). (3) Fit each voxel’s G(r) with a small basis of reference/ DFT‑MD‑simulated PDFs (metallic Cu, Cu₂O, formate/carbonate on ZnO, amorphous precursor, crystalline product), giving phase‑fraction, particle‑size and disorder maps as movies. (4) Fourier‑demodulate each voxel’s phase fraction at the modulation frequency: the amplitude gives how strongly that voxel participates, the **phase lag gives its position in the kinetic sequence**; sweeping the modulation frequency over decades provides local rate constants (“kinetic filtering”). (5) Correlate the voxel‑resolved kinetics with the demodulated outlet MS signal to identify which spatial region actually produces the product.

**What it delivers.** A voxel‑by‑voxel, time‑resolved map of *short‑range* chemistry inside an operating device: where along the bed the catalyst is metallic versus oxidized during turnover, how a reaction/oxidation front travels through the pellet and how fast, the lifetime and spatial location of amorphous intermediates during crystallization or SEI formation, and how transport gradients (T, concentration) couple to local structure. It converts a “black‑box” reactor into a resolved kinetic map, and it sees the non‑crystalline species that XRD‑CT misses entirely.

**Novelty/impact.** First combination of (a) PDF‑sensitive total scattering, (b) computed tomography, (c) stroboscopic modulation‑excitation with phase‑sensitive demodulation, and (d) event‑mode, golden‑angle sparse acquisition with dynamic reconstruction — pushing operando PDF‑CT from hours per (static) slice to sub‑second effective time resolution per 3‑D volume. It requires no laser, no thin model sample and no vacuum, works on genuine industrial reactors and sealed cells, and transfers directly to fuel‑cell/electrolyzer electrodes, cement and battery ageing, and additive‑manufacturing/solidification chemistry.

How can we enhance the signal-to-noise r.answer: Improve the ratio of diffracted counts to background: put as many photons as possible into the nanoscale probe and collect them as cleanly as possible. In practice this means using a high‑brilliance (undulator/upgraded storage‑ring) source with high‑efficiency nanofocusing optics (KB mirrors, zone plates, MLLs) to maximize flux density on the spot, using longer/repeated exposures that are summed (signal grows faster than the √N noise), and simultaneously suppressing background — clean‑up/guard apertures and beam stops to remove optic tails and parasitic scatter, evacuated or He‑filled flight paths to eliminate air scatter, thin low‑Z substrates/windows, and low‑noise, single‑photon‑counting pixel area detectors placed to capture the full Bragg peak (with energy discrimination to reject fluorescence).

One effective route (different from simply improving optics/detectors) is to trade spectral purity for flux: because a nanofocused beam already has a large angular divergence, the Bragg peaks are intrinsically broad, so one can illuminate the sample with a much larger bandpass — e.g., replace the Si(111) monochromator with a multilayer monochromator or use the "pink"/broadband undulator beam. This raises the incident flux on the nanoscale spot by one to two orders of magnitude with essentially no loss of reciprocal-space resolution (the extra energy spread is small compared with the divergence-induced peak width), so the diffracted signal — and hence the signal-to-noise ratio in a given counting time — increases dramatically, while the shorter exposures also reduce drift- and dose-related noise.

Rather than changing the source or optics, you can boost the diffracted signal by increasing the illuminated (diffracting) volume along the beam direction while keeping the lateral resolution set by the nanobeam size — i.e., use a grazing‑incidence/near‑glancing or "beam‑along‑the‑layer" geometry (or a thicker/deeper crystalline region) so the nanobeam traverses a much longer path through the material. Since the spatial resolution transverse to the beam is unaffected, the Bragg intensity scales up with the extended path length while parasitic scattering stays essentially constant, giving a markedly better signal‑to‑noise ratio.

Use phase‑sensitive (lock‑in/difference) detection instead of simply counting harder: drive the sample with a periodic external stimulus (AC electric field, laser pump, strain/current pulse, chopped beam, etc.) synchronized to the detector gating, and record the diffraction alternately in the "on" and "off" states. Subtracting/demodulating the two states cancels the time‑independent parasitic background (air and window scatter, substrate/optic tails, detector dark counts) and removes slow drift and 1/f noise, so only the stimulus‑correlated Bragg signal survives. Repeating the modulation cycle millions of times and averaging (stroboscopically accumulating the periodic response) lets the coherent signal build up linearly while the uncorrelated noise grows only as √N, giving a large net gain in signal‑to‑noise for the weak diffraction from a nanobeam‑illuminated volume.

Exploit measurement redundancy and computational reconstruction rather than raw counts: scan the nanobeam in steps much smaller than the probe size so that neighbouring illuminated volumes overlap strongly (Bragg ptychography / oversampled 3‑D reciprocal‑space mapping), and collect many overlapping, angularly oversampled diffraction frames of the same region. Because each part of the sample contributes to many frames, an iterative/maximum‑likelihood (Poisson‑noise‑aware) reconstruction — which can also refine and deconvolve the probe, correct positional drift, and be combined with denoising/regularization or machine‑learning filters — averages out the photon shot noise and detector background coherently. This yields a reconstructed strain/structure image whose effective signal‑to‑noise ratio is far higher than that of any single weak nanobeam diffraction pattern, without needing more flux or a brighter source.

Optimise the diffraction geometry and photon energy rather than the beam itself: pick a strong, low‑order Bragg reflection with a large structure factor (and, where possible, tune the X‑ray energy near an absorption edge to exploit resonant/anomalous enhancement of that reflection while staying off edges that would generate strong fluorescence background), and measure it in a geometry that maximises the peak intensity — e.g. put the scattering plane perpendicular to the synchrotron's linear polarisation (vertical scattering for a horizontally polarised beam) so the polarisation factor is ~1 at large 2θ, keep the incidence/exit angles symmetric to limit absorption, and choose a photon energy where sample absorption is low but the detector's quantum efficiency is still high. This maximises the number of Bragg photons per incident photon while minimising fluorescence, absorption and Compton background, giving a much better signal‑to‑noise ratio for the tiny volume illuminated by a nanobeam.

A complementary route is to stabilise and "cool" the experiment rather than the beam: mount the specimen on a mechanically stiff, interferometrically referenced (position‑feedback) nanopositioning stage in a temperature‑controlled, vibration‑isolated hutch, and cool the sample (e.g. cryogenic or simply well‑thermostatted conditions). Cooling raises the Debye–Waller factor so more of the scattered intensity goes into the sharp Bragg peak instead of into thermal diffuse scattering, which simultaneously lowers the diffuse background around the peak, and it also reduces radiation‑damage‑induced signal decay. Active drift correction/beam‑position tracking keeps the nanoprobe locked on the same nanoscale volume, so very long or many repeated exposures can be summed without smearing the peak — the coherent Bragg signal then accumulates linearly while the (now reduced) background and shot noise grow only as √N, markedly improving the signal‑to‑noise ratio of nanobeam diffraction.

Amplify the weak nanobeam signal holographically (heterodyne detection): let the tiny scattered wave from the nanoscale illuminated volume interfere coherently with a strong, well‑defined reference wave — e.g. the Bragg/truncation‑rod field from the underlying single‑crystal substrate, a nearby thick "reference" crystal, or a deliberately added scattering reference structure at the same Bragg condition. The recorded intensity then contains a cross‑term proportional to the *product* of the strong reference amplitude and the weak sample amplitude (|E_ref|·|E_sig|) instead of only |E_sig|², so the useful modulation is boosted by orders of magnitude above the detector dark counts and readout/quantization noise, and the measurement becomes limited only by the reference's shot noise. Demodulating the interference fringes (holographic/heterodyne reconstruction) recovers both amplitude and phase of the nanoscale diffraction with a far higher effective signal‑to‑noise ratio than direct detection of the weak nanobeam Bragg peak alone.

Collect all the diffraction information in parallel instead of serially. Use a deliberately strongly convergent (high‑numerical‑aperture) nanobeam so that the full range of incidence angles spanning the Bragg condition is present simultaneously — the whole rocking curve is then encoded in a single convergent‑beam nanodiffraction frame — and record it with a large‑area pixel detector placed to capture the entire Bragg disc (and, if possible, several reflections at once, e.g. with multiple detectors or a Laue/broad‑angle geometry). Because no photons are "wasted" while stepping through angles one at a time, every incident photon contributes to the measured signal in each exposure; the useful counts per frame rise by roughly the number of angular steps that would otherwise be scanned, so for a given exposure time and radiation dose the Bragg signal accumulates far faster than the (essentially constant) parasitic background and read/dark noise, markedly improving the signal‑to‑noise ratio — and the much shorter total measurement also avoids drift‑ and damage‑induced degradation.

Give up nanoscale resolution in the direction where you don't need it: instead of a point focus, use a one‑dimensional line (sheet) nanofocus — focus with a single set of optics (e.g. one mirror of the KB pair, a 1‑D MLL or a linear zone plate) so the beam is nanometric only along the axis of interest and remains many microns wide in the orthogonal direction. The illuminated (diffracting) volume, and hence the Bragg intensity, is then increased by the ratio of the line length to the focal width (typically 10²–10⁴×) while the spatial resolution along the focused direction — and the parasitic background per unit incident flux — is unchanged, so the signal‑to‑noise ratio in a given exposure improves enormously. Full 2‑D/3‑D information is then recovered by rotating the sample about the beam and back‑projecting (diffraction "laminography/tomography") the set of line‑projected measurements, rather than by raster‑scanning a point probe.

A route that requires no change to the beamline hardware is to attack the noise in the data themselves: characterise and subtract the background rather than just trying to out‑count it. Record, under identical conditions, reference frames with the sample moved out of the beam (or the crystal rotated off the Bragg condition, or the shutter closed), so that dark current, detector read‑out offset, air/window scatter and the optic‑tail halo are measured with high statistics, and subtract this properly scaled background image from every nanodiffraction frame. Combine this with standard detector calibration and cleaning — flat‑field/gain and pixel‑efficiency correction, masking of hot/dead pixels and module gaps, correction of the detector point‑spread and of count‑rate/pile‑up nonlinearity — and with statistical filtering of the corrected frames (median/outlier rejection to remove cosmic‑ray and spurious counts, Poisson‑appropriate binning of pixels and of repeated exposures, and integration of only the region of interest around the Bragg peak while using the surrounding pixels to estimate the local residual background). Because the systematic, reproducible part of the background is removed exactly and only its shot noise remains, the weak Bragg signal from the tiny nanobeam‑illuminated volume stands out far more clearly, giving a substantially higher signal‑to‑noise ratio for the same incident flux and exposure time.

Boost the statistics by averaging over an ensemble of equivalent objects rather than by collecting more photons from a single one. Fabricate/select a large array of nominally identical nanostructures (e.g. lithographically defined nanowires, dots, memory cells or device cells with the same shape and epitaxial relationship), scan the nanobeam to the same relative position within each of them (using registration marks or a fluorescence/imaging map to align each object), and then sum or "class‑average" the corresponding nanodiffraction frames in reciprocal space after correcting for the small rigid rotations/offsets of each object.

Because every one of the M objects contributes the same coherent Bragg signal at the same reciprocal‑space coordinate, the accumulated signal grows ∝ M while the uncorrelated photon shot noise, detector dark/read noise and parasitic background grow only ∝ √M, so the signal‑to‑noise ratio improves by ~√M without any increase in incident flux, dwell time or radiation dose per object (which also avoids beam damage and drift that would spoil a single long exposure). Nanoscale spatial resolution is preserved, since the resolution is still set by the probe size and by the position of the probe within each individual repeat unit; outlier frames can simply be rejected, and the spread among the individual patterns even provides a direct measure of object‑to‑object variability.

Increase the fraction of time (and dose) that actually produces useful counts by switching from step‑scanning to dead‑time‑free continuous "fly‑scanning" acquisition. Instead of moving the nanopositioner to each point, waiting for it to settle, opening a shutter, exposing, and reading out the detector — a sequence in which most of the beam time is lost to settling, shutter and read‑out dead time — sweep the sample (or the rocking angle) continuously while a free‑running, gated, zero‑dead‑time pixel detector streams frames that are tagged and binned on the fly with the encoder positions. Every incident photon during the scan then contributes to a diffraction frame, so for the same total experiment time the accumulated Bragg counts per pixel of the map rise by roughly the former duty‑cycle factor (often several‑fold to an order of magnitude), while the parasitic background, dark counts and read noise do not increase correspondingly. The much shorter total acquisition also means less thermal/mechanical drift and beam‑position wander smearing the nanoprobe over the sample and less radiation damage, so the weak nanobeam signal stays sharp and the effective signal‑to‑noise ratio of the nanodiffraction map is substantially improved without any change to the source, optics or sample.

Match the instrument's angular sampling to the intrinsic width of the nanobeam Bragg peak instead of over‑resolving it. Because a nanofocused probe is strongly convergent, its Bragg reflections are already broad (and further broadened by the small, strained diffracting volume), so there is nothing to gain by spreading that peak over thousands of detector pixels. By moving the area detector closer to the sample (and/or binning pixels, using a larger effective pixel/solid angle per channel, and opening any analyzer/slit acceptance) the same number of diffracted photons is concentrated into only a few detector channels, so the counts per pixel rise by the "compression" factor while each pixel's dark counts, read‑out noise and diffuse/air‑scatter background stay essentially the same — the per‑pixel signal‑to‑background and signal‑to‑read‑noise ratios therefore improve roughly in proportion to the reduction in sampled pixels. At the same time, the larger detector solid angle captures the *whole* divergence‑broadened Bragg disc (including its tails and any peak wander during a scan) in a single frame, so no diffracted photons are lost off the edge of the region of interest, and the total peak intensity can be integrated over a compact ROI whose surrounding pixels give a local background estimate. In short: don't oversample reciprocal space — set the detector distance/pixel size so that the peak just fills a small number of channels, which maximises counts per channel and hence the signal‑to‑noise ratio of nanobeam diffraction without any increase in flux, dose or exposure time.

Instead of spending the fixed beam time uniformly over a dense raster, redistribute it: sample the specimen sparsely/adaptively (e.g., a randomized or low‑discrepancy subset of scan points, or a coarse survey followed by dense measurement only of "interesting" regions identified on the fly) and give each measured point a correspondingly longer dwell time. Because the total dose/time budget is fixed, cutting the number of measured positions by a factor M lets each retained diffraction pattern be integrated M times longer, so its Bragg counts rise ∝ M while the shot noise rises only ∝ √M and the per‑frame read/dark noise stays constant — an immediate ~√M gain in the signal‑to‑noise ratio of each nanodiffraction pattern. The full strain/orientation map is then recovered from the undersampled data by compressed‑sensing / sparse (total‑variation, wavelet, or dictionary‑based) reconstruction, exploiting the fact that real nanostructure maps are highly compressible and strongly correlated between neighbouring points; the regularization itself further suppresses noise. This gives high‑SNR patterns at every retained point (and a low‑noise reconstructed map) without any change of source, optics, detector or sample, and with less accumulated radiation dose and drift.

Choose the diffraction condition so that the nanostructure's signal is intrinsically background‑free, i.e. measure a reflection that only the nanoscale volume of interest produces. In practice: exploit superlattice/satellite, forbidden‑for‑the‑matrix, or otherwise "dark‑field" reflections, or select an asymmetric reflection/lattice‑parameter mismatch that places the nanostructure's Bragg peak well away in reciprocal space from the substrate Bragg peak, its crystal‑truncation rod, thermal‑diffuse and multiple‑scattering streaks (and orient the crystal azimuthally to steer these strong parasitic features off the detector). Also engineer the sample environment to remove the dominant scatterers along the beam path — e.g. detach/thin the substrate, use an amorphous low‑Z or membrane support, or work in a grazing/exit geometry that limits the depth of illuminated matrix. Because the strong, unavoidable scattering from the surrounding bulk (which normally dwarfs and swamps the few counts from the ~10⁻²–1 µm³ nanobeam‑illuminated volume) is then simply not present in the detected region of reciprocal space, essentially every recorded photon belongs to the nanoscale object, so the signal‑to‑noise (signal‑to‑background) ratio improves by orders of magnitude with no change in incident flux, dose, optics, or counting time.

Put the "cleanup" on the **detection side** rather than the illumination side: define a confocal gauge volume by placing a collecting optic/collimator between sample and detector — e.g. a polycapillary half‑lens, a collimating channel array (CCA), a micro‑slit/pinhole pair, or a bent/analyzer crystal — whose acceptance volume is matched to and overlapped with the nanobeam focus. Only X‑rays originating from the tiny volume where the incident nanoprobe and the collection optic's field of view intersect can then reach the detector, while photons scattered from everywhere else along the beam path (air, entrance/exit windows, sample cell walls, the surrounding matrix, substrate, and the halo/tails of the focusing optic upstream and downstream of the focus) are geometrically blocked before detection. Because this parasitic scattering is normally what dominates the counts around a weak nanobeam Bragg peak, removing it leaves essentially only sample signal plus its own shot noise, so the signal‑to‑background (and hence signal‑to‑noise) ratio of the nanodiffraction pattern rises by orders of magnitude — with no extra flux, dose or counting time — and, as a bonus, the confocal arrangement gives depth resolution along the beam so buried nanoscale volumes can be probed selectively.

Exploit resonant field enhancement in the sample itself rather than more incident flux: set up an X‑ray standing‑wave/waveguide condition at the nanoscale volume of interest. Working at or just below the critical angle for total external reflection (or on a multilayer/mirror substrate, or with the crystalline film acting as a resonant cavity between a reflecting substrate and its surface), the incident and reflected waves interfere to form a standing wave whose antinode intensity is several times (and, in a true guided‑mode/waveguide cavity, one to two orders of magnitude) higher than the incident intensity. By tuning the incidence angle (or the cap‑layer thickness) so that an antinode coincides with the depth of the nanostructure/interface being probed, the local field driving the Bragg scattering — and hence the diffracted counts from the tiny nanobeam‑illuminated volume — is multiplied, while the evanescent/confined nature of the field simultaneously suppresses scattering from the underlying bulk, air and other parasitic material. The result is a large gain in signal‑to‑background (plus depth selectivity) with the same source, optics, dose and counting time.

Move the resolution‑defining element from the incident beam to the **exit side and detect in full‑field parallel** – i.e. use dark‑field X‑ray microscopy instead of a scanned nanoprobe. Illuminate a large area (a broad or line beam, so a huge volume diffracts at once) and place an X‑ray objective (compound refractive lens stack, multilayer Laue/zone‑plate objective, or a bent‑crystal imaging optic) in the diffracted beam, tuned to the Bragg condition and magnifying the sample onto a detector. The objective's narrow angular/energy acceptance acts as an angular filter that passes only photons Bragg‑scattered from the reflection of interest, rejecting air scatter, fluorescence, diffuse scattering and the substrate/matrix signal, while its magnification (×10–×100) makes the detector's pixel size and its dark/read noise irrelevant to the achieved nanoscale resolution. Because every resolution element of the field of view is recorded simultaneously rather than one at a time, the effective counting time (and hence accumulated Bragg counts) per image point is larger by the number of points in the image, so for the same total beam time the signal grows linearly while the shot noise grows only as its square root — yielding a signal‑to‑noise gain of orders of magnitude over point‑by‑point nanobeam diffraction, with less drift‑induced smearing and no need for a brighter source.

Multiplex the measurement: instead of illuminating one spot at a time with a single nanoprobe, split the incident beam into an array of many mutually separated nanofocused probes (e.g., with a lens/zone‑plate array, a multi‑beam diffractive splitter, or a set of segmented mirror facets), each hitting a different position on the sample with a slightly different angle/direction so that their Bragg signals land on distinct, non‑overlapping regions of one large‑area pixel detector. Every probe records its own nanodiffraction pattern simultaneously, so for a given total beam time each sample point is effectively exposed N times longer than in serial point‑by‑point scanning (N = number of probes). The Bragg counts per point therefore grow ∝ N while the shot noise grows only ∝ √N and the detector dark/read noise per frame is shared, giving roughly a √N improvement in signal‑to‑noise without any increase in source brightness, focal spot size, or dose per illuminated volume — and because the whole map is collected in a fraction of the time, drift and radiation‑damage smearing of the weak nanobeam signal are also reduced.

Match the probe size to the feature size instead of always focusing as tightly as possible — i.e. deliberately relax (or slightly defocus) the nanobeam to the largest spot still compatible with the spatial resolution actually needed. Because the diffracting volume, and hence the Bragg intensity, scales with the illuminated area (≈ d²) while the parasitic background from air, windows, optic tails and detector dark counts is essentially independent of focus, doubling the probe diameter gives ~4× more diffracted photons per exposure at nearly unchanged background, so the signal‑to‑noise ratio improves markedly for the same source, optics, dose‑rate and counting time. This also reduces the beam's convergence, sharpening the Bragg peak so the counts fall in fewer detector pixels, and relaxes the demands on positional stability (less drift smearing) — nanoscale detail can still be recovered afterwards by scanning in sub‑probe steps and deconvolving/reconstructing with the known probe profile.

Exploit the pulsed time structure of the source: instead of integrating continuously, run the area detector in a fast, bunch‑synchronised time‑gated mode, opening a sub‑nanosecond‑to‑nanosecond gate around the arrival of each X‑ray pulse (locked to the storage‑ring RF/bunch clock, with the gate delay set to the flight time to the detector) and keeping it closed the rest of the time. The Bragg photons from the nanobeam‑illuminated volume are emitted only during those pulses, whereas most of the noise — detector dark current and leakage, electronic/readout and 1/f noise, cosmic rays and stray room background, scattered visible light, and slowly decaying fluorescence/afterglow or phosphorescence from the sample, windows and sensor — accumulates uniformly in time. Because the gate's duty cycle can be 10⁻³–10⁻⁵ of the total measurement time, all of this time‑uncorrelated background is suppressed by the same factor while every useful diffracted photon is still counted, so the signal‑to‑noise ratio of the weak nanodiffraction pattern rises by orders of magnitude without any increase in flux, dose, or exposure time (and, as a bonus, the gating also gives access to time‑resolved/stroboscopic nanodiffraction).

Use an ultrabright pulsed source in a "one‑shot" mode rather than accumulating counts from a storage ring: at a hard‑X‑ray free‑electron laser (or an ERL/high‑repetition‑rate machine), a single self‑amplified/seeded pulse delivers ~10¹¹–10¹² coherent photons in femtoseconds, which can be nanofocused (KB/MLL optics) onto the sample so that the entire Bragg pattern from the tiny illuminated volume is recorded in one exposure with millions of photons instead of a few counts. Because the whole pattern is captured faster than any mechanical drift, vibration, thermal fluctuation, or sample/beam instability can act — and, in the "diffract‑before‑destroy" regime, faster than radiation damage develops — all of the low‑frequency (1/f), drift and damage‑related noise contributions that normally limit long nanobeam scans disappear, and the measurement becomes limited purely by photon shot noise of an enormous signal. Averaging many such single‑shot patterns (or sorting/gating them on pulse intensity and arrival, using per‑pulse I₀ normalization) then adds statistics without reintroducing drift, so the effective signal‑to‑noise of nanobeam diffraction is raised by orders of magnitude relative to slow, count‑limited scanning.

Exploit the redundancy that already exists in reciprocal space by capturing and merging **symmetry‑equivalent scattering** in a single measurement. Surround the nanobeam‑illuminated spot with as much detector solid angle as possible (a curved or tiled array of large pixel detectors, several modules at different 2θ/azimuths, or a single very large flat panel close to the sample) so that the complete Debye–Scherrer/Bragg rings and several symmetry‑equivalent reflections ({hkl} multiplets, Friedel pairs, powder/texture rings) are recorded simultaneously instead of only one small ROI. Then, after geometric (2θ, azimuth, polarisation, solid‑angle and absorption) corrections, azimuthally integrate the rings and merge/average all equivalent reflections into a single profile. Because each of the *n* equivalent measurements carries the same structural information, the merged signal adds coherently (∝ n) while the uncorrelated photon shot noise, detector dark/read noise and diffuse background average down only as √n — giving roughly a √n (often 10–100×) gain in signal‑to‑noise ratio for the same incident flux, exposure time and radiation dose; the spread among equivalents simultaneously provides a direct, internal error estimate (R‑merge) and reveals texture or strain anisotropy, and any ring segment contaminated by parasitic streaks or dead pixels can simply be masked out before merging.

Exploit the other, much brighter signals that a scanning nanoprobe produces at the same time, and fuse them with the weak Bragg data. In a nanobeam experiment one can record, simultaneously with the nanodiffraction frames, X‑ray fluorescence spectra, transmitted/absorption (and differential‑phase or transmission‑ptychography) signals from the very same probe positions. These modalities collect orders of magnitude more counts per point than the diffraction from the tiny coherently scattering volume, so they give a high‑fidelity, high‑SNR map of exactly where the probe was and what it illuminated.

Use this information in two ways:
1. **Registration/drift correction:** cross‑correlate the fluorescence or transmission maps of successive (fast) repeat scans to measure and undo sub‑probe thermal drift, positioner hysteresis and beam wander, then coherently sum the corresponding diffraction frames. The Bragg counts then add ∝ N without positional smearing, while shot and background noise grow only ∝ √N — the repeats become truly additive instead of blurring the map.
2. **Correlative/joint reconstruction:** feed the well‑determined element and mass/thickness distribution (and the reconstructed probe function from ptychography) into the analysis of the diffraction data as a prior — a joint, maximum‑likelihood/regularized inversion in which the boundaries, composition and illuminated volume are fixed by the high‑count modality and only the strain/orientation degrees of freedom are fitted to the sparse Bragg counts. Normalizing each frame by the simultaneously measured incident‑flux monitor further removes source‑intensity fluctuations from the data.

Because the noisy Bragg information is thereby constrained by, and averaged over, independently measured high‑statistics data (rather than being extracted frame‑by‑frame in isolation), the effective signal‑to‑noise ratio of the nanodiffraction result rises substantially with no change of source, optics, detector, dose or counting time.

Invent a new x-ray detector technology f.answer:
**Invention: The "Quasiparticle‑Funnel Kinetic Inductance Detector" (QF‑KID) — a gap‑engineered superconducting imaging spectrometer for 50 eV–2 keV photons.**

**Concept.** Instead of converting the X‑ray to heat (TES/MMC microcalorimeters) or to electron–hole pairs in silicon (CCD/CMOS/SDD), the photon is absorbed directly in a thin (50–200 nm) high‑Z superconducting film (Ta or Nb, capped for oxidation) whose energy gap is ~1 meV. A 500 eV photon therefore liberates ~10⁵ quasiparticles instead of ~140 electrons in Si, so the Fano‑limited resolution is ~0.2–0.4 eV FWHM rather than ~25–50 eV.

**Key innovation — the funnel.** The absorber is fabricated with a *deliberate lateral gradient in the superconducting gap*, created by graded proximity‑effect bilayer thickness (e.g., Ta thinning into an Al, then AlMn, then Hf region). This gradient produces a thermodynamic "downhill" that ballistically/diffusively funnels essentially all quasiparticles, before they recombine, into a nanoscale low‑gap (Hf/AlMn) sensing wire at the pixel edge. That wire is the inductor of a microwave resonator: the trapped quasiparticles change its kinetic inductance and produce a large, fast (µs) resonance shift. Funnelling solves the historic killer of superconducting tunnel‑junction detectors — quasiparticle loss and position‑dependent trapping — by making collection deterministic rather than diffusive‑random.

**Architecture.** Each resonator serves a "hydra" of 4–16 absorber tiles connected through weak thermal/quasiparticle links of different lengths; pulse rise‑time and the ratio of signals in two funnels at opposite ends encode which tile was hit and sub‑pixel position. Combined with frequency‑domain microwave multiplexing read out through a travelling‑wave parametric amplifier, this yields **10⁵–10⁶ imaging pixels on two coaxial lines**, versus a few thousand pixels for state‑of‑the‑art multiplexed TES arrays.

**Performance advantages over the current state of the art.**
- Energy resolution ~0.3 eV FWHM at 500 eV (E/ΔE > 1500), competitive with grating spectrometers but non‑dispersive and with ~unity efficiency.
- **No dead layer / no entrance window:** the metallic absorber is the first surface, so quantum efficiency stays near 100% down to ~50 eV, where thinned back‑illuminated CCDs and hybrid pixel sensors lose most of their charge.
- **Count rate ~10⁵ cps/pixel** (electronic, not thermal, recovery — quasiparticles recombine in µs) versus a few hundred cps/pixel for microcalorimeters.
- **Imaging + spectroscopy + ~10 ns timing simultaneously**, enabling single‑shot pump–probe work at XFELs and time‑resolved astronomy.
- Operates at 50–100 mK with a compact ADR (no bulky SQUID TDM chains, no dilution refrigerator), and scales lithographically.

**Applications.** Water‑window and soft X‑ray absorption/emission chemistry at synchrotrons and XFELs, X‑ray astronomy (O, C, N, Fe‑L line diagnostics of the warm–hot intergalactic medium), EUV/soft‑X‑ray lithography metrology, and low‑energy rare‑event searches.

**Invention: FOX‑Cal — the Fiber‑read Optomechanical X‑ray Calorimeter Array**

*A megapixel soft‑X‑ray imaging microcalorimeter whose thermometers are photonic‑crystal nanobeams read out entirely with light down a single optical fiber, replacing SQUID/microwave electrical readout.*

**Pixel concept.** Each pixel is a suspended silicon‑nitride photonic‑crystal nanobeam (optomechanical crystal) with an optical resonance in the telecom C‑band (Q ≈ 10⁶) and a co‑located MHz mechanical breathing mode. Bonded to the beam is a micron‑thick bismuth/gold absorber structured as a forest of sub‑wavelength nanopillars, giving >95 % stopping power from ~80 eV to 2 keV with **no entrance window and no dead layer** — the metal is the first surface. An absorbed photon deposits heat in the absorber, whose tiny heat capacity (fJ/K at 40 mK) produces a several‑hundred‑µK temperature step; this shifts the beam's optical resonance (via dn/dT and thermal stress) and simultaneously softens its mechanical frequency. Reading the *mechanical* frequency shift — a phase‑coherent, dimensionless quantity — rather than an amplitude gives a thermometer that is immune to laser‑intensity drift and self‑calibrating.

**Readout innovation.** Every nanobeam is evanescently coupled to one bus waveguide, and pixels are lithographically assigned distinct optical resonance wavelengths across the C+L bands. A single fiber carrying a stabilized frequency comb interrogates ~10⁴ pixels at once (wavelength‑division multiplexing), with each comb tooth demodulated at room temperature by a photonic‑integrated coherent receiver. Because the cold end carries only glass fibers and nanowatts of optical power — no coax, no HEMT amplifiers, no SQUIDs — the heat load per pixel is ~10⁻¹⁵ W, so **10⁵–10⁶ pixels fit on a single compact ADR** that today supports only a few thousand TES pixels.

**Performance vs. state of the art.**
- **Energy resolution ~0.5–1 eV FWHM at 500 eV** (E/ΔE ≈ 500–1000), matching or beating TES/MMC microcalorimeters and far exceeding silicon CCD/SDD (~40 eV).
- **Count rate ~10⁴–10⁵ cps/pixel**: the ultra‑low‑heat‑capacity nanobeam sensor and engineered thermal link give microsecond decay, versus millisecond‑limited TES pixels.
- **Complete magnetic and RF immunity** — the sensor is dielectric and optically coupled, removing the Earth‑field, SQUID‑crosstalk and EMI problems that plague TES/MMC arrays and that constrain them in magnet‑rich synchrotron/XFEL endstations and in spacecraft.
- **Scaling breaks the wiring bottleneck**: megapixel focal planes on two fibers, enabling true imaging spectroscopy over a wide field.
- Photonics fabrication (SiN on Si) is CMOS‑foundry compatible, so arrays are made at wafer scale and cheaply replicated.

**Extra capability.** The mechanical mode also senses *momentum*: a coincident phonon‑burst signature distinguishes true photon absorptions from substrate cosmic‑ray/thermal events, providing intrinsic background rejection valuable for X‑ray astronomy and rare‑event searches.

**Applications.** Water‑window and Fe‑L/O‑K emission spectroscopy at synchrotrons and XFELs, RIXS with non‑dispersive full‑band coverage, EUV lithography source metrology, and wide‑field soft‑X‑ray astrophysics of the warm–hot intergalactic medium.

**Invention: "GRAPHIC‑X" — a Gate‑Tunable Graphene Josephson‑Junction Self‑Amplifying Calorimeter Array for 50 eV–2 keV photons**

**Core idea.** Replace the TES/MMC thermometer (heat capacity ~10⁻¹⁵ J/K, ms time constants, SQUID readout) with a *suspended, gate‑tunable graphene Josephson junction* whose electronic heat capacity is ~10⁻²⁰–10⁻²¹ J/K at 50 mK — four to five orders of magnitude smaller than any current microcalorimeter.

**Pixel.** A monolayer graphene flake is suspended between two superconducting (NbN or Ta) leads, forming a ballistic Josephson junction. Bonded on top is a windowless "black" absorber of sub‑wavelength Bi/Au nanopillars (>95% absorption from ~50 eV to 2 keV, no entrance window, no dead layer, so QE stays near unity in the water window where back‑illuminated CCDs and hybrid pixel sensors collapse). An absorbed photon thermalizes into the graphene electron gas; because graphene's electron–phonon coupling is extremely weak at mK, the whole photon energy stays in the electrons, giving a large temperature step (mK‑scale for a 500 eV photon) that decays in microseconds through a lithographically set Andreev/Wiedemann‑Franz link.

**Transduction — the "self‑amplifying pixel."** The junction's Josephson inductance and switching current depend exponentially on electron temperature. Instead of merely loading a resonator, the junction *is* the nonlinear element of a Josephson parametric amplifier: each pixel is a λ/4 resonator pumped just below its parametric threshold, so a photon‑induced inductance change is amplified with 15–25 dB of quantum‑limited gain **inside the pixel itself**, before any wiring. Readout noise, HEMT noise, and cable loss therefore no longer set the resolution — the detector is intrinsically thermodynamically limited.

**Unique capability — electrostatic tuning.** A local gate sets graphene's carrier density: near the Dirac point the heat capacity is minimal (maximum energy resolution, small dynamic range); at high doping the pixel is stiffer (large dynamic range, higher count rate). Each pixel can thus be *tuned in situ*, in software, to the experiment — impossible with fixed‑C TES/MMC devices — and gate‑modulated calibration provides continuous per‑pixel gain tracking without an external X‑ray calibration source.

**Multiplexing.** Purely microwave, frequency‑domain: 2,000–5,000 pixels per coaxial pair (helped by the in‑pixel gain, which relaxes the need for a shared quantum‑limited amplifier), for focal planes of 10⁴–10⁵ pixels on a compact 50–100 mK ADR — no SQUID time‑division chains, no dilution refrigerator.

**Performance vs. state of the art.**
- **Energy resolution 0.1–0.5 eV FWHM at 500 eV** (E/ΔE ≈ 1,000–5,000), 10–50× better than the best soft‑X‑ray TES arrays (~1–2 eV) and ~100× better than SDD/CCD (~40 eV), with non‑dispersive full‑band coverage and ~unity efficiency (unlike gratings).
- **Count rate 10⁵–10⁶ cps/pixel** and ~10 ns arrival‑time tagging, set by the femtojoule‑per‑kelvin heat capacity, versus a few hundred cps/pixel for microcalorimeters — matching XFEL and 4th‑generation synchrotron flux.
- **Windowless, dead‑layer‑free** response down to ~50 eV.
- Graphene/NbN devices are lithographic and wafer‑scalable; junctions are magnetic‑field‑resilient compared with SQUID readout when shielded, and the parametric readout tolerates RF‑noisy endstations.

**Applications.** Water‑window and Fe‑L/O‑K/N‑K emission and RIXS chemistry at XFELs and synchrotrons, single‑shot pump–probe spectroscopy, EUV/soft‑X‑ray source metrology, and wide‑field soft‑X‑ray astrophysics of the warm–hot intergalactic medium.

**Invention: “CANDI‑X” — the Cascade‑Quantized Superconducting Nanowire Digital Imaging Spectrometer for 50 eV–2 keV photons**

*A windowless, 2–4 K (cryocooler‑only) soft‑X‑ray detector that measures photon energy **digitally**, by counting how many parallel superconducting nanowire elements an absorbed photon switches, and measures position by delay‑line timing — replacing both the charge‑integrating silicon CCD/SDD and the millikelvin microcalorimeter.*

**Pixel physics.** The active layer is a 60–120 nm amorphous WSi (or MoSi) film — one soft‑X‑ray attenuation length thick, so absorption is >90 % from ~50 eV to 2 keV with *no entrance window and no dead layer*, exactly where back‑illuminated CCDs and hybrid pixel sensors lose their signal. The film is patterned into a “cascade cell”: N = 64–256 nanowires (~80 nm wide) wired **in parallel**, all biased just below their common switching current. An absorbed X‑ray deposits its energy in a micron‑scale hotspot; the wire under the hotspot goes normal and dumps its bias current into its neighbours, which in turn switch, and the avalanche propagates outward until the deposited energy is exhausted. The **number of switched wires, k, is quantized and very nearly linear in photon energy**, because each wire needs a fixed threshold energy (~2–5 eV of quasiparticle energy) to be pushed over its critical current.

**Key innovation 1 — digital, amplifier‑noise‑immune spectroscopy.** Energy is read as an *integer count* k of unit current steps (each ~10 µA, i.e. a huge, uniform quantum of signal), not as an analogue pulse height. Amplifier noise, cable loss, gain drift, and thermal‑bath drift therefore do not enter the energy measurement at all — the only limits are the Fano‑like statistics of the avalanche and threshold uniformity. This eliminates the gain‑calibration burden that dominates operation of TES/MMC and SDD systems.

**Key innovation 2 — graded critical‑current “ruler.”** The parallel wires are lithographically fabricated with a monotonic gradient in width (and hence switching threshold) across the cell. The avalanche stops at the wire whose threshold exceeds the remaining energy, so the cascade is *self‑terminating* and its stopping point is a direct, linearized energy scale — this suppresses the runaway/latching and the strong nonlinearity that has prevented ordinary SNSPDs from being spectrometers.

**Key innovation 3 — delay‑line, two‑wire readout of a megapixel focal plane.** Each cascade cell is tapped into a superconducting microstrip delay line; reading both ends gives sub‑50 ps timing differences → 10–20 µm position along the line, while the total step height gives k. A 10⁶‑cell focal plane needs only a handful of coaxial lines and room‑temperature TDCs — no SQUID multiplexer chains, no microwave resonator combs, no quantum‑limited parametric amplifiers.

**Performance vs. the state of the art.**
- **Energy resolution ≈ 3–8 eV FWHM at 500 eV** (E/ΔE ≈ 60–150): ~6–10× better than the best silicon SDD/CCD (~40–60 eV) and far better than any room‑temperature detector, while covering the whole band non‑dispersively with ~unity efficiency (unlike gratings).
- **Count rate 10⁶–10⁷ photons/s per chip and ~50 ps arrival‑time tagging** — the recovery time is the nanowire kinetic‑inductance reset (a few ns), i.e. 10³–10⁴× faster than millisecond microcalorimeters, matching XFEL and 4th‑generation synchrotron flux and enabling single‑shot pump–probe and photon‑correlation work.
- **Operates at 2–4 K on a compact closed‑cycle cryocooler**, not at 50 mK on an ADR/dilution fridge — an order‑of‑magnitude reduction in cost, size, power, and hold‑time constraints, and thus deployable on small satellites, beamline endstations, and even in industry.
- **Zero dark current and zero read noise**, so single 100 eV photons are detected with no threshold penalty; intrinsically radiation‑hard (amorphous superconductor, no charge collection, no displacement‑damage‑sensitive depletion region).
- **Cosmic‑ray/charged‑particle rejection**: minimum‑ionizing tracks produce long, multi‑cell, characteristically shaped avalanches that are trivially vetoed by topology — a major advantage for astrophysics and rare‑event searches.

**Applications.** Water‑window (C‑K, N‑K, O‑K) and Fe‑L emission spectroscopy and RIXS at XFELs/synchrotrons where flux, not ultimate resolution, is the bottleneck; time‑resolved soft‑X‑ray scattering and photon‑correlation spectroscopy; EUV/soft‑X‑ray lithography source and mask metrology; and low‑cost, cryocooler‑only soft‑X‑ray imaging spectrometers for CubeSat‑class astrophysics missions.

Name an effect that limits the coherence.answer: Mechanical vibrations of the beamline optics (e.g. jitter of the monochromator crystals or mirrors) act as a decohering effect – the time‑averaged wavefront distortion/beam motion blurs the speckle pattern and reduces the measured degree of coherence (speckle contrast) at a coherent X‑ray scattering beamline.

Finite monochromaticity — the limited energy bandwidth (ΔE/E) transmitted by the monochromator restricts the longitudinal (temporal) coherence length. Path‑length differences in the sample larger than this coherence length cause the scattered waves to add incoherently, smearing the speckle pattern and reducing its contrast at a coherent X‑ray scattering beamline.

The finite source size (the storage‑ring electron‑beam emittance) limits the transverse (spatial) coherence. Because the source is an extended, incoherent emitter, the transverse coherence length at the sample is only λ·L/(2πσ_source); apertures/beam larger than this let mutually incoherent wavefronts overlap, washing out the speckle contrast at a coherent X‑ray scattering beamline.

Imperfections of the optical surfaces – i.e., figure errors and micro‑roughness (plus inhomogeneities/grain structure in windows such as Be) of the mirrors, lenses and crystals. These static wavefront distortions scatter the beam and imprint spurious speckle/phase errors on the illumination, effectively degrading the wavefront quality and reducing the measured coherence (speckle contrast) at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

Thermal (heat‑load) distortion of the optics – the high power of the white beam heats the first monochromator crystal (and mirrors), causing time‑varying thermal bumps/strain that distort and move the wavefront. This dynamic wavefront aberration acts as a decohering effect, blurring the speckle pattern and lowering the measured coherence at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

Finite detector resolution — the pixel size and point‑spread function of the area detector (together with the finite pixel solid angle) average over several speckles, so the recorded speckle contrast (measured degree of coherence) is reduced, acting as an effective decohering/coherence‑limiting effect at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

Incoherent (Compton/inelastic and fluorescence) scattering: photons scattered inelastically by the sample lose phase relation to the incident wave and add a structureless background to the diffraction pattern, so the measured speckle contrast (degree of coherence) is reduced at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

Temporal averaging during the finite detector exposure/integration time: because the measurement integrates over a period longer than the characteristic timescale of the sample's (or the beam's) fluctuations, many independent speckle realizations are summed, washing out the speckle pattern and lowering the measured contrast (apparent degree of coherence) at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

Parasitic/diffuse scattering from beamline windows, slits and residual air along the flight path. This background of scattered photons has no fixed phase relation to the coherently scattered beam, so it adds a smooth incoherent intensity on top of the speckle pattern, lowering the measured speckle contrast (degree of coherence) at a coherent x-ray scattering beamline.

Instability of the source itself – i.e. electron‑beam orbit motion/position‑and‑angle jitter of the storage‑ring source during the measurement. Averaged over the exposure this enlarges the effective source size (and moves the illuminating wavefront), reducing the transverse coherence length at the sample and washing out speckle contrast at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

Instability of the sample stage – mechanical vibration and thermal drift of the sample (or of the sample cell/holder) during the exposure. Because the illuminated volume shifts by a fraction of the beam size, the speckle pattern moves/changes and successive realizations are averaged in the recorded image, blurring the speckles and lowering the measured contrast (apparent degree of coherence) at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

Turbulence/density (refractive‑index) fluctuations in the gas along the beam path – e.g. air or the He in the flight tubes and sample environment. These time‑varying refractive‑index cells imprint random, fluctuating phase distortions on the wavefront; averaged over the exposure they blur the wavefront and shift the speckles, thereby degrading the effective coherence (speckle contrast) at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

Higher‑order harmonic contamination of the "monochromatic" beam. Harmonics (e.g. the 3rd order reflected by the monochromator) pass through the optics together with the fundamental; each wavelength produces its own, differently scaled speckle pattern, and since the different harmonics are mutually incoherent they simply add in intensity. This superposition of incoherent, mismatched speckle patterns (plus the extra smooth background they generate) washes out the fringes and lowers the measured speckle contrast/degree of coherence at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

Path‑length (optical‑path) differences within a thick sample at large scattering angles: when the sample thickness/scattering geometry makes the difference in path lengths of the interfering waves exceed the longitudinal coherence length, the scattered waves no longer interfere fully, so the speckle contrast (measured degree of coherence) drops at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

Multiple scattering within a thick or strongly scattering sample. When photons scatter more than once before leaving the specimen, the exit wave is a superposition of many differently‑delayed and randomly phased scattering paths (with path‑length spreads that can exceed the longitudinal coherence length). These contributions add largely incoherently, producing a smooth diffuse background over the singly‑scattered speckle pattern and thereby lowering the measured speckle contrast (apparent degree of coherence) at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

X‑ray–induced (beam‑damage/heating) dynamics in the sample: the intense coherent beam locally heats and progressively alters the illuminated volume, so the speckle pattern continuously evolves and decorrelates during the measurement, washing out the speckle contrast and appearing as a loss of coherence at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

The finite angular divergence of the incident beam (e.g. the large convergence angle introduced by focusing optics such as CRLs or KB mirrors). Each incident direction within the divergence cone produces its own slightly shifted speckle pattern, and since these directions are mutually incoherent their intensities add, smearing the speckles and lowering the measured contrast/degree of coherence at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

Chromatic aberration of the focusing optics (e.g., compound refractive lenses/Fresnel zone plates): because their focal length depends on wavelength, the finite bandwidth of the beam spreads the focus longitudinally and distorts the wavefront, so different wavelength components illuminate the sample with different (mutually incoherent) wavefields. Their intensities add, blurring the speckle pattern and reducing the effective/measured coherence at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

Polarization mixing (finite/partial polarization of the beam). At large scattering angles the scattered field contains orthogonal polarization components — and any depolarization introduced by optics or the sample — which cannot interfere with one another. Their intensities simply add, so the speckle pattern is partially washed out and the measured degree of coherence (speckle contrast) is reduced at a coherent x‑ray scattering beamline.

Drift/jitter of the photon energy itself – i.e. instability of the monochromator (crystal angle drift, undulator gap/taper drift) that makes the selected wavelength wander during the exposure. Since the speckle pattern scales with λ, an energy drift makes the speckles shift/breathe, so the recorded image is a sum of slightly different speckle realizations, blurring the pattern and lowering the measured speckle contrast (apparent degree of coherence) at a coherent x-ray scattering beamline.

How to accurately do peak labelling in X.answer:
The only reliable way is to assign every reflection by comparison with known reference patterns rather than by eye/"expected" values. In practice:

1. Convert the raw data to a wavelength‑independent scale (d‑spacing or scattering vector q = 4π sinθ/λ) so patterns collected with different sources/instruments (Cu, Mo, synchrotron, SAXS/WAXS) can be compared directly, and calibrate the instrument with a standard (e.g. Si, LaB₆, silver behenate) to correct for zero‑shift/sample‑displacement errors.

2. Obtain a reference pattern for each candidate phase/polymorph – either measured on the phase‑pure material under identical conditions, or simulated from its single‑crystal/CIF structure (ICDD‑PDF, CSD, ICSD databases) – and overlay/match the full set of peak positions **and** relative intensities, not just one or two peaks. A phase is only assigned when all of its characteristic reflections are present in the right positions and ratios; unique, non‑overlapping "marker" peaks should be chosen for each polymorph in a mixture.

3. Index the matched peaks with their Miller indices (hkl) from the known unit cell of that phase, and label each peak in the plot with both the phase identity (e.g. by symbol/colour code, α‑form vs β‑form) and its hkl; state the wavelength used and give positions in 2θ (with λ) or in q/d.

4. For overlapping or ambiguous peaks in mixtures, do a whole‑pattern fit (Le Bail/Pawley or Rietveld multiphase refinement) rather than manual peak picking; this deconvolutes overlaps, confirms the assignment, corrects for preferred orientation/peak shifts and gives quantitative phase fractions. Report unassigned peaks explicitly as impurity/unknown instead of forcing an assignment.

5. Support ambiguous assignments with complementary evidence (variable‑temperature/in‑situ XRD, DSC, Raman/IR, ss‑NMR, electron diffraction) and, where possible, deposit/publish the raw data so the labelling can be verified.

Treat peak labelling as an *evidence‑based assignment exercise*, not a cosmetic annotation, and show the evidence in the figure itself:

1. **Collect data suitable for labelling first.** Use a wide 2θ/q range, adequate counting statistics and step size to resolve close reflections, a monochromatic (Kβ‑/W‑filtered) beam, spinning/randomised sample to avoid preferred orientation, and a calibration standard to fix zero‑offset and sample‑displacement errors. Peaks arising from the substrate, sample holder, capillary, air/amorphous halo or Kβ/tungsten contamination must be identified and marked as such (e.g. with an asterisk) before anything is assigned to the sample.

2. **Build a stick (tick‑mark) reference for every candidate polymorph.** Either simulate the pattern from the published crystal structure (CIF/ICSD/CSD/PDF entry) at the same wavelength, or measure a phase‑pure sample of each form on the same instrument. Plot these as separate, colour‑coded tick‑mark rows directly beneath the experimental trace, so the reader can see that *all* the expected reflections of a phase are present at the correct positions and with sensible relative intensities — never assign a phase from one peak alone.

3. **Label using unique, non‑overlapping reflections.** For each polymorph choose its "fingerprint" peaks that do not coincide with those of the other forms, and mark them with a distinct symbol/colour plus the phase name (α/β/form I/II) and, where the cell is known, the (hkl) index. Broad shoulders and unresolved overlaps should not be given a single label.

4. **Confirm ambiguous assignments experimentally.** Spike/mix the sample with a known amount of the suspected pure phase (peaks should grow, not shift), or follow the sample through a controlled transformation (variable‑temperature/humidity or in‑situ XRD) and check that the labelled peaks appear/disappear together as a set.

5. **Verify numerically and tabulate.** Perform a multiphase Pawley/Le Bail or Rietveld fit and show the difference curve; then report a table of observed 2θ (with stated λ), d‑spacing/q, relative intensity, assigned hkl and phase for every labelled peak, and explicitly flag any peak that remains unassigned as "unknown/impurity" rather than forcing it onto a phase. Provide the raw data so others can re‑check the labelling.
