**Why it hasn't been discovered:** Noble gases have filled shells, the highest ionisation energies and the lowest polarisabilities in the periodic table; helium's is so extreme that any species electrophilic enough to bind it would normally rip apart its own ligands, solvent or counterion first. Known noble‑gas compounds require the most oxidising elements, cryogenic matrices, or extreme pressure, and are neither catalytic nor reversible. Realising it requires ligand frameworks that can support a naked, unquenched electrophilic centre in bulk matter, nanoconfinement that supplies the missing binding energy through compression and dispersion, and a predictive theory of very weak, dispersion‑ and relativity‑dominated covalency — in short, a chemistry of bonding to atoms that, by definition, do not want to bond.

**Proposed reaction class: "concerted multi‑electron/multi‑proton transfer" — a genuinely many‑body elementary step in which four, six or eight electrons and their protons are exchanged simultaneously in one act, with no high‑energy one‑electron intermediate, allowing redox chemistry to run at essentially zero overpotential.**

**What it is:** Every redox reaction we know is stitched together from one‑electron (or at best two‑electron) elementary steps. Chemistry's foundational assumption is that elementary events are unimolecular or bimolecular, so a 4e⁻/4H⁺ transformation such as 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, or N₂ → 2NH₃ (6e⁻/6H⁺), or CO₂ → CH₃OH, must pass through fragile radical intermediates (•OH, *OOH, diazenyl, CO₂•⁻). Because the free energies of those intermediates are locked to one another by scaling relations, every catalyst — natural or synthetic — must overshoot the thermodynamic potential by 0.3–0.5 V just to make the worst intermediate accessible. That overshoot is the single largest, most universal energy tax in chemistry.

The undiscovered reaction would abolish the intermediates altogether. It requires a catalyst that behaves as a *collective electron and proton reservoir*: a redox‑non‑innocent cluster or delocalised lattice that can hold several electrons at nearly the same potential (an "electron sponge" with no energetic staircase), rigidly coupled to a pre‑organised hydrogen‑bond network that positions all the protons in advance, so that bond breaking and bond making across four or more atoms occur in one concerted, low‑barrier passage over a single transition state. The reaction coordinate is a correlated motion of many nuclei and electrons at once — energy being exchanged with a collective mode of the catalyst rather than being dumped into and retrieved from a discrete radical. Because no intermediate is ever populated, the reaction is microscopically reversible and runs at, or within millivolts of, its equilibrium potential in both directions.

**Why it will be essential in 100 years:** A civilisation running on renewable electricity is a civilisation that continuously converts electrons into bonds and back — water into hydrogen, air into ammonia and fertiliser, CO₂ into fuels, polymers and food precursors, and all of these back into power on demand. Every one of those conversions is today throttled by overpotential: electrolysers, fuel cells, CO₂ reducers and flow batteries typically lose 25–40 % of their energy at the electrode, and lose it *twice* in any storage cycle. Zero‑overpotential chemistry would roughly halve the primary energy needed by the entire electrified chemical and energy economy, make long‑duration storage round‑trip efficient enough to replace fossil firming, allow seasonal energy to be shipped as chemical bonds without penalty, and make ambient‑condition synthesis of ammonia, fuels and carbon feedstocks cheaper than the fossil routes they must replace. It would also remove the need for scarce precious‑metal catalysts, whose value lies almost entirely in mitigating this same intermediate problem, and it would make each reaction cleanly reversible — so a single device could be an electrolyser at noon and a fuel cell at midnight, and a single reactor could both fix and release carbon or nitrogen.

**Why it hasn't been discovered:** Nothing in current theory tells us how to make a truly multi‑body elementary step. Transition‑state theory, mechanism determination and catalyst design are all built on sequential single‑electron events; concerted proton–electron transfer is known only in its 1e⁻/1H⁺ form. Nature has never solved it either — photosystem II's manganese cluster still accumulates four charges in discrete S‑states and still pays an overpotential. Realising it demands materials that can store multiple electrons with degenerate redox potentials without disproportionating, proton wires with sub‑ångström positional discipline, and, most fundamentally, a new kinetic theory of correlated many‑particle transition states that goes beyond the one‑bond‑at‑a‑time picture chemistry has used since Eyring.

**Proposed reaction class: "catalytic bond‑order inversion" — the ambient‑condition, catalytic conversion of a stable multiply‑bonded molecule into a metastable single‑bonded extended solid, and its catalysed reversion on demand (the archetype: N₂ ⇌ polymeric "cubic‑gauche" nitrogen).**

**What it is:** Every reaction chemists run today ends in the thermodynamic sink; we have no general way to *deliberately climb* into a deep kinetic trap and then hold matter there. This reaction class would do exactly that. A catalyst — most likely a two‑dimensional templating surface or a nanoconfined framework that supplies the missing compression through chemical rather than mechanical pressure — would bind N₂ end‑to‑on, back‑donate enough electron density to depopulate the π system, and then *stitch* the resulting nitrogen atoms into a three‑dimensional network of N–N single bonds, propagating the polymerisation autocatalytically along the growing lattice edge. Today this requires >110 GPa and ~2000 K in a diamond anvil cell and yields micrograms; the undiscovered chemistry would do it at one atmosphere and room temperature, driven by renewable electricity or light, with the catalyst supplying the electronic (not the physical) pressure. The mirror half of the reaction is equally new: a second catalyst that *lowers* the enormous kinetic barrier back down, so the metastable solid can be depolymerised at a chosen rate rather than detonating — "catalysed uncontrolled‑release prevention," turning an explosive into a fuel. Generalised, the same principle would apply to metallic/polymeric hydrogen, extended‑solid CO, carbon nitrides and other high‑enthalpy allotropes: a chemistry whose product variable is not composition but *bond order and kinetic depth*.

**Why it will be essential in 100 years:** Single‑bonded nitrogen stores roughly 10 kJ/g — several times the best chemical explosives and far above any battery — and releases it by reverting to ordinary N₂ gas. Its only combustion product is air. A catalytic route to it would give the twenty‑second century (i) a gravimetric energy store that beats lithium chemistry by an order of magnitude, making electric aviation, heavy shipping and grid‑scale seasonal storage genuinely possible; (ii) a clean, high‑specific‑impulse propellant that emits nitrogen, ending the dependence of spaceflight and defence on carbon‑ and toxin‑laden propellants; (iii) a way to store renewable electricity as a *solid* that can be stockpiled indefinitely, shipped in a sack rather than a cryogenic tank, and consumed anywhere without infrastructure; and (iv) more broadly, control of the kinetic dimension of matter — the ability to park energy in a metastable phase and withdraw it catalytically, which is the missing capability in a civilisation whose energy supply is intermittent but whose demand is not.

**Why it hasn't been discovered:** Nothing in chemistry currently substitutes for pressure. Catalysts lower barriers; they do not change which phase is thermodynamically preferred, and here the target phase lies ~200 kJ/mol *above* the reactant and is separated from it by the strongest bond in main‑group chemistry. Achieving it needs a catalyst that acts as a chemical analogue of a megabar — confinement plus electron back‑donation sufficient to invert the relative stability of N≡N and N–N *within the catalyst's coordination sphere* — plus templated, self‑propagating growth so the network extends beyond the active site instead of relaxing back to gas, plus a theory of how to design and then *stabilise* deep kinetic traps rather than avoid them. It is the inverse of everything catalysis has been for two centuries: a reaction engineered not to reach equilibrium but to escape it, and to be held there until called upon.

**Proposed reaction class: "quantum‑light‑driven synthesis" — chemistry driven by entangled and squeezed photon pairs, in which two (or more) correlated photons deliver their combined energy to a molecule as a single, cooperative event.**

**What it is:** All photochemistry today is one‑photon chemistry. To do anything genuinely hard — split N≡N, break a C–F bond, cleave a Si–O or a lattice metal–oxide bond, drive a 4‑electron oxidation in one go — you need a UV photon that sunlight barely supplies and that indiscriminately damages everything it hits. Multiphoton routes exist but scale with the *square* of intensity, so they require lasers and are useless at ambient light levels. The undiscovered reaction class exploits *nonclassical* light: time‑ and energy‑entangled photon pairs (and squeezed, number‑correlated beams) arrive at a chromophore within femtoseconds of each other and with anticorrelated energies, so their absorption is a linear, not quadratic, process. Two cheap red or infrared photons then perform the chemistry of one expensive ultraviolet one, at vanishing photon flux. Because the pair is entangled, the *pair itself* is the reagent: its joint spectral correlations can be shaped so that only one specific two‑quantum transition in one specific molecule or one specific site of a solid is addressed, and the two photons can even be routed to two different centres of a catalyst so that a two‑electron or two‑bond step is triggered in a single concerted act rather than through a radical intermediate. Selectivity comes from quantum correlation — from the *state* of the light, not its colour or intensity — and reaction "recipes" become photon‑state recipes, generated by a nonlinear crystal or a quantum light source rather than mixed in a flask.

**Why it will be essential in 100 years:** It removes the fundamental mismatch between the energy of sunlight and the energy of the bonds we most need to break. A civilisation that must run its entire chemical industry on ambient renewable photons cannot afford to convert them first to electricity, then to heat, then to UV; entangled‑pair chemistry lets low‑energy, abundant photons do high‑energy work directly and at near‑unity quantum yield, because no energy is wasted populating hot, damaging intermediates. That means solar destruction of PFAS, dioxins and pharmaceutical residues in dilute water; direct photo‑activation of N₂, CO₂ and CH₄ under sunlight; photolithography‑free, light‑programmed fabrication of solids; and — because the quadratic intensity requirement disappears — deep‑tissue photochemistry and photodynamic medicine driven by faint, harmless near‑infrared light that becomes reactive only where the photon pairs are focused. Equally important, the correlations of the light survive scattering statistics, so reactions can be initiated deep inside opaque, turbid, or living media, and the same light source can be reprogrammed to address a different bond by re‑engineering the entanglement rather than the catalyst.

**Why it hasn't been discovered:** Entangled two‑photon absorption cross‑sections measured so far are extremely small and fiercely contested — many early large values have failed replication — and bright, broadband, tunable sources of entangled light are laboratory instruments, not process equipment. There is as yet no theory that tells a chemist which molecular or catalytic architectures have large *entangled* (as opposed to classical) two‑photon cross‑sections, no design rules for matching a photon pair's joint spectral amplitude to a molecule's virtual‑state structure, and no way to keep quantum correlations alive in a warm, dense, scattering reaction medium. The breakthrough will require chromophores and catalysts engineered as quantum‑optical antennas, macroscopic sources of correlated photons, and a merged discipline of quantum optics and reaction kinetics in which the entangled state of the light is written into the mechanism itself.

**Proposed reaction class: "catalytic carbon‑atom transfer from elemental carbon" — the ambient‑condition, catalytic abstraction of single carbon atoms out of a solid carbon lattice (graphite, soot, char, diamond, amorphous carbon) and their direct insertion into growing molecules.**

**What it is.** Elemental carbon is, chemically speaking, a dead end: sp² sheets held by ~5–7 eV C–C bonds that nothing attacks except O₂ at high temperature. To use carbon as a feedstock today we must first burn or gasify it to CO/CO₂, then laboriously re‑reduce that carbon back down through syngas, Fischer–Tropsch or methanol chemistry — paying a huge oxidation/re‑reduction energy round trip and emitting CO₂ at every stage. The undiscovered reaction would skip the oxide entirely. A "carbon‑abstraction catalyst" — a metal or main‑group centre with a vacant, carbyne‑stabilising orbital manifold, working at a lattice edge or defect and assisted by strain, electrochemical bias, or a redox‑cycling shuttle — would grip a single edge carbon, cleave its remaining lattice bonds, and carry it away as a bound carbide/carbyne (M≡C) fragment. That fragment is then delivered, catalytically and stereospecifically, into an organic substrate: inserted into a C–H bond, coupled to a second carbon to extend a chain, converted to a carbene for cyclopropanation, or strung into an alkyne or aromatic ring. The catalyst is regenerated, and the solid simply erodes, atom by atom, into designed molecules. Run in reverse, the same catalyst *deposits* atoms — writing graphite, diamond or carbyne one carbon at a time at room temperature instead of by CVD at 1000 °C. Selectivity would come from which lattice site the catalyst can reach and which acceptor bond it can bind, so a single "carbon‑mining" catalyst plus a library of acceptors would replace whole sectors of petrochemistry.

**Why it will be essential in 100 years.** The twenty‑second century's carbon problem is not making CO₂ — it is that carbon, once captured, has nowhere useful to go. The cheapest, safest and most permanent way to take carbon out of the air is to reduce it all the way to a solid (biochar, pyrolysis black, methane‑pyrolysis carbon, mineralised soot) — but that solid is then inert waste to be buried, and the chemical industry meanwhile still digs up oil for its carbon atoms. Catalytic carbon‑atom transfer would fuse the two halves: sequestered solid carbon becomes the *only* feedstock the chemical industry needs, and every polymer, pharmaceutical, fibre and fuel is built directly from it, atom by atom, with no gasification, no syngas, no fossil hydrocarbon, and no oxidation penalty. Carbon becomes a genuinely circular, stockpilable currency — mined from the air, stored as an inert black solid indefinitely, and drawn down on demand. It also makes carbon the *ideal* material for a closed economy: waste plastics, tyres and composites can be pyrolysed to crude char and then re‑issued as pure atoms rather than sorted and re‑purified. And because the reverse direction writes carbon lattices at ambient temperature, it delivers atomically perfect diamond, graphene and carbyne structural materials, electronics and membranes without furnaces — decisive for space habitats and lunar/Martian settlements, where carbon is scarce, energy is precious, and regolith‑derived char plus this reaction is the whole organic chemistry supply chain.

**Why it hasn't been discovered.** Removing one atom from a graphite sheet costs roughly 7 eV and leaves three dangling bonds; no known catalyst can pay that with chemical driving force at ambient temperature, and the intermediate — a naked, terminally bound carbon atom — is one of the most reactive species conceivable, so it would immediately insert into the catalyst's own ligands or re‑deposit as soot. Metal carbides, the obvious precedent, are thermodynamic sinks that release carbon only via oxidation. Realising it requires ligand architectures that can stabilise a metal–carbide fragment while still making it transferable (a "carbon shuttle" with tuned M≡C bond strength, analogous to the hydride shuttles of hydrogenation), edge/defect engineering that turns the lattice into a reagent with definable site reactivity, and electrochemical or photochemical driving that supplies the abstraction energy in single‑atom increments. Above all it needs a theory of *solid‑to‑molecule atom transfer* — a chemistry in which a bulk element, not a molecule, is the substrate and its individual atoms have turnover numbers.

**Proposed reaction class: "directed radiolytic catalysis" — selective, catalyst‑controlled synthesis driven directly by ionizing radiation, in which the MeV energy of a nuclear decay or cosmic particle is captured, down‑converted, and funnelled into one designated bond of one designated molecule.**

**What it is:** Today, ionizing radiation is chemically useless except as a blunt instrument: a single alpha, beta or gamma quantum carries millions of electron‑volts, ~10⁵ times a bond energy, and dumps it along a random track as a chaotic spray of ionizations, hot electrons and radicals. The result is indiscriminate damage — the reason radiation sterilizes, degrades polymers, and corrodes reactors. The undiscovered reaction class would tame it. The "catalyst" is a hybrid antenna–reactor material: a dense scintillator or high‑Z semiconductor lattice that stops the particle and converts its energy into a large population of excitons and thermalized charge carriers, coupled through engineered energy‑transfer channels to molecular active sites that can only accept quanta of one specific energy and geometry. Radicals and hot carriers formed off‑target are quenched and recycled back into the exciton pool rather than reacting; only the resonant, pre‑organized site opens a chemical channel. One decay event would then produce not scattered damage but a stoichiometric burst of hundreds of identical, chosen bond‑forming events — N₂ → NH₃, CO₂ → C–C, H₂O → H₂/O₂, or a designed C–H functionalization — with quantum yields approaching the thermodynamic limit rather than the ~1–5% of present radiolysis. Selectivity would come from the energy‑transfer architecture (which acceptor states exist and where they sit), not from thermal activation barriers, so the reaction runs at any temperature, including cryogenic, and needs no electricity, light, or high‑grade heat.

**Why it will be essential in 100 years:** It would make radioactivity a synthetic reagent instead of a liability. Spent nuclear fuel and fission products contain enormous, continuously delivered energy that we currently spend money and concrete to *throw away* as decay heat over centuries; directed radiolytic catalysis would let a waste canister itself become a chemical plant, quietly manufacturing hydrogen, ammonia or fuels for decades with no moving parts, no turbines, and no conversion losses — turning the century's most expensive waste stream into distributed, weather‑independent chemical production, and shortening its custodial burden by consuming the energy rather than storing it. The same principle powers deep‑space and outer‑planet operations, where sunlight is negligible but radioisotopes and cosmic/Jovian radiation are ubiquitous: habitats and probes could synthesize propellant, oxygen and organics directly from the radiation field that presently only harms them, so shielding mass becomes productive infrastructure. On Earth it enables sealed, gridless, maintenance‑free reactors for remote or emergency use, and — run in the protective direction — the same energy‑funnelling materials would make polymers, electronics and biological tissue radiation‑immune by harvesting incoming quanta before they can damage anything, which is the key enabling technology for long‑duration human spaceflight and for reactor and fusion‑blanket materials that must survive decades of flux.

**Why it hasn't been discovered:** Radiation chemistry has no concept of selectivity. The initial event is nonequilibrium, femtosecond, and spatially inhomogeneous — a dense track of ions and excited states whose fate is decided long before any catalyst can intervene — and no theory currently connects track structure to product distribution well enough to design against it. We would need materials that stop particles, convert their energy into a coherent, transferable form faster than radical chemistry occurs (sub‑picosecond), transport it many nanometres to a chosen site without loss, and simultaneously self‑heal the lattice damage every event creates — a fusion of scintillator physics, exciton engineering, and catalysis that does not exist as a discipline. It is chemistry in which the reagent is a decaying nucleus and the mechanism is energy flow through a solid, not a collision between molecules.

**Proposed reaction class: "tunnelling‑controlled catalysis" — catalysis that works by making a barrier *thin* rather than *low*, so that whole heavy atoms (C, N, O, even fragments) quantum‑mechanically tunnel through the transition state instead of climbing over it.**

**What it is:** Every catalyst ever designed operates on one principle inherited from Arrhenius and Eyring — lower the activation *energy* and let thermal collisions supply the rest. This new class would exploit the other axis of the barrier: its *width* and the mass that must move across it. The catalyst would be a rigid, pre‑organised host that clamps reactants into a geometry in which the reaction coordinate is compressed to a few tenths of an ångström, couples a designed low‑frequency "promoting vibration" of the scaffold to that coordinate so it rhythmically squeezes the barrier thinner, and suppresses the environmental fluctuations that normally destroy nuclear coherence. Reaction then proceeds by heavy‑atom tunnelling with a rate that is nearly *temperature‑independent* — as fast at 100 K as at 300 K — and whose selectivity is set by geometry and reduced mass rather than by activation energy. Two competing pathways of identical thermodynamics and near‑identical barrier heights could be separated by orders of magnitude simply because one requires a shorter, lighter atomic displacement. Heavy‑atom tunnelling is already known in exotic cases (ring‑opening of cyclopropylcarbinyl radicals, carbene rearrangements at 10 K), but only as a curiosity in frozen matrices; nobody can yet *design* it, catalyse it, or use it to make anything.

**Why it will be essential in 100 years:** It would decouple chemistry from heat. Essentially all industrial energy use exists to push molecules over barriers thermally — and heat is indiscriminate, so it also drives every side reaction, decomposes every fragile product, and is the reason synthesis of complex matter is a cascade of protecting groups and purifications. A catalyst that makes barriers transparent rather than surmountable would run bulk transformations at ambient or even sub‑ambient temperature with no thermal input at all, approaching the thermodynamic minimum energy cost of manufacturing and eliminating thermal side products, so yields approach unity and separations largely vanish. It would allow chemistry to be performed on and inside things that cannot be heated: living tissue, cryopreserved organs, quantum devices, spacecraft electronics, and food. It is the only plausible chemistry for the outer solar system and for cryogenic planetary environments, where energy is scarce and temperatures are 90–200 K — Titan's hydrocarbon feedstocks, cometary ices, and shadowed lunar volatiles are all frozen out of reach of thermally activated catalysis. And because tunnelling rates depend steeply on the mass and distance moved rather than on bond strength, it gives a completely new selectivity handle for reactions that thermal chemistry cannot distinguish at all, plus reactions that are literally impossible to run hot because the product decomposes above its own formation temperature — an entire region of accessible molecules and metastable materials that no thermal route can ever reach.

**Why it hasn't been discovered:** We have no theory that lets a chemist *design* a barrier's width, only its height; potential‑energy‑surface intuition, Hammond's postulate, linear free‑energy relationships and every catalyst design rule in use are height‑based, and standard transition‑state theory formally has no width in it. Achieving it requires scaffolds stiffer than kT that hold two reacting atoms within tunnelling distance without simply forming a bond, engineered promoting modes that modulate the donor–acceptor distance coherently, protection of nuclear coherence in a warm condensed phase where it currently dies in femtoseconds, and a predictive multidimensional theory of nuclear quantum dynamics in catalysis. Enzymes hint that nature partially exploits this for hydrogen transfer, but no known system does it for heavy atoms, catalytically, at turnover‑relevant rates — it would be a chemistry in which the mechanism is the wavefunction of the nuclei, not the energy of the transition state.

**Proposed reaction class: "chronoselective cascade chemistry" — reactions whose selectivity is encoded in *time* rather than in structure, so that a single sealed vessel containing all reagents at once executes a long, multistep synthesis autonomously, step by step, on a chemical clock.**

**What it is:** Today selectivity is spatial and structural — we isolate, purify, and add reagents in order, because any two reactive partners in the same flask will react immediately. The new reaction class would use catalysts and reagents that are *generated and destroyed on schedule* by coupled, fuel-consuming clock reactions: a reagent exists only in a defined time window, is quenched by a delayed antagonist, and the next catalyst is switched on by the appearance of the previous step's product (product-triggered feedback). Each elementary step would be gated not by a barrier but by a transient, self-limiting concentration pulse, with threshold and hysteresis behaviour giving digital on/off character, and with error-correction loops that re-run a step if an intermediate's concentration signature is wrong. The "recipe" becomes a waveform of chemical activity in one pot rather than a sequence of physical operations.

**Why it will be essential in 100 years:** Separations and purifications — not bond-making — consume the majority of the energy, solvent, and mass loss of chemical manufacturing, and they are exactly what cannot be done inside a sealed capsule, a spacecraft, a habitat, or a human body. Chronoselective chemistry collapses an entire multistep plant into a single vessel with near-total atom economy: complex pharmaceuticals, polymers, and food molecules made on demand from generic feedstocks in a device the size of a cartridge; drugs assembled inside the patient in the right order at the right time; materials that build themselves through a programmed sequence of phases; closed-loop life support that manufactures whatever is needed without stockrooms of reagents.

**Why it hasn't been discovered:** It requires reaction networks that are robustly out of equilibrium — with clocks, thresholds, feedback, and antagonists that keep working through twenty steps without drifting, cross-talking, or dying — plus catalysts that are chemically activated and deactivated by other species in the same soup. Cells do this, but abiotic chemistry has no design theory for programmed non-equilibrium networks, only isolated oscillators. It is chemistry in which the mechanism includes a schedule.

**Proposed reaction class: "chemotactic (gradient‑seeking) catalysis" — a self‑propelled catalytic cycle that uses part of its own reaction free energy to actively hunt and pre‑concentrate its substrate, so that turnover no longer obeys ordinary mass‑action kinetics at vanishing concentration.**

**What it is:** All chemistry today is passive and statistical: a catalyst waits for a substrate to collide with it, so rate falls linearly (or worse) with dilution, and below roughly micromolar concentrations useful chemistry effectively stops — which is why we must first concentrate a feedstock (by distillation, adsorption, evaporation, ion exchange) before we can react it, at enormous energy cost. The new reaction class would fuse transport and catalysis into one mechanism. The catalyst is an asymmetric molecular or colloidal object whose catalytic turnover generates a local product/ion/thermal gradient that propels it, with the propulsion vector coupled to a binding‑site occupancy signal so that motion is biased *up* the substrate gradient (true chemotaxis, not random self‑diffusiophoresis). Bound substrate is then held in a high‑local‑concentration antechamber and funnelled to the active site, so the effective local concentration at the reaction centre is orders of magnitude above the bulk. Kinetically this is a genuinely new rate law: turnover becomes nearly independent of bulk concentration down to parts‑per‑trillion, and the catalyst population self‑organises into swarms that converge on, and consume, dilute plumes.

**Why it will be essential in 100 years:** The century's chemical problems are almost all *dilution* problems. CO₂ is 0.04 % of air; lithium, uranium, magnesium, rubidium and phosphorus in seawater are present in oceans‑worth of quantity but at ppb–ppm; PFAS, pharmaceuticals, heavy metals and microplastics matter at parts per trillion; nutrient runoff, methane leaks and stratospheric aerosols are diffuse by nature; and the resource base left after high‑grade ores are exhausted is precisely low‑grade, dispersed matter. Today the energy cost of *finding and concentrating* these species dwarfs the cost of reacting them, and thermodynamics guarantees that bulk separation of a ppt contaminant is ruinously expensive. A catalyst that pays a tiny fraction of its own reaction enthalpy to locate its substrate inverts the economics: remediation, mining and carbon removal become chemistry rather than separation engineering. It would allow direct air capture without fans and sorbent regeneration, seawater as a general ore body, self‑navigating decontamination of soil, groundwater and oceans, and — in medicine — therapeutic catalysts that swim to a tumour, a plaque, or a pathogen at its own local concentration signature instead of being dosed systemically. It also makes closed‑loop life support possible in habitats, where every trace contaminant must be scavenged to near zero from large volumes with almost no energy budget.

**Why it hasn't been discovered:** At molecular scale, propulsion is drowned by Brownian motion (a nanoscale swimmer randomises direction in microseconds), and existing "chemically powered nanomotors" show only enhanced *random* diffusion or crude phoretic drift, not genuine sensing‑and‑steering; there is no theory linking a catalytic mechanism to a directed force vector, and no design rule for coupling occupancy of a binding site to the asymmetry that generates thrust. It requires molecular machines that can integrate a signal over times longer than their rotational relaxation (memory/ratcheting), propulsion efficient enough that the energy spent swimming is a small fraction of the bond energy released, and a kinetics that treats the catalyst as an agent moving through space rather than a species at uniform concentration — a merger of stochastic transport theory with catalysis in which the reaction's rate‑determining step is *arrival*.

**Proposed reaction class: "catalytic chemical stasis" — a single, reversible reaction that simultaneously caps *every* reactive group in a complex system, freezing all of its chemistry in place, and a paired catalytic trigger that un‑caps them all on command with perfect fidelity.**

**What it is:** Today a protecting group is stoichiometric, site‑specific, and installed one functional group at a time under conditions no living or complex system could survive. The undiscovered reaction would be the opposite: a small, membrane‑permeant "stasis reagent" that diffuses through an entire object — a tissue, an organ, a food, a soil sample, a half‑finished reaction mixture — and, in one pass, forms weak, uniform, reversible covalent adducts with every nucleophile and electrophile it meets (amines, thiols, carbonyls, phosphates, water itself), while a companion dynamic‑covalent network locks the solvent into a non‑crystallising, glass‑like state. The result is not a killed or dried system but a *paused* one: every molecule remains in its exact position and conformation, but no reaction — hydrolysis, oxidation, racemisation, enzymatic turnover, microbial growth, radical chain propagation — has any accessible pathway, because no reactive partner is exposed. Reversal is the genuinely new part: a catalyst (or a light/pH/redox pulse) that strips all the caps in a rapid, near‑quantitative, cooperative wave, restoring the original bonding pattern everywhere at once without leaving a single scar, cross‑link, or altered stereocentre. Selectivity comes not from choosing a target but from *touching everything identically and reversibly* — chemistry whose product is a state of matter, not a compound.

**Why it will be essential in 100 years:** Almost everything of value degrades on a clock, and our only defence is to spend continuous energy fighting it — refrigeration and freezing consume a large share of global electricity, roughly a third of all food is lost to spoilage, transplantable organs survive hours, biological samples and vaccines demand unbroken cold chains, and reagents, batteries, drugs, and archives all quietly decay on the shelf. A chemical pause button would replace the entire cold chain with a room‑temperature, energy‑free one: food, blood, vaccines, and pharmaceuticals stored indefinitely without a single watt; organs and whole tissues banked for years rather than hours, which is the missing step that would make transplantation and engineered‑tissue medicine universally available; unstable intermediates, catalysts, and radicals stockpiled and shipped rather than made on demand; ecological, forensic, and medical samples archived without loss of information. In a century where energy is the binding constraint and where refrigeration is both a major emitter and the fragile foundation of medicine and food security, the ability to stop time chemically — and to restart it — is worth more than most new molecules. It is also the only credible route to long‑duration human spaceflight, to closed habitats that cannot run continuous cold storage, and to a materials economy in which durability is a switch rather than an inherent property.

**Why it hasn't been discovered:** The requirements are mutually contradictory. The capping bond must be weak enough to be removed quantitatively and instantly, yet strong enough to survive years of storage; it must form with thousands of chemically distinct groups at comparable rates, yet leave none permanently modified; it must penetrate dense, heterogeneous, water‑rich matter faster than the system can be damaged by its own arrival; and its removal must be a synchronised, near‑error‑free event across ~10²⁰ sites, since even 0.1 % residual modification would destroy an enzyme or a genome. Water — the most abundant and most reactive participant — must be immobilised without ice crystals or osmotic collapse. Nature offers only crude partial analogues (anhydrobiosis with trehalose, spore dormancy, tardigrade proteins), all of which merely slow chemistry rather than switching it off, and none of which is reversible on demand. Realising it requires a general theory of *reversible, non‑selective* covalent chemistry — dynamic bonds with tunable, uniform lifetimes across all functional group classes — plus cooperative, autocatalytic uncapping cascades so that release is a phase transition rather than a slow, incomplete equilibrium. It is chemistry whose purpose is not to make anything, but to hold everything still.

**Proposed reaction class: "coherent chemomechanical catalysis" — a reversible reaction in which bond making/breaking is coupled directly and losslessly to macroscopic mechanical work, so chemistry and motion interconvert without ever passing through heat or electricity.**

**What it is:** Today every reaction dumps its free energy into heat or into an electrochemical potential; to get work we must burn fuel and run a Carnot-limited engine, or make electricity and run a motor. This new reaction would be an *allosteric solid*: a catalytic, covalently switchable material (a cooperative framework, ferroelastic molecular crystal, or dynamic-covalent polymer network) in which a single catalytic turnover at an active site does not release its energy locally but launches a coherent strain wave through a domain of ~10⁹ coupled units, all of which switch together. The chemical step and the mechanical step are then the *same* elementary event: substrate binding shortens the lattice, product release lengthens it, and the reaction coordinate literally is the material's macroscopic dimension. Because the coupling is cooperative and near-equilibrium, it is microscopically reversible — applying force to the material drives the reaction backwards uphill, so mechanical energy becomes a *reagent* that synthesises high-energy bonds directly, and the same block of matter is an engine in one direction and a synthesiser in the other. Selectivity and "gearing" come from domain size and elastic coupling constants, not from activation barriers; efficiency is set by hysteresis in the switching, not by temperature ratio.

**Why it will be essential in 100 years:** Roughly two-thirds of the energy humanity converts is lost as heat in the chemical-to-mechanical step — engines, turbines, and even electric drivetrains all pay conversion tolls. Isothermal chemomechanical coupling has no Carnot ceiling, so transport, pumping, compression and industrial motion could run at 90%+ efficiency from fuels, ammonia, or metabolites, with no combustion, no rotating machinery, no rare-earth magnets and no thermal signature. Run in reverse, it is the missing technology for harvesting *diffuse mechanical* energy — waves, tides, wind, footfall, vibration, blood pressure, breathing — as chemical bonds directly, skipping generators, power electronics and batteries entirely, and giving seasonal storage in the very act of collection. It makes true artificial muscle possible: soft, silent, self-healing actuators for prosthetics, implanted pumps and hearts, exoskeletons, surgical and deep-sea/space robotics that are powered by ordinary chemical fuel at biological energy density instead of by motors. And it turns force into a general synthetic driving force, so pressing, stretching or sonicating a material becomes a way to push endergonic reactions — a mechanically driven chemical industry with no reactors, no heating and no solvent.

**Why it hasn't been discovered:** Molecular conformational changes are individually tiny (~ångströms, ~kT of work) and stochastic; in every known material they decohere into heat within nanoseconds, so single-molecule events average out instead of adding up. We have no design theory for cooperativity that spans twelve orders of magnitude in length scale, no way to build switching that is simultaneously fast, high-force, and free of hysteresis (all known actuating materials — shape-memory alloys, liquid-crystal elastomers, muscle itself — waste most of their energy in irreversibility and top out near 40%), and no framework for kinetics in which the reaction coordinate is a bulk strain field rather than a molecular geometry. Achieving it requires catalysis embedded in a genuinely allosteric solid, elastic networks that transmit chemical events without dissipating them, and a merged science of chemical kinetics and continuum mechanics — chemistry in which the product of the reaction is not a molecule but motion.

Come up with a simple chemical process t.answer:
Stir in a food‑grade powdered cation‑exchange material – e.g. a fine clinoptilolite (zeolite) powder or an edible sulfonated ion‑exchange resin pre‑loaded with calcium (or potassium) ions – then strain/filter it out.

How it works: the powder's negatively charged aluminosilicate (or sulfonate) sites hold Ca²⁺/K⁺ loosely. When mixed into the moist/liquid food, dissolved Na⁺ from the salt exchanges onto the solid:

2 R–Ca + 2 Na⁺(aq) → 2 R–Na + Ca²⁺(aq)

Sodium ions are locked onto the insoluble grains, so when the powder is filtered off (or settles and is decanted), the sodium leaves with it. Since saltiness is perceived mainly from free Na⁺ (with Cl⁻), removing it lowers the salty taste without diluting or adding volume to the dish; the small amount of released calcium/potassium is harmless and largely masked by the food. A quick stir of 1–2 minutes with a few grams per liter, followed by straining, is enough.

Sprinkle in food‑grade powdered **alginic acid** (the free‑acid form of seaweed alginate; low‑methoxyl pectin works similarly), stir ~1 min, then lift/scoop out the gel that forms.

How it works: alginic acid is a polymer full of –COOH groups. In the moist food the carboxyls ionize and their –COO⁻ sites grab the dissolved sodium:

R–COOH + Na⁺(aq) → R–COO⁻Na⁺ + H⁺

As it binds Na⁺ (and traps water) the powder swells into a firm, rubbery sodium‑alginate gel that holds the salty liquid inside it. Because that gel is insoluble and cohesive, you can simply lift it out with a spoon or strainer, carrying the sequestered sodium out of the dish. The small amount of H⁺ released gives a faint tartness, and acidity is known to suppress the perception of saltiness, so the food tastes even less salty than the sodium removal alone would suggest. A few grams per litre is enough, and alginate is a common, harmless food additive (E400–E404), so any residue is safe.

**Add powdered tartaric acid / cream of tartar (potassium bitartrate) and chill, then filter off the crystals.**

How it works: sodium hydrogen tartrate (sodium bitartrate) is one of the few sparingly soluble sodium salts, especially in cold, alcohol‑ or sugar‑rich liquid. When you stir a few grams per litre of the fine acid‑tartrate powder into the salty soup/sauce, the dissolved salt reacts:

Na⁺(aq) + HC₄H₄O₆⁻ → NaHC₄H₄O₆(s)↓  (and KHC₄H₄O₆ + Na⁺ → NaHC₄H₄O₆↓ + K⁺)

Cooling the pot for a few minutes drops the solubility further, so the sodium precipitates out as gritty crystals (the same "wine diamonds" that form in chilled wine). Straining the liquid through a fine sieve or cloth physically removes the crystallized sodium from the dish, lowering the free Na⁺ that the tongue's salt receptors detect.

Two bonuses: any potassium released tastes far less salty than sodium, and the slight tartness left behind by the tartaric acid further suppresses the perception of saltiness. Tartaric acid and cream of tartar are ordinary baking ingredients (E334/E336), so residues are completely harmless.

**Convert the chloride into a "non‑salty" anion using a powdered edible anion exchanger (protonated chitosan in the acetate/citrate form).**

Sprinkle 2–5 g per litre of food‑grade chitosan powder that has been pre‑swollen in a little vinegar (so its amine groups are protonated, –NH₃⁺, with acetate as the counter‑ion) into the warm soup/sauce, stir 1–2 minutes, then strain the flakes out with a fine sieve.

Chemistry: the positively charged chitosan backbone is an anion‑exchange resin. When it meets dissolved NaCl it swaps its acetate (or citrate) counter‑ion for chloride:

R–NH₃⁺·CH₃COO⁻ + Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → R–NH₃⁺·Cl⁻(s) + Na⁺ + CH₃COO⁻

The chloride is locked onto the insoluble solid and leaves the pot when you strain it, while the sodium stays behind paired with acetate. This matters because saltiness is an anion‑dependent sensation: the small, mobile Cl⁻ ion permeates the tongue's salt‑taste channels and gives NaCl its sharp salty punch, whereas sodium acetate (or sodium citrate/gluconate) is only mildly, roundly savoury — a fraction as salty at the same sodium level. So without removing any liquid, diluting, or adding bulk, the dish's perceived saltiness drops sharply, and the trace of acetate/citrate left behind gives a pleasant tang that further suppresses the salty note. Chitosan is a common, harmless dietary fibre supplement (avoid for shellfish allergies), and any residue is simply filtered off.

**Stir in a pinch of powdered xanthan gum (or another cold‑swelling hydrocolloid such as gum arabic/pre‑gelatinised starch) – about 1–3 g per litre – and let it hydrate for a minute.**

How it works: xanthan is a long, highly hydroxylated (and carboxylated) polysaccharide. On contact with the liquid it hydrogen‑bonds huge amounts of water and its side‑chain –COO⁻ groups weakly coordinate the hydrated Na⁺ ions, building a three‑dimensional entangled network throughout the dish. This does two chemical things:

1. It lowers the **water activity and the effective (thermodynamic) activity of the free Na⁺** – much of the sodium is now held in the polymer's solvation shell rather than freely dissolved.
2. It drastically slows **ion diffusion**: in the viscous, gel‑like matrix Na⁺ can no longer migrate quickly out of the food bolus into the saliva film on the tongue, so far fewer ions reach the ENaC salt receptors in the few seconds a mouthful is tasted.

The result is that the same amount of salt registers as markedly less salty, and the effect is instant, reversible‑free and needs no straining. Xanthan is a standard, harmless food additive (E415), tasteless in these amounts, and it simultaneously gives the dish a pleasant body/mouthfeel that further rounds off the sharp salty edge.

**Stir in a spoonful of powdered glycine (plus a little powdered L‑arginine or L‑lysine) — roughly 2–5 g per litre — and let it dissolve; nothing has to be strained out.**

Chemistry: glycine is a zwitterion (⁺H₃N–CH₂–COO⁻) and arginine/lysine carry a protonated side chain. Once dissolved, the huge dipole of the zwitterion and the charged –COO⁻ / –NH₃⁺ ends form ion‑pairs and ion–dipole solvation shells around the dissolved salt:

Na⁺(aq) + ⁻OOC–CH₂–NH₃⁺ ⇌ [Na···OOC–CH₂–NH₃⁺]  and  Cl⁻(aq) + ⁺H₃N–R ⇌ [R–NH₃⁺···Cl⁻]

Sodium and chloride are thus tied up in loose complexes rather than existing as fully free, hydrated ions, which lowers their **thermodynamic activity** and slows their delivery to the ENaC salt channels on the tongue — the taste receptors only respond to free, mobile Na⁺/Cl⁻.

On top of that, glycine is intrinsically sweet and arginine slightly bitter‑alkaline; both compete with and cross‑suppress the salty channel at the receptor level (sweet–salty mixture suppression), and the basic amino acids are known "salt‑taste modifiers" that blunt the sharp NaCl bite.

Result: the dish tastes noticeably less salty within seconds, with no dilution, no change in volume, no filtering, and no bulk added — and amino acids are ordinary, harmless food components that simply add a mild savoury‑sweet roundness.

**Stir in a few spoonfuls of finely powdered sugar (icing sugar/sucrose, or powdered erythritol or maltodextrin if you want less sweetness) — roughly 10–20 g per litre — and let it dissolve completely. Nothing has to be strained out.**

Chemistry/mechanism: sucrose is a small, extremely hydroxyl‑rich molecule (8 –OH groups). When it dissolves, each molecule hydrogen‑bonds and immobilises a shell of ~5–10 water molecules, so a large fraction of the solvent is "tied up" as sugar hydration water. Because Na⁺ and Cl⁻ need bulk free water to stay fully hydrated and dissociated, removing that water **lowers the water activity and raises the ionic activity coefficients**, which pushes the equilibrium

Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) ⇌ [Na⁺···Cl⁻] (contact/solvent‑separated ion pairs)

to the right. The tongue's ENaC salt‑taste channels only respond to free, mobile hydrated Na⁺, so with more of the sodium locked into neutral ion pairs (and diffusing more slowly through the now more viscous, sugar‑thickened liquid), fewer ions reach the receptors during a mouthful.

On top of that purely physicochemical effect, the dissolved sugar activates the sweet (T1R2/T1R3) pathway, which produces classic sweet–salt mixture suppression in the taste system, further blunting the salty note.

Result: the dish tastes distinctly less salty within seconds, with no filtering, no precipitate and no change in volume — and sugar is a completely ordinary, harmless kitchen ingredient that simply rounds the flavour out.

**Stir in a small amount of powdered food‑grade calcium (or magnesium) lactate/gluconate — about 1–2 g per litre — and let it dissolve. Nothing needs to be strained out.**

Chemistry/mechanism: these powders dissolve to give divalent cations, Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, together with a harmless, non‑salty organic anion (lactate/gluconate):

Ca(C₃H₅O₃)₂(s) → Ca²⁺(aq) + 2 C₃H₅O₃⁻(aq)

Saltiness is generated when free Na⁺ passes through the ENaC sodium channels in the tongue's taste cells. Divalent cations are much more strongly charged and bind far more tightly at the negatively charged carboxylate sites in the mouth of that channel pore than Na⁺ does, so they sit there and **electrostatically plug/compete for the channel**, sharply cutting the Na⁺ current that the brain reads as "salty" — the same competitive‑block chemistry by which Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ inhibit other cation channels. In addition, Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ cross‑link and ion‑pair with the food's own anionic components (proteins, pectins, phosphates, organic acids), and the added lactate/gluconate ion‑pairs with Na⁺, so a little of the sodium is also tied up as weakly dissociated, slowly diffusing complexes instead of free hydrated ions.

Result: the dish tastes distinctly less salty within seconds, with no filtering, no precipitate, no dilution and no change in volume. Keep the dose low (calcium/magnesium salts turn chalky‑bitter in excess), and use calcium lactate rather than chloride, since chloride would restore the salty bite.

What is a molecule that becomes more den.answer: Water (H₂O) — losing a hydrogen atom (e.g., going to the hydroxyl/peroxide form) breaks up its open hydrogen‑bonded structure, giving a denser substance.

Ammonia (NH₃). Liquid ammonia is quite light (≈0.68 g/cm³) because its hydrogen‑bonded network keeps the molecules loosely packed. Strip one hydrogen atom away (giving NH₂ units, which pair up as hydrazine, N₂H₄) and the resulting substance is much denser (≈1.02 g/cm³).

Benzene (C₆H₆). Liquid benzene has a density of only ~0.88 g/cm³, but take away one hydrogen atom — the resulting phenyl units join to form biphenyl (C₆H₅–C₆H₅) — and the substance is a solid with a density of about 1.04 g/cm³, i.e. noticeably denser.

Methane (CH₄). Liquid methane is extremely light (~0.42 g/cm³) because its small, symmetric, non‑polar molecules pack loosely. Take away one hydrogen and the resulting methyl units join into ethane (C₂H₆), whose liquid density (~0.55 g/cm³) is appreciably higher — so removing an atom makes the substance denser.

Methanol (CH₃OH). Liquid methanol has a density of only ~0.79 g/cm³; remove one hydrogen atom and the resulting •CH₂OH units combine into ethylene glycol (HOCH₂–CH₂OH), a liquid with a density of about 1.11 g/cm³ — so taking away an atom yields a considerably denser substance.

Toluene (C₆H₅CH₃). Liquid toluene has a density of only ~0.87 g/cm³, but remove one hydrogen atom — the resulting benzyl units pair up as bibenzyl (C₆H₅CH₂–CH₂C₆H₅) — and you get a solid with a density of about 0.98 g/cm³, i.e. denser than the original.

Suggest a new scanning probe measurement.answer:
**Scanning Entropy (Caloric) Microscopy — a nanoscale probe of the local entropy landscape.**

Concept: a sharp tip carrying both a field‑delivering electrode/actuator and an ultrasensitive thermometer (e.g., a nanoscale thermocouple, SQUID‑thermometer, or NV‑center thermometry tip) is scanned over the sample. The tip applies a small *oscillating* thermodynamic conjugate field to the nanoscale volume beneath it — AC electric field, strain from a piezo/vibrating tip, magnetic field from a tip coil, or a gate‑induced chemical‑potential modulation — and the resulting adiabatic temperature oscillation δT(x, y) is detected at the drive frequency by lock‑in.

Because under adiabatic conditions δT ∝ −(T/C)·(∂S/∂X)·δX, the image directly maps the local entropy derivative (electrocaloric, elastocaloric, magnetocaloric, or "entropy‑vs‑carrier‑density" response) with the spatial resolution of the tip–sample junction (10–100 nm), and, with a bias/gate sweep, yields S(x, y; n, T, B) — a quantity no existing SPM measures.

Why it is useful (what it sees that STM/AFM/NSOM/MIM cannot):
- Distinguishes phases by their *entropy* rather than their density of states or conductivity: local spin entropy (k_B ln 2 per moment) in flat‑band and moiré systems, Pomeranchuk‑type isospin transitions, and Wigner‑crystal/spin‑liquid regions.
- Images latent heat and entropy jumps at first‑order structural, ferroelectric, magnetic, or metal–insulator transitions domain‑by‑domain, revealing nucleation sites and hysteresis at individual defects.
- Provides a route to detect fractionalized or non‑Abelian excitations through their quantized residual entropy (e.g., ½ k_B ln 2 from Majorana modes) at a specific location.
- Directly maps caloric‑effect efficiency in solid‑state cooling materials and thermal dissipation "hot spots" tied to entropy production in operating devices.

Implementation is compatible with existing cryogenic AFM/STM platforms: a qPlus or cantilever tip metallized for field application, with the thermometer integrated at the apex; operation in vacuum ensures near‑adiabatic conditions, and higher‑harmonic detection separates the caloric signal from ordinary Joule heating (which appears at 2ω and is field‑direction independent, whereas the caloric signal is linear in and reverses with the applied field).

**Scanning Quantum‑Noise Microscopy (SQNM) — imaging the local *fluctuations* of charge, rather than its average.**

Concept: a cryogenic tip (metallic tunnel tip, or a nano‑antenna/quantum‑dot/ NV‑ or graphene‑bolometer‑terminated tip) is coupled to a current‑carrying sample, but instead of recording the DC tunnel current or impedance, the tip's local signal is fed into a broadband, GHz‑bandwidth cross‑correlation amplifier and its **noise power spectral density** S(f, r) is measured point‑by‑point. Raster scanning yields real‑space maps of (i) the local shot‑noise Fano factor, (ii) the local Johnson–Nyquist noise (hence an absolute, contactless electron‑temperature map), and (iii) the local low‑frequency 1/f and telegraph‑noise spectra.

What it measures that no existing SPM does: STM/AFM/NSOM/MIM all sense mean quantities (LDOS, force, near‑field permittivity, conductivity); SQNM senses the *second moment* of the current, which contains information invisible in the mean:
- **Local effective quasiparticle charge** e\* from the shot‑noise slope — direct, spatially resolved detection of e/3 Laughlin quasiparticles, Cooper‑pair (2e) and Andreev (multiple‑e) processes, and charge‑e/2 or Majorana‑related noise at specific edges or vortices.
- **Where dissipation actually happens**: Johnson‑noise thermometry maps electron temperature with tens‑of‑nm resolution, distinguishing ballistic, hydrodynamic (Poiseuille‑flow) and diffusive transport, and revealing hot spots and non‑local cooling in graphene/2D devices.
- **Individual fluctuators**: single two‑level systems, mobile ions, trapped charges and domain‑wall creep events appear as localized Lorentzian/telegraph noise, pinpointing the microscopic sources of 1/f noise and decoherence in qubits, transistors, and memristive devices.
- **Correlations**: noise suppression/enhancement identifies interaction‑ and statistics‑driven bunching/antibunching and non‑equilibrium criticality region by region.

Implementation is compatible with existing dilution‑refrigerator STM/AFM platforms: it requires only a low‑loss, impedance‑matched coaxial/resonant‑tank coupling to the tip and cross‑correlated HEMT amplification, with tip‑height and bias‑symmetry checks used to separate genuine sample noise from amplifier and cable backgrounds.

**Scanning Positron‑Annihilation Microscopy (SPAM) — a "matter–antimatter" scanning probe that maps local open volume and electron momentum density.**

Concept: the probe is a hollow, field‑emission‑type nanotip that acts as a *nanoscale slow‑positron source*. Positrons from a ²²Na/⁶⁴Cu source (or a compact pair‑production/trap‑based reservoir) are moderated, guided down a magnetically/electrostatically focusing nanocapillary tip, and emitted from the apex at a few eV, so their implantation spot and stopping depth (nm–tens of nm) are set by the tip–sample geometry rather than by a far‑field beam optic. The positrons thermalize under the apex, diffuse a short distance, and annihilate; a segmented array of coincident γ detectors (511 keV) records, pixel by pixel, (i) the annihilation **lifetime**, (ii) the **Doppler broadening / angular correlation** of the two γ's, and (iii) the 3γ (ortho‑positronium) fraction. Raster scanning yields images of the local positron trapping and annihilation spectrum.

What it measures that STM/AFM/NSOM/MIM cannot — those probe surface LDOS, force, near‑field permittivity or conductivity, all essentially *surface and electron‑charge* quantities. SPAM is uniquely sensitive to **open volume and to the momentum distribution of the electrons that the positron annihilates with**:
- Real‑space maps of **single vacancies, vacancy clusters, dislocation cores, nanovoids and free volume** buried tens of nm below the surface — the defects that control mechanical failure, radiation damage, dopant activation and ion‑battery/memristor degradation, and which are invisible to all charge‑ or force‑based SPMs.
- **Locally resolved electron momentum density / Fermi‑surface information** (from angular correlation), i.e. a real‑space image of how the Fermi surface or valence‑electron momentum distribution changes across a grain boundary, a strained domain, a buried interface, or a phase‑separated region.
- **Chemical identification of the defect environment**: the Doppler high‑momentum tail carries the core‑electron signature of the atoms surrounding each vacancy, giving element‑specific defect chemistry (e.g. vacancy–dopant complexes) at ~10 nm scale.
- **Positronium formation maps** in porous, molecular and amorphous films, giving pore‑size and free‑volume distributions (o‑Ps lifetime → pore radius) point by point, plus buried‑interface adhesion and voiding in packaged devices.
- Combined with a bias/gate sweep, the positron affinity shift reports the **local electrostatic potential and work function deep inside** the material, not just at the surface.

Implementation builds on existing technology: nanocapillary/remoderator positron optics, tuning‑fork tip–sample distance control for positioning, and fast coincidence γ spectroscopy; tip‑retraction and implantation‑energy nulls separate the genuinely localized annihilation signal from the diffuse background.

**Scanning Nonlocal Correlation Microscopy (SNCM) — a two‑tip (or multi‑tip) probe that measures the *two‑point* correlation function of a material in real space.**

Concept: instead of one apex, two independently positioned nanotips (dual‑tip STM/AFM heads, or a monolithic tip pair with ~5–50 nm controllable separation) are simultaneously coupled to the same sample at positions r₁ and r₂. Rather than reading each tip's mean signal, the two channels are fed into a cross‑correlation (coincidence) detector: one records ⟨δI₁(t) δI₂(t+τ)⟩, the cross‑spectrum S₁₂(ω, r₁, r₂), and the coincidence rate of individual tunneling events, as a function of the tip separation vector **d** = r₂ − r₁, bias, and delay τ. Scanning **d** yields a direct image of the nonlocal correlator G(r₁, r₂); Fourier transforming over **d** gives a *local* momentum‑resolved response — a nanoscale "scattering experiment" performed with two tips.

What it measures that no existing SPM does: STM, AFM, NSOM and MIM all record a single‑point, one‑body quantity (LDOS, force, permittivity, conductivity). SNCM measures genuinely **two‑body, nonlocal quantum correlations**:
- Real‑space maps of the electron **pair correlation and coherence length** — e.g., splitting a Cooper pair between the two tips gives a positive cross‑correlation that decays over ξ, imaging the pairing coherence length and its variation across a single grain boundary, vortex, or doped region.
- **Hanbury Brown–Twiss statistics of electrons**: antibunching vs. bunching between the two tips distinguishes free quasiparticles from interaction‑ and statistics‑driven correlated transport (anyonic/fractionalized carriers, hydrodynamic electron flow, Cooper‑pair or Andreev processes).
- **Entanglement witnesses** at the nanoscale: violation of classical bounds on the cross‑correlation certifies spatially separated entangled electron pairs emitted from a superconductor, quantum dot, or topological edge.
- **Nonlocal susceptibility / local band structure**: injecting current at tip 1 and detecting at tip 2 versus **d** gives the real‑space Green's function G(r₁, r₂, E) — hence electron focusing, Fermi‑surface anisotropy, quasiparticle mean free path, and coherence, all measured *inside* a single micro‑domain instead of averaged over a contacted device.
- **Correlation‑length imaging of order parameters**: how charge‑density‑wave, magnetic, or nematic fluctuations decay in space and time, pixel by pixel, near a defect or a quantum critical region.

Implementation is compatible with existing multi‑probe cryogenic SPM platforms: it requires nanoscale, drift‑stable tip–tip positioning (SEM‑ or interferometrically monitored), low‑capacitance wiring with HEMT amplifiers, and cross‑correlated GHz detection; tip separation sweeps and tip‑retraction nulls separate genuine sample correlations from capacitive crosstalk and amplifier background.

**Scanning Casimir–Lifshitz (Vacuum‑Fluctuation) Spectroscopy Microscopy (SCVM) — imaging matter through the quantum‑fluctuation force spectrum rather than through charge, current, force‑of‑contact, or light.**

**Concept.** A smooth, well‑characterized micro‑sphere/flat‑punch tip on an ultrasoft, high‑Q cryogenic resonator (or a levitated nanoparticle acting as the "tip") is held in the 20 nm–1 µm non‑contact range above the sample, with all electrostatic patch potentials nulled in situ by a Kelvin‑probe feedback and modulated‑bias compensation. Instead of recording the force at one gap, the instrument sweeps the tip–sample separation *d* and records the full distance dependence of the dispersion (Casimir–Lifshitz) force and force gradient at every pixel, F_C(d, r), together with (i) its temperature dependence (thermal‑fluctuation, low‑frequency part), (ii) its dependence on a set of exchangeable tip coatings/materials, and (iii) the **Casimir torque** on an optically anisotropic (birefringent or ferromagnetic) tip as it is rotated. Because F_C(d) is a Lifshitz integral over the sample's reflection coefficients at imaginary frequencies, r(iξ, k), the measured F_C(d, r) can be inverted, pixel by pixel, into the **local, broadband (IR‑to‑UV) dielectric/magnetic response function and its wavevector (nonlocal) dependence** of the material volume within ~d of the surface.

**What it gives that STM/AFM/NSOM/MIM cannot.** STM sees surface LDOS, AFM the mechanical/electrostatic force, NSOM the near‑field optical response in a narrow laser band, MIM the GHz conductivity. SCVM measures the *zero‑point and thermal electromagnetic fluctuation spectrum* of the material, integrated over all frequencies and, crucially, over evanescent wavevectors — a quantity no scanning probe currently accesses. It would provide:

- **Buried, contactless spectroscopy:** because the range of the integral is set by the gap, varying *d* performs depth tomography of the dielectric function tens to hundreds of nm *below* the surface (buried interfaces, oxide layers, voids, delamination in packaged devices) without any tunneling or optical access.
- **Maps of "fluctuation phases":** the low‑frequency/Matsubara‑zero term is exquisitely sensitive to free carriers, so metal–insulator, superconducting, and charge‑ordered domains show up as distinct Casimir contrast (a superconducting transition changes the reflection coefficients at ξ ≲ Δ/ħ), giving a genuinely non‑invasive order‑parameter map.
- **Topology and magnetoelectricity:** Chern insulators, axion insulators and magnetoelectric materials produce Hall‑conductivity–dependent, quantized contributions and even Casimir *repulsion/torque* signatures — a real‑space read‑out of the local axion coupling θ(r) and of edge/domain‑wall regions.
- **Nematicity and anisotropy imaging** via the Casimir torque on a birefringent tip: the torque angle directly maps the local optical‑anisotropy axis (nematic domains, strain, liquid‑crystal and molecular alignment) with no polarized light required.
- **Nonlocal/hydrodynamic electrodynamics:** the evanescent‑wavevector weighting makes SCVM sensitive to spatial dispersion, hydrodynamic electron flow and plasmon nonlocality — inaccessible to far‑field or single‑frequency near‑field optics.
- **Engineering payoff:** direct measurement of the fluctuation‑induced stiction/adhesion budget in NEMS/MEMS, and of the vacuum‑fluctuation forces and patch‑potential landscapes that limit precision force experiments and trapped‑ion/levitated‑particle qubits.

**Feasibility.** Everything needed exists separately: sub‑aN/√Hz cryogenic cantilevers or levitated optomechanics, in‑situ electrostatic patch compensation, sub‑nm gap metrology by fiber interferometry, and Lifshitz‑theory inversion algorithms. Systematics (residual electrostatics, hydrodynamic damping, tip roughness) are separated by their distinct power laws in *d*, by bias‑polarity symmetry, and by tip‑material substitution nulls — the same strategy that has already validated Casimir force measurements at the few‑percent level, now performed as a raster‑scanned, spectroscopic imaging mode.

**Scanning Gravimetric (Mass‑Density) Microscopy — "gravity SPM": imaging local mass density through the Newtonian force gradient rather than through any electromagnetic interaction.**

**Concept.** The probe is not a sharp electrical tip but a dense, compact test mass (e.g., a µm‑scale tungsten/osmium or gold sphere, or a levitated nanoparticle) mounted on an ultrasoft, high‑Q cryogenic torsional/optomechanical resonator with sub‑zeptonewton force sensitivity. The test mass is scanned tens to hundreds of nanometres above the sample and its resonance frequency/phase is read out interferometrically. Crucially, the tip–sample gap contains a **thin superconducting (and grounded, magnetically shielded) membrane** that screens electrostatic patch potentials, Casimir–Lifshitz forces, and magnetic interactions, but is transparent to gravity. The sample (or the test mass) is modulated — mechanically dithered, or the sample is a rotating/translating structure — so the gravitational signal appears at a chosen sideband frequency far from thermal and 1/f backgrounds, and is recovered by long‑integration lock‑in detection. Raster scanning maps the local Newtonian force gradient ∂²Φ/∂z², which inverts to the **mass density distribution ρ(r)** beneath the probe, with depth information obtained from the height dependence of the gradient (deeper structures produce a slower fall‑off with gap), i.e. gravitational tomography.

**What it measures that STM/AFM/NSOM/MIM cannot.** All existing SPMs sense electromagnetic quantities — tunnelling current (LDOS), surface forces, near‑field permittivity, GHz conductivity — and are therefore blind beyond the first few nanometres and sensitive only to charge/spin. Gravity couples to **mass–energy alone**, is unscreenable, and penetrates arbitrarily deep. This modality would provide:
- **Composition‑independent, truly buried imaging:** voids, delamination, density fluctuations, inclusions and phase‑separated regions tens to hundreds of nm below the surface or beneath opaque metal/encapsulation layers — invisible to every charge‑ or photon‑based probe.
- **Isotope and packing‑density contrast:** two chemically identical, electronically indistinguishable regions differing in isotopic composition or atomic packing (amorphous vs crystalline, porous vs dense) show direct gravitational contrast.
- **Absolute local density metrology** for thin films, batteries, membranes and biological/soft matter, without models of dielectric function or contact mechanics.
- **A short‑range fundamental‑physics search built into an imaging tool:** any deviation of the measured force map from the electromagnetically determined mass distribution constrains Yukawa‑type "fifth forces", extra dimensions, chameleon/axion‑mediated interactions, and gravitational decoherence at the 10 nm–1 µm scale, region by region.
- **A route to source‑mass gravity of quantum objects:** with a levitated tip prepared in a spatial superposition, the same platform tests whether gravity from a nanoscale mass is coherent — a scanning‑probe assault on quantum gravity.

**Feasibility.** The required pieces exist separately: levitated optomechanics and cryogenic torsion balances already reach ~10⁻²¹ N/√Hz, gravitational coupling between mm‑ and now sub‑mm‑scale masses has been measured, and superconducting shields plus modulation at a mechanical sideband are the standard tools for rejecting Casimir/patch backgrounds. The pathway is to scale the source mass down and the integration time up; systematics are discriminated by their distinct gap scaling (Newtonian gradient ∝ 1/d³–1/d⁴ vs Casimir ∝ 1/d⁴–1/d⁵), by shield thickness/material substitution nulls, and by replacing the sample region with an equal‑permittivity, different‑density reference.

**Scanning Angular‑Momentum Microscopy (SAMM) — a nanoscale Einstein–de Haas/Barnett probe that images where angular momentum resides and where it flows.**

**Concept.** The probe is not a current‑ or force‑sensing tip but an ultrasensitive *torsional* optomechanical resonator: a nanoscale disk/paddle (SiN, diamond, or a levitated nanoparticle) whose rotational degree of freedom is read out interferometrically at the zeptonewton‑metre level, terminated by a sharp apex that carries a microwave/optical near‑field antenna. The apex delivers a resonant microwave (or ultrafast optical) pulse that coherently flips or demagnetizes the spins in a ~10–50 nm volume directly beneath it; conservation of total angular momentum means the flipped spins deposit a *mechanical torque impulse* into the lattice, which is transmitted to (or, in the inverted geometry, exerted on) the torsional probe and detected phase‑sensitively at the pulse repetition frequency. Conversely, driving the probe into rotation (Barnett effect) imprints an effective field on the local spins, whose response is read back. Raster scanning and sweeping pulse frequency/delay yields maps of ΔL(r) — the angular momentum exchanged per unit area — versus field, temperature, and time delay.

**What it measures that no existing SPM does.** STM sees LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near‑field optics, MIM conductivity, MFM/MRFM the *magnetic moment*. SAMM measures the **absolute angular momentum budget** and its transfer channels:
- **Local separation of spin vs orbital angular momentum:** because the Einstein–de Haas ratio gives the gyromagnetic ratio directly, a single scan returns the local g‑factor map, i.e. the orbital contribution to magnetism in 4f/5d magnets, altermagnets, single‑molecule magnets, and moiré flat bands — a decomposition currently only available from element‑averaged XMCD sum rules.
- **Where angular momentum goes during switching:** imaging, domain by domain, the lattice as the angular‑momentum sink in ultrafast demagnetization, spin–orbit‑torque switching, and skyrmion nucleation/annihilation, including the still‑unresolved role of phonon angular momentum (chiral phonons) and magnon–phonon conversion.
- **Nanoscale spin‑current metrology without electrical contacts:** a spin current entering a region shows up as a steady mechanical torque, giving an absolute, calibration‑free measurement of spin injection, spin Hall/Edelstein efficiency, and spin‑pumping losses at individual interfaces and defects.
- **Detection of "hidden" order that carries angular momentum but little net moment:** antiferromagnetic, altermagnetic, and orbital‑loop‑current domains, and chirality/handedness of molecular and helimagnetic textures, all produce a torque signature while being nearly invisible to MFM.
- **Angular‑momentum noise:** the fluctuating torque spectrum gives the local spin‑lattice relaxation channel (Gilbert damping) with nanometre resolution.

**Feasibility.** All ingredients exist separately: torsional optomechanics and levitated rotors already resolve ~10⁻²⁷ N·m/√Hz (single‑spin‑flip torque impulses at kHz repetition), pulsed ESR/FMR near‑field antennas on scanning tips are standard, and Einstein–de Haas has been demonstrated on micromechanical cantilevers. Backgrounds (Ampère‑force, thermal expansion, magnetic gradient force) are separated by their distinct symmetry under field reversal, by their scaling with tip–sample gap, and by nulling on a nonmagnetic reference region.

**Scanning Mössbauer (Nuclear‑Resonance) Microscopy — a scanning probe whose contrast comes from the *nucleus*, not the electrons.**

**Concept.** The tip is a nanoscale source/detector of recoil‑free resonant γ‑rays: either (i) an apex‑mounted radioactive nanocrystal (e.g. ⁵⁷Co → ⁵⁷Fe, or ¹¹⁹mSn, ¹⁵¹Eu, ¹⁶¹Dy sources) driven on a fast piezo that Doppler‑sweeps the γ energy over the ~10⁻⁸ eV nuclear line, or (ii) a nano‑aperture/waveguide tip that funnels a focused synchrotron/X‑ray‑free‑electron‑laser nuclear‑resonant beam into a ~10–30 nm spot. Tip–sample distance is regulated by a standard tuning‑fork/AFM feedback. At each pixel one records the resonant absorption/nuclear forward‑scattering spectrum (energy domain) or the quantum‑beat pattern of the delayed nuclear decay (time domain) with a fast avalanche‑photodiode detector.

**Observable.** Raster scanning yields real‑space maps of the *hyperfine interaction parameters of individual isotopes*: isomer shift (local s‑electron density → oxidation state, bonding, charge transfer), quadrupole splitting (local electric‑field‑gradient → site symmetry, strain, distortion, orbital order), magnetic hyperfine field with its full **vector direction** (from the relative intensities of the Zeeman lines), and the Lamb–Mössbauer factor / line width (local lattice stiffness, mean‑square displacement, spin‑fluctuation and relaxation rates in the 10⁻⁹–10⁻⁷ s window).

**What no existing SPM can do.** STM sees surface LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near‑field optics, MIM permittivity, MFM/NV a stray dipole field — none is isotope‑specific, none reads the electric‑field gradient, and none is quantitatively sensitive to atoms buried tens to hundreds of nanometres deep, since γ‑rays penetrate freely. This modality would provide: element‑ and isotope‑labelled chemical‑state maps (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ domains in battery cathodes, catalysts and corrosion layers) *inside* an operating, encapsulated device; local Néel‑vector and spin‑canting imaging in antiferromagnets and multiferroics, where the moment is compensated and MFM is blind; absolute, calibration‑free hyperfine‑field magnetometry at buried interfaces of spintronic stacks (with isotopic ⁵⁷Fe delta‑layers used as depth markers, giving nuclear‑resonance depth tomography); nanoscale strain/EFG mapping at dislocations and phase boundaries; and spatially resolved spin‑dynamics/relaxation spectroscopy across a magnetic or valence‑ordering transition, domain by domain.

**Feasibility.** All ingredients exist separately: nuclear‑resonant scattering with sub‑100 nm focused synchrotron beams, X‑ray waveguide/nano‑aperture optics, milli‑Curie microsource Mössbauer spectrometers, and tuning‑fork distance control. The chief development is the high‑specific‑activity apex source (or efficient nano‑waveguide tip) plus long per‑pixel integration; genuine near‑field nuclear signal is separated from the far‑field background by tip‑retraction nulls, by the Doppler‑velocity resonance condition, and by time‑gating on the delayed nuclear decay.

**Scanning Fermi‑Surface (Quantum‑Oscillation) Microscopy, "SFSM" — a probe that measures de Haas–van Alphen/Shubnikov–de Haas oscillations locally, turning a scanning tip into a real‑space Fermi‑surface tomograph.**

**Concept.** The sample sits in a swept magnetic field in a dilution refrigerator, and the tip reads out an *oscillatory* local thermodynamic response rather than a static one. Two complementary apex designs: (i) a SQUID‑on‑tip or NV/graphene‑Hall nanomagnetometer that senses the local oscillatory magnetization M(1/B, r) (nanoscale dHvA), and (ii) a metallized tip run as a single‑electron‑transistor/capacitance sensor that records the oscillations of the local electronic compressibility ∂μ/∂n and local chemical potential as Landau levels sweep through E_F. At every pixel the signal is Fourier transformed in 1/B; the oscillation frequencies F = (ħ/2πe)A_k give the *local* extremal Fermi‑surface cross sections, the temperature damping (Lifshitz–Kosevich) gives the local cyclotron effective mass m*, the field damping gives the local Dingle/quantum lifetime τ_q, and the oscillation phase gives the local Berry phase (π for Dirac carriers) and spin‑splitting/g‑factor.

**What no existing SPM delivers.** STM gives LDOS at a point, AFM force, NSOM near‑field optics, MIM local conductivity — none returns a momentum‑space object. SFSM produces a **map of k‑space over real space**: A_k(r), m*(r), τ_q(r), Berry phase(r), with ~50–100 nm resolution. This would let one image how the Fermi surface itself reconstructs across a single domain wall of a charge‑/spin‑density‑wave or nematic order; watch Fermi‑surface reconstruction at a phase‑separated boundary in cuprates, kagome metals or Kondo systems; measure how strain gradients, twist‑angle disorder or gate inhomogeneity locally deform A_k and m* in moiré and rhombohedral graphene devices; separate "bulk" from surface/interface pockets in topological and heterostructure samples by scanning across an edge; and identify whether transport disorder comes from long‑range potential fluctuations (uniform τ_q, varying F) or from local scattering centres (varying τ_q).

**Feasibility.** All components exist: SQUID‑on‑tip magnetometry with nT/√Hz at ~50 nm standoff, scanning SET/capacitance compressibility probes, and standard field sweeps with lock‑in modulation at ~10 mK.
