The chief development is per‑pixel field sweeping (or rapid field‑modulation with 1/B‑synchronous detection) to keep acquisition times practical; genuine sample oscillations are separated from tip/background artefacts by their strict periodicity in 1/B, their Lifshitz–Kosevich temperature dependence, and tip‑retraction nulls.

**Scanning Muon‑Spin‑Rotation Microscopy ("scanning µSR") — a spin‑polarized muon implanted point‑by‑point as a local, contact‑free magnetometer inside the sample.**

**Concept.** A low‑energy (eV–keV), 100% spin‑polarized surface‑muon beam is funneled through a nanocapillary/electrostatic‑lens tip that is held above the sample by conventional tuning‑fork distance feedback. The tip focuses and steers the muons into a ~10–50 nm implantation spot (depth set by the implantation energy, 1–200 nm), so the implantation site is defined by tip position rather than by far‑field beam optics. Each implanted muon precesses in the *local internal field at its interstitial stopping site* and then decays (τ = 2.2 µs), emitting a positron preferentially along its instantaneous spin direction; a segmented positron detector array records the asymmetry vs. time at every pixel, in zero, longitudinal, or transverse applied field.

**Observable.** Raster scanning gives real‑space maps of: the local internal‑field distribution P(B) and its width (magnetic order, disorder, vortex‑lattice field profile), the **magnetic volume fraction** (fraction of muons seeing a static field — i.e. how phase separation is distributed spatially), the local spin‑relaxation rates λ and 1/T₁ (probing spin fluctuations in the 10⁻⁶–10⁻¹¹ s window, complementary to Mössbauer/NMR), and, in a superconductor, the local **magnetic penetration depth λ_L (→ superfluid density n_s/m\*)** and the presence of spontaneous time‑reversal‑symmetry‑breaking fields in zero field.

**What no existing SPM can do.** STM sees surface LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near‑field optics, MIM conductivity, MFM/NV only *stray* fields outside the sample. The muon sits *inside* the lattice, so it senses fields that are fully compensated externally: antiferromagnetic, altermagnetic and loop‑current order, spin‑glass and spin‑liquid dynamics, and the absolute superfluid density — none of which produce stray flux for a magnetometer tip. Scanning µSR would therefore image, domain by domain and with depth control: superfluid‑density inhomogeneity across a single grain boundary or interface in cuprates/nickelates, the coexistence versus phase separation of magnetism and superconductivity, the nucleation of hidden TRSB order at defects, and the spatial variation of spin dynamics through a quantum‑critical or glassy region.

**Feasibility.** All ingredients exist separately: high‑intensity low‑energy muon beams (LEM at PSI) with tunable few‑nm–200 nm implantation depth, muon microbeam focusing to ~µm (nanocapillary/immersion‑lens optics are the development step), fast segmented positron detection, and tuning‑fork tip–sample control. Long per‑pixel counting is the price; genuine localized signal is verified by tip‑retraction and implantation‑energy nulls and by the strict Larmor periodicity of the asymmetry.

**Scanning Magnon Microscopy (SMM) — a "spin‑wave STM" that locally injects and phase‑coherently detects magnons to map the magnetic system's own excitation spectrum in real space.**

**Concept.** The apex carries a nanoscale microwave near‑field element — a lithographed loop/stripline antenna or a magnetic nano‑pillar/vortex tip driven at GHz–THz — that launches a *coherent, narrow‑band spin‑wave packet* into a magnetic sample from a ~10–30 nm source spot. The same (or a second, co‑located) apex element detects the local magnetization dynamics phase‑sensitively: inductively at the drive frequency, via an NV centre in a diamond pillar (magnon‑induced field/relaxometry), or via tip‑enhanced Brillouin light scattering. Sweeping drive frequency, applied field, and source–detector separation at each pixel and lock‑in detecting amplitude *and* phase yields the local magnon Green's function G(r, r′, ω) — the magnetic analogue of dI/dV maps.

**Observables.** Real‑space, mode‑resolved maps of: the local magnon dispersion ω(k) and hence local exchange stiffness, anisotropy field and interfacial Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya constant (from the nonreciprocal k ↔ −k asymmetry of the dispersion); the local Gilbert damping/magnon lifetime; magnon band gaps, standing modes and confinement in magnonic crystals, nanodots and domain patterns; magnon transmission, reflection, refraction and phase shift at *individual* domain walls, skyrmions, grain boundaries and interfaces; magnon–phonon and magnon–magnon (nonlinear, parametric) coupling pixel by pixel.

**Why it is new.** STM sees electronic LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near‑field optics, MIM conductivity, MFM/NV only static or noise‑averaged stray fields — none resolves the *magnetic excitation spectrum* with wavevector and phase resolution in real space (far‑field FMR/BLS averages over microns and is diffraction limited). SMM would show where magnons are actually scattered and where damping originates in spintronic and magnonic devices, image the spin‑wave optics of topological textures, reveal local exchange/DMI disorder in antiferromagnets, altermagnets and van der Waals magnets, and directly probe magnon condensates and magnon‑mediated coupling in hybrid quantum circuits.

**Feasibility.** All ingredients exist separately: scanning nano‑antenna ESR/FMR tips, NV magnetometry with nT/√Hz at 50 nm standoff, GHz vector (phase‑sensitive) detection, and tuning‑fork distance control. Genuine magnon signal is separated from direct antenna crosstalk by tip‑retraction nulls, by the field‑dependent resonance condition, and by the linear phase accumulation with source–detector distance.

**Scanning Mass‑Spectrometric Microscopy (SMSM) — an SPM whose contrast is the *mass/isotope* of the atoms directly under the apex.**

**Concept.** A sharp tip is operated in normal AFM/STM feedback a few nm above the surface, but the apex is also the extraction electrode of a miniaturized time‑of‑flight (or Orbitrap‑like) analyzer built into the scan head. At each pixel the feedback is briefly paused and a single, calibrated nanosecond voltage pulse (optionally assisted by a plasmonically enhanced femtosecond pulse delivered through the tip, or by a low‑energy He⁺ nano‑jet) field‑desorbs/ionizes only the few atoms or the single molecule in the ~1 nm² region of highest field beneath the apex. The ions are accelerated through the tip aperture into the TOF drift tube and mass‑analyzed with single‑ion counting; the tip then re‑engages and the scan continues. Because the desorption field is highly nonlinear in tip–sample gap, the analyzed volume is set by the apex geometry, not by any beam optic.

**Observables.** Pixel‑by‑pixel: (i) elemental and **isotopic** identity (m/z) of the topmost atoms, and, with repeated pulsing, layer‑by‑layer depth profiles — 3‑D chemical tomography with sub‑nm lateral and single‑monolayer depth resolution; (ii) molecular fragment fingerprints for organic/2‑D and biological surfaces; (iii) the *sub‑threshold* (non‑destructive) observable: the local **field‑evaporation threshold and ion charge‑state ratio**, which map local bond strength, cohesive energy, work function and surface electric field; (iv) correlation of each ion's identity with the simultaneously recorded AFM force/STM dI/dV signature of the very same atom, giving an in‑situ calibration of chemical contrast in force and tunneling maps.

**What existing SPMs cannot do.** STM sees LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near‑field optics, MIM permittivity — none identifies *what element or isotope* an atom is, none distinguishes ¹²C from ¹³C, ⁶Li from ⁷Li, or H from D, and none gives molecular composition. SMSM would give: isotope‑labelled tracking of single dopants, Li/H diffusion pathways and grain‑boundary segregation in batteries and alloys; direct chemical identification of individual catalytic sites, adatoms and point defects previously assigned only by DFT‑matched force curves; hydrogen mapping (hydrogen embrittlement, hydride formation) at the atomic scale; and sequence/composition read‑out of single adsorbed molecules combined with their imaged conformation.

**Feasibility.** All parts exist separately — atom‑probe field evaporation from nanotips, laser‑assisted and pulsed‑field desorption, compact TOF analyzers with single‑ion detection, and cryogenic UHV AFM/STM heads; the development steps are integrating a short, high‑transmission ion optic around the tip and operating the desorption pulse without destabilizing the feedback. The genuine local signal is verified by tip‑retraction nulls, by the sharp field threshold versus gap, and by cross‑checking the removed‑atom site against the before/after topographic images.

**Scanning Rydberg‑Atom Microscopy (SRAM) — using a single laser‑cooled atom, not a solid tip, as the scanning probe.**

**Concept.** The "tip" is one neutral atom (Rb, Cs, or Sr) held in an optical tweezer and positioned 50 nm–1 µm above the sample with nanometre accuracy by scanning the trap beam (the tweezer itself is the positioning stage; no mechanical apex ever touches the surface). At each pixel the atom is excited to a Rydberg state (n ≈ 30–100) and interrogated by optical/microwave Ramsey spectroscopy; the enormous Rydberg polarizability (∝ n⁷) and dipole moment (∝ n²) convert the local environment into measurable Stark/Zeeman shifts, level mixing, and state‑transfer rates, read out by state‑selective fluorescence with quantum‑projection‑limited sensitivity.

**Observables mapped pixel by pixel.**
- Local **DC and low‑frequency electric field vector** with µV/cm‑level sensitivity — patch potentials, adsorbate dipoles, trapped charges, ferroelectric/polarization domains, and buried charge — measured absolutely (atomic units, no tip‑shape calibration) and *without* the tip‑induced band bending, contact potential, or capacitive back‑action that plague KPFM/scanning‑gate.
- **Electric‑field noise spectral density** S_E(ω, r) over MHz–GHz, obtained from Rydberg dephasing/state‑transfer rates — i.e. a real‑space map of the "anomalous heating" sources that limit trapped‑ion and superconducting qubits, localized to individual surface contaminants or grain boundaries.
- **Microwave–THz near‑field spectroscopy** in a regime no photodetector reaches: Rydberg–Rydberg transitions lie at 1 GHz–1 THz, so the atom acts as a tunable, quantum‑calibrated antenna sensing the sample's local THz permittivity, surface‑phonon‑polariton and plasmon fields, and even the **local blackbody/thermal‑photon occupation** (contactless near‑field radiative thermometry).
- **Atom–surface quantum interactions**: Casimir–Polder/van der Waals level shifts and surface‑modified spontaneous emission (Purcell) rates, giving the local vacuum mode density.
- With two atoms in adjacent tweezers, **surface‑mediated Rydberg interactions** report the sample's ability to screen or transmit dipolar coupling — a direct probe of local dielectric screening and decoherence.

**Why it is genuinely new.** STM measures LDOS, AFM force, NSOM optical near fields at fixed laser bands, MIM GHz conductivity — all with a solid, invasive, hard‑to‑calibrate tip. SRAM replaces the tip with a *single quantum object of exactly known internal structure*, giving SI‑traceable, non‑perturbative measurements of DC‑to‑THz electric fields, their noise spectra, and the local vacuum/thermal photon environment — quantities central to quantum‑device surface science yet inaccessible to every existing scanning probe.

**Feasibility.** All ingredients exist separately: tweezer arrays with single‑atom control, Rydberg electrometry already demonstrated at µV/cm sensitivity and used for microwave sensing, and atom trapping within a few hundred nm of dielectric/nanophotonic surfaces. Development steps are stable trapping close to conducting surfaces (blue‑detuned/nanophotonic traps), UV‑light‑induced adsorbate control, and photon‑budget‑efficient repetition; spurious signals are nulled by retracting the tweezer and by the strict n‑scaling (n⁷ for Stark, n² for microwave coupling) of the genuine surface response.

**Scanning Entangled‑Photon (Quantum‑Coherence) Near‑Field Microscopy — "SEPM": using one half of an entangled photon pair as the probe and reading out the *quantum state* it comes back in, rather than the intensity it produces.**

**Concept.** A nonlinear crystal (or a quantum‑dot/SPDC source) fed into the scan head generates correlated photon pairs: a "signal" photon (visible, kept in the instrument and detected by efficient single‑photon detectors) and an "idler" photon (mid‑IR/THz, where detectors are poor) that is funnelled through a plasmonic/adiabatic taper tip and interacts with the sample in a ~10–30 nm near‑field spot. The tip is held in standard tuning‑fork feedback. The returning idler is recombined with a second, coherently pumped pair source (an "induced‑coherence / undetected‑photon" interferometer) so that the *visible* signal photon's interference fringe amplitude and phase encode the sample's local mid‑IR/THz complex response — never requiring an IR detector. In parallel, the pair's polarization/time‑bin entanglement is tomographed pixel by pixel, and coincidence statistics (g⁽²⁾, Hong–Ou–Mandel dip position and visibility) are recorded.

**Observables mapped pixel by pixel.** (i) The full complex local susceptibility ε(ω, r) across the molecular‑fingerprint mid‑IR/THz range — vibrational, phonon‑polariton and free‑carrier spectroscopy — with amplitude *and* phase obtained from a visible‑light measurement; (ii) the **local decoherence/entanglement‑degradation map**: concurrence, purity and HOM visibility loss quantify how strongly a nanoscale region dephases a photonic quantum state, i.e. a direct image of the sample's fluctuation/loss channels rather than its mean absorption; (iii) sub‑shot‑noise (squeezed/photon‑number‑correlated) absorption imaging, giving quantum‑enhanced sensitivity at photon fluxes low enough not to perturb photosensitive, soft‑matter, or cryogenic quantum samples; (iv) local nonlinear susceptibility χ⁽²⁾/χ⁽³⁾ read out as the local pair‑generation or pair‑absorption rate; (v) HOM time‑delay shifts giving absolute, calibration‑free nanoscale optical path/thickness metrology at the attosecond level.

**Why it is new.** STM measures LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near‑field *intensity* with classical light, MIM GHz admittance — all are mean, single‑photon‑number quantities in a narrow band with detector‑limited spectral reach. SEPM measures the *quantum state* of light after nanoscale interaction: it accesses spectral regions with no good detectors, obtains phase without a reference arm, delivers genuinely quantum‑limited sensitivity for damage‑free imaging of biological and photoresist samples, and produces a uniquely new contrast channel — the spatial map of where a material destroys photonic coherence and entanglement, which is exactly the figure of merit for quantum photonic circuits, single‑photon emitters and low‑loss cryogenic optics.

**Feasibility.** All ingredients exist separately: bright SPDC sources, induced‑coherence ("quantum") IR spectroscopy with undetected photons, plasmonic tips that funnel mid‑IR to ~20 nm, superconducting nanowire single‑photon detectors, and tuning‑fork tip control. Genuine near‑field quantum signal is isolated by tip‑retraction nulls, tip‑dither (higher‑harmonic) demodulation of the coincidence rate, and the requirement that the contrast appear only in the *correlated*, not the accidental, coincidence channel.

**Scanning Attosecond Chronoscopy (SAC) — "time-domain SPM": mapping the local *attosecond time delays* of electron dynamics instead of any static amplitude.**

**Concept.** A plasmonic nanotip is held in normal AFM/STM feedback and illuminated by carrier-envelope-phase-stable, few-cycle laser pulses. The apex field-enhancement confines the light-driven electron emission/tunneling to a ~1–10 nm spot. A second, phase-locked pulse (or the same field's next half-cycle) acts as an attosecond "streaking/attoclock" gate: the emitted electron's final momentum, recorded by a small time-of-flight/energy analyzer in the scan head — or, in the all-solid-state version, the sub-cycle-resolved current through the junction as a function of the delay between the two pulses — encodes *when* the electron left, with 10–100 attosecond precision. Raster scanning and delay-scanning at each pixel gives τ(r, E), the local Wigner/Eisenbud–Smith delay and its energy dependence.

**Observable.** Real-space maps of characteristic *times* rather than densities or forces: the local tunneling/emission delay, the dynamical screening (build-up) time of the electron gas, plasmon and exciton dephasing times, electron–electron and electron–phonon scattering times, and the initial-state-resolved delays that distinguish localized (d/f) from delocalized (sp) orbitals and surface from bulk/buried-interface emission. Sub-cycle current maps additionally give the local field-enhancement vector and the light-field-driven (petahertz) conductivity.

**Why it is new.** STM measures LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near-field amplitude, MIM permittivity — all time-averaged, steady-state quantities; ultrafast STM/THz-STM reaches ~ps–fs but images *populations*, not phase delays. SAC makes the *attosecond response time* itself the contrast channel, allowing one to see, region by region: where screening is fast (metallic) versus slow (correlated/Mott, excitonic insulator); how long a plasmon or exciton survives at an individual defect, grain boundary or moiré domain; the site-resolved orbital character of emission through its delay fingerprint; the speed limit of charge transfer across a single molecule–metal contact or a single 2D heterostructure interface — the key figure of merit for petahertz electronics, photocatalysis and light-wave switching.

**Feasibility.** All ingredients exist separately: CEP-stable few-cycle nanotip photoemission, attosecond streaking and attoclock metrology, sub-cycle-resolved tip currents, and compact electron energy analyzers on UHV AFM/STM heads. Genuine local signal is verified by tip-retraction nulls, CEP-reversal antisymmetrization, and the strict scaling of the delay with tip–sample gap.

**Scanning Coherent‑Electron‑Holography Microscopy (SCEHM) — a tip used as a coherent electron *point source* whose contrast is the quantum (Aharonov–Bohm/inner‑potential) phase of the electron wave, not a current or force.**

**Concept.** A single‑atom‑terminated field‑emission nanotip (W(111)/Ir or a carbon nanocone), held at 1–100 nm from the sample by tuning‑fork/tunneling feedback, emits a highly coherent, divergent low‑energy electron wave (20 eV–2 keV) from an effective source size < 0.3 nm. Part of the wave passes through or grazes the nanoscale region under the apex; the rest propagates as an unscattered reference wave. A pixelated single‑electron‑counting detector placed downstream (transmission geometry for membranes/2D materials, or a backscatter/low‑energy‑diffraction detector for bulk samples) records the in‑line hologram at each tip position. Because the tip *is* the source, the illuminated volume and the magnification are set by the tip–sample gap rather than by any lens, and gap scanning provides tomographic (through‑focus) depth sectioning. Numerical phase retrieval at every pixel converts the holograms into the local complex electron wave, and raster scanning stitches these into a map.

**Observables (per pixel).** The *phase* of the electron wave, which contains: (i) the local mean inner potential and electrostatic potential integrated along the path — hence buried charge, space‑charge layers, p–n junction and ferroelectric polarization fields, work‑function/patch potentials, with sub‑nm lateral and mV·nm sensitivity; (ii) the **magnetic Aharonov–Bohm phase**, ∮A·dl, i.e. direct real‑space imaging of enclosed flux — single vortices, skyrmion and domain‑wall flux, persistent currents, flux quantization at individual grain boundaries — a *gauge‑field* quantity no scanning probe measures; (iii) amplitude/diffraction contrast giving local atomic arrangement, strain and lattice orientation of *buried* layers, because low‑energy electrons emitted at the apex penetrate and diffract from subsurface planes; (iv) decoherence contrast: the loss of fringe visibility maps where the sample dephases an electron wave (fluctuating charges, thermal and current noise), the analogue of a local "which‑path" measurement.

**Why it is genuinely new.** STM reads surface LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near‑field optics, MIM permittivity — all are local *intensity/response* quantities, and all are confined to the topmost atomic layers. SCEHM measures the **quantum phase accumulated by a charged particle traversing the sample's electromagnetic potentials**, giving contactless, model‑free access to potentials and vector potentials (not just fields), to buried structure tens of nanometres deep, and to local electron decoherence — with no lenses and hence no aberration limit.

**Feasibility.** All parts exist separately: single‑atom coherent field emitters, low‑energy point‑projection electron holography of graphene and single proteins, off‑axis holography's AB‑phase sensitivity in TEM, delay‑line single‑electron detectors, and standard tip–sample distance control. Genuine local phase signal is verified by tip‑retraction nulls, by the strict scaling of fringe spacing with tip–sample gap, and by field/polarization‑reversal antisymmetrization to separate the magnetic AB phase from the electrostatic term.

**Scanning Quantum‑Fisher‑Information Microscopy (SQFIM) — a scanning probe whose contrast is the *local entanglement depth* of the many‑body state.**

**Concept.** A single apex carries two co‑located functions: (i) a nanoscale *drive* (a loop/stripline microwave antenna, a gate electrode, or a strain actuator) that applies a weak, frequency‑swept perturbation to a ~10–50 nm volume, and (ii) a quantum *sensor* (NV centre in a diamond pillar, SQUID‑on‑tip, or GHz‑matched tunnel junction) that reads the resulting local response and, with the drive off, the equilibrium fluctuation spectrum of the same volume. At every pixel one therefore records both the **local dynamical susceptibility χ″(r, ω)** (drive‑on, lock‑in, phase‑sensitive) and the local noise power S(r, ω) (drive‑off, relaxometry/spectrum analysis) over a broad frequency band, at controlled temperature, field and gate voltage.

**Observable.** Combining the two, pixel by pixel, gives the **quantum Fisher information density**

f_Q(r) = (4/π) ∫ dω tanh(ħω/2k_BT) χ″(r, ω),

whose consistency with S(r,ω) also provides an in‑situ fluctuation–dissipation check. Because f_Q/n > m certifies at least (m+1)‑partite entanglement, raster scanning produces a **real‑space map of the entanglement depth** — a quantum‑information observable, not a charge, force, optical or thermodynamic one — together with maps of the local spectral weight distribution, the local violation of the fluctuation–dissipation theorem (an effective‑temperature/entropy‑production image in driven or nonequilibrium regions), and the divergence of f_Q on approach to a quantum critical point.

**What no existing SPM gives.** STM sees LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near‑field optics, MIM conductivity, MFM/NV stray field — all are *classical, one‑body* quantities that cannot say whether a region of the sample is entangled. SQFIM would image: where multipartite entanglement actually lives in a quantum spin liquid or frustrated magnet (and whether it survives at defects, edges and grain boundaries); the spatial extent of the quantum‑critical "fan" around a single impurity or strain gradient; entanglement‑depth contrast between coexisting phases in phase‑separated correlated materials; and, in engineered devices, the pixel‑resolved loss of entanglement (decoherence hot spots) in qubit arrays and superconducting circuits.

**Feasibility.** Every ingredient exists separately: broadband NV/SQUID‑on‑tip noise spectroscopy with nT/√Hz at 50 nm standoff, scanning nano‑antenna FMR/ESR drive tips, cryogenic phase‑sensitive GHz detection, and QFI extraction already validated from bulk neutron‑scattering χ″ data. Genuine local signal is isolated by tip‑retraction nulls, drive‑amplitude linearity checks, and the strict tanh(ħω/2k_BT) temperature scaling that distinguishes the quantum from the thermal part of the response.

**Scanning Qubit‑Decoherence (Loss‑Tangent) Microscopy — "SQDM": a superconducting qubit itself is the scanning probe.**

**Concept.** The apex of a cryogenic scan head carries a miniaturized, frequency‑tunable superconducting qubit (transmon or flux qubit) fabricated on a sharp dielectric/Si probe chip, with its electric‑field antinode (a nanoscale shunt‑capacitor claw) or its flux loop protruding at the very tip. The probe is held 5–100 nm above the sample by tuning‑fork feedback, coupled to the sample only through its own evanescent electric/magnetic field, and read out dispersively through an on‑chip resonator and a Josephson parametric amplifier. At each pixel one performs a full qubit‑metrology sequence — T₁ relaxometry, Ramsey/spin‑echo dephasing, and qubit‑frequency spectroscopy — while sweeping the qubit frequency across 3–12 GHz (and sweeping temperature, magnetic field, gate bias, or drive power).

**Observable.** Rather than a current, force, optical field, or admittance, the contrast channel is the *decoherence the sample imposes on a quantum state*, resolved in frequency and separated by channel:
- **Local dielectric loss tangent tan δ(r, ω)** and **local magnetic/flux loss** at the single‑microwave‑photon level, obtained from Γ₁(r, ω), with absolute, calibration‑free units set by the known qubit dipole moment.
- **Individual two‑level‑system (TLS) defects**: as the qubit is tuned, each nearby TLS appears as a resolved avoided crossing, giving its transition frequency, coupling strength (hence dipole moment), position (from the height dependence), and its strain/electric‑field tuning — the first direct, one‑by‑one real‑space spectroscopy of the amorphous defects that limit superconducting qubits.
- **Local low‑frequency charge and flux noise spectra** S_Q(r, f), S_Φ(r, f), from Ramsey/echo/dynamical‑decoupling filter functions — a map of the 1/f fluctuators themselves.
- **Local quasiparticle density and pair‑breaking**, from the parity‑switching rate and the sub‑gap Γ₁ contribution, imaging where non‑equilibrium quasiparticles are generated and trapped in a superconducting film.
- **Coherent (non‑dissipative) coupling**: the qubit frequency shift maps the local dielectric constant, kinetic inductance and vortex/flux landscape, and strong coupling to a sample mode (magnon, phonon, plasmon, spin ensemble) yields a vacuum‑Rabi splitting image.

**Why it is new.** STM measures LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near‑field optics, MIM permittivity — all are mean, classical, essentially lossless‑limit responses. SQDM makes the *microwave‑frequency dissipation and dephasing experienced by a coherent quantum state* the imaging observable, at the single‑photon powers where TLS physics is nonlinear and where all other probes are blind. It would show, pixel by pixel, where the loss actually lives in a superconducting qubit chip — surface oxide, metal–substrate interface, resist residue, a single grain boundary, a Josephson junction barrier, a wirebond, an airbridge — turning "loss budget" from a device‑averaged number into a picture, and providing the same map for low‑loss dielectrics, kinetic‑inductance detectors, and quantum‑limited amplifiers.

**Feasibility.** All ingredients exist separately: flip‑chip and cantilever‑mounted qubits, qubit‑based sensing of single TLS and of quasiparticle bursts, JPA readout in dilution refrigerators, and tuning‑fork positioning at mK. The development steps are a mechanically robust qubit‑on‑tip with the field antinode at the apex and vibration isolation compatible with millisecond coherence. Genuine sample signal is isolated by tip‑retraction nulls, by the characteristic power‑law height dependence of surface dielectric loss (∝1/d for a dipole coupling to a lossy half‑space), and by TLS saturation/temperature scaling that distinguishes sample loss from intrinsic probe loss.

**Scanning Condensate‑Phase Interferometry Microscopy (SCPIM) — a scanning probe whose contrast is the *phase* of the superconducting (or superfluid) order parameter, φ(r), rather than its magnitude.**

**Concept.** A superconducting tip is coupled to the sample through a tunable tunnel junction (as in Josephson‑STM), but instead of reading only the critical‑current/pair‑density signal, the tip junction is wired as *one arm of a scanning DC SQUID*: the second, fixed reference junction contacts the sample at a stationary point, so the tip and reference form a closed superconducting loop. The critical current of this loop oscillates as I_c(Φ, r) ∝ |cos[(φ(r) − φ_ref + 2πΦ/Φ₀)/2]|, so at every pixel the position of the interference pattern in applied flux directly yields the **gauge‑invariant phase difference between the tip location and the reference**, while its amplitude gives the local pair amplitude. Phase resolution is set by flux noise, not by tunneling resolution; heights/junction resistance are swept to null background flux and to verify the sinusoidal current–phase relation. Adding a fast, low‑noise readout of the same loop records the phase *fluctuation* spectrum S_φ(r, ω) at each pixel.

**Observables (per pixel).** The real‑space map of φ(r); its gradient ∇φ, i.e. the **local superfluid velocity and supercurrent field** (magnitude *and* direction) without contacts; the winding of φ around individual vortices and antivortices, including fractional and half‑quantum vortices; the *sign* of the order parameter across domains — π versus 0 regions in s± iron‑based superconductors, sign‑changing d‑wave lobes, pair‑density‑wave (PDW) sign alternation, and the sign structure of proposed chiral/triplet states; the local phase‑coherence length and the spatial onset of phase stiffness in granular, underdoped or pseudogap films (where |Δ| is finite but the phase is not ordered); local phase‑slip and telegraph events; and the spatially resolved current–phase relation of a single grain boundary, twin boundary, or engineered weak link.

**Why it is genuinely new.** STM measures LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near‑field optics, MIM conductivity, and even Josephson‑STM measures only the *modulus* of the pair wavefunction; scanning SQUID measures stray magnetic field, not the condensate phase. SCPIM makes the **quantum phase of the macroscopic wavefunction — the quantity that actually orders at T_c and that carries all topological information (vortices, sign changes, phase stiffness)** — the imaging channel, turning long‑standing indirect sign‑structure arguments (tricrystal experiments, quasiparticle interference phase analysis) into a direct picture.

**Feasibility.** All ingredients exist separately: superconducting‑tip Josephson STM with mK stability, nano‑SQUID readout with µΦ₀/√Hz sensitivity, and flux‑modulated lock‑in detection. Genuine phase signal is verified by tip‑retraction nulls, by the strict Φ₀ periodicity of the interference, and by loop‑area/reference‑point substitution.

**Scanning Exciton‑Transfer Microscopy (SXTM) — a single quantum emitter on the tip that injects and re‑absorbs *excitons*, making energy (not charge, force, light intensity, or impedance) the contrast channel.**

**Concept.** The apex carries one well‑characterized emitter — a single dye molecule, colloidal quantum dot, or a diamond/hBN color center — mounted on a nanopillar and held 2–20 nm above the sample by tuning‑fork feedback. The emitter is optically pumped and its excitation is transferred to the sample *non‑radiatively*, by Förster (dipole–dipole, ∝1/d⁶) or, at sub‑nm gaps, Dexter (exchange) coupling, so a single exciton is deposited into a ~2–10 nm spot far below any optical diffraction or even plasmonic near‑field limit. The read‑out is the tip emitter itself: its fluorescence lifetime, intensity, and photon statistics are recorded at every pixel, while a pulsed pump–probe (or a second emitter/collection channel a controlled distance away) times how long an injected exciton takes to reappear, and a tunable pump/detection window resolves the transfer spectrum.

**Observables per pixel.** The local energy‑transfer rate k_ET(r) (hence the local acceptor density and the sample's local optical density of states at the emitter frequency, in absolute units set by the known donor dipole); the **local exciton diffusion tensor D(r) and diffusion length**, from the delay/arrival statistics between injection and detection points; local exciton energy, binding energy, and the depth of trap states (from the spectral dependence of transfer); the branching into dark/triplet states, singlet‑fission and triplet‑fusion yields; the **orientation of the local transition dipole** (from the tip‑dipole‑angle dependence); and exciton–exciton annihilation, seen as a density‑dependent nonlinearity in the transfer rate.

**What existing SPMs cannot do.** STM images LDOS, AFM force, NSOM the *radiative* near field (still limited by the plasmonic tip mode and blind to non‑radiative channels), MIM the GHz admittance. None of them injects a *neutral* excitation, and none measures where energy — rather than charge — actually flows. SXTM would map, defect by defect, why excitons die in OLED and photovoltaic films; image exciton funneling and trapping in moiré TMD heterostructures, single grain boundaries, and molecular aggregates; visualize energy transport in photosynthetic light‑harvesting complexes and in perovskite grains; and quantify the "dark" (non‑radiative) loss landscape of single‑photon sources and quantum emitters — a quantity that is invisible to every photon‑counting far‑field or near‑field technique because it never produces a photon in the sample.

**Feasibility.** All parts exist separately: single‑molecule/QD‑functionalized SPM tips, nanopillar NV probes, single‑molecule FRET with nm sensitivity, and picosecond time‑correlated single‑photon counting on scan heads. Genuine local transfer is verified by the strict 1/d⁶ (Förster) or exponential (Dexter) gap scaling, by spectral‑overlap detuning nulls, and by tip‑retraction controls that separate energy transfer from radiative (Purcell/near‑field) modification of the emitter.

**Scanning Irreversibility Microscopy (SIM) — a scanning probe whose contrast is the *local rate of entropy production*, i.e. the degree to which detailed balance (time‑reversal symmetry of fluctuations) is broken under the tip.**

**Concept.** The apex carries two (or more) closely spaced, independently read‑out sensing channels — e.g. a soft cantilever/nanomechanical mode plus a co‑located electrical (tunnel/capacitive) or optical channel, or two nanoelectrodes ~20–50 nm apart. No drive is applied to the sample; instead, at each pixel the instrument records long, simultaneous *time series* of the spontaneous fluctuations in both channels, x₁(t) and x₂(t), at MHz–GHz bandwidth. Rather than reducing these to a mean value or to a noise power (which are time‑reversal symmetric), the analysis reconstructs the two‑dimensional phase‑space trajectory and extracts the **cyclic probability current** and the antisymmetric part of the cross‑correlation, C₁₂(τ) − C₂₁(τ) ≠ 0 — the unambiguous signature of broken detailed balance. Equivalently, one computes the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the forward and time‑reversed trajectory ensembles, which lower‑bounds the local entropy production rate σ(r) = (dS/dt)(r) in units of k_B/s, and the corresponding local violation of the fluctuation–dissipation theorem (an "effective temperature" map).

**Observables per pixel.** σ(r) (entropy production / arrow‑of‑time strength); the phase‑space circulation loops that identify *which* microscopic cycle is being driven; the local effective temperature T_eff(r,ω) versus the true bath temperature; the frequency band in which irreversibility resides; and the crossover radius at which activity decays back to equilibrium around a driven site.

**What no existing SPM gives.** STM (LDOS), AFM (force), NSOM (near‑field optics), MIM (admittance) and even noise/thermometry probes all measure quantities that are invariant under t → −t; none can tell whether a nanoscale region is in equilibrium or is being actively driven, nor how much free energy it is dissipating. SIM would image: the energy‑consuming machinery of living cells (molecular motors, active membranes, cytoskeletal remodeling) with the "activity" itself as contrast; where in a battery, memristor, catalyst or electrochemical interface the free energy is actually being burned rather than stored; nonequilibrium steady states and their spatial extent around a single defect, hot spot, or current‑carrying channel; the microscopic dissipative cycles behind 1/f noise and decoherence in qubits; and the local thermodynamic cost of computation and of information erasure in nanodevices, providing a real‑space test of stochastic‑thermodynamic uncertainty relations.

**Feasibility.** All ingredients exist separately: high‑bandwidth multi‑channel SPM readout, sub‑pN/√Hz cantilevers and low‑noise cryogenic amplifiers, and the trajectory‑based irreversibility estimators already validated in single‑molecule and active‑matter experiments. Genuine sample irreversibility is isolated by tip‑retraction nulls, by verifying that the measured circulation vanishes on an equilibrium reference region at the same temperature, and by checking that the instrument's own back‑action drive (which would fake a current) scales with tip stiffness/bias while the sample signal scales with the applied chemical or electrical driving.

**Scanning Chirality Microscopy (SChM) — a parity-sensitive scanning probe that images the *absolute handedness* of matter, pixel by pixel.**

**Concept.** The apex is made *enantiopure*: a single chiral molecule (e.g., a helicene, binaphthyl, or peptide helix) or a chiral plasmonic nano-helix/gammadion is grafted onto an otherwise standard AFM/STM/qPlus tip, and an identical tip carrying the *mirror-image* enantiomer is mounted alongside (or the tip is exchanged in situ). At each pixel the instrument records the difference between the two handedness channels — Δ = S(L-tip) − S(R-tip) — in one or more coupled read-outs: (i) the diastereomeric short-range force/adhesion and higher-harmonic stiffness from the chiral tip–sample contact, (ii) the chirality-induced spin-selectivity (CISS) signal, i.e. the tunneling current asymmetry when the tip (or a ferromagnetic back-contact) is spin-polarized and the magnetization is reversed, and (iii) tip-enhanced circular-dichroism/optical-rotation of light funneled through the chiral apex. Because parity, not time reversal, is the symmetry being tested, the genuine signal is odd under **tip-enantiomer exchange** and even under magnetic-field reversal — a background-free null unavailable to any other probe.

**Observables per pixel.** The sign and magnitude of the local enantiomeric excess (absolute configuration of individual adsorbed molecules); the handedness of chiral crystal domains, twisted/moiré stacking, screw dislocations, and chiral surface reconstructions; local spin-filtering efficiency (CISS asymmetry) and its correlation with molecular conformation; chiral phonon/plasmon activity through the frequency-resolved tip-enhanced dichroism; and racemization or chirality-switching events followed in real time at a single site.

**What existing SPMs cannot do.** STM sees LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near-field intensity, MIM admittance — none of them is *parity-odd*, so none can distinguish an enantiomer from its mirror image except indirectly through imaged geometry (which fails for buried, disordered, or dynamically racemizing species). SChM makes handedness itself the contrast channel, enabling: single-molecule assignment of absolute configuration in pharmaceuticals and on chiral catalysts; mapping enantioselective active sites and how they are poisoned; imaging chiral symmetry breaking during crystallization and in chiral magnets/chiral topological materials; and locating where spin filtering actually occurs in CISS-based spintronic and chiral-induced spin devices.

**Feasibility.** All parts exist separately: chemically functionalized (CO-, molecule-terminated) tips, chiral plasmonic nano-antennas, tip-enhanced circular dichroism, and spin-polarized STM. Genuine chiral signal is verified by tip-enantiomer swap antisymmetrization, by nulling on an achiral reference region, and by tip-retraction and racemic-tip controls.

**Scanning Anyon‑Braiding (Exchange‑Statistics) Microscopy — a tip that physically drags a quasiparticle around a closed loop and reads out the statistical (Berry) phase it accumulates, mapping exchange statistics in real space.**

**Concept.** In a dilution‑refrigerator scan head, a metallized apex acts as a mobile, few‑nanometre‑deep potential well (a "quasiparticle tweezer") over a fractional quantum‑Hall, fractional‑Chern‑insulator, spin‑liquid, or vortex‑carrying topological‑superconductor sample. Biasing the tip nucleates and traps a single localized excitation (an e/3 Laughlin quasihole, a vison, or a vortex‑bound Majorana mode); the tip then adiabatically transports it along a programmable closed path that encircles a chosen set of other pinned quasiparticles. The accumulated phase is read out interferometrically by a *second*, co‑located sensor on the same apex — a scanning single‑electron transistor / quantum‑dot charge sensor forming a nanoscale Fabry–Pérot or Mach–Zehnder loop with the sample edge, or a Josephson/compressibility read‑out — which registers the oscillation of the local chemical potential, compressibility, or edge‑interference conductance as the enclosed statistical flux changes by one quasiparticle at a time. Subtracting the Aharonov–Bohm part (measured by encircling a *charge‑free* region of identical area, and by field/area scaling) leaves the pure exchange phase.

**Observables per pixel.** (i) the local statistical phase θ per enclosed excitation — 2π/3, π/2, π, or the θ of an unknown state — i.e. a direct, real‑space measurement of anyonic statistics; (ii) maps of where individual quasiparticles are pinned and how many are enclosed (statistical‑flux counting, quantized in units of θ); (iii) for non‑Abelian candidates, the *non‑commutativity* of two braids, tested by executing braid sequences in both orders at the same site and detecting the resulting state change (a topological‑qubit read‑out, e.g. fermion parity of a vortex pair); (iv) the local topological gap and decoherence, from the maximum braiding speed and the loss of phase coherence as a function of path length and temperature; (v) the pinning landscape and quasiparticle mobility, from the tip force/current required to drag the excitation.

**Why it is genuinely new.** STM reads LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near fields, MIM admittance — all are local, one‑body, geometry‑independent quantities that carry no information about *particle exchange*. Statistics has so far been inferred only indirectly and device‑averaged (edge interferometry, current cross‑correlations). Making the braiding phase itself the imaging channel would directly certify fractional and non‑Abelian statistics, image how it survives at disorder, edges and domain walls, locate the "good" regions of a device for topological qubits, and turn braiding from a global transport signature into a spatially resolved picture.

**Feasibility.** All ingredients exist separately: scanning‑gate control of individual localized states, scanning SET/compressibility probes with sub‑e sensitivity at 10 mK, quasiparticle‑trapping by local potentials, and edge interferometers showing anyonic phase slips. Genuine statistical signal is isolated by tip‑retraction nulls, by loop‑area and loop‑orientation scaling (the exchange term is area‑independent while the Aharonov–Bohm term is not), and by reversing the braid direction, which must flip the sign of θ.

**Scanning Chemical‑Potential (Nano‑Osmometry) Microscopy — "SCPM": a probe that measures the local *electrochemical potential of a chosen chemical species*, μ̃_i(r), at zero net flux, rather than any current, force, optical field, or impedance.**

**Concept.** The apex is a species‑selective *equilibrium* sensor rather than a current collector: a sub‑100 nm nanopipette or hollow tip whose orifice is closed by an ionophore‑loaded membrane, a solid‑electrolyte/ion‑insertion nanocrystal (e.g. LixFePO₄ for Li⁺, YSZ or a perovskite for O²⁻, IrOx for H⁺), or a hydrogel/osmotic nanocell for neutral species such as H₂O or O₂. Tip–sample distance is held by tuning‑fork/shear‑force or ionic‑conductance feedback. At each pixel the tip is allowed to come to local equilibrium with the sample and its open‑circuit (zero‑current, zero‑flux) potential — or, for neutral species, the osmotic pressure/mechanical deflection of the nanocell — is read out against a distant reference electrode. Because the measurement is made at null flux, the reading is a genuine thermodynamic potential, not a transport signal.

**Observable.** Real‑space maps of μ̃_i(r) = μ_i⁰ + k_BT ln a_i(r) + z_i eφ(r) for the selected species — i.e. the local *activity* a_i(r) (not merely concentration) and, by using a second, charge‑insensitive channel or an inert reference ion, its separation into the chemical part (ln a_i) and the local electrostatic potential φ(r). Sweeping temperature at each pixel gives the local **partial molar entropy** s_i(r) = −∂μ_i/∂T; applying a tip load or hydrostatic modulation gives the local **partial molar volume** v_i(r) = ∂μ_i/∂P; comparing μ̃_i(r) with the simultaneously measured ionic/electronic current gives the local **overpotential and thermodynamic efficiency**, and the gradient ∇μ̃_i(r) gives the true, spatially resolved **driving force** for diffusion and reaction.

**What no existing SPM provides.** STM reads LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near‑field optics, MIM admittance, KPFM the electron work function, and SECM/SICM an amperometric *flux* or a conductance — none returns the equilibrium chemical potential of a specified ion or molecule, and therefore none can say whether a nanoscale region is uphill or downhill in free energy. SCPM would image: where the free‑energy losses (overpotential) actually occur in an operating battery electrode — particle by particle, at a single grain boundary, cathode–electrolyte interphase or crack tip; the true Li⁺/H⁺/O²⁻ activity landscape that drives dendrite nucleation, phase separation in intercalation compounds, and degradation; the local water and ion activity across membranes, fuel‑cell ionomers and biological tissue (nano‑osmometry of a single cell or organelle); the chemical‑potential drop across a catalyst–support interface that sets turnover; and, with the entropy/volume derivatives, a pixel‑resolved local equation of state and Gibbs free‑energy map of heterogeneous materials.

**Feasibility.** All parts exist separately: ion‑selective nanopipette electrodes with tens‑of‑nm tips, solid‑electrolyte and ion‑insertion microreferences, SICM distance control, and high‑impedance electrometer readout. Genuine local equilibrium signal is verified by tip‑retraction nulls, by Nernstian calibration in known‑activity standards, by checking null‑flux (no measurable current) operation, and by the required Nernst‑slope temperature scaling that distinguishes true chemical‑potential contrast from junction/streaming‑potential artifacts.

**Scanning Thermal‑Hall / Heat‑Current‑Vector Microscopy (STHM) — a probe that images the *local thermal conductivity tensor*, including its antisymmetric (thermal‑Hall, Righi–Leduc) component κ_xy(r), rather than temperature, force, current, or permittivity.**

**Concept.** The apex combines (i) a nanoscale point heat source — a resistive nano‑heater, a pulsed‑laser‑absorbing plasmonic apex, or a Joule‑heated tunnel junction — with (ii) a multi‑point thermometry array that resolves not just T but its *gradient vector*: several NV centres in a diamond nanopillar, a co‑located thermocouple pair/quadrupole, or a scanning SQUID/Johnson‑noise thermometer that is stepped around the injection point. Heat is injected at r₀ with kHz modulation, and the resulting temperature field δT(r₀ + d) is mapped as a function of the offset vector **d**, at each pixel, in a swept magnetic field and at mK–300 K.

**Observable.** Inverting the measured local heat‑diffusion Green's function gives, pixel by pixel: the full thermal conductivity tensor κ_ij(r); the *antisymmetric* part κ_xy(r), extracted as the component of the temperature pattern that swirls around the heat source and is odd under B‑reversal (a genuinely background‑free null, since ordinary diffusion is symmetric); the local thermal diffusivity and phonon/magnon mean free path from the frequency (or time) dependence of the thermal wave; and the local heat‑current *direction* in an operating device.

**Why it is new and useful.** STM sees LDOS, AFM force, NSOM near fields, MIM admittance, SThM only a scalar temperature — none returns the transverse, time‑reversal‑odd sector of heat transport. STHM would: test whether the half‑quantized thermal Hall signal κ_xy/T = (π/12)(k_B²/ħ) claimed for α‑RuCl₃ and cuprates is intrinsic and spatially uniform or comes from particular domains, twins, or stacking faults (the central controversy in the field, currently addressed only by device‑averaged bulk measurements); image chiral‑phonon and magnon‑Berry‑curvature contributions separately by their different length/frequency scales; map where Majorana edge modes, if present, actually carry heat; visualize ballistic vs. hydrodynamic (phonon Poiseuille) heat flow and heat funnelling around single grain boundaries, interfaces, and hot spots in power devices and thermoelectrics.

**Feasibility.** All pieces exist separately: NV thermometry with mK sensitivity at ~50 nm standoff, scanning Johnson‑noise thermometry, nano‑heater tips, and lock‑in thermal‑wave detection; the development step is the vector (multi‑point) thermometer at the apex. Artifacts (heater asymmetry, tip drift, magnetothermal response of the probe itself) are removed by B‑reversal antisymmetrization, heater/thermometer swap, and tip‑retraction nulls.

**Scanning Coulomb‑Drag Microscopy (SCDM) — imaging the *interlayer momentum/energy transfer rate* between a probe electron gas and the sample.**

**Concept.** Instead of a metal tip, the apex carries a small, separately contacted two‑dimensional conductor (a graphene or TMD flake on an hBN‑clad nanopillar, ~50–100 nm across) held 1–10 nm above the sample by tuning‑fork feedback. A current is driven through the sample (or, in the "passive" variant, only its equilibrium/nonequilibrium current fluctuations are used), and the **open‑circuit drag voltage induced in the probe flake by pure Coulomb (and plasmon‑mediated) coupling** is recorded with a lock‑in at every pixel. No tunneling, no contact, no light: the only coupling is the interlayer electron–electron interaction, whose strength falls off steeply with the gap, so the signal comes from a patch of sample the size of the flake–sample separation.

**Observables per pixel.** The local drag resistivity ρ_D(r, T, n, ω) and its sign, which give: the local carrier density *and carrier polarity* (drag reverses sign for electrons vs holes, mapping p–n puddles and charge‑neutrality regions); the local momentum‑relaxation and electron–electron scattering rates (drag ∝ τ_ee) — a direct, contactless map of *interaction strength* rather than conductivity; the local plasmon dispersion and interlayer screening (from the frequency and density dependence of the drag peak); "energy drag"/noise drag, which images hot‑electron and hydrodynamic regions; giant/negative drag signatures of exciton condensation, Wigner crystallization and correlated insulating states in moiré and double‑layer systems; and, with a magnetic field, the local *Hall* drag component, sensitive to composite‑fermion and excitonic order.

**Why it is beyond STM/AFM/NSOM/MIM.** All of those measure a one‑body response of the sample to a probe field (LDOS, force, near‑field permittivity, admittance). SCDM measures the rate at which the sample's carriers **exchange momentum and energy with an external electron gas**, i.e. the Coulomb interaction and screening function itself, χ(q, ω), locally — a two‑body, interaction‑resolved quantity that is invisible to every existing scanning probe, and one that requires no electrical contact to, or tunneling into, the region being imaged.

**Feasibility.** All parts exist separately: hBN‑encapsulated graphene "probe" layers, van der Waals pick‑up onto AFM pillars, bulk Coulomb‑drag measurements at nV sensitivity, and cryogenic tuning‑fork positioning. Genuine drag is verified by tip‑retraction and gap‑scaling nulls (ρ_D ∝ 1/d⁴ for momentum drag), by Onsager reciprocity under swapping drive and detection layers, by the T² temperature law, and by the sign reversal on crossing the sample's charge‑neutrality point — all of which separate it from capacitive crosstalk or thermoelectric artifacts.

**Scanning Distribution‑Function Microscopy (SDFM) — a probe whose contrast is the *electron energy‑occupancy function* f(E, r), not the density of states.**

**Concept.** The apex is an energy‑*filtering* tunnel probe rather than a broadband metallic tip: either a superconducting tip (whose sharp BCS gap edge acts as a ~10–100 µeV‑wide energy filter) or a tip terminated by a single quantum dot / molecular level whose discrete resonance is Stark‑tuned by the bias. Held in normal STM feedback over an *operating* device (current‑biased, illuminated, or microwave‑driven), the tip records I(V) and dI/dV at each pixel; because the tunneling current is a convolution of the known tip filter with the sample's occupancy, deconvolution returns the full nonequilibrium electron energy distribution f(E) at that point, with meV–µeV resolution. The occupancy (odd‑in‑energy, bias‑antisymmetric) part is separated from the LDOS (even) part by bias‑polarity antisymmetrization and by normalizing against a reference region of known equilibrium occupancy; tip retraction and drive‑off nulls confirm the local origin.

**Observables per pixel.** The shape of f(E, r) itself: the local electron temperature *and* whether the distribution is even Fermi–Dirac at all — double‑step (two‑terminal, non‑thermalized) distributions, hot‑carrier tails, photon‑assisted/Floquet sidebands at ±nħΩ, population inversion, and the local effective chemical potential μ(r) (i.e., contactless four‑probe voltage measurement inside a device). Spatial evolution of the steps gives the *energy relaxation length* and separates electron–electron from electron–phonon thermalization; in superconductors it gives the local quasiparticle occupation and charge‑imbalance profile.

**Why it is new.** STM measures the density of *available* states, AFM force, NSOM near fields, MIM admittance, SThM/Johnson noise only a scalar temperature that presupposes thermal equilibrium. None reports *which states are actually occupied*. SDFM would image where and how electrons thermalize in graphene and 2D devices, map hot‑carrier extraction in photovoltaics and hot‑electron bolometers, locate quasiparticle poisoning sources in superconducting qubits, visualize the breakdown of the quantum‑Hall state and of hydrodynamic flow, and provide the first real‑space test of nonequilibrium Boltzmann/Keldysh theory.

**Feasibility.** All ingredients exist separately: superconducting‑tip STM at mK, quantum‑dot‑terminated tips, and tunnel‑probe extraction of f(E) already demonstrated in lithographic mesoscopic wires with fixed probes — the step is to make that probe scannable.

**Scanning Quantum‑Coherence Microscopy (SQCM) — "holographic tunneling": imaging the *off‑diagonal* single‑particle density matrix, ρ(r₁,r₂;E) = ⟨ψ†(r₁)ψ(r₂)⟩, i.e. the amplitude *and phase* of the electronic wavefunction, rather than |ψ|².**

**Concept.** The probe is a *double‑apex* ("dimer") tip: two atomically sharp emitters separated by a controllable 0.3–5 nm, fabricated as a nano‑machined tip pair, a molecule‑bridged double apex, or a single tip carrying a phase‑reference quantum‑dot level. Both apexes tunnel simultaneously into the sample at the same bias, so a single electron has two coherent paths and the current contains, besides the incoherent sum of the two LDOS terms, an interference cross‑term I_int ∝ 2 Re[t₁t₂* ρ(r₁,r₂;eV)]. This cross‑term is isolated background‑free by threading a small magnetic flux through the tip–sample loop and lock‑in detecting at the Φ₀‑periodic Aharonov–Bohm modulation (or by piezo/bias modulation of one path's phase), which also sweeps the relative phase and therefore yields both Re and Im parts. Scanning the apex‑separation vector **d** = r₂ − r₁ at each pixel, and sweeping bias, gives the complex, energy‑resolved coherence function; Fourier transforming over **d** returns a *local* momentum‑space object.

**Observables per pixel.** The phase of the Bloch/molecular wavefunction and hence the *sign* of orbital lobes and nodal planes (orbital symmetry/parity of a single adsorbed molecule, defect state or impurity resonance, without DFT matching); the sign structure of order parameters (d‑wave lobes, s± inter‑pocket sign change, pair‑density‑wave sign alternation) read directly rather than inferred from quasiparticle‑interference intensity; the real‑space **single‑particle coherence length** and its decay law, distinguishing Anderson‑localized, diffusive and ballistic regions and imaging where the electron's phase is destroyed (decoherence hot spots, magnetic impurities, fluctuating charges); the Berry/geometric phase winding accumulated around a Dirac point, vortex, or domain wall; and the local band structure via the **d**‑Fourier transform, i.e. E(k) measured inside one micro‑domain.

**Why it is genuinely new.** STM measures the *diagonal* of the density matrix (LDOS, |ψ|²), AFM force, NSOM near‑field intensity, MIM admittance — all are phase‑blind, positive‑definite quantities. SQCM makes the *quantum phase and the off‑diagonal coherence of the electronic state itself* the contrast channel, turning sign structure, orbital parity and phase‑coherence — quantities currently obtained only indirectly (tricrystal experiments, QPI phase analysis, weak‑localization transport averages) — into direct images.

**Feasibility.** All ingredients exist separately: multi‑apex and nanofabricated double tips, atomically defined molecular tip terminations, sub‑Φ₀ flux modulation in nanoscale loops, and cryogenic mK STM stability. Genuine coherence signal is certified by its strict Φ₀ periodicity in flux, its exponential dependence on apex separation and temperature (thermal dephasing length), and by tip‑retraction and single‑apex nulls that remove the incoherent LDOS background and capacitive crosstalk.

**Proposal: Acoustically‑directed self‑assembly ("sono‑epitaxy") using standing surface‑acoustic‑wave (SAW) fields.**

Instead of pre‑patterning the substrate chemically or topographically, the BCP film is spin‑cast onto a piezoelectric substrate (e.g., 128° Y‑cut LiNbO₃ or a ZnO/AlN‑coated Si wafer) carrying interdigitated transducers. During thermal or solvent‑vapour annealing, counter‑propagating RF signals (tens of MHz–GHz) generate a **standing surface acoustic wave**, i.e. a spatially periodic, dynamically tunable field of nodes and antinodes. Three coupled effects register the microdomains to this virtual template: (i) the periodic in‑plane strain/stress field, which couples to the chain stretching and interfacial tension of the ordering domains (an elastic analogue of an electric field's dielectric coupling); (ii) acoustic radiation pressure and acoustic streaming in the softened/solvent‑swollen film, which biases domain orientation and accelerates defect annihilation by driving polymer flow; and (iii) the mild periodic acoustothermal heating that modulates the local χN, creating a "thermal chemoepitaxy" pattern without any surface chemistry.

Key advantages: the template is *non‑contact, erasable, and reconfigurable in real time* — the pitch is set simply by the SAW wavelength (λ_SAW/2), so density multiplication is achieved by matching L₀ to integer fractions of the acoustic period, and the alignment direction can be rotated or switched off electronically using orthogonal transducer pairs. Because ordering is driven by mechanical energy rather than by a lithographically defined guide, no guiding pattern must be removed afterwards, and defect annealing is greatly enhanced by the oscillatory shear, which "shakes" the film out of metastable defect states — potentially yielding sub‑10 nm line/space and hole arrays over wafer scale with a single, reusable piezoelectric chuck.

**Proposal: "Charge‑epitaxy" – DSA guided by a rewritable pattern of trapped electrostatic charge in an electret underlayer.**

Coat the substrate with a thin electret film (e.g., Teflon AF, CYTOP, or SiO₂/Si₃N₄ with deep traps) that is chemically uniform and topographically flat, then *write* into it a periodic pattern of immobilized space charge — by biased‑AFM/conductive‑stamp charge injection, focused electron‑beam charging, corona discharge through a mask, or contact electrification with a patterned elastomeric stamp. The frozen charge creates a spatially periodic in‑plane/fringing electric field at the film–substrate interface with a pitch set by the writing pattern (which can be a multiple of L₀ for density multiplication). When the BCP is spin‑cast and annealed, the blocks segregate according to their dielectric constants and dipole/ion partitioning: the higher‑permittivity (or ionically doped/salt‑complexed) block is drawn to the high‑field regions, while the low‑ε block is expelled, so the microdomains register to the charge pattern exactly as they would to a chemical prepattern — but through purely electrostatic, non‑contact, chemistry‑free guiding. Adding a small amount of a salt (e.g., LiTFSI in a PEO block) or using a polyelectrolyte/ionic‑liquid‑containing block strongly amplifies the coupling, allowing very low charge densities to be effective.

Distinct advantages: the "template" is written and erased rather than lithographically fabricated — heating above the electret's charge‑relaxation temperature, UV flood exposure, or ion‑ambient neutralization wipes the pattern, so a single substrate can be reprogrammed for different pitches, orientations and geometries (lines, dots, bends, gradients) and reused after the polymer is stripped; no guide stripes remain in the final pattern, eliminating the pattern‑transfer artifacts of graphoepitaxy/chemoepitaxy; and the charge pattern can be written with sparse, low‑resolution features while the field's smooth periodic modulation supports large density multiplication. The same trapped‑charge field also supplies a thermodynamic driving force during annealing that helps annihilate dislocations/disclinations, improving long‑range order.

**Proposal: "Opto‑epitaxy" – DSA templated by a holographic interference light field (virtual, reconfigurable optical template).**

Rather than pre‑patterning the substrate, the guiding pattern is projected *into* the film as light. A two‑ (or three‑) beam interference pattern from a UV/visible laser is imaged onto the BCP during thermal or solvent‑vapour annealing, producing a periodic array of bright/dark fringes whose pitch (λ/2sinθ) is continuously tunable and whose orientation, symmetry (lines, square/hexagonal dot lattices, gradients, bends) and phase can be changed on the fly by rotating/adding beams or using an SLM/DMD for arbitrary "maskless" layouts.

Coupling to the microdomains is achieved by making one block photo‑responsive: e.g. an azobenzene‑ (or spiropyran‑/coumarin‑) containing block, or a block loaded with a photothermal/photoacid additive. In the bright fringes, trans–cis photo‑isomerization photo‑fluidizes and photo‑softens that block, changes its polarity/solubility parameter and hence χ, and drives athermal photo‑induced mass transport toward (or away from) the illuminated regions; photothermal absorbers additionally create a periodic temperature modulation that locally tunes χN, ordering kinetics and the solvent‑swelling ratio. The result is a spatially periodic chemical/mobility "pseudo‑prepattern" that registers the microdomains exactly as a chemical prepattern would, with density multiplication when L₀ is an integer fraction of the optical period. Polarized light additionally sets an in‑plane easy axis via photo‑orientation (Weigert effect), aligning cylinders/lamellae normal to the polarization.

Key advantages: the template is written by light and disappears when the light is switched off (cis→trans relaxation), so it leaves no residual guiding stripes or trenches to strip; it is fully rewritable and reusable, allowing several different patterns to be explored on one wafer, in‑situ pattern correction (feedback from real‑time GISAXS/reflectivity), and dynamic "moving‑fringe" annealing in which the interference pattern is slowly translated or its pitch swept—an optical analogue of zone annealing—that sweeps defects out of the film and yields long‑range order without any lithographic pre‑pattern.

**Proposal: "Solidification (eutectic) epitaxy" – DSA templated by a directionally crystallized, sacrificial molecular crystal that is removed by sublimation.**

The BCP is blended with (or overcoated/underlaid by) a sacrificial, volatile small molecule that crystallizes in well‑defined lamellae or forms a eutectic with the polymer — e.g. benzoic acid, anthracene, succinonitrile, camphor, urea, or even water/ice. The sample is heated above the additive's melting point (the BCP is then swollen/plasticized and disordered) and pulled at constant velocity through a sharp thermal gradient, so a **planar crystallization front sweeps across the wafer**. Two effects direct the assembly: (i) the growing crystal *rejects* the polymer into the intercrystalline channels, producing a self‑generated, periodic array of "trenches" and chemically distinct crystal walls whose spacing is set by the classic Jackson–Hunt relation (λ² v ≈ const., i.e. tunable from ~1 µm to tens of nm simply by changing the pulling speed and gradient), and (ii) the moving front itself imposes a directional confinement and a solute/solvent‑concentration gradient that continuously orders the microdomains behind it, in a zone‑refining fashion that sweeps dislocations and disclinations out of the film. The BCP thus templates on a *transient, self‑organized* mould rather than on a lithographic one, with the crystal facets/growth direction fixing the in‑plane orientation and the confining width fixing the number of domain rows (density multiplication when λ = n·L₀).

After ordering, the template is simply **sublimed or washed away** (all the candidate additives are volatile/soluble), leaving a clean, guide‑free BCP pattern on a flat, chemically uniform substrate.

Advantages: no e‑beam/EUV pre‑patterning, no residual guiding stripes or trenches to strip, wafer‑scale and roll‑to‑roll compatible (a moving hot/cold bar is all that is needed), pitch and orientation are set by processing parameters (front velocity, gradient, pulling direction) rather than by a fabricated mask, and the moving front provides simultaneous defect annihilation — an intrinsically "self‑templating" DSA in which the guiding pattern is grown, used, and then evaporated.

**Proposal: "Magneto‑epitaxy" – DSA guided by a rewritable pattern of magnetic bits written into a perpendicular‑magnetic‑recording (PMR) underlayer.**

Instead of a topographic or chemical prepattern, the substrate is a chemically uniform, atomically flat hard‑disk‑type stack (CoCrPt or FePt/Co‑Pd multilayer with a thin carbon/SiO₂ overcoat). Using an ordinary HDD write head (or a Bloch‑line/spin‑orbit‑torque writer, or a magnetic‑force‑microscope tip), a periodic array of up/down magnetized bits — line stripes or dot lattices with pitches down to ~15–20 nm and arbitrary layout — is *written* into the layer. The resulting stray (fringing) fields form a virtual template that decays over only a few nanometres above the surface, exactly matching BCP film thicknesses.

Coupling to the microdomains is provided by making one block magnetically responsive: a block selectively loaded with superparamagnetic nanoparticles (Fe₃O₄, FePt, Co), a metallo‑block containing high‑spin paramagnetic ions (Fe(III), Gd(III), Co(II) complexes or ferrocene/cobaltocenium units), or simply exploiting the diamagnetic‑susceptibility contrast between blocks. During thermal or solvent‑vapour annealing the magnetophoretic force (∝ ∇|B|², which is enormous at bit‑transition edges) pulls the magnetic block onto the written transitions/bit centres, pinning and registering the microdomain lattice to the magnetic pattern; density multiplication follows when the bit period is an integer multiple of L₀. The same field gradients also bias domain orientation and drive dislocation glide, accelerating defect annihilation.

Distinct advantages: the template is *written, erased and rewritten* magnetically (a DC erase field or heating above the medium's blocking/Curie temperature wipes it), so one substrate can be reprogrammed for different pitches, symmetries, bends and gradients and reused after stripping the polymer; the guiding "pattern" is buried and non‑topographic, leaving no residual guide stripes or trenches to remove before pattern transfer; writing is maskless, serial‑but‑fast (GHz write rates over a spinning/scanning stage) and needs no e‑beam/EUV resist step; and the magnetic contrast is orthogonal to the chemistry, so surface energies stay perfectly neutral for perpendicular lamellae/cylinders. It is also naturally suited to fabricating bit‑patterned magnetic media, where the magnetic prepattern and the final device pattern are one and the same.

**Proposal: "Moiré epitaxy" – DSA guided by the periodic potential of a twisted 2D‑material (van der Waals) moiré superlattice underlayer.**

Instead of writing a guiding pattern lithographically, the substrate is made to *self‑generate* one at the sub‑10‑nm scale: a stack of two van der Waals layers (e.g. graphene/hBN, twisted bilayer graphene, MoS₂/WSe₂, or graphene on a metal such as Ru(0001)/Ir(111)) is transferred onto the wafer with a controlled twist angle θ (or lattice mismatch). The lattice mismatch produces a *moiré superlattice* whose period is set purely by geometry, λ_moiré ≈ a/√(θ² + δ²), and is therefore continuously tunable from ~1 nm (large θ) to >100 nm (θ → 0) simply by the transfer angle — spanning exactly the L₀ range of high‑χ BCPs, including pitches below the resolution limit of e‑beam/EUV.

The moiré is not just structural: it imposes a strictly periodic modulation of the **local surface potential/work function, charge‑puddle density, adsorption energy, polarizability and out‑of‑plane corrugation (0.1–1 nm)** in AA‑, AB‑ and saddle‑point stacking regions. This is a genuine "chemical" prepattern in the sense that the two blocks have different preferential wetting/adsorption energies on the different stacking regions (amplified by choosing one block with π‑interacting, polar or ionic/metallated units, or by seeding one block with a moiré‑pinned adsorbate such as metal clusters or a small‑molecule adsorbate lattice). On annealing, the microdomains register to the moiré lattice — hexagonal moirés template dot/cylinder arrays, uniaxially strained or 1D‑mismatched moirés template line/lamellar patterns, and density multiplication is obtained when λ_moiré = n·L₀. The single‑crystal orientation of the 2D layers also fixes the global in‑plane orientation over the whole flake/wafer‑scale CVD film, so grain orientation is inherited from the underlayer rather than from a written template.

Distinct advantages: the guiding template is created by *stacking, not patterning* — no e‑beam/EUV, no resist, no trenches or guide stripes to strip before pattern transfer; it is atomically flat and topographically negligible, so surface‑energy neutrality for perpendicular domains is easy to maintain; the pitch, symmetry (hexagonal, stripe, quasi‑periodic), and even in‑plane strain gradients are "programmed" by twist angle, heterostrain and layer choice, and can be reprogrammed on a new sample by simply re‑twisting; the moiré potential can additionally be *tuned in situ* (electrostatic gating of the bilayer, or piezo/strain tuning) to switch the guiding strength on and off during annealing, providing dynamic defect annealing; and the underlayer is reusable — the BCP can be stripped and a new film cast on the same 2D template many times.

**Proposal: "Liquid‑crystal (LC) fingerprint epitaxy" – DSA directed by the periodic elastic/anchoring field of a cholesteric liquid‑crystal top‑coat.**

Instead of patterning the substrate, the BCP film is capped with a thin, immiscible cholesteric (chiral‑nematic) liquid‑crystal layer (e.g. 5CB/E7 + chiral dopant, or a smectic‑A layer forming a focal‑conic domain array). With degenerate planar anchoring, the cholesteric spontaneously develops a **"fingerprint" texture**: a defect‑free, self‑organized stripe pattern of alternating splay/bend director orientation whose period is exactly half the helical pitch, p/2, and is set continuously from ~10 nm to microns simply by the chiral‑dopant concentration, temperature, or an applied electric/magnetic field. Smectic focal‑conic or blue‑phase textures give square/hexagonal lattices instead of stripes.

The fingerprint acts as a *soft, virtual prepattern* through three coupled couplings at the LC–BCP interface: (i) a strictly periodic modulation of interfacial tension/surface energy, since the LC presents alternately its aromatic mesogen cores (edge‑on) and aliphatic tails (end‑on) to the polymer, so the two blocks preferentially wet alternating stripes — a chemoepitaxy‑like pattern generated by self‑assembly rather than lithography; (ii) a periodic elastic (Frank) stress and orientational torque that biases microdomain orientation and drives dislocation glide; (iii) a periodic solvent/plasticizer partitioning (the LC is a good solvent for one block), which modulates local χN and mobility during annealing. Registration follows the standard commensurability rules, with density multiplication when p/2 = n·L₀. Aligning the fingerprint globally (rubbed/photo‑aligned LC command layer, shear, or a field) fixes the in‑plane orientation over the whole wafer; a small AC field can be swept to translate the fingerprint stripes ("moving‑template" annealing) and sweep defects out of the film.

Advantages: the template *builds itself* at sub‑20 nm pitches inaccessible to e‑beam/EUV, is set by chemistry/field rather than fabrication, is fully reconfigurable (pitch tuned by dopant/temperature, symmetry switched between stripes, focal conics and blue phases, orientation rotated by field), and is removed after ordering by a simple solvent rinse or by heating above T_NI — leaving no guide stripes or trenches on a flat, chemically uniform substrate before pattern transfer. It is also inherently roll‑to‑roll compatible, since the LC top‑coat can be coated, cured/aligned, and washed off continuously.

**Proposal: "Convecto‑epitaxy" – DSA templated by self‑organized Bénard–Marangoni convection cells in the solvent‑swollen film.**

Instead of fabricating a guide, let the *fluid itself* generate the periodic template. The BCP is solvent‑vapour annealed (or cast from a volatile solvent) while a controlled vertical temperature/evaporation gradient is imposed across the swollen layer — e.g. a heated chuck plus a cooled/vapour‑saturated lid, or uniform IR/photothermal heating from below. Above a critical Marangoni number the swollen film spontaneously breaks into a **regular array of Bénard–Marangoni convection cells or rolls**, whose wavelength is set almost purely by the swollen‑film thickness and the Marangoni/Rayleigh numbers (λ ≈ 2–4 h_swollen), and can therefore be dialled continuously from microns down to tens of nanometres by controlling the degree of swelling, the surface‑tension gradient (dγ/dT, dγ/dc), the solvent volatility and the added surfactant/co‑solvent. Cells give a hexagonal lattice; a small lateral gradient (thermal, vapour‑pressure, or a moving cold bar) converts them into straight, globally aligned rolls.

The convection pattern acts as a *virtual, dynamically maintained prepattern* through three coupled effects: (i) a strictly periodic in‑plane **solvent‑concentration modulation** (solvent‑rich upwellings vs. solvent‑poor downwellings), which periodically modulates the effective χN, L₀ and mobility, i.e. a self‑generated "chemoepitaxy" pattern written in solvent rather than in surface chemistry; (ii) periodic **selective solvent partitioning** — with a block‑selective solvent, the block that the solvent prefers is thermodynamically drawn to the upwelling stripes/cells, registering the microdomains one‑to‑one (or n‑to‑one, giving density multiplication when λ = n·L₀); and (iii) the periodic **shear/extensional flow and surface‑tension (Marangoni) stress** at the free surface, which orients cylinders/lamellae along the roll axes and drives dislocation glide, actively annihilating defects. Slowly translating the convection pattern (by sweeping the thermal gradient or the vapour front across the wafer) gives a "moving‑template" zone anneal that sweeps grain boundaries out of the film.

Distinct advantages: the guiding pattern is *hydrodynamically self‑generated at the required nanoscale pitch*, so no e‑beam/EUV pre‑patterning, no resist, and no residual guide stripes or trenches to strip before pattern transfer; the substrate stays flat and chemically neutral (ideal for perpendicular domains); pitch, symmetry (hexagons ↔ rolls ↔ squares) and orientation are set purely by processing knobs (thickness, gradient, solvent selectivity, sweep direction) and can be changed wafer‑to‑wafer without new hardware; and when the solvent is removed the template simply evaporates, leaving the ordered BCP behind. The approach is intrinsically large‑area, low‑cost and roll‑to‑roll compatible, since all it requires is a controlled evaporation/thermal‑gradient stage.

Propose a way to induce a self-assemblin.answer: Use a linear ABC triblock terpolymer instead of a simple AB diblock. If the two end blocks (A and C) are minority components of roughly equal volume fraction and are strongly incompatible with each other as well as with the majority middle block (B), each will form its own set of domains dispersed in the B matrix. Because like-domains repel and unlike-domains attract, the two interpenetrating cylinder (or sphere) arrays pack in an alternating "checkerboard" fashion, which is a tetragonal/square lattice rather than the hexagonal lattice preferred by a single population of domains. Casting this terpolymer as a monolayer film on a surface-neutral (or lightly templated, e.g., square chemical-pattern/graphoepitaxial) substrate and solvent/thermal annealing it orients the cylinders perpendicular to the film and yields a square-symmetry in-plane pattern.
