Rather than changing the polymer chemistry, impose the symmetry from the substrate: use directed self‑assembly (chemo‑ or grapho‑epitaxy) with a square‑symmetry template. For example, define a chemical pre‑pattern by e‑beam/interference lithography (two orthogonal exposures) consisting of a square array of "pinning" spots (or crossed stripes) whose spots are preferentially wetted by the minority block, with the surrounding brush made non‑preferential/neutral. Spin‑coat a thin (monolayer‑thick) film of a sphere‑ or perpendicular‑cylinder‑forming diblock (e.g., PS‑b‑PMMA or PS‑b‑P2VP) whose natural domain spacing L₀ matches the template pitch (or an integer sub‑multiple of it for density multiplication, e.g. pitch = √2·L₀ or 2L₀), then thermally or solvent anneal. The pinning sites register the minority domains onto the square lattice, and the intervening domains fill in on the same tetragonal grid, so the film adopts a square (4‑fold) array of dots instead of the equilibrium hexagonal packing. Equivalently, topographic trenches/pits patterned as square wells (graphoepitaxy) with commensurate wall spacing will force the same square packing by confinement.

Keep the chemistry simple (an ordinary sphere‑forming AB diblock, e.g. PS‑b‑PMMA or PS‑b‑P2VP) and instead exploit thin‑film confinement to select the lattice plane that lies parallel to the substrate. The bulk spheres pack on a body‑centred‑cubic lattice; the {110} planes (hexagonal in‑plane) are the usual choice, but the {100} planes of a bcc lattice have four‑fold, square symmetry. By tuning the film thickness so that it is commensurate with the (100) interplanar spacing (i.e. an integer number of a₀/2 layers, with the surfaces "flattening" the layer spacing) and by using top and bottom interfaces of matched (both slightly minority‑block‑attractive, or a free surface plus a coated top layer) so that the confining walls impose the same registry on successive layers, the spheres reorganise with their (100) planes parallel to the substrate. Annealing (thermal or solvent‑vapour, with slow solvent removal to lock in the confined spacing) then produces a film whose surface layer is a square array of dots; in the extreme of a single confined layer the same commensurability trick converts the monolayer of spheres from hexagonal to tetragonal packing, and the square lattice can be further perfected by applying a shear or electric field along one of the desired <100> directions.

Use a **binary blend of two sphere/micelle‑forming block copolymers of different core sizes** so that the film crystallizes as a two‑component (binary) nanoparticle‑like superlattice rather than a single‑component hexagonal one.

Practically: mix a "large" sphere‑forming diblock (e.g., a high‑MW PS‑b‑P2VP or PS‑b‑PDMS) with a "small" sphere‑forming diblock built on the same matrix block but with a mutually immiscible or simply much smaller core (e.g., a low‑MW PS‑b‑P2VP or PS‑b‑PEO), choosing the core–core size ratio in the range ~0.4–0.6 and the number ratio ~1:1. Spin‑coat a monolayer‑thick film onto a substrate/brush that is neutral to the matrix block and solvent‑vapor anneal (slow deswelling) so the two micelle populations can co‑crystallize in‑plane. Under these conditions the large cores adopt a **square (tetragonal) lattice with the small cores sitting in the interstitial sites of that lattice** — a 2‑D "NaCl/AB‑type" checkerboard — because filling the interstices with the second species removes the packing‑frustration penalty that otherwise makes hexagonal packing optimal. If desired, the minority small‑core domains can afterwards be selectively removed (UV/ozone, ozonolysis, or solvent rinse) or selectively metal‑loaded, leaving a clean square array of dots for pattern transfer. The lattice constant is set simply by the size and ratio of the two blends, and adding a small amount of matrix homopolymer helps relieve stretching and improves square‑lattice grain size.

Impose the symmetry mechanically, by anisotropically straining an already-ordered hexagonal film. Cast a monolayer of a perpendicular-cylinder- (or sphere-) forming diblock such as PS-b-PDMS or PS-b-P2VP onto a compliant elastomer (e.g., a pre-strained PDMS sheet) with a neutral surface treatment, and thermally/solvent anneal so it first orders into the usual close-packed hexagonal dot array. Then release/apply strain along one lattice direction: because a hexagonal (6-fold) lattice becomes a square (4-fold) lattice when it is compressed by ~13–15 % along one ⟨10⟩ direction (or equivalently stretched ~15 % along the orthogonal direction, ratio √3:√2 → 1:1), a uniaxial deformation of this magnitude applied while the film is soft (solvent-swollen or above Tg) converts the row spacing to the dot spacing and locks the domains onto a tetragonal grid. Quenching/de-swelling under strain (and, if desired, transferring the film to a rigid substrate) freezes in the square-symmetry array, which can then be used directly for pattern transfer.

Switch from a linear diblock to a **three‑miktoarm star terpolymer (μ‑ABC)**, in which the A, B and C arms are all joined at a single junction point.  Because the junction is a point rather than a chain, all three interfaces must meet along common lines, and the domains are forced to tile the plane as prisms (perpendicular "columns") with Archimedean tiling symmetry rather than as a hexagonal array of one minority domain.  By choosing the arm volume fractions so that two of the components are minority and comparable in size while the third forms the continuous phase – e.g. an A (matrix) arm of roughly 50–60 vol % with B and C arms of ~20–25 vol % each (such as polyisoprene‑arm‑polystyrene‑arm‑poly(2‑vinylpyridine) or a PI/PS/PDMS star) and with χ<sub>BC</sub> large so B and C cannot mix – the system adopts the [4.8.8] (or [4.6.12]) tiling, a **p4mm, four‑fold‑symmetric arrangement in which square B (or C) columns alternate with octagonal columns on a square lattice**.

To realise it in a film: spin‑coat the star terpolymer to a thickness of about one prism period on a substrate coated with a brush that is non‑preferential (neutral) for all three blocks, and solvent‑vapour anneal (with a solvent slightly selective for the matrix arm) and de‑swell slowly, so that the prisms orient perpendicular to the substrate rather than lying down.  The result is a surface pattern with square‑lattice symmetry; selectively removing or staining one arm (e.g. ozonolysis of PI, or metal loading of P2VP) converts it into a square array of dots suitable for pattern transfer.  Tuning the arm ratios shifts the tiling between [4.8.8] (square) and the hexagonal [6.6.6] tiling, giving a direct chemical "knob" for selecting four‑fold symmetry.

Instead of trying to make a 2‑D array of dots pack tetragonally, use a **3‑D network‑forming block copolymer and orient one of its four‑fold crystallographic axes normal to the film**. The double gyroid (Ia3̄d) has 4‑fold screw axes along ⟨100⟩, so a gyroid film whose {100} planes lie parallel to the substrate presents a *square* (p4) array of channels/pores at its surface, rather than the usual hexagonal or "wagon‑wheel" (211) motif.

Practically: choose a diblock in the gyroid window (f_minor ≈ 0.33–0.37) with an etchable/removable minority block, e.g. PS‑b‑PLA, PS‑b‑PDMS, or PS‑b‑P4VP. Spin‑coat onto a substrate coated with a random‑copolymer brush that is non‑preferential (neutral) for both blocks and use a neutral top interface as well (a second brush‑coated/“sandwiched” top plate, a neutral top‑coat layer, or a solvent‑vapour atmosphere that neutralizes the free surface) so that no surface field forces the low‑free‑energy {211} orientation. Set the film thickness commensurate with an integer number of (100) d‑spacings (i.e. ~n·a₀ of the cubic cell, typically 40–100 nm) so that {100} stacking is the only thickness‑commensurate orientation, and anneal slowly in solvent vapour (or thermally, with slow deswelling/cooling through the order–disorder transition) so the network can nucleate in registry with the two flat, thickness‑quantized interfaces; a slow, directional (zone) anneal or a field applied along the desired ⟨100⟩ direction improves grain size and in‑plane registration.

Finally, remove the minority network (UV/ozone or base hydrolysis of PLA, ozonolysis, or reactive‑ion etching) to reveal a square lattice of pores at the film surface, ready for pattern transfer. Because the square symmetry comes from the intrinsic cubic symmetry of the gyroid unit cell, no special chemistry, blending, template, or mechanical strain is required—only orientation and thickness control.

Exploit a **tetragonal Frank–Kasper phase (the σ phase, space group P4₂/mnm) instead of the usual bcc/hexagonal sphere packing**, and orient its unique four‑fold (c) axis normal to the film.

How: choose a sphere‑forming diblock with strong conformational asymmetry between the blocks — e.g. poly(isoprene‑b‑lactide), poly(styrene‑b‑dimethylsiloxane), or a "wedge/dendron‑coil" type copolymer — with the minority volume fraction near the sphere/cylinder boundary (f ≈ 0.12–0.20). Conformational asymmetry (and, if needed, deliberately broadening the dispersity of the matrix block or blending in a small amount of matrix homopolymer, which lets the micelle cores adopt several slightly different sizes) stabilizes the σ Frank–Kasper packing over bcc, because unequal‑volume, low‑surface‑area Voronoi cells relieve the packing frustration. σ is a **tetragonal** lattice, so its (001) plane has genuine four‑fold, square symmetry.

To lock that plane parallel to the substrate in a thin film, cast the polymer on a brush that is weakly attractive to the matrix block, use a neutral or free top surface, and set the film thickness to an integer multiple of the c‑axis repeat (only a few nm, since c ≈ 0.5a for σ) so that (001) stacking is the thickness‑commensurate, lowest‑free‑energy orientation; anneal slowly in solvent vapour with controlled de‑swelling (or thermally just below the order–order transition) so the σ grains nucleate in registry with the two flat interfaces, optionally aided by zone annealing or an electric/shear field to enlarge and align the grains. The exposed surface layer is then a square (p4) array of micellar domains, which can be stained/metal‑loaded or etched for pattern transfer — square symmetry obtained from the intrinsic tetragonal unit cell of the Frank–Kasper phase, with no template, blend of two copolymers, strain, or extra blocks required.

Build the square lattice by "crossing" two aligned one‑dimensional (line) patterns instead of trying to force a single dot array off its hexagonal packing.

Take an ordinary lamellae‑ or in‑plane‑cylinder‑forming diblock (e.g., PS‑b‑PMMA, PS‑b‑PDMS) and cast a very thin, single‑layer film. Give it long‑range unidirectional alignment using a directional field — cold/hot zone annealing with a sharp thermal gradient, shear (a soft PDMS pad dragged across the swollen film), or a directional solvent‑vapor front — so the stripes run along, say, x. Then lock this layer in (UV or thermal crosslinking of the matrix block, or convert it to an inorganic replica by sequential infiltration synthesis/metal loading and etching, so it can no longer reflow). Rotate the substrate 90°, spin‑coat a second layer of the same copolymer on a neutral brush over the first, and repeat the same directional annealing so the second layer's stripes run along y (the underlying stiffened stripes also act as a weak topographic/chemical guide reinforcing orthogonal registry).

The superposition of the two orthogonal stripe sets is a mesh with four‑fold, p4mm symmetry: the intersections and the enclosed openings form a square lattice with pitch equal to L₀. A single pattern‑transfer etch through both layers then gives a square array of posts (or, with the tone reversed, of holes) whose lattice constant is set simply by L₀ — no new chemistry, blend, template or strain is required, only two sequential orthogonal alignment steps.

Use light, rather than the substrate or the chemistry, to impose four‑fold symmetry: build the copolymer with a photo‑responsive (azobenzene‑containing) block — e.g. PS‑b‑poly(methacrylate‑azobenzene) or an azo‑functionalized PS‑b‑P4VP supramolecular complex — and photo‑direct its assembly with a four‑fold‑symmetric optical field.

Practically: spin‑coat a monolayer‑thick film of the sphere/perpendicular‑cylinder‑forming azo‑BCP on a neutral brush, then, while the film is mobile (solvent‑vapour swollen or just above Tg), expose it to two crossed two‑beam interference patterns of linearly polarized light at 488–532 nm, the second rotated 90° from the first (or a single four‑beam interference exposure that directly generates a square intensity/polarization grid), with the interference period set to L₀ (or √2·L₀ or 2L₀ for density multiplication). Trans–cis photoisomerization drives directional mass transport and photo‑orientation of the azo mesogens, creating an in‑situ, erasable "virtual" chemical/topographic grid with p4mm symmetry; the minority domains migrate into the dark (or bright) nodes of that grid and lock onto the square lattice, which the surrounding domains then propagate. Cooling below Tg (or de‑swelling) with the light on, followed by a brief unpolarized exposure or thermal quench, freezes the tetragonal array; the azo/matrix block can then be stained or etched for pattern transfer. Because the symmetry is written optically and can be reconfigured or rotated simply by changing the beam geometry, no pre‑patterned substrate, blend, extra block, or mechanical strain is needed.

Blend two different diblock copolymers that share a common majority (matrix) block but have mutually immiscible minority blocks — i.e., co‑assemble A‑b‑B with A‑b‑C (for example PS‑b‑P2VP + PS‑b‑PEO, or PS‑b‑PDMS + PS‑b‑P4VP) at a ~1:1 molar ratio, with the two minority blocks of comparable volume and χ_BC large.

Because the A blocks are identical, the two copolymers mix into a single continuous PS matrix, but B and C cannot mix with each other, so each forms its own separate population of perpendicular cylinders/spheres. Like domains repel while unlike domains are effectively "attracted" (interfacial tension is lowered by placing a B domain next to a C domain rather than next to another B), so the two equal‑sized domain populations interdigitate in an alternating checkerboard. The B sublattice and the C sublattice each end up on a square (p4mm, tetragonal) grid rotated 45° from one another, instead of the single hexagonal array a one‑component diblock would give. Adding a small amount of a B–C‑bridging additive (e.g., a hydrogen‑bond donor/acceptor pair such as P4VP with a phenolic or carboxylic small molecule, or a common metal salt that coordinates both) further stabilizes the alternating arrangement.

Practically: spin‑coat the blend to about one domain period thick on a brush that is non‑preferential for all components, solvent‑vapor anneal in a solvent slightly selective for the matrix and de‑swell slowly so the two cylinder populations orient normal to the film and can re‑arrange into registry. Selectively removing or staining just one of the two minority blocks (UV/ozone, hydrolysis, or selective metal loading of P4VP/PEO) leaves a clean square array of dots or holes at pitch √2·L₀ for pattern transfer — obtained purely by blending two off‑the‑shelf diblocks, with no terpolymer synthesis, template, strain, or field required.

Build the square symmetry into the domain shapes themselves by using a side‑chain **liquid‑crystalline block copolymer**, so that mesogenic order — not sphere packing — dictates the lattice.

Synthesize an AB diblock in which the minority (or matrix) block carries smectic mesogens, e.g. polystyrene‑*b*‑poly(methacrylate) bearing cyanobiphenyl or azobenzene side groups (PS‑*b*‑PMACB), with f_minor ≈ 0.2–0.3 so the minority block would normally form hexagonally packed cylinders. Below the smectic–isotropic transition the mesogens must stack into flat, parallel layers with a fixed director; this rigid, uniaxial LC order is geometrically incompatible with the circular cross‑section and 6‑fold packing of ordinary cylinders. The system relieves the frustration by flattening the domain cross‑sections into rectangular/square prisms whose faces are parallel to the smectic layers, and these prisms tile the plane on a **tetragonal (p4mm‑like) lattice** rather than a hexagonal one; the LC layer spacing sets one lattice vector and the block‑copolymer period the other, and choosing the mesogen/spacer length so these two lengths match gives a true square (a = b) cell.

To realize it in a thin film: spin‑coat a monolayer‑to‑few‑layer film onto a rubbed polyimide (or photo‑aligned azobenzene) alignment layer with a neutral brush underneath, anneal above the isotropic point, then cool slowly through the smectic phase in the presence of the alignment layer (or under a magnetic/electric field) so the LC director is fixed uniformly in one in‑plane direction and the prismatic domains all register to the same tetragonal grid. Slow cooling with a controlled top interface (neutral topcoat or solvent atmosphere) keeps the prisms perpendicular to the substrate. Staining or etching the non‑LC block then reveals a square array of dots/holes for pattern transfer — the four‑fold symmetry arising purely from coupling mesogenic smectic order to microphase separation, with no template, blend, extra block, or applied strain.

**Route: evaporation‑induced co‑assembly of the block copolymer with an inorganic (sol–gel) precursor, using the film's uniaxial drying contraction to lock in a tetragonal lattice.**

Instead of annealing the neat polymer, dissolve an amphiphilic BCP (e.g., Pluronic F127/P123, or PS‑*b*‑PEO) together with a hydrolyzed sol–gel precursor (TEOS/TiCl₄/aluminate, acid‑catalyzed, in an ethanol–water solution) and dip‑ or spin‑coat it. As the volatile solvent evaporates, the surfactant‑like BCP micellizes and co‑organizes with the condensing inorganic species (evaporation‑induced self‑assembly, EISA): the hydrophilic block (PEO) sits with the silica/metal‑oxide, the hydrophobic block forms the micelle cores, and the micelles crystallize into a body‑centered‑cubic (Im3̄m) mesostructure with its {100} planes lying parallel to the substrate (the flat air and substrate interfaces select this orientation).

The key step is the drying/ageing/calcination stage: because the film is clamped to the substrate, all of the shrinkage that accompanies inorganic condensation occurs **uniaxially, normal to the film**. This compresses the cubic cell only along the film normal and converts it into a *body‑centered tetragonal* lattice whose in‑plane unit cell is unchanged — i.e., the surface layer of micelles/pores is a genuine **square (p4mm, four‑fold) array** rather than the hexagonal packing a free‑standing film would adopt. The degree of contraction (and hence how "square" the in‑plane cell is) is tuned by the polymer/precursor ratio, the relative humidity and ageing time before condensation is complete, and the calcination ramp; working near the higher‑surfactant end of the phase field also gives the 2‑D square‑packed (p4mm) cylinder mesophase directly.

Burning out or solvent‑extracting the polymer leaves a rigid oxide replica containing a square lattice of perpendicular pores at the surface — square symmetry obtained purely from constrained shrinkage of an inorganic‑hybrid mesophase, needing no lithographic template, extra block, blend, strain, or applied field. (The pattern can then be used as a hard mask, or refilled/back‑filled for further pattern transfer.)

**Route: use "commensurability squeezing" of *parallel* (in‑plane) cylinders in a hard‑confined film, so that the cylinder lattice seen in cross‑section is tetragonal rather than hexagonal.**

Take an ordinary cylinder‑forming AB diblock (f_minor ≈ 0.3; e.g. PS‑*b*‑PMMA, PS‑*b*‑PDMS, PS‑*b*‑P2VP) and deliberately make **both** interfaces strongly preferential for the *majority* block — a majority‑block homopolymer/brush on the wafer plus a rigid, wetting top layer (a cross‑linked top‑coat, an evaporated/laminated capping layer, or a flat second wafer pressed onto the film). Such symmetric wetting forces the cylinders to lie parallel to the substrate and to stack in discrete layers whose number, *n*, is fixed by the confinement.

Now exploit the fact that the film thickness, not the polymer, sets the *inter‑layer* spacing. In bulk the hexagonal packing has layer spacing (√3/2)L₀ ≈ 0.87 L₀, i.e. smaller than the in‑plane cylinder–cylinder distance L₀. If the gap is set instead to h ≈ n·L₀ + (wetting layers) — that is, the layer separation is dilated by ~15 % relative to the hexagonal value — the only way the chains can fill space uniformly is for each cylinder to sit directly above the one below rather than in the hollow between two: the layers register **AAA (eclipsed) instead of ABAB**, and the cross‑sectional lattice becomes **square (tetragonal, p4mm), with equal spacings L₀ along the film normal and in the film plane**. Practically, one prepares a thickness gradient or a series of gaps/spacers, anneals (thermal or solvent‑vapour with slow de‑swelling, so the domains can re‑register while the walls hold the thickness), and selects the thickness windows where cross‑sectional SEM/TEM or GISAXS shows the tetragonal (rather than hexagonal) reflections; two or three layers already suffice, and the effect is strengthened by using a slightly incommensurate gap that penalises the hexagonal stacking.

Cleaving or sectioning the film (or etching the minority block after removing the cap) then exposes a square array of cylinder cross‑sections, i.e. a square‑lattice morphology obtained purely from thickness‑commensurability under symmetric hard confinement — no new chemistry, blend, lithographic template, field or strain required.

**Route: use a kinetically controlled, "epitaxial" order–order transition from an aligned lamellar film — i.e., break up pre‑aligned lamellae into rows of dots that stay in register.**

Start with a *lamella‑forming* diblock (e.g. PS‑*b*‑P2VP, PS‑*b*‑P4VP, PS‑*b*‑PEO, or PS‑*b*‑PMMA) cast as a thin film on a neutral brush so the lamellae stand perpendicular to the substrate, and give the stripes long‑range unidirectional alignment (cold/hot‑zone annealing with a sharp thermal gradient, shear with a soft PDMS pad, a directional solvent‑front anneal, or a coarse 1‑D guiding grating). This fixes one lattice vector exactly at the lamellar period L₀ and, importantly, fixes it *identically for every stripe*.

Now push the film across the lamella→cylinder (or lamella→sphere) boundary **after** the stripes are aligned, rather than assembling the dot phase from scratch: swell the film in a vapour of a solvent that is selective for the majority block (or blend in a modest amount of majority‑block homopolymer, or simply raise the temperature toward the order–order transition). The effective minority volume fraction drops, and each lamella becomes unstable to a peristaltic (undulation) instability and pinches off into a line of discrete domains. Because the transition is epitaxial — the new domains nucleate inside the parent lamella and the undulations of neighbouring lamellae couple in phase through the thin matrix walls — the resulting dots sit in straight rows separated by the parent lamellar spacing L₀, with the dots of adjacent rows *eclipsed* (aligned side by side) rather than nested in the hollows. If the composition/solvent selectivity is tuned so that the pinch‑off wavelength along each stripe also equals L₀ (this ratio is set by the minority fraction and by how much the matrix is swollen), the two spacings are equal and the array is a genuine **square (p4mm) lattice**, rotated 0°/90° to the original stripe direction.

Freeze it in by de‑swelling rapidly (or quenching below Tg) once the square pattern appears, so the array cannot relax back to its equilibrium hexagonal packing; cross‑linking the matrix (UV) or converting the minority domains to an inorganic replica (metal loading/sequential infiltration) permanently locks the tetragonal symmetry for pattern transfer.

The key point is that the square symmetry comes from *pathway and memory*: a 1‑D aligned lamellar precursor supplies one lattice vector and enforces in‑phase, eclipsed row registry, while the order–order transition supplies the second, equal lattice vector — no new chemistry, blend, square template, external field, or mechanical strain is required.

Propose a novel use for the all-optical.answer: One novel use is as a **dynamically re‑writable topographic "cell‑instruction" substrate for live‑cell mechanobiology**. Because SRGs form all‑optically at room temperature (well below Tg) through light‑driven mass transport, the surface corrugation can be inscribed, re‑oriented, changed in period/amplitude, or completely erased *in situ* with visible light while living cells are already cultured on the azo‑polymer film — something impossible with etched or embossed static topographies. A cytocompatible azo‑polymer (or azo‑functionalized biopolymer) coating placed on a microscope stage could be patterned with an interference pattern to create nanoscale grooves that guide cell adhesion, cytoskeletal alignment and migration; then, mid‑experiment, the grating could be rotated by 90°, its amplitude ramped, or flattened, allowing real‑time observation of how cells sense, re‑align to, and remember changing topographic cues (contact guidance, focal‑adhesion remodelling, stem‑cell differentiation). Spatial light modulators would allow different cells in the same dish to experience individually programmed, time‑varying topographies, turning the photo‑induced SRG effect into a "topography‑on‑demand" platform for tissue engineering, wound‑healing/cell‑sorting devices and reconfigurable organ‑on‑chip surfaces.

**Use SRG inscription as a light‑programmable "fluidic circuit board": an erasable, electrode‑free platform for droplet routing via reconfigurable anisotropic wetting.**

Because sinusoidal surface relief can be written, rotated, chirped, and erased all‑optically at room temperature, an azo‑polymer‑coated chip lid or channel floor can be patterned *in operando* with grating tracks whose groove direction, period, and amplitude set the local contact‑angle anisotropy and pinning strength. Droplets placed on the film spread and slide preferentially along the grooves, so a projected interference pattern (or an SLM/DMD‑generated holographic pattern) becomes a "virtual wire" that guides a droplet from point A to B; writing a chirped grating creates a wettability gradient that drives spontaneous, pump‑free droplet motion toward the shallower/denser region, while locally flattening the relief makes a "gate" that releases or traps the droplet. Because the same area can be re‑written thousands of times, one blank chip can execute arbitrary, dynamically re‑routed protocols—merging, splitting, mixing, sorting, and dead‑end‑free rerouting around a fouled region—without any pre‑fabricated electrodes, valves, or microstructures (unlike electrowetting or static superhydrophobic tracks). Adding a photo‑responsive azo surface chemistry means the same light also modulates polarity, so topographic and chemical wettability cues can be combined and time‑multiplexed.

Applications: reprogrammable digital microfluidics for combinatorial assays and point‑of‑care diagnostics, self‑cleaning/anti‑fogging surfaces whose drainage direction can be re‑aimed with light, condensation‑harvesting surfaces optimized on the fly, and "write‑once‑per‑experiment" disposable chips whose layout is defined by software rather than by lithography.

**Novel use: an all‑optically re‑writable "graphoepitaxy template" for *in‑operando* control of crystallization and directed self‑assembly — including chiral/polymorph selection.**

Since SRGs are inscribed by light at room temperature (far below Tg) and can be rotated, chirped, deepened, made chiral (with circularly/vector‑polarized beams), or completely erased *while a liquid or solution sits on the film*, an azo‑polymer surface can serve as a nucleation substrate whose nanotopography is reprogrammed during the assembly process itself. Concretely: (i) a solution of a pharmaceutical, protein, or perovskite is deposited on the azo film and a projected interference pattern writes grooves whose period/depth is tuned in real time to match a specific crystal face spacing, so that nucleation is templated toward one desired polymorph or crystal orientation; changing the period mid‑experiment lets one "walk" the system through, and select among, competing polymorphs on a single chip — an optical polymorph screening platform. (ii) Writing helically modulated/chiral relief with circularly polarized light imprints a handed surface geometry that biases enantioselective nucleation, giving a light‑switchable route to chirality control (switch handedness by switching light polarization, with no change of substrate chemistry). (iii) The same trick templates block‑copolymer microdomains, liquid‑crystal director fields, colloidal crystals, or 2D‑material/organic‑semiconductor grain alignment, and because the grating can be erased and rewritten thousands of times, one substrate supports combinatorial, software‑defined assembly experiments and allows "annealing" of defects by dynamically translating or rotating the confining topography (a moving‑template, zone‑refining approach impossible with etched, static trenches).

This turns photo‑induced mass transport from a passive patterning method into an active, feedback‑controlled handle on nucleation and self‑assembly: microscopy or diffraction monitors the growing phase, and the SRG parameters are updated on the fly by a spatial light modulator to steer the outcome — useful for drug polymorph/enantiomer control, high‑quality organic semiconductor and perovskite films, protein crystallography, and reconfigurable nanolithography masters.

**Novel use: a "travelling‑wave" SRG as an all‑optical, contactless nano‑conveyor / peristaltic surface pump for matter transport.**

Instead of using the grating as a static optical element, exploit the *dynamics* of the photo‑induced mass transport itself: by slowly sliding the phase of the recording interference pattern (e.g., with an electro‑optic phase shifter, an SLM/DMD, or two slightly detuned beams), the corrugation crests of the azo‑polymer film can be made to march continuously across the surface. Because SRG formation happens below Tg and generates real mechanical stress and micron‑scale displacements of polymer material, the moving relief acts like a peristaltic wave that physically pushes objects riding on the film — nanoparticles, quantum dots, colloids, protein aggregates, adsorbed thin liquid films, or even adherent cells — along programmable trajectories, at speeds set by the phase‑shift rate and with directionality set by the beam geometry. Crossed or vector‑polarized beams give 2‑D travelling ripple fields, so material can be steered, focused into "corrals" (nodes of the standing pattern), sorted by size/adhesion (large or strongly pinned objects lag behind the wave, small ones follow), and delivered to a chosen collection site, then released by erasing the grating.

This converts photo‑isomerization into a *mechanical* actuator that works at ordinary light intensities (mW/cm²–W/cm²), thousands of times lower than optical tweezers, needs no electrodes, no fluid flow, and no plasmonic heating, and works on dry, adhered objects that conventional trapping cannot move. Potential applications: light‑programmable assembly and positioning of nanoparticles/2‑D flakes for device fabrication, contactless cleaning/de‑fouling of surfaces (sweeping dust or biofilm off optics and sensors), continuous separation of nanoparticle mixtures on an open surface, delivery of single emitters onto photonic structures, and light‑driven "conveyor belts" for lab‑on‑a‑chip solid‑phase assays — with the added ability to reverse direction or reprogram the route in real time simply by changing the illumination.

**Novel use: light‑written, erasable surface‑relief gratings as a *reconfigurable phononic metasurface* for surface‑acoustic‑wave (SAW) circuits.**

Coat a piezoelectric SAW substrate (e.g., LiNbO₃, ST‑quartz, or AlN/Si) with a thin azo‑polymer film and use an interference/SLM‑projected pattern to inscribe corrugations *in operando*. Because a periodic mass‑and‑stiffness corrugation on the surface acts as a Bragg reflector/scatterer for Rayleigh waves, the optically written SRG becomes a **software‑defined acoustic mirror, waveguide, lens or cavity** whose period (hence stop‑band frequency), depth (reflectivity), orientation (beam‑steering direction) and chirp (dispersion/focусing) can be reprogrammed in seconds with light, and completely erased with uniform or circularly polarized illumination — all at room temperature, with no lithography, no electrodes and no change of chip.

What this enables that fixed etched grooves cannot:
- **Frequency‑agile SAW resonators/filters**: tune the resonance by simply rewriting the grating period, or trim/de‑trim a fabricated device post‑hoc (optical "acoustic trimming" to correct fabrication error or temperature drift).
- **Movable acoustic cavities and reprogrammable phononic waveguide routes**: shifting the phase of the writing pattern translates a resonant cavity across the chip, allowing standing‑wave pressure nodes in acoustofluidics/acoustic tweezers to be swept and re‑aimed optically, so particles, droplets or cells can be routed along arbitrary, rewritable paths.
- **Acoustic holography**: a computer‑generated, non‑periodic relief pattern written by an SLM shapes an arbitrary SAW wavefront (focal spots, vortices, multi‑beam patterns) for on‑chip acoustic imaging, mixing or patterned particle assembly.
- **Coupling/decoupling elements for hybrid quantum and optomechanical devices**: an optically placed, removable grating mirror can define a SAW Fabry–Pérot cavity around a chosen quantum emitter, defect centre or nanomechanical element, letting the acoustic mode be aligned to the device after the device is characterized.
- **Combinatorial phononic‑crystal research**: hundreds of lattice geometries (square, hexagonal, quasi‑periodic, graded, topologically non‑trivial interfaces) can be tested on one blank substrate by successive write–measure–erase cycles, giving rapid experimental exploration of phononic band structures and topological edge states.

In short, photo‑induced mass transport turns a passive piezoelectric chip into a **rewritable acoustic “printed circuit board,”** where the entire phononic layout is defined and re‑defined by projected light rather than by permanent etching.

**Novel use: an all‑optically re‑programmable dry‑adhesion/friction pad — a "light‑switchable gecko gripper" for micro‑transfer printing.**

Since SRGs can be written, deepened, rotated and completely erased at room temperature with mW‑level light, an azo‑polymer‑coated stamp face can have its *real contact area* and *interfacial stiffness* reprogrammed in seconds. A flat (erased) pad makes intimate, conformal, van‑der‑Waals contact and therefore grips strongly; writing a grating of chosen period/amplitude under the pad reduces the true contact area and introduces crack‑initiating asperities, dropping the pull‑off force by orders of magnitude — so pick‑up and release are controlled purely by projected light rather than by stamp velocity, temperature, vacuum or peel geometry (the usual, unreliable "kinetic" transfer‑printing tricks). Because a spatial light modulator defines the pattern, adhesion can be set *pixel‑by‑pixel*: a single blank stamp can grab a selected subset of micro‑LEDs, chiplets, thin‑film sensors, 2‑D‑material flakes or micro‑optics from a source wafer, carry them, and release them one at a time by locally re‑writing the relief — enabling deterministic, sequential, defect‑repair assembly with one universal stamp instead of a library of custom‑etched ones. Grating orientation additionally gives *anisotropic* friction (easy sliding along the grooves, high resistance across them), so the same surface can act as a light‑steerable directional‑friction skin for micro‑robot feet, crawling actuators, or conveying/aligning parts on a vibrating tray, with the "tread pattern" re‑aimed on the fly. Adhesion switching is reversible over thousands of write/erase cycles, requires no electrodes, heat or chemistry, and works in vacuum, making it attractive for cleanroom pick‑and‑place, in‑space assembly, and reconfigurable end‑effectors for micromanipulation.

**Novel use: a "self‑writing," self‑healing holographic interconnect that doubles as an in‑material photonic synapse (analog optical learning layer).**

Instead of writing an SRG once and then using it as a fixed optical element, exploit the fact that the relief is written *by the very light that later reads it*: place a thin azo‑polymer film at the coupling plane between two photonic chips/fibers/free‑space terminals and simply let the signal beam and a reference (or the receiver's beacon) beam interfere on it. The photo‑induced mass transport spontaneously grows exactly the surface corrugation whose period and orientation phase‑match those two beams, so the link "grows its own grating" and aligns itself. Because writing continues during operation, any drift — thermal bending of a board, vibration, a change of wavelength, a slightly moved receiver — immediately produces a new fringe geometry that rewrites the relief, so the coupler continuously re‑optimizes and *heals* its own misalignment with no actuators, feedback electronics, or alignment stages. Aberrated or scattering media can be compensated the same way (the scattered field itself records the compensating relief), giving a passive, all‑optical "digital‑optical‑phase‑conjugation without a computer."

The same physics makes the film an analog memory element: relief amplitude (hence diffraction efficiency = "synaptic weight") grows with the correlation between two beams — a direct optical Hebbian update — saturates, and decays/erases under uniform or circularly polarized light or mild heating, giving short‑term vs. long‑term plasticity, forgetting, and paired‑pulse facilitation. A stack or array of such films addressed by an SLM therefore implements a rewritable, non‑volatile, low‑power (mW/cm²) weight matrix for optical vector–matrix multiplication and *in‑situ* trained optical neural networks, where training and inference happen in the same medium and the weights are stored as topography rather than in electronics. Being surface (not volume) relief, it is thin, broadband, polarization‑sensitive (a bonus degree of freedom for multiplexing weights by polarization), and can be read non‑destructively at a wavelength outside the azo absorption band.

Applications: self‑aligning chip‑to‑chip and satellite/UAV free‑space optical links, adaptive fiber‑bundle and endoscope imaging through moving scatterers, self‑tuning laser cavity output couplers, and rewritable, self‑training photonic synapse arrays for edge optical computing.

**Novel use: an all‑optically re‑writable "thermal metasurface" for dynamic radiative heat management and infrared signature control.**

Coat a spacecraft radiator panel (or a building/vehicle skin, or the lid of a chip package) with a thin azo‑polymer film and inscribe SRGs into it with projected interference/SLM patterns. Because the corrugation period, depth, orientation and chirp set how the surface diffracts, traps and re‑emits mid‑ and far‑infrared radiation — grating‑coupling to surface phonon‑polariton and polymer vibrational modes, plus a "moth‑eye"‑like graded index that suppresses reflection — the spectral emissivity, its angular lobe pattern and the solar‑absorptivity/IR‑emissivity ratio (α/ε) of the panel can be tuned continuously by simply rewriting the relief. Since writing occurs at room temperature with mW‑level visible light and the pattern can be erased and re‑written thousands of times, the same blank surface becomes a **software‑defined, moving‑part‑free variable‑emittance device**: flatten the film (low ε, "insulating" state) to retain heat during eclipse or cold soak, write a deep grating (high ε, "radiating" state) to dump heat during a high‑power burn, and grade the pattern spatially so different zones of one radiator run at different set points. Feedback is trivial — a thermistor or IR camera drives the SLM, giving closed‑loop thermal control that replaces mechanical louvers, electrochromic/MEMS shutters or heat pipes, with far lower mass and no electrodes.

The same principle gives **reprogrammable IR camouflage and anti‑counterfeit thermal tagging**: local grating patterns modulate apparent thermal radiance, so an object can be made to display an arbitrary, re‑drawable "thermal image" (matching background clutter, or displaying a covert code visible only to a thermal camera), and the pattern can be erased and re‑written on demand. Adding the grating's polarization and angular selectivity lets emission be steered into a chosen solid angle — e.g., aiming waste heat away from a sensitive instrument or toward the cold sky for daytime radiative cooling — and the anisotropic relief simultaneously creates directional wetting/anti‑icing behaviour on the same skin.

This turns photo‑induced mass transport from a photonics‑only patterning trick into an **actuator for heat**, enabling combinatorial, on‑the‑fly optimisation of emissivity spectra on a single sample (write–measure–erase screening of thermal metasurface designs) without any lithography.

**Novel use: turn the SRG‑writing process itself into an all‑optical nanorheometer — using photo‑induced mass transport as a contact‑free probe of local viscoelasticity, free volume and glass‑transition behaviour in ultrathin films and at buried interfaces.**

Instead of caring about the grating as an optical element, use its *growth kinetics* as the measurement. Because SRG formation is driven by a known, calibrated opto‑mechanical driving force (the light‑induced pressure/stress from repeated trans–cis–trans isomerisation) acting against the material's own resistance to flow, the rate at which the corrugation amplitude rises, the saturation depth reached for a given fluence/period, and the relaxation (decay) of the relief after the writing beams are switched off constitute a direct, quantitative read‑out of the local viscosity, shear modulus, free volume and molecular mobility of the film — over length scales set simply by the fringe spacing (100 nm–several µm), and read *in situ* and non‑destructively by first‑order diffraction efficiency, with sub‑nanometre sensitivity and millisecond time resolution.

Because the excitation is light, this "grating rheometer" reaches regimes conventional rheology, nanoindentation or AFM cannot: (i) it measures mobility in films only tens of nanometres thick, and — by using an azo‑doped tracer layer sandwiched under or over another material — probes *buried* interfaces, confinement‑induced Tg shifts, surface‑enhanced mobility, and the mobility gradient near a substrate or free surface; (ii) it applies stress at a chosen spatial wavelength, so the wavevector dependence of the response gives the length scale of cooperative rearrangement (dynamic heterogeneity) in glasses; (iii) since a spatial light modulator can write at many periods/orientations simultaneously and the pattern can be erased and rewritten thousands of times on the same spot, it gives combinatorial, mapped, time‑resolved mechanical imaging of a whole sample — following physical ageing, plasticiser or solvent uptake, crosslinking/curing of an adhesive or photoresist, degree of cure of a coating, or damage/embrittlement — all with no contact, no electrodes and no tip wear.

Practical spin‑offs: an all‑optical, self‑reporting **environmental/chemical dosimeter** (sorbed vapour, humidity, or radiation‑induced chain scission plasticise the matrix, so the grating grows faster or decays sooner — the diffracted spot brightness reports exposure quantitatively and can be optically reset); an in‑line quality‑control tool for coating cure and ageing on production lines; a probe of interfacial mobility in polymer nanocomposites, membranes and photoresists (directly relevant to line‑edge roughness and pattern collapse in lithography); and a fundamental experimental handle on the long‑standing question of how confinement and interfaces alter the glass transition.

**Novel use: an all‑optically written, erasable SRG as a "strain‑engineering pad" for 2‑D materials — light‑programmable periodic strain superlattices, exciton funnels and single‑photon‑emitter arrays.**

Exploit the fact that SRG formation is a genuine *mechanical* event: photo‑induced mass transport moves polymer below Tg and generates micron‑scale surface displacements and large local stresses. If a monolayer of graphene, WSe₂/MoS₂, hBN, or a thin perovskite/organic‑semiconductor membrane is van‑der‑Waals‑transferred onto a flat azo‑polymer film, then writing an interference pattern makes the substrate corrugate *underneath the already‑bonded 2‑D crystal*, forcing it to conform and acquire a sinusoidal, periodically modulated strain field whose period (∼200 nm–several µm), amplitude (0→hundreds of nm), orientation relative to the crystal axes, and chirp are all set by the writing beams — and which can be increased, rotated, translated, or completely erased with circularly polarized/uniform light, thousands of times, at room temperature and with mW‑level power, with no electrodes, no piezo stage, no bending rig and no lithography.

This turns strain, normally a "fabricate‑once and hope" parameter, into a *continuously tunable, spatially patterned, real‑time* knob inside a cryostat or under a microscope objective:
- **Band‑structure and exciton engineering on demand:** the strain modulation locally shifts the bandgap, so the grating becomes an array of tunable exciton funnels/traps; sweeping amplitude while recording photoluminescence gives a full strain–optical response curve on a *single* flake, replacing whole sample libraries.
- **Deterministic, repositionable quantum‑emitter arrays:** strain maxima nucleate localized single‑photon emitters in WSe₂/hBN at optically defined positions; shifting the writing pattern's phase *moves* the emitter lattice, allowing an emitter to be walked into registry with a pre‑characterized photonic cavity or waveguide after the device is made — and erased if the placement is wrong.
- **Pseudo‑magnetic fields and synthetic gauge potentials in graphene**, plus optically switchable one‑dimensional superlattice/mini‑band formation, flat‑band and topological‑transition studies, where the superlattice period is scanned continuously instead of being fixed by etching.
- **Reversible tuning of moiré/twisted bilayers, ferroelastic domains and piezo/flexoelectric response**, strain‑controlled catalysis and hydrogen‑evolution activity, and strain‑gated tunnel junctions or nanomechanical resonators.
- **Combinatorial "write–measure–erase" screening:** an SLM writes different periods/orientations in different regions of one flake, so the entire strain phase diagram of a material can be mapped in a single experiment with in‑situ Raman/PL/transport feedback closing the loop.

In short, photo‑induced surface‑relief formation is repurposed from a photonics patterning trick into a **contactless, reconfigurable nano‑actuator for straintronics**, giving software‑defined, erasable strain superlattices for quantum photonics and 2‑D‑materials physics.

Propose an application for 3D nanoscale.answer: The periodic empty "cages" can serve as a designer host lattice — a 3D molecular scaffold whose regularly spaced internal cavities are used to capture and precisely position guest species (e.g., gold/silver nanoparticles, quantum dots, enzymes or other proteins) at defined lattice sites. Because the DNA cage walls can be functionalized with sequence‑specific capture strands, guests of chosen size and chemistry can be loaded into every unit cell, converting the origami superlattice into a programmable 3D array of nano‑objects. Such an assembly would be useful, for example, as a plasmonic/photonic metamaterial (ordered nanoparticle arrays with engineered optical response, SERS substrates) or, after silica/metal templating, as a mold for casting inorganic 3D nanostructures; alternatively, loading with enzymes gives an ordered porous host for multi‑enzyme cascade catalysis or for structural studies (crystallographic "scaffolding") of encapsulated biomolecules.

Because every unit cell contains an identical, precisely sized empty cavity connected through the lattice, such a "caged" origami superlattice can be used as a **nanoporous membrane / molecular sieve for size‑ and shape‑selective separation**. The DNA framework gives a monodisperse, genetically programmable pore diameter (tunable simply by redesigning the block/vacancy dimensions), so a thin film of the crystal supported on a porous substrate — optionally rigidified by silicification or metal/polymer coating to survive drying and flow — would act as a filtration/chromatographic medium that sorts proteins, viruses, polymers, or nanoparticles by hydrodynamic size, while lining the cage walls with aptamers or complementary strands adds chemical selectivity (affinity capture/release, desalting, or purification of biomolecules).

They could serve as a programmable **drug‑storage and triggered‑release depot**: the periodic, uniformly sized vacancies act as a huge number of identical nanoreservoirs that can be loaded with small‑molecule drugs, siRNA/antisense oligos, peptides or contrast agents at very high, precisely quantifiable capacity (one defined dose per unit cell). Because the cage openings are lined with designed single‑stranded DNA, they can be "gated" with hybridized locking strands, aptamer switches, i‑motif/triplex pH sensors or nuclease‑ or ATP‑cleavable motifs, so cargo is retained until a specific biochemical cue (target miRNA/protein, acidic tumour or endosomal pH, enzyme activity) unzips the gates and releases the payload with programmable kinetics. Crystal size, cage dimension and gate design independently tune loading, diffusion rate and trigger specificity, and the crystals can be coated (e.g., silica, oligolysine–PEG) for serum stability — giving a stimuli‑responsive, sequence‑addressable carrier for targeted therapy or for in‑vitro sensing where cargo release reports on the presence of an analyte.

Use the caged crystals as a sacrificial template for **3D ordered nanoporous electrodes in electrochemical energy storage/conversion**. Because the DNA framework is a periodic, fully addressable scaffold whose backbone phosphates readily bind metal ions, the origami walls can be seeded and electrolessly plated (or coated by atomic‑layer/sol–gel deposition) with metals, metal oxides or conductive polymers; burning off or enzymatically digesting the DNA then leaves an inverse replica in which the former "cage" vacancies become an interconnected, monodisperse pore network of precisely designed size and symmetry. Such a material combines an extremely high, geometrically uniform surface area with continuous, straight ion‑transport channels and a continuous conductive skeleton — exactly the architecture desired for supercapacitor and battery electrodes, fuel‑cell/electrocatalytic supports, or gas‑storage/sensing media. Crucially, unlike colloidal‑ or block‑copolymer‑templated porous metals, the pore diameter, wall thickness, lattice symmetry and even chemical patterning of individual pore faces are set independently by DNA sequence design, so charge‑storage capacity, rate capability (ion diffusion length) and catalytic site placement can be systematically optimized by simply redesigning the origami block and its vacancy.

Use them as a **reconfigurable photonic‑crystal (Bragg‑diffraction) sensor/actuator**. Because each unit cell contains a large empty cage, the lattice is highly "compressible": the low‑density, solvent‑filled voids allow the crystal to swell or contract substantially without losing long‑range order, and the periodic dielectric contrast between the DNA walls and the empty cavities gives a well‑defined optical/X‑ray diffraction signature. If the struts framing the cages are built with responsive elements — toehold‑mediated strand‑displacement linkers, i‑motif/triplex pH switches, aptamer or riboswitch modules, temperature‑ or ion‑sensitive duplexes — binding of a specific analyte (target DNA/RNA, protein, small molecule, metal ion, or a change in pH, ionic strength or temperature) collapses or expands the vacancies, shifting the lattice constant by tens of nanometres. This produces a large, continuously tunable shift in the diffracted wavelength/structural colour (or SAXS peak position) that can be read out optically as a label‑free, amplified sensing signal, and, run in reverse, the same cage‑mediated volume change makes the crystal a soft, chemically driven nanoactuator or a switchable "gate" material whose porosity and optical properties are toggled on demand.

Use the caged superlattice as a **3D nanoscale metrology/calibration standard ("molecular ruler phantom") for high‑resolution imaging and scattering instruments.** Because the DNA‑origami block dimensions and the size of the central vacancy are defined by base‑pair geometry, the crystal has exactly known, uniform lattice constants and void diameters (tens of nanometres) repeated over micrometre distances in all three directions. A thin section or a vitrified/embedded crystal therefore provides an absolute, self‑referencing length scale in x, y and z that can be used to calibrate magnification, pixel size and distortion in cryo‑electron tomography and SEM/TEM, to measure and validate the point‑spread function, axial resolution, drift and refractive‑index/depth‑dependent aberrations of super‑resolution fluorescence microscopes (STORM/PALM/STED/MINFLUX) when selected cage corners are labelled with dyes, and to serve as a q‑axis calibrant for small‑angle X‑ray/neutron scattering. The empty cages also make the object low‑contrast and stain‑free, and the walls can be sparsely decorated with gold nanoparticles or fluorophores at chosen sites so that the same specimen doubles as a fiducial marker array for tomographic alignment and for benchmarking correlative and 3D single‑molecule‑localization workflows, with the "resolution target" spacing tunable simply by redesigning the block and its vacancy.

They could be used as an **ultralight, programmable mechanical (auxetic/phononic) metamaterial**. Because a large fraction of each unit cell is empty space, the caged origami crystal is an extremely low‑density but ordered solid whose elastic response is set entirely by the geometry of the struts framing the vacancies and by the stiffness of the DNA duplex/holliday‑junction linkers connecting neighbouring blocks. By redesigning the block shape, the vacancy size and the connection angles, one can dial in the effective Young's modulus, anisotropy, and even negative Poisson's ratio (re‑entrant, auxetic cage geometries) or negative thermal/ionic expansion, since the hollow cells can hinge and fold rather than stretch. Such crystals — reinforced by silicification or metal coating and used as a template for an inorganic replica if higher stiffness is needed — provide a route to nanoscale architected foams with record stiffness‑to‑density ratios, tunable energy absorption and shock damping, and periodic void spacing on the tens‑of‑nanometre scale, which also creates hypersonic phononic band gaps for controlling GHz–THz acoustic waves (nanoscale acoustic filters, thermal‑conductivity suppression for thermoelectrics). Uniquely, the mechanical response is sequence‑programmable and can be switched in situ (e.g., strand displacement or ion‑induced stiffening), giving an actively reconfigurable mechanical metamaterial.

Use the periodic vacancies as a **3D array of zeptoliter "nanoreactors" for confined, single‑molecule chemistry and templated nucleation.** Each identical cage is a sealed‑but‑diffusively‑accessible reaction chamber of exactly known volume, so reagents can be admitted (and then trapped by hybridizing "lid" strands or by pH/ion‑triggered closure of the cage openings) at Poisson‑limited occupancy, giving millions to billions of physically isolated, addressable compartments per crystal. Two payoffs follow: (i) *digital, massively parallel assays* — a single enzyme, ribozyme, PCR/ELISA target or catalytic nanoparticle per cage produces a compartment‑confined fluorescent product that can be counted optically or by super‑resolution imaging, enabling absolute quantification and single‑turnover kinetics with far higher compartment density (and 3D packing) than droplet or microwell platforms, and allowing directed‑evolution style screening where the cage walls also carry the DNA "barcode" of the encapsulated variant; and (ii) *size‑monodisperse synthesis* — because nucleation and growth of an inorganic phase (metal, semiconductor, metal–organic or protein crystal) is geometrically limited by the cage walls, each vacancy templates a particle whose diameter and shape are set by the origami design rather than by kinetics, yielding ultra‑narrow size distributions and, since the particles are formed in register with the lattice, an automatically ordered 3D nanoparticle array. Confinement itself is a chemical tool here: crowding, restricted diffusion and the highly charged DNA walls can accelerate or steer reactions, stabilize otherwise unstable intermediates/polymorphs, and prevent aggregation, while the cage size, wall chemistry and gating chemistry are all reprogrammable by simply redesigning the origami block.

Use the caged superlattice as an **ultrahigh‑density, addressable 3D digital information‑storage medium ("DNA‑origami memory crystal")**. Every unit cell contains one identical, precisely located vacancy that can be either empty or occupied, so each cage acts as a physical bit: writing is done by diffusing a "filler" guest into selected cages (a metal/gold nanocluster, dye, quantum dot, or a short oligonucleotide that hybridizes to capture strands lining only certain cage walls), and erasing/rewriting is done by toehold‑mediated strand displacement or a pH/thermal trigger that ejects the guest. Because the cages are spaced by only tens of nanometres and the medium is filled in all three dimensions, the areal/volumetric bit density greatly exceeds that of planar optical or magnetic media (~10^15–10^17 bits cm^-3), and the DNA sequence design gives every lattice plane/sublattice a distinct chemical "address," enabling random access to blocks of data rather than the bulk‑pool, sequencing‑only readout of conventional DNA data storage. Read‑out is non‑destructive and parallel: occupied cages change the structure factor of the crystal, so the stored pattern can be interrogated by X‑ray/electron diffraction or SAXS, by the shift in plasmonic/photonic (Bragg) response when metal or dielectric guests fill the voids, or bit‑by‑bit by super‑resolution/cryo‑EM imaging of fluorophore‑ or nanoparticle‑filled sites. Multilevel (not just binary) encoding is possible by loading guests of different size, scattering power or emission colour into the same cage, and the crystals can be silicified or metal‑coated for long‑term, dry, archival stability — giving a rewritable, energy‑free‑to‑store, molecularly programmable 3D memory.

Use the caged crystals as a template for an **ultralow‑dielectric‑constant ("air‑gap"/low‑k) and thermally insulating nanoporous film for microelectronics.** Because each unit cell is mostly empty space, the material is a periodic solid–void composite with an extremely high, perfectly monodisperse void fraction. Conformally coating the DNA walls (e.g., by silicification, sol–gel or atomic‑layer deposition of SiO₂/organosilicate) and then removing the DNA leaves a mechanically self‑supporting inorganic replica whose pores are ordered, closed‑off and uniform on the tens‑of‑nanometre scale — exactly the architecture needed for back‑end‑of‑line interlayer dielectrics, where k can be pushed toward 1.5–2 (air k ≈ 1) to cut interconnect RC delay and crosstalk. Unlike surfactant‑ or porogen‑templated low‑k films, which have random, polydisperse and often interconnected pores that cause metal‑precursor intrusion, moisture uptake and dielectric breakdown, the origami‑defined lattice sets pore size, spacing, wall thickness and symmetry independently by sequence design, so porosity (and hence k) can be dialled in while keeping wall connectivity — and therefore Young's modulus and breakdown strength — optimized. The same ordered nanovoid architecture strongly scatters phonons, so the film simultaneously serves as a nanoscale thermal barrier/insulating layer (or as a low‑thermal‑conductivity, high‑porosity aerogel‑like coating), and the periodic void pattern can additionally be exploited as an antireflective/low‑index optical layer.

**Build a 3D "artificial quantum/excitonic solid": a lattice of identical cages, each hosting exactly one quantum emitter, so that dipole–dipole coupling can be engineered by design.**

Because every unit cell contains one geometrically identical vacancy at a crystallographically defined position, each cage can be loaded (via capture strands or size-selective encapsulation) with a *single* quantum object — a colloidal quantum dot, nanodiamond NV centre, perovskite nanocrystal, rare-earth/lanthanide complex, or a single dye/chromophore. The DNA design fixes the emitter–emitter separation (and hence the dipolar coupling strength) with sub-nanometre precision in all three directions, while the empty cage isolates each emitter from its neighbours' surfaces, suppressing aggregation, charge transfer and non-radiative quenching that plague close-packed nanocrystal solids.

The result is a *programmable* quantum-optical medium: at spacings in the strong-coupling/Förster regime the array supports coherent exciton delocalization, superradiance and directional energy funnelling (an artificial light-harvesting antenna in which alternating cages carry donor and acceptor species to steer excitons toward a designed "reaction centre"); at larger spacings it behaves as a dilute, ordered emitter array for narrow-line collective emission, single-photon sources arranged on a known 3D grid, or a solid-state platform for optically addressable spin qubits/quantum registers and analogue quantum simulation of dipolar spin lattices. Since lattice constant, symmetry, cage occupancy and even the sequence-encoded chemical identity of each sublattice are set independently by the origami design, one can systematically map how geometry controls coherent energy transport — knowledge directly transferable to photon-upconversion media, exciton-transport wires and quantum photonic metamaterials — and the crystal can be silicified or resin-embedded to give a robust, optically transparent device layer.

**Use the caged crystal as a 3‑D charged‑nanochannel (nanofluidic/ionotronic) material for osmotic energy harvesting and ionic circuitry.**

Because every unit cell contains an identical vacancy and the cages interconnect through the lattice, the crystal is effectively a periodic network of tens‑of‑nanometre channels whose walls are DNA — i.e. uniformly and densely negatively charged by the phosphate backbone. When the cage dimension is comparable to the Debye length, the electric double layers overlap inside each void, so ion transport becomes strongly *unipolar* (cation‑selective) and surface‑charge‑governed rather than bulk‑governed. A thin, mechanically stabilised film of such crystals (silicified or resin‑supported, mounted between two reservoirs) therefore behaves as a highly permselective nanofluidic membrane that can convert a salinity gradient into electrical power by reverse electrodialysis ("blue energy"), with the advantage over polymer or track‑etched membranes that pore size, pore density, tortuosity, lattice symmetry and surface‑charge density are all set independently and reproducibly by origami sequence design, allowing the selectivity–conductance trade‑off to be optimised rationally rather than empirically.

The same architecture provides programmable **ionic logic elements**: asymmetric cage geometries or chemically asymmetric sublattices (e.g. one face of each cage decorated with polycationic peptides, i‑motif/triplex pH switches, or aptamers) give ionic‑current rectification (nanofluidic diodes), gate‑tunable ionic transistors, and memristive/hysteretic conduction useful for neuromorphic ionic devices and for iontronic sensing. Because the channel chemistry is addressable by strand displacement, the ion selectivity and conductance can be switched *in operando* by adding a DNA or small‑molecule trigger — yielding a chemically reconfigurable ionic conductor, and, in a biomimetic mode, an artificial analogue of ion‑channel arrays for studying and exploiting confined ion/water transport (including selective Li⁺/Na⁺/K⁺ or heavy‑metal‑ion recovery from brines).

**Use the caged superlattice as a multivalent "pathogen‑trap sponge" for antiviral therapy and diagnostic capture of intact virions/exosomes.**

Each unit cell's vacancy can be designed to match the diameter of a target particle (≈30–100 nm: dengue, influenza, SARS‑CoV‑2, AAV, or extracellular vesicles), and the interior cage walls can be decorated—at DNA‑programmed spacings that exactly mirror the icosahedral or spike‑protein geometry of the virion surface—with antibodies, nanobodies, aptamers, or glycan/sialic‑acid ligands. Because dozens of ligands engage one particle simultaneously with the correct geometric registry, the avidity is enormous (picomolar–femtomolar apparent K_D), so a virus that diffuses into a cage is essentially irreversibly held and sterically blocked from binding or fusing with a host‑cell membrane. A microcrystal thus contains millions of identical binding pockets in three dimensions, giving a far higher trap density per unit volume—and far better size/shape selectivity—than soluble antibodies or single origami shells, and the sponge neutralizes by physical sequestration rather than by targeting a single epitope, making it less vulnerable to escape mutations (its specificity can be reprogrammed in days by swapping ligand strands for a new variant or a new pathogen).

Practical embodiments: (i) a prophylactic/therapeutic "decoy" material for nasal sprays, wound irrigation, or blood/plasma detoxification cartridges that strip virions, bacterial toxins, or inflammatory cytokines from a fluid stream; (ii) a sample‑preparation and diagnostic medium that concentrates whole virus particles or tumour‑derived exosomes from dilute clinical samples for downstream PCR, sequencing, or mass spectrometry, with capture read out label‑free as a change in the crystal's Bragg/SAXS structure factor or refractive index when the cages fill; and (iii) an environmental/water‑safety filter for enteric viruses. The empty, solvent‑accessible cages also mean captured particles remain hydrated and intact, so the same crystal can serve as a holder that orients trapped virions in a periodic array for cryo‑EM/tomographic imaging, and the trapped cargo can be released on demand by toehold‑mediated strand displacement of the capture ligands for recovery and analysis.

**Use the "cage" crystals as a designer mesoscale model solid for experimental solid‑state/soft‑matter physics — i.e., a tunable‑vacancy crystal in which defect thermodynamics and mass transport can be watched directly.**

In atomic crystals, point defects (vacancies, interstitials, Frenkel/Schottky pairs), their formation energies, diffusion and clustering govern properties such as ionic conductivity, creep, sintering and phase transformation kinetics — yet they occur at ångström length scales and picosecond time scales and are essentially impossible to observe individually. A DNA‑origami superlattice built from blocks with a deliberate central vacancy reproduces exactly this physics on a length scale of tens of nanometres and a time scale of seconds to hours, where cryo‑EM, electron tomography, in‑situ SAXS/GISAXS and even super‑resolution optical microscopy can resolve individual lattice sites.

Because the "atoms" (origami blocks), their bond strengths (number, length and sequence of hybridizing sticky ends), their coordination geometry, and — uniquely here — the *size and concentration of the vacancies* are all set independently by sequence design, one can deliberately dope the crystal with an arbitrary, known fraction of empty cages or of "guest" blocks that fit into them, and then measure: how vacancy concentration and cage size shift the melting/annealing temperature and the elastic constants; how defects migrate, coalesce into voids, or mediate diffusion of guest particles hopping cage‑to‑cage (a direct, single‑particle visualization of vacancy‑mediated diffusion and of Frenkel‑type disorder); how grain boundaries, dislocations and stacking faults nucleate and heal; and how open, low‑coordination "zeolitic" lattices remain thermodynamically stable rather than collapsing to close packing. Since the bond energy (base pairing) is tunable in units of k_BT simply by changing sticky‑end length or salt, the same crystal can be driven reversibly through order–disorder and open‑to‑close‑packed transitions in situ.

The payoff is both fundamental and practical: it provides quantitative, real‑space benchmarks for statistical‑mechanical and simulation models of crystallization, defect equilibria and self‑assembly pathways that currently rest on indirect data, and it yields design rules for making *any* open, low‑density programmable lattice (colloidal, nanoparticle, or metal–organic) robust — telling engineers how large a void a self‑assembled framework can tolerate before it collapses, which is the key limitation for all of the functional (photonic, catalytic, host–guest) uses of porous nanomaterials.

**Use the caged origami crystal as a self‑assembled, sub‑20‑nm "stencil mask" for nanolithography and pattern transfer onto device substrates.**

A single (or few) monolayer‑thick slab cleaved from the superlattice is a mechanically continuous DNA film perforated by a perfectly periodic array of identical through‑holes — the central vacancies of the constituent blocks. Deposited flat on a wafer (Si, SiO₂, graphene, a magnetic or superconducting film) and lightly rigidified (Mg²⁺/oligolysine, silicification or a thin metal skin), it acts exactly like a shadow/stencil mask in which the hole diameter, hole‑to‑hole pitch, lattice symmetry (square, hexagonal, rectangular) and even deliberate registry marks are set purely by the origami sequence design rather than by an exposure tool. Evaporating or sputtering metal, ALD‑depositing an oxide, or ion/plasma‑etching through the openings, then digesting away the DNA with nuclease or an oxygen plasma, transfers the pattern into the substrate as a wafer‑scale, long‑range‑ordered array of nanodots, nanopores or nanopillars with a pitch well below the resolution and far below the throughput cost of e‑beam or EUV lithography.

Because the "resist" is a molecular object, the achievable feature size and placement precision are set by base‑pair geometry (~2–5 nm), the pattern is produced in parallel over macroscopic areas by simple self‑assembly and drop‑casting, and the mask is reprogrammable in days by redesigning the block/vacancy — no new photomask or write step is needed. Target uses include bit‑patterned magnetic recording media (one magnetic island per cage, at densities of several Tb in⁻²), ordered quantum‑dot or nanowire seed arrays for optoelectronics, catalyst‑particle arrays of uniform size for CVD growth of carbon nanotubes/2D materials, plasmonic and SERS nanodot arrays, and ordered solid‑state nanopore arrays for sequencing or single‑molecule sensing. The empty cages are essential: they provide the open, through‑thickness apertures that make the film a mask rather than a solid layer, and stacking several offset layers of the crystal even allows multilevel or 3D (Moiré‑ and vertical‑registry‑controlled) patterning that planar lithography cannot easily achieve.

**Use the caged superlattice as a programmable multivalent immunogen ("nanocrystal vaccine") for immune‑engineering.**

Each unit cell's vacancy provides an identical, solvent‑accessible pocket whose walls can be decorated by hybridization with antigens (viral glycoproteins/RBDs, peptides, glycans, haptens) or with immunostimulatory motifs (CpG oligos, TLR agonists), and the same chemistry decorates the crystal's outer faces. Because DNA origami fixes the inter‑antigen spacing with ~2–5 nm precision and the lattice repeats that spacing in three dimensions, the crystal presents thousands of copies of an antigen at exactly the geometry that optimally cross‑links B‑cell receptors (~5–15 nm pitch is known to maximize B‑cell activation), while the cages let one systematically vary valency, spacing, antigen orientation and antigen/adjuvant ratio — variables that are essentially uncontrollable in conventional protein nanoparticle or virus‑like‑particle vaccines. Colocalizing antigen and adjuvant in the same cage guarantees they are delivered together to the same antigen‑presenting cell, and the micron‑scale, low‑density crystal is efficiently taken up by dendritic cells and drains to lymph nodes, where gradual nuclease erosion of the lattice gives sustained antigen release (germinal‑centre "depot" effect) without a separate excipient. Multiple antigen variants can be loaded into distinct sublattices to make a defined mosaic/multivalent immunogen for broadly protective (e.g., pan‑influenza or pan‑sarbecovirus) responses, and the design can be reprogrammed for a new pathogen simply by swapping the antigen‑conjugated capture strands. The same platform serves as a research tool for quantitatively mapping how antigen geometry controls B‑cell activation, affinity maturation and antibody breadth, and, with peptide–MHC and costimulatory ligands in the cages, as an artificial antigen‑presenting scaffold for expanding T cells in immunotherapy.

Use the caged crystals as a **cell‑instructive, biodegradable 3D "artificial extracellular‑matrix" scaffold for tissue engineering and stem‑cell biology.** Because the lattice is mostly open space, a micron‑to‑millimetre aggregate of such crystals (crosslinked or embedded in a hydrogel) forms a highly hydrated, mechanically compliant matrix whose interconnected cage network is permeable to nutrients, oxygen and metabolites, while its walls present adhesion ligands (RGD peptides, laminin/collagen mimetic peptides, cadherin or Notch ligands) at spacings defined with ~2–5 nm precision by origami sequence design — exactly the parameter (ligand nanospacing, clustering and valency) that controls integrin clustering, focal‑adhesion maturation and mechanotransduction, but which cannot be controlled in natural or polymer matrices. Simultaneously, each identical vacancy serves as a nanoreservoir preloaded with morphogens or growth factors (BMP, VEGF, FGF, Wnt), so the same material delivers a defined dose per unit volume with programmable release kinetics set by gating strands, nuclease‑cleavable linkers or pH/enzyme‑responsive locks; loading different sublattices or different crystal batches with distinct factors allows spatially graded, multi‑cue microenvironments to be built up layer by layer. Lattice geometry additionally tunes the bulk stiffness and pore size independently of chemistry, letting one decouple matrix mechanics from ligand density — the classic confound in stem‑cell fate studies. As cells secrete nucleases and remodel the scaffold, the DNA framework is degraded into non‑toxic nucleotides at a rate that can be programmed through duplex stability and chemical protection, providing a matrix that "hands over" mechanical support to newly deposited native ECM. Applications include quantitative screening of how ligand geometry and stiffness direct differentiation, organoid and vascular‑network guidance, and implantable, fully resorbable regenerative patches whose biochemical program can be rewritten simply by changing the origami strand set.

**Use the caged superlattice to build a three‑dimensional artificial spin lattice / magnonic crystal for nanomagnetism and magnon‑based computing.**

Every unit cell contains one identical, crystallographically fixed vacancy, so a single magnetic nanoelement can be placed in (or grown inside) each cage: a superparamagnetic or ferrimagnetic nanoparticle (Fe₃O₄, CoFe₂O₄, FePt) captured by cage‑lining sequences, or a magnetic phase nucleated in situ by mineralizing the void (e.g., ferritin‑like iron loading, or electroless/ALD deposition on the cage walls). The result is a true 3D periodic array of nanomagnets whose lattice constant, symmetry (cubic, tetragonal, distorted), inter‑magnet spacing and even sublattice composition are set purely by the origami block/vacancy design rather than by lithography — something planar patterning fundamentally cannot deliver in the third dimension at sub‑50‑nm pitch.

Because dipolar coupling strength scales steeply with separation, and the DNA design fixes that separation with base‑pair (~2–5 nm) precision, one can deliberately engineer frustrated coordination geometries and realize **3D artificial spin ice** — a long‑sought experimental platform for studying emergent monopole‑like excitations, magnetic Coulomb phases, frustration and ordering/relaxation dynamics in bulk rather than on a surface — and systematically tune frustration simply by rewriting the strand set. Filling only selected sublattices, mixing hard/soft or magnetic/non‑magnetic guests, or leaving a designed fraction of cages empty introduces controlled "spin vacancies" and disorder for testing statistical‑mechanical models.

Functionally, the same periodic modulation of magnetization makes the crystal a **magnonic band‑gap material**: spin waves propagating through the ordered dipolar array experience Bragg scattering at GHz frequencies, giving designable magnon band gaps, waveguiding and reconfigurable filters/interconnects for magnon spintronics, as well as tunable microwave/absorbing metamaterials and negative‑permeability elements. Since the cages can also be gated by strand displacement or pH/ion triggers, guests can be loaded, ejected or shifted in situ, making the magnetic band structure chemically reconfigurable — and, once silicified or resin‑embedded, the assembly becomes a robust device layer. Additional payoffs include a uniform, ordered 3D array of identical magnetic labels for MRI/magnetic‑particle‑imaging calibration and hyperthermia dose studies, and, if the crystal is used as a sacrificial template, an inverse magnetic nanostructure with periodic voids for vortex‑pinning or bit‑patterned media.
