Use the caged crystals as a **precision‑pore sorbent for vapour/gas capture — e.g. atmospheric water harvesting, dehumidification and direct‑air CO₂ capture.** Because every unit cell contributes an identical, tens‑of‑nanometre cavity, the lattice (or, for dry‑state robustness, its silica/alumina replica made by conformally mineralising the DNA walls and burning the template out) is a sorbent with an essentially perfectly monodisperse pore size and an enormous internal surface area. Sorption in such uniform mesopores is dominated by capillary condensation, which occurs at a sharp, well‑defined relative humidity/partial pressure set by the Kelvin equation — and since the pore diameter here is dialled in by simply redesigning the origami block and its vacancy, that uptake–release threshold can be tuned by design rather than by empirical synthesis. The practical consequence is a sorbent with a **step‑like isotherm**: it fills completely at the humidity of night/ambient air and empties completely with only a few degrees of solar or waste‑heat warming, giving high working capacity with very low regeneration energy — the key bottleneck for passive water‑from‑air devices and for DAC. Additional selectivity is programmable chemically: the cage walls can be functionalised through hybridised strands with amines/guanidinium or carbonic‑anhydrase‑mimetic Zn sites for chemisorptive CO₂ binding, with hydrophilic/hydrophobic patches to shift the condensation point, or with aptamers for capturing specific volatile organics, so the same platform serves as a regenerable VOC scrubber or as the sensing layer of a highly selective gravimetric (QCM/microcantilever) vapour sensor, where filling of the ordered voids also produces a readable shift in the crystal's Bragg/refractive‑index response.

**Use the caged superlattice (or its silica/alumina replica made by mineralising the DNA walls) as a host for *nanoconfined phase‑change materials* — a programmable latent‑heat thermal‑storage and thermal‑management medium.**

Because every unit cell contributes an identical, tens‑of‑nanometre cavity, infiltrating the cages with a phase‑change medium (paraffin/fatty acid, salt hydrate, polyethylene glycol, water, or a low‑melting metal/alloy such as Ga or Bi–Sn) gives a composite in which *every* PCM domain has exactly the same, designer‑set volume and surface‑to‑volume ratio. Nanoconfinement then does three useful things at once: (i) the Gibbs–Thomson depression shifts the melting/freezing point by an amount fixed by the cage diameter, so the transition temperature can be *dialled in* simply by redesigning the origami block and its vacancy rather than by searching for a new chemistry; (ii) the monodisperse pores give an extremely sharp, reproducible transition (in bulk or randomly porous hosts the size distribution smears it out) and the DNA/oxide walls act as uniform heterogeneous nucleation sites that suppress the large, erratic supercooling that plagues salt hydrates and paraffins; and (iii) capillary forces and the rigid framework prevent leakage, phase segregation and volume‑change damage on cycling, so the material is form‑stable over many thousands of melt–freeze cycles.

Practically this yields a “shape‑stabilised” PCM with a tunable, narrow set‑point for isothermal buffering of hot spots in microelectronics and photonics, for solar‑thermal and waste‑heat storage, for cold‑chain/biologics shipping, and for thermal‑protection coatings; combining sublattices or crystal batches with different cage sizes gives a *cascade* of set‑points and hence a broad, staged storage window. Since the empty voids also scatter phonons while the molten phase conducts, the same material acts as a solid‑state **thermal switch/regulator** whose conductivity changes abruptly at the designed temperature. As a research tool, the perfectly monodisperse, sequence‑tunable cavities provide an ideal model system for measuring how confinement size and wall chemistry (which can be made hydrophilic/hydrophobic or ligand‑decorated by hybridised strands) control freezing, ice nucleation, glass formation and interfacial premelting — questions relevant to cryopreservation, anti‑icing surfaces and geochemistry.

**Use the caged crystals as covert, dual‑mode anti‑counterfeiting taggants / physical‑unclonable authentication labels.**

Because the lattice constant, symmetry, cage diameter and cage occupancy are all set by origami sequence design, each production batch of "cage" superlattices can be given a deliberately chosen, hard‑to‑replicate structural fingerprint: the periodic void array produces a sharp, characteristic Bragg/SAXS diffraction pattern and, when the cages are left empty versus loaded with high‑index, plasmonic or fluorescent guests (Au/Ag nanoparticles, quantum dots, dyes, upconverting nanocrystals), a distinctive refractive‑index contrast, structural colour, SERS signature or multi‑colour emission spectrum. Filling only selected sublattices, or mixing several crystal populations with different cage sizes, encodes a multiplexed optical/scattering "barcode" that is read out non‑destructively in seconds with a handheld spectrometer, portable Raman reader or lab diffractometer.

The tag carries a second, orthogonal layer of security that no inorganic microparticle taggant can offer: the origami staple strands themselves constitute a cryptographic DNA key that can be PCR‑amplified and sequenced for forensic‑grade verification, and additional "message" oligos can be hidden inside the cages and released only by a specific toehold/primer, so authentication requires knowing both the physical (lattice/optical) and the molecular (sequence) code. Because self‑assembly of billions of crystals is stochastic in grain shape, size and defect/vacancy filling pattern, an individual crystal's imaged cage‑occupancy map is effectively unclonable, giving a true PUF for item‑level serialization.

Practically, a trace amount of such crystals (optionally silicified or resin‑embedded for dry, thermal and shelf stability) can be blended into pharmaceutical tablet coatings, inks, polymers, packaging films, banknote fibres, explosives or agrochemicals to authenticate products, trace supply chains and identify diversion or adulteration — with the whole code reprogrammable in days by simply redesigning the block/vacancy and its guest set, keeping counterfeiters permanently a generation behind, and with the biodegradable, non‑toxic DNA framework being safe for food‑, drug‑ and environment‑contact use.

**Use the caged superlattice as a self‑assembled, three‑dimensional diffractive optic for short‑wavelength radiation — i.e. a "soft‑X‑ray/EUV and cold‑neutron Bragg element" (monochromator, beam splitter/phase grating, or volume hologram).**

The periodic alternation of DNA walls and empty (or selectively filled) cages creates a genuine 3‑D modulation of electron density / neutron scattering‑length density with a lattice constant of tens of nanometres — precisely the period range needed to Bragg‑diffract extreme‑ultraviolet and soft‑X‑ray photons (λ ≈ 1–30 nm) and to give measurable small‑angle diffraction of cold neutrons (λ ≈ 0.4–2 nm), a regime where conventional optics are limited to painstakingly sputtered multilayers or e‑beam‑written gratings. Because the *vacancy* is what produces the contrast, the "index step" per unit cell can be made very large and, crucially, tuned: leaving the cages empty gives a low‑absorption, high‑Δρ phase grating, whereas infiltrating them with high‑Z guests (Au, W, Pt clusters) or, for neutrons, with H₂O/D₂O or Gd/B‑containing species dials the amplitude‑ versus phase‑contrast and even switches the diffraction on and off in situ by strand‑displacement‑gated loading/unloading. Since d‑spacing, lattice symmetry, crystal thickness and the shape of the scattering unit are all set independently by origami sequence design (and can be graded or chirped between sublattices), one can specify Bragg angle, bandwidth, diffraction order and dispersion by design rather than by deposition tolerance, and produce the elements in parallel over macroscopic areas by simple self‑assembly (with silicification or metal coating to make them robust, dry, radiation‑hard device layers).

Applications include compact EUV/soft‑X‑ray monochromators, order‑sorting and beam‑splitting phase masks for tabletop high‑harmonic and free‑electron‑laser beamlines, gratings and analyser elements for X‑ray phase‑contrast/Talbot interferometry, and transmission gratings/phase objects for cold‑neutron interferometry and ultra‑small‑angle scattering instrumentation — as well as reference diffraction standards for calibrating those instruments.

**Use the caged superlattice as a template for a three‑dimensional Josephson‑junction array / superconducting quantum metamaterial.**

Each unit cell's identical, crystallographically fixed vacancy is loaded with (or used to nucleate) a single superconducting nanograin — e.g. Al, Sn, Pb, Nb or NbN nanoparticles captured by cage‑lining capture strands, or a superconducting phase grown in situ by electroless/atomic‑layer deposition on the cage walls followed by removal of the DNA. Because the origami design fixes the grain size, the inter‑grain separation and the lattice symmetry with base‑pair (~2–5 nm) precision in all three directions, the barrier thickness — and hence the Josephson coupling energy E_J and charging energy E_C of every junction — is set uniformly and by design, something that lithography cannot achieve in the third dimension at sub‑50‑nm pitch. The result is a macroscopic, self‑assembled 3D network of nominally identical, tunable Josephson junctions.

Scientifically, such an array is a clean experimental platform for the E_J/E_C‑driven superconductor–insulator quantum phase transition, Cooper‑pair localization and charge/vortex duality, and for analogue quantum simulation of frustrated XY (phase) models — with frustration, dimensionality and disorder engineered simply by rewriting the strand set (e.g. leaving a designed fraction of cages empty to create "grain vacancies", or filling alternating sublattices with normal‑metal or magnetic guests to make SNS/SFS junctions and study π‑junction and triplet physics). Technologically, the periodic void/metal architecture gives a bulk superconducting metamaterial with engineered kinetic inductance and strongly nonlinear, low‑loss microwave response — useful for compact high‑inductance elements, travelling‑wave parametric amplifiers, tunable microwave filters/left‑handed media for circuit‑QED, and, in the inverse (voided) replica, an ordered array of vortex‑pinning sites for high‑critical‑current superconducting films. Since the cages can be gated by toehold‑mediated strand displacement or pH/ion triggers, guests can be inserted or ejected in situ, making the coupling — and thus the superconducting/insulating state — chemically reconfigurable, and the crystal can be silicified or resin‑embedded to yield a robust cryogenic device layer.

**Use the caged crystal as a solid‑state "Anfinsen cage" — a GroEL‑mimetic chaperone matrix for encapsulating, refolding and stabilizing aggregation‑prone proteins.**

Each unit cell provides an identical, solvent‑accessible cavity of designer diameter (a few tens of nm) whose walls are a rigid, highly charged DNA framework. Threading a single unfolded or partially folded polypeptide into each cage — through pores sized to admit monomers but not oligomers, or by tethering the chain to a capture strand on one cage wall — confines it to a volume that holds only one molecule, so the dominant failure mode of protein folding, *inter*molecular collision and aggregation, is physically abolished while *intra*molecular folding proceeds freely. Steric confinement additionally destabilizes expanded misfolded states and shifts the folding funnel toward the compact native state (the entropic "cage effect" exploited by chaperonins), and the cavity walls can be chemically programmed by hybridized strands (hydrophobic patches, polyanionic/polycationic surfaces, arginine or osmolyte‑mimetic groups, or grafted Hsp70/DnaJ‑derived peptides and disulfide‑isomerase mimics) to tune whether the wall is inert or transiently binds exposed hydrophobic segments in a bind‑and‑release cycle. Because the cages are periodic and identical, the crystal offers billions of equivalent folding chambers per particle, and cargo can be released on demand by toehold‑mediated strand displacement or a pH/ionic trigger.

Practical payoffs: (i) a reusable, flow‑through "refolding column" for recovering active protein from bacterial inclusion bodies and for high‑throughput screening of refolding conditions, replacing dilute‑refolding and detergent/chaotrope protocols; (ii) a formulation matrix that suppresses aggregation of therapeutic proteins, antibodies and vaccines during storage, freeze–drying and shipping, and that can sequester amyloidogenic species (Aβ, α‑synuclein, IAPP) as an anti‑aggregation agent or as a platform for screening aggregation inhibitors; and (iii) a uniquely quantitative research tool — since cage volume, wall chemistry, tether geometry and crowding are all set independently by sequence design, one can systematically measure how confinement dimension and surface chemistry alter folding rates, stability, misfolding pathways and single‑molecule folding trajectories (read out by FRET, cryo‑EM of the ordered lattice, or diffraction), testing chaperonin theory in a way that natural GroEL, which has one fixed cavity size, cannot.

**Use the caged crystals as a high‑capacity, chemically selective sorbent for water remediation and critical‑metal recovery.**

Every unit cell donates an identical, solvent‑accessible cavity, so a gram of crystals (or of its silicified/crosslinked, flow‑stable form packed into a column or cast as beads/foam) presents an enormous number of uniform, freely accessible binding pockets rather than the tortuous, polydisperse pores of activated carbon or ion‑exchange resins. Two features make this a genuinely selective extractor: (i) the DNA walls are intrinsically polyanionic, giving strong generic affinity for cations, and (ii) each cage can be lined, by simple hybridization of modified strands, with a *designed constellation* of chelators — lanthanide‑binding peptide tags, siderophore/hydroxamate or catechol groups, amidoxime for uranyl, phosphonates, thiol/cysteine motifs for Hg²⁺/Pb²⁺/Cd²⁺, or metal‑specific DNAzymes and aptamers. Because origami fixes the number, spacing and three‑dimensional geometry of these ligands with ~2 nm precision, the pocket can be built to match the coordination number and ionic radius of one target ion (e.g. discriminating individual lanthanides from one another, or Au³⁺/Pd²⁺ from base metals), achieving the multidentate, "pre‑organized" recognition that gives natural metalloproteins their selectivity but that is impossible to control in a random polymer resin.

Practically this yields a regenerable extraction medium for: stripping Pb, Hg, Cd, As or Cr from drinking and waste water below ppb levels; capturing uranium, technetium or actinides/⁹⁰Sr–¹³⁷Cs from seawater, mine tailings and nuclear‑decommissioning effluent; and recovering rare‑earth and platinum‑group elements from e‑waste leachates, coal ash and geothermal brines — an urgent need for supply‑chain security where current solvent extraction requires dozens of energy‑intensive stages. Recovery is programmable rather than harsh: instead of concentrated acid elution, the bound metal can be released by toehold‑mediated strand displacement of the chelator strand, or by a pH/competitive‑ligand trigger, so the same framework is reloaded with a *different* ligand set to target a different element without resynthesizing the material. Sorption is also self‑reporting, since filling of the ordered voids with heavy ions changes the crystal's structure factor and diffraction/optical response, letting the column signal its own breakthrough point; and the DNA scaffold is biodegradable, so spent, non‑silicified sorbent can be nuclease‑digested to liberate a concentrated metal stream with minimal secondary waste.

**Use the caged crystals as monodisperse "gas‑trap" ultrasound contrast and cavitation agents.** Because every unit cell contains an identical, precisely sized cavity, the lattice can be made hydrophobic on the inner cage walls (by hybridizing cholesterol‑, fluoroalkyl‑ or perfluorocarbon‑modified strands) so that each vacancy stably nucleates and retains a nanoscale gas pocket (air, SF₆, C₃F₈) when the crystal is degassed/re‑equilibrated or exposed to a perfluorocarbon nanodroplet that vaporizes on demand. The result is a 3D periodic array of billions of *identical* nanobubbles held at fixed spacing — something impossible with lipid microbubbles, which are inherently polydisperse and coalesce.

The payoff is acoustic: because bubble resonance frequency is set by radius, a population of cages with one designed diameter gives an extremely narrow, tunable resonance, so the agent produces a strong, spectrally sharp, harmonic/subharmonic echo at a frequency chosen by origami design. This yields (i) high‑sensitivity, frequency‑multiplexed ultrasound contrast imaging in which several crystal batches with different cage sizes act as independently addressable "colours" for simultaneous imaging of different targets (the outer faces being decorated with antibodies or aptamers for molecular ultrasound of tumour vasculature, thrombi or inflammation); (ii) predictable, low‑threshold inertial cavitation under focused ultrasound, enabling controlled sonoporation, blood–brain‑barrier opening, sonodynamic/histotripsy therapy and simultaneous release of drugs co‑loaded in the same cages, with the cavitation dose set by the designed bubble size rather than by an uncontrolled size distribution; and (iii) very efficient photoacoustic/acoustic droplet‑vaporization response for image‑guided therapy. The DNA framework also makes the agent biodegradable and its acoustic signature self‑reporting, since loss of the ordered voids changes both the echo spectrum and the crystal's diffraction pattern, allowing bubble persistence and agent clearance to be quantified directly.

**Use the caged superlattice as a three‑dimensional *chiral* nanoporous framework — a "programmable chiral sponge" for enantioselective separation/catalysis and for chiroptical (circular‑dichroic) metamaterials.**

DNA is intrinsically chiral, and because the origami blocks can be assembled with a designed handedness (twisted/skewed struts, helically offset connections between neighbouring blocks, or a chiral arrangement of the openings into each vacancy), every one of the millions of identical cages in the crystal becomes a chiral pocket of exactly the same size, shape and handedness. Lining those pockets by hybridization with chiral recognition elements — L‑ or D‑peptides, aptamers, cyclodextrin/crown‑ether or amino‑acid–modified strands placed at ~2 nm‑precise positions and orientations — creates a pre‑organized, three‑point binding site whose geometry can be matched to one enantiomer of a target molecule. Packed into a column or cast as a membrane (silicified or crosslinked for flow stability), the crystal then acts as a chiral stationary phase that resolves racemic drugs, agrochemicals and amino acids with selectivity set by *design* rather than by empirical screening, and the same pockets, loaded with a metal complex or organocatalyst held in a fixed chiral environment, function as an ordered heterogeneous asymmetric catalyst in which confinement plus ligand geometry enforce facial selectivity (an artificial enzyme active site replicated billions of times). Because the recognition strands can be swapped or ejected by toehold‑mediated strand displacement, the same framework can be re‑programmed for the opposite enantiomer or a different substrate without resynthesizing the material, and bound guests can be released under mild, non‑denaturing conditions.

The same handed, periodic void architecture also gives strong bulk chiroptical response: filling selected cages with plasmonic or dielectric guests (Au/Ag nanoparticles, quantum dots) that inherit the lattice's helical arrangement produces a 3D chiral metamaterial with giant circular dichroism, optical rotation and superchiral near‑fields — useful as a broadband circular polarizer/optical isolator layer, a wavelength‑tunable CD reference standard, and, most powerfully, as an enhancement substrate that amplifies the weak CD/Raman‑optical‑activity signals of trace chiral analytes trapped inside the cages, enabling chirality sensing (e.g. enantiomeric‑excess monitoring in pharmaceutical process control) at concentrations far below conventional CD detection limits.

**Use the caged crystal as a spin‑engineered host matrix for magnetic‑resonance spectroscopy — a "DNP/NMR alignment medium" in which every guest molecule sits at a designed distance from a polarizing radical.**

Because each unit cell contains one identical vacancy at a crystallographically fixed position, a guest molecule (a small‑molecule drug, peptide, RNA, membrane protein in a nanodisc, or a catalytic complex) can be loaded one‑per‑cage, while the surrounding DNA walls are decorated by hybridization with polarizing agents (TEMPO/trityl/AMUPol biradicals, Gd³⁺ or Mn²⁺ chelates) or with paramagnetic/spin‑label strands at sequence‑chosen sites. This solves the central problem of dynamic nuclear polarization and paramagnetic NMR/EPR: instead of randomly dispersing radicals and analyte in a frozen glass, the origami design sets the radical–analyte distance, the radical–radical distance (which governs the electron dipolar coupling that drives cross‑effect DNP), and the analyte concentration/dilution independently and with ~1–2 nm precision, so polarization transfer can be optimized rationally and paramagnetic quenching of the signal avoided. The lattice repeats these identical local environments billions of times, giving a homogeneous, monodisperse sample rather than the distribution of geometries that broadens lines and limits enhancement.

Additional payoffs: (i) the anisotropic, magnetically alignable crystal (DNA duplexes orient in high fields, and the crystal can be strained or shear‑cast in a film) acts as a **programmable alignment medium** that imposes a controlled partial ordering on the encapsulated guest, yielding residual dipolar couplings, chemical‑shift‑anisotropy and quadrupolar information for structure determination — with the degree and direction of alignment tuned by redesigning the block/cage rather than by trial‑and‑error choice of bicelles, phage or gels, and with the inert, empty cage preventing the guest–medium sticking that plagues conventional alignment media; (ii) spin‑diffusion pathways and nuclear relaxation can be sculpted by isotopically labelling (²H/¹³C/¹⁵N) selected staple strands, making the walls either a proton "spin bath" for polarization relay or a deuterated silent matrix; (iii) for EPR/DEER, placing exactly two spin labels per cage at a designed separation provides distance‑measurement calibration standards and a way to study dipolar coupled spin networks; and (iv) the same host, loaded with pyruvate or metabolite guests, serves as a reusable, filterable polarizing matrix for producing hyperpolarized solutions for metabolic MRI, since the radicals stay bound to the framework and are removed with it. In short, the periodic vacancies convert the superlattice into a magnetic‑resonance "test tube array" with sequence‑programmable spin geometry, boosting sensitivity for trace/precious analytes and enabling systematic studies of how radical geometry controls DNP efficiency.

**Use the caged crystals (after conversion to an inorganic replica) as a monodisperse ultralow‑density nanofoam for inertial‑confinement‑fusion and high‑energy‑density‑physics targets.**

Because every unit cell of the superlattice contributes one identical vacancy, the material is a perfectly periodic solid–void composite with an extremely high void fraction and a cell size fixed at tens of nanometres by base‑pair geometry. Conformally coating the DNA walls (silicification, sol–gel, ALD of SiO₂/Al₂O₃, or carbonization/metal plating for CH‑, C‑ or high‑Z foams) and then removing the template yields a self‑supporting foam of ~1–100 mg cm⁻³ density whose cell diameter, wall thickness, lattice symmetry and elemental composition are all set independently by origami sequence design rather than by the stochastic phase separation that governs conventional aerogels, divinylbenzene/resorcinol‑formaldehyde foams and CH aerogel shells.

This matters because the single biggest defect in current ICF foam ablators and wicking layers is pore polydispersity: cells of variable, sometimes micron‑scale size seed density perturbations that grow via Rayleigh–Taylor/Richtmyer–Meshkov instability during implosion and quench fusion yield. An origami‑templated foam offers cells that are uniform to within a nanometre and far smaller than the shell thickness and than the relevant instability wavelengths, so the foam ablates and shock‑homogenizes as an effectively continuous medium. The same open, interconnected void network wicks liquid DT fuel uniformly by capillarity to form a smooth cryogenic ice layer, and the designed cell size lets one dial in the capillary pressure and fill/vent kinetics. Because the walls can be built from low‑Z (CH, C, SiO₂) or, by loading the cages with metal/cluster guests, mid‑ and high‑Z materials, and because different sublattices can be doped independently, one can engineer graded‑density and doped ablators, X‑ray converters, radiation‑transport (supersonic Marshak wave) samples, and laser‑driven electron/ion‑acceleration targets with controlled, reproducible microstructure — turning "foam quality" from an empirical synthesis lottery into a programmable design parameter, and providing standard, well‑characterized nanofoams for benchmarking radiation‑hydrodynamics codes.

**Use the caged superlattice as the host framework for a nanostructured, photonically engineered scintillator for X‑ray/γ‑ray and particle detection.**

Because every unit cell contains one identical, crystallographically fixed vacancy, each cage can be loaded (via sequence‑specific capture strands) with exactly one scintillating emitter — a perovskite or CdSe/ZnS quantum dot, a Ce³⁺/Tb³⁺/Eu³⁺ lanthanide complex, a high‑Z Bi/Hf/W cluster paired with an organic fluorophore, or a nanoparticle scintillator. The DNA design fixes emitter size, one‑per‑cell occupancy and inter‑emitter spacing with ~2 nm precision, which directly addresses the three limitations of conventional scintillator films: (i) *concentration quenching and aggregation* — the empty cage walls keep every emitter optically isolated at a chosen separation, so loading can be pushed to high volumetric density without self‑absorption or Förster quenching, giving high light yield and fast, non‑degraded decay times; (ii) *stopping power vs. transparency* — high‑Z converter species can be placed on the cage walls (or in alternating sublattices) while the emitters sit in the voids, decoupling X‑ray absorption from luminescence and allowing graded/multi‑element "stacks" to be designed rather than empirically mixed; and (iii) *light spreading, which blurs images* — the periodic tens‑of‑nanometre modulation of refractive index between DNA walls and voids constitutes a genuine 3D photonic crystal, so the same lattice that hosts the emitters can be designed to suppress isotropic emission into guided modes and instead funnel/beam scintillation photons toward the photodetector (Purcell‑enhanced, directional emission), improving both light‑collection efficiency and spatial resolution.

Practically, thin films or resin/silica‑stabilised slabs of such crystals coupled to CMOS/SiPM arrays would give high‑resolution, high‑efficiency detectors for medical X‑ray and CT imaging, PET and Compton cameras, security screening, X‑ray free‑electron‑laser and synchrotron beam diagnostics, and neutron detection (by loading ⁶Li‑ or ¹⁰B‑containing guests into the cages). Multiplexed spectral discrimination is possible by loading different sublattices or different crystal batches with emitters of distinct emission wavelength and decay constant, so photon energy or particle type can be encoded in colour/timing; and because pore size, emitter identity, spacing and lattice symmetry are all reprogrammed simply by redesigning the origami block and its vacancy, the detector's stopping power, emission wavelength, decay time and photonic outcoupling can be optimised by design rather than by materials screening. The same architecture, with a persistent‑luminescence or thermoluminescent guest, yields a reusable, tissue‑compatible nanoscale dosimeter for radiotherapy dose mapping.

**Use the caged crystal as a three‑dimensional entropic‑trap array for long‑polymer (genomic DNA/chromatin) separation, stretching and single‑molecule optical mapping.**

The lattice naturally alternates wide, identical cavities (the block vacancies) with the much narrower necks/openings between neighbouring blocks — exactly the "wide well / narrow slit" geometry used in entropic‑trap electrophoresis chips, but with a period of tens of nanometres (set by base pairing to ±2 nm) instead of the hundreds of nanometres achievable by lithography, and repeated in all three dimensions instead of one plane. A thin, field‑spanning film of the crystal (mechanically fixed by silicification, oligolysine–PEG coating or resin embedding, and mounted in a microfluidic cell) therefore forces a migrating polymer to repeatedly coil in a cage and then pay an entropic penalty to squeeze a "beachhead" through a neck. Because that escape probability depends steeply on molecular length and stiffness, the film fractionates long DNA, RNA, chromatin fragments, plasmids, polysaccharides or synthetic polymers in a length regime (>20–50 kb) where conventional gel and capillary electrophoresis lose all resolution and where pulsed‑field runs take days — here separation is fast, isocratic and tunable simply by redesigning the cage/neck dimensions rather than by casting a new gel.

The same confinement stretches molecules: a DNA strand threading the neck series is held near‑linearised and in register with the periodic lattice, so fluorescently labelled sequence motifs (nick‑labelling, CRISPR‑Cas tags, methylation marks) appear at physically calibrated intervals — the lattice constant itself serves as an internal ruler — giving high‑accuracy optical genome mapping, structural‑variant and epigenetic‑pattern detection without amplification, plus controlled feeding of single molecules toward downstream nanopores or sequencing chemistry. Lining the necks with hybridised sequence‑, methyl‑ or protein‑specific ligands adds affinity‑based retardation, so the material becomes a programmable chromatographic medium (e.g. capturing only methylated or protein‑bound fragments).

Scientifically, the perfectly monodisperse, sequence‑tunable cavity/neck geometry provides the long‑missing model system for testing polymer‑physics theory of confinement — de Gennes vs. Odijk regimes, hernia/nucleation‑limited escape, reptation and DNA knotting/unknotting — because cage size, neck width, connectivity and wall charge/chemistry can each be varied independently while every trap in the sample is identical.

**Use the caged superlattice as a nanostructured, low‑density solid target for directional detection of rare nuclear‑recoil events (WIMP dark‑matter searches, coherent neutrino–nucleus scattering, and neutron/α dosimetry).**

A recoiling nucleus in an ordinary solid travels only tens of nanometres, so its *direction* — the key signature that would distinguish a galactic dark‑matter "wind" from radioactive backgrounds — is normally unrecoverable. A crystal built from origami blocks with periodic central vacancies solves this on two counts. First, because most of each unit cell is empty, the material has a very low but *exactly known and uniform* mass density, so recoil tracks are stretched to hundreds of nanometres to micrometres, spanning many unit cells; and because the vacancies form a perfectly periodic 3‑D lattice with a base‑pair‑defined constant, the crystal is its own built‑in coordinate grid, letting the track's start point, length and polar/azimuthal angles be reconstructed with nanometre accuracy. Second, the DNA framework itself is the sensor: a recoil that passes through a cage wall severs single‑stranded "tracer" segments hybridised at designed positions, and the released, sequence‑barcoded oligos (each barcode encoding the x,y,z address of the lattice site it came from) are collected and read out by high‑throughput sequencing or by PCR amplification — giving effectively single‑ion sensitivity with amplification built in, and a spatial resolution set by molecular design rather than by pixel size. Loading the cages with chosen guests tunes the target nucleus (e.g. hydrogen‑rich polymers or high‑Z Au/W clusters for different WIMP mass ranges, ⁶Li/¹⁰B or Gd complexes for neutron capture), while leaving alternate sublattices empty controls stopping power and track length; the same crystal, silicified for robustness, also serves as a solid‑state track‑etch/neutron dosimeter and as a calibration standard for stopping‑power and radiation‑damage models, since every damage site occurs in an identical, precisely known local environment.

**Use the caged crystals as a sacrificial template for a 3D‑ordered porous ferro‑/piezoelectric film — i.e. a "designer piezo‑foam" for mechanical energy harvesting, self‑powered sensing and electromechanical transducers.**

Because every unit cell contributes one identical vacancy, the superlattice is a periodic solid–void composite whose void size, wall thickness, spacing and symmetry are set purely by origami sequence design. Conformally coating the DNA walls with a ferroelectric by sol–gel/ALD (BaTiO₃, PZT, KNN, ZnO, HfO₂/HZO, or an infiltrated β‑PVDF‑TrFE) and then burning out or digesting the DNA leaves an inverse replica: a self‑supporting, monodisperse‑pore piezoelectric skeleton with tens‑of‑nanometre cells.

Why the *cages* are the point: in dense ceramics the piezoelectric voltage coefficient g = d/ε is limited by the very high permittivity of the material. Introducing an ordered, high‑fraction void network drops ε dramatically while the continuous ceramic struts still carry the load, so g₃₃ (and the figure of merit d·g for harvesting/sensing) can rise by an order of magnitude. Moreover, the periodic voids act as designed stress concentrators, funnelling applied strain into the struts and amplifying the local field; because every cell is identical (unlike random, polydisperse sacrificial‑porogen or freeze‑cast foams), the stress distribution, poling behaviour and depolarisation fields are uniform, which raises breakdown strength, reduces fatigue/cracking hot spots and makes the response reproducible and predictable rather than empirical. The open network also makes the film compliant and conformable (good acoustic/mechanical impedance match to skin, tissue and air) and easy to pole and to back‑fill with a polymer or liquid electrolyte for 0‑3/3‑3 composite designs.

Practical payoffs: flexible nanogenerators and self‑powered strain/pressure/touch sensors and e‑skin; low‑impedance ultrasonic and photoacoustic transducers and hydrophones (where high g and low ε are exactly what is wanted); MEMS/NEMS actuators and resonators; vibration and acoustic energy scavengers for wireless/implantable microdevices; and, with ferroelectric HfO₂ walls, ordered 3D arrays of nanoscale ferroelectric capacitors for high‑density non‑volatile memory and neuromorphic synapses. Since porosity, cell size, wall thickness and lattice symmetry (including deliberately anisotropic or auxetic geometries that convert transverse loading into extra axial strain) are all reprogrammed simply by redesigning the origami block and its vacancy, the dielectric constant, compliance, resonance frequency and d/g coefficients can be optimised independently by design — turning "porous piezoceramic processing" from a stochastic foaming problem into a programmable one. The same platform doubles as a model system for quantifying how pore geometry controls domain‑wall motion, poling efficiency and electromechanical coupling in porous ferroelectrics.

**Use the caged superlattice as a self‑assembled "artificial photosynthetic membrane" — a 3D array of identical photocatalytic compartments for solar‑fuel production (H₂ evolution, CO₂ reduction).**

Each unit cell's vacancy is an identical reaction pocket whose walls can be decorated, by hybridizing modified strands at sequence‑chosen positions, with a complete, spatially organized photosystem: an antenna array of chromophores on the outer struts that funnels absorbed light to a photosensitizer (Ru/Ir complex, porphyrin, quantum dot) anchored on one cage face, an electron‑relay/redox mediator midway, and a catalyst (Pt, Ni‑ or Co‑bis(dithiolene)/cobaloxime, [FeFe]‑hydrogenase mimic, Mn‑oxo or CO₂‑reduction complex) fixed on the opposite face. Because DNA origami sets the donor–acceptor separations and mutual orientations with ~2 nm precision, forward electron transfer can be made fast and vectorial while the *long, empty* cage span suppresses the back‑electron transfer and recombination that limit all randomly mixed homogeneous photocatalytic systems — the same trick natural reaction centres use, but with the geometry as a programmable design variable rather than a fixed protein architecture.

The lattice adds what a single origami device cannot: billions of identical, perfectly registered photosystems per crystal give macroscopic light absorption and a measurable turnover rate; the periodic void network is an interconnected, solvent‑filled channel system that supplies water/CO₂/sacrificial donor and lets gaseous products escape without bubble‑induced catalyst fouling; different sublattices can carry the oxidation and reduction half‑reactions separately (an origami "Z‑scheme"), so oxygen and fuel are generated in chemically distinct, spatially separated compartments and cross‑reaction is minimized; and the periodic dielectric/plasmonic contrast between walls and voids can be designed to slow light or concentrate near‑fields at the catalyst sites, boosting absorption at the photosensitizer's weakly absorbing edges.

Practically this yields a printable photocatalyst film or slurry for solar hydrogen/syngas generation and photoelectrochemical cells (the crystal can be deposited on a transparent conducting electrode and silicified or resin‑stabilized for durability), and, just as importantly, a *quantitative platform for optimizing artificial photosynthesis*: because antenna number, chromophore spacing, relay identity, donor–catalyst distance and cage size are each varied independently simply by rewriting the strand set, one can map how molecular geometry controls quantum yield, charge‑separation lifetime and catalytic turnover — and swap in a new catalyst or sensitizer by toehold‑mediated strand displacement without resynthesizing the material.

**Use the caged superlattice as a template for a three‑dimensional photonic‑crystal "thermal‑emission engineer" — i.e., a spectrally selective radiative‑cooling / thermophotovoltaic coating.**

Because every unit cell donates one identical vacancy, the crystal is a periodic solid–void composite whose void diameter, wall thickness, filling fraction and lattice symmetry are all set by base‑pair geometry rather than by stochastic foaming. Conformally coating the DNA walls (silicification, sol–gel, or ALD of SiO₂/Al₂O₃/TiO₂ for cooling, or refractory HfO₂/W/TaN for high‑temperature use) and then burning out the template yields a self‑supporting inverse replica: a mechanically continuous inorganic skeleton perforated by a monodisperse, ordered network of tens‑of‑nanometre pores. Such a structure is precisely what is needed to sculpt a surface's spectral emissivity, which is the central design problem of radiative thermal management.

Two payoffs follow directly from the *ordered, monodisperse* cages. (i) **Passive daytime radiative cooling:** the periodic sub‑wavelength void array gives strong, broadband Mie/Bragg scattering across the solar spectrum (0.3–2.5 µm) — so a thin, thermally insulating film reflects >95 % of sunlight without any pigment — while the polar Si–O/Al–O wall phonon resonances provide near‑unity emissivity in the 8–13 µm atmospheric transparency window. The result is a paint‑like coating that radiates heat to deep space and cools below ambient under full sun, for zero‑energy building, vehicle, solar‑panel and cold‑chain cooling. Crucially, because scattering strength and the spectral cut‑off depend on pore diameter and pitch — which here are *identical for every pore and reprogrammable simply by redesigning the origami block and its vacancy* — the solar‑reflection band and the IR emission band can be optimized independently and predictably, instead of by the empirical, polydisperse phase‑inversion or porogen routes used for current cooling paints (whose broad pore‑size distributions blur the spectral response and waste reflectance).

(ii) **Selective emitters/absorbers for thermophotovoltaics and solar‑thermal conversion:** built from refractory walls, the same periodic void lattice creates a genuine 3D photonic band structure that suppresses emission below the PV cell's band‑gap wavelength and concentrates it just above, sharply raising TPV and solar‑TPV efficiency; run in reverse, it is a broadband solar absorber with suppressed IR re‑radiation for concentrated‑solar receivers. Cage size and lattice symmetry set the band edge, wall material sets the emissivity amplitude, and different sublattices or stacked crystal layers give graded/multi‑band responses.

The same platform also serves as a research tool for quantifying how ordered versus disordered porosity, pore size and wall chemistry control scattering, emissivity and phonon transport — a comparison that is impossible in conventional foams, where pore size and disorder cannot be varied independently.

**Use the caged superlattice as a 3‑D array of supported lipid‑bilayer "nanodiscs" — a self‑assembled membrane‑protein chip.**

Each identical vacancy is an ideal, pre‑formed aperture: by hybridizing cholesterol‑, alkyl‑ or lipid‑anchored strands around the rim of every cage opening, a lipid bilayer patch can be templated so that it spans (or lines) each cavity, giving billions of geometrically identical, mechanically supported free‑standing membranes of a diameter set purely by the origami design. Reconstituting membrane proteins into these patches — ion channels, transporters, GPCRs, receptors, or pore formers such as α‑hemolysin/MspA/CsgG — at Poisson‑limited occupancy places roughly one protein per cage in a native‑like lipid environment, with the cage interior acting as the sealed *cis* compartment and the interconnected lattice as the *trans* side.

Payoffs: (i) **massively parallel single‑molecule electrophysiology/biosensing** — a thin crystal film mounted between electrodes becomes an array of nanopore/channel sensors with far higher density than lithographic bilayer chips, for high‑throughput ion‑channel drug screening, toxin and analyte detection, or parallel nanopore sequencing, with each cage optically addressable (Ca²⁺/voltage‑dye fluorescence read‑out) so the "current" of individual channels can be imaged rather than wired; (ii) **stable, monodisperse membrane mimics** — because the DNA framework mechanically clamps each patch, the notoriously fragile bilayer survives handling, drying‑resistant coatings, and long recordings, and the lattice's uniform curvature/tension can be *designed* (cage size sets patch diameter and hence membrane tension and curvature), letting one systematically measure how bilayer geometry, thickness and lipid composition control channel gating, protein oligomerization and mechanosensation; (iii) **structural biology** — the periodic, pre‑oriented arrangement of one membrane protein per unit cell provides an in‑register lattice for cryo‑EM/tomography averaging and for solid‑state NMR of membrane proteins in a real bilayer; and (iv) **biomimetic energy/transport devices** — loading opposite sublattices with proton pumps (bacteriorhodopsin) and ATP synthase creates an ordered, macroscopic artificial‑organelle film that converts light into a proton gradient and ATP, or acts as a selectively permeable "smart" biomembrane for separations. Membrane composition, patch size and protein identity are all reprogrammed simply by redesigning the block, its vacancy and the anchor strands.

**Use the caged superlattice as the resonator of a self‑assembled, three‑dimensional distributed‑feedback (photonic‑crystal) laser and optical amplifier.**

Loading each identical vacancy with gain material — laser dyes, colloidal quantum dots, perovskite nanocrystals, or upconverting/rare‑earth emitters captured by cage‑lining strands — gives a gain medium in which the emitters sit at crystallographically defined positions, one (or a fixed, known number) per unit cell. The periodic tens‑of‑nanometre modulation of refractive index between the dense DNA/guest walls and the empty voids simultaneously provides the optical feedback: light at the Bragg condition is coherently back‑scattered in all three directions, so the same lattice that holds the gain also forms the cavity, eliminating the need for mirrors, etched gratings or an external microcavity. Because the emitters are held apart by the empty cages, they cannot aggregate or self‑quench, which permits very high volumetric gain densities (and hence low lasing thresholds) that are unattainable in close‑packed dye or quantum‑dot films, while the slow‑photon modes at the photonic band edge further amplify the light–matter interaction and give directional, narrow‑linewidth, low‑divergence emission.

The unique advantage over conventional DFB lasers is programmability: the lattice constant, symmetry, void filling fraction and emitter identity are all set independently by origami sequence design, so the resonance wavelength, mode structure, polarisation and output direction can be specified computationally rather than by lithographic tolerance, and different sublattices can be given different emitters for multi‑wavelength or cascaded (energy‑transfer‑pumped) lasing. Since the cages are chemically addressable, the device is also *dynamically tunable and switchable*: toehold‑mediated strand displacement, pH/ion triggers, or infiltration of high‑index liquids or plasmonic nanoparticles change the index contrast and lattice spacing in situ, shifting or quenching the lasing line. This converts the laser into a label‑free, amplified biosensor (analyte binding inside the cages shifts the lasing wavelength or turns emission on/off with the sharp threshold nonlinearity providing far greater sensitivity than fluorescence read‑out), and, run as a passive element, the same crystal serves as a photonic‑bandgap waveguide/filter or a quasi‑phase‑matched host for nonlinear frequency conversion. Silicification or resin embedding yields a robust, drop‑cast thin film, giving printable, biocompatible microlasers for on‑chip photonics, lab‑on‑chip diagnostics, laser‑based barcoding of cells or samples, and low‑cost coherent light sources produced entirely by self‑assembly.

**Use the caged crystals as a programmable ice‑control / vitrification matrix for cryopreservation (and anti‑icing).**

Because every unit cell contains an identical vacancy only tens of nanometres across, water taken up into the lattice is split into billions of monodisperse, geometrically identical nanodroplets. Confinement of this size strongly suppresses ice: the Gibbs–Thomson effect depresses the freezing point by an amount fixed by the designed cage diameter, homogeneous nucleation becomes improbable in such small volumes, and any nucleus that does form is geometrically capped by the cage walls so it cannot grow into the large, membrane‑shearing crystals or propagate between compartments. The material therefore promotes glass formation (vitrification) at far lower cooling rates and with far less toxic penetrating cryoprotectant (DMSO/glycerol) than current protocols, and it blocks the devitrification/ice‑recrystallization during warming that is the main cause of cell and tissue damage.

Crucially, the ice behaviour is *designable* rather than empirical: cage diameter sets the nucleation temperature and the maximum possible crystal size, while the cage walls can be decorated by hybridizing modified strands with antifreeze‑protein/ice‑binding peptides, trehalose or polyampholyte groups, or hydrophobic/hydrophilic patches, so both nucleation control and ice‑face binding are tuned independently by rewriting the strand set. Practical embodiments include a cryoprotectant additive or scaffold in which cells, organoids, embryos, sperm, platelets or engineered tissue are embedded for banking and cold‑chain shipping of biologics and vaccines; a vitrification aid for cryo‑EM grid preparation that guarantees amorphous ice of reproducible thickness; and, in silicified or coated form, an anti‑icing surface layer for aircraft, wind turbines and heat exchangers. Because every cavity is identical and sequence‑tunable, the same crystals also provide the long‑missing model system for measuring how confinement dimension and wall chemistry control ice nucleation, supercooling and the liquid–glass transition of water.

**Use a thin film of the caged crystals (silicified or metal‑coated for laser/vacuum robustness) as an ordered, matrix‑free laser‑desorption/ionisation surface for mass spectrometry — a "programmable NIMS/DIOS chip".**

In nanostructure‑initiator and desorption‑ionisation‑on‑silicon MS, analytes are ionised directly from a nanoporous surface that traps an "initiator" liquid and confines the laser‑deposited energy, avoiding the matrix crystals that dominate MALDI spectra in the low‑mass region and make signal intensity irreproducible. The origami cage lattice is an almost ideal version of such a surface: every pore has the *same*, sequence‑designed diameter, depth and spacing, so the amount of initiator/analyte held per unit area, the local heating and the desorption plume are uniform across the whole target — giving flat, reproducible ion yields (good quantitation and imaging) instead of the "sweet‑spot" hunting caused by the stochastic pore‑size distribution of etched silicon or of sputtered nanoparticle films.

The cages also act as the sample‑preparation step: analytes diffuse in and are concentrated from dilute solution, while cage‑lining capture strands (aptamers, antibodies, chelators, boronate or lectin groups, or complementary oligos) make the capture chemically selective, so salts, detergents and abundant proteins can be rinsed away and only the target class (metabolites, drug/drug metabolites, phosphopeptides, glycans, miRNA) is retained and then blasted off by the laser — an on‑target purification/enrichment that normally requires separate SPE or affinity beads. Size exclusion by the cage opening adds a second selectivity axis, and different sublattices or spotted crystal batches with different ligands give a multiplexed array in which each spot reports on a different analyte.

Because pore diameter, wall chemistry, plasmonic loading (Au/Ag guests in the cages to tune absorption at the laser wavelength) and the ligand set are all reprogrammed simply by redesigning the origami block and its vacancy, the ionisation efficiency, mass range and analyte specificity become design parameters rather than empirical process variables. Practical targets: high‑throughput, low‑femtomole metabolomics and drug‑screening plates; clean small‑molecule analysis below m/z 500 where MALDI matrix ions interfere; and mass‑spectrometry imaging, where the tens‑of‑nanometre, perfectly periodic void array supplies both a homogeneous ionisation layer and a built‑in spatial calibration grid.

**Use the caged superlattice (silicified or carbon/metal‑coated for robustness) as an ultralow‑density "capture foam" for intact collection of hypervelocity particles — a next‑generation cosmic‑dust/space‑debris and aerosol collector for sample‑return missions.**

Because each unit cell is mostly empty space, a monolith of these crystals is an aerogel‑like medium of only a few mg cm⁻³, but unlike stochastic silica aerogel its density, cell diameter, wall thickness and lattice symmetry are exactly uniform and set by origami sequence design. A micrometeoroid, comet grain, or orbital‑debris fragment striking at km s⁻¹ is decelerated gradually as it crushes one identical nanocell after another, so the peak deceleration, heating and shock pressure per unit path length are homogeneous and *calculable*, rather than varying with the random pore structure of conventional aerogel. This maximizes the chance of capturing the grain intact (preserving mineralogy, organics, isotopic and volatile content instead of melting/vaporizing it, the main limitation of the Stardust collections), and by grading cell size or wall composition between stacked crystal layers one can build a designed deceleration ramp (soft, large‑cage entrance layers followed by denser, smaller‑cage stopping layers).

Crucially, the periodic vacancy array is also the *instrument*: the lattice constant is a built‑in nanometre‑accurate 3D coordinate grid, so the entry point, track length, taper and entry angle of each impact can be reconstructed from tomography or optical/electron imaging to give particle mass, speed and trajectory (and hence the parent body or debris orbit). Sequence‑barcoded "tracer" strands hybridized at designed lattice positions can be released by the impact and read out by PCR/sequencing, amplifying each track into a position‑encoded molecular signal for automated flux mapping over large collector areas. The cage walls can additionally be functionalized to trap and preserve volatiles and organics released on impact, and the low‑Z, contaminant‑free, biodegradable DNA framework (or its pure SiO₂/C replica) can be chosen so as not to interfere with subsequent isotopic and organic analysis of the captured grain.

The same material serves terrestrially as a low‑backscatter collector for high‑altitude/stratospheric aerosol and micrometeorite sampling, for engine/exhaust and clean‑room particulate capture, and as a calibrated standard for hypervelocity‑impact and light‑gas‑gun experiments, since every impact occurs in an identical, precisely known microstructure.

**Use the caged crystal (with one plasmonic/photothermal guest per cage, and silicified or resin‑stabilised for wet robustness) as a solar‑driven interfacial evaporator for desalination and wastewater purification.**

Because every unit cell donates an identical, tens‑of‑nanometre void and the voids interconnect through the lattice, a floating film of these crystals is simultaneously (i) a capillary pump — the monodisperse, straight, hydrophilic (polyanionic DNA/silica) channels wick brine from the bulk to the illuminated top surface at a rate set by the designed cage diameter, with no random, clogging‑prone pore distribution; (ii) a thermal insulator — the high, ordered void fraction and phonon‑scattering walls confine the absorbed heat to a thin surface layer instead of losing it to the underlying water, which is the key efficiency lever in interfacial evaporation; and (iii) a broadband absorber — a single Au/Ag/carbon or semiconductor nanoparticle captured by cage‑lining strands in each vacancy gives a periodic, non‑aggregated array of plasmonic heaters whose spacing (and hence coupling, near‑field enhancement and absorption band) is fixed with ~2 nm precision, so near‑unity solar absorption is achieved with very little absorber mass and without the self‑quenching/aggregation of drop‑cast nanoparticle films.

The decisive advantage of the cages is thermodynamic: water confined in uniform nanocavities exists as small, weakly hydrogen‑bonded clusters, so its effective enthalpy of vaporisation drops, allowing evaporation rates that exceed the nominal solar‑thermal limit — and because every cavity is identical and its size is reprogrammed simply by redesigning the origami block and its vacancy, this "reduced‑enthalpy" effect, the wicking rate and the salt‑rejection behaviour can be optimised by design rather than by empirical foaming or freeze‑casting. The continuous, uniform channel network also permits convective back‑diffusion of concentrated brine, giving long‑term, salt‑fouling‑free operation in hypersaline feeds, while cage walls functionalised by hybridised strands (chelators, aptamers, catalytic or photocatalytic guests) let the same film simultaneously trap heavy metals or photodegrade organic contaminants as the water passes through — yielding an off‑grid, low‑cost, biodegradable evaporator for drinking‑water production, brine mining and zero‑liquid‑discharge treatment, as well as a model system for quantifying how confinement dimension and wall chemistry control the vaporisation enthalpy of nanoconfined water.

**Use the caged crystal (converted to a robust silica/carbon replica by mineralising the DNA walls and burning out the template) as an ordered nanoconfinement scaffold for solid‑state hydrogen storage in metal/complex hydrides.**

Every unit cell contributes an identical, tens‑of‑nanometre cavity, so melt‑ or solution‑infiltrating a hydride (MgH₂, NaAlH₄, LiBH₄, Mg(BH₄)₂, ammonia borane) fills the lattice with billions of hydride nanoparticles that all have exactly the same, designer‑set diameter and are held apart by the framework walls. This directly attacks the three failure modes of bulk hydride storage: (i) *thermodynamics* — at these sizes the surface/interface energy term measurably destabilises the hydride, lowering the desorption enthalpy and hence the release temperature, and because the cage diameter is dialled in simply by redesigning the origami block and its vacancy, the operating temperature/plateau pressure becomes a design parameter rather than an empirical result; (ii) *kinetics* — the nanometre diffusion path for H atoms and the huge, uniform interfacial area give absorption/desorption rates orders of magnitude faster than bulk powder, and the pore walls can be pre‑decorated (through hybridised, metal‑binding strands before mineralisation) with atomically dispersed Ti/Ni/Pd catalytic sites at DNA‑programmed spacing right at every particle's surface; and (iii) *cycling stability* — the rigid, monodisperse cages act as anti‑sintering "corrals" that prevent the particle coarsening, phase segregation and release of unwanted by‑products (B₂H₆, NH₃) that degrade capacity over hundreds of cycles, while the interconnected void network still allows H₂ to diffuse in and out.

Because, unlike carbon aerogels or mesoporous silica templates, *every* pore is identical and its size, wall thickness, symmetry and surface chemistry are set independently by sequence design, the same platform is also the long‑missing model system for quantifying how confinement dimension and wall chemistry control hydride thermodynamics, hysteresis and reaction pathways — turning nanoconfined hydrogen‑storage development (for fuel‑cell vehicles, portable power and seasonal energy storage) from a screening exercise into a rational design problem.

**Use the caged crystal as a recoil‑retaining radionuclide carrier for targeted alpha‑particle therapy (and as a nanoscale brachytherapy "seed").**

The single biggest obstacle in ²²⁵Ac/²²³Ra/²¹²Pb therapy is not delivering the parent isotope but retaining its **recoiling daughters**: each alpha decay imparts ~100 keV of recoil energy to the daughter nucleus, which breaks any chelate bond and escapes the carrier, then redistributes to kidneys, marrow and bone, causing dose‑limiting off‑target toxicity. A superlattice of origami blocks with periodic central vacancies solves this geometrically. The parent radionuclide is loaded one‑per‑cage (chelator‑ or DNAzyme‑modified strands lining each vacancy bind Ac³⁺/Ra²⁺/Bi³⁺ with defined stoichiometry, so the activity per crystal is exactly countable and reproducible — a real advantage over stochastically loaded liposomes or polymer nanoparticles). Because the recoil range of the daughter is only tens of nanometres in condensed matter, and the lattice presents many DNA (or, after silicification/metal coating, silica/metal) walls and successive cages within that distance, the daughter is simply stopped in a neighbouring cage of the *same* crystal rather than being ejected into the bloodstream. Crystal radius, wall density and cage size — all set independently by origami sequence design — can therefore be dialled to exceed the recoil range for every member of the decay chain, converting daughter retention from an empirical formulation problem into a calculable design parameter; a graded, denser outer shell of small cages can be added as a dedicated "recoil stopper."

The outer faces of the same crystal are decorated by hybridisation with antibodies, nanobodies, peptides (PSMA, somatostatin, folate) or aptamers for tumour targeting, while the interconnected voids still admit solvent so the crystal is small and porous enough for tumour penetration; alternatively, a micron‑sized crystal injected intratumourally acts as a fully biodegradable, self‑contained brachytherapy source that irradiates locally and then dissolves, avoiding surgical seed removal. Extra payoffs: co‑loading distinct sublattices with a therapeutic alpha emitter and a diagnostic gamma/PET nuclide (or a Gd/Au contrast guest) gives a matched theranostic pair with identical biodistribution; radiosensitising high‑Z guests or drugs can be placed in adjacent cages for combination therapy; and because the daughters remain in a periodic, crystallographically defined array, the same material serves as a well‑defined experimental platform for measuring recoil ranges, radiolytic damage and daughter‑retention efficiency as a function of confinement geometry — knowledge directly transferable to all nanocarrier designs for alpha therapy and to the safe encapsulation of alpha‑emitting waste.

**Use the caged superlattice (converted into a silica/aerogel‑like inorganic replica by conformally mineralising the DNA walls and burning out the template) as a refractive‑index‑tunable, low‑scattering Cherenkov radiator for particle‑identification detectors (RICH/threshold counters).**

Cherenkov detectors covering the "gap" momentum range between gases (n ≈ 1.001) and liquids/solids (n ≥ 1.3) require radiators with refractive indices of roughly 1.01–1.1, a regime accessible only to silica aerogels. But conventional aerogels are made by stochastic sol–gel phase separation: their pore/strand sizes are broadly distributed and comparable to visible wavelengths, so Rayleigh scattering (the "clarity" term) severely attenuates and smears the Cherenkov ring, and index uniformity across a tile is hard to control. A crystal built from origami blocks with periodic central vacancies fixes both problems at their root. Because *every* unit cell contributes an identical vacancy whose diameter, wall thickness, lattice symmetry and hence void fraction are set by base‑pair geometry, the replica is a solid–void composite with (i) an effective refractive index that follows directly and predictably from the designed filling fraction — so n can be dialled anywhere from ~1.01 to ~1.2 simply by redesigning the block and its cage, and graded/multi‑layer "focusing" radiators (index increasing layer by layer to make all Cherenkov photons land on one ring) can be built by stacking crystal batches of different cage size; and (ii) scattering centres that are monodisperse and *ordered* rather than random, with a period well below optical wavelengths, which strongly suppresses the incoherent Rayleigh scattering that limits aerogel transmission length — yielding much better photon yield, ring sharpness and therefore π/K/p separation power at higher momenta.

The same designed nano‑architecture also gives the mechanical and optical uniformity aerogel tiles lack (no density striations, controllable wall connectivity for crack resistance), makes the material radiation‑hard and non‑hygroscopic once mineralised, and lets the wall chemistry be doped by sequence‑programmed metal binding before mineralisation (e.g. adding high‑Z or wavelength‑shifting species in selected sublattices to tune dispersion, absorb UV, or shift photons into the sensitive band of SiPM readout). Beyond collider and fixed‑target RICH systems, such programmable ultralow‑index, high‑clarity blocks serve as index‑matching/antireflection layers, as calibration standards for optical scattering and effective‑medium theory, and as a research platform for quantifying how ordered versus disordered porosity controls light transport — a comparison impossible in conventional aerogels, where pore size and disorder cannot be varied independently.

**Turn the caged crystal into a self‑assembled "nano‑channel plate" electron/ion multiplier for imaging detectors.** Because every unit cell contributes an identical vacancy and the cages interconnect through the lattice, conformally coating the DNA walls by ALD (a resistive layer such as Al‑doped ZnO plus a high secondary‑electron‑yield emissive layer such as MgO/Al₂O₃) and then burning out the template leaves a rigid inorganic film perforated by a perfectly periodic array of straight, monodisperse channels — the same architecture as a microchannel plate, but with a pore pitch of tens of nanometres rather than 5–10 µm. Biased across its thickness in vacuum, each channel cascades an incident photon, electron or ion into a measurable charge pulse, so the plate provides single‑particle gain with spatial resolution set by the origami design rather than by glass‑fibre drawing, plus uniform gain (no pore‑size scatter), low crosstalk and low dark noise. Uses: photon‑counting and UV/X‑ray imaging, night vision, time‑of‑flight mass‑spectrometry and electron‑microscope detectors, and ultrafast timing (TOF‑PET), with pore diameter, pitch, aspect ratio and wall chemistry all reprogrammable by redesigning the block and its vacancy.

**Use the caged superlattice as a self‑assembled zero‑mode‑waveguide (ZMW) array — a nanophotonic "observation‑volume" chip for single‑molecule fluorescence and real‑time sequencing at physiological concentrations.**

Coat the DNA walls of a thin, single‑ or few‑layer slab of the crystal with a conformal metal film (electroless Au/Ag or ALD/evaporated Al) and remove or leave the template: each central vacancy becomes a metal‑clad, sub‑wavelength aperture of identical, sequence‑defined diameter (~10–50 nm) and depth, arrayed with tens‑of‑nanometre pitch over macroscopic areas. Because such an aperture is far below the cut‑off diameter for propagating light, laser illumination decays evanescently inside it and only a zeptolitre‑to‑attolitre volume at the aperture floor is excited — exactly the trick that makes single‑molecule real‑time (SMRT) sequencing possible. The key advantage over the e‑beam/photolithographically milled ZMWs used today is that here the hole diameter, depth, pitch, symmetry and even the chemistry of the aperture floor are set by base‑pair geometry rather than by an exposure tool: every well is *identical* (so the illumination profile, background and photon‑count statistics are uniform across the chip, which is the main source of well‑to‑well variability today), the apertures can be made smaller and far denser than lithography allows (millions to billions of wells per chip, and stacked/offset layers give multi‑level arrays), and the whole "mask" is produced in parallel by drop‑casting a self‑assembled crystal at negligible cost.

Functionally, the cage floor can be pre‑functionalised through hybridised capture strands so that exactly one polymerase, ribosome, enzyme, receptor or target molecule is immobilised per well at Poisson‑controlled occupancy, while the metal rim additionally provides plasmonic near‑field enhancement (nanoantenna effect) that boosts fluorophore brightness and shortens lifetimes. Applications: massively parallel, amplification‑free long‑read DNA/RNA sequencing and direct detection of base modifications; real‑time single‑molecule enzymology (transcription, translation, helicase, protease kinetics) and protein sequencing/fingerprinting; single‑molecule FRET and fluorescence‑correlation spectroscopy at micromolar ligand concentrations, where conventional confocal detection is swamped by background; and high‑throughput digital immunoassays or drug‑binding screens, with the periodic lattice doubling as an in‑built spatial calibration grid for image registration and drift correction. Since the aperture size and surface chemistry are reprogrammed simply by redesigning the origami block and its vacancy, the observation volume, background suppression and analyte specificity become design parameters rather than fabrication limits.

**Use the caged superlattice as a three‑dimensional hardware substrate for spatially localized DNA computing — a self‑assembled "molecular processor/neuromorphic circuit board."**

Every unit cell provides one identical, sequence‑addressable cavity, so each cage can be equipped (via hybridized strands on its inner walls) with a distinct computational element: a strand‑displacement logic gate, a seesaw/threshold gate, a DNAzyme, a hairpin amplifier, or a memory element that stores a binary state as the presence/absence of an output strand. Crucially, the cages are not stirred‑pot compartments but a *wired* network: neighbouring cavities are separated by fixed, tens‑of‑nanometre distances, so a signal strand released in one cage reaches its neighbour by short‑range tethered hopping rather than bulk diffusion. This is the key advantage — localized (surface‑tethered) DNA circuits react orders of magnitude faster than solution circuits, avoid concentration dilution, and allow the *same* gate sequence to be reused in different places without crosstalk, which is the leakage/sequence‑exhaustion bottleneck that currently limits solution‑phase DNA computers to a few dozen gates. Here the wiring topology, fan‑in/fan‑out, gate spacing (and hence signal delay and coupling weight) and circuit depth are set purely by the origami block/vacancy design and the lattice symmetry, so a circuit is literally laid out in 3D — with vertical interconnects and crossovers that planar DNA "circuit boards" cannot provide — and a single microcrystal contains billions of identical, parallel copies of the circuit.

Functionally this yields: (i) massively parallel molecular pattern recognition and classification (a 3D winner‑take‑all/perceptron network in which cage‑to‑cage coupling strengths are programmed by linker length and toehold strength, giving a chemically implemented neural network that reads a multiplexed miRNA/protein signature directly in a sample and outputs a fluorescent or diffraction‑readable diagnosis); (ii) reaction–diffusion computing and cellular‑automaton dynamics — travelling waves, oscillators, Turing patterns and logic cascades propagating through the periodic cage lattice can be imaged in real space by super‑resolution microscopy, making the crystal a physical testbed for excitable‑media and morphogenesis models; (iii) rewritable state and learning, since toehold‑mediated strand displacement, pH/ion triggers or photocleavable linkers can add, delete or re‑weight connections in operando, allowing the same crystal to be reprogrammed for a new computation without resynthesizing the material; and (iv) an integrated readout, because occupancy of the cages by output strands (or by output‑recruited nanoparticles/fluorophores) changes the crystal's structure factor and optical response, so the computation's result can be read non‑destructively by diffraction, colour change or single‑cage imaging. The result is a self‑assembled, energy‑efficient, autonomously operating chemical computer that works inside a droplet or a cell lysate — turning circuit layout, wiring length and signal timing into DNA‑sequence design parameters.

**Build a biomimetic "nuclear‑pore‑complex (NPC) array" — a receptor‑gated, ultraselective transport membrane and a platform for decoding NPC physics.**

Each unit cell's vacancy is an identical, tens‑of‑nanometre channel of exactly the dimensions of a real nuclear pore's central conduit, and — uniquely — its walls are chemically addressable at ~2 nm precision. By hybridising strands conjugated to FG‑repeat nucleoporin domains (Nsp1, Nup98, Nup153 fragments) or synthetic FG‑mimetic polymers onto the cage interior, every cavity can be filled with a cohesive FG hydrogel/polymer brush of *designed* grafting density, anchoring pattern, length and cohesiveness. The resulting film (mounted between two reservoirs, silicified or resin‑supported at the rim for flow stability) reproduces the defining property of the NPC: it is a soft, saturated meshwork that blocks inert macromolecules above ~40 kDa almost completely, yet allows cargo bound to nuclear transport receptors (importin‑β/karyopherins, NTF2, or engineered FG‑philic binders) to partition into and cross the barrier within milliseconds, with thousands of translocations per pore per second and essentially no size penalty.

Why this beats a passive sieve: selectivity is *affinity‑based and signal‑encoded*, not merely steric. Practical uses include (i) an ultraselective purification/concentration membrane in which only NLS‑ or NTR‑tagged proteins, viral vectors, mRNA–LNP cargo or therapeutic biologics are pulled out of a crude lysate or fermentation broth against a background of similarly sized contaminants, with release triggered by RanGTP or by toehold displacement of the receptor strand; (ii) a programmable "gate" for artificial cells and synthetic organelles, giving a nucleus‑like compartment whose import/export permissions can be rewritten by swapping strands; (iii) a highly selective biosensor/logic element in which passage of a reporter is licensed only when a specific analyte‑bound receptor is present, read out electrically (channel conductance) or optically (Bragg/refractive‑index shift as the cages fill); and (iv) an anti‑fouling, self‑cleaning separation layer, since the FG phase resists nonspecific adsorption.

Scientifically, it is the experiment the native NPC cannot provide: channel diameter, FG type, grafting density, anchor position (rim vs. mid‑channel), stoichiometry of different Nup species and the fraction of "empty" control cages are all set independently by origami sequence design and repeated identically billions of times per crystal. That allows direct, quantitative discrimination between the competing "selective‑phase/hydrogel," "virtual‑gate/polymer‑brush" and "forest/reduction‑of‑dimensionality" models of nucleocytoplasmic transport, measurement of how geometry sets the size cut‑off and receptor flux, and rational engineering of the selectivity–permeability trade‑off — plus a route to study how nuclear transport is hijacked by viruses or disrupted in ALS/FTD‑associated Nup pathology, all in a synthetic, single‑pore‑resolvable, three‑dimensionally ordered mimic.

**Use the caged superlattice (or a silica/ceramic replica made by mineralising the DNA walls) as a 3‑D‑ordered nanochannel separator / single‑ion‑conducting electrolyte host for lithium‑metal and lithium‑sulfur batteries.**

Because every unit cell contributes one identical vacancy and the vacancies interconnect, a thin film of the crystal is a membrane pierced by a perfectly periodic, monodisperse, low‑tortuosity channel network whose diameter, pitch, symmetry and wall chemistry are set by origami sequence design rather than by the stochastic phase‑inversion process that makes today’s polyolefin or ceramic‑coated separators. Three battery problems are addressed at once by that uniformity:

1. **Dendrite suppression.** Lithium dendrites nucleate where the Li⁺ flux at the anode is locally concentrated — i.e. at the large, randomly distributed pores of conventional separators. Here every channel delivers exactly the same current density over the whole electrode area, so plating is forced to be spatially homogeneous and planar; the rigid framework simultaneously provides a mechanical block against any protrusion that does form, and the channel size can be dialled below the critical dimension for dendrite penetration.

2. **Near‑unity Li⁺ transference number.** The DNA backbone (or the sulfonated/anion‑grafted wall of the mineralised replica) is intrinsically polyanionic, so counter‑anions are electrostatically immobilised on the channel walls while Li⁺ hops along them. When the channel diameter approaches the Debye length the double layers overlap and transport becomes essentially unipolar, eliminating the salt‑concentration gradients and polarisation that limit fast charging — the same “single‑ion conductor” behaviour sought in block‑copolymer and MOF electrolytes, but with the charge density, pore size and spacing tunable independently.

3. **Shuttle/crossover blocking.** The uniform, chemically addressable cages sterically and electrostatically reject polysulfides in Li–S cells (and vanadium ions in flow batteries, methanol in DMFCs), and cage‑lining strands can add specific chelating or redox‑mediating groups; the same voids can be infiltrated with a gel, ionic‑liquid or polymer electrolyte to give a mechanically robust, thermally stable composite with straight, short ion paths (high conductivity at low tortuosity), or with Li⁺‑philic seeds so the cages act as a 3‑D “host” that accommodates lithium’s volume change during cycling.

Because pore diameter, wall charge density, porosity and thickness are all reprogrammed simply by redesigning the origami block and its vacancy, separator design becomes a rational, parametric exercise instead of an empirical one — and the same perfectly monodisperse channels provide the long‑missing model system for measuring how confinement dimension and surface charge control Li⁺ desolvation, transference and interfacial (SEI) formation.

**Use a thin, mineralised film of the caged crystal as the membrane of a solid‑state, moving‑part‑free "Knudsen pump" (thermal‑transpiration gas compressor).**

Because each origami block contributes an identical central vacancy and the vacancies interconnect through the lattice, a slab of the superlattice — conformally coated by silicification/ALD (SiO₂, Al₂O₃) and the DNA burned out for thermal robustness — is a membrane pierced by a perfectly periodic array of straight channels only tens of nanometres wide. That is exactly the regime needed for *free‑molecular (Knudsen) flow*: the channel diameter is far below the mean free path of air at atmospheric pressure (~68 nm), so gas molecules collide with the walls rather than with each other. Imposing a modest temperature gradient across the film (a few tens of K from a thin resistive heater or absorbed sunlight on one face) then drives **thermal transpiration**: molecules creep along the walls from the cold side to the hot side, producing a net gas flow and a pressure rise with no pistons, valves, diaphragms or moving parts.

The cages are the essential ingredient.
