Pumping efficiency and the achievable compression ratio per stage depend steeply and non‑monotonically on the ratio of channel radius to mean free path and on channel length/tortuosity; in conventional Knudsen pumps these are set by porous ceramics, aerogels or track‑etched films whose pore sizes are broadly distributed, so most pores operate off‑optimum, viscous back‑flow through the largest pores cancels the transpiration flow through the smallest, and performance is empirical and irreproducible. Here every channel is identical, straight and of a diameter chosen by *design* (simply by redesigning the block and its vacancy), so all pores work at the same optimum, back‑leakage is eliminated, and the pump's operating pressure range, flow rate and stage compression ratio become calculable design parameters. Stacking crystal batches with progressively different cage sizes gives a multistage cascade tuned to the changing mean free path as pressure rises, and the wall chemistry can be tailored (hydrophobic/hydrophilic strands before mineralisation, or catalytic/adsorptive coatings) to tune momentum accommodation at the surface — the microscopic parameter that sets transpiration strength — or to add selectivity.

Practical payoffs: chip‑scale vacuum and gas‑handling for portable micro gas chromatographs, mass spectrometers and ion‑mobility spectrometers; sample‑drawing pumps for wearable and distributed air‑quality, breath‑analysis and chemical‑threat sensors; propellant feed and micro‑thrusters for CubeSats; and heat‑driven, electricity‑free pumping that runs directly on waste heat or sunlight — with the added benefit that the same ordered nanochannel array separates gases by Knudsen (mass‑dependent) effusion, allowing isotope or light‑gas enrichment in the same element. Scientifically, the monodisperse, sequence‑tunable channels provide the long‑missing model system for testing rarefied‑gas (Boltzmann/DSMC) transport theory, since channel size, length, symmetry and surface accommodation can each be varied independently while every pore in the sample is identical.

**Use the caged crystals as a sacrificial template for an ordered mesoporous electron‑transport scaffold in thin‑film photovoltaics (perovskite / dye‑sensitised solar cells).**

Because every unit cell donates one identical, interconnected vacancy, conformally coating the DNA walls (sol–gel or ALD of TiO₂, SnO₂ or ZnO) and then removing the template yields a self‑supporting inorganic scaffold whose pore diameter, wall thickness, porosity and lattice symmetry are set by origami sequence design rather than by the random sintered‑nanoparticle or block‑copolymer routes used today. Back‑filling those pores with a perovskite (or dye/solid hole conductor) gives a solar‑cell absorber layer with several design advantages that follow directly from the *monodispersity and order* of the cages:

- **Complete, void‑free infiltration and uniform absorber grains:** every cavity is the same size and openly connected, so the precursor melt/solution fills all of them and each cage templates one perovskite nanocrystal of identical volume — eliminating the pinholes, grain‑size scatter and shunt paths that dominate device‑to‑device variability, and allowing quantum‑confinement tuning of the band gap (and hence tandem‑cell band‑gap matching) simply by redesigning the block and its vacancy.
- **Decoupled optimisation of light absorption and charge collection:** the straight, short, low‑tortuosity walls give every photogenerated electron a nanometre‑scale path to a continuous conducting skeleton, while the huge, uniform heterojunction area maximises exciton splitting; scaffold thickness, pore size and wall thickness can be varied independently to balance absorption depth against diffusion length.
- **Built‑in photonic light trapping:** the periodic tens‑of‑nanometre index modulation acts as a 3D photonic structure that scatters/slow‑lights photons near the absorber's weak band edge, boosting absorption without adding thickness (an ordered analogue of inverse‑opal light management, but with a pitch chosen by design).
- **Stability:** the rigid, chemically inert framework physically confines each perovskite domain, suppressing grain coarsening, ion migration, phase segregation and moisture ingress — the main degradation modes — and its walls can be pre‑decorated (via metal‑binding or functional strands before mineralisation) with passivating or dipole‑forming groups at DNA‑programmed spacing to lower interfacial recombination.

The same platform doubles as a research tool: because pore size, spacing, symmetry and surface chemistry are reprogrammable and every pore is identical, it provides a clean model system for quantifying how mesoscale geometry controls charge collection, recombination and hysteresis in mesostructured solar cells — turning scaffold design from empirical nanoparticle sintering into a parametric, computable exercise.

**Use the caged superlattice (or, for high‑temperature service, the inorganic replica made by conformally coating the DNA walls with a semiconductor and removing the template) as a 3D‑ordered nanoporous "phonon‑glass/electron‑crystal" thermoelectric material.**

The figure of merit ZT = S²σT/κ is limited by the fact that, in bulk semiconductors, the same crystal that conducts electricity also conducts heat. The key to breaking that coupling is a length scale: in good thermoelectrics (Bi₂Te₃, PbTe, SiGe, half‑Heuslers, Mg₃Sb₂) the heat‑carrying acoustic phonons have mean free paths of ~10–300 nm, whereas the charge carriers have mean free paths of only ~1–10 nm. A DNA‑origami crystal of blocks with periodic central vacancies is exactly a solid–void composite whose feature size sits in that window — and, uniquely, whose void diameter, wall thickness, inter‑void spacing and lattice symmetry are set independently by sequence design rather than by the stochastic ball‑milling, spark‑plasma sintering or porogen routes used today.

Two implementations follow. (i) *Template route*: sol–gel/ALD or electroless deposition of the thermoelectric phase on the cage walls, then burn‑out of the DNA, giving a continuous, electrically percolating skeleton perforated by a monodisperse, ordered nanopore network. (ii) *Backfill route*: infiltrating the cages with the thermoelectric material so that each vacancy templates one identical nanoinclusion embedded in a matrix, or with a second phase (e.g. a heavy‑element cluster) to create ordered "rattler"/nano‑inclusion scattering centres.

The payoff of the *ordered, monodisperse* cages is spectral selectivity of phonon scattering. Because every scatterer is identical and periodically placed, the void lattice acts as a designed phononic/Bragg scatterer that removes a chosen band of phonon wavelengths (and, through coherent zone‑folding and boundary scattering, flattens the acoustic branches and reduces group velocities) while leaving carrier transport comparatively intact — pushing κ_lattice toward the amorphous limit at a porosity far lower than random foams require, and hence with much smaller penalty to σ. In randomly porous or nanograined thermoelectrics the pore/grain size distribution is broad, so only a fraction of the phonon spectrum is targeted and much of the electrical conductivity is sacrificed; here the "cut" in the phonon spectrum can be dialled in by simply redesigning the block and its vacancy, and stacking sublattices or crystal batches with several different cage sizes gives a hierarchical, multi‑band scatterer that attacks short‑, mid‑ and long‑wavelength phonons simultaneously. The high, uniform internal surface area also provides an enormous density of identical, chemically addressable interfaces: decorating the cage walls with metal‑binding or dopant‑carrying strands before mineralisation places dopants, energy‑filtering barriers or modulation‑doped shells at DNA‑programmed spacing, allowing carrier‑energy filtering that raises the Seebeck coefficient S without collapsing σ.

Practically this yields printable, self‑assembled thermoelectric films for waste‑heat harvesting (engine, industrial‑flue and data‑centre heat), for self‑powered wearables and IoT sensors (where the low‑density, compliant, conformable porous film also matches skin mechanics and provides the large ΔT‑sustaining thermal resistance that dense ceramics lack), for solid‑state Peltier micro‑coolers for chips and photonic devices, and for radioisotope thermoelectric generators. Equally important, since pore size, porosity, symmetry, wall thickness and surface chemistry can each be varied independently while every pore in the sample is identical, the platform is the long‑missing model system for measuring the phonon mean‑free‑path spectrum and for testing coherent (wave‑like) versus incoherent (particle‑like) nanoscale phonon transport — turning nanostructured‑thermoelectric development from empirical processing into parametric design.

**Use the caged superlattice as a "smart nanocontainer" additive for self‑healing, corrosion‑protective and self‑lubricating coatings.**

Because every unit cell contains an identical, precisely sized vacancy, a microcrystal of these origami blocks is effectively a reservoir array with a known, quantifiable volume of storage per particle. Dispersing such crystals (silicified, oligolysine–PEG‑ or resin‑stabilised so they survive cure and service conditions) into an epoxy, polyurethane or sol–gel primer gives a coating whose interior is uniformly loaded with cargo held in the cages: corrosion inhibitors (benzotriazole, 8‑hydroxyquinoline, Ce³⁺/molybdate), polymerisable healing agents (dicyclopentadiene, silanes, thiol–ene monomers plus catalyst in a separate sublattice), solid or liquid lubricants (ionic liquids, PFPE, MoS₂ precursors), or biocides/antifouling agents.

The key advantage over conventional halloysite, mesoporous‑silica or layered‑double‑hydroxide containers is that release is *programmed rather than diffusive*: the cage openings are lined with designed single strands, so they can be gated with i‑motif/triplex pH switches that unzip in the locally acidic (or alkaline cathodic) microenvironment of a corrosion pit, with metal‑ion‑responsive DNAzymes that sense Fe²⁺/Cl⁻ ingress, or with duplex "locks" that shear open only when a crack propagates through the crystal. Cargo is therefore delivered on demand, only at the damaged spot, and in a dose set by cage volume and crystal loading — eliminating the premature leaching and inhibitor‑induced blistering that limit directly doped coatings. Cage size, gate chemistry and inhibitor identity are all reprogrammed simply by redesigning the origami block, so the same platform can be re‑tuned for a different alloy, lubricant or trigger without new synthesis chemistry, and different sublattices can carry two mutually reactive components (monomer/initiator) that meet only upon rupture.

Two bonuses follow from the periodicity: the ordered voids give the filler an intrinsically low density and act as crack‑deflecting, energy‑absorbing inclusions that toughen the film rather than weakening it, and, because the empty‑versus‑filled lattice has a distinct Bragg/structural‑colour and SAXS signature, the coating is *self‑reporting* — the colour or diffraction change as cages empty provides an optical readout of where and how much healing agent has been consumed, i.e. a built‑in damage/remaining‑protection sensor for marine, aerospace, pipeline and biomedical‑implant coatings.

**Use the caged superlattice as a sacrificial/structural template for a 3D‑ordered nanoporous electrochromic film for dynamic ("smart") windows and reflective displays.**

Conformally coating the DNA walls (sol–gel/ALD of WO₃, NiO, V₂O₅, Nb₂O₅ or an infiltrated conducting polymer) and then removing the template leaves an inverse replica in which every former cage becomes an identical, interconnected electrolyte‑filled channel. Because the pores are monodisperse, straight and short, Li⁺/H⁺ insertion–extraction is fast and, crucially, *spatially uniform*, so the film switches in seconds rather than minutes, colours evenly without the blotchy "iris" fronts of dense or randomly porous films, and resists the cracking/ion‑trapping that limits cycle life, while the huge uniform interfacial area gives high optical contrast and coloration efficiency at very small material thickness. Since pore size, wall thickness, porosity and lattice symmetry are all reset simply by redesigning the origami block and its vacancy, switching speed, charge capacity and the periodic index contrast (which adds tunable structural colour / NIR‑selective Bragg reflection) become design parameters — enabling energy‑saving architectural glazing, automotive/aircraft dimmable windows, variable‑emissivity spacecraft radiators, and low‑power reflective e‑paper.

**Use a cleaved slab of the caged crystal (or its silica/metal replica) as a self‑assembled "strain‑engineering substrate" for 2D materials — a periodic nano‑dimple array that creates ordered quantum‑emitter and pseudomagnetic superlattices.**

Because a single layer of the superlattice is a continuous film perforated by a perfectly periodic array of identical vacancies, transferring a monolayer 2D crystal (WSe₂, MoS₂, hBN, graphene) onto it makes the membrane drape into — or suspend across — every cage. Each vacancy therefore imprints an identical, nanometre‑scale strain well or "drumhead" whose diameter, depth, pitch and lattice symmetry are set purely by origami sequence design (and can be varied systematically, or tuned in situ by swelling/collapsing the cages with ion, pH or strand‑displacement triggers) rather than by e‑beam lithography, nanopillar arrays or random wrinkling.

Payoffs: (i) in WSe₂/WS₂ the local tensile strain funnels excitons into each dimple, creating a **deterministic, wafer‑scale array of identical single‑photon emitters** at a pitch of tens of nanometres — far denser and more uniform than lithographically defined nanopillar arrays — for quantum‑photonic sources and correlated emitter lattices; (ii) in graphene the periodic strain generates **pseudomagnetic field superlattices** (hundreds of tesla equivalent) and a designer periodic potential, giving flat bands, Landau‑level and Hofstadter‑type physics with a lattice constant that is *programmable* instead of being fixed by a moiré twist angle; (iii) the suspended membrane patches form a huge array of identical **nanomechanical resonators** for mass/force/pressure sensing and phonon–photon transduction, and the underlying open cages act as sealed reference volumes for pressure/gas sensing or as reservoirs for gating molecules; (iv) the periodic strain also modulates band gap and catalytic activity, patterning arrays of reactive "hot spots" for electrocatalysis and for site‑selective functionalisation of the 2D sheet.

Because every cage is identical and reprogrammable by rewriting the strand set, emitter spacing, strain magnitude, band‑structure modulation and resonator frequency become design parameters — turning strain engineering of 2D materials from a lithography‑limited, stochastic process into a self‑assembled, parametric one, and providing a clean model system for measuring how strain geometry controls exciton localisation, electronic band structure and mechanical response.

**Use the caged superlattice as the template for a radiation‑damage‑tolerant nanostructured material — an engineered lattice of "defect‑sink" voids for fission/fusion reactor and space‑electronics components.**

Conformally coating the DNA walls of the crystal (electroless plating or ALD of a structural metal/ceramic such as W, Mo, Cu, SiC, TiN or a ferritic alloy precursor) and then burning out the template leaves an inverse replica: a continuous inorganic skeleton perforated by a perfectly periodic, monodisperse array of tens‑of‑nanometre voids and internal surfaces, with the void diameter, wall thickness (i.e. ligament dimension) and lattice symmetry all set by origami sequence design rather than by dealloying, ball‑milling or oxide‑dispersion processing.

Why the cages matter: the lifetime of a material under neutron, ion or proton irradiation is limited by the accumulation of displacement damage — vacancies and interstitials that cluster into dislocation loops and voids (swelling), and transmuted helium/hydrogen that collects at grain boundaries and causes embrittlement and blistering. Damage is annihilated only if a point defect can reach a *sink* before it clusters, so the governing parameter is the mean distance from any lattice site to a free surface. Here that distance is a design variable: because the ligament thickness can be made comparable to or smaller than the defect diffusion length (a few tens of nanometres), essentially every Frenkel pair produced in a collision cascade migrates to a cage wall and is absorbed, giving "self‑healing" behaviour, while the ordered voids serve as pre‑formed, uniformly distributed helium traps that hold gas in many small, harmless bubbles instead of a few large, boundary‑decorating ones. Crucially, unlike nanoporous foams or nanocrystalline metals — whose pore/grain size distributions are broad, so only part of the microstructure sits in the tolerant regime, and whose sinks coarsen under irradiation and heat — every cell here is identical and the periodic framework resists coarsening, so sink strength, swelling resistance and mechanical stiffness can be optimised independently and predictably (and graded by stacking crystal batches of different cage size, e.g. a fine‑cage plasma‑facing layer over a coarser, more compliant substrate).

Practical targets: plasma‑facing and first‑wall/divertor coatings and neutron‑multiplier structures for fusion devices, cladding and in‑core sensor components for advanced fission reactors, spallation‑target and accelerator beam‑window materials, and radiation‑hard interconnect/insulator layers for satellite and deep‑space electronics; the low density and ordered ligament network additionally give good thermal‑shock compliance and phonon scattering. Just as valuable, since void size, spacing, symmetry, surface chemistry and even deliberate "missing‑cage" defect concentrations are reprogrammed simply by redesigning the origami block, the material is the long‑missing model system for quantitatively testing rate‑theory and cluster‑dynamics models of radiation damage — measuring how sink spacing and geometry control defect recombination, helium bubble nucleation and swelling under ion‑beam irradiation, with every sink in the sample identical and its position known a priori.

**Use the caged crystal (or the robust silica/alumina/carbon replica obtained by mineralising the DNA walls and burning out the template) as a "designer mesoporous zeolite" — a shape‑selective heterogeneous catalyst for cracking and upcycling bulky molecules such as waste plastics, lignin and heavy petroleum fractions.**

Conventional zeolites owe their selectivity to uniform micropores, but those pores (<1–2 nm) are far too small to admit polyolefin chains, lignin fragments or asphaltenes, so plastic pyrolysis and biomass depolymerisation today rely on amorphous mesoporous solids with broad, random pore‑size distributions that give poor, unpredictable product slates and rapid coking. A superlattice of origami blocks with periodic central vacancies provides exactly what is missing: millions of *identical*, interconnected cavities whose diameter, window (neck) size, spacing and lattice symmetry are set by base‑pair geometry and can be dialled anywhere from a few nanometres to tens of nanometres simply by redesigning the block and its vacancy. Because every cage is the same, a molecule of a given size and shape either fits or does not, and every product molecule experiences the same confinement and residence time — so the carbon‑number distribution of the cracked products (e.g. selectively making C₅–C₁₂ gasoline‑range or C₁₀–C₂₀ wax/lubricant‑range hydrocarbons from polyethylene, or monomeric aromatics from lignin) becomes a geometric design parameter rather than a kinetic accident.

Catalytic sites are equally programmable: before mineralisation, hybridised metal‑binding, peptide‑ or chelator‑modified strands place acid sites, single metal atoms or small clusters (Pt, Ru, Ni, Zn, Al, Zr) at chosen positions and *known spacings* on the cage walls, so bifunctional (metal + acid) tandem chemistry — hydrogenolysis/isomerisation/aromatisation cascades — can be built with the metal‑to‑acid‑site distance, which is known to control product selectivity, fixed by sequence design instead of by impregnation statistics. The wide, straight, monodisperse channel network gives short diffusion paths and low tortuosity, suppressing over‑cracking and coke formation and allowing viscous polymer melts to reach the active sites, while the rigid framework prevents the site sintering that deactivates supported metals.

The same platform doubles as the long‑missing model system for confinement catalysis: since cavity size, window size, wall chemistry and active‑site spacing are varied independently while every pore in the sample is identical, one can measure quantitatively how mesopore geometry controls transition‑state stabilisation, diffusion‑limited selectivity and deactivation — turning catalyst design for chemical recycling of plastics and biomass valorisation from empirical screening into a parametric, computable exercise.

**Use the caged superlattice as a template/host for a three‑dimensionally ordered "nano‑energetic" (reactive/thermite) composite with a programmable burn rate.**

In nanothermites and other reactive composites (Al/CuO, Al/Bi₂O₃, Al/PTFE, Al/MoO₃), the energy‑release rate, ignition threshold and combustion‑front velocity are governed almost entirely by one geometric parameter — the diffusion distance between fuel and oxidizer domains — yet in conventional powders that distance is set by stochastic particle mixing, so mixtures are inhomogeneous, contact area is poor, and performance is irreproducible and inherently limited by mass‑transport. A DNA‑origami crystal built from blocks with periodic central vacancies solves this by construction: the fuel and the oxidizer can be placed on opposite sides of a designed, identical gap in every unit cell. In practice, the DNA walls are conformally mineralized/metallized (sol–gel, ALD or electroless plating with the oxidizer phase, e.g. CuO, Fe₂O₃, Bi₂O₃, or with the metal fuel), the template is removed, and the complementary reactant is then infiltrated into every cage (metal nanoparticles captured by cage‑lining strands before mineralization, melt‑infiltrated Al/Mg, or a fluoropolymer/oxidizer melt). The result is a macroscopic solid in which billions of fuel–oxidizer interfaces are *identical*, intimately contacting, and separated by a distance chosen by base‑pair geometry rather than by milling statistics.

The payoffs follow directly from the monodispersity and periodicity of the cages: (i) **rate by design** — since the reaction is diffusion/interface‑limited, the flame‑propagation velocity, pressurization rate, ignition delay and sensitivity become continuous design variables set simply by redesigning the block and its vacancy, allowing anything from a slow, controlled gasless heat source to a near‑detonative reactive material, and permitting graded or layered "burn‑rate ramps" by stacking crystal batches with different cage sizes; (ii) **reproducibility and safety** — every reaction site is equivalent, so batch‑to‑batch variability, hot‑spot‑driven accidental ignition and the notorious sensitivity scatter of hand‑mixed nanopowders are suppressed, and the rigid framework prevents the agglomeration/segregation that ages conventional nanothermites; (iii) **stoichiometric precision** — the cage volume fixes the amount of reactant per unit cell, so the fuel/oxidizer ratio is exact and quantifiable rather than nominal, and unreacted mass (a major loss channel) is minimized; (iv) **added functionality** — catalytic or ignition‑promoting species (Pd, iodine/biocidal agents for agent‑defeat, gas‑generating additives) can be hybridized onto specific cage faces at DNA‑programmed positions, and the interconnected void network vents product gases and provides a designed void fraction that tunes pressure output and shock coupling.

Applications include chip‑scale igniters, initiators and micro‑thrusters for CubeSats and MEMS propulsion; on‑chip nanojoule heat sources for microelectronic self‑destruct/data‑sanitization and for reactive joining/soldering of dissimilar materials; airbag and pyrotechnic initiators with tightly specified timing; welding/brazing foils; and biocidal agent‑defeat and thermal‑pulse formulations. Equally valuable, because interfacial spacing, contact area, void fraction, wall thickness and lattice symmetry can each be varied independently while every reaction cell in the sample is identical, the material is the long‑missing model system for measuring how nanoscale geometry actually controls ignition, condensed‑phase mass transport and flame propagation in reactive composites — turning energetic‑material formulation from empirical powder mixing into a parametric, computable design problem.

**Use the caged superlattice (metal‑ or dielectric‑coated by ALD/electroless plating, with the DNA template then removed) as a self‑assembled array of billions of *identical* vacuum nanogaps — a bulk "Casimir/van der Waals metamaterial" and a platform for quantum‑vacuum force engineering.**

Casimir and van der Waals forces between surfaces scale steeply (≈1/d⁴ per unit area) with separation, so they are only measurable — and only useful — when two surfaces are held parallel at a precisely known distance of tens of nanometres. Achieving that today requires heroic single‑cavity experiments (AFM sphere–plate, MEMS torsional oscillators) in which alignment, roughness and patch potentials dominate the error budget, and only one gap is probed at a time. A crystal of origami blocks with periodic central vacancies solves this by construction: every unit cell contributes a cavity whose wall separation, shape and orientation are fixed by base‑pair geometry to ~1–2 nm and repeated identically throughout a macroscopic solid. Because the coated walls are atomically smooth (ALD‑grown) and the gap population is monodisperse rather than log‑normal, the Casimir stress of each gap adds coherently, converting a force that is normally a single‑cavity curiosity into a *bulk*, measurable mechanical property of the material — the crystal's compressive stiffness, internal stress and even its equilibrium lattice constant then contain a directly readable quantum‑vacuum contribution.

Payoffs: (i) **precision metrology** — the same specimen gives an ensemble‑averaged Casimir measurement with enormously improved statistics, and, since gap size, wall material (Au, Al, Si, SiO₂, graphene, ITO, magnetic or chiral coatings), gap symmetry and even a deliberately chirped set of spacings are all reprogrammed simply by redesigning the block and its vacancy, one can map the force law versus separation, material dispersion and geometry systematically — testing Lifshitz theory, geometry (non‑additivity/"proximity‑force") corrections, thermal Casimir contributions and searches for new short‑range (non‑Newtonian gravity, chameleon/axion) forces, where the periodic lattice also supplies a natural modulation frequency for lock‑in detection; (ii) **force engineering** — alternating sublattices of different wall materials, or filling selected cages with a high‑index fluid, permits *repulsive* Casimir configurations and Casimir torque between birefringent walls, giving an ordered material with designed internal quantum pressure that can be used to build stiction‑free, quasi‑frictionless nanoscale bearings, levitated MEMS/NEMS elements and low‑adhesion contact layers (stiction from Casimir/vdW attraction is the principal failure mode of MEMS); (iii) **switchability** — because the cages remain chemically addressable before mineralisation (or through openings afterwards), toehold‑mediated strand displacement, pH/ion triggers or infiltration/ejection of a dielectric fluid change the gap's dielectric function *in operando*, yielding a material whose Casimir adhesion, stiffness and vacuum‑gap thermal conductance can be switched on demand — the basis for Casimir‑actuated switches, tunable adhesion surfaces and vacuum‑gap thermal diodes.

In short, the empty cages are exploited not as containers for matter but as containers for *vacuum*: a periodic, monodisperse, sequence‑programmable array of nanoscale voids turns quantum‑vacuum forces from a nuisance to be avoided in nanodevices into a designable bulk material property.

**Use the caged crystal as a xenon‑hosting "hyperCEST" reporter for ultrasensitive molecular MRI with hyperpolarized ¹²⁹Xe.**

Hyperpolarized ¹²⁹Xe gives NMR/MRI signals ~10⁴–10⁵ times stronger than thermal‑equilibrium nuclei, but it needs a host cavity that reversibly binds xenon and shifts its resonance — today's only options are cryptophane cages, which are hard to synthesize, hold one Xe each, and offer almost no tunability. A DNA‑origami superlattice whose every unit cell contains an identical vacancy is a natural, massively multivalent alternative: line the cage interior by hybridizing hydrophobic/fluoroalkyl‑, cucurbituril‑ or cryptophane‑modified strands so each void becomes a xenon "pocket," and a single microcrystal then provides billions of *identical* binding sites with a fast, tunable in/out exchange rate through the interconnected channel network.

The payoff is amplification plus programmability. In hyperCEST, RF saturation of the bound‑Xe resonance is continuously carried into the free dissolved‑Xe pool by chemical exchange, so one host reports through thousands of Xe atoms per second — allowing picomolar‑to‑femtomolar detection of the reporter, far below the millimolar sensitivity floor of conventional Gd/¹⁹F MRI agents. Because the cage diameter, wall chemistry and window (neck) size are set by base‑pair design, the bound‑Xe chemical shift and the exchange rate — the two parameters that determine hyperCEST contrast and saturation efficiency — become design variables rather than synthetic accidents; crystal batches with different cage sizes give spectrally resolved "colours," so several targets can be imaged simultaneously in one scan (multiplexed molecular MRI). Decorating the outer faces with antibodies, nanobodies, peptides or aptamers targets the crystal to tumour markers, thrombi or inflamed endothelium, while adding responsive gates (i‑motif/pH switches, protease‑ or miRNA‑cleavable locks, aptamer switches) makes the contrast *activatable*: the analyte opens or closes the cage windows, switching Xe access and hence the CEST signal on or off, turning the crystal into an in‑vivo sensor for pH, enzyme activity or specific nucleic acids.

The same material also serves ex vivo as a Xe‑storage/relaxation‑protective matrix and as a calibration phantom for hyperCEST instrumentation, and — since cavity volume, hydrophobicity and neck size can be varied independently while every cage in the sample is identical — as the model system for quantifying how confinement geometry controls xenon binding affinity, chemical shift and exchange kinetics, knowledge directly transferable to designing next‑generation ¹²⁹Xe biosensors.

**Use the caged superlattice as a 3‑D array of identical nanoscale confinement chambers for studying and engineering biomolecular condensates (liquid–liquid phase separation) — a "condensate‑on‑a‑crystal" platform and route to synthetic membraneless organelles.**

Because every unit cell contains one geometrically identical, solvent‑accessible vacancy of sequence‑defined volume, infiltrating the crystal with condensate‑forming components (intrinsically disordered proteins such as FUS/hnRNPA1/DDX4, RNA, poly‑Arg/poly‑Asp or PEG–dextran systems, or client enzymes) partitions the mixture into billions of *equal‑volume*, wall‑defined droplets rather than the broad, coalescing, Ostwald‑ripening size distribution seen in bulk. Confinement at tens of nanometres is exactly the regime in which surface‑to‑volume ratio, wall chemistry and finite molecule number dominate phase behaviour, so the lattice gives what bulk tubes and microfluidic droplets cannot: identical, arrested droplets whose size is set by design, cannot fuse, and are held at fixed, known spacing for direct real‑space imaging.

The payoff is threefold. (i) *Quantitative biophysics*: cage diameter, wall charge/hydrophobicity (tuned simply by hybridising modified strands), crowding and the number of nucleation‑competent surfaces are each varied independently while every chamber in the sample is identical, allowing systematic measurement of how confinement and surface wetting shift the saturation concentration, phase boundary, nucleation barrier, internal dynamics and the liquid‑to‑gel/amyloid ageing transition that underlies ALS/FTD and other condensate‑linked diseases — with readouts by FRAP/single‑molecule imaging, cryo‑EM of the ordered lattice, or the crystal's diffraction/refractive‑index change as the voids fill. (ii) *High‑throughput screening*: each cage is an independent, addressable femto‑/atto‑litre assay well, so libraries of small molecules, RNAs or peptides can be tested for their ability to promote, dissolve or harden condensates (a major and currently hard‑to‑assay drug‑discovery target), with digital, Poisson‑limited single‑condensate statistics. (iii) *Synthetic biology/biotechnology*: pre‑loading the cages with a condensed phase that concentrates enzymes and substrates hundreds‑fold creates an ordered array of artificial membraneless organelles for accelerating multi‑step biocatalytic cascades, for sequestering toxic intermediates, or for building compartmentalised artificial cells — with cargo loading and release programmed by toehold‑mediated strand displacement or pH/ion triggers on the cage openings.

**Use the caged superlattice (converted into a rigid silica/alumina replica by conformally mineralising the DNA walls and burning out the template) as an *ordered, monodisperse confinement matrix for quantum fluids* — an "engineered aerogel" for superfluid ³He/⁴He and other confined quantum-liquid physics.**

Superfluid ³He is the archetypal p-wave, spin-triplet condensate, and its order parameter is exquisitely sensitive to confinement on the scale of the Cooper-pair coherence length (ξ ≈ 20–80 nm) — exactly the cavity size that DNA-origami blocks with central vacancies produce. Confining ³He in silica aerogel is currently the only way to explore this, and it has revealed dramatic effects (suppressed T_c, the stabilised "polar" phase, half-quantum vortices, Weyl/Majorana surface states). But aerogel is a *stochastic* medium: its strand and pore sizes are broadly distributed, its anisotropy can only be imposed crudely by uniaxial straining, and the resulting impurity/disorder correlations cannot be varied independently — so comparison with theory (Ginzburg–Landau with anisotropic quenched disorder) is largely qualitative.

An origami-templated replica fixes this at the root. Because every unit cell contributes an identical vacancy, the pore diameter, wall (strut) thickness, connectivity, lattice symmetry and hence the *anisotropy tensor* of the scattering medium are all set a priori by base-pair geometry and reprogrammed simply by redesigning the block and its cage. One can therefore: (i) dial the confinement dimension D through ξ to map, quantitatively, the A–B, planar and polar phase boundaries and the confinement-induced stabilisation of otherwise inaccessible order-parameter states; (ii) build *deliberately anisotropic or chiral* cage lattices (elongated, sheared, or helically stacked vacancies) that impose a designed, uniform orientational field on the order parameter — the key ingredient for stabilising the polar phase and for creating a bulk lattice of half-quantum vortices and their bound Majorana modes, a candidate platform for topological quantum information; (iii) introduce a *known, tunable* concentration of "missing-cage" defects or of selectively filled sublattices to interpolate cleanly between the ordered and disordered (aerogel-like) limits, giving the first controlled test of quenched-disorder theories of unconventional superfluids/superconductors; and (iv) exploit the periodicity itself, since a lattice of pores connected by narrow necks is a natural array of weak links — i.e. a macroscopic 3D Josephson-junction network for ³He/⁴He, useful for studying phase slips, π-states and quantum turbulence, and as the basis of superfluid interferometers (SHeQUIDs) for rotation/gravity sensing.

The same ordered, monodisperse nanoporous host also serves for confined ⁴He (Kosterlitz–Thouless and "supersolid"/localisation questions in a geometry where every pore is identical), for adsorbed helium/hydrogen monolayers as a model 2D quantum solid, and, more practically, as a well-characterised low-density heat-exchange/wicking matrix for dilution refrigerators and superfluid-based cryogenic devices. In short, the periodic vacancies convert an inherently random confinement problem into a *programmable* one, turning "aerogel disorder" from an uncontrolled nuisance into a designable parameter of quantum-fluid physics.

**Use the caged crystal (converted to a robust silica/oxide replica by conformally mineralising the DNA walls and burning out the template) as a positronium‑forming converter/moderator for antimatter and fundamental‑physics experiments.**

When slow positrons are implanted into a nanoporous oxide film, they capture an electron to form positronium (Ps), which then diffuses into the voids, thermalises by repeated wall collisions, and is emitted into vacuum. The efficiency, the emission energy and — critically — the *energy spread* of the Ps beam are governed almost entirely by the pore diameter: quantum confinement sets a zero‑point energy of order tens of meV that is released as the atom leaves, and the wall‑collision rate sets the cooling time before the 142 ns ortho‑Ps lifetime expires. In today's converters (mesoporous silica films, aerogels, oxidised porous Si) the pore sizes are stochastic and broadly distributed, so the emitted Ps has an uncontrolled, inhomogeneously broadened energy/velocity distribution and a poorly reproducible yield.

A superlattice of origami blocks with identical central vacancies fixes this by construction: every cavity has the same, base‑pair‑defined diameter, the cavities interconnect into straight, low‑tortuosity escape channels, and pore size, wall thickness, film thickness, channel orientation and lattice symmetry are each reprogrammed simply by redesigning the block and its vacancy. One therefore obtains a monoenergetic, forward‑directed, high‑yield Ps source whose emission energy is a *design parameter*, and can map Ps confinement energy versus cavity size quantitatively (impossible in polydisperse media). Practical payoffs: efficient production of cold, dense Ps clouds for antihydrogen formation (AEgIS/GBAR‑type experiments) and for antimatter gravity measurements; narrow‑linewidth Ps beams for precision 1S–2S and hyperfine spectroscopy tests of QED and of matter–antimatter symmetry; a route toward the long‑sought Ps Bose–Einstein condensate and γ‑ray "annihilation laser," where a fixed number of Ps atoms per identical cavity gives uniform density in every pocket; plus Ps‑annihilation lifetime spectroscopy standards — the same perfectly monodisperse voids serve as calibration samples for PALS, which is routinely used to measure free volume in polymers, low‑k dielectrics and glasses but currently lacks well‑defined reference pore sizes. The cage walls can additionally be doped (via metal‑binding strands before mineralisation) with hydrophobic, fluorinated or low‑Z terminations to suppress Ps pick‑off annihilation and quenching, tuning Ps survival independently of geometry.

**Use a single, mineralised layer of the caged crystal as a precision vacuum‑gap spacer for near‑field thermophotovoltaic (nTPV) and thermionic energy conversion.**

Near‑field radiative heat transfer exceeds the blackbody limit by 1–2 orders of magnitude only when a hot emitter and a photovoltaic (or collector) chip are held apart by a *uniform* vacuum gap of tens to ~100 nm over centimetre areas — the single unsolved engineering obstacle for nTPV waste‑heat and solar‑thermal converters. A slab cleaved from an origami superlattice of blocks with central vacancies is exactly such a spacer: the block height sets the separation with base‑pair (~2 nm) precision, the periodic lattice guarantees the same separation everywhere (no tilt, sag, or particulate‑induced shorts), and, crucially, the *cages* make the layer mostly empty space, so the spacer occupies only a few percent of the interface area. That minimises the two things that ruin real devices — parasitic solid (phonon) heat conduction across the spacer, which short‑circuits the thermal gradient, and dielectric material blocking the evanescent‑wave coupling — while the DNA walls, once conformally silicified/ALD‑coated (SiO₂, Al₂O₃) and the template burned out, give a refractory, electrically insulating, mechanically stiff skeleton able to hold the gap against thermal expansion, electrostatic attraction and Casimir/van der Waals collapse at emitter temperatures of several hundred °C.

Because gap height, wall thickness, contact‑area fraction and lattice symmetry are each set independently simply by redesigning the block and its vacancy, the trade‑off between mechanical stability and parasitic conduction — currently handled by ad hoc lithographic pillars or microspheres with poor size uniformity — becomes a parametric design problem, and graded/stacked layers give different gaps in one device. The same self‑assembled spacer enables micron‑gap thermionic and thermo‑photonic converters, near‑field thermal diodes/switches and transistors, nanogap electrostatic and vacuum‑gap MEMS actuators, and heat‑assisted magnetic recording heads; and since every gap in the sample is identical and known a priori, the material is also a clean experimental standard for measuring near‑field radiative heat flux versus separation and testing fluctuational‑electrodynamics theory.

**Use the caged crystals as an artificial oxygen carrier — a "synthetic red‑blood‑cell" for transfusion, organ preservation and tumour oxygenation.**

Each unit cell's identical vacancy is loaded with exactly one oxygen‑binding payload — a haemoglobin tetramer or myoglobin captured by cage‑lining strands, a synthetic Fe‑ or Co‑porphyrin/picket‑fence complex hybridised to the cavity wall, or a perfluorocarbon nanodroplet condensed into the hydrophobically modified void — so a single microcrystal carries a huge, exactly countable number of O₂ sites at a defined stoichiometry rather than the stochastic loading of liposome‑ or polymer‑encapsulated haemoglobin. The empty, solvent‑connected cage network is essential: it lets O₂ and CO₂ diffuse in and out within milliseconds (short, straight, monodisperse channels give near‑capillary gas exchange kinetics) while the DNA/silicified walls physically sequester the haem from the vasculature, which solves the two problems that killed earlier haemoglobin‑based substitutes — extravasation of free haemoglobin and its scavenging of endothelial nitric oxide, which causes vasoconstriction and hypertension. Because the cage window size is set by base‑pair design, it can be made permeable to O₂/CO₂/NO‑gas diffusion but impermeable to the protein itself, and the wall can carry reductases, catalase/SOD‑mimetic or ascorbate‑bearing strands adjacent to every haem to suppress methaemoglobin formation and oxidative damage.

Crucially, the *oxygen affinity and release profile become design parameters*: P₅₀ and cooperativity can be tuned by the cage's confinement dimension, wall charge and by allosteric effectors (2,3‑DPG analogues, inositol phosphates) tethered at DNA‑programmed distances from the bound protein, so the material can be built to unload O₂ only at hypoxic tissue pO₂ — and made *responsive* by pH‑ (i‑motif/triplex) or lactate‑/enzyme‑gated cage openings that mimic the Bohr effect and dump oxygen preferentially in ischaemic or acidic tumour tissue. Loading different sublattices with distinct carriers gives a graded, multi‑affinity release cascade, and the outer faces can be PEGylated/oligolysine‑coated for circulation half‑life and decorated with targeting ligands.

Applications: a universally compatible, pathogen‑free, room‑temperature‑storable transfusion alternative for trauma, battlefield and low‑resource settings; a perfusate additive that oxygenates donor organs during normothermic machine perfusion and extends preservation time; tumour re‑oxygenation to radiosensitise hypoxic tumours before radiotherapy; treatment of ischaemia, stroke, sickle‑cell crisis and carbon‑monoxide poisoning (cages loaded with high‑affinity scavengers that strip CO or excess NO); and oxygen supply to engineered tissues and organoids inside 3D scaffolds. Because every cavity is identical and its size, wall chemistry and gating are reprogrammed simply by redesigning the origami block and its vacancy, the platform is also the long‑missing model system for quantifying how nanoconfinement and local electrostatics control haem ligand binding, cooperativity and autoxidation.

**Use a single cleaved layer of the caged crystal as a self‑assembled, affinity‑functionalised support film for cryo‑electron microscopy (a "programmable Quantifoil").**

Because one monolayer of the superlattice is a continuous, mechanically coherent DNA film perforated by a perfectly periodic array of identical through‑holes (the block vacancies), it can be laid over a standard EM grid — optionally stiffened by a thin carbon/graphene or silica skin — to give holes whose diameter, pitch and lattice symmetry are set by base‑pair design (±2 nm) rather than by photolithographic patterning of a polymer film. Each cage then acts as a hole in which a thin film of vitreous ice is suspended for imaging.

The cages solve the two dominant problems of cryo‑EM specimen preparation. (i) *Ice thickness and particle distribution*: identical, sub‑100‑nm holes give uniform, reproducibly thin ice across the whole grid, so blotting becomes far less of a black art and far more of the grid area is usable. (ii) *Air–water‑interface damage and preferred orientation*: the cage walls can be decorated by hybridisation with capture ligands (complementary oligos, aptamers, nanobodies, Ni‑NTA/His‑tag, streptavidin, or lipid/detergent anchors for membrane proteins), so the target particle is tethered inside the void, away from the denaturing, orientation‑biasing air–water interface, at a controllable surface density; placing ligands at DNA‑programmed positions and spacings can even bias particles into a chosen orientation or hold them in a defined pose, directly attacking missing‑cone artefacts. Because the lattice constant is known exactly, the periodic film simultaneously serves as an in‑image magnification/distortion calibrant and as a fiducial grid for tomographic alignment and drift correction, and because it is a low‑Z, thin, largely empty framework it adds little background scattering.

Since hole size, spacing, wall chemistry and ligand identity are reprogrammed simply by redesigning the origami block and its vacancy, grids can be tailored per specimen (small proteins, ribosomes, virions, membrane‑protein nanodiscs, in‑cell lamellae supports), and the same film enables on‑grid sample purification: capture the target directly from crude lysate in the cages, wash away contaminants, then vitrify — turning grid preparation from empirical screening into a designable, single‑step affinity workflow.

**Use a thin film of the caged crystals (mineralised/metal‑coated for robustness and rendered hydrophobic) as a pressure‑stable "plastron" surface — a self‑assembled air‑retaining skin for underwater drag reduction, antifouling and gas‑exchange membranes.**

Because every unit cell contributes an identical, tens‑of‑nanometre vacancy, coating the cage walls with fluoroalkyl‑/alkyl‑modified strands (or silanising the silica replica after burning out the DNA) turns the lattice into a periodic array of monodisperse, non‑wetting nanocavities that each trap and hold a stable pocket of gas when the film is immersed. The key advantage over conventional micro/nano‑textured superhydrophobic coatings is hydrostatic robustness: the Laplace pressure that pins the meniscus scales as ~2γ/r, so cavities of a few tens of nanometres resist wetting (Cassie→Wenzel collapse) at pressures of many atmospheres, and because *every* cavity is the same size — instead of the broad, defect‑prone size distribution of etched, sprayed or phase‑separated textures — there is no population of large pores that floods first and nucleates catastrophic, spreading plastron loss. The interconnected void network also lets the gas layer self‑replenish laterally and be actively re‑pressurised, and the meniscus curvature, gas volume per unit area and collapse pressure all become design parameters set simply by redesigning the origami block and its vacancy.

Practical payoffs: (i) a continuous air–water slip layer that cuts skin‑friction drag on ship hulls, pipelines, torpedo/AUV bodies and microfluidic channels, saving fuel and pumping energy; (ii) passive antifouling and anticorrosion, since barnacle larvae, bacteria, proteins and salt water never contact the solid surface (and the same non‑wetting cages resist ice nucleation and give self‑cleaning behaviour); (iii) an artificial "gill"/gas‑exchange membrane, in which the stable plastron acts as a permanent gas–liquid interface for extracting dissolved O₂ or stripping CO₂ from water — useful for underwater vehicles, bioreactor aeration, membrane oxygenators and degassing units — with the huge, uniform interfacial area giving high transfer rates without bubble formation; and (iv) an anti‑cavitation/heat‑transfer surface where the identical, pre‑formed vapour pockets serve as uniform, reproducible boiling nucleation sites, raising critical heat flux in a predictable way. Because cavity size, wall chemistry and lattice symmetry are reprogrammed by rewriting the strand set, the material is simultaneously the model system for quantifying how pore geometry and surface chemistry govern Cassie‑state stability, plastron lifetime and slip length — turning superhydrophobic‑surface design from empirical texturing into a parametric exercise.

**Use the caged crystal (or the rigid silica/carbon replica made by mineralising the DNA walls and burning out the template) as a host for *nanoconfined gas‑hydrate (clathrate) formation* — a "designer ice cage" for high‑density, low‑pressure storage and transport of methane/natural gas, and for CO₂ capture‑and‑sequestration by hydrate exchange.**

Gas hydrates store an extraordinary amount of gas (~160 v/v for methane) in a solid, non‑flammable, water‑based form, but they are almost unusable in practice because their formation from bulk water is plagued by hours‑to‑days stochastic nucleation induction times, severe hysteresis, incomplete conversion (unreacted water becomes a diffusion‑blocking "shell"), and the need for high pressure and low temperature. Every one of these failures is a *geometry* problem, and a superlattice of origami blocks with identical central vacancies attacks it directly: water taken up into the lattice is divided into billions of monodisperse, tens‑of‑nanometre droplets, each in contact with a huge, uniform wall area and connected to a straight, low‑tortuosity gas‑supply channel network. Confinement of this size (i) supplies an enormous density of identical heterogeneous nucleation sites so hydrate nucleates promptly and reproducibly rather than stochastically, (ii) makes the water film thin enough that gas diffusion never becomes rate‑limiting, giving near‑complete water‑to‑hydrate conversion and fast charge/discharge cycling without the self‑preserving crust that stalls bulk reactors, and (iii) shifts the hydrate equilibrium curve by a Gibbs–Thomson term fixed by the designed pore diameter — so the storage pressure/temperature set‑point becomes a *design variable* dialled in by redesigning the block and its vacancy, rather than something tuned empirically with promoters like THF or SDS.

Because every cavity is identical (unlike silica gels, activated carbons, hydrogels or dry‑water systems, whose broad pore‑size distributions smear the phase transition and leave much of the water inactive), the material gives a sharp, reproducible, fully reversible uptake–release step with low hysteresis, and the cage walls can be independently programmed by hybridised strands (hydrophobic/fluoroalkyl patches, amphiphilic kinetic promoters, or anti‑agglomerant motifs at DNA‑defined spacings) to tune wettability, nucleation rate and the structure I/II/H polymorph that forms.

Practical payoffs: solid‑state natural‑gas and hydrogen/CH₄ storage for vehicles, stranded‑gas monetisation and "solidified natural gas" shipping at moderate pressure instead of −162 °C LNG; CO₂ capture from flue gas by hydrate crystallisation and CO₂–CH₄ swap chemistry for producing methane from natural hydrate reservoirs while sequestering CO₂; and gas separation (CH₄/CO₂/N₂) by selective hydrate formation. Scientifically, since cavity size, wall chemistry, connectivity and water loading are each varied independently while every pore in the sample is identical, it is the long‑missing model system for measuring how confinement and surface chemistry control clathrate nucleation kinetics, memory effects and phase stability — knowledge equally relevant to flow‑assurance (hydrate plug prevention in pipelines) and to planetary/permafrost hydrate science.

Suggest a high-value, near-term research.answer:
**Project: An experimental demonstration of positionally‑controlled diamond mechanosynthesis — a closed, recyclable "hydrogen‑abstraction + carbon‑dimer‑placement" tool cycle on a passivated diamond surface, run in a cryogenic UHV scanning‑probe microscope.**

**What it would do.** Using a low‑temperature (~5–80 K) ultra‑high‑vacuum AFM/STM with sub‑ångström positioning and force/current feedback, mount chemically well‑defined molecular tooltips on the probe apex (e.g., an ethynyl/adamantane‑based radical abstraction tip and a DCB6‑Ge‑type carbon‑dimer deposition tip, both proposed and quantum‑chemically vetted by Freitas and Merkle). On a hydrogen‑terminated diamond C(110)/C(100) surface, execute in sequence: (1) site‑specific abstraction of a single hydrogen atom to create an isolated surface radical, (2) mechanically forced deposition of a C₂ dimer at that exact site, (3) verification of the added atoms by non‑contact AFM imaging/spectroscopy, and (4) tooltip *recharge* (re‑hydrogenation / re‑loading of the dimer feedstock) so the same tip can perform many cycles. Success criterion: statistically characterized per‑operation yield and error rates over hundreds of repetitions, culminating in the automated, machine‑controlled construction of a small three‑dimensional diamondoid structure (e.g., a few hundred atoms) built atom‑by‑atom to a pre‑specified design.

**Why it is high‑value and near‑term.** All of the enabling pieces already exist: sub‑ångström SPM positioning, demonstrated single‑atom manipulation and hydrogen depassivation lithography on Si(100), CO‑functionalized tips with atomic‑resolution imaging, and a decade of DFT work showing that the required mechanosynthetic reactions have adequate barriers, positional error tolerances, and no serious pathological side reactions. The project therefore needs no new physics — only careful integration and engineering — yet it converts the central premise of Drexlerian nanotechnology (site‑specific, positionally controlled covalent bond formation with reusable tools) from theory into a measured, reproducible laboratory process. It also produces exactly the quantitative inputs a scale‑up program requires: reaction reliability, error rates, cycle times, and the feasibility of tool re‑use — and it directly seeds the bootstrap path, since the first structures built can be improved tooltips and the rigid diamondoid handles/frames of a second‑generation positional device, opening the road to parallel arrays and, eventually, self‑replicating atomically precise manufacturing systems.

**Project: Use modern de‑novo protein design to build a self‑assembled, atomically precise "molecular positioning device" — a rigid designed protein frame carrying an actuated arm and a reactive tool tip — and demonstrate that it can perform programmed, site‑specific covalent chemistry on a held substrate.**

**What it would do.** Exploit the now‑mature deep‑learning protein design stack (RFdiffusion / ProteinMPNN / AlphaFold‑class validation, plus high‑throughput gene synthesis and yeast/E. coli expression) to design: (1) an ultra‑stiff, hyperstable scaffold — e.g., a designed helical‑bundle or β‑sandwich truss assembled into a ~10–30 nm rigid baseplate with sub‑ångström RMS thermal fluctuation at the working point; (2) a two‑ or three‑degree‑of‑freedom arm built from designed hinge/latch domains that switch between discrete, well‑defined conformational states under external control (pH, ion, small‑molecule effector, or a light‑switchable/DNA‑strand‑displacement input), so that the tip position is *digitally* selected rather than diffusively sampled; (3) a tool site — a designed metal centre, organocatalytic residue triad, or covalently tethered reactive group — mounted at the arm's apex; and (4) a substrate‑clamping site on the baseplate that holds a growing oligomer in a fixed, known register. The demonstration target is the stepwise, machine‑directed synthesis of a short non‑biological polymer (say, an unnatural backbone or a branched oligomer) in which each monomer addition is placed at a *selected* site by moving the arm to a chosen state, with the product sequence programmed by the order of external control inputs. Success criteria: near‑atomic cryo‑EM (and ideally cryo‑ET of individual devices) confirming the designed geometry and each discrete arm state; measured per‑step yield, positional error, and cycle time; and mass‑spectrometric/sequencing proof that the product's monomer order tracks the commanded input order rather than solution chemistry alone.

**Why it is high‑value and near‑term.** It attacks the true bottleneck on the Drexlerian path — *positional control of chemistry by a machine*, with a reusable tool and a stiff frame — but does so in the one construction medium where we already possess reliable, cheap, massively parallel atomic‑precision fabrication: designed polypeptides self‑assembling from encoded sequences. Every ingredient exists today (designed hyperstable folds, designed ligand‑ and light‑switchable conformational switches, designed metalloenzyme active sites, single‑particle cryo‑EM at 2–3 Å, DNA‑origami mounting for arraying), so no new physics is needed. Yet the payoff is decisive: it converts positional assembly from a scanning‑probe curiosity performed one tip at a time into a *molecular* machine present at 10¹⁵ copies per litre, running in parallel, and it delivers the quantitative engineering data (stiffness, error rate per operation, tool lifetime, cycle time) that any scale‑up requires. Crucially, it is the natural bootstrap step: such devices can be used to synthesize stiffer, non‑biological atomically precise components (rigid polycyclic frameworks, ladder polymers, organometallic tool tips) that in turn form the second‑generation, stiffer positional machinery — the standard "soft machines build hard machines" route out of the current impasse — while also being manufacturable, evolvable, and testable on academic budgets and timescales of a few years.

**Project: Build a wafer‑scale, massively parallel "nanofactory‑on‑a‑chip" — a UHV MEMS/CMOS array of tens of thousands to millions of independently addressed, closed‑loop atomic‑precision probes — to solve the *throughput and scale‑up* bottleneck of positional assembly.**

**What it would do.** Rather than improving a single tip's chemistry, this project industrializes positional control. Fabricate on one silicon wafer a dense array (starting at 10²–10³ units, scaling to 10⁵–10⁶) of monolithic MEMS nanopositioners, each carrying a sharp tip, each with (i) integrated 3‑DOF electrostatic/piezoelectric actuation with ≥100 kHz bandwidth, (ii) on‑chip capacitive or piezoresistive displacement sensing plus tunneling‑current/force feedback giving closed‑loop positional noise below ~30–50 pm at cryogenic UHV operating conditions, (iii) stiff, low‑thermal‑drift single‑crystal Si or diamond flexure structures whose creep and thermal expansion are characterized and compensated, and (iv) monolithically integrated (or flip‑chip‑bonded) CMOS drive/readout electronics so that all tips are addressed in parallel from a digital "instruction stream" without an external wiring bottleneck. The demonstration milestone: run the whole array simultaneously performing an already‑proven atomic‑precision operation — hydrogen depassivation lithography on H:Si(100), with automated tip‑condition monitoring, error detection, and error correction — and measure the aggregate figures of merit that matter for manufacturing: operations per second per chip, per‑operation yield and error rate as a function of tip number, tip lifetime, drift‑limited duty cycle, and cost per atomically placed feature. The capstone: use the chip to write, in parallel, the atomically precise patterned templates (followed by selective atomic layer epitaxy) for the *next* generation of stiffer, smaller, better nanopositioners and tool‑tip mounts — an explicit self‑improvement/bootstrapping loop.

**Why it is high‑value and near‑term.** Single‑tip atomic manipulation has been reproducible for three decades; what has never been demonstrated is doing it *in parallel, cheaply, and reliably enough to build macroscopic quantities of atomically precise matter*. That, not any missing physics, is the reason Drexlerian manufacturing remains hypothetical: one tip performing ~10 operations/s cannot build anything of consequence, whereas 10⁶ tips at 10⁴ operations/s is ~10¹⁰ placements/s — the regime where atomically precise components become an engineering material rather than a stunt. Every enabling technology already exists in mature form (IBM "Millipede" thousand‑tip MEMS arrays, MEMS scanning probes with integrated actuation and sensing, cryo‑UHV STM stability at the tens‑of‑picometres level, automated tip conditioning and machine‑learning SPM control, CMOS‑MEMS integration, ALE/ALD for converting patterns into 3D structure), so the work is systems integration, metrology, and yield engineering — exactly the kind of problem semiconductor manufacturing knows how to attack, on a 3–5 year timescale and a modest capital budget. The deliverable is tool‑independent and compounding: whatever mechanosynthetic chemistry (Si, diamondoid, or otherwise) turns out to be best, it plugs into this platform, and the platform can be used to make its own successors — converting positional assembly from a laboratory curiosity into an exponentially improving manufacturing technology.

Propose a new nanofabrication technique.answer:
**Proposed technique: Parallel “atom‑lattice” scanning‑probe chemical lithography — STM hydrogen‑depassivation patterning coupled to area‑selective atomic‑layer deposition/etching (ALD/ALE), scaled up with MEMS tip arrays.**

**Concept.** Instead of exposing a polymer resist with a focused electron beam (whose ultimate resolution ~3–5 nm is set by forward/backscattered and secondary‑electron blur, resist molecular size and shot noise), the pattern is written directly into a *monatomic* resist: a hydrogen‑terminated Si(100) or H/Ge surface in UHV. A scanning tunneling microscope tip injects low‑energy (<10 eV) electrons that desorb individual H atoms via vibrational‑ladder excitation. Because the electrons are emitted into a tunneling gap of ~0.5 nm and the "resist" is one atom thick, there is no proximity effect and the smallest writable feature is a single dangling bond — i.e., the silicon lattice constant (~0.38 nm), roughly an order of magnitude below EBL.

**Pattern transfer.** The depassivated dangling‑bond regions act as chemically selective nucleation sites: precursors such as TiCl₄/TMA/PH₃ adsorb only on bare Si, so area‑selective ALD grows the pattern with atomic‑layer thickness control, and self‑limiting ALE removes material atom‑layer by atom‑layer. Resolution is therefore set by surface chemistry and the crystal lattice, not by beam optics or resist stochastics.

**Throughput solution (the key innovation).** Massively parallel MEMS/NEMS cantilever arrays (10³–10⁵ independently actuated, individually current‑controlled tips, as in millipede‑style probe storage) write in parallel, each tip closed‑loop registered to the atomic lattice using the tunneling signal itself as a self‑calibrating metrology reference. Machine‑learning tip‑state classification and autonomous tip reconditioning maintain single‑atom apex sharpness across the array, addressing the historic throughput and reliability barriers.

**Expected performance.** Sub‑nanometer (single‑atom, ~0.4 nm) placement precision, deterministic dopant/defect positioning for quantum devices, and zero line‑edge roughness from resist polymer blur — capabilities inaccessible to EBL, EUV, or even helium‑ion beams.

**Proposed technique: “Sequence‑programmed DNA‑origami molecular stencil lithography” — wafer‑scale, massively parallel patterning in which the mask itself is a self‑assembled biomolecular template whose resolution is set by the DNA double‑helix pitch (~2 nm) and base spacing (~0.34 nm) rather than by beam optics.**

**Concept.** A long scaffold strand plus ~200 short staple strands folds into a rigid 2D/3D origami tile. Because every staple has a unique sequence and a known coordinate on the tile, *each* of the thousands of addressable sites can be chemically functionalized independently (thiol, azide, biotin, aptamer, or metal‑binding peptide handles). The arbitrary pattern is therefore written **once, in software, as DNA sequence**, and then reproduced in ~10¹² identical copies in a single self‑assembly reaction — i.e., the pattern generation step is chemical and parallel, not serial like e‑beam writing, so there is no shot noise, no proximity effect, and no secondary‑electron blur.

**Placement and registration (key innovation).** The origami tiles are docked onto a substrate pre‑patterned with coarse, low‑resolution (cheap, ≥50 nm) optical/nanoimprint “landing pads” whose size, shape and electrostatic charge match a single tile, giving deterministic single‑tile placement with defined orientation (chiral or asymmetric pad geometry breaks the two‑fold degeneracy). Hierarchical assembly of tiles into super‑origami arrays bridges the gap between the 2 nm intrinsic feature scale and the micron scale of device layout — the fine resolution comes from chemistry, the long‑range order from inexpensive lithography.

**Pattern transfer.** Functional handles nucleate the hard pattern: (i) site‑selective electroless/vapor metallization or seeded ALD grows metal or oxide only where handles exist; (ii) alternatively the origami is used as a self‑limiting “molecular hard mask” for a low‑bias, low‑temperature plasma or atomic‑layer etch, after conversion to a carbonized/silicified replica (e.g., by TMA/H₂O infiltration or silica encapsulation, which stiffens the DNA and gives ~10:1 etch contrast). Single‑molecule components — quantum dots, single‑walled nanotubes, molecular magnets, colour centres, single dopant atoms — can be tethered at chosen bases before transfer, giving *deterministic single‑emitter placement* that no beam technique can achieve.

**Expected performance.** Half‑pitch ~2 nm and placement precision ~0.5 nm, set by helix geometry rather than resist stochastics; throughput of the order of a full wafer per assembly bath (≥10¹⁰ features/s effective), with the "mask" cost reduced to DNA synthesis. Line‑edge roughness is eliminated because every feature is a chemically identical molecule.

**Main challenges to address:** defect and yield statistics of self‑assembly (mitigated by error‑correcting staple design and post‑assembly purification/annealing), tile placement fidelity, and DNA‑to‑inorganic transfer contrast — all engineering problems rather than physical resolution limits.

**Proposed technique: “Cold‑atom de Broglie (matter‑wave) lithography with optical‑lattice atom lenses” — massively parallel, charge‑free patterning by laser‑cooled neutral atoms focused with light rather than electrostatics.**

**Concept.** A laser‑cooled, velocity‑selected beam of neutral atoms (e.g., metastable He*/Ar*, or Cr, Al, In for direct deposition) is launched at a substrate. Because the atoms are ~10⁴–10⁵ times heavier than an electron and are slowed to mK temperatures, their de Broglie wavelength is only ~1–100 pm, and — crucially — they carry no charge. This removes at a stroke the three physical limits of EBL: (i) Coulomb (Boersch) blur and space‑charge in the beam, (ii) forward/backscattered‑electron proximity exposure, and (iii) the ~5–10 nm range of secondary electrons that smears any electron‑exposed resist.

**Focusing element (key innovation).** Instead of magnetic lenses, the atoms are focused by a **far‑detuned optical standing wave acting as an array of conservative dipole‑force lenses**: each node/antinode of the light field is a cylindrical or 2‑D lens that channels atoms into a focal spot far narrower than the optical period (λ/2). Spot size is set by atom temperature and dipole‑potential curvature, not by λ_light, giving ~1 nm focal widths already demonstrated in atom‑lithography experiments; adding a “STED‑like” second, blue‑detuned lattice that repels atoms from the wings of each channel (an optical *dark‑spot* mask) narrows the deposited line to the sub‑nanometre regime. Arbitrary (non‑periodic) patterns are written by holographically shaping the light field with a spatial light modulator and/or by scanning the substrate under a phase‑stepped lattice — i.e., **the “mask” is reconfigurable light, and 10⁶–10⁸ lens channels expose in parallel**, so throughput scales like an imaging tool, not a serial writer.

**Resist / pattern transfer.** Metastable rare‑gas atoms carry ~8–20 eV of internal energy released only on contact, cleanly cleaving a single self‑assembled‑monolayer resist (a “resist” one molecule thick, hence no polymer swelling, no molecular‑size blur, no line‑edge roughness from polymer aggregates); the damaged/undamaged SAM then serves as a wet‑etch or area‑selective‑ALD mask. Alternatively, reactive metal atoms are deposited directly, so the pattern is formed additively with no resist at all.

**Expected performance.** Sub‑nanometre half‑pitch and placement precision, limited by atom transverse temperature and surface diffusion (suppressed by cryogenic substrates) rather than by beam optics or resist stochastics; zero proximity effect on any substrate, including insulators, since no charge is deposited; and area throughput orders of magnitude above EBL because millions of optical lens channels expose simultaneously.

Suggest a nanoscale system that could mi.answer:
A good candidate is a **redox‑driven rotaxane‑based artificial molecular pump** – i.e., a mechanically interlocked molecule in which positively charged macrocycles (e.g., cyclobis(paraquat‑p‑phenylene) rings) are threaded onto a molecular "dumbbell" axle bearing a redox‑active recognition site, a steric speed bump, and a "collecting chain," anchored at one end (for example, to a gold electrode or embedded in a lipid‑bilayer/membrane scaffold).

How it mimics a biological motor/pump: Cycling the redox state (electrochemically, chemically, or photochemically – the analogue of ATP hydrolysis) alternately switches the ring–axle attraction on and off, while the asymmetric energy barriers along the axle act as a ratchet that biases Brownian motion in one direction. Each redox cycle therefore drives a ring from solution onto the collecting chain and traps it there, pumping rings *against* their concentration gradient and storing free energy — exactly the information/energy‑ratchet principle used by ATP‑powered ion pumps and by linear motors such as kinesin and myosin. Chaining many such units or coupling the ring translation to a membrane‑spanning channel would give directed transport of ions or cargo, i.e., a synthetic active transporter; running it on a circular track instead yields unidirectional rotation like ATP synthase's F₁ motor.

**A DNA‑origami rotary "nanoturbine" docked in a solid‑state nanopore (or a membrane‑spanning DNA nanopore), driven by a transmembrane electrochemical/ion‑flux gradient.**

Design: a self‑assembled DNA origami rotor with chiral, pitched blades (like a turbine/propeller) is mounted on a stiff DNA or protein axle that sits in the constriction of a nanopore in a solid‑state (SiN/graphene) or lipid membrane; a rigid origami stator plate anchors the axle and defines the rotation axis. Applying a voltage/salt gradient across the pore creates an electro‑osmotic and ionic flux through the chiral blades, which converts the down‑gradient flow of ions/water into continuous unidirectional rotation (tens to hundreds of rev/s), directly analogous to the proton‑motive‑force–driven c‑ring of F₀‑ATP synthase or the bacterial flagellar motor. The rotation can be read out by attaching a fluorescent or gold‑nanoparticle marker, and coupling the axle to a second, cam‑shaped origami element lets each turn cyclically open/close a DNA "gate," so that reversing the drive (mechanically torquing the rotor with magnetic tweezers or an optical trap) makes the device run backwards and actively pump ions or small cargo *against* their gradient—i.e., a fully synthetic, reversible rotary motor/pump built from programmable DNA.

**A light‑driven overcrowded‑alkene (Feringa‑type) rotary motor embedded as the "rotor" of a synthetic transmembrane ion channel.**

Design: a sterically overcrowded alkene molecular motor — two half‑units joined by a central C=C bond with stereogenic methyl groups — is covalently built into an amphiphilic, membrane‑spanning scaffold (e.g., a bola‑amphiphilic peptide/crown‑ether or pillararene channel) inserted into a lipid bilayer. The upper half acts as the rotor bearing a charged/ion‑binding "arm" (a crown ether or carboxylate cage), while the lower half is anchored to the channel wall as the stator.

Operation: each absorbed photon (the energy input, replacing ATP hydrolysis or the proton‑motive force) drives a photochemical E/Z isomerization, and the subsequent thermal helix inversion — which is irreversible because of the molecule's built‑in chirality — completes a 180° step. Repeated photon absorption therefore produces continuous **unidirectional 360° rotation** rather than random back‑and‑forth motion, i.e., a chemically ratcheted power stroke. As the arm sweeps through the channel it alternately exposes its ion‑binding site to one side of the membrane, changes its binding affinity as the ring/arm is strained during the rotation cycle, and releases the ion on the opposite side — an alternating‑access, "bind‑high‑affinity / release‑low‑affinity" cycle exactly like the E1/E2 conformational cycle of a P‑type ATPase (Na⁺/K⁺ pump) or the c‑ring of F₀F₁‑ATP synthase.

Because the rotation direction is set by the molecule's stereochemistry, ions are moved **against** their electrochemical gradient, storing free energy as a transmembrane potential/pH gradient that could, in a vesicle, be used to drive downstream chemistry — a fully synthetic, photon‑powered active transporter. Reversing the illumination wavelength or the load lets the device be run as a motor that harvests the gradient instead.

**A DNA "molecular walker" (bipedal burnt‑bridge nanowalker) striding along a nanoparticle‑ or origami‑patterned track – a synthetic analogue of kinesin/myosin.**

Design: two single‑stranded DNA "legs" (each bearing a DNAzyme or nicking‑enzyme recognition sequence) are joined by a short rigid duplex "body" that carries a cargo attachment site (quantum dot, gold nanoparticle, or a protein). The "track" is a DNA‑origami tile or nanotube decorated with a periodic row of complementary single‑stranded RNA/DNA "footholds" spaced ~6 nm apart, exactly like the 8‑nm tubulin repeat of a microtubule.

Operation: each leg binds a foothold; the bound DNAzyme (or an added nicking endonuclease/strand‑displacement fuel strand) then cleaves that foothold, destroying it and lowering its affinity so the rear leg detaches while the free leg searches forward and binds the next intact site. Because a used foothold cannot be re‑bound ("burnt bridge"), the chemical energy of hydrolysing/hybridising the fuel strands (the analogue of ATP hydrolysis) is converted into a Brownian ratchet that biases stepping in one direction only, giving processive, unidirectional, hand‑over‑hand transport of cargo along the track — precisely the mechanochemical cycle of kinesin.

Pump mode: anchoring an array of such walkers around the mouth of a membrane‑spanning DNA‑origami channel, so that each fuel‑driven step drags bound ions/molecules from one side of the track through the pore and releases them (low‑affinity state) on the far side, converts the linear motor into a vectorial active transporter that moves solutes **against** their concentration gradient, storing free energy as a transmembrane gradient. Step size, speed and directionality can be programmed simply by changing sequence spacing and fuel concentration, and steps can be read out single‑molecule by FRET or by tracking the attached nanoparticle.

**A catalytic bimetallic (Pt–Au) nanorod / Janus nanoparticle motor driven by self‑electrophoresis, which becomes a surface‑anchored "nanopump" when immobilized.**

Design: a ~300 nm‑diameter, 1–2 µm‑long rod (or a silica sphere half‑coated with Pt) with one catalytic Pt segment and one Au segment, dispersed in dilute hydrogen peroxide (or, in bio‑compatible versions, an enzyme pair such as catalase/urease/glucose oxidase grafted asymmetrically onto the particle so the fuel is urea or glucose).

Operation: the catalytic face decomposes the fuel asymmetrically (H₂O₂ → O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ at Pt, reduction at Au), setting up a local proton/ion flux and self‑generated electric field and concentration gradient across the particle. The resulting electro‑/diffusio‑phoretic slip flow propels the particle at tens of body‑lengths per second, converting chemical energy directly into directed mechanical motion — the same chemomechanical conversion a flagellar motor or myosin performs, but with a phoretic rather than a conformational ratchet. Directionality can be steered by embedding a ferromagnetic Ni segment and applying a weak external magnetic field, and cargo (drug, DNA, bead) can be docked on the inert end for transport, mimicking kinesin‑style cargo hauling.
