Pump mode: when the same catalytic particle (or a patterned patch of enzyme/metal) is tethered to a surface or to the rim of a nanochannel, it cannot move, so its self‑generated ion gradient instead drives the surrounding fluid — producing a steady electro‑osmotic/diffusio‑osmotic convective flow that draws tracers and solutes toward or away from the catalytic site. This turns the motor into a fuel‑powered, chemically gated micro/nanopump that transports solutes without any moving parts, functionally analogous to a proton‑pumping membrane ATPase; the pumping rate is switchable by fuel (substrate) concentration, giving built‑in "metabolic" regulation.

**A carbon‑ (or boron‑nitride‑) nanotube nanochannel lined with azobenzene "gates" that are photo‑isomerized in a travelling wave — a synthetic peristaltic proton/ion pump inspired by bacteriorhodopsin.**

Design: a ~1–2 nm inner‑diameter nanotube (or a single conical solid‑state nanopore) spans a lipid bilayer or a thin membrane separating two reservoirs. Along the inner wall, at three or four axially spaced positions, azobenzene units bearing charged/ion‑coordinating groups (carboxylates or crown‑ether caps) are covalently grafted. In the *trans* state each azobenzene lies flat against the wall (channel segment open, low ion affinity); on absorbing a photon it switches to the bulky, dipolar *cis* state, constricting that segment and raising its ion affinity.

Operation: the gates are made spectrally distinguishable (different substituents → different absorption maxima) or are addressed sequentially with a scanned/pulsed multi‑wavelength illumination, so the constrictions open and close in a phased sequence from one membrane face to the other. This creates a travelling "peristaltic" wave of binding sites and constrictions: an ion is captured at the high‑affinity *cis* site near the cis‑side entrance, the next gate downstream opens while the upstream gate closes behind it (a hard, energy‑ratcheted barrier preventing back‑slip), and the ion is handed forward and released at a low‑affinity *trans* site on the far side. Photon energy — rather than ATP hydrolysis — supplies the free energy, and the *spatiotemporal asymmetry of the illumination sequence*, not the geometry alone, sets the direction, so ions are translocated **against** their electrochemical gradient, building a transmembrane pH/potential difference exactly as the retinal‑driven proton relay of bacteriorhodopsin does.

Readout/utility: reconstituted in vesicles the device can be monitored by pH‑sensitive dyes or single‑channel current recording; reversing the phase of the light sequence reverses the pumping direction, and letting the built‑up gradient relax through the channel lets it run "downhill" as a motor that could drive coupled chemistry (e.g., a co‑reconstituted ATP synthase), giving a fully synthetic, optically programmable active transporter with no macroscopic moving parts.

**A nested (multi‑walled) carbon‑nanotube rotary nanomotor with a helical "impeller" paddle — an all‑solid‑state analogue of the bacterial flagellar motor / F₀ rotary pump.**

Design: a multi‑walled carbon nanotube is anchored at both ends to electrodes on a chip; the outer shell(s) are etched away in the middle so that the inner shell acts as an atomically smooth, nearly frictionless axle (the "bearing"), while a lithographically defined metal (Au) plate or a chirally pitched helical blade is welded to the free outer shell to form the rotor. Three or four stator electrodes are patterned around the rotor.

Operation: phased AC voltages on the stator electrodes (or a DC electron wind / thermal gradient along the tube, or an off‑axis laser‑induced optical torque) generate a rotating electrostatic field that drags the charged/polarizable rotor around the nanotube axle, giving continuous, reversible unidirectional rotation at up to kHz–MHz rates with essentially no wear, exactly as the proton‑motive‑force–driven stator ring turns the flagellar rotor. Direction and speed are set simply by the phase sequence and amplitude of the drive — the electrical analogue of ATP hydrolysis or the proton gradient.

Pump mode: if the rotor blade is made helical (an Archimedes screw) and the whole assembly is placed at the mouth of a nanofluidic channel or a membrane‑spanning pore, each revolution sweeps a fixed volume of water/ions from one side to the other, driving solute **against** its concentration gradient — a synthetic rotary active transporter. Run in reverse, a pressure‑ or gradient‑driven flow through the helix spins the rotor and generates electricity, mimicking how F₀ harvests the proton‑motive force to power F₁. Rotation is read out by tracking the paddle in a TEM/SEM or by the modulated electrostatic signal on the stators.

**A magnetically driven chiral nanohelix ("nanoscrew") propeller — a synthetic analogue of the bacterial flagellum that becomes a rotary Archimedes‑screw pump when tethered.**

Design: a ~200–500 nm‑diameter, 1–3 µm‑long helical ribbon (glancing‑angle‑deposited SiO₂, or a template‑grown/3D‑laser‑written polymer coil) carrying a soft‑ferromagnetic head or a thin Ni/Fe₃O₄ coating whose easy magnetization axis is fixed perpendicular to the helix axis. The helix has a well‑defined pitch and handedness, giving it a chiral (screw‑like) mobility matrix.

Operation: a weak (few‑mT) rotating external magnetic field exerts a torque on the embedded magnetic moment, spinning the helix synchronously at up to hundreds of Hz. Because the body is chiral, in the low‑Reynolds‑number regime rotation is hydrodynamically coupled to translation, so the corkscrew "swims" forward along the field's rotation axis — exactly the non‑reciprocal, torque‑to‑thrust conversion the proton‑motive‑force–driven flagellar motor achieves with its helical filament. Direction and speed are set by the field's rotation sense and frequency (the external field replacing the ion gradient/ATP as the energy input), and steering is fully remote, allowing cargo (drug, gene, single cell) to be hauled through viscous biological fluids like a motile bacterium.

Pump mode: clamping the helix inside or at the mouth of a nanochannel/membrane pore so it can spin but not translate turns it into a rotary displacement pump — each revolution screws a fixed volume of fluid and its dissolved ions from one reservoir to the other, moving solute *against* its pressure/concentration gradient with no valves, a purely mechanical mimic of an active transmembrane transporter. Run in reverse, an imposed flow through the helix spins it and induces a detectable magnetic/inductive signal, i.e., a nanoscale turbine that harvests a gradient much as F₀ harvests the proton‑motive force. Arrays of such screws in a membrane give tunable, magnetically gated active transport.

**A "flashing‑ratchet" nanofluidic pump: an array of asymmetric (sawtooth) nanoelectrodes lining a nanochannel that switches its potential on and off to rectify Brownian motion.**

Design: a fluidic nanochannel (or nanopore array through a thin membrane) whose walls carry lithographically patterned, interdigitated electrodes shaped as a periodic sawtooth (spatially asymmetric, period ~100 nm–1 µm, no mirror symmetry along the channel axis). Charged cargo — ions, DNA, proteins, or charged nanoparticles — diffuses freely in the channel.

Operation: the electrode array is cycled between "ON" (a periodic asymmetric potential with steep and shallow flanks, trapping cargo in the potential minima) and "OFF" (flat potential, cargo spreads by free diffusion). Because the wells are asymmetric, during the OFF period a particle is statistically more likely to diffuse past the *nearby shallow* barrier than the far steep one; when the field is switched ON again it is recaptured in the next well downstream. Each ON/OFF cycle therefore rectifies thermal noise into a net directed step — no net force is ever applied, exactly as in biological motors, where ATP hydrolysis (here, the electrical switching energy) does not push the motor but merely raises and lowers binding/energy barriers to bias Brownian excursions.

Why it mimics a biological motor/pump: this is a literal implementation of the Brownian‑ratchet/power‑stroke‑free mechanism proposed for kinesin stepping and for alternating‑access transporters — cyclic switching between a high‑affinity "bound" state and a low‑affinity "released" state within an asymmetric energy landscape. Spanning a membrane, the same device performs active transport, moving ions or solutes **against** their electrochemical gradient (a synthetic ATPase), and the direction and speed can be reversed simply by changing the flashing frequency, duty cycle, or the sign/steepness of the sawtooth — allowing separation, concentration, or gradient generation, with transport read out by fluorescence tracking or by the channel's ionic current.

**A chemically‑fuelled [3]catenane rotary motor — interlocked rings that ratchet around a macrocyclic "track," mimicking the rotational catalysis of F₁‑ATP synthase.**

Design: a large macrocycle (the "stator ring/track") carries two or three recognition stations separated by cleavable/formable chemical barriers (e.g., hydroxyl and amine groups that can be transiently acylated), with two smaller macrocycles threaded onto it as the "rotors." The whole assembly is anchored — for instance grafted onto a gold surface, a nanoparticle, or embedded in the head‑group region of a vesicle bilayer.

Operation: a chemical fuel (a carbodiimide, an activated ester, or a pulse of acid/base — the surrogate for ATP hydrolysis) reacts with the barrier sites, transiently installing and then hydrolytically removing bulky blocking groups. Because the kinetics of barrier formation depend on which side the ring occupies (a *kinetically asymmetric information ratchet*), a ring is far more likely to be "gated through" in one sense than the other, so each fuel‑consumption cycle drives the rings **360° unidirectionally** around the track and drives the system away from equilibrium, with waste product released just as ADP + Pᵢ is. The steric interaction between the two rings enforces a sequential, out‑of‑phase 120°‑style stepping, exactly like the three catalytic β‑subunits of F₁.

Motor/pump use: the rotating ring can be coupled through a rigid linker to a cam or paddle that cyclically deforms a co‑attached crown‑ether/pillararene channel, alternately exposing a high‑affinity ion site to one face of the membrane and a low‑affinity site to the other. The fuel‑driven rotation therefore imposes an alternating‑access cycle that translocates ions or small molecules **against** their electrochemical gradient, converting chemical fuel into a stored transmembrane gradient — a fully synthetic, chemically powered rotary pump. Run in reverse (letting the gradient or an applied torque turn the rings) it can be used to drive coupled synthesis, mirroring how proton flux through F₀ makes F₁ produce ATP; progress is monitored by NMR/CD of the ring positions or by single‑channel current and pH‑dye readout in vesicles.

**A de‑novo–designed transmembrane peptide "alternating‑access" nanopump — a self‑assembling four‑helix coiled‑coil bundle that switches conformation on metal‑ion (or pH) cycling.**

Design: four (or six) computationally designed amphipathic α‑helices, each ~30 residues with a heptad‑repeat sequence, self‑assemble in a lipid bilayer into a barrel with a narrow central lumen. Midway down the lumen a ring of His/Glu residues forms a high‑affinity ion/substrate binding site (the "occluded" site). Above and below it, two designed "gate" layers of bulky Leu/Trp residues act as hydrophobic seals. A separate allosteric ring of Cys/His residues on the periplasmic face binds a trigger ion (Zn²⁺, or is protonated at low pH); binding rotates the helices by ~25° about the bundle axis (a designed knobs‑into‑holes register shift), which opens the outer gate while closing the inner one, and vice versa when the trigger is released.

Operation: the device is driven by an externally imposed, spatially asymmetric chemical oscillation — e.g., periodic Zn²⁺/EDTA or acid/base pulses applied to one side only, or a photoacid/photobase caged compound released by light on the *cis* face. Each cycle runs the classic alternating‑access sequence: (1) outward‑open, high‑affinity state captures the cargo ion from the outside; (2) trigger binding closes the outer gate and *lowers* the affinity of the central site (strain built into the redesigned helix packing supplies the "power stroke"); (3) the inner gate opens and the cargo is released into the cytoplasmic side at low affinity; (4) trigger dissociation resets the bundle. Because gate opening is kinetically coupled to the affinity change (a chemical information ratchet), the cargo is released preferentially on the far side, so ions are moved **against** their electrochemical gradient, exactly as a P‑type ATPase or a secondary transporter does.

Why it is a good mimic: it reproduces the actual physical principle of biological pumps — coupled conformational gating plus affinity modulation within a lipid membrane — but with a fully synthetic, sequence‑programmable protein whose gate residues, binding‑site selectivity (Na⁺ vs K⁺ vs Cl⁻), and switching thermodynamics can be tuned by mutation. Reconstituted in vesicles, pumping is read out by pH‑ or Na⁺‑sensitive dyes and by single‑channel electrophysiology; letting the built‑up gradient run back downhill turns the same bundle into a motor element that can drive coupled conformational work or, in a vesicle co‑reconstituted with ATP synthase, actual ATP synthesis.

**A pH‑/redox‑switchable [c2]daisy‑chain rotaxane "molecular muscle" array — a synthetic sarcomere that contracts and, when it squeezes a pore, acts as a peristaltic pump.**

**Design.** Each monomer is a self‑complementary "hermaphrodite" molecule: a thread bearing two recognition stations (e.g., an ammonium station and an adjacent triazolium/viologen station) capped with a bulky stopper, whose own macrocycle (crown ether or cucurbituril) is threaded onto the partner's thread. Two such units interlock head‑to‑tail to give a doubly threaded [c2]daisy chain that can slide telescopically between an extended (~4 nm) and a contracted (~2.5 nm) state. Hundreds of these units are polymerized end‑to‑end into a linear "myofibril," and many such fibrils are bundled and anchored between a rigid substrate/origami frame and a movable element — for example the lid of a membrane‑spanning nanopore or a deformable vesicle patch.

**Operation.** A chemical or electrochemical stimulus (acid/base pulses, or one‑electron reduction/oxidation of the viologen station — the surrogate for ATP hydrolysis) switches which station the macrocycle prefers, so every unit slides ~1.5 nm inward; reversing the stimulus re‑extends it. Because the sliding amplitude is summed over hundreds of interlocked units in series, the bundle undergoes a large (tens of %) macroscopic contraction/extension stroke that generates piconewton‑to‑nanonewton forces — exactly the way myosin's small per‑head power strokes are amplified along a thick filament in a sarcomere. Making the switching kinetically asymmetric (station A can only be released when the ring has passed a gate) turns the cycle into a ratchet, so work is done against a load rather than dissipated.

**Pump mode.** Coupling the contracting bundle to an elastic membrane channel or a soft nanochannel wall makes each contraction cycle constrict the lumen behind a captured ion/solute and each extension re‑open it further along — a peristaltic, valve‑free displacement pump. Combined with binding sites whose affinity is modulated by the same mechanical strain (high‑affinity in the extended state, low‑affinity in the contracted state), the device performs an alternating‑access cycle that moves ions or small molecules **against** their electrochemical gradient, storing free energy as a transmembrane gradient. Contraction can be read out by SAXS/AFM force spectroscopy or FRET between the two ends of each daisy chain, and running the device backwards (letting the load or gradient stretch the muscle) recovers work, just as an actomyosin system can be driven in reverse.

**A single‑molecule electrically driven rotor on a metal surface, powered by inelastic tunnelling electrons from an STM tip (a "molecular turnstile" array that can act as a surface conveyor/pump).**

Design: a small chiral adsorbate — e.g., butyl methyl sulfide, a thioether whose S atom binds to a Cu(111) atom, or a designed molecule with an asymmetric "paddle" arm — is chemisorbed at a well‑defined surface site. The S–metal bond serves as the *bearing/stator*, and the asymmetric alkyl arm is the *rotor*. The molecule's chirality (and the registry of its arm with the underlying lattice) makes the rotational potential‑energy landscape a **sawtooth (ratchet) rather than symmetric**.

Operation: electrons tunnelling from the STM tip (or, in a device version, from a nanogap electrode or a hot‑electron injection contact) deposit ~0.1–0.3 eV of vibrational energy into the C–S torsional mode. Each inelastic electron therefore acts as a discrete quantum of "fuel," exactly as one ATP hydrolysis event does for kinesin or F₁: it does not push the rotor directly but excites it over the low barrier of the asymmetric landscape, so thermal/vibrational excursions are rectified into **net unidirectional rotation** whose sense is set by the molecule's handedness and by the tip position/bias polarity (a true chemically‑analogous Brownian ratchet, with electron energy replacing chemical free energy). Rotation rate scales with current (fuel flux) and rotation direction reverses with the opposite enantiomer — direct proof of ratchet, not driven, motion.

Motor/pump function: coupling the rotating arm to a neighbouring adsorbate (or building a linear array of such rotors along a nanochannel/graphene nanoribbon groove) means each turn cyclically grips, displaces and releases a physisorbed atom or molecule, handing it to the next rotor — a nanoscale "hand‑over‑hand" conveyor that transports surface species **against** their concentration gradient, i.e., a synthetic active transporter/2‑D pump. Because the rotors are read out atom‑by‑atom with the STM, one can measure the stepping statistics, efficiency and stall behaviour of a single motor in the same way single‑molecule assays characterise myosin or the flagellar motor.

**A thermophoretic (phonon‑driven) carbon‑nanotube shuttle — a short outer nanotube "cargo carrier" riding along a long inner nanotube axle under a thermal gradient, which becomes a nanopump when the shuttle is fixed and the fluid inside is driven instead.**

Design: a long single‑walled nanotube (or a nanotube "rail" suspended between two microfabricated pads, one resistively heated and one heat‑sunk) serves as the atomically smooth track; a short concentric outer nanotube sleeve — or a metal/fullerene/water nanodroplet cargo — sits on it and can slide or rotate with essentially zero static friction because of the incommensurate van der Waals interface. Cargo (a gold nanocrystal, a drug‑loaded fullerene, a DNA strand) is welded or physisorbed to the sleeve.

Operation: a temperature difference of a few tens of kelvin along the track sets up a directional phonon flux ("phonon wind") and a gradient in the interfacial free energy. Momentum transfer from the ballistic phonons, plus the entropic drive of the sleeve toward the cold (lower‑free‑energy) end, produces steady unidirectional translation at metres per second, with the thermal gradient playing the role of the proton‑motive force or ATP hydrolysis: energy is fed in as a non‑equilibrium *gradient*, and the built‑in asymmetry (the imposed temperature slope plus any chirality/defect ratchet patterned on the tube) rectifies the otherwise random thermal fluctuations into directed transport — the same nonequilibrium‑gradient‑to‑work conversion used by kinesin on a microtubule.

Pump mode: if the sleeve is clamped and the nanotube interior is filled with water or an electrolyte, the identical thermo‑osmotic/thermophoretic driving force acts on the confined fluid instead, and water molecules and solvated ions are dragged from the hot side to the cold side through the ~1 nm lumen in single‑file fashion. Spanning a membrane, such a tube translocates ions or small solutes **against** their concentration/electrochemical gradient purely by an applied heat flux, storing free energy as a transmembrane osmotic/pH difference — a valve‑free, moving‑part‑free synthetic active transporter analogous to a heat‑driven membrane ATPase. Direction and speed are set simply by the sign and magnitude of ΔT (reversing ΔT reverses pumping), throughput scales by bundling many tubes into an array, and transport can be read out by ionic‑current recording, pH‑sensitive dyes in vesicles, or TEM/fluorescence tracking of the shuttle, allowing the stall force and efficiency of a single "motor" to be measured just as in single‑molecule motor assays.

**An optically driven spinning nanoparticle rotor in a nanoaperture — a circularly‑polarized‑light‑powered rotary nanopump ("optical F₀").**

Design: a birefringent/chiral‑plasmonic nanoparticle (e.g., a vaterite or rutile nanocrystal, or a gold nanorod/gammadion with a chiral plasmonic response) ~100–200 nm across is held in the constriction of a nanochannel or membrane‑spanning pore by a plasmonic optical trap formed in a metallic bowtie/nanohole aperture, which acts as the stator/bearing and fixes the rotation axis.

Operation: circularly polarized (or orbital‑angular‑momentum‑carrying) laser light transfers spin angular momentum to the particle; because of its optical anisotropy it absorbs/retards one handedness preferentially and experiences a constant torque, so it spins continuously and unidirectionally at up to kHz–MHz. Photons here replace ATP hydrolysis or the proton‑motive force as the energy input, and the sense of rotation is set simply by the handedness of the polarization — a directionality "ratchet" imposed by the drive rather than by geometry.

Pump/motor function: at low Reynolds number the spinning particle drags the surrounding fluid, and if its surface is patterned with a shallow helical groove (or the pore wall is threaded), each revolution screws a fixed volume of water and its dissolved ions through the constriction, moving solute **against** its concentration/pressure gradient — a valve‑free rotary active transporter directly analogous to the c‑ring of F₀‑ATP synthase or the bacterial flagellar motor. Reversing the polarization handedness reverses the pumping direction; letting an imposed flow spin the particle instead makes it a turbine whose rotation (read out by the flicker of scattered light or by ionic‑current modulation) reports the harvested gradient, exactly as F₀ harvests proton flux to power F₁. Arrays of such trapped rotors in a nanoporous membrane give remotely and instantly switchable, light‑gated active transport with no chemical fuel and no wear.

**An ultrasound‑powered ("acoustic") nanomotor: a shape‑asymmetric, concave‑ended gold nanorod driven by acoustic streaming in a standing‑wave field, which becomes an acoustic nanopump when tethered at the mouth of a nanopore.**

**Design.** A ~300 nm × 2 µm metallic nanorod is electrodeposited so that one end is flat and the other is concave/cup‑shaped (a sacrificial Ag‑template step gives the hollow end); a thin Ni stripe can be embedded for magnetic steering and a polymer/DNA cargo dock placed on the inert end. The rods are suspended in an aqueous chamber (or a lipid‑bilayer‑spanning nanochannel array) driven at a few MHz by a piezo transducer that sets up a standing pressure wave.

**Operation.** The MHz acoustic field is the energy input, replacing ATP hydrolysis or the proton‑motive force. Radiation force first levitates and aligns the rod at a pressure node; because the two ends scatter sound asymmetrically, the oscillating flow around the concave end rectifies into a steady second‑order "acoustic streaming" jet. This time‑averaged, *non‑reciprocal* flow — a purely hydrodynamic Brownian/ratchet‑like rectification of a symmetric oscillatory drive — propels the rod axially at tens of body‑lengths per second and can also spin it, exactly as a flagellum converts periodic actuation into net thrust at low Reynolds number. Speed scales with acoustic power (the "fuel flux"), and direction is set by the rod's shape asymmetry and by a weak magnetic field on the Ni segment, so cargo (drug particles, cells, DNA) can be hauled directionally, mimicking kinesin‑style transport but fuel‑free and fully biocompatible in serum or tissue.

**Pump mode.** When the same rod is anchored (tethered to a substrate, or clamped in the constriction of a nanopore/membrane channel) it cannot translate, so its streaming jet instead drives the surrounding fluid: a persistent microvortex draws solute in at one face and expels it at the other, giving valve‑free, moving‑part‑free convective transport of ions and molecules **against** their concentration gradient — a synthetic active transporter functionally analogous to a membrane ATPase or a ciliary pump. Because the drive is remote and instantaneous, pumping can be switched, reversed (by changing the node position/frequency/phase) and multiplexed across an array of pores; transport is read out by ionic‑current recording, tracer‑particle velocimetry, or pH/ion‑sensitive dyes in vesicles, allowing stall pressure and efficiency to be measured as in single‑molecule motor assays.

**An artificial photosynthetic "redox‑loop" proton pump: a porphyrin–carotenoid–quinone (C–P–Q) triad plus a mobile quinone shuttle reconstituted in a liposome membrane.**

**Design.** Amphiphilic molecular triads — a carotenoid electron donor covalently linked to a porphyrin chromophore, which is in turn linked to a naphthoquinone acceptor — are inserted into the bilayer of a ~100 nm unilamellar vesicle with a fixed (vectorial) orientation, the carotene end facing outward and the quinone end facing the lumen. A pool of freely diffusing lipophilic quinones (e.g., ubiquinone‑type) dissolved in the bilayer serves as the mobile proton carrier, and a small amount of a soluble redox mediator sits inside the vesicle.

**Operation.** Light absorbed by the porphyrin (the energy input, replacing ATP hydrolysis) triggers sequential photoinduced electron transfer to give a long‑lived, membrane‑spanning charge‑separated state C•⁺–P–Q•⁻. The reduced quinone end picks up an electron and the oxidized carotenoid end oxidizes the mobile quinol; the mobile quinone is thereby reduced at the *inner* leaflet, where it takes up two protons from the vesicle interior, diffuses across the bilayer as quinol, and is re‑oxidized at the *outer* leaflet by the carotenoid radical cation, releasing its protons to the external medium. Each photon therefore drives one turn of a chemiosmotic "Q‑cycle": charge separation across the membrane is converted into vectorial proton translocation, exactly as in a photosynthetic reaction centre/cytochrome *bc*₁ complex or bacteriorhodopsin.

**Why it is a good mimic.** Directionality comes not from a mechanical ratchet but from the *asymmetric insertion* of the triad and from the spatial separation of the protonation and deprotonation steps (a redox‑loop ratchet), so protons are pumped **against** their electrochemical gradient, building a ΔpH/Δψ of >100 mV. The stored gradient is genuine free energy: co‑reconstituting F₀F₁‑ATP synthase in the same vesicle lets the pumped protons flow back and drive real ATP synthesis, demonstrating a fully synthetic light‑to‑chemical energy transducer coupled to a natural rotary motor. Pumping is read out with pH‑sensitive dyes (pyranine) or potential‑sensitive probes, and rate/direction are controlled by light intensity, wavelength and the quinone pool size.

**A carpet of magnetically actuated artificial cilia — superparamagnetic nanofilaments that beat non‑reciprocally to pump fluid, mimicking ciliary/flagellar propulsion.**

**Design.** Anchor an array of flexible nanofilaments (~100–500 nm diameter, 5–20 µm long) to a surface or to the mouth of a membrane/microchannel. Each filament is either a chain of self‑assembled superparamagnetic beads linked by DNA/biotin–streptavidin hinges, or a PDMS/hydrogel nanorod loaded with aligned Fe₃O₄ nanoparticles, so that its magnetic easy axis lies along the filament and its bending stiffness gives a sperm number ≈1–4 (elastic and viscous timescales comparable).

**Operation.** A weak (mT), rotating or precessing external magnetic field — the energy input replacing ATP hydrolysis in dynein — applies a distributed torque along the filament. Because the filament is elastic and the surrounding fluid is viscous, the induced bending wave lags the field, so the stroke is **non‑reciprocal**: a stiff, extended "effective stroke" that sweeps a large volume of fluid, followed by a curled, low‑drag "recovery stroke" close to the wall. Scallop‑theorem symmetry is thereby broken and each beat cycle produces a net displacement of fluid at low Reynolds number, exactly as in a beating cilium or eukaryotic flagellum. Phasing the field (or exploiting hydrodynamic coupling between neighbours) makes the array self‑organize into **metachronal waves**, the travelling‑wave coordination that biological ciliated epithelia use to boost transport efficiency.

**Pump/motor function.** Because the filaments are tethered and cannot swim, their beating drives directed flow parallel to the surface — a valve‑free, sub‑micron peristaltic/ciliary pump that transports solutes, particles, or cells through a nanochannel and, if it feeds a membrane pore, can concentrate solute on one side, i.e. active transport against a concentration gradient (mucociliary‑clearance‑like vectorial pumping). Direction and rate are set instantly by the field's rotation sense, frequency and tilt; reversing the field reverses the flow, and an imposed flow that bends the filaments generates a detectable inductive/optical signal, letting the same device work as a flow sensor. Pumping is read out by particle‑image velocimetry, tracer transport, or fluorescent dye fronts, and throughput scales simply by increasing cilia density.

**A nanoelectromechanical "single‑electron/ion shuttle": a nanocluster suspended on molecular springs that oscillates between two electrodes (or two faces of a membrane) and ferries charge one quantum at a time.**

**Design.** A ~5–20 nm gold nanoparticle (or a C₆₀ / metal‑cluster "bob") is tethered by two flexible molecular springs — alkanedithiol or oligo(phenylene‑ethynylene) linkers, or a short DNA/peptide hinge — inside a nanogap between a source and a drain electrode, or inside a nanopore spanning a lipid/solid‑state membrane. The shuttle's surface is decorated with a receptor: a redox‑active site (ferrocene/viologen) for electrons, or a crown‑ether/cryptand cage for a specific cation such as K⁺.

**Operation.** A DC bias (or the transmembrane potential) is the energy input, replacing ATP hydrolysis. At the negative electrode the shuttle touches down, is loaded with charge by tunnelling (or binds its cation in the *high‑affinity*, un‑charged state); the resulting Coulomb force accelerates it across the gap; at the far electrode it unloads the charge (or, being now electrostatically strained/oxidized, switches to a *low‑affinity* state and releases the ion), and the elastic restoring force plus the reversed Coulomb force sends it back. The cycle is self‑exciting, giving stable limit‑cycle oscillations at MHz–GHz, and each stroke transfers an integer number of charges — a discrete, quantized "power stroke" with load/transport/release/reset steps that reproduce exactly the alternating‑access, affinity‑switching cycle of a P‑type ATPase, and the vectorial charge translocation of cytochrome *c* oxidase or a mobile carrier like valinomycin (but actively driven rather than passive).

**Motor/pump character.** Directionality comes from the asymmetry of the two contacts (different work functions, tunnel barriers, or protonation environments), so the device is a genuine ratchet: with a suitable phase lag between mechanical position and charge state, an AC drive or a thermal/redox gradient can be rectified to move ions **against** their electrochemical gradient, building up a transmembrane potential/ΔpH that could be discharged through a co‑reconstituted ATP synthase. Mechanical oscillation is read out by the shuttle current (quantized steps of *Ne f*) or by optical/SEM tracking, and the stall force, step size and efficiency can be measured just as in single‑molecule motor assays; reversing the bias reverses the pumping direction, and letting an existing ion gradient drive the shuttle turns it into a nanogenerator that harvests the gradient.

**A chemically‑fuelled supramolecular/DNA "polymerisation ratchet" nanomotor — a synthetic mimic of the actin/microtubule (and ParM/FtsZ) pushing motors.**

**Design.** A nucleating "seed" (a short DNA‑origami or peptide‑amphiphile stub) is anchored on a rigid wall, and a load — a bead, vesicle membrane, or the piston plate of a nanochannel — is held loosely a few nanometres in front of it. The growth medium contains monomers kept in a metastable, kinetically trapped state: e.g. hairpin‑protected DNA tiles/strands, or dicarboxylate peptide monomers that only polymerise once "activated" by a chemical fuel (a carbodiimide, ATP itself, or a photoacid pulse). Fibre growth is thus strictly templated, occurring only at the free (barbed) end of the growing filament.

**Operation.** Thermal fluctuations of the load transiently open a gap larger than one monomer at the filament tip; a monomer inserts and is locked in place, so the load can no longer fluctuate back — a classic **Brownian ratchet** in which the free energy of monomer addition (fuel hydrolysis/hairpin opening replacing ATP hydrolysis) is rectified into directed force. Each insertion event advances the load by one subunit (~3–6 nm) and generates piconewton‑scale pushing force; bundling many filaments multiplies the force, exactly as an actin comet tail propels *Listeria* or a lamellipodium pushes a membrane. Fuel depletion/deactivation at the anchored end causes treadmilling, so the filament reaches a steady state and can run continuously as long as fuel is supplied.

**Pump mode.** Placing the filament bundle inside a nanochannel so that the pushed plate acts as a piston converts each growth‑and‑treadmill cycle into a displacement stroke that sweeps a fixed volume of solvent and solute from one reservoir to the other; alternatively, growing/depolymerising the fibre against a deformable membrane patch cyclically constricts and reopens a pore behind a captured ion, giving valve‑free peristaltic active transport of solute **against** its concentration gradient. Direction is set by which end is anchored and by the spatial pattern of fuel delivery, force and step size are read out by optical‑trap or AFM force spectroscopy (stall force, velocity–load curve) exactly as for real cytoskeletal motors, and the whole device is programmable through monomer sequence/chemistry and fuel concentration.

**A stimuli‑responsive polymer‑brush "gating ratchet" in an asymmetric (conical) nanopore — a soft‑matter mimic of an alternating‑access ion pump.**

**Design.** A single conical (or bullet‑shaped) nanopore in a track‑etched polymer or SiN membrane is grafted on its inner wall with a responsive polyelectrolyte brush: e.g. poly(N‑isopropylacrylamide)‑*co*‑acrylic acid, or a spiropyran/azobenzene‑functionalised brush, denser near the narrow tip than near the wide base. The brush chains carry ionisable groups (–COO⁻ or amine) that provide the ion‑binding/"affinity" element, while the cone's geometric and surface‑charge asymmetry provides the built‑in structural bias (ionic‑current rectification).

**Operation.** The membrane is exposed to a periodic, spatially asymmetric stimulus — a temperature, light, or pH/CO₂ oscillation applied from one face (the energy input replacing ATP hydrolysis). In the swollen, extended state the brush is highly charged, the tip constriction is nearly closed, and cations are captured with high affinity in the brush's counter‑ion cloud. On switching (heating above the LCST, or *trans→cis* photo‑isomerisation), the brush collapses: the effective pore opens, the local charge density and dielectric environment change, and the bound ions are released with low affinity — but because the collapse front propagates from the illuminated/heated face toward the other, and because the conical geometry makes the escape barrier much lower toward the base than toward the tip, the released ions preferentially leave on the far side. Reswelling closes the gate behind them, preventing back‑slip.

**Why it mimics a pump/motor.** Each swell–collapse cycle executes exactly the biological alternating‑access sequence — high‑affinity capture on one side, gated occlusion, affinity drop, low‑affinity release on the other side, reset — with the conformational "power stroke" of a P‑type ATPase replaced by the coil–globule transition of the brush, and directionality supplied by the kinetic/structural asymmetry rather than by any net applied force (an energy ratchet). Ions are therefore translocated **against** their electrochemical gradient, building a measurable transmembrane potential/concentration difference; reversing which face is stimulated (or the sign of the brush charge) reverses the pumping direction, and letting the accumulated gradient relax through the open pore runs the device downhill as a soft "motor" whose swelling strokes can also do mechanical work on an attached load. Pumping is read out by ionic‑current recording, ion‑selective electrodes, or fluorescent ion dyes in vesicle/two‑chamber assays, and throughput scales simply by using a multipore membrane.

**A feedback‑controlled ("Maxwell's‑demon") nanopore transporter: a solid‑state nanopore with an integrated single‑molecule sensor and gate electrode that rectifies thermal motion by information rather than by a net applied force.**

**Design.** A ~5–20 nm pore is drilled through a thin SiN/graphene/MoS₂ membrane and instrumented with two elements: (i) a *sensor* — the pore's own ionic‑current channel, or an embedded nanoribbon FET/plasmonic hot‑spot — that reports, with microsecond time resolution, whenever a single ion, charged nanoparticle, protein or DNA molecule enters the constriction and on which side it sits; and (ii) an *actuator* — a ring gate electrode (or a co‑located electro‑responsive polymer/plasmonic heating pad) that can raise or drop a local electrostatic barrier in the pore within a few microseconds. A fast FPGA/lock‑in feedback loop links the two.

**Operation.** The cargo is allowed to diffuse purely by Brownian motion; no directional force is ever applied. The controller continuously "watches" the sensor signal, and *only when* a fluctuation has already carried the particle past the pore's midplane in the desired direction does it switch the gate on, erecting a barrier behind the particle so that the favourable fluctuation cannot be undone. The barrier is then dropped and the loop repeats. Free energy is thus extracted from thermal noise at the cost of measurement and (Landauer) erasure of the acquired information, so solute is accumulated on one side of the membrane **against** its concentration/electrochemical gradient.

**Why it mimics a biological motor/pump.** This is the physical embodiment of the *information‑ratchet* mechanism that molecular biologists invoke for transporters and motors: biological pumps do not push their substrate, they cyclically gate it — the conformational state of the protein "knows" whether the substrate is bound and opens the outward or inward gate accordingly (alternating access, kinetic gating in kinesin's neck‑linker, or the "ratchet" of the Sec/Hsp70 translocon that traps forward Brownian excursions of a polypeptide). Here the protein's internal chemical logic is replaced by external electronics: the sensor is the substrate‑binding "sensing" step, the gate is the occlusion/gating step, and the electrical switching energy plays the role of ATP hydrolysis. Direction and pumping rate are reversed or tuned simply by flipping the feedback rule, latency, or barrier height; transport is read out from the same ionic current or by ion‑selective/fluorescent dyes in a two‑chamber or vesicle assay, allowing the device's thermodynamic efficiency to be benchmarked directly against the Landauer/Sagawa–Ueda information bounds and against real pumps such as the Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase.

**A self‑oscillating Belousov–Zhabotinsky (BZ) gel nanoactuator — a chemically fuelled "peristaltic" nanopump/artificial muscle.**

**Design.** Graft the redox catalyst Ru(bpy)₃²⁺ covalently into a thin (tens–hundreds of nm) poly(N‑isopropylacrylamide) hydrogel layer, patterned as an array of asymmetric (wedge‑ or cilium‑shaped) nanopillars, or as the deformable lining of a nanochannel/membrane pore. The gel is bathed in a solution of the BZ reactants (malonic acid, bromate, acid) — the chemical "fuel," the surrogate for ATP.

**Operation.** The Ru catalyst drives the autocatalytic BZ reaction inside the gel, so its oxidation state (Ru²⁺ ⇄ Ru³⁺) oscillates spontaneously with a period of tens of seconds. Because the oxidized Ru³⁺ form is more hydrophilic, the local LCST shifts and the gel cyclically swells and deswells with no external stimulus at all — the system runs continuously and autonomously as long as fuel is present, exactly as a muscle or motor protein turns over while substrate lasts. Crucially, the BZ chemistry propagates as a *travelling* chemical wave through the gel, so the swelling is not synchronous but arrives as a phased contraction wave sweeping from one end of the film/channel to the other — the direct chemical analogue of a peristaltic wave or of the metachronal beating of cilia.

**Why it mimics a motor/pump.** The travelling swell–collapse wave is *non‑reciprocal* (it has a definite propagation direction set by the wave source/gradient of fuel), so it breaks time‑reversal symmetry and can do net work at low Reynolds number: shaped nanopillars beat with an effective/recovery stroke and push fluid along the surface, while a wave running down a gel‑lined nanochannel squeezes a fixed slug of solvent and solute from one reservoir to the other in a valve‑free, moving‑part‑free displacement stroke. If the gel also carries ionisable groups, the swollen (high‑affinity) and collapsed (low‑affinity) states bind and then release cations at different points along the wave, giving an alternating‑access capture‑occlude‑release cycle that translocates ions **against** their electrochemical gradient — chemical free energy converted directly into vectorial transport, as in a P‑type ATPase; free gel strips instead undergo worm‑like self‑propulsion, mimicking muscle/flagellar motility.

**Control and readout.** Wave direction (hence pumping direction) is set by where the wave is nucleated or by a fuel/temperature gradient; rate is tuned by fuel concentration or by light, since Ru(bpy)₃²⁺ is photosensitive, allowing optical pacing and phase locking of arrays. Transport is monitored by particle‑image velocimetry, tracer/dye fronts, ionic‑current recording, or the colour change of the Ru oscillation itself, and force/stroke can be measured by AFM against a load.

**A piezoelectric "inchworm" nanoactuator driving a valveless nozzle–diffuser nanopump — an all‑solid‑state, electrically fuelled mimic of myosin's clamp‑and‑stroke cycle and of an alternating‑access transporter.**

**Design.** Grow a ZnO/AlN/PZT nanowire (or a stack of few‑nanometre ferroelectric films) as the active element, and pattern it as three series segments — a rear "clamp," a central "extender," and a front "clamp" — sitting in a nanofluidic slot whose walls it can grip. The slot narrows at each end into an asymmetric, funnel‑shaped constriction (nozzle in one direction, diffuser in the other), and one wall of the chamber is a flexible piezo‑driven membrane; the chamber connects two reservoirs (or the two faces of a membrane containing an ion‑selective sub‑nanometre orifice lined with carboxylate/crown‑ether binding sites).

**Operation (motor mode).** A four‑phase voltage sequence — the electrical surrogate for ATP hydrolysis — runs the cycle: front clamp grips (high‑affinity "bound" state) → the central segment expands by a few nanometres (the power stroke) → rear clamp releases (low‑affinity state) and is dragged forward → rear clamp re‑grips and the extender relaxes, advancing the body. Because the grip/release steps are *phase‑locked* to the extension step, the strokes are non‑reciprocal and the actuator walks processively along the track, generating nN forces with nanometre steps — exactly the attach–stroke–detach–reprime mechanochemical cycle of myosin or kinesin, with electrical energy replacing chemical fuel.

**Pump mode.** Anchor the actuator so it cannot translate and let it instead oscillate the chamber membrane. The symmetric volume oscillation is rectified by the asymmetric nozzle/diffuser ends (higher flow resistance one way than the other), so each cycle nets a fixed slug of fluid, ions and solute from one reservoir to the other — a valve‑free, wear‑free displacement pump. Phasing the two constrictions' gating with the volume stroke (open inlet while expanding, open outlet while contracting) plus strain‑modulated affinity of the binding sites (high affinity when the lumen is dilated, low when compressed) reproduces the capture–occlude–release–reset alternating‑access cycle of a P‑type ATPase, so solute is moved **against** its concentration/electrochemical gradient, storing free energy as a transmembrane gradient.

**Control/readout.** Direction and rate are set instantly by the drive phase sequence and frequency (kHz–MHz), reversing the phase reverses pumping, and an imposed pressure or gradient that flexes the piezo generates a measurable voltage — i.e., the same device run backwards is a nanogenerator harvesting the gradient, just as F₀ harvests the proton‑motive force. Stepping, stall force and efficiency are read out by AFM/interferometry, and transport by ionic‑current recording or ion‑selective dyes in a two‑chamber assay.

**A surface‑acoustic‑wave (SAW) "quantized charge pump" in a semiconductor nanowire/quantum‑dot channel — a solid‑state, single‑particle‑per‑cycle analogue of an ion pump.**

**Design.** Define a narrow (~50–100 nm) one‑dimensional channel in a GaAs/AlGaAs two‑dimensional electron gas (or in a Si/graphene nanoribbon) by split gates, so that a tunable tunnel barrier pinches the channel into a small quantum dot connected to a "source" reservoir on one side and a "drain" reservoir on the other. Interdigitated transducers patterned on the piezoelectric substrate launch a GHz surface acoustic wave that travels along the channel, creating a moving sinusoidal electrostatic potential (a train of travelling potential minima) superimposed on the static barrier. In a nanofluidic version of the same concept, the moving potential wave is applied to a nanochannel filled with electrolyte so that solvated ions, rather than electrons, are the cargo.

**Operation.** Each travelling minimum arrives at the source reservoir, scoops up carriers, and then rises as it climbs the static barrier; Coulomb blockade (the charging energy of the tiny moving dot) causes all but an integer number *n* of carriers to spill back, so exactly *n* charges are "occluded" in the moving well, carried adiabatically over the barrier, and released on the far side. The result is a precisely quantized current *I = nef* — one packet of cargo per acoustic cycle — that flows **even against an opposing bias**, i.e. uphill in electrochemical potential. The RF power driving the SAW (or the phase‑shifted AC gate voltages in a purely electrostatic "turnstile" version) is the energy input replacing ATP hydrolysis.

**Why it mimics a biological motor/pump.** This is the exact physics of alternating access with stoichiometric turnover: (1) a high‑capacity "outward‑open" state loads cargo from one reservoir; (2) the barrier rises behind it and the cargo is *occluded* in a closed cavity; (3) the cavity's energy is raised (affinity lowered) as it is translocated; (4) it opens to the opposite side and releases a fixed number of particles per cycle — the direct analogue of the 3 Na⁺/2 K⁺ per ATP stoichiometry of the Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase, or of the c‑ring of F₀ carrying one proton per site per turn. Directionality comes from the *travelling‑wave* (spatiotemporal) asymmetry of the drive rather than from any net static force, so it is a true energy ratchet, and reversing the SAW propagation direction (or the gate phase sequence) reverses the pumping direction, just as a gradient‑driven pump can be run backwards as a motor/synthase.

**Readout/utility.** Pumping is quantified simply as plateaus in the DC current at *I = nef* (metrological accuracy <1 ppm), giving a direct measure of "turnover number," stall (the counter‑bias at which pumping ceases) and thermodynamic efficiency, exactly as stall‑force and step‑size assays characterize kinesin or F₁; arrays of such channels give scalable, electrically gated active transport with no moving parts.

**A vectorially oriented photoacid/photobase "proton‑relay" membrane — a synthetic bacteriorhodopsin built from spiropyran–merocyanine switches wired to a hydrogen‑bonded proton wire.**

**Design.** Amphiphilic spiropyran (SP) molecules bearing a sulfonate/phenolate head are inserted with a fixed orientation into a lipid bilayer (or grafted asymmetrically into the mouth of a sub‑2‑nm nanoporous/peptide‑nanotube membrane). Each switch sits at the end of a short, pre‑organized chain of hydrogen‑bond donors/acceptors (ordered water plus carboxylate/imidazole "relay" residues), forming a Grotthuss proton wire that spans the membrane. A second, complementary photobase (or a simple pKa‑shifted acceptor) is placed at the opposite face so the wire is chemically asymmetric.

**Operation.** Light — replacing ATP hydrolysis or the proton‑motive force as the energy input — isomerizes SP to the merocyanine (MC) form, dropping its pKa by several units so that the group *releases* a proton into the wire on the inner face. The proton then hops Grotthuss‑style along the pre‑oriented hydrogen‑bond chain and is expelled on the outer face, because the relay's pKa values are deliberately graded (high → low) in that direction. Thermal (or second‑wavelength) back‑isomerization to SP restores the high‑pKa state, which now re‑protonates only from the *inner* reservoir, because the outer access path is sterically/electrostatically occluded in that conformer. Thus each photocycle executes a full alternating‑access sequence — high‑affinity uptake on one side, occlusion, affinity drop, low‑affinity release on the other side, reset — identical in logic to the retinal Schiff‑base/Asp85/Asp96 proton relay of bacteriorhodopsin.

**Why it is a good mimic.** Directionality arises not from an applied field but from the *structural asymmetry of insertion plus the kinetic asymmetry of the pKa cycle* (a chemical energy‑ratchet), so protons are translocated **against** their electrochemical gradient, building a ΔpH/Δψ of >100 mV across a vesicle. The stored gradient is real free energy: co‑reconstituting F₀F₁‑ATP synthase in the same liposome lets the pumped protons flow back downhill and make ATP, proving genuine active transport. Pumping rate and stoichiometry are read out with pyranine/pH‑sensitive dyes or patch‑clamp photocurrents; the direction reverses if the switches are inserted with opposite orientation, and illumination intensity/wavelength gives instantaneous, fuel‑free "metabolic" control with no moving parts.

**A de‑novo–designed protein "axle‑and‑rotor" nanomachine (a computationally designed rotary assembly) driven by a proton/pH gradient across a membrane — a fully synthetic protein analogue of F₀‑ATP synthase / the flagellar motor.**

**Design.** Use Rosetta/deep‑learning protein design to build two interlocking components: (i) a rigid C₃‑ or C₅‑symmetric α‑helical *axle* whose surface is decorated with a helical ladder of buried carboxylates (Asp/Glu "proton sites"), and (ii) a matched cyclic *rotor ring* that encircles the axle with a designed, deliberately "loose" knobs‑into‑holes interface, so the two parts are held together by shape complementarity but can slip rotationally with a shallow, sawtooth‑shaped (asymmetric) energy landscape. The ring is anchored in a lipid bilayer (or in the constriction of a solid‑state/DNA nanopore) by a designed transmembrane β‑barrel or amphipathic belt, which acts as the *stator*; a half‑channel in the stator gives access to one membrane face only near the interface, and a second offset half‑channel opens to the other face.

**Operation.** A proton entering from the acidic side through the first half‑channel protonates a carboxylate on the axle, neutralising its charge and allowing that site to rotate into the hydrophobic ring interior; it can only be deprotonated after ~one step of rotation, when it reaches the second half‑channel facing the basic side. Because protonation/deprotonation is *kinetically gated by position* (an information/energy ratchet built into the designed pKₐ ladder and the asymmetric interface potential), thermal fluctuations are rectified into continuous unidirectional rotation — exactly the mechanism of the c‑ring of F₀ or the MotA/B stator of the flagellar motor, with the transmembrane proton‑motive force replacing ATP.

**Motor and pump modes.** Coupled through a designed coiled‑coil shaft to a downstream cam or to a designed "clamp" domain, the rotation performs cyclic mechanical work (turning a fluorescently labelled bead/DNA‑origami paddle for single‑molecule readout, or driving a conformational cycle in a synthetic catalytic ring). Run **in reverse** — by torquing the shaft with magnetic tweezers or by coupling it to a chemically driven module — the same device pumps protons (or a designed Na⁺‑selective site) *against* their electrochemical gradient, building a ΔpH/Δψ in reconstituted vesicles that can be read out with pyranine or by single‑channel electrophysiology, and even used to drive a co‑reconstituted ATP synthase.

**Why it is a good mimic.** It reproduces the actual architecture and physics of biological rotary transporters — rotor/stator, half‑channels, position‑gated protonation, Brownian ratcheting — but every element is sequence‑programmable, so step size (ring symmetry), ion selectivity (binding‑site chemistry), torque and directionality (interface asymmetry/handedness) can be systematically tuned and tested.

**A photo‑responsive liquid‑crystal‑elastomer (LCE) nanofibre "artificial muscle" lining a nanochannel — a light‑driven peristaltic nanopump/contractile motor.**

**Design.** Synthesise nematic elastomer nanofibres/nanotubes (~50–200 nm across) from acrylate mesogens crosslinked while the director is aligned along the fibre axis, with azobenzene mesogens (or a molecular photoswitch dopant) copolymerised into the network. Either (i) bundle thousands of such fibres in parallel between a fixed anchor and a movable load (a piston plate, a bead, or a membrane patch), or (ii) use the elastomer as the compliant lining of a sub‑micron fluidic channel/pore, with the director patterned azimuthally so that local contraction pinches the lumen. Ionisable comonomers (–COO⁻/sulfonate) in the network give ion‑binding sites whose affinity depends on the network's strain and mesophase.

**Operation.** Light (or a thermal/electrical pulse) is the energy input replacing ATP hydrolysis: photoisomerisation of the azobenzene units disrupts nematic order, driving a nematic→isotropic transition that makes the network contract by 20–50 % along the director within milliseconds; back‑isomerisation in the dark (or with a second wavelength) restores order and re‑extends the fibre. Because contraction is anisotropic and molecular‑scale ordering is amplified over the whole fibre length, each cycle produces a genuine power stroke — nanometre–micrometre displacements at 10⁵–10⁶ N/m² stress — exactly the way summed myosin power strokes shorten a sarcomere.

**Motor/pump mode.** Scanning or phase‑delaying the illumination (a moving light spot, an interference pattern, or spectrally distinguishable switches addressed in sequence) creates a *travelling* contraction wave down the elastomer‑lined channel. This wave is non‑reciprocal, so at low Reynolds number it squeezes a fixed slug of fluid and solute from one reservoir to the other — a valve‑free, moving‑part‑free peristaltic pump, the soft‑matter analogue of ciliary/gut peristalsis. If the network's ionisable sites bind cations strongly in the swollen, ordered (extended) state and weakly in the collapsed, disordered state, each wave performs a capture → occlude → affinity‑drop → release cycle displaced in space, i.e. an alternating‑access transport cycle that moves ions **against** their electrochemical gradient and stores free energy as a transmembrane gradient. Reversing the direction of the light wave reverses pumping; free‑standing patterned fibres instead crawl or swim, mimicking muscle‑powered motility. Stroke, force and stall load are read out by AFM/optical‑trap force spectroscopy, and transport by tracer PIV, ionic‑current recording, or ion‑sensitive dyes in a two‑chamber/vesicle assay.

**An AC‑field–driven Janus metallodielectric nanorotor working by induced‑charge electro‑osmosis (ICEO)/Quincke rotation — a "field‑fuelled" rotary nanomotor that becomes an electro‑osmotic nanopump when anchored in a pore.**

**Design.** A ~100–300 nm particle made half of a polarizable conductor (Au or doped Si) and half of a dielectric (silica/polystyrene), or a similarly shape‑asymmetric metal nanostructure (L‑shaped or "carrom‑disc" rod), is suspended in a low‑conductivity electrolyte between coplanar microelectrodes, or is tethered by a short molecular/DNA hinge inside the constriction of a nanopore that spans a membrane. Interdigitated electrodes on the pore rim supply a modest AC field (kHz–MHz, a few V).

**Operation.** The applied field polarizes the metal face and charges its own electrical double layer; the field then acts on these *induced* counter‑ions, driving a steady second‑order slip flow over the metal hemisphere only (ICEO). Because the particle is Janus, the slip is spatially asymmetric and does not average to zero even under a symmetric AC drive — the classic broken‑symmetry rectification of an oscillatory input, exactly the non‑reciprocity that a flagellum needs at low Reynolds number. At higher fields/lower frequencies the same particle undergoes Quincke rotation (spontaneous symmetry breaking of the induced dipole), spinning continuously about an axis perpendicular to the field, with the handedness selected by an initial fluctuation or by a small DC/magnetic bias. Electrical energy replaces ATP hydrolysis or the proton‑motive force, and speed/direction are set instantly by frequency, amplitude and electrode phasing.

**Pump mode.** When the rotor is clamped in the pore it cannot translate, so its ICEO slip layer instead drives the surrounding electrolyte: a persistent, valve‑free electro‑osmotic jet carries water and dissolved ions from one reservoir through the constriction to the other. Making the pore wall or the particle surface chemically asymmetric (charged/ion‑binding patches whose occupancy is modulated in phase with the field) adds a capture–occlude–release cycle on top of the convection, so solute can be accumulated **against** its concentration/electrochemical gradient — a synthetic active transporter functionally analogous to a rotary membrane ATPase, but with no chemical fuel, no wear and no moving mechanical parts.

**Readout/control.** Rotation is tracked optically (scattering flicker or a fluorescent marker on the dielectric face), pumping by tracer PIV, ionic‑current recording or ion‑selective dyes in a two‑chamber/vesicle assay; reversing the electrode phase reverses the flow, and a pressure‑driven flow that spins the rotor generates a measurable impedance/streaming signal, letting the device also run "backwards" as a gradient‑harvesting turbine. Arrays of such rotors in a nanoporous membrane give scalable, electrically gated active transport.

**A light‑driven semiconductor‑nanowire "photoelectrochemical proton pump" membrane — an inorganic redox‑loop mimic of a photosynthetic/bacteriorhodopsin proton pump.**

**Design.** Fabricate a dense, vertically aligned array of ~100 nm Si (or TiO₂/Ta₃N₅–Si tandem) nanowires that penetrate a thin, otherwise ion‑impermeable polymer/oxide membrane, so each wire forms a nanoscale p–n (or semiconductor–electrolyte) junction whose two ends face opposite reservoirs. The end facing side A is coated with an oxidation catalyst (IrOₓ/CoPi, or a quinone/hydroquinone monolayer); the end facing side B carries a reduction catalyst (Pt or a Ni‑bis(diphosphine) complex). The built‑in junction field is oriented so that photogenerated holes are swept to the A end and electrons to the B end. A thin proton‑conducting (Nafion/graphene‑oxide) skirt seals the wires into the membrane so that the only route for ions is through the catalytic reactions themselves.

**Operation.** Absorbed photons — the energy input replacing ATP hydrolysis or the proton‑motive force — create electron–hole pairs; the internal junction field vectorially separates them (this asymmetry is the "ratchet" that sets direction, exactly as the fixed orientation of a reaction centre does in a thylakoid). At the A face, holes drive an oxidation that *releases* protons into reservoir A (e.g. hydroquinone → quinone + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻, or water oxidation); the electrons travel through the nanowire and at the B face drive a reduction that *consumes* protons from reservoir B (quinone/H⁺ reduction or H⁺ → ½H₂). Each electron transferred through the wire therefore moves one proton's worth of charge from B to A without the proton ever diffusing through the membrane — a solid‑state "redox loop," the same chemical logic used by complex I and cytochrome *bc*₁.

**Why it mimics a biological pump.** Directionality comes from vectorial insertion and the spatial separation of protonation/deprotonation steps rather than from any applied force, so protons are translocated **against** their electrochemical gradient, building a ΔpH/Δψ of hundreds of millivolts across the membrane. The stored free energy is genuine: co‑reconstituting F₀F₁‑ATP synthase in a lipid patch on the membrane (or feeding the gradient to a downstream nanofluidic diode) lets the pumped protons run back downhill to do chemical or mechanical work, just as a proton gradient powers ATP synthesis or the flagellar motor.

**Control/readout.** Pumping rate scales with light intensity and wavelength (instant, fuel‑free "metabolic" control); direction reverses if the wire polarity/catalyst placement is flipped or if the membrane is illuminated from the opposite face. Transport is quantified with pyranine/pH microelectrodes in a two‑chamber cell, by short‑circuit photocurrent (giving turnover number and stoichiometry), and by the stall condition — the counter‑ΔpH at which net pumping ceases — the analogue of a stall‑force measurement on a single motor protein.

**A light‑driven "shuttle carrier" nanotransporter: an azobenzene–crown‑ether (photoswitchable ionophore) mobile carrier operating in a lipid bilayer under asymmetric illumination — a synthetic mimic of a carrier‑type (valinomycin/P‑type‑ATPase‑like) ion pump.**

**Design.** A lipophilic amphiphile is built from a cation‑binding macrocycle (an 18‑crown‑6 or calixarene/cryptand cage selective for K⁺ or Na⁺) tethered to an azobenzene (or a hemithioindigo/donor–acceptor Stenhouse adduct) photoswitch, with a second, cooperative binding arm (e.g., a carboxylate or a second crown) positioned so that the *cis* isomer forms a closed, high‑affinity sandwich cage around the ion, whereas the *trans* isomer is extended and binds it only weakly. The carrier is highly hydrophobic, so it partitions into and diffuses freely within the bilayer of a ~100 nm liposome (or a supported/black lipid membrane) but cannot leave it — exactly like a natural mobile ionophore.

**Operation.** Light is the energy input, replacing ATP hydrolysis. The outer face of the vesicle is illuminated at the wavelength that generates the *cis*, high‑affinity form; there the carrier picks up the cation (with its counter‑charge neutralised by the ligand's own carboxylate, so no net charge is dragged). The loaded complex diffuses down the ~4 nm hydrophobic slab to the inner leaflet, where — in the dark/shaded interior, or under a second wavelength or simply by fast thermal *cis→trans* relaxation timed to match the transit — the cage springs open, the affinity drops by several orders of magnitude, and the ion is released into the lumen. The empty *trans* carrier diffuses back, is re‑isomerised at the illuminated face, and the cycle repeats.

**Why it mimics a biological pump.** Each turnover reproduces the canonical alternating‑access sequence — high‑affinity capture on one side, occlusion during translocation, photochemically/kinetically triggered affinity drop, low‑affinity release on the other side, reset — but with the protein's conformational change replaced by a molecular photoisomerisation. Crucially, directionality does *not* come from any applied force: it comes from the **spatial asymmetry of the light field combined with the kinetic asymmetry of the switching cycle** (an energy/information ratchet), so the carrier's own Brownian diffusion is rectified and ions are accumulated **against** their electrochemical gradient, building a measurable ΔpM/Δψ (tens to >100 mV) across the membrane. Unlike valinomycin, which can only dissipate a gradient, this device *creates* one.

**Control and readout.** Rate scales with photon flux (the "fuel flux") and carrier loading; the pumping direction reverses if the vesicle is illuminated from the inside or if the two wavelengths are swapped; selectivity is programmed by the macrocycle cavity size (K⁺ vs Na⁺ vs Ca²⁺). Transport is quantified with ion‑selective fluorescent dyes (PBFI, pyranine for a coupled H⁺ antiport) or ion‑selective electrodes in a two‑chamber assay, the stall condition (the back‑gradient at which net flux ceases) gives the analogue of a stall‑force measurement, and co‑reconstituting F₀F₁‑ATP synthase lets the stored gradient run back downhill to make real ATP — proving genuine, light‑powered active transport with no moving mechanical parts.

**A synthetic "translocase/packaging‑motor": a clamp‑and‑ratchet nanoring that threads a polymer chain through a pore, mimicking the φ29 DNA‑packaging motor / SecA–Hsp70 translocon.**

**Design.** A rigid DNA‑origami (or designed protein) ring ~20 nm across is mounted on the rim of a membrane‑ or solid‑state nanopore. The ring carries two independently addressable, sequence‑programmed "clamp" arms (single‑stranded gripper domains, or intercalator/aptamer jaws) spaced one step apart along the lumen, plus a compliant "lever" element between them that can extend and retract. A guest polymer — duplex DNA, a synthetic polyelectrolyte, or an unfolded peptide — is threaded through the ring and pore, with a bead/vesicle load on the far side.

**Operation.** A fuel cycle (pulses of a hairpin fuel strand consumed by toehold exchange, an ATP/carbodiimide‑activated acylation, or alternating pH/light pulses — the surrogate for ATP hydrolysis) runs a strictly ordered four‑stroke sequence: (1) the trailing clamp grips the chain (high‑affinity state); (2) the lever contracts, pulling a fixed ~2–5 nm segment of chain through the pore (power stroke); (3) the leading clamp closes behind it and the trailing clamp is switched to its low‑affinity state and released; (4) the lever re‑extends and re‑grips further back, resetting the machine. Because grip/release is kinetically coupled to the lever stroke, back‑slip is blocked and thermal fluctuations of the chain are rectified — a hand‑over‑hand Brownian ratchet with a defined step size and stoichiometry (one step per fuel turnover), exactly like the pentameric φ29 ATPase compressing DNA into a capsid or the Hsp70 "trapping ratchet" that pulls polypeptides through the ER/mitochondrial translocon.

**Motor/pump character.** Because it pulls the chain against a tethered load or against the entropic/osmotic back‑pressure of an already‑crowded compartment, it does real work — packaging polymer into a vesicle at densities far above equilibrium, i.e. transporting matter *against* its chemical potential, the polymeric analogue of an ion pump. Running the ring in the opposite phase order reverses translocation (ejection), and letting a pre‑stressed, loaded vesicle drive the ring backwards turns the device into a gradient‑harvesting motor. Step size, stall force and turnover are read out directly by nanopore ionic current, magnetic/optical tweezers on the chain end, or FRET between the two clamps — the same single‑molecule assays used on real packaging motors.

**A bubble‑propelled tubular nanojet engine — a rolled‑up (or template‑grown) microtube/nanotube with a catalytic inner wall, which becomes a "bubble pump" when anchored.**

**Design.** A conical tube ~100–500 nm inner diameter and 2–10 µm long is made by rolling up a strained metal/polymer nanomembrane or by electrodepositing Pt (or Mg/Zn, or immobilised catalase/urease) inside a template pore, so that the *interior* is catalytic while the exterior is inert; a Ni layer can be added for magnetic steering and a cargo dock (antibody, DNA, drug capsule) on the outer wall. The engine is suspended in dilute H₂O₂ (or, in biocompatible versions, water/gastric fluid or urea solution, where Mg/Zn or urease generates H₂/CO₂/NH₃).

**Operation.** Fuel entering the wide opening is decomposed on the inner catalytic wall, so gas becomes supersaturated *inside the confined lumen*, nucleating microbubbles that grow, are pushed asymmetrically toward the wider end by the conical geometry and Laplace‑pressure gradient, and are ejected as a periodic bubble train. Each ejection imparts recoil momentum and drags fluid behind it, giving a **non‑reciprocal, cyclic power stroke**: chemical free energy → a discrete mechanical impulse, repeated at tens to hundreds of hertz, propelling the tube at hundreds of body‑lengths per second even in serum or viscous media. Fuel concentration sets the "turnover rate" exactly as substrate concentration sets a motor protein's stepping rate, the conical asymmetry (not an external field) sets the direction — a purely geometric ratchet — and a weak magnetic field on the Ni layer steers it, so cargo is hauled directionally like kinesin hauling a vesicle, or like a bacterium swimming up a gradient (the tubes even show chemotaxis toward fuel).

**Pump mode.** Anchor the same tube (or an array of catalytic conical pores) in the wall of a nanochannel or across a membrane so it cannot translate: the periodic bubble growth‑and‑ejection now acts as a valve‑less positive‑displacement stroke, each cycle sweeping a fixed slug of liquid and its dissolved solutes from the narrow to the wide end, with the conical taper providing the flow‑rectifying (nozzle/diffuser) asymmetry that prevents backflow. The result is a steady, fuel‑gated convective flux that can accumulate solute on one side **against** its concentration gradient — a chemically powered active transporter, functionally analogous to a membrane ATPase, but built with no moving mechanical parts. Pumping switches on/off with fuel supply (built‑in "metabolic" regulation), reverses if the cone orientation is flipped, and is read out by tracer particle‑image velocimetry, ionic‑current recording, or dye fronts; stall pressure and per‑cycle displacement give the analogues of stall force and step size in single‑molecule motor assays.

**A chemically fuelled Marangoni ("surface‑tension‑gradient") active droplet — a self‑propelling nanodroplet swimmer that becomes an interfacial nanopump when pinned.**

**Design.** A ~100–500 nm oil (or aqueous‑in‑oil) droplet is dispersed in a surfactant solution above its critical micelle concentration, or is loaded with a precursor that is slowly converted at the interface (e.g., micellar solubilisation/monomer of the droplet, hydrolysis of an ester surfactant, or a catalytic patch on one face). The droplet interface therefore carries a self‑generated, self‑sustaining gradient of surfactant coverage rather than any fabricated moving part.

**Operation.** Consumption/production of surfactant at the interface (the chemical fuel, standing in for ATP hydrolysis) depletes surfactant at the droplet's leading pole and enriches it at the trailing pole. The resulting interfacial‑tension difference drives a Marangoni slip flow along the surface from low to high tension, which propels the droplet in the opposite direction at tens of body‑lengths per second. The symmetry is broken **spontaneously**, by an advection–diffusion instability that amplifies any fluctuation in the concentration field (or is imposed by a Janus catalytic cap), so a symmetric object converts isotropic chemical free energy into persistent, directed motion — the same spontaneous polarity‑and‑flow mechanism that drives amoeboid cell crawling and cytoplasmic streaming, and, like a real motor protein, it runs autonomously as long as fuel lasts, shows chemotaxis up fuel/surfactant gradients, and stops when the fuel is exhausted.

**Pump mode.** Pin the same droplet in the mouth of a nanopore or at a patterned wettability patch on a channel wall so that it cannot translate: its Marangoni slip layer then drives the surrounding liquid instead, producing a steady, valve‑free interfacial jet and toroidal vortex that convects water, ions and solutes from one reservoir through the constriction into the other. If the droplet interface additionally carries an ionisable/complexing surfactant whose ion affinity is high in the compressed (surfactant‑rich) trailing region and low in the depleted leading region, each circulation of the interface executes a capture → transport → release cycle, so solute can be accumulated on one side **against** its concentration gradient — a fuel‑powered, moving‑part‑free active transporter functionally analogous to a membrane ATPase.

**Control/readout.** Speed and pumping rate scale with fuel (surfactant/substrate) concentration, giving built‑in "metabolic" regulation; direction is set by the catalytic cap orientation or by an external chemical gradient and reverses when the gradient is flipped; flow is measured by tracer particle‑image velocimetry, dye fronts, or ionic‑current recording across the pore, and the stall pressure and per‑cycle displacement give the analogues of stall force and step size in single‑molecule motor assays.

**A "molecular‑gyroscope" MOF membrane: a metal–organic framework (amphidynamic crystal) whose channel walls are lined with dipolar rotor linkers that are driven by a rotating/phased electric field to ratchet guests through the pores.**

**Design.** Grow an oriented, defect‑free MOF (or covalent‑organic‑framework) thin film — e.g. a pillared‑paddlewheel framework with 1–2 nm one‑dimensional channels — spanning a support so it separates two reservoirs. Each channel wall linker is a "molecular gyroscope": a bulky, rigid stator cage (triptycene/bicyclic struts fixed into the framework lattice) enclosing a freely rotating dipolar rotator (a fluorinated/nitro‑substituted phenylene or a bistable dipolar switch) mounted on a low‑barrier alkyne axle, so it spins almost frictionlessly inside the crystal. The rotors are arranged as a helical ladder down each channel, and their local torsional potential is made asymmetric (sawtooth) by substituent/lattice registry. Interdigitated electrodes on the two faces of the film, or a graded set of spectrally distinct rotors, allow the rotor layers to be addressed sequentially.

**Operation.** A rotating (or phase‑stepped, MHz–GHz) electric field — the energy input replacing ATP hydrolysis — torques the permanent dipoles, so each rotor layer flips in a programmed phase sequence from one face of the membrane to the other. Because each rotor's dipole simultaneously creates a local electrostatic well (a high‑affinity binding site for a cation or polar guest) and a steric constriction when it lies across the channel, the phased flipping produces a **travelling wave of binding sites and gates** through the pore: a guest is captured at a rotor pointing "in," is occluded as the upstream rotor rotates shut behind it, is handed to the next site downstream as that rotor's dipole reorients and its affinity drops, and is finally expelled on the far face. The built‑in sawtooth torsional landscape plus the spatiotemporal asymmetry of the drive make this an energy ratchet, not a driven flow, so no net static force is ever applied to the guest.

**Why it mimics a biological motor/pump.** Each rotor executes the exact alternating‑access cycle of a P‑type ATPase (high‑affinity capture → occlusion → affinity drop → release → reset), while the phased array reproduces the proton‑relay/hand‑over‑hand logic of bacteriorhodopsin and the rotor–stator gating of the F₀ c‑ring — with a genuine, atomically defined rotary element (the gyroscope) as the moving part. Ions or small polar molecules are therefore translocated **against** their electrochemical gradient, storing free energy as a transmembrane ΔpM/Δψ.

**Control/readout.** Direction and rate reverse instantly with the field's rotation sense, phase order and frequency; selectivity is programmed by channel aperture and rotor substituents. Rotor dynamics are measured by variable‑temperature ²H/¹³C solid‑state NMR and dielectric spectroscopy (the "turnover number"), transport by ionic‑current recording or ion‑selective/pH dyes in a two‑chamber assay, and the counter‑gradient at which pumping ceases gives the analogue of a stall‑force measurement; an imposed gradient driving the rotors backwards makes the film a gradient‑harvesting nanogenerator.

**A VO₂ (phase‑change/shape‑memory) nanobeam actuator lining a nanochannel — an electro‑thermally "fuelled" power‑stroke motor/pump.**

**Design.** Single‑crystal vanadium‑dioxide nanobeams (~100 nm × 50 nm cross‑section, a few µm long) — or NiTi shape‑memory nanowires — are clamped at one end to a rigid frame and at the other to a paddle/piston, or are used as the deformable lining of a sub‑micron channel that connects two reservoirs through an asymmetric (nozzle–diffuser or conical) constriction. Each beam carries a resistive contact for microsecond Joule pulses (or is heated by a plasmonic antenna/laser), and its surface is functionalised with carboxylate/crown‑ether ion‑binding groups whose affinity is strain‑ and temperature‑dependent.

**Operation.** A short electrical (or optical) pulse — the surrogate for ATP hydrolysis — drives the beam through its first‑order insulator‑to‑metal structural transition at ~68 °C: the lattice snaps from the monoclinic to the rutile phase, producing a fast (<µs), essentially digital ~1 % axial contraction/bending stroke that develops GPa‑scale stress and nN forces. Cooling between pulses restores the original phase and re‑primes the beam.
