Because the transition is hysteretic and first order, the "attach–stroke–release–reset" sequence is intrinsically non‑reciprocal and bistable — a true two‑state power stroke with a latch, exactly like the lever‑arm swing of myosin (and the hysteresis blocks back‑slip, giving the ratchet).

**Motor/pump function.** Phasing the pulses along a row of beams creates a travelling contraction wave that peristaltically squeezes a fixed slug of fluid and solute through the channel (valve‑free), while the asymmetric constriction rectifies the volume oscillation of a single beam into net flow. Because the binding sites are high‑affinity in the cool, dilated monoclinic state and low‑affinity in the hot, compressed rutile state, each pulse cycle executes a capture → occlude → affinity‑drop → release → reset sequence displaced in space, i.e. an alternating‑access cycle that moves ions **against** their electrochemical gradient, storing free energy as a transmembrane/interchamber gradient.

**Control/readout.** Direction and rate are set by the pulse phase sequence and repetition rate (kHz), and reverse when the phase order is reversed; stroke, stall force and efficiency are measured by AFM/interferometry, and transport by ionic‑current recording or ion‑selective dyes in a two‑chamber assay. An imposed strain that switches the beam back generates a measurable resistance change, so the same element run backwards reports (and can harvest) the gradient.

**A conducting‑polymer "redox ion pump": a PEDOT:PSS (organic electronic ion pump, OEIP) nanochannel that cycles its oxidation state to load, occlude and expel ions across a membrane — an electrically fuelled mimic of a P‑type ATPase/neurotransmitter transporter.**

**Design.** A thin (tens of nm) ion‑selective conducting‑polymer film — PEDOT doped with immobile polyanionic PSS⁻ (or a polycationic analogue for anion pumping) — is patterned as the lining of a sub‑100 nm channel or as a plug filling a pore through an otherwise impermeable membrane, connecting a "source" reservoir to a "target" reservoir. Two nanoelectrodes contact the polymer at its two ends; the fixed PSS⁻ sulfonates in the matrix are the cation‑binding sites, and cross‑linking makes the film permselective, so only counter‑ions (K⁺, Na⁺, Ca²⁺, H⁺, or protonated neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine or glutamate) can move through it while co‑ions and solvent bulk flow are excluded.

**Operation.** A small applied voltage (a few hundred mV, the electrical surrogate for ATP hydrolysis) drives the reversible redox reaction PEDOT⁺ + e⁻ + M⁺ ⇌ PEDOT⁰·M⁺. When a segment is electrochemically **reduced**, the polymer backbone loses its positive charge, the fixed sulfonates become uncompensated, and the segment switches to a *high‑affinity, "outward‑open"* state that draws a cation in from the source side and swells to trap it. Propagating the redox front along the channel (by phasing the two electrode potentials, or by using a series of independently addressed polymer segments) carries the bound ion through an **occluded** interior in which neither reservoir has access, exactly as in the E1P→E2P occluded intermediate of a P‑type ATPase. When the segment is then **oxidized**, the backbone regains its positive charge, electrostatically displaces the cation from the sulfonate site (*affinity drops by orders of magnitude*) and the deswelling film expels it into the target reservoir; the electrode then resets the segment for the next cycle. Because charge injection at the electrodes and the redox‑front direction are set by the applied waveform, the sequence is strictly ordered and non‑reciprocal — an energy ratchet with a defined stoichiometry of roughly one ion per electron transferred, i.e. a measurable "turnover number" and coupling ratio.

**Why it mimics a biological pump.** It reproduces the actual physical logic of active transport — high‑affinity capture on one face, occlusion during translocation, electrochemically triggered affinity switch, low‑affinity release on the far face, reset — with the protein's conformational change replaced by a redox‑driven swelling/charge switch of the polymer. Ions are therefore delivered **against** their concentration/electrochemical gradient with zero convective solvent flow (no "leak"), building a ΔpM/Δψ across the membrane; the same device run in reverse (letting the built‑up gradient discharge through the polymer) produces a current, harvesting the gradient just as F₀ harvests the proton‑motive force.

**Control and readout.** Rate scales linearly with current (the "fuel flux"), direction reverses instantly with the sign of the bias, and selectivity is programmed by the fixed‑charge chemistry and mesh size of the polymer. Transport is quantified by ion‑selective electrodes, pH/Ca²⁺ fluorescent dyes or amperometric detection in a two‑chamber or vesicle assay, and the counter‑gradient at which net flux ceases gives the analogue of a stall‑force measurement — while, practically, such pumps already deliver neurotransmitters to single cells on demand, functioning as an artificial synapse.

**A suspended‑graphene (or MoS₂) "ripple‑wave" nanochannel — an electrostatically driven flexural‑wave peristaltic pump.**

**Design.** Two atomically thin 2‑D membranes are suspended a few nanometres apart to form a slit nanochannel spanning two reservoirs (or bridging a lipid‑bilayer/solid‑state pore). Beneath the lower sheet sits a row of independently addressable nanogate electrodes spaced ~20–50 nm apart; the channel walls are functionalized with a periodic ladder of charged/ion‑coordinating groups (carboxylates, crown‑ether or oxygen‑functionalized sites) whose ion affinity depends on local strain and wall separation.

**Operation.** Applying phase‑shifted AC voltages (MHz–GHz) to the gate array electrostatically pulls the graphene sheet down at successive positions, launching a **travelling flexural ripple** (a nanoscale surface wave) along the channel — the electrical surrogate for ATP hydrolysis. Because the deformation wave moves in a definite direction, the sequence of local constrictions and dilations is non‑reciprocal, so at essentially zero Reynolds number it squeezes a fixed slug of water and solute from one reservoir to the other, valve‑free — exactly the peristalsis used by gut smooth muscle and the metachronal ripples of ciliated epithelia, and the same "travelling‑wave" symmetry breaking a flagellum uses to generate thrust.

**Why it mimics a pump/motor.** Each wall segment cycles through dilated (wide gap, hydrated, **high‑affinity** binding site occupied) → constricted/occluded (ion sealed off from both reservoirs, dragged forward with the ripple) → compressed (dehydrated, strained site, **affinity drops**, ion expelled) → reset — i.e. the canonical capture–occlude–affinity‑switch–release–reset alternating‑access cycle of a P‑type ATPase, but with the protein's conformational change replaced by an electro‑mechanical ripple of a 2‑D crystal. Directionality comes purely from the spatiotemporal phase asymmetry of the gate sequence (an energy ratchet), not from any net static field on the ions, so solute can be accumulated **against** its electrochemical gradient, storing free energy as a Δψ/ΔpM.

**Control and readout.** Direction and rate reverse instantly by reversing the gate phase order and scale with drive frequency ("turnover rate"); selectivity is set by slit width (sub‑nanometre confinement gives K⁺/Na⁺ discrimination). Ripple amplitude and phase velocity are measured by interferometry/AFM or by the gates' capacitance, transport by ionic‑current recording, tracer PIV or ion‑selective dyes in a two‑chamber/vesicle assay, and the back‑gradient at which net flux stops gives the analogue of a stall‑force measurement — while an externally imposed pressure‑driven flow that flexes the membrane generates a measurable capacitive/streaming signal, letting the identical device run backwards as a gradient‑harvesting nanogenerator, just as F₀ harvests the proton‑motive force.

**A small‑molecule bipedal "nanowalker" that strides along a molecular track by dynamic‑covalent foot exchange (a synthetic kinesin), and, arrayed inside a nanochannel, acts as a hand‑over‑hand solute escalator.**

**Design.** The walker is a short rigid organic "body" (e.g., a stilbene/biphenyl strut) terminating in two chemically *orthogonal* feet: one foot bearing a thiol (able to form/break disulfide bonds) and the other a hydrazide (able to form/break hydrazone bonds). The track is a rigid oligomeric molecular strand — a rod‑like oligo(phenylene‑ethynylene) or a peptide/DNA‑supported strand — presenting an alternating sequence of complementary footholds (thiol, aldehyde, thiol, aldehyde…) spaced ~1 nm apart, anchored at one end so the track has a defined polarity.

**Operation.** The two chemistries are switched on and off by *different* external conditions: disulfide exchange is turned on by base/thiol catalyst and frozen by acid, whereas hydrazone exchange is turned on by acid and frozen by base. Alternating acid and base pulses (the surrogate for ATP hydrolysis) therefore release and re‑attach only one foot at a time, so the walker never fully detaches and moves processively, hand over hand, exactly like kinesin's coordinated two‑head cycle. Making one of the exchange steps *kinetically* rather than thermodynamically controlled — for example by adding a photochemical E→Z isomerisation of the body, or a fuel‑driven activation that biases which foothold the freed leg can reach — converts the random shuffle into a **ratcheted, directional** stride: the free foot is preferentially delivered to the next foothold forward, and closing the bond behind it blocks back‑slip. The chemical energy of the fuel is thus not used to push the walker but to bias its Brownian excursions, the defining physics of biological motors.

**Pump mode.** Graft a dense ladder of such walkers (or their track‑bound "gripper" feet) along the inner wall of a sub‑2‑nm nanochannel or membrane pore, with each foot carrying a crown‑ether/carboxylate ion‑binding site whose affinity is high in the bound (closed) state and low in the released (open) state. Driving the acid/base (or light) cycle as a *travelling phase wave* down the channel means each site captures an ion at one position, hands it to the next site downstream, and releases it — a capture → occlude → affinity‑drop → release → reset alternating‑access relay that translocates ions **against** their electrochemical gradient, storing free energy as a transmembrane ΔpM/Δψ, just as a P‑type ATPase does.

**Readout/control.** Stepping is followed by HPLC/NMR analysis of the isomeric track‑bound species (giving directionality bias and "turnover number") or by single‑molecule FRET/STM imaging; pumping is read out by ionic‑current recording or ion‑selective dyes in a two‑chamber/vesicle assay, and reversing the order of the acid/base pulses (or the light wavelength sequence) reverses the direction of both walking and transport.

Propose a method to create a self-healin.answer:
**Method: Encapsulated‑healing‑agent nanocomposite (autonomic "microvascular‑free" self‑healing material).**

1. **Make the nanocapsules.** Prepare an oil‑in‑water miniemulsion in which the disperse phase is a liquid healing agent (e.g., dicyclopentadiene, DCPD, or an epoxy monomer/amine pair). Using a surfactant (e.g., sodium dodecyl sulfate or gum arabic) and high‑shear/ultrasonic homogenization, form droplets of 100–500 nm, then grow a rigid shell around them by in‑situ interfacial polymerization (urea–formaldehyde or poly(urea‑urethane)) or by sol–gel condensation of TEOS to give a silica shell. Wash, filter and dry to obtain free‑flowing nanocapsules with a shell thin enough (tens of nm) to rupture under crack stress but strong enough to survive processing.

2. **Add the trigger/catalyst.** Disperse a complementary component—e.g., Grubbs' ruthenium metathesis catalyst nanoparticles for DCPD, or capsules of a hardener for the epoxy system—separately in the matrix (or graft it to nanofillers such as functionalized graphene oxide/silica nanoparticles, which also reinforce the composite).

3. **Compound the material.** Blend 5–15 wt % of the nanocapsules plus catalyst into the host polymer (epoxy, PDMS, polyurethane) with vacuum degassing to ensure uniform dispersion and good capsule–matrix adhesion (silane coupling agents help), then cure.

4. **Healing mechanism.** When a microcrack propagates, it ruptures the embedded nanocapsules; capillary action wicks the released monomer into the crack plane, where it contacts the catalyst and polymerizes (ROMP of DCPD), chemically bonding the crack faces and restoring mechanical integrity autonomously at room temperature.

5. **Optional enhancement.** Build the matrix itself from reversible chemistry—Diels–Alder furan/maleimide adducts, disulfide exchange, or hydrogen‑bonding/host–guest supramolecular links—so that mild heat or light gives repeated (multi‑cycle) healing in addition to the one‑shot capsule healing.

6. **Validation.** Measure healing efficiency as the recovery of fracture toughness/tensile strength (tapered double‑cantilever beam or tensile tests) of virgin vs. healed samples, and image crack closure and capsule rupture by SEM/TEM.

**Method: A dynamic‑covalent "nanoparticle‑crosslinked" network healed remotely by magnetic‑induction heating (intrinsic, repeatable self‑healing).**

1. **Build the nano‑crosslinkers.** Synthesize ~10–15 nm superparamagnetic Fe₃O₄ nanoparticles by co‑precipitation, coat them with a thin silica shell (Stöber/TEOS), then graft aminopropyl‑silane (APTES) so each particle carries a dense corona of –NH₂ groups. (Alternatively use amine‑ or boronic‑acid‑functionalized silica/cellulose nanocrystals or graphene oxide as reinforcing nano‑nodes.)

2. **Design a reversible‑bond matrix.** Prepare a soft, low‑Tg polymer (e.g., a telechelic polyurethane, PDMS, or poly(ethylene glycol) prepolymer) end‑capped with aldehyde (or benzaldehyde/diol) groups so it forms **imine (Schiff‑base)** — or equivalently boronic‑ester/disulfide/Diels–Alder — linkages, which are covalent yet exchange dynamically.

3. **Assemble the nanocomposite.** Mix 3–10 wt % of the functionalized nanoparticles into the prepolymer with sonication and solvent‑assisted dispersion; the surface amines condense with the polymer aldehydes so that the *nanoparticles themselves become the crosslink junctions* of the network. Cast/mold and cure, removing solvent under vacuum. Result: a gel/elastomer whose entire connectivity is made of exchangeable bonds anchored on well‑dispersed, reinforcing nanoparticles.

4. **Healing mechanism and trigger.** After a cut or crack, press the surfaces together and apply a low‑power **alternating magnetic field (≈100–300 kHz)** (or NIR light if plasmonic Au/graphene nanofillers are used). The nanoparticles convert the field into localized hysteresis/Néel heat only at the damage site, raising the local temperature above the bond‑exchange threshold. Imine metathesis/transamination lets chains detach from one particle and reattach across the interface; polymer chains interdiffuse and the network re‑forms, welding the crack shut. Switching off the field re‑vitrifies the network. Because no reagent is consumed, healing is repeatable at the same location, is spatially selective (no bulk heating), and the nanoparticles simultaneously act as mechanical reinforcement.

5. **Optional enhancement.** Incorporate a shape‑memory segment (e.g., crystallizable PCL blocks) so the same induction heating drives "close‑then‑heal": the material first recovers its programmed shape to bring crack faces into contact, then bond exchange re‑bonds them; adding a trace of catalyst (e.g., scandium triflate or an amine) accelerates the exchange.

6. **Validation.** Track healing by optical/SEM imaging of the scar, recovery of tensile strength/elongation and storage modulus (DMA) over multiple damage–heal cycles, stress‑relaxation/Arrhenius analysis to confirm bond‑exchange kinetics, and IR thermography to verify localized nanoparticle heating.

**Method: “Damage‑seeking” nanoparticle segregation — self‑repair by thermodynamically driven migration of functionalized nanoparticles into nascent cracks (a nano‑scale “white‑blood‑cell” repair mechanism).**

1. **Make the repair particles.** Synthesize monodisperse 3–10 nm cores (silica by a Stöber route, or CdSe/Au quantum dots for optical tracking) and graft them with a short polymer brush that is *just* compatible with the matrix — e.g., low‑molecular‑weight polystyrene or PEG chains attached by ATRP/“grafting‑to” thiol or silane chemistry. Keep the brush density low enough that the particles are dispersed but only marginally soluble, so the free energy penalty of staying in the bulk is small.

2. **Add a latent reactive shell.** Terminate a fraction of the brush chains with reactive end groups (epoxide, thiol, catechol, or maleimide) that are inert inside the bulk polymer but react rapidly with complementary groups (amines/enes) exposed on a freshly created fracture surface, or with atmospheric oxygen/moisture at the crack face.

3. **Formulate the nanocomposite.** Disperse 1–5 vol % of these particles in the host polymer melt or solution (sonication + solvent casting), then crosslink lightly and anneal above Tg so the film is a soft, mobile network with a uniform particle distribution.

4. **Healing mechanism (autonomic, no external agent).** When a nanocrack nucleates, it creates new free surface. Because the grafted particles lower the interfacial energy of that surface (an enthalpic gain plus the entropic gain of brush chains spreading into free volume), they spontaneously diffuse down the resulting chemical‑potential gradient and accumulate at the crack walls. They jam into a densely packed monolayer/plug that mechanically bridges and fills the void, blunting and arresting the crack; the latent reactive end groups then covalently tether the plug to both crack faces, converting the physical filling into a permanent weld. Repair is triggered only by damage, is localized, and can occur repeatedly as long as reservoir particles remain.

5. **Optional enhancements.** Use a gradient/bimodal particle size (small ones for fast diffusion, larger ones for load transfer); place a sacrificial reservoir layer of particles beneath the surface of a coating; or use hollow mesoporous nanoparticles loaded with a corrosion inhibitor/monomer so migration also delivers a chemical healing agent to the defect.

6. **Validation.** Track particle accumulation at cracks by cross‑sectional TEM, EDX mapping, or fluorescence/confocal imaging of the quantum‑dot particles; quantify repair by recovery of barrier properties (gas/ion permeation, electrochemical impedance for coatings) and of modulus/fracture toughness before and after damage, and compare with a particle‑free control.

**Method: A nano‑“vascular” network of coaxially electrospun core–shell nanofibers that bleed and refill healing agent (bio‑inspired capillary repair).**

1. **Spin the hollow nano‑vessels.** Use coaxial (core–shell) electrospinning: pump a healing liquid (e.g., epoxy resin DGEBA, or an isocyanate/thiol prepolymer, optionally with a solvent to lower viscosity) through the inner needle and a polymer shell solution (poly(ε‑caprolactone), PAN, PMMA, or PVDF in DMF/chloroform) through the outer needle at ~10–20 kV. This yields continuous 200–800 nm fibers with a mechanically robust shell (~50 nm) and a liquid‑filled lumen. Electrospin a second, chemically complementary mat whose cores carry the curing agent (amine hardener or catalyst).

2. **Build the interpenetrating network.** Alternately deposit the two fiber populations (or use dual‑spinneret simultaneous spinning) to form a randomly interwoven, spatially interlaced mat in which resin‑ and hardener‑filled fibers cross thousands of times per mm². Align some fibers in‑plane to also serve as reinforcement.

3. **Integrate into the host.** Infiltrate/laminate this nanofiber mat into the matrix (epoxy laminate, coating, or elastomer film) by vacuum‑assisted resin infusion or as an interleaf between composite plies, curing below the shell’s softening point so the lumens stay filled. Surface‑treat the shells (plasma or silane) for good interfacial bonding so cracks *cut* rather than debond the fibers.

4. **Healing mechanism.** A propagating crack severs the nanofibers; capillary pressure in the sub‑micron lumens (which is very large, ∝1/r) rapidly wicks resin and hardener out of the cut ends into the crack plane, where the two streams meet, mix at the nanoscale (short diffusion distances give fast, complete reaction) and polymerize, re‑bonding the fracture surfaces. Because the fibers are *continuous* and can be connected at the panel edge to an external micro‑reservoir/pump, the network can be re‑pressurized and refilled after each event—giving repeated healing at the same location, unlike one‑shot capsules.

5. **Optional enhancements.** Add a UV/thermally triggered latent catalyst or fluorescent dye in the core for “damage indication + on‑demand cure”; use shape‑memory fibers (PCL) that contract on heating to first pull the crack closed before the resin cures; or fill some fibers with conductive silver/liquid‑metal (EGaIn) nanoparticles to restore electrical as well as mechanical continuity.

6. **Validation.** Confirm hollow core–shell morphology by TEM/cryo‑SEM and core loading by TGA; verify agent release with fluorescence microscopy of a cracked sample; quantify performance as recovery of Mode‑I fracture toughness/interlaminar shear strength over multiple damage–refill cycles versus a solid‑fiber control.

Suggest a novel method for visualizing i.answer:
**Proposal: Laser‑triggered "4D" atomic movies in a graphene nanoreactor cell (stroboscopic ultrafast STEM with event‑driven detection and AI denoising).**

Encapsulate the reagents in a graphene "liquid/gas cell" — two atomically thin, electron‑transparent graphene sheets sealing a picoliter pocket — which confines molecules to a quasi‑2D layer so that every heavy atom is individually resolvable and the windows contribute almost no background. Anchor the reactant molecules to the graphene via engineered defect or ligand sites so they stay in the field of view and in a known orientation.

Image with an aberration‑corrected scanning transmission electron microscope operated in a photon‑pump/electron‑probe (ultrafast 4D‑EM) mode: a femtosecond laser pulse triggers each reaction cycle (photochemically, or by plasmonic/thermal or electrochemical bias jumps for non‑photochemical reactions), and a synchronized, delayed picosecond electron pulse takes a snapshot. Scanning the pump–probe delay and summing over many identical, self‑resetting reaction cycles builds a stroboscopic movie with picosecond time resolution and sub‑ångström spatial resolution, while a fast event‑driven direct‑electron (pixelated 4D‑STEM/ptychography) detector records the full diffraction pattern at every probe position for continuous, dose‑efficient real‑time imaging of single events.

Keep the dose below the damage threshold by using low‑voltage (30–80 kV) operation, ptychographic phase retrieval (which extracts maximum information per electron and reveals light atoms such as C, N, O and even H), and a machine‑learning denoiser/tracker trained on simulated image series that assigns atomic identities and coordinates frame‑by‑frame from very sparse data.

The result is a directly observed, atom‑by‑atom movie of bond breaking and forming — trajectories, transient intermediates and transition‑state geometries — which can be cross‑validated against simultaneous electron energy‑loss spectroscopy for chemical/oxidation‑state identification of each atom.

**Proposal: "Single‑spin MRI movies" — atom‑resolved nuclear‑spin imaging of a tethered molecule using a diamond NV‑centre quantum sensor array with nanoscale field gradients.**

Instead of hitting the molecule with electrons or X‑rays (which damage it), read out each atom *magnetically*, so the imaging is completely non‑destructive and works at room temperature in solution.

1. **Sample stage:** the reactant is covalently tethered by a rigid linker onto the (111) surface of an ultrapure diamond chip so that it sits 2–5 nm above an array of shallow, implanted nitrogen‑vacancy (NV) centres. Isotopic labelling (¹³C, ¹⁵N, ¹⁷O, ²H, ³¹P) gives every atom of interest a nuclear spin "tag," and the different gyromagnetic ratios make the readout intrinsically element‑specific.

2. **Spatial encoding:** a magnetic nanotip (or lithographed current wires) applies a static field gradient of ~10⁶–10⁷ T/m across the molecule, so each nucleus precesses at a Larmor frequency set by its position — a true atomic‑scale MRI *k*‑space encoding, with pulsed gradients along three axes giving 3D Fourier reconstruction at sub‑ångström resolution.

3. **Detection:** each NV centre, driven by dynamical‑decoupling (XY8/CPMG) microwave sequences resonant with the encoded nuclear frequencies, senses the a.c. magnetic field of individual nuclei; the NV's optically detected spin state is read out continuously by confocal or wide‑field fluorescence. Correlation ("qdyne"/weak‑measurement) spectroscopy on the NV array records the frequency *and* phase of every nuclear spin simultaneously, and the array geometry provides triangulation redundancy.

4. **Reaction triggering and timing:** the reaction is initiated repeatedly by a photocaged reagent (uncaged by a laser pulse), a pH/redox jump, or an electrochemical potential step at the diamond electrode. Between trigger events the nuclear spins are re‑polarised by NV‑mediated dynamic nuclear polarisation, so each cycle starts with a fresh, hyperpolarised, high‑signal molecule. Time‑stamping of every photon (event‑driven readout) yields microsecond frames; stroboscopic averaging over many cycles sharpens them to sub‑microsecond, and compressed‑sensing/Bayesian reconstruction converts the sparse spin‑frequency data into a frame‑by‑frame set of atomic coordinates.

5. **Output:** a real‑time, element‑labelled 3D movie of atomic positions — showing bond lengths and angles changing, atoms transferring between partners, and transient intermediates — with the bonus that the nuclear chemical shifts and dipolar couplings measured in the same experiment report directly on the changing electronic structure and bond order of each atom. Because photons, not ionising particles, do the sensing, the same single molecule can be watched through thousands of turnovers.

**Proposal: "Lightwave‑gated atomic cinematography" — single‑cycle THz‑driven scanning probe microscopy with a CO‑functionalized tip (THz‑STM/AFM plus tip‑enhanced Raman readout).**

Put a single reactant molecule on a bilayer of insulating NaCl (or hBN) grown on a metal crystal in a cryogenic UHV microscope; the decoupling layer preserves the molecule's frontier orbitals and keeps its atomic framework rigid enough to image. Terminate the probe apex with a single CO molecule, whose lateral stiffness makes non‑contact AFM frequency‑shift maps resolve each individual atom and even the bond orders between them (Pauli‑repulsion imaging).

Give this static atomic‑resolution probe femtosecond time resolution by driving it with light rather than with an electronic bias: focus a single‑cycle THz pulse onto the junction, where its carrier field acts as an ultrafast, sub‑picosecond bias transient that opens a ~100 fs tunnelling "shutter." A synchronized visible/UV pump pulse (or a voltage/electric‑field pulse from the tip itself) triggers the reaction — photoisomerization, tautomerization, hydrogen or halogen transfer, cycloaddition — and the delayed THz pulse reads out the instantaneous atomic configuration at that pixel. Sweeping the pump–THz delay while raster‑scanning the tip assembles a stroboscopic movie with ångström spatial and femtosecond temporal resolution; because each frame is built from a reversible, tip‑resettable reaction (the reverse step is driven by a second pulse or a controlled bias ramp), the *same* molecule is filmed over thousands of cycles.

Two additions make the movie chemically, not just geometrically, informative: (i) the same tip performs tip‑enhanced Raman/inelastic‑tunnelling spectroscopy at every delay, so vibrational fingerprints identify which bonds are breaking or forming as the atoms move; and (ii) a neural network trained on DFT‑simulated AFM/THz‑STM contrast inverts the sparse, distorted probe images into true 3D atomic coordinates and charge distributions frame by frame, correcting for CO‑tip bending artefacts.

The result is a non‑destructive, all‑optical‑timing atom‑by‑atom movie of a single molecule reacting — transition‑state geometries, transient intermediates and even the electron density redistributing between atoms — obtained without any ionizing radiation.

Propose a way to achieve dynamic reconfi.answer: Build the origami with mechanically compliant joints (e.g., single‑stranded scaffold "hinges" or flexible connections between rigid helix bundles) and hold the object in a given conformation with a small set of "lock" staples that bridge the movable parts through short complementary sticky‑end/latch duplexes carrying single‑stranded toehold overhangs. Adding a complementary "key"/fuel strand removes a lock by toehold‑mediated strand displacement, releasing the joint and letting the structure switch to its alternative configuration (open/closed, extended/compact, chiral inversion, etc.); adding an "anti‑key" strand that strips off the invader restores the original lock, so the device can be cycled reversibly many times (with the waste duplex simply accumulating in solution). The same latch chemistry can be made to respond to other triggers instead of DNA inputs — e.g., i‑motif/triplex latches that open and close with pH, azobenzene‑modified staples switched by UV/visible light, aptamer latches opened by a target molecule/protein, or Mg²⁺/Na⁺‑dependent stacking bonds — so the origami reconfigures autonomously on sensing an environmental cue. Conformational change can be verified in real time by placing a FRET dye pair (or plasmonic nanoparticles) across the hinge and by TEM/cryo‑EM of the two states.

Build the origami as a rigid "robot arm" mounted on a low‑friction pivot and actuate it with an **external electric field instead of chemical fuel**. Concretely: fold a stiff multi‑helix‑bundle lever (tens to hundreds of nm long) and join it to a large, flat origami baseplate through a short, flexible single‑stranded scaffold pivot that permits nearly free rotation but keeps the two parts tethered; the baseplate is immobilized on a surface (e.g., biotin–streptavidin or cholesterol anchors on a supported lipid bilayer) inside a microfluidic cross‑ or multi‑electrode cell. Because DNA is highly negatively charged, the arm behaves as a charged, polarizable rod: applying a modest external electric field (a few V/cm, dc or ac, from orthogonal electrode pairs) exerts an electrophoretic/dielectrophoretic torque that swings the arm to an angle set by the field vector, and rotating the field vector rotates the arm continuously; switching the field off lets thermal fluctuations return it to a random/relaxed state. Because the drive is purely physical, the reconfiguration is fuel‑free, fully reversible, repeatable indefinitely without waste‑product accumulation, and occurs on millisecond timescales—orders of magnitude faster than diffusion‑limited chemical switching. Discrete, latchable states can be added by placing shape‑complementary blunt‑end stacking "docking sites" at defined positions on the baseplate, so the field steers the arm into a chosen dock where it is transiently held; changing the field releases and re‑docks it elsewhere. Motion is read out in real time by attaching a fluorophore (or gold/fluorescent nanoparticle) to the arm tip and imaging with TIRF/FRET, allowing single‑molecule tracking of each switching event and use of the device as a nanoscale robotic manipulator, force sensor, or reconfigurable plasmonic/photonic element.

Make the shape "rewritable" by competitive staple‑set exchange rather than by hinges or fields. Fold the scaffold so that a defined sub‑region (a "reprogrammable domain") is addressed by a first set of staples that specifies shape A — for example crossovers that fold the sheet into a tube, or that place a set of helices in a particular curvature/twist. Design a second, alternative staple set for the same scaffold segment that encodes shape B (different crossover positions, different insertions/deletions of bases per turn), and give these "rewriting" staples a clear thermodynamic advantage: longer binding domains, higher GC content, extra clamp/locking segments, or LNA/2′‑OMe‑modified bases so that their duplex with the scaffold is significantly more stable than that of the incumbent staples.

Reconfiguration is then driven by adding the alternative staples in excess and applying a mild, isothermal‑or‑ramped thermal (or formamide/urea, or low‑Mg²⁺) "soft‑annealing" pulse — well below scaffold denaturation, just above the melting point of the weaker incumbent staples. The incumbent staples release, the stronger invaders take their place, and the structure re‑folds into shape B; the displaced staples remain inert in solution or can be removed by a complementary magnetic‑bead/biotin pull‑down or by a nuclease that recognizes only their unique 3′ tag. Because each staple set can be made mutually orthogonal and stability‑ranked (set 1 < set 2 < set 3 …), successive additions with successive gentle thermal pulses drive the same scaffold through a programmed sequence of many discrete shapes — a "shape stack" — and the process is repeatable on a single object population without any bespoke hinge or latch geometry. Ordered, monotonic re‑writing can also be implemented locally: only the domain whose staples are competed out re‑folds, so different regions can be rewritten independently to give combinatorial multi‑state structures. Each state is verified by AFM/TEM imaging and by agarose‑gel mobility shifts, and the transition kinetics tracked with a fluorophore–quencher pair spanning the rewritten domain.

**Enzyme‑driven, transcriptionally programmed reconfiguration (an RNA/enzyme "chemical clock" built into the origami).**

Instead of hinges that must be opened by hand‑added DNA keys, encode the switching instructions in the origami itself and let enzymes execute them:

- Build the object from two (or more) rigid origami domains connected by flexible scaffold hinges, and fix the initial conformation (state A) with a small set of **hybrid "staple‑locks" made of RNA or containing an RNA/2′‑OH window** that clamp the domains together.
- Place a **T7 (or SP6) promoter duplex plus a short DNA template on the origami surface**. Adding T7 RNA polymerase + NTPs makes the object continuously transcribe its own RNA "trigger" strands, which are complementary to the toehold of the DNA locks; these locally produced RNAs invade the locks and release the hinge, switching the object to state B without any user intervention. Because transcription is autocatalytic in time, the shape change is programmable in *when* and *how fast* it happens (set by promoter strength, template copy number, NTP concentration).
- Reset/cycle the device with a second enzyme: **RNase H** selectively hydrolyses the RNA in any RNA:DNA duplex, chewing up the spent RNA triggers (and the RNA locks), so the waste never accumulates and the freed DNA locks can re‑hybridise, returning the structure to state A. Running RNA polymerase and RNase H (or an RNA‑degrading exonuclease) together in the same pot creates a **dissipative, fuel‑consuming reaction network** in which the origami oscillates or steps autonomously between conformations for as long as NTPs are supplied — a genuine molecular machine rather than a one‑shot switch.
- Multiplexing: give each hinge its own promoter/terminator pair and orthogonal RNA sequence, so different regions open in a defined *temporal order* (a shape "program"), and add restriction‑enzyme or DNAzyme cut sites for irreversible, checkpoint‑type transitions.
- Readout: FRET pairs or plasmonic Au‑rod pairs spanning each hinge report the state kinetics in bulk and at the single‑molecule level (TIRF), with cryo‑EM/AFM confirming the discrete conformations.

This gives dynamic reconfigurability that is autonomous, timed, cyclable and biologically compatible (it runs on NTPs and natural enzymes), making it directly usable inside cells or in cell‑free gene circuits where the origami shape becomes an output of a transcriptional program.

**Make the reconfigurability hierarchical – i.e., reconfigure the *bonds between* origami modules rather than hinges inside one object.**

Fold a set of rigid origami "voxel" tiles (e.g., helix‑bundle bricks or plates) whose faces carry two independent, orthogonal classes of interaction patches: (i) patterned **shape‑complementary blunt‑end stacking patches** (protrusion/recess pairs whose binding strength is tuned by the number of stacking contacts and is strongly dependent on cation concentration and temperature), and (ii) a second set of **short sticky‑end codes** placed on other faces, each code being weak enough that its binding is only marginally favourable at working temperature.

Because the two bond types respond to different physical variables, the *connectivity* of the superstructure becomes a programmable variable: at high Mg²⁺ (or low temperature) the stacking patches dominate and the tiles assemble into architecture A (say a closed ring or a filament); lowering Mg²⁺/raising Na⁺ or applying a mild temperature step selectively melts the stacking bonds while leaving the individual origami and the sticky‑end code intact, so the same tiles re‑sort and re‑knit through their sticky‑end interfaces into a different topology B (a lattice, tube, or dimer). Adding "capping" or "linker" tiles, or short displacement strands that mask/unmask a given code, re‑routes the assembly again, so a single population of building blocks can be cycled through many distinct higher‑order shapes without ever refolding the scaffolds.

Practically: encode several mutually orthogonal stacking‑patch geometries and codes so different joints have separated melting/ion thresholds; run the cycles isothermally by simply exchanging buffer in a microfluidic chamber or by adding chelator/Mg²⁺; verify each state by AFM/TEM, DLS and gel mobility, and follow switching kinetics with FRET or gold‑nanoparticle plasmon coupling placed across the inter‑tile interfaces. This yields fuel‑free, waste‑free, many‑cycle reconfiguration of *architecture* (topology, porosity, chirality, lattice constant), useful for switchable metamaterials, reconfigurable nanoreactors and stimuli‑responsive scaffolds.

**Remote, fuel‑free actuation with magnetic nanoparticles ("magneto‑origami").**

Fold the object as two (or more) stiff helix‑bundle domains joined by a flexible single‑stranded‑scaffold pivot/hinge, immobilise one domain (biotin–streptavidin, cholesterol‑lipid bilayer, or a glass/gold surface anchor), and site‑specifically conjugate a superparamagnetic nanoparticle or magnetic bead (via a DHLA/streptavidin‑ or click‑functionalised staple protruding at a chosen address) to the tip of the mobile domain. An external magnet or a set of orthogonal electromagnetic coils then exerts a magnetic force/torque on the bead, bending, rotating or stretching the hinge to a defined angle set by the field direction and magnitude; reversing or rotating the field drives the reverse motion, and switching the field off lets the elastic hinge (or thermal fluctuation) relax the structure to its resting state. Discrete, "latched" states are obtained by placing shape‑complementary blunt‑end stacking docks (or weak sticky‑end catches) at chosen positions on the baseplate, so the field steers and parks the arm in a specific dock and a stronger/rotated field pops it out again. Adding an alternating (rather than static) field allows the same particle to be used for local hyperthermia, which can melt weak lock duplexes only in the immediate vicinity of the particle, giving a second, sequence‑addressable switching channel.

Because actuation is purely physical, it is instantaneous (ms), infinitely cyclable, produces no waste strands, penetrates tissue and turbid media, and is orthogonal to the buffer chemistry — so the same population can be switched thousands of times in situ. Multiplexing is achieved by using particles of different size/coercivity on different hinges (each responding at a different field threshold or frequency). States are read out by FRET or plasmon coupling across the hinge, magnetic tweezers force–extension curves, and cryo‑EM/AFM of the trapped conformations, making the device usable as a nanoscale force transducer, switchable plasmonic element, or remotely triggered drug‑release container.

**Use grafted stimuli‑responsive polymers as built‑in "muscles" that mechanically drive the origami between shapes.**

Fold the object as rigid multi‑helix‑bundle segments (plates, arms, or a barrel) joined by short flexible single‑stranded scaffold hinges, and then site‑specifically graft a thermo‑/pH‑responsive polymer — e.g. PNIPAM (LCST ≈ 32 °C), PDEAEMA, or a polyzwitterion — onto selected staple extensions using click/NHS chemistry, so that each polymer chain spans a pair of anchor points across the joint (a "polymer tendon"). In the swollen, hydrated state the extended coils exert an entropic pushing/spacer pressure that holds the joint open (state A). When the trigger is applied — warming above the LCST, a pH or ionic‑strength change, or, if an azobenzene/spiropyran comonomer is included, a pulse of light — the chains undergo a coil‑to‑globule collapse and contract, generating pN‑scale entropic forces that pull the anchor points together and fold the origami into the compact conformation B (closing a lid, contracting an arm, collapsing a tube). Restoring the original conditions re‑swells the polymer and the elastic hinge springs the structure back, so the device works like a reversible artificial muscle.

Key features: actuation force and stroke are tuned by chain length, grafting density and anchor spacing; several polymers with different LCSTs/pKa values can be grafted at different hinges so that individual joints switch at distinct thresholds (multi‑state, orthogonal addressing); and because the driving force is a physical phase transition of the polymer rather than hybridisation, the cycle is fuel‑free, waste‑free, fast (sub‑second) and can be repeated indefinitely. Additionally, the collapsed polymer layer simultaneously shields the DNA from nucleases and low‑Mg²⁺ media, so the same modification that actuates the device also stabilises it for use in physiological conditions (e.g. thermally triggered cargo release from a polymer‑actuated origami capsule). States are verified by FRET across the hinge, AFM/TEM/cryo‑EM of the two conformations, and DLS/gel mobility shifts as a function of temperature or pH.

**Engineer the free‑energy landscape itself: build the origami as a pre‑strained, bistable compliant mechanism that "snaps" between shapes when the elasticity of its own DNA is tuned.**

Design the object as stiff multi‑helix‑bundle struts connected not by free hinges but by *compliant* elements — short single‑stranded scaffold segments acting as entropic springs and thin, few‑helix flexure beams — arranged in a geometry that is over‑constrained (e.g., a curved/arched beam pinned at both ends, a crossed four‑bar linkage, or a "buckled" plate). Program a defined amount of built‑in mechanical pre‑stress by using base insertions/deletions to over‑ or under‑wind helices, by setting the ssDNA tether contour length slightly shorter than the strut spacing, and by choosing crossover spacing that forces global twist/curvature. The result is a double‑well energy landscape: the mechanism has two (or more) locally stable, strain‑relieved conformations (e.g., arch‑up vs. arch‑down, expanded vs. collapsed, left‑ vs. right‑handed twist) separated by a designed energy barrier of a few k_BT, so that no bonds have to be broken or made to switch — only elastic energy is redistributed.

Reconfiguration is then triggered simply by changing a global physical variable that alters DNA elasticity and the balance between the two wells: Mg²⁺/Na⁺ concentration (which sets ssDNA persistence length, electrostatic repulsion between helices, and hence the spring constants and the equilibrium helix spacing), temperature (entropic spring stiffness and helical twist density), or a small externally applied load/flow/AFM tip push. Because the transition is a cooperative snap‑through rather than a diffusion‑limited hybridization event, it is fast (µs–ms), completely fuel‑free and waste‑free, and infinitely cyclable; the barrier height (i.e., how sharply it switches and how well each state is retained) is tuned at design time by strut stiffness, flexure length, and the magnitude of the pre‑strain, and hysteresis can be deliberately built in to make each state latch (mechanical memory). Multi‑state and large‑scale behaviour is obtained by tiling many identical bistable units into a lattice or tube so that individual snaps propagate as a domain wall, producing a global, amplified shape change (auxetic expansion, chirality inversion, tube opening) from a tiny stimulus — a DNA mechanical metamaterial. States and switching kinetics are verified by cryo‑EM/AFM of the two conformations, FRET or plasmon coupling across the bistable element, and single‑molecule magnetic/optical‑tweezer force–extension curves that map the double‑well landscape directly.

**Build a protein–DNA hybrid origami in which the actuator is a genetically encoded, light‑switchable protein dimer rather than a DNA lock.**

Fold the object as two (or more) stiff multi‑helix‑bundle domains joined by a flexible scaffold pivot, and site‑specifically conjugate one half of an optogenetic binding pair to a staple extension on one domain and its partner to a staple on the facing domain (e.g., via SNAP/HaloTag, sortase, or click chemistry to 5′‑modified staples, or by DNA‑zip‑code hybridization of oligo‑labelled proteins). Suitable pairs include phytochrome B–PIF6 (associates under 660 nm red light, dissociates under 740 nm far‑red), the LOV2–Zdk pair (blue light releases), Dronpa domains (violet/cyan light toggles dimerization), or a Ca²⁺‑switched calmodulin–M13 peptide clamp.

Illuminating at the "on" wavelength makes the two proteins heterodimerize, tethering the domains together and pulling the origami into the closed/compact conformation; illuminating at the "off" wavelength (or removing Ca²⁺ with EGTA in the calmodulin version) breaks the protein–protein bond and the hinge relaxes to the open state. Because the switch lives in a protein whose association/dissociation is intrinsically reversible and photochromic, the reconfiguration is fuel‑free and waste‑free (no accumulating duplex by‑products), occurs on sub‑second timescales, and can be cycled thousands of times, patterned with diffraction‑limited spatial precision in a microscope, and driven with tissue‑penetrating red/far‑red light. Multiple hinges can be addressed orthogonally by using pairs with different action spectra (blue LOV2 vs. red PhyB) or different chemical triggers, giving multi‑state shape programs; supplying the light through a chromophore‑supplemented buffer (PCB for PhyB) makes it compatible with in‑cell operation. States and kinetics are verified with FRET dyes flanking the hinge, TIRF single‑molecule tracking, and AFM/cryo‑EM of the illuminated versus dark conformations.

**Use covalent photochemistry as the actuator: “photo‑welded/photo‑cut” joints that let light write and erase the shape.**

Fold the object as stiff multi‑helix‑bundle domains joined by flexible single‑stranded scaffold pivots, and control each joint with two chemically orthogonal light‑responsive staples instead of toehold locks:

- **Photo‑weld staples:** incorporate an ultrafast photo‑crosslinking nucleoside such as 3‑cyanovinylcarbazole (^CNVK) (or a psoralen/coumarin unit) at the position where a bridging staple faces a thymine on the partner domain. A few seconds of 365 nm light drives a [2+2] cycloaddition that covalently welds the two domains into the closed conformation; irradiation at ~312 nm (or a brief warm 312 nm pulse) cleanly reverses the cycloaddition and unwelds the joint, so the same bond can be made and broken repeatedly.
- **Photo‑cleave staples:** in the *complementary* joint (the one that holds the open/alternative state) place an o‑nitrobenzyl (or coumarin‑ or thioacetal‑) photocleavable spacer in the staple backbone, and/or a nitrobenzyl‑caged base that blocks hybridization until uncaged. A pulse at a different wavelength severs or activates these bridges.

Because the two photochemistries respond to different colours and thresholds, a simple wavelength sequence (λ1 welds state B while λ2 cuts the state‑A bridges, and vice versa) toggles the structure between defined conformations. Multiple hinges are addressed orthogonally by using chromophores with separated action spectra (or two‑photon/upconversion excitation for depth), giving multi‑state “shape programs.”

Key advantages: actuation is **fuel‑free and waste‑free** (no invader/anti‑invader duplexes accumulate), occurs in **seconds**, works at physiological salt/temperature, and — uniquely — is **spatially addressable**: illuminating through a photomask or with a scanning laser/DMD reconfigures only the origami in the illuminated region, so a surface‑immobilized array of identical devices can be patterned into arbitrary maps of state A and state B (or written line‑by‑line like lithography). The covalent welds also mechanically lock and nuclease‑stabilize the chosen conformation, so each state persists indefinitely in the dark until the next light pulse — i.e., optical *memory* as well as switching.

Readout: FRET dye pair (or coupled Au nanorods) across each hinge for real‑time kinetics, plus AFM/TEM/cryo‑EM and gel‑mobility shifts (crosslinked joints survive denaturing gels, giving a direct assay of weld efficiency).

**Actuate the origami with metal‑ion–mediated artificial base pairs ("metallo‑DNA latches").**

Fold the object as stiff multi‑helix‑bundle domains joined by flexible single‑stranded scaffold pivots, and bridge each joint with short latch/bridge staples that are *deliberately mismatched*: the bridging duplex is designed with a run of C–C mismatches (and/or T–T mismatches) instead of Watson–Crick pairs, so at neutral pH in ordinary buffer it is too unstable to hybridize and the hinge stays open. Adding Ag⁺ converts every C–C mismatch into a stable C–Ag⁺–C metallo‑base pair (and Hg²⁺ converts T–T into T–Hg²⁺–T), instantly "zipping" the latch shut and locking the structure into its closed/compact conformation. Sequestering the ion with a chelator (cysteine, glutathione, EDTA/EGTA) strips the metal out, the mismatched bridge melts, and the elastic hinge springs the device back to the open state — a fully reversible, many‑cycle switch driven only by ion addition/removal. Ligand‑modified staples (e.g., terpyridine‑ or hydroxyquinoline‑bearing nucleotides that form Fe²⁺/Ni²⁺/Zn²⁺ complexes) can be used the same way for still stronger, redox‑tunable crosslinks.

Because Ag⁺ works only on C–C, Hg²⁺ only on T–T, and terpyridine only on transition metals, several hinges on the same object can be addressed **orthogonally with different ions**, giving multi‑state shape programs (e.g., Ag⁺ closes the lid, Hg²⁺ contracts the arm, both together give a third conformation), and the number of metallo‑pairs per latch sets its ion threshold so that joints switch sequentially as the ion concentration is titrated. The mechanism adds no invader/anti‑invader strands, so **no waste duplexes accumulate**; switching is fast (seconds, limited only by ion diffusion), isothermal, and compatible with physiological salt. As a bonus, the same construct doubles as a shape‑changing heavy‑metal sensor/scavenger, and the ions can be delivered or removed locally (photolabile metal cages, electrochemical Ag⁺ generation at an electrode) for spatially patterned reconfiguration.

Readout: FRET dye pair or coupled Au nanorods across each hinge for real‑time kinetics and titration curves, plus AFM/TEM/cryo‑EM of the metal‑bound versus chelated conformations and gel‑mobility shifts.

**Use redox‑switchable disulfide (thiol–disulfide) bridges as the actuating joints — a "redox latch" origami.**

Fold the object as two (or more) stiff multi‑helix‑bundle domains connected by flexible single‑stranded scaffold pivots, then place pairs of thiol‑modified staples (C6‑SH or thiol‑dPEG extensions) at defined addresses so that a thiol on one domain sits directly opposite a thiol on the facing domain. Mild oxidation (air/O₂ with trace Cu²⁺, or a small amount of oxidized glutathione/H₂O₂, or simply holding the object at a positively poised electrode) forms covalent S–S crosslinks that staple the two domains together and lock the structure in its compact/closed conformation (state A). Adding a reducing agent — TCEP, DTT, or physiological millimolar glutathione — quantitatively cleaves the disulfides, the elastic hinge relaxes, and the device springs open into state B; re‑oxidation re‑welds it, so the same population can be cycled many times simply by toggling the redox potential of the buffer, with no invader/anti‑invader strands and therefore **no accumulating waste duplexes**.

Key design handles:
- **Graded thresholds / multi‑state programs:** the number of disulfide bridges per joint and their chemistry set the reduction potential at which each joint opens (few‑bridge joints and sterically strained aryl disulfides reduce first; bulky/hindered or multi‑bridge joints last), so titrating the reductant walks the structure through a defined sequence of conformations. Orthogonality can be extended with a second, non‑redox joint chemistry (e.g., a diselenide, which reduces at a different potential, or a boronate–diol bridge switched by sugar/pH) so different hinges respond to different chemical channels.
- **Spatial addressing:** because the trigger is an electron transfer, the state can be written locally by electrochemistry — origami immobilized on a patterned microelectrode array is opened only over the electrodes held at reducing potential and closed again by stepping the potential, giving lithography‑like maps of state A/state B; photoredox catalysts or caged reductants allow the same with light.
- **Biological payoff:** the cytosol is strongly reducing (~1–10 mM glutathione) while blood/extracellular space is oxidizing, so a disulfide‑locked origami capsule stays covalently closed and nuclease‑protected during circulation and **auto‑opens only after cellular uptake/endosomal escape**, releasing its cargo — an intrinsically "smart," fuel‑free, environment‑sensing reconfiguration. The covalent locks also stabilize the folded state against low‑Mg²⁺ media and thermal denaturation.

Readout/validation: FRET dye pair (or coupled Au nanorods) spanning each hinge for real‑time switching kinetics and redox titration curves; non‑reducing versus reducing SDS/agarose gel‑mobility shifts as a direct assay of crosslink efficiency; AFM/TEM/cryo‑EM of the oxidized versus reduced conformations; cyclic voltammetry for the electrochemically driven version.

**Drive the shape change with small‑molecule intercalation that re‑programs the helical twist of the origami ("torsion‑tuned" origami).**

Design the object so that its global geometry is dictated by *twist strain* rather than by hinges or latches: use crossover spacings and base insertions/deletions that deliberately over‑ or under‑wind the helices (e.g., 10.0 vs 10.5 bp/turn domains), so the folded sheet/bundle adopts a defined curvature, global twist, tube diameter, or lattice pitch that is exquisitely sensitive to the average number of base pairs per helical turn. Then actuate it chemically by adding a DNA intercalator (ethidium, doxorubicin, SYBR/YOYO dyes, or a photo‑switchable azobenzene‑ or spiropyran‑intercalator). Each intercalated molecule locally unwinds the duplex by ~10–27°, lengthening it and changing bp/turn; because the crossovers rigidly enforce a fixed inter‑helix register, this accumulated unwinding is converted into a large, cooperative global deformation — the structure untwists, straightens, changes chirality (right‑ to left‑handed supertwist), expands its lattice constant, or opens/uncoils a tube — with the magnitude tuned continuously by intercalator:bp ratio, giving analogue (not just two‑state) reconfiguration.

Reversal/cycling is fuel‑free and waste‑free: dilute or dialyse/absorb the dye away (activated charcoal, cyclodextrin or micellar scavenger, or competitive binding by excess free DNA/heparin), or, with an azobenzene‑type intercalator, simply irradiate at ~450 nm so the *cis* isomer no longer intercalates and the structure snaps back — allowing many repeat cycles and even light‑patterned, spatially addressed reconfiguration across a surface‑immobilised array. Orthogonal, multi‑state behaviour is obtained by giving different domains different crossover densities/strain (they respond at different intercalator loadings, so domains untwist sequentially during a titration) or by using groove‑binder versus intercalator ligands that act on AT‑rich versus GC‑rich sub‑domains selectively.

Validation/readout: cryo‑EM and AFM of the twisted vs untwisted states, TEM tomography of curvature, gel mobility shifts, circular dichroism and single‑molecule magnetic‑tweezer twist measurements, and FRET dyes (or coupled Au nanorods giving a switchable plasmonic chiroptical/CD signal) placed across the deforming region for real‑time kinetics — yielding a reconfigurable chiral metamaterial and, since doxorubicin is the actuator in one version, a drug‑loading‑coupled shape switch.

**Make the reconfigurability topological: build the origami as a mechanically interlocked machine (a DNA‑origami rotaxane/catenane shuttle) whose parts slide and rotate along a track rather than opening on a hinge.**

Fold a stiff multi‑helix‑bundle "axle" (or a closed origami ring) and, in a separate step, fold a second origami ring/collar *around* it, closing the ring's last few staple connections only after threading so that the two objects are permanently interlocked without any covalent or base‑pairing link between them (bulky origami "stoppers" folded onto the axle ends prevent de‑threading). Because the collar is held on only by topology, it is free to shuttle along the axle and to rotate about it over tens–hundreds of nanometres with almost no energy barrier — a genuine mechanical bond, exactly as in synthetic rotaxanes.

Program discrete conformational states by writing a series of "stations" along the axle: short single‑stranded or duplex patches, or shape‑complementary blunt‑end stacking docks, each complementary to a matching patch on the inner face of the collar. The device is reconfigured by switching which station is *available*: e.g., blocking strands, pH‑responsive triplex/i‑motif station clamps, or restriction/nicking sites that deactivate a station, so the collar hops from station 1 to station 2 to station 3, translating and/or twisting the whole assembly (extending a filament, changing the pitch/chirality of a helical superstructure, sliding a cargo platform, or driving a rotary motion of an attached arm). Because the two components can never fall apart, the machine tolerates conditions that would dissociate a hybridization latch (low Mg²⁺, high temperature, nuclease attack on one station) and can be cycled indefinitely, and a directional bias — an asymmetric station sequence combined with an energy‑consuming input (fuel strands, transcription, or a thermal/ion ratchet) — turns the shuttle into a processive linear/rotary motor rather than a two‑state switch.

Multiple collars on one axle, or catenated ring pairs, give combinatorial multi‑state architectures (a "molecular abacus" whose state is set by bead positions), and the same interlock can be used to make reconfigurable, topologically robust origami chain‑mail/polycatenane materials whose stiffness and dimensions change when the sliding freedom is locked or released.

Validation/readout: cryo‑EM/AFM and TEM of the different collar positions, single‑molecule FRET or plasmon coupling between a dye/Au nanoparticle on the collar and one on the axle to follow shuttling kinetics in real time, and gel‑mobility/denaturation assays showing that the two objects co‑migrate even under conditions that break all base pairing — the signature of a mechanical, non‑hybridization linkage.

**Actuate the origami by switching designed regions between single‑stranded and double‑stranded DNA ("stiffness/length switching" of the scaffold itself), using polymerase‑ or HCR‑driven strand growth.**

Design the object so that its geometry is set not by latches but by a few defined **scaffold loops of controlled contour length** placed at the joints/edges between rigid multi‑helix‑bundle segments. In the ssDNA state these loops are floppy (persistence length ~1 nm) and their entropic coiling holds the segments close together / at a relaxed angle (state A). To reconfigure, convert those exact loops into duplex: add a short primer that anneals in the loop plus a strand‑displacing DNA polymerase (Bst/phi29) and dNTPs, or feed a set of metastable hairpins that zip up the loop by hybridization chain reaction/primer‑exchange extension. The ss→ds conversion increases the persistence length ~50‑fold and lengthens the segment to ~0.34 nm/bp, so the loop is transformed into a **rigid strut that straightens the joint, splays the plates apart, extends a telescoping arm, or sets a precise inter‑segment angle** determined simply by how many base pairs are laid down (state B). Because the stroke is proportional to the number of nucleotides polymerized, the motion is *analogue and programmable* — stopping the reaction with a chain terminator, a blocking base (e.g., an abasic/iso‑dG stop), or a limiting hairpin supply defines a discrete intermediate state, so titrating templates and stop sites gives a whole series of shapes from one folded object.

Reset the device enzymatically: a nicking endonuclease plus 5′→3′ exonuclease (or RNase H if the invading strand is RNA, or a strand‑displacing "eraser" strand released from a helicase) chews the new duplex back to ssDNA, and the entropic loop re‑collapses the structure to state A; running the polymerase and the nuclease together in one pot makes the origami cycle autonomously as long as dNTPs are supplied (a dissipative, fuel‑driven machine).

Orthogonality/multiplexing is achieved by giving each loop a unique primer/hairpin sequence and a different programmed extension length, so different joints extend by different amounts, in a chosen temporal order, in response to different molecular inputs — the primer can itself be a biomarker RNA/DNA, making the shape change a direct amplified readout of a nucleic‑acid target. Validation: AFM/TEM/cryo‑EM of the compact vs extended conformations, gel‑mobility shifts as the loops become duplex, and FRET (or Au‑nanorod plasmon coupling) across each joint to follow the extension kinetics in real time.

Suggest a novel nanoscale mechanism to h.answer:
**Proposal: A "flexo‑ionic peristaltic nanogenerator" — self‑rectifying ion pumping in sub‑10 nm asymmetric nanochannels gated by membrane flexoelectricity.**

**Architecture.** Fabricate a dense array (10⁹–10¹⁰ cm⁻²) of funnel‑shaped (conical, tip ≈2–5 nm, base ≈50 nm) nanochannels through a thin dielectric membrane (e.g., HfO₂ or h‑BN/MoS₂ stack), filled with a concentrated ionic liquid or aqueous electrolyte. Each channel mouth is capped by a suspended, ultrathin 2D membrane (few‑layer MoS₂ or graphene/BN) that acts as the vibration‑coupled drumhead, and asymmetric (dissimilar‑work‑function) electrodes contact the two reservoirs.

**Mechanism.** Ambient vibration deflects the drumhead, doing two things *simultaneously and in phase*:
1. **Mechanical pumping:** the deflection compresses the fluid, driving an oscillating pressure‑driven ion flow through the conical channel, which produces a streaming current (convection of the electric double layer, EDL).
2. **Flexoelectric gating:** the *bending* of the nanomembrane creates a large strain gradient (10⁶–10⁷ m⁻¹ at nanoscale thickness), and flexoelectricity — which requires no non‑centrosymmetric material and grows as 1/thickness — generates a transient surface polarization that modulates the channel's surface charge density and hence the EDL/ionic selectivity.

Because the flexoelectric sign flips with the direction of bending, the channel is *ion‑selective for cations on the compression half‑cycle and for anions (or blocking) on the rebound half‑cycle*. The conical geometry adds a static ionic‑diode asymmetry. The result is that forward and reverse strokes no longer cancel: the device acts as its own synchronous rectifier, converting symmetric AC vibration into a **net DC ionic current** that is collected as electron current at the asymmetric electrodes — no external diode bridge, no ferroelectric poling, no triboelectric contact wear.

**Why it is novel/advantageous.** Existing nanogenerators rely on piezoelectricity (needs non‑centrosymmetric crystals, poling, high stiffness), triboelectricity (contact wear, AC output needing rectification), or passive streaming potentials (symmetric, self‑cancelling under vibration). Here, flexoelectric gating and mechanical pumping are *phase‑locked by construction* because both derive from the same membrane deflection — a mechanically driven ionic ratchet. It works in centrosymmetric, CMOS‑compatible dielectrics, at low frequencies (1–100 Hz, typical of ambient vibration) and sub‑nm strains where piezoelectrics give negligible output, and the 1/thickness scaling of flexoelectricity means performance *improves* as the device shrinks.

**Expected performance & tests.** Ionic conduction of the array gives low internal impedance (unlike high‑impedance piezo/tribo devices), easing impedance matching to CMOS power management; estimated open‑circuit output ~0.1–1 V with power densities of order µW–mW cm⁻² at 0.1 g excitation. Key validation experiments: (i) show DC (not AC) short‑circuit current whose sign reverses when the cone orientation or the electrolyte's dominant ion charge is reversed; (ii) confirm output scales as 1/membrane thickness (flexoelectric fingerprint) rather than with piezoelectric coefficient; (iii) demonstrate that output vanishes for symmetric cylindrical channels or for rigid (non‑bending) caps.

**Main risks.** Ionic‑liquid leakage/evaporation and electrode polarization (mitigate with sealed, redox‑active or capacitive electrodes such as MXene/Prussian‑blue), viscous drag limiting high‑frequency operation (mitigate by parallelizing many short channels), and dielectric breakdown/fatigue of the suspended membrane.

**Proposal: A "sliding‑ferroelectric superlubric shear nanogenerator" — ambient vibration converted to electricity by sub‑ångström interlayer sliding of parallel‑stacked van der Waals bilayers (slidetronic polarization pumping).**

**Architecture.** A stack of parallel‑stacked (AB/BA, ~0.1–1° twist) bilayer h‑BN (or 3R‑MoS₂/WTe₂) is sandwiched between graphene electrodes on a rigid substrate. The top layer is clamped to a lithographically defined inertial proof mass (a Si or metal nanopillar, ~pg–ng), while the bottom layer is anchored to the substrate. Crucially, the two layers are *not* bonded — they contact through an incommensurate, structurally superlubric van der Waals interface with friction coefficients of 10⁻⁴–10⁻⁶ and essentially zero wear. The moiré superlattice is made deliberately asymmetric (a gradient in twist angle, or a one‑sided strain/ripple gradient imposed by a sawtooth‑patterned substrate), creating a ratchet‑shaped moiré potential landscape for domain walls.

**Mechanism.** Ambient vibration accelerates the proof mass, applying an in‑plane *shear* to the bilayer. In parallel‑stacked vdW bilayers, an interlayer slide of only ~1–2 Å (one third of a lattice vector, AB→BA) reverses the out‑of‑plane electric polarization (~0.5–2 pC/m, i.e., ~10¹² e/cm² of bound charge) — sliding ferroelectricity. Because superlubric sliding costs almost no energy, even sub‑nm, sub‑nN vibrational excursions are enough to nucleate and translate moiré domain walls. Each wall sweeping across the electrode area flips the local polarization, and the compensating screening charge on the graphene electrodes must be re‑supplied through the external circuit: the vibration therefore *pumps* a displacement current I = A·dP/dt directly into the load. The engineered asymmetric moiré potential makes domain‑wall propagation easier in one shear direction than the other (a Brownian‑ratchet/"polarization ratchet"), so the forward and backward halves of the vibration cycle do not cancel and the device self‑rectifies to a net DC output without a diode bridge.

**Why it is fundamentally different.** This is neither piezoelectricity (no bulk lattice strain — the layers themselves are undeformed and centrosymmetric individually), nor triboelectricity (no contact electrification, no charge transfer across an asperity, no wear or degradation), nor electromagnetic induction. The energy conversion is *interfacial and topological*: it comes from translating a stacking‑order domain wall, not from deforming a crystal. The consequences are: (i) the transducer is mechanically ultra‑soft in shear yet electrically stiff, so it couples efficiently to the tiny forces of ambient vibration (µg–mg levels) that piezoelectric cantilevers cannot exploit; (ii) superlubricity means no fatigue, no wear‑out, and >10¹² switching cycles; (iii) the output is atomically thin (<1 nm active layer) and CMOS/BEOL‑compatible; (iv) energy per unit area per cycle is set by 2P_s·V, giving projected ~10–100 µW cm⁻² at 10–1000 Hz, with an extremely wide bandwidth because the switching is not resonance‑limited (domain‑wall speeds reach km/s).

**Validation experiments.** (1) Show short‑circuit current proportional to shear amplitude and frequency, and that it vanishes for antiparallel (2H, centrosymmetric) stacking of the identical device; (2) image moiré domain‑wall motion in situ (SHG, KPFM, or 4D‑STEM) synchronously with the current; (3) demonstrate DC (unipolar) output whose sign flips when the substrate sawtooth/twist‑gradient asymmetry is reversed; (4) verify wear‑free operation over 10⁹ cycles, distinguishing it from triboelectric decay.

**Risks/mitigations.** Depolarization‑field suppression of P (mitigate with graphene screening electrodes in direct contact), pinning of domain walls by adsorbates or bubbles (mitigate with encapsulated, annealed, ultraclean transfer), and the small energy per unit area (mitigate by 3D stacking of many bilayer repeats in parallel, which multiplies output while keeping the device sub‑micron thick).

**Proposal: a "magnetic‑mousetrap" straintronic spin‑pumping nanogenerator — low‑frequency vibration is up‑converted to GHz magnetization precession in magnetostrictive nanomagnets and rectified into DC by the inverse spin Hall effect.**

**Architecture.** On a thin flexible membrane (SiN, PET or Kapton, with an integrated proof mass) deposit a heavy‑metal spin‑sink strip (Pt, β‑W, or Bi₂Se₃, 3–5 nm) and on it a dense array (10⁹–10¹⁰ cm⁻²) of elliptical, single‑domain magnetostrictive nanomagnets (FeGa, Terfenol‑D or Ni, ~100 × 60 × 8 nm, λ_s ≈ 10⁻⁴–10⁻³). The ellipse long axis is deliberately tilted (~10–20°) with respect to the strain axis, and the nanomagnets are dipole‑chained so the array behaves as one coherent, biased ensemble; no external magnet is needed because a thin exchange‑bias (IrMn) underlayer supplies the symmetry‑breaking field. Many Pt strips are wired in series/parallel to sum the DC output.

**Mechanism (the novelty).** Ambient vibration (1–200 Hz) bends the membrane and strains each nanomagnet. Via inverse magnetostriction (Villari effect) the strain modulates the *magnetic anisotropy*, not the charge. The key trick is **mechanical‑to‑magnetic frequency up‑conversion by an anisotropy "snap"**: strain is stored slowly (Hz) until the stress‑induced easy axis rotates past a critical angle, at which point the magnetization is suddenly left far from equilibrium and undergoes free precessional ringing at its GHz ferromagnetic‑resonance frequency (~2–10 GHz) — a magnetic analogue of a mousetrap or a snapping buckled beam. Slow mechanical charging is thus released as a fast magnetic burst, an up‑conversion of ~10⁸ in frequency, exactly the regime where magnetodynamic transduction is efficient and where conventional piezoelectric/triboelectric harvesters fail (their output scales with frequency, so Hz excitation gives negligible power).

Each GHz precession burst **spin‑pumps** a pure spin current into the adjacent Pt layer, j_s ∝ g↑↓ (m × dm/dt). The **inverse spin Hall effect** converts this spin current into a transverse *charge* current, j_c ∝ θ_SH (j_s × σ). Because ⟨m × dm/dt⟩ is a rectified (second‑order, non‑zero DC average) quantity, the output is intrinsically **DC** — the device self‑rectifies without diodes. The tilted anisotropy/exchange bias ensures the precession cone has the same handedness on the compression and tension half‑cycles, so the two halves of the vibration cycle add rather than cancel.

**Why it is fundamentally different.** No piezoelectric poling, no non‑centrosymmetric crystal, no contact electrification/wear, no electromagnetic coil or magnet, and no charge separation across an insulator. The energy path is mechanical → magnetic‑anisotropy → magnon/spin current → charge current. Consequences: (i) the source impedance is metallic (Ω–kΩ), so it impedance‑matches directly to CMOS power management, unlike the GΩ–MΩ, capacitively limited output of piezo/tribo nanogenerators; (ii) the output is DC and unipolar, eliminating rectifier losses that dominate at low voltages; (iii) it is broadband and non‑resonant in the mechanical domain (any stroke that exceeds the snap threshold produces the same GHz burst), so it works over the messy, drifting spectrum of real ambient vibration; (iv) it is fully thin‑film, BEOL/CMOS‑compatible, and improves on scaling because spin pumping is an interface effect (output ∝ interface area, not volume).

**Estimates.** Per snap, each nanomagnet releases ~10²–10³ k_BT of anisotropy energy; with 10¹⁰ magnets cm⁻² snapping twice per cycle at 100 Hz and 5–10 % magnetoelastic→spin→charge conversion, the projected output is ~10–100 mV per series‑connected chain and ~1–50 µW cm⁻², at strains of only 10⁻⁴ (accelerations of ~0.01–0.1 g).

**Validation.** (1) The DC voltage must reverse sign when Pt (θ_SH > 0) is replaced by β‑W (θ_SH < 0) — the ISHE fingerprint; (2) it must vanish for zero‑magnetostriction permalloy (Ni₈₀Fe₂₀) nanomagnets of identical geometry, ruling out piezo/tribo/electromagnetic artefacts; (3) output should scale with λ_s·σ and show a threshold in strain amplitude (the snap condition) rather than a linear strain dependence; (4) time‑resolved MOKE or ferromagnetic‑resonance spectroscopy should show GHz ringing bursts phase‑locked to the Hz mechanical drive; (5) the sign should invert when the exchange‑bias direction (set during field cooling) is reversed.

**Risks/mitigations.** Thermal‑fluctuation‑induced random snapping and incoherent precession across the array (mitigate with dipole‑coupled chains and slightly larger, thermally stable magnets); magnetoelastic fatigue and clamping by the substrate (mitigate with free‑standing membranes and low‑Young's‑modulus polymer supports); spin‑memory loss at the FM/HM interface (mitigate with a thin Cu or Hf dusting layer); and possible thermoelectric (spin‑Seebeck/Nernst) artefacts, which the θ_SH‑reversal and λ_s = 0 control experiments explicitly exclude.

**Proposal: a "vibration‑driven adiabatic quantum charge pump" — ambient vibration used not to *strain* a material but to *cyclically modulate two out‑of‑phase parameters of a nanogap tunnel junction*, so that a geometric (Berry‑phase/Thouless) pumping cycle transports a fixed packet of electrons per vibration cycle, giving DC power with no piezoelectric, triboelectric, or inductive element.**

**Architecture.** Fabricate a dense array (10⁹–10¹⁰ cm⁻²) of vacuum/air nanogap tunnel junctions: a rigid substrate electrode of one metal (e.g., Pt, φ ≈ 5.6 eV) faces a suspended, ultrathin cantilever/drumhead electrode of a dissimilar metal (e.g., Hf or Al, φ ≈ 3.9–4.2 eV) with an equilibrium gap of 0.8–1.5 nm. Between them sits a single monolayer of quantum dots (or a self‑assembled redox/fullerene monolayer) bound to the moving electrode, forming an asymmetric double‑barrier (metal–dot–metal) junction with a discrete level ε₀ near the Fermi energy. Each suspended element carries a nanoscale proof mass placed **off‑axis**, so that a single ambient acceleration excites simultaneously a *flexural* mode (which changes the tunnel gap d, hence the barrier transparencies Γ_L, Γ_R) and a *torsional/rocking* mode (which tilts the dot in the built‑in contact‑potential field, hence Stark‑shifts the dot level ε₀). Because the two modes have different resonant frequencies and quality factors, they respond to the same broadband excitation with an intrinsic **phase lag of ≈ 90°**.

**Mechanism (the novelty).** The junction's transported charge depends on the two parameters (Γ_asymmetry, ε₀). Modulating either one alone gives only reactive, cycle‑averaged‑zero current. But modulating them *in quadrature* makes the system trace a **closed loop of finite area in parameter space**, and adiabatic quantum pumping theory says the charge transferred per cycle is Q = (e/2π)∮ (∂θ/∂X₁ ∂/∂X₂ − …) dX₁dX₂ — i.e., proportional to the *enclosed area*, not to the modulation frequency or to any material polarization. Physically: on the half‑cycle when the gap narrows, the level is pushed below E_F and the dot loads an electron preferentially from the low‑work‑function electrode; on the return half‑cycle the level is pushed up while the barrier asymmetry has reversed, so the electron unloads into the high‑work‑function electrode. Each vibration cycle therefore ratchets a well‑defined electron packet "uphill" against the load, and the built‑in contact potential difference (0.5–1.5 V) sets the available voltage. **The device is intrinsically self‑rectifying and DC** — reversing the vibration direction does not cancel the output, because the sign is set by the *handedness of the loop* (the sign of the mode phase lag and the direction of the work‑function gradient), not by the sign of the stroke.

**Why this is fundamentally different.** (i) No non‑centrosymmetric crystal, no poling, no contact electrification/wear (electrodes never touch — tunneling is a non‑contact interaction), no coils or magnets. (ii) The transduction is *exponentially* sensitive: tunneling current varies e‑fold per ~0.05 nm, so sub‑ångström vibrational amplitudes — far below the strain needed for any piezoelectric response — already produce order‑unity modulation. (iii) Output charge per cycle is *amplitude‑insensitive and quantized‑like* once the loop encloses the resonance, which stabilizes power against the erratic amplitude of real ambient vibration.
