(iv) The source impedance is set by tunnel resistance (kΩ–MΩ per junction, and ~Ω–kΩ for a massively parallel array), a far better match to CMOS power management than the GΩ, capacitive source of piezo/tribo nanogenerators, and it needs no diode bridge (whose ~0.2–0.3 V drop kills millivolt harvesters). (v) It is a genuinely non‑resonant, broadband harvester in the mechanical domain: any excitation that drives both modes with a phase difference pumps charge.

**Estimates.** With Q ≈ 0.1–1 e per junction per cycle, 10¹⁰ junctions cm⁻², 100 Hz ambient vibration and ~0.7 V contact potential, the projected output is ~0.1–1 µA cm⁻² at ~0.5 V, i.e. ~0.05–0.5 µW cm⁻² per layer, multiplied by vertical stacking of many layers in a BEOL‑compatible 3D array.

**Validation experiments.** (1) The DC short‑circuit current must **reverse sign when the relative phase of the two mechanical modes is inverted** (achieved by driving above vs. below the torsional resonance, or by mirroring the off‑axis proof mass) — the unambiguous fingerprint of geometric pumping, which no piezoelectric, triboelectric, thermoelectric, or capacitive‑generator artefact can reproduce. (2) Output must be roughly independent of drive frequency (charge/cycle constant) rather than ∝ f, distinguishing it from displacement‑current mechanisms. (3) It must vanish for symmetric junctions (same metal on both sides, or single‑barrier junctions with no dot level). (4) Output must peak when a DC gate bias tunes ε₀ through E_F, mapping out the pumping resonance. (5) Wear‑free operation over >10¹⁰ cycles, in contrast to triboelectric decay.

**Risks/mitigations.** Non‑adiabaticity and decoherence at room temperature (mitigate by using strongly coupled, large‑charging‑energy dots or molecular redox centres with level spacing ≫ k_BT, and by operating deep in the adiabatic regime, f ≪ Γ/ħ, which is trivially satisfied at Hz–kHz); stiction/collapse of the suspended electrode (mitigate with mechanical stops, hydrophobic/vacuum encapsulation, and stiff SiN or graphene membranes); rectification of thermal (Johnson) noise mimicking a signal (excluded by the phase‑reversal control, which no equilibrium ratchet can pass); and gap drift from adsorbates or thermal expansion (mitigate with hermetic vacuum sealing and a slow electrostatic servo that re‑centres the gap using a fraction of the harvested power).

Propose a way to achieve high-resolution.answer:
Use femtosecond‑laser two‑photon (multiphoton) polymerization direct laser writing, and then shrink the printed object to push the features below the optical diffraction limit.

Concretely: a tightly focused near‑IR femtosecond beam is scanned point‑by‑point through a photosensitive resin/hydrogel precursor. Because polymerization requires simultaneous absorption of two (or more) photons, cross‑linking occurs only in the tiny central region of the focal volume where the intensity is highest, so a single voxel is already sub‑micron (~100–200 nm) and can be written anywhere inside the transparent volume, giving true layer‑free 3D freedom. Resolution is further improved by (i) working just above the polymerization threshold with low dose and high‑contrast/high‑threshold resists containing radical quenchers, (ii) adding a doughnut‑shaped depletion/inhibition beam (STED‑inspired lithography) that switches off polymerization at the focus periphery, and (iii) using high‑NA immersion optics and precise piezo/galvo scanning with adaptive optics for aberration correction.

Finally, "implosion fabrication": write the pattern into a swollen, water‑filled polyacrylate/polyacrylamide hydrogel scaffold (depositing the desired material—metal ions, nanoparticles, quantum dots, biomolecules—at the addressed voxels), then dehydrate/de‑swell the gel with acid or divalent salts so it contracts isotropically 10–20× in each dimension. All written features and their spacings scale down accordingly, converting ~½‑micron writing into ~10–50 nm final structures, while the material densifies into a solid nanostructure. Development/rinsing and optional pyrolysis or metallization then yield the finished high‑resolution 3D nanostructure.

Use **focused‑electron‑beam‑induced deposition (FEBID) as a direct "3D nano‑printer"** inside a scanning electron microscope.

How it works: a gas‑injection needle supplies a volatile organometallic precursor (e.g., Me₃PtCpMe, Co₂(CO)₈, W(CO)₆, Fe(CO)₅) that physisorbs on the substrate in a monolayer. A tightly focused, high‑energy (5–30 keV) electron beam is parked/scanned point‑by‑point; the secondary electrons generated in a nanometre‑sized spot dissociate the adsorbed molecules, leaving a solid deposit only where the beam dwells while the volatile ligands are pumped away. Because deposition is driven by the secondary‑electron cloud rather than by an optical focus, the voxel size is set by the beam and the electron interaction volume — a few nanometres — so features of ~5–20 nm and freestanding vertical, tilted, or branched nanowires can be built.

To make it truly 3D: the deposit grows toward the beam, so by moving the beam very slowly the pillar grows vertically, and by increasing the scan speed the growing tip bends at a controlled angle. Combining calibrated dwell times, beam‑speed/angle relationships, and simulation‑generated beam‑path files (3D CAD sliced into a stream of x, y, dwell‑time points, with compensation for substrate heating, precursor depletion/replenishment and proximity/secondary‑electron scattering) allows the direct writing of complex free‑space 3D meshes, helices, nanobridges and lattices in a single step without supports, layers or resist development.

Post‑processing — in‑situ electron‑beam or O₂/H₂O purification, or annealing — removes residual carbon and converts the deposit into a pure metal (Pt, Co, Fe, W) or oxide, giving functional plasmonic, magnetic or mechanical 3D nanostructures with sub‑10 nm resolution, and the same platform allows immediate SEM/STEM inspection and correction during printing.

**Use electrochemical (meniscus‑confined) 3D nanoprinting with a nanopipette – i.e., localized electrodeposition of metal ions from an attoliter liquid meniscus.**

A glass/quartz capillary is pulled to a nozzle only ~30–250 nm across and filled with a metal‑salt electrolyte (e.g., Cu²⁺, Ag⁺, Ni²⁺, Au³⁺, or mixed salts). The nozzle is brought within nanometres of a conductive substrate on a piezo stage; capillary forces form a tiny liquid bridge (meniscus) between the pipette tip and the surface, which confines the electrochemistry to a spot roughly the size of the aperture. Applying a small voltage (a few volts) between a counter/reference electrode inside the pipette and the substrate reduces the ions exactly within that meniscus, so a metal voxel of tens of nanometres nucleates only there. The deposition current (or ion‑ejection current in the electrohydrodynamic‑redox variant, where ions are ejected from the tip by a field and reduced on landing) is monitored in a feedback loop that senses when a voxel is complete and retracts the tip by exactly one voxel height, letting the structure grow continuously upward.

By scanning the nozzle along a sliced CAD path, one writes voxel‑by‑voxel free‑standing pillars, helices, overhangs, cantilevers, lattices and even hollow shells in pure, dense, polycrystalline metal — no resist, no photopolymer binder, no sacrificial support and no pyrolysis/burn‑out step, so the printed object is immediately electrically and mechanically functional. Because the printing happens at room temperature from solution, multi‑metal and compositionally graded objects can be made simply by using a multi‑barrel (theta) pipette and switching or mixing the electrolytes voxel‑by‑voxel, enabling alloy gradients and later selective etching of one metal to leave nanoporous or hollow architectures.

Resolution is set by the nozzle diameter, the meniscus size and the ion flux rather than by any diffraction limit, so features of ~25–100 nm with aspect ratios above 10 are attainable; further reduction of the aperture, use of low‑concentration electrolytes and tight current feedback push it toward sub‑20 nm. Printing in a humidity‑controlled chamber (or fully immersed, "electrohydrodynamic in‑liquid" mode) stabilizes the meniscus, and in‑situ SEM/AFM monitoring allows closed‑loop correction during the build.

**Use DNA‑origami self‑assembly as a "molecular 3D printer": build a programmable DNA mold and cast the desired material inside it.**

Design the object in CAD‑like DNA design software (caDNAno/vHelix/ATHENA): a long single‑stranded M13 scaffold (~7,000 nt) is folded by hundreds of computer‑designed short "staple" strands into a rigid, hollow 3D box/mold whose interior cavity has exactly the shape of the nanostructure you want (pillars, rings, chiral helices, cubes, branched frames). Because the position of every helix is fixed by Watson–Crick base pairing, the shape is defined with ~2 nm (single‑base, 0.34 nm axial) precision — far beyond any beam‑ or optics‑limited printer — and the whole batch self‑assembles in one annealing step (95 °C → 20 °C over a few hours in Mg²⁺ buffer), giving 10¹²+ identical copies in parallel rather than one voxel at a time.

To turn the DNA "print" into a functional solid: place gold‑nanoparticle seeds on interior staple strands modified with thiol/amine handles, then add a growth solution (HAuCl₄/AgNO₃ + ascorbic acid or hydroxylamine) so the metal grows only inside the confined cavity until it fills the mold, faithfully replicating its shape (or, alternatively, silicify the DNA with TMAPS/TEOS to make a rigid silica replica, or use it as a template for ALD of Al₂O₃/TiO₂ and subsequent metallization). Finally remove the DNA by enzymatic digestion (DNase), oxygen plasma, or calcination, leaving the free‑standing inorganic nanostructure.

Multi‑material and hierarchical "printing" comes free: different staples can be labelled with different chemistries so metals, quantum dots, proteins, or fluorophores are placed at defined coordinates within the same object; and origami units can carry complementary sticky ends so they hierarchically assemble into larger, micron‑scale 3D lattices/superlattices. Deposit the assembled origami on a lithographically patterned substrate (with binding sites of matching shape/charge) to register the nanostructures at chosen locations, then image by cryo‑EM/AFM to verify the print.

This gives true 3D architectures with sub‑5 nm feature control, massively parallel throughput, and arbitrary chemical addressability — resolution limited by molecular dimensions rather than by a focused beam or nozzle.

**Use electrohydrodynamic (EHD) jet nanoprinting — "near‑field electrospinning" of a charged nano‑jet — to stack sub‑100 nm filaments into 3D nanostructures.**

A polymer/nanoparticle ink (e.g., PEO, PVDF, polymer–quantum‑dot or metal‑nanoparticle suspension) is fed through a fine, conductive‑coated glass or metal nozzle (0.5–2 µm inner diameter) held only tens of microns above a grounded, piezo‑driven substrate. A DC bias of a few hundred volts to ~2 kV deforms the ink into a Taylor cone whose apex emits a jet far *thinner* than the nozzle itself; because the nozzle–substrate gap is smaller than the jet's instability (whipping) onset length, the jet lands straight and stably, so line widths of ~20–100 nm are written deterministically rather than randomly deposited. Resolution is set by the Taylor‑cone apex, ink viscosity/conductivity and field strength — not by any diffraction limit or beam optics.

To go 3D, exploit **self‑aligned charge focusing**: solvent evaporates in flight so the arriving filament is already solidified, and the residual charge on the freshly deposited tip locally concentrates the electric field, steering each subsequent jet segment onto the previous one. By retracting the stage (or nozzle) at exactly the deposition rate under current/field feedback, the filament grows vertically as a free‑standing nanowire, and by translating laterally during growth one writes arches, zig‑zags, helices, woodpile lattices, high‑aspect‑ratio pillar arrays and hollow scaffolds directly from a sliced CAD path, without supports, resist, developer or a photopolymer matrix.

Multi‑material printing is achieved with multi‑barrel nozzles or by switching inks mid‑build; functional nanostructures follow from post‑processing — sintering or reductive annealing of nanoparticle inks to give dense metal (Ag, Au, Cu) nanowire architectures, or pyrolysis of polymer prints to yield glassy‑carbon/ceramic nanolattices. Environmental control (humidity, temperature), pulsed‑voltage "drop/segment‑on‑demand" operation for discrete voxels, and in‑situ optical/SEM monitoring with closed‑loop tuning of the standoff distance keep the jet stable and enable nanometre‑accurate registration on pre‑patterned electrodes, all at ambient conditions, high speed and low cost compared with vacuum beam‑based nanofabrication.

**Use thermal scanning‑probe lithography (t‑SPL) as a "nano‑3D‑printer": a heated AFM tip that sculpts 3D relief in a self‑amplified depolymerizing resist, repeated layer‑by‑layer.**

Coat the substrate with a thermally labile resist (e.g., polyphthalaldehyde/polycarbonate or a cross‑linkable molecular glass) on a thin transfer/sacrificial underlayer. A silicon cantilever with an integrated resistive heater terminating in a tip of ~5 nm radius is heated in microsecond pulses to ~300–700 °C and pressed into the film with nanonewton force. Where the hot tip touches, the polymer unzips into volatile monomers that evaporate instantly, so material is *removed* (or, with a "nano‑extrusion"/ink‑coated tip, locally *deposited*) with no chemical development, no beam, and no diffraction or proximity‑scattering limits — the voxel is set by the tip–surface contact area and the thermal decay length, giving lateral features of ~10 nm and depth control of ~1 nm.

3D shaping comes from grayscale dose modulation: pit depth is a smooth, calibrated function of tip temperature, force and dwell time, so a sliced CAD height map is converted directly into a pulse map and a full 3D surface profile (ramps, curved lenses, chirped gratings, overlapping multi‑level cavities) is written in a single pass rather than by stacking binary layers. Because the same cantilever carries a thermoelectric/piezoresistive height sensor, the just‑written topography is read back in‑line during writing, enabling closed‑loop correction of depth errors and overlay alignment to previously written layers with sub‑5 nm accuracy — something no optical or e‑beam tool does simultaneously.

True volumetric structures are then built by iteration: after each patterned layer, transfer the relief into a functional material by directional dry etching, lift‑off, or by spinning/evaporating the next material (metal, oxide, polymer) and planarizing, then spin a fresh resist and align the next grayscale layer to the buried markers read by the same tip. Stacking such registered grayscale layers yields multi‑material 3D nanoarchitectures (photonic crystals, plasmonic stacks, nanofluidic channels, nano‑optical elements).

Throughput is scaled by operating parallel arrays of independently addressed heated cantilevers (thousands of tips writing simultaneously, "millipede"‑style), and the whole process runs in ambient air at low tip temperatures without vacuum, charging, resist chemistry variability, or damage to sensitive substrates such as 2D materials, organics and biomolecules.

**Use laser‑induced forward transfer (LIFT) of molten sub‑micron droplets — a "nano‑inkjet" that prints pure metal voxel by voxel.**

Set‑up: a thin (20–100 nm) donor film of the desired metal (Au, Ag, Cu, Al, Cr, or an alloy/multilayer) is evaporated onto a transparent carrier (glass/sapphire). The carrier is placed film‑side‑down a few microns above the receiver substrate, which sits on a piezo/nanopositioning stage. A femtosecond or picosecond laser pulse is focused through the carrier onto the back of the donor film; the confined absorption melts and pressurizes a tiny disc of metal that is ejected as a **single molten nanodroplet** that flies across the gap and solidifies on impact within nanoseconds.

Why it can be high resolution: by working just above the ejection threshold with a tightly focused, near‑Gaussian beam, only the very centre of the spot exceeds the ejection fluence, so the transferred droplet is much smaller than the focal spot (a few hundred down to ~50–100 nm in diameter, i.e. attolitre volumes). Resolution is set by the ejected melt volume — film thickness × threshold area — not by the diffraction limit, and can be tuned continuously by thinning the donor film and lowering the pulse energy. Each pulse deposits one droplet, so the process is inherently digital and drop‑on‑demand (kHz–MHz repetition rates).

Going 3D: because each droplet arrives molten and freezes immediately on the previously deposited one, droplets stack on top of each other and self‑align by surface tension. Firing repeated pulses on the same (x,y) point while retracting the stage grows a free‑standing vertical nanowire/pillar; translating laterally between pulses writes tilted rods, arches, zig‑zags, helices, coils, meshes, cantilevers and lattices directly from a sliced CAD droplet map — with no support material, no resist, no developer and no binder to burn out. The donor ribbon is translated to expose fresh film for every shot, and pulse energy/gap/droplet spacing are held in closed loop using in‑situ imaging (or plasma/acoustic shot‑to‑shot monitoring) to keep droplet size and placement uniform.

Advantages/extension: the printed material is dense, pure, fully crystalline metal that is immediately electrically and mechanically functional (no sintering or pyrolysis step); multi‑material and compositionally graded structures are made simply by switching to a different donor region mid‑build; and printing works in air on almost any receiver, including flexible polymers, fibres, membranes, or the facet of an optical fibre/AFM tip — enabling 3D plasmonic antennas, nanoelectrode arrays, interconnects, and inductor/coil nanostructures written directly onto pre‑existing devices.

**Print in the gas phase: "ion‑assisted aerosol nanoparticle 3D printing," in which electrostatic funnels focus charged nanoparticles onto a substrate and grow the structures by self‑focused accretion.**

Generate a continuous aerosol of nanoparticles (Au, Ag, Si, TiO₂, Ni…) by spark discharge, laser ablation or atomization, size‑select them with a differential mobility analyzer, and unipolarly charge them. The receiving substrate is a conductor covered with a thin insulating (photoresist/oxide) film that has been pre‑patterned by conventional lithography with openings only tens of nanometres wide. A separate corona/soft‑X‑ray ion source floods the chamber with ions of the *same* polarity as the particles; these ions charge the exposed dielectric surface, so the insulator becomes strongly repulsive while the grounded openings remain attractive. The resulting three‑dimensional field landscape acts as an "electrostatic funnel/lens" that steers essentially every incoming particle into the small conductive window — deposition is therefore *concentrating* rather than diffraction‑ or nozzle‑limited, and features can be considerably **narrower than the lithographic opening (≈20–50 nm)**.

Building in 3D is automatic and self‑correcting: as particles pile up, the growing tip is the most field‑enhanced, least‑screened point, so incoming particles are guided preferentially to the apex, producing free‑standing vertical nanopillars/nanowires whose height simply scales with deposition time. Tilting or scanning the substrate, applying an in‑plane bias, or changing the ion‑flux/particle‑charge ratio during growth bends the electric field and hence bends the growing structure, giving curved, slanted, spiral, branched or "nanotree" architectures; switching the aerosol source mid‑run yields axially multi‑material or core–shell structures (e.g., magnetic base, plasmonic tip).

Because the entire wafer is patterned in parallel by one particle stream (no point‑by‑point serial writing, no vacuum beam column, no resin, developer or support material), millions of identical 3D nanostructures are produced simultaneously in minutes at near‑ambient pressure. A final low‑temperature sintering (thermal or photonic) densifies the particle assembly into a mechanically robust, electrically conductive solid, and stripping the dielectric mask releases free‑standing 3D nano‑arrays for plasmonic sensors, field emitters, superhydrophobic/antireflective surfaces or nanoelectrode arrays.

**Build the object atom‑by‑atom with a scanning tunnelling microscope: hydrogen‑depassivation lithography combined with selective atomic‑layer growth and epitaxial overgrowth ("atomically precise 3D printing").**

Start with a clean Si(100) (or Ge/ diamond) surface in ultrahigh vacuum, terminated with a single monolayer of hydrogen that acts as an atomically thin, perfectly uniform resist. An STM tip is then used as the "print head": at a few volts and nanoampere current the tunnelling electrons desorb individual H atoms, so a pattern of bare, chemically reactive dangling bonds is written with true single‑atom (≈0.4 nm) placement accuracy — resolution set by the atomic lattice itself, not by a focused beam, meniscus, droplet or optical spot. The same tip immediately images the written pattern with atomic resolution, giving in‑line, closed‑loop verification and error correction (missing/extra atoms can be re‑written or re‑passivated) before the next step.

The bare patch is then dosed with a precursor gas (PH₃, AsH₃, B₂H₆, or an ALD metal/oxide precursor such as TMA, TiCl₄, Me₃PtCpMe). The molecules chemisorb and incorporate **only** on the depassivated atoms — the H monolayer blocks reaction everywhere else — so a single atomic layer of dopant or material is deposited exactly in the printed shape (area‑selective ALD/atomic‑layer epitaxy). A brief thermal incorporation anneal locks the atoms into the lattice.

To make it three‑dimensional, repeat: grow a few nanometres of epitaxial silicon (or ALD oxide) over the finished layer at low temperature to bury it without diffusing the pattern, re‑passivate the new surface with atomic hydrogen, re‑locate the buried layer using pre‑written fiducial markers imaged by the same tip, and write the next atomic plane in registry. Stacking tens to hundreds of such registered atomic layers—each with its own shape and its own material/dopant chemistry—yields a fully embedded, monolithic 3D nanostructure with ~1 nm vertical and sub‑nm lateral control: 3D dopant/qubit arrays, vertically stacked atomic wires and tunnel junctions, single‑atom transistors, and 3D photonic/quantum devices. Throughput is scaled by running arrays of independently addressed tips (and by using the tip only to write "seed" patterns that are subsequently amplified by selective growth), and because everything happens in UHV with a monolayer resist there is no developer, no proximity scattering, no shrinkage and no support material.

**Make it 2‑D first, then fold it: "nano‑origami" — pattern ultrathin membranes with planar lithography and then transform them into 3‑D by controlled stress/ion‑beam folding.**

Start with a sacrificial‑layer/thin‑film stack (e.g., Si₃N₄, SiO₂, Al₂O₃, Au, or a bilayer of two materials with different intrinsic stress or expansion coefficients) on a wafer. Use the highest‑resolution *planar* tools available — electron‑beam or EUV/He‑ion lithography, block‑copolymer or nanoimprint templating — to define the flat "unfolded" precursor: panels, ribbons, hinges, tabs and slits, with feature sizes of 5–20 nm written over a full wafer in parallel. Because all the fine patterning is done in a single plane, one keeps the ultimate resolution, overlay accuracy and throughput of 2‑D nanolithography instead of paying the resolution penalty of serial voxel‑by‑voxel 3‑D writing.

The flat sheet is then converted into a true three‑dimensional object by *actuating the hinges*:

- **Focused‑ion‑beam folding:** a low‑dose Ga⁺/He⁺ scan along a designated hinge line implants ions and creates a compressive/tensile stress gradient through the film thickness, so the panel bends by an angle that is a calibrated, monotonic function of ion dose. Dose maps therefore act as a "fold program" (mountain/valley folds, curved creases), giving boxes, tetrahedra, helices, split‑ring resonators, chiral plasmonic gyroids and cantilevered nano‑machines.
- **Residual‑stress / bilayer roll‑up:** releasing the sacrificial layer (HF or XeF₂) lets pre‑stressed bilayers curl into tubes, spirals and coils with radii set simply by film thickness and mismatch strain (nm‑scale curvature control).
- **Compressive buckling / pop‑up assembly:** bond selected pads of the 2‑D precursor to a pre‑stretched elastomer or a shape‑memory layer; relaxing the strain makes the untethered segments pop out of plane into ribbons, arches, cages and multi‑storey lattices, with the final geometry predicted quantitatively by finite‑element mechanics.
- **Capillary or magnetic/electrostatic folding** of surface‑tension‑driven hinges (a melting solder/polymer pad at each crease) for self‑assembling, self‑latching closure.

Locking, verification and function: after folding, the joints are fixed by a brief ALD conformal coating, a second FIB "weld", or by shape‑memory/latch tabs, so the structure is mechanically rigid; ALD also lets you conformally coat the folded object with a second material (metal, oxide, catalyst) to make it functional. Because the panels were patterned when flat, each face can carry its own high‑resolution decoration — gratings, antennas, nanopores, electrodes, dopant patterns, multilayers — which is essentially impossible with any direct 3‑D writing method. In‑situ SEM imaging during FIB folding provides closed‑loop control of the fold angle, and fiducial marks guarantee registry between faces.

The result is wafer‑scale, massively parallel production of complex, multi‑material 3‑D nanostructures (3‑D metamaterials, chiral photonic elements, nano‑cages/drug carriers, 3‑D nanoelectrode and MEMS/NEMS architectures) whose resolution is inherited from 2‑D lithography — sub‑10 nm features with atomically smooth surfaces — rather than being limited by a focal spot, nozzle, droplet or voxel.

**Print at cryogenic temperature with "ice lithography": use condensed ice films as a resist‑free, layer‑by‑layer 3D nano‑printing medium in an electron/ion microscope.**

Mount the substrate on a cryo‑stage (~100 K or below) inside an SEM/STEM equipped with a gas‑injection/condensation nozzle. Leak in a vapour (H₂O, or an organic such as nonane/anisole, or an organometallic vapour) that condenses as a smooth, amorphous, few‑nanometre‑thick "ice" film — a perfectly uniform, spin‑free, contaminant‑free resist that conforms even to non‑flat and fragile substrates.

A tightly focused electron (or He⁺) beam is then scanned over the frozen film according to a sliced CAD path. Where the beam dwells, the ice is either (i) locally desorbed/sublimed, opening a nanometre‑scale window through which an evaporated material is deposited (a self‑developing, resist‑stripping‑free stencil), or (ii) cross‑linked/decomposed so that the exposed voxel remains as a solid deposit while the unexposed ice simply sublimes away on warming — no wet developer, no rinsing, hence no capillary collapse of high‑aspect‑ratio features. Because the beam spot and the very thin, low‑Z film give almost no proximity scattering or beam broadening, the voxel is set by the electron probe (~5–20 nm; ~1 nm with He⁺).

Three‑dimensionality is achieved by *iterating the cycle in situ*: after each written and metallised/deposited layer, condense a fresh ice film of controlled thickness (thickness = layer height, monitored interferometrically or by beam transmission), realign to fiducials imaged by the same beam, and write the next slice in registry. Sacrificial ice can also be printed deliberately as a support material for overhangs, bridges and hollow shells, and it disappears completely by sublimation when the stage is warmed — a support that needs no chemical removal. Switching the condensed vapour or the evaporant between layers gives multi‑material, compositionally graded 3D objects (metal/oxide/organic), and the low temperature preserves beam‑ and solvent‑sensitive materials (2D crystals, organics, biological specimens).

The result is genuinely additive, resist‑ and developer‑free 3D nanoprinting with sub‑20 nm features, in‑line SEM verification after every layer, and clean release of free‑standing nanoarchitectures simply by letting the ice evaporate.

**Use a plasmonic near‑field "nano‑pen" printhead: beat the diffraction limit by writing with an evanescent hot‑spot from a nanoantenna/nanoaperture flying just above the resin, and stack the layers.**

Fabricate the printhead by placing a resonant plasmonic element — a bowtie or "C"/ridge aperture (gap 10–30 nm) milled in a metal film, or a metal‑coated tapered fiber/AFM tip with a sub‑50 nm aperture — at the apex of a scanning probe (or on an air‑bearing "flying head" like a hard‑disk slider). Illuminate it from behind with a CW or femtosecond laser polarized along the antenna axis; at resonance the field is squeezed and enhanced 10²–10³× in the gap, producing an evanescent hot‑spot only ~10–30 nm wide that decays within ~20 nm of the tip. Because the exposure volume is set by the antenna gap and the near‑field decay length — not by λ/2NA — a single voxel is an order of magnitude smaller than any far‑field focus, and the strong intensity enhancement lets you exploit the nonlinear/threshold response of the photoresin (two‑photon absorption or radical‑threshold polymerization) so only the very core of the hot‑spot cross‑links, trimming the voxel to <20 nm.

Printing procedure: spin (or dispense) an ultrathin film of photopolymer, metal‑ion photoreduction ink, or nanoparticle photoresin; bring the antenna into contact/near‑contact under AFM force or gap feedback (shear‑force, tunneling, or optical‑gap servo holds the standoff constant to ~1 nm, which is essential because the dose depends exponentially on tip–surface distance); raster the head along a sliced CAD path while gating the laser per voxel. Develop or simply add the next thin layer, re‑register to fiducials read by the same probe, and repeat — building true 3D architectures (woodpiles, helices, nanolattices, plasmonic/photonic elements) layer by layer with ~20 nm lateral and ~10–20 nm vertical resolution. Using a metal‑salt ink (Ag⁺/Au³⁺ + photoreducer) prints conductive metal directly; a nanoparticle or preceramic ink plus low‑temperature sintering/pyrolysis gives metal or ceramic nanostructures.

Throughput, which is the usual weakness of serial near‑field writing, is recovered by parallelization: mold an elastomeric "beam‑pen" array of thousands of pyramidal tips, each with a sub‑100 nm aperture at its apex, and address them individually with a digital micromirror device, so thousands of near‑field voxels are exposed simultaneously over a wafer‑scale area; head arrays on flying sliders can be scanned at m/s speeds. In‑line control comes from monitoring the antenna's scattering/reflectance (which shifts as the resin polymerizes) for closed‑loop dose feedback, and from imaging the just‑written layer with the same probe.

The key advantages: it uses ordinary low‑power light and ambient conditions (no vacuum, no electron beam, no charging or damage), the resolution is set by a lithographically defined nanogap that can be shrunk at will, and it can print on curved, flexible, or pre‑patterned substrates and on top of existing devices.

**Use bottom‑up "self‑assembly printing": directed self‑assembly (DSA) of block copolymers combined with sequential infiltration synthesis (SIS)/backfilling to cast 3D nanostructures with ~5–20 nm features over whole wafers.**

Design the geometry through polymer chemistry rather than a writing beam. Synthesize a block copolymer (e.g., PS‑b‑PMMA, PS‑b‑P4VP, PS‑b‑PDMS, or an ABC triblock/blend) whose block molecular weights and volume fractions are chosen so that microphase separation produces the desired equilibrium morphology — vertical cylinders, lamellae, spheres, or genuinely three‑dimensional bicontinuous networks such as the double gyroid, diamond, or alternating‑gyroid phase. Because the domain period is set by the polymer chain dimensions (L₀ ≈ 5–50 nm, tunable by N and χ, with high‑χ systems reaching sub‑10 nm), the "printed" feature size is defined thermodynamically, not by any focal spot, nozzle, droplet or probe — and the entire pattern forms simultaneously everywhere on the wafer in a single anneal (thermal or solvent‑vapour), giving trillions of identical, defect‑healing nanofeatures in minutes.

Impose deterministic placement and orientation (this is what turns self‑assembly into *printing*): pre‑pattern the substrate by a coarse, easy lithography step — chemoepitaxial chemical stripes/brush patterns or graphoepitaxial trenches with a pitch that is an integer multiple of L₀ — so the self‑assembled domains register to the guiding pattern with sub‑nanometre placement accuracy and pitch multiplication (the template does the "addressing," the polymer does the "resolution"). Electric fields, shear, thermal gradients or topographic guides can be used to align 3D network domains along chosen crystallographic directions.

Convert the soft polymer template into a robust inorganic 3D nanostructure by **sequential infiltration synthesis**: expose the annealed film to alternating ALD‑style pulses (e.g., trimethylaluminium + H₂O, TiCl₄ + H₂O, or diethyl zinc) that selectively coordinate to and grow inside only one block (the ester‑ or pyridine‑containing domain). After a few cycles the chosen domain is filled with Al₂O₃/TiO₂/ZnO; removing the polymer by an O₂ plasma or calcination leaves a free‑standing, mechanically stiff inorganic replica of the 3D morphology. Alternatively, selectively etch one block and backfill the interconnected void by electrodeposition or ALD with metals (Au, Ni, Pt) to obtain 3D metallic gyroid networks, or use the inorganic replica as a hard mask for deep anisotropic etching to transfer the pattern into silicon.

Extend to arbitrary, multi‑level 3D architectures by iteration and hierarchy: planarize each completed layer, deposit a new brush/guiding pattern aligned to buried fiducials, and self‑assemble the next layer with a different polymer (different L₀, morphology, or orientation), stacking registered nanoscale layers into woodpile‑like or graded 3D architectures; blends, triblock terpolymers and solvent‑annealing paths give core–shell, multi‑material and hierarchical (nanostructure‑within‑microstructure) motifs.

Advantages: massively parallel and inexpensive (no vacuum column, no serial voxel writing, no diffraction limit); sub‑10 nm resolution set by molecular size with atomically smooth interfaces; and it directly yields functional 3D metamaterials — optical gyroid metamaterials with chiral/negative‑index response, 3D photonic crystals, nanoporous membranes and battery/catalyst electrodes, and high‑surface‑area 3D interconnected networks that would be impractical to write point‑by‑point.

**Use a matter‑transporting scanning probe as the printhead: thermal dip‑pen nanolithography (tDPN) — an ink‑coated, resistively heated AFM tip that "extrudes" attolitre volumes of molten ink point‑by‑point and stacks them into 3D nanostructures.**

Coat a cantilever having a heater‑integrated tip (apex radius ~10–20 nm) with a solid "ink" that is a solid at room temperature but flows when warm — e.g. a low‑melting polymer (polyethylene, PCL, polystyrene oligomer), an organometallic/metal‑nanoparticle paste, a molten metal alloy (In, Bi–Sn), a preceramic polymer, or a phase‑change chalcogenide. Because the ink is solid at ambient temperature, nothing leaks: writing is switched **on and off electronically** by pulsing the tip heater (µs pulses, 50–300 °C). When the tip is heated in contact with the surface, a nanoscopic molten meniscus forms and a voxel of ink is transferred; when the pulse ends the ink re‑solidifies instantly and the transfer stops. The voxel volume is set by the tip–surface contact area, the pulse temperature and the dwell time — not by any beam, focal spot, or diffraction limit — giving lateral features of ~10–50 nm and sub‑nanometre control of the deposited height per pulse. (In the classical room‑temperature DPN variant, a water meniscus instead carries molecular, nanoparticle, protein, or sol–gel inks by diffusion, with the humidity and dwell time setting the dot size.)

**Building the third dimension:** because each pulse adds material rather than removing it, the tip simply retracts by one voxel height under z‑feedback and fires again on the same spot, growing a free‑standing nanopillar; translating laterally between pulses writes tilted rods, arches, bridges, helices, meshes and woodpile lattices directly from a sliced CAD path. The same cantilever is a force/height sensor, so after every voxel or layer the just‑printed topography is imaged in‑line with nanometre accuracy, enabling closed‑loop correction of layer height, overlay to buried fiducials, and repair of defects during the build — a self‑metrology capability no beam‑based printer has. Multi‑material and compositionally graded structures are made by shuttling between several inkwells (microfluidic ink reservoirs on the chip) or by using multiple cantilevers, each carrying a different ink, so metal, polymer, and functional (magnetic, fluorescent, biological) voxels can be interleaved within one object. Post‑processing — mild thermal sintering, reductive annealing of nanoparticle inks, or pyrolysis of preceramic ink — densifies the print into solid metal, oxide, or glassy‑carbon nanoarchitectures.

**Throughput:** the usual serial bottleneck is removed by massive parallelization — 2D arrays of thousands to millions of independently heated cantilevers, or elastomeric "polymer‑pen"/"beam‑pen" arrays individually actuated by a digital micromirror device — so an entire wafer of identical (or individually addressed) 3D nanostructures is printed simultaneously.

**Advantages:** it operates in ambient air with no vacuum, no charged beam (hence no charging, scattering, or radiation damage), no photoresist, no developer, no support material and no wet chemistry; it prints on curved, flexible, fragile, or pre‑patterned substrates and directly onto existing devices; and the resolution is set by a nanoscale tip apex that can be sharpened at will, making it suitable for 3D plasmonic antennas, nanoelectrodes, phase‑change memory cells, nano‑optical elements, and biomolecule arrays.

**Use single‑exposure holographic (multi‑beam interference) lithography — specifically phase‑mask "proximity‑field nanopatterning" (PnP) with short‑wavelength light — to optically "print" an entire 3D nanostructure at once.**

Coat the substrate with a thick (1–20 µm) transparent photoresist (SU‑8, HSQ, or a chalcogenide/hybrid sol–gel film). Instead of scanning a focal spot, generate several mutually coherent plane waves that overlap inside the resist volume: either by splitting a UV/DUV (or EUV/X‑ray) laser beam into 4–7 arms with prisms/beamsplitters and steering them onto the film at chosen angles, or — far simpler and phase‑stable — by placing a conformable elastomeric (PDMS) phase mask with a sub‑wavelength relief grating in optical contact with the resist and illuminating it with a single collimated beam. The mask diffracts the light into multiple orders that interfere in the near field, reproducing a Talbot‑type 3D intensity distribution throughout the film thickness.

The resulting periodic light field is a true volumetric hologram: its lattice symmetry, unit‑cell shape and fill fraction are set by the number, direction, polarization, amplitude and relative phase of the beams (equivalently by the mask period/duty cycle and the illumination wavelength and angle), so face‑centred‑cubic, diamond, woodpile, gyroid‑like, chiral and graded lattices can all be programmed by optical design rather than by tool‑path slicing. Because the resist responds only where the dose exceeds a threshold (enhanced by using a chemically amplified or two‑photon/nonlinear resist and working near threshold), features far smaller than the fringe period are retained; a single wet development in one step leaves a fully connected, free‑standing 3D nanolattice with ~50–100 nm struts (down to sub‑20 nm using EUV/X‑ray interference where the period is λ/2‑limited).

Aperiodic or device‑level features are added by combining the interference exposure with a conventional mask/e‑beam exposure (double exposure), by spatially modulating the beams with an SLM, by tiling multiple exposures at different orientations, or by using multi‑level/pixelated phase masks that locally change the diffraction and hence the local lattice — giving embedded waveguides, cavities and defects inside the photonic crystal.

Finally, convert the polymer template into a functional material: conformal ALD (TiO₂, Al₂O₃, ZnO) or electrodeposition/CVD backfilling followed by burn‑out of the polymer yields inverse ceramic, metallic or semiconductor 3D nanoarchitectures; pyrolysis yields glassy‑carbon nanolattices.

Key advantage: the whole 3D structure over square centimetres is written in a **single, seconds‑long parallel exposure** with no serial voxel writing, no vacuum, no supports and no stitching — resolution is set by the optical wavelength/interference period and the resist threshold, and throughput is orders of magnitude higher than point‑by‑point 3D nanoprinting.

**Build the object out of pre‑made nanoparticles: "colloidal 3D printing" by capillary‑assisted particle assembly (CAPA) plus sequential transfer printing.**

Instead of writing with a beam, nozzle or focal spot, use monodisperse colloids (5–100 nm Au, Ag, SiO₂, TiO₂, quantum dots, magnetite, polymer latex) as ready‑made, atomically smooth "voxels," so the printed feature size equals the particle size rather than any optical, electron‑probe or nozzle limit.

*Step 1 – template.* Mold a PDMS (or hard‑silicon) stamp bearing topographic traps — holes, slits, grooves — whose dimensions are matched to hold exactly one particle (or a defined small cluster) per site; the trap array is defined once by e‑beam/nanoimprint lithography and reused thousands of times, so the expensive high‑resolution step is amortized.

*Step 2 – assembly.* Drag a droplet of colloidal suspension slowly across the template at controlled temperature, humidity and contact‑angle (the "accumulation zone" of a receding meniscus). Convective/capillary forces at the pinned contact line drive particles into the traps with essentially 100 % yield and sub‑10 nm placement accuracy; surplus particles are swept away by the moving meniscus, giving a deterministic, defect‑free 2‑D "layer file" of single particles in the programmed pattern. Different colloids can be assembled in successive passes (or from a multi‑channel meniscus) to give multi‑material, chemically addressed layers.

*Step 3 – transfer print.* Bring the loaded stamp into contact with the receiving substrate and delaminate at high/low rate (kinetically controlled adhesion switching), or use a thin thermoplastic/PVA adhesion layer, so the whole particle pattern is released in one shot onto the target. Alignment to fiducials with a mask‑aligner/nanopositioner gives <20 nm overlay.

*Step 4 – iterate to 3‑D.* Print the next particle layer directly on top of the previous one, using the corrugation of the underlying layer as a self‑registering template (particles nest in the hollows, giving automatic close‑packed or programmed stacking), and repeat. Layers of different symmetry, particle size or material can be interleaved, and sacrificial polymer‑latex particles can be printed as removable support for overhangs, bridges and hollow shells, later burned out. This yields woodpile, diamond, chiral and graded 3‑D architectures, particle by particle.

*Step 5 – consolidate.* A brief thermal/photonic sintering, ligand‑exchange necking, or a few cycles of conformal atomic‑layer deposition (Al₂O₃/TiO₂) welds the particles into a mechanically robust, electrically continuous solid; the sacrificial particles and stamp residues are removed by calcination or plasma, leaving free‑standing inorganic 3‑D nanostructures.

Advantages: resolution and surface quality are set by colloid synthesis (monodisperse, crystalline, sub‑10 nm particles) rather than by a diffraction limit or beam spot; the assembly + transfer steps are massively parallel (a full wafer of identical 3‑D objects per print cycle, seconds each) instead of serial voxel writing; it runs in ambient conditions with no vacuum, resist, developer or photopolymer binder; and each layer can carry a different functional material (plasmonic, magnetic, luminescent, catalytic), enabling 3‑D photonic crystals, metamaterials, SERS substrates, nanoelectrodes and quantum‑dot devices.

**Use MeV ion‑beam (proton‑beam) writing with energy‑modulated depth control — "3D lithography by the Bragg peak."**

Spin a thick (1–50 µm) high‑resolution resist (PMMA, HSQ, SU‑8) on a conductive/plating base and expose it with a focused beam of MeV light ions (H⁺ or He⁺) from a nuclear‑microprobe: a small accelerator whose beam is demagnified by a high‑precision quadrupole/Oxford‑triplet lens system to a spot of ~10–30 nm and scanned electrostatically over the sample from a sliced CAD file.

Why this gives high resolution *and* true 3D:
- Unlike keV electrons, MeV ions travel in essentially **straight lines** with negligible lateral scattering until the very end of their range, so the exposed track is a nearly perfect cylinder with vertical, smooth sidewalls and aspect ratios >50 — no proximity effect, no forward/backscatter blurring, no need for thin films.
- The energy deposition is strongly peaked at the end of range (**Bragg peak**), and the range is a deterministic function of ion energy and species. Therefore, by tuning the accelerator energy (or inserting calibrated degrader foils) during the scan, the exposed voxel can be placed at a *chosen depth inside the resist*, leaving the material above and below unexposed. Modulating (x, y, energy, fluence) writes buried voxels, stacked levels, undercuts, embedded channels, tilted struts and continuously graded ("stepless") 3D reliefs in a **single resist layer with a single development step**, rather than by stacking aligned 2D layers.
- Grey‑scale dose control gives analog height variation (dose → local scission/cross‑link density → developed depth), and tilting/rotating the stage between energy steps adds slanted and helical elements.

Process completion: after one wet development the free‑standing polymer 3D nanostructure is used directly, or is (i) electroplated (Ni, Au, Cu) to make a metallic replica/mould for nanoimprint mass replication, (ii) backfilled by ALD and burned out to give ceramic/inverse structures, or (iii) pyrolysed (HSQ → SiO₂‑like, polymer → glassy carbon) with the known isotropic shrinkage further reducing all features by 2–4×, pushing struts below 20 nm.

Extras: the same beam simultaneously produces ionoluminescence/backscatter signals for in‑line imaging and alignment to fiducials; using an ion species that also modifies the substrate (e.g., direct proton‑beam writing of buried porous‑silicon or refractive‑index‑changed waveguides in glass) lets the technique write functional 3D structures *inside* a bulk material without any resist at all.

The result is resist‑ or bulk‑based 3D nanofabrication in which resolution is set by the focused ion probe and the ion straggling (a few nanometres) rather than by diffraction, and the third dimension is addressed by beam energy rather than by layer stacking.

**Assemble the object one nanoparticle at a time with light: "optical printing" using a focused laser beam / holographic optical tweezers as a contact‑free nano‑pick‑and‑place tool.**

Immerse the substrate in a dilute colloidal suspension of pre‑synthesized building blocks (5–100 nm Au, Ag, Si, TiO₂, up‑conversion or quantum‑dot particles). A tightly focused CW laser tuned near — but slightly red of — the particle's plasmon/Mie resonance is aimed at the chosen (x, y) coordinate a few hundred nanometres above the surface. A particle that diffuses into the beam is trapped by the optical gradient force and then driven to the substrate by radiation pressure (scattering force) plus thermophoretic/optothermal flows, where it is immobilized irreversibly by van der Waals/electrostatic adhesion (tuned via salt concentration, pH or a thin polyelectrolyte/thiol adhesion layer). The laser is then blinked off and the stage/beam moved to the next site. Because the printed feature is a single pre‑made, monodisperse, crystalline particle, the **feature size is set by colloid chemistry (down to a few nm), not by the diffraction‑limited spot**; placement accuracy of ~50 nm is achieved by the trap stiffness and can be pushed to <10 nm by using a plasmonic/near‑field trap (nanoaperture, bowtie, or a photonic‑crystal cavity) or by "self‑registered" printing, in which the field enhancement at the edge of an already‑printed particle steers the next arriving particle into the nanogap.

**Getting the third dimension:** holographic optical tweezers (an SLM splitting the beam into many independently steerable 3D traps) hold and stack particles above the substrate, so each new particle is deposited on top of the previous one; the growing structure's own optical near field focuses the incoming particles onto its apex, letting free‑standing pillars, chains, arches, helices and lattices grow voxel‑by‑voxel from a sliced CAD path. Overhangs are supported by sacrificial polymer‑latex or ice particles, or by printing inside a photo‑crosslinkable hydrogel that is gelled point‑by‑point around the assembly.

**Multi‑material and functionalization come free:** switching the wavelength selects which particle species is resonant, so different materials can be printed from a mixed suspension by colour alone (spectrally multiplexed printing) — plasmonic, magnetic, luminescent and catalytic voxels can be interleaved in one object with a controlled nanogap between them.

**Consolidation and verification:** a brief laser or photonic sintering pulse, ligand‑exchange necking, or a few cycles of conformal ALD welds the particles into a mechanically robust, electrically continuous solid; the process is monitored in real time by dark‑field scattering/optical microscopy of the same beam, giving closed‑loop confirmation that each particle has landed before the next is printed, and the whole process runs in ambient liquid at room temperature with no vacuum, resist, developer or photopolymer binder — ideal for 3D plasmonic antennas, chiral metamolecules, SERS hot‑spot arrays and quantum‑emitter/cavity devices.

**Print with electrons inside a liquid: electron‑beam‑induced reduction of metal‑salt solutions in a sealed liquid cell ("in‑situ liquid‑phase STEM 3D nanoprinting").**

Enclose a dilute precursor solution (e.g., HAuCl₄, AgNO₃, Na₂PdCl₄, CuSO₄, or a mixed‑salt/organometallic electrolyte, buffered and dosed with a controlled amount of radical scavenger such as isopropanol/formate) between two electron‑transparent Si₃N₄ or graphene windows in a microfluidic liquid cell mounted in a (S)TEM or environmental SEM. A finely focused electron probe (sub‑nanometre in STEM) passing through the liquid radiolyses water in a tiny volume around the beam path, generating hydrated electrons and H• radicals that reduce metal ions **only where the probe dwells**; the metal nucleates and grows there as a solid deposit while unirradiated regions stay liquid and untouched. Because the writing agent is a chemically short‑lived radical cloud rather than an optical focus, the voxel size is set by the probe diameter and the radical diffusion length — a few nanometres — with no diffraction limit, no resist, no developer and no polymer binder.

Three‑dimensionality: the deposit grows back up the beam toward the source (self‑focusing at the field‑enhanced, most‑irradiated tip), so parking the probe and slowly withdrawing the focal plane grows a free‑standing nanowire, while translating the beam between pulses writes tilted rods, arches, helices, meshes and lattices directly from a sliced CAD dwell‑map. Key control knobs are dose rate, dwell time, precursor and scavenger concentration and pH: keeping the dose just above the nucleation threshold and adding scavengers to quench radicals that stray outside the probe sharpens the voxel and prevents unwanted background nucleation; flowing fresh electrolyte through the cell replenishes ions and avoids depletion, and switching the flow to a different salt mid‑build gives multi‑material, alloyed or core–shell architectures. A conductive working electrode in the cell can bias the substrate to bias/assist (or suppress) reduction electrochemically, giving an extra on/off gate.

Unique advantage: the same electron beam that prints also **images the growing object in real time with atomic/nanometre resolution**, so nucleation, growth rate, crystallinity and defects are monitored shot‑by‑shot and the tool‑path is corrected in closed loop during the build — true in‑line metrology no other nanoprinter offers. When finished, the cell is flushed with water/ethanol and dried (critical‑point or freeze drying to avoid capillary collapse), leaving dense, ligand‑free, polycrystalline metal nanostructures that are immediately conductive; a brief anneal completes densification. This yields 3D plasmonic antennas, nanoelectrodes, catalytic scaffolds and interconnects with sub‑10–50 nm features, written in liquid at room temperature without vacuum‑incompatible chemistry, resists, supports or pyrolysis.

**Grow the 3D nanostructures by shadow‑controlled vapour deposition: seeded glancing‑angle deposition (GLAD / oblique‑angle "dynamic shadowing growth").**

Idea: instead of writing voxel‑by‑voxel, let ballistic self‑shadowing of an atomic vapour flux do the 3D "printing" in parallel over a whole wafer, with the shape programmed by the substrate's tilt and rotation trajectory rather than by any focused beam.

How it is done:
1. **Seed the print sites.** Define an array of nucleation dots (10–50 nm) on the substrate by e‑beam/nanoimprint lithography, block‑copolymer micelle patterning, or self‑assembled nanosphere monolayers. These seeds fix where every 3D object will grow, its pitch and its lateral registry, so the "resolution" is inherited from a single cheap 2‑D patterning step.
2. **Deposit at a steep oblique angle.** In a high‑vacuum e‑beam evaporator/sputter system, direct a collimated atomic flux (Si, SiO₂, TiO₂, Al₂O₃, Au, Ag, Mg, Co, Ni, ITO, or organics) onto the substrate at α ≈ 80–89° from normal, with the substrate cooled so adatom surface diffusion is suppressed. Each seed casts a geometric shadow, so incoming atoms can only land on the already‑protruding tip; growth is therefore self‑focusing and columns grow *only* from the seeds, with the surrounding area starved of flux. Column diameters of ~10–50 nm and interpillar gaps of a few nanometres are obtained routinely.
3. **Program the shape with the stage motion.** The instantaneous growth direction follows the flux direction, so a computer‑controlled polar (α) and azimuthal (φ) trajectory acts as the "G‑code":
 - continuous slow φ rotation → **helices/springs** (pitch = deposition rate ÷ rotation rate);
 - fast φ rotation → **vertical posts**;
 - discrete 180° φ flips → **zig‑zag/chevron stacks**;
 - φ swept with varying α → **tapered, curved, S‑shaped or branched (nano‑tree) columns**;
 - stopping rotation → slanted struts, and periodic modulation gives chiral, graded or "woodpile‑like" layers.
4. **Multi‑material and functional segments.** Switching the evaporation source mid‑run writes axially heterostructured or core–shell objects (e.g., magnetic base + plasmonic helical tip, metal–dielectric–metal chiral stacks); a conformal ALD coat afterwards adds a second material, stiffens the columns and tunes the gap size down to the sub‑nanometre level.
5. **Finish.** Low‑temperature annealing/sintering densifies and crystallizes the deposit; selective etching of a sacrificial segment releases free‑standing or hollow architectures; the seed layer can be dissolved to lift the array off.

Why it gives high resolution: the feature size is set by nucleation‑seed size, atomic shadowing length and adatom diffusion — not by diffraction, a beam probe, a nozzle, a droplet or a meniscus — and the growth is inherently additive with nanometre height control (sub‑monolayer per rotation), monitored in real time by a quartz crystal microbalance and verified by SEM.

Advantages: millions of identical, complex chiral 3‑D nanostructures are grown **simultaneously** in one vacuum run in minutes (no serial writing, no resist, no developer, no support material, no shrinkage), on almost any substrate including flexible or curved ones — ideal for chiral/circular‑dichroism metamaterials, 3‑D photonic and SERS substrates, nanospring mechanical elements, magnetic helices and high‑surface‑area electrodes.

**Use laser‑induced chemical vapour deposition (LCVD) as a "3‑D nano‑pen": grow the structure from a gas precursor at a laser‑heated hot spot, exploiting the exponential (Arrhenius) threshold of the pyrolytic reaction and self‑focused tip growth.**

Place the substrate in a small cold‑wall reaction cell filled with a low‑pressure precursor gas (a hydrocarbon such as C₂H₂/C₂H₄ for carbon, SiH₄ for silicon, WF₆ or W(CO)₆, Fe(CO)₅, Ni(CO)₄, TMA/TEOS for oxides). Focus a CW or pulsed laser (visible/near‑IR, often through the transparent backside of the substrate or delivered by a tapered/lensed optical fibre) to a diffraction‑limited spot on the surface. The precursor decomposes only where the local temperature exceeds the pyrolysis threshold; because the deposition rate depends *exponentially* on temperature, only the very peak of the Gaussian temperature profile is above threshold, so by working just above threshold with short dwell times the deposited voxel is an order of magnitude smaller than the optical spot — tens of nanometres rather than a micron — with no need for vacuum electron optics, resist, developer or binder.

The third dimension comes free from **self‑focused tip growth**: the freshly deposited nanotip absorbs light more strongly and is thermally isolated from the substrate, so it is the hottest point in the field and all subsequent deposition occurs at its apex. Parking the beam and translating the stage (or the focus) downward/away at exactly the axial growth rate pulls a continuous free‑standing nanowire upward; moving laterally during growth writes tilted rods, arches, zig‑zags, helices, meshes and lattices directly from a sliced CAD path, with no support material and no layer stacking. Growth rate (and hence pull speed) is regulated in closed loop by monitoring the laser light scattered/reflected from the growing tip or its incandescence, and the axial "fibre‑pulling" geometry, low precursor pressure and short pulse trains keep the diameter constant and prevent lateral overgrowth; pulsing the laser also allows discrete "voxel‑on‑demand" deposition.

Multi‑material and graded structures are made simply by switching or mixing the precursor gases mid‑build (e.g. a magnetic Fe segment on a conductive carbon stalk, or a metal core with an oxide shell), and a final low‑temperature anneal (or brief H₂/O₂ treatment) purifies and densifies the deposit into pure, dense, immediately conductive metal, semiconductor or ceramic nanostructures — useful for 3‑D field emitters, nanoelectrodes, AFM/plasmonic tips, interconnects and nanomechanical elements grown directly on existing devices, fibres or curved substrates in a simple gas cell at atmospheric‑to‑low pressure.

**Replicate, don't write: use multi‑tier / layer‑by‑layer nanoimprint lithography (3D NIL) — molding the nanostructure from a reusable master, and stacking imprinted layers by reverse‑imprint transfer bonding.**

*Master.* Invest the high‑resolution effort only once: fabricate a hard mold (Si, SiO₂, quartz, Ni, or diamond‑like‑carbon‑coated) carrying the negative of the object. Its relief is defined by the sharpest available planar tools — e‑beam or He‑ion lithography, grayscale EBL, block‑copolymer templating, or anisotropic KOH/atomic‑layer‑controlled etching — giving 5–20 nm lateral features with atomically smooth sidewalls. Multi‑level ("stepped") and continuously graded (grayscale) reliefs are built into the same mold by multiple aligned etch steps or by dose‑modulated writing, so a *single press* already produces a genuinely three‑dimensional, multi‑height object rather than a binary pattern. Shrinking the master by pyrolysis/oxidation or coating it conformally with ALD trims the mold features (and thus every future copy) below 10 nm.

*Imprint.* Spin or ink‑jet a thin UV‑curable or thermoplastic resist onto the substrate, press the mold at modest pressure (or use soft, conformable PDMS/ETFE/h‑PDMS working stamps for curved and flexible substrates), cure with UV or by cooling through T_g, and demold. Because the pattern is defined by *mechanical displacement of the resist*, resolution is set by molecular/mold dimensions — not by diffraction, beam scattering, a nozzle, a droplet or a voxel — and sub‑10 nm fidelity is routinely transferred. Anti‑sticking fluorosilane monolayers, controlled resist viscosity and vacuum/gas‑dissolution (He or condensable gas) imprinting eliminate trapped bubbles and defects.

*Third dimension.* Build the volume by **reverse (transfer) imprinting**: imprint the layer on a low‑adhesion carrier, then bring it into contact with the growing stack and release it, so each fully patterned layer — including free‑standing bridges and overhangs, which are supported by the sacrificial residual resist — is bonded on top of the previous one. Align successive layers to buried fiducials in a nanoimprint aligner (moiré/interferometric overlay, <20 nm). Alternating layer orientations gives woodpile photonic crystals, chiral and helical stacks, membranes, nanofluidic channels and closed cavities; layers of different materials (imprinted nanoparticle, sol–gel, preceramic, metal‑precursor or quantum‑dot inks) give multi‑material 3D architectures. Residual‑layer removal by a brief anisotropic O₂ descum, then pattern transfer by RIE, lift‑off, electroplating, or conformal ALD backfilling + polymer burn‑out, converts the polymer stack into metal, oxide, semiconductor or glassy‑carbon nanostructures.

*Why this is attractive.* The expensive, slow, atom‑precise step happens once; thereafter every press replicates the entire 3D nanostructure over a full wafer (or continuously, roll‑to‑roll) in seconds, with thousands of copies per mold. It needs no vacuum, no charged beam, no photochemistry threshold engineering and no serial voxel scanning, yet delivers sub‑10 nm features with smooth surfaces — making it the practical route to mass‑produced 3D metamaterials, photonic crystals, nanofluidic and nanoelectrode devices.

**Grow the nanostructures inside a programmable nanoporous template: "3‑D printing by template‑assisted electrodeposition" in anodic aluminium oxide (AAO) or ion‑track‑etched membranes.**

Instead of writing voxel‑by‑voxel, first *print the mold electrochemically*. Anodize high‑purity aluminium (or a Ta/Ti film) in oxalic/sulfuric/phosphoric acid: self‑ordered hexagonal pore arrays form spontaneously, with pore diameter (5–200 nm), interpore spacing and length set simply by the anodizing voltage, electrolyte and time — resolution defined by electrochemical self‑organization, not by any beam, nozzle or focal spot. Pre‑indenting the aluminium with a nanoimprint stamp or an FIB‑written dot array forces the pores to nucleate exactly where wanted, converting the random array into a deterministic, registered "print bed."

The third dimension is *programmed into the template as a function of time*: because pore diameter tracks the instantaneous anodizing potential, a computer‑controlled voltage/current waveform (a "G‑code" in time rather than in space) writes, along the depth of every pore simultaneously, modulated diameters, tapers, periodic necks, chambers, and — by stepping the voltage down by a factor of √2 — controlled Y‑branching, giving hierarchical dendritic and 3‑D interconnected pore networks. Cyclic anodization/etching, multi‑step widening, or crossing two ion‑irradiation directions in a polymer track‑etched foil (irradiate at several tilt angles, then etch) produces genuinely three‑dimensional, interpenetrating channel architectures.

Then fill the mold: sputter a conductive back electrode and electrodeposit (or electroless‑plate / ALD‑coat) the desired material into the pores — Au, Ni, Co, Cu, Bi₂Te₃, conducting polymer, or, by pulsing the potential between two electrolytes, axially multilayered/segmented and core–shell nanowires (e.g., magnetic/nonmagnetic superlattices, plasmonic barcodes). Partial filling plus a conformal ALD shell gives hollow nanotubes; sequential filling of a branched template gives multi‑material junctions at predefined depths.

Finally, selectively dissolve the alumina (NaOH/CrO₃–H₃PO₄) or the polymer (organic solvent/plasma), using critical‑point drying to avoid capillary collapse, and release free‑standing arrays of 3‑D nanostructures — modulated, branched, helical or networked nanowires with sub‑20 nm features, high aspect ratios (>1000), dense crystalline material and immediate electrical functionality.

Advantages: **billions of identical 3‑D nano‑objects are "printed" in parallel in one bench‑top electrochemical run** — no vacuum, no resist, no developer, no serial scanning and no pyrolysis — with feature size set by anodization physics (down to a few nanometres) and the vertical architecture set by a time‑programmed voltage waveform; the template is also reusable as a stencil/mask for depositing registered nanodot and nanomesh layers on top, and the released structures serve as 3‑D magnetic memory/racetrack elements, thermoelectric and battery electrodes, plasmonic and SERS arrays, and nanofluidic/filtration membranes.

**Sculpt the 3D object with dose‑modulated (grayscale), multi‑angle electron‑beam lithography in a thick resist, then shrink it by pyrolysis.**

Spin a single thick (0.5–5 µm) high‑contrast resist — HSQ (negative, inorganic, ~2 nm intrinsic resolution) or PMMA (positive) — onto the substrate. Instead of writing a binary 2‑D pattern, treat the exposure as a *volumetric dose problem*: the local degree of cross‑linking (or chain scission) is a smooth, calibrated function of the deposited energy density, and the developer removes material to a depth set by that dose. A sliced CAD model is therefore converted, via Monte‑Carlo (CASINO/proximity‑effect) simulation of the electron energy‑deposition kernel, into a per‑pixel dose map — effectively a deconvolution/"tomographic" inverse problem — so that after a single develop step the resist relief reproduces continuous ramps, curved surfaces, multi‑level terraces, sloped struts and buried‑profile geometries in one layer, with no layer stacking.

Push the resolution and the true 3‑D freedom with three tricks:
1. **High‑energy (50–100 keV) beams and thin/low‑Z stacks** to keep forward scattering minimal (few‑nm probe, straight trajectories), with proximity‑effect correction removing the backscatter background so 5–10 nm features survive in dense arrangements.
2. **Multi‑angle (tilted/rotated stage) exposures**: writing the same resist volume from several tilt angles lets exposure "rays" intersect only where the accumulated dose crosses the development threshold, so voxels can be placed *inside* the film to create undercuts, overhangs, bridges, chiral and woodpile motifs that a normal‑incidence exposure cannot produce.
3. **Threshold engineering**: cold development (IPA/water or salty developers at low temperature), ultrasonic agitation and high‑contrast tone give a sharp dose threshold, so the written feature is far narrower than the energy‑deposition profile; critical‑point drying prevents collapse of high‑aspect‑ratio features.

Finally, convert and shrink: pyrolyse/anneal the developed HSQ (→ dense SiO₂‑like glass) or the polymer (→ glassy carbon) at 600–1100 °C. The known, isotropic 2–5× volumetric shrinkage scales every feature and gap down proportionally, pushing struts below 10 nm while densifying and stiffening the structure. Optional conformal ALD (Al₂O₃/TiO₂), metallization or backfill‑and‑burn‑out turns the template into a ceramic, metallic or inverse 3‑D nanostructure; the same e‑beam column images and aligns to fiducials for in‑line verification.

This gives beam‑limited (few‑nm), resist‑based 3‑D nanoprinting in one exposure/one development cycle, using standard EBL hardware and no diffraction‑limited optics, nozzles, supports or serial voxel stacking.

**Sculpt the object subtractively with a focused ion beam: "3‑D nano‑milling" using a tomographic (depth‑calibrated) sputter‑dose map on a tilt/rotate stage.**

Start from a dense, homogeneous blank of the final functional material itself — a single‑crystal Si/diamond/sapphire pillar, an evaporated metal film, a suspended Si₃N₄/graphene membrane, or a pre‑grown micro‑pillar/optical‑fibre facet — mounted on a eucentric 5‑axis piezo stage in a FIB/SEM dual‑beam microscope. Because the workpiece is already solid, fully dense material, there is no resist, no developer, no binder, no support, no shrinkage and no post‑sintering/pyrolysis step: what you carve is immediately mechanically, electrically and optically functional.

**Writing:** a liquid‑metal (Ga⁺), gas‑field (He⁺/Ne⁺) or Xe‑plasma ion source is focused to a probe of ~0.5–5 nm (He⁺) to ~5–25 nm (Ga⁺). Each ion impact removes a few atoms by momentum‑transfer sputtering, so the "voxel" is set by the ion probe size and the collision cascade (a few nanometres), not by any diffraction limit, meniscus, droplet or chemical threshold. The removed depth at every pixel is a calibrated, essentially linear function of the local ion dose (dose = beam current × dwell time / pixel area ÷ sputter yield). A sliced CAD model is therefore inverted into a **grayscale dose/dwell‑time bitmap** — a "milling tomogram" — using Monte‑Carlo (SRIM/TRIM) sputter‑yield data plus a redeposition‑and‑angle‑of‑incidence model, so that curved surfaces, smooth ramps, blazed and Fresnel profiles, tapered nano‑cones, hollow shells and multi‑level terraces emerge after a single continuous pass rather than by stacking binary layers. Multi‑pass, low‑dwell‑time serpentine scanning (many fast passes instead of one slow one) spreads the dose in time so sputtered atoms are pumped away instead of re‑depositing, keeping sidewalls vertical and surfaces atomically smooth.

**Getting true 3‑D (undercuts, overhangs, closed cavities):** rotate and tilt the stage between (or during) milling passes and re‑register to fiducial marks imaged by the electron column, so the beam attacks the workpiece from many directions — a "reverse tomography" in which material is removed along intersecting ray paths. Grazing‑incidence passes cut undercuts, cantilevers, free‑standing bridges, chiral helices, split‑ring and gyroid‑like unit cells, and re‑entrant nanolattices that no normal‑incidence tool can make; annular/spiral scan paths turn a pillar into an axially symmetric 3‑D body (nano‑lathe machining) such as a lens, ogive tip, coil or nozzle. Gas‑assisted etching (XeF₂, Cl₂, H₂O, I₂ injected through a GIS needle) raises the yield 5–20×, suppresses redeposition and adds material selectivity, so one material can be cleared out of a stack while its neighbour is untouched; conversely, switching the same GIS to a deposition precursor lets you add material (FIBID) in the same run, giving mixed additive/subtractive builds. Low‑energy (1–5 keV) or light‑ion (He⁺) finishing passes strip the ion‑damaged/implanted surface layer, leaving crystalline, contamination‑free faces.

**Closed‑loop control and finishing:** the coincident SEM (and, on a lamella, STEM) images the workpiece after every slice at nanometre resolution, and end‑point detection via the secondary‑electron/ion or EDS signal tells you exactly when an interface is reached, so depth errors, drift and beam‑current decay are corrected during the build — in‑line metrology impossible in most nanoprinters. A brief low‑temperature anneal (or hydrogen/oxygen plasma) removes residual implanted Ga and heals point defects; a conformal ALD coating can then add a functional skin (Al₂O₃, TiO₂, Pt) or shrink every gap to the sub‑nanometre level.

**Result:** deterministic, arbitrary 3‑D nano‑objects with ~5–20 nm (down to sub‑5 nm with He⁺) features and optically smooth surfaces, machined directly into the functional material and directly on top of existing devices, fibres, AFM tips or membranes — ideal for 3‑D photonic/plasmonic elements, nano‑mechanical metamaterial unit cells, solid‑state nanopores, micro‑optics and prototype masters that can subsequently be replicated.

**Nanorobotic pick‑and‑place assembly inside an electron microscope — build the 3D nanostructure by robotically stacking pre‑grown nano‑building‑blocks and welding them together.**

Instead of forming material voxel‑by‑voxel, first synthesize near‑perfect building blocks by bulk chemistry/growth: CVD carbon nanotubes, VLS‑grown Si/GaN/ZnO nanowires, exfoliated 2D flakes (graphene, MoS₂, hBN), nanoribbons, nanospheres and single‑crystal nanoplates. Because these are grown, not written, their diameters (1–50 nm), crystallinity and surface quality are set by chemistry — far beyond any beam, nozzle or focal‑spot limit — so the printed "filament" is already an atomically defined object.

Load them onto a stage inside an SEM (or a TEM holder for atomic‑resolution work) together with several independently driven piezo‑nanomanipulators (coarse stick‑slip + fine piezo, 1–0.1 nm steps, 3–6 DOF each) carrying sharpened tungsten/AFM tips, nanotweezers (two closable, electrically biased tips) or a gripper. Under live electron imaging the operator/robot picks a single nanowire from the source substrate — adhesion is switched by van der Waals contact, electrostatic bias on the tip, or a spot of electron‑beam‑induced carbon "glue" — lifts it, rotates and translates it, and places it exactly where the sliced CAD model says, with placement accuracy of a few nanometres verified in‑line by the same electron beam (true closed‑loop metrology during assembly).

Each placed element is then **joined**: a short electron‑beam‑induced deposition of Pt/W/C at the joint, a Joule‑heating current pulse through the two contacting members (nanowelding/soldering), local electromigration, or in‑situ e‑beam‑induced amorphous‑carbon welding fuses the junction into a mechanically rigid, electrically ohmic contact. Repeating pick–place–weld builds genuinely free‑standing 3D architectures — crossed‑wire lattices, cantilevers, bridges, tripods, helical coils, nano‑tweezers/actuators, tetrapods and hierarchical trusses — with no supports, no resist, no developer, no shrinkage and no sintering, since every strut is already dense, single‑crystalline, functional material.

Multi‑material and functional heterostructures come naturally: different feed substrates supply metal, semiconductor, insulator, magnetic or luminescent blocks, so p–n junctions, tunnel gaps, quantum emitters and 2D/1D hybrids can be placed at chosen coordinates within one object, and precise gaps (sub‑nm to tens of nm) can be set by feedback on the tunnelling current between manipulated tips. In‑situ electrical/mechanical testing (force sensing on the tip, I–V across the structure) lets each junction be characterized and, if faulty, un‑welded and re‑made before the build continues.

Throughput — the obvious weakness of serial manipulation — is addressed by automating the pick‑place‑weld cycle with machine‑vision tracking of the SEM image, by using arrays of manipulators working in parallel, and by using robotic assembly only to make one master 3D object that is subsequently replicated by molding/imprinting.

The result is deterministic, defect‑by‑defect‑correctable 3D nanoprinting whose resolution is inherited from the diameter of a chemically grown nanocrystal (down to ~1 nm for a nanotube), giving 3D NEMS, nanoelectrode and nanoprobe assemblies, 3D transistor/interconnect prototypes, plasmonic antennas with atomically defined gaps, and mechanical metamaterial unit cells built directly onto existing chips, fibres or TEM grids.

**Use dynamic (programmable) nanostencil lithography — resist‑free shadow‑mask evaporation through a movable nano‑aperture membrane — to build 3D nanostructures layer by layer.**

Fabricate the "printhead" as an ultrathin (50–200 nm) low‑stress Si₃N₄ or SiO₂ membrane perforated with apertures of 10–100 nm (defined once by e‑beam/He‑ion milling or FIB, and further shrunk to sub‑20 nm by conformal ALD or a self‑limiting oxide/metal closure coating). Mount this stencil on a 6‑axis piezo nanopositioner a few hundred nanometres above the substrate inside a UHV evaporator/sputter/PLD chamber, with capacitive or interferometric gap sensing and in‑situ SEM/optical alignment to fiducials.

Printing: a collimated atomic vapour beam (Au, Ag, Al, Pt, Cr, SiO₂, MgF₂, organic semiconductors, superconductors such as Nb/Al) passes only through the open apertures and condenses on the substrate as an exact, resist‑free copy of the aperture pattern. Because the deposit's edge sharpness is set by the aperture size, the stencil–substrate gap and the source's angular divergence — not by any diffraction limit, resist chemistry, developer, lift‑off or beam scattering — features of 10–30 nm with atomically clean interfaces are obtained on any substrate, including fragile, flexible, curved, organic or 2D materials that cannot survive resist processing.

Getting the third dimension (this is what turns a stencil into a 3D printer):
1. **Thickness modulation ("grayscale by time"):** the deposited height at each aperture is simply flux × open time, so a shutter/quartz‑monitor‑controlled dose per aperture gives multi‑level and graded reliefs.
2. **Stencil translation between/during deposition:** shifting the membrane by a fraction of an aperture width and depositing again lets partially overlapping shadows sum into continuously varying, curved and tapered profiles ("moving‑mask" grayscale deposition), while stacking translated exposures builds staircases, ramps, bridges and overhangs.
3. **Tilting the substrate/source:** oblique‑incidence deposition through the same aperture displaces the landing spot laterally with height, so tilted struts, slanted pillars, split‑ring resonators and — with continuous azimuthal rotation — helices and chiral unit cells are grown; combined with shadow evaporation this also produces self‑aligned nanogaps and tunnel junctions of a few nanometres without any lithographic alignment.
