Because these terms cost essentially nothing to evaluate yet capture the physics that would otherwise force enormous simulation cells and long trajectories, they typically cut the number of atoms treated quantum‑mechanically by an order of magnitude (with the cubic scaling of DFT turning that into two to three orders of magnitude in time) while often *improving* agreement with experiment; and since they only modify the external potential and the total‑energy expression, they stack with every other acceleration strategy.

A route not yet used is to **attack the exact‑exchange (Fock‑exchange) bottleneck of hybrid functionals directly, by evaluating it in a cheaper, screened and auxiliary‑basis form instead of exactly.** Hybrids are typically 10–100× more expensive than semilocal DFT solely because of the four‑index exchange term, which couples every occupied orbital pair and, in plane‑wave/periodic codes, requires an FFT pair for every band and k/q combination. This term can be made almost as cheap as a GGA without abandoning hybrid accuracy by: (i) **range separation/screening** — use a short‑range‑only exchange operator (HSE‑type erfc screening, or truncation of the Coulomb kernel at a finite radius), so the number of interacting pairs becomes O(N) and the slowly convergent long‑range q→0 divergence and the huge k‑point/q‑mesh requirement disappear; (ii) the **auxiliary density‑matrix method (ADMM)** — project the density matrix onto a much smaller, more compact auxiliary basis, compute the expensive exchange there, and correct the difference with a cheap (semi)local exchange functional, cutting the cost by 1–2 orders of magnitude with errors of a fraction of a kcal/mol; (iii) **seminumerical / semi‑analytic exchange** (chain‑of‑spheres COSX, occ‑RI‑K, pseudospectral, tensor‑hypercontraction, interpolative separable density fitting), where one index of the integral is evaluated on a coarse numerical grid so the formal N⁴ integral cost drops toward N²–N³ with a tiny prefactor; (iv) **localized‑orbital exchange with rigorous screening** — rotate to maximally localized/Wannier or Cholesky orbitals, exploit the exponential decay of the exchange kernel, and skip all pairs below a threshold, giving linear scaling in insulators; and (v) evaluating the exchange **less often** — freeze or update it only every few SCF cycles (nested/multi‑rate SCF), or reuse the exchange operator between MD steps. All of these are systematically controllable by a single screening/truncation/auxiliary‑basis parameter, introduce errors far below the intrinsic error of the functional, and stack with any other acceleration strategy, making hybrid‑quality calculations affordable for systems where only GGAs were previously feasible.

A route not yet used is to **speed up the per‑iteration numerical work of building the Kohn–Sham matrix by exploiting *incremental* (differential) updates and optimized exchange–correlation quadrature.** Two complementary ideas:

(i) **Incremental/differential Fock–KS builds.** After the first few SCF cycles the density matrix barely changes, so instead of rebuilding the Coulomb and exchange–correlation contributions from the full density P at every cycle, build them only from the *difference* ΔP = P(n) − P(n−1) and add the result to the previous matrix. Because ΔP becomes very small and sparse near convergence, integral prescreening (Schwarz/QQR bounds, distance and density‑weighted thresholds) discards the overwhelming majority of shell pairs, so later SCF iterations cost a small fraction of the first one. The same "reuse the previous operator and update only the change" logic applies between geometry‑optimization or MD steps (the density, KS matrix, and even the exchange operator can be propagated and only differentially corrected).

(ii) **Cheaper, smarter integration grids for the XC term.** The XC energy/potential is evaluated by numerical quadrature over atom‑centered (Becke/Lebedev–Gauss) or real‑space grids, which can dominate the cost for large systems. Use *pruned* grids (few angular points near the nucleus and in the far tail, many only in the valence region), atom‑ and element‑adapted radial maps, batching of grid points into spatial blocks with per‑block screening of basis functions and of small density values (making the quadrature strictly linear‑scaling), coarse grids in the early SCF cycles with a switch to a fine grid only for the last cycles and for the final energy/forces, and tabulated/spline‑evaluated functional kernels with vectorized (SIMD/GPU) inner loops. Grid‑weight derivatives can then be added only where they matter for forces.

Both tricks are purely numerical bookkeeping — they leave the functional, basis, and physics untouched and introduce errors controlled by a single threshold well below the intrinsic error of the functional — yet they routinely cut total SCF time by factors of several to an order of magnitude, and they stack with every other acceleration strategy.

A route not yet used is **alchemical (chemical‑space) perturbation theory — "APDFT"**: instead of re‑running DFT for every compound in a screening campaign, run it once for a single reference system and then obtain the energies of *many chemically different* compounds analytically by perturbing the nuclear charges. Because the external potential depends linearly on the nuclear charges {Z_I}, the derivatives of the total energy with respect to Z are given by simple Hellmann–Feynman‑type expressions: the first derivative is just the electrostatic potential of the reference density evaluated at the nucleus (∂E/∂Z_I = ∫ρ(r)/|r−R_I| d³r, essentially free once ρ is converged), and the higher orders follow from cheap coupled‑perturbed/Sternheimer response equations (or from finite differences in the *fractional* nuclear charge, which is a continuous, smooth variable). A Taylor expansion in ΔZ then predicts the energies, and with the same machinery the densities, forces and relative stabilities, of every iso‑electronic "alchemical neighbour" — B/N substitution in carbon frameworks, dopants and substitutional defects in a host lattice, transition‑metal swaps in catalysts, alloy compositions, ligand mutations — at essentially zero additional cost per compound. Related exact constraints (alchemical enantiomers, Levy/Hellmann–Feynman symmetry rules, linear‑in‑ΔZ relations, and Δ‑machine‑learning corrections trained on a few exact points) further tighten the predictions, and the reference can be chosen as a "mean" or fractionally charged system so that the whole target set lies within a small ΔZ.

Since a high‑throughput study of *N* candidate stoichiometries normally means *N* independent self‑consistent calculations, replacing them with one converged SCF plus a handful of linear response solves reduces the cost by two to four orders of magnitude, converts a combinatorial search into a smooth, differentiable optimization over a continuous nuclear‑charge (and hence compositional) space that can be attacked with gradient‑based inverse‑design, and introduces no approximation to the underlying Kohn–Sham method beyond the truncation order of the expansion — so it stacks with any per‑calculation speed‑up.

A route not used before is to **work in the time domain / with polynomial (kernel‑polynomial) expansions instead of doing eigen‑decompositions and many separate frequency‑ or perturbation‑resolved runs.** Rather than diagonalizing the Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian and then repeating a linear‑response calculation for every frequency, perturbation direction, temperature or energy point of interest, one applies a short "kick" (or an explicit time‑dependent field) to the ground state and propagates the orbitals in real time with a matrix‑free integrator (Crank–Nicolson, Magnus, Taylor or, most efficiently, a Chebyshev expansion of exp(−iHΔt)), then Fourier‑transforms the resulting dipole/current to obtain the entire absorption, dielectric, conductivity or nonlinear‑response spectrum from a *single* run. The same polynomial idea works for static quantities: the density of states, the density matrix, the local moments and the Fermi‑level occupation can be obtained from a Chebyshev/Lanczos "kernel‑polynomial" expansion of the desired function of H, evaluated with random or localized probe vectors.

The advantage is that every operation reduces to cheap Hamiltonian–vector products (FFTs or short stencils plus local multiplications): no diagonalization, no orthogonalization, no explicit unoccupied states (which are the real bottleneck of Casida/Sternheimer‑type response calculations), and memory scaling only with the occupied manifold. The cost therefore grows roughly linearly with system size and with the number of spectral points is essentially *free*, whereas frequency‑domain approaches cost one full linear solve per frequency and per perturbation. It is also embarrassingly parallel — each orbital, probe vector, or time segment propagates independently — maps perfectly onto GPUs, and the accuracy is controlled by two transparent knobs (time step / polynomial order and total propagation time, which sets the spectral resolution). Because it is an exact reformulation of the same Kohn–Sham (or time‑dependent Kohn–Sham) problem, it introduces no new physical approximation and stacks with linear‑scaling, GPU, pseudopotential and basis‑compression strategies, giving one to three orders of magnitude savings for spectra, transport, strong‑field/nonlinear response, electron–ion dynamics and finite‑temperature/warm‑dense‑matter calculations that would be prohibitive by repeated static diagonalization.

A route not used before is to **reformulate Kohn–Sham DFT in the Green's‑function / multiple‑scattering (KKR) language and integrate on a complex‑energy contour, so that one never computes wavefunctions or eigenvalues at all.** In multiple‑scattering theory the electronic structure of each atom is encoded once per energy in a small single‑site scattering matrix (t‑matrix, obtained from a cheap radial Schrödinger/Dirac solve inside each atomic sphere, truncated at ℓ ≤ 2–3), while the geometry enters only through purely structural, energy‑independent‑by‑construction structure constants; the Green's function then follows from a small Dyson equation, G = g + g·T·g, whose dimension is only (ℓ_max+1)² per atom — typically 9–16 — instead of thousands of plane waves per atom. All observables (density, DOS, total energy via Lloyd's formula, magnetic moments, exchange couplings, transport) are obtained as energy integrals of G, and the crucial trick is that this integral can be deformed into the **complex plane**: on a semicircular contour well away from the real axis the Green's function is analytic and extremely smooth, so Gauss–Legendre quadrature with only ~20–40 complex energy points (plus a few Matsubara poles at finite temperature) converges the integral to high precision — replacing the need for dense real‑axis energy meshes, large numbers of empty bands, fine k‑meshes and eigen‑decompositions. Because the imaginary part of the energy damps the real‑space Green's function exponentially, the site–site blocks become short‑ranged, so the Dyson equation can be solved by real‑space cluster truncation, screened/tight‑binding structure constants, or sparse block inversion — giving O(N) scaling with almost perfect parallelism over the (completely independent) energy points, k‑points and atomic sites.

Beyond raw speed, this formulation removes whole classes of calculations that would otherwise require huge supercells or repeated SCF runs: embedding a defect, impurity, surface or interface directly in the Green's function of the infinite host (no supercell, no vacuum padding, no artificial periodic images), configurational averaging over disorder in a single primitive cell (CPA), and direct access to spectral functions, lifetimes, magnetic exchange parameters (Liechtenstein formula) and Landauer transport from the same converged G. Since it is an exact reformulation of the same Kohn–Sham problem — only the representation of the electronic structure changes — the accuracy is controlled by the transparent knobs ℓ_max, contour points and cluster radius, and the approach stacks with GPU acceleration, symmetry reduction and any other strategy.

Another distinct route is to **attack the eigenvalue problem with "spectrum‑slicing," contour‑integral eigensolvers running on highly optimized parallel dense/sparse linear‑algebra libraries.** Instead of computing all occupied Kohn–Sham states with one global diagonalization (whose O(N³) cost and, worse, whose global orthogonalization forces all‑to‑all communication and limits scaling), the occupied spectrum is cut into many narrow energy windows, and each window's eigenpairs are extracted independently and simultaneously by a filter that suppresses everything outside it — a shift‑and‑invert (sparse LU/Cholesky factorization) filter, a polynomial/rational filter, or a contour‑integral projector à la FEAST/Sakurai–Sugiura, where the resolvent (zI−H)⁻¹ is evaluated at a handful of quadrature points on a circle enclosing the window. Because the states within different slices are automatically orthogonal to one another, orthogonalization is needed only inside each small window: the O(N³) work with a large prefactor is replaced by many small, nearly independent subspace problems that can be spread over separate groups of nodes/GPUs with almost no communication between them, on top of the usual parallelism over k‑points, spins and bands. Implemented through mature, machine‑tuned libraries (ELPA/ELSI, ScaLAPACK/MAGMA/SLATE, SLEPc, FEAST, with two‑stage tridiagonalization, cache‑blocked kernels and mixed precision), and combined with reuse of the previous SCF cycle's subspace as the starting guess and with loose residual tolerances in early cycles, this typically gives an order of magnitude reduction in diagonalization time and enables strong scaling to hundreds of thousands of cores. Since it is exact linear algebra on the same Hamiltonian — with accuracy controlled only by the filter degree/quadrature and residual threshold — it introduces no physical approximation and multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

A route not yet used is to **stop computing DFT along the sampling trajectory at all and instead obtain DFT‑quality ensemble averages by *reweighting* from a cheap reference potential.** Most of the cost in finite‑temperature/condensed‑phase DFT studies (free energies, solvation and adsorption free energies, phase diagrams, melting points, defect formation entropies, reaction barriers in solution, IR/NMR ensemble averages) is not one expensive energy evaluation but the millions of correlated ones needed to converge a statistical average. Instead: run the long, well‑converged sampling (MD or Monte Carlo, including enhanced sampling) entirely on a cheap surrogate — a classical/polarizable force field, a semiempirical/tight‑binding Hamiltonian, or a machine‑learned potential — then recover the exact DFT ensemble by performing full DFT single‑point (energy‑only) calculations on a small set of *decorrelated* snapshots and applying free‑energy perturbation / Zwanzig reweighting, Bennett acceptance ratio or MBAR, thermodynamic integration along a λ path connecting the cheap and the DFT Hamiltonians, or a Δ‑correction (fit the DFT–surrogate energy difference and add it perturbatively). Because the free‑energy difference between the reference and the DFT surface is a smooth, low‑variance quantity when the reference is reasonably good, only 10²–10³ DFT single points — each *independent* and therefore embarrassingly parallel, with no need for forces, no need to be sequential in time, and no need to restart the SCF from the previous step — suffice where a direct ab initio MD would need 10⁵–10⁷ sequential force evaluations. The statistical overlap can be improved systematically (train/refit the surrogate on the same DFT snapshots in an active‑learning loop, use multiple intermediate λ states or "targeted"/map‑based reweighting, or use umbrella‑style stratification), so the result converges to the true DFT answer with a controllable and *measurable* error bar rather than an uncontrolled approximation. This attacks the number and the serial dependency of DFT calls in statistical‑mechanical applications — typically two to four orders of magnitude fewer self‑consistent solves and near‑perfect parallel efficiency — and it stacks with every per‑calculation speed‑up.

A route not yet used is **error‑controlled, "just‑enough‑accuracy" computing: let rigorous a‑posteriori error estimators decide, on the fly, how much numerical effort each part of the calculation actually deserves.** In practice most DFT runs are grossly over‑converged because users set one safe global value for every knob (plane‑wave cutoff/grid spacing, k‑mesh, SCF and eigensolver residual thresholds, quadrature grid, real‑space cutoffs, augmentation/projector accuracy, force/stress tolerances) and keep it fixed from the first iteration to the last. Instead, equip the code with computable estimates of the individual error contributions — discretization/basis‑incompleteness estimators (residual‑based or dual‑weighted‑residual "goal‑oriented" estimators in finite‑element/real‑space DFT), SCF and eigen‑residual bounds propagated to the *target* quantity through perturbation theory (the energy is second order, but forces and gaps are first order, so each needs a different tolerance), and statistical estimates of quadrature and truncation noise — and then adapt every parameter so that each error sits just below the accuracy the user actually asked for in the quantity of interest, no tighter. This naturally produces a cascadic/continuation strategy: converge cheaply on a coarse grid, small basis and sparse k‑mesh, interpolate the density and orbitals as the starting guess for the next finer level, and pay for the finest discretization only in the last one or two iterations; it also tightens thresholds progressively during the SCF and during a geometry relaxation or MD run (loose early, tight only near convergence), refines the mesh/basis only in the spatial regions and only for the states that dominate the error, and deliberately exploits systematic error cancellation by using *identical, moderately converged* settings for the two sides of a difference (reaction energy, defect formation energy, adsorption energy) rather than converging each absolute total energy to μeV. Because the estimators also give an honest, reportable error bar, the accuracy is not merely preserved but becomes *verifiable*, and since this is purely a matter of choosing numerical parameters — no change to the functional, basis type, solver or hardware — it typically saves factors of several to tens and multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

A route not yet used is to **parallelize in the *time*/trajectory dimension rather than in space — i.e., harvest the parallelism that a single DFT run cannot use.** Every DFT code hits a strong‑scaling wall (beyond a few hundred–thousand cores per SCF the communication in FFTs, orthogonalization and diagonalization dominates), so on a large machine the extra nodes are best spent on *concurrent* work along the simulation timeline: (i) **parallel‑in‑time integration (parareal / PFASST‑type schemes)**, where a cheap coarse propagator (classical force field, DFTB, or an on‑the‑fly machine‑learned potential) sweeps serially over the whole trajectory to give predicted states at many time slices, and full DFT fine propagators then run *simultaneously* on all slices, with an iterative correction sweep that provably converges to the exact DFT trajectory in a few iterations — turning a strictly sequential chain of 10⁵ force calls into a handful of sequential sweeps over many parallel segments; (ii) **ensemble/replica parallelism** — many independent walkers, replica‑exchange/parallel‑tempering, multiple‑walker metadynamics, parallel‑replica dynamics and transition‑interface/forward‑flux sampling for rare events, and independent seeds for statistical averages — which cuts the *wall‑clock* time to a converged free energy or rate by the number of replicas, since the trajectories never have to talk to each other except through occasional swaps; (iii) **speculative/pipelined execution and asynchronous task‑based scheduling**, in which candidate future configurations (e.g. several trial steps of an optimizer, several stretched/compressed cells, several k‑point or spin blocks) are launched pre‑emptively and the unused branches discarded, keeping the machine saturated instead of idling during serial phases. Because the physics, functional, basis and solver are untouched and the parareal correction converges to the same trajectory, the accuracy is unchanged; what improves is *time‑to‑solution*, typically by one to two orders of magnitude on machines whose node count far exceeds the strong‑scaling limit of one SCF calculation — and this multiplies with every per‑call speed‑up.

A route not yet used is **pure performance engineering of the existing code — profiling‑driven, low‑level optimisation of the *implementation* rather than of the physics or the algorithm.** Production DFT codes typically run at a small fraction of the peak throughput of the machine they sit on, and the gap is recovered by systematic software work: profile first to find the true hot spots (usually a handful of GEMM‑like loops, the 3‑D FFTs, the XC quadrature and the integral kernels), then (i) replace hand‑written loops with vendor‑ and architecture‑tuned libraries (MKL/OpenBLAS/BLIS, libxsmm for the many *small* matrix products, FFTW/heFFTe with pre‑planned, reused transform plans, ELPA/ELSI for eigensolves) and recast as many operations as possible from BLAS‑1/2 into blocked BLAS‑3 form with batched calls; (ii) optimise for the memory hierarchy — cache blocking and loop fusion/tiling so that data are touched once, contiguous, aligned, structure‑of‑arrays data layouts that allow full SIMD (AVX‑512/SVE) vectorisation, elimination of temporary array copies and of repeated re‑computation of quantities that can be tabulated once; (iii) fix the parallel plumbing — NUMA‑aware allocation, thread/core pinning, hybrid MPI+OpenMP instead of pure MPI to cut message counts, non‑blocking collectives and communication/computation overlap, load balancing of grid points, bands and shell pairs, task‑based asynchronous runtimes so no rank idles in serial phases; (iv) remove I/O entirely — keep wavefunctions, integrals and densities in core (or in compressed/reduced‑precision storage) rather than streaming them to scratch disk, which on large runs is often the single biggest bottleneck; and (v) exploit build‑time gains — aggressive compiler flags, link‑time and profile‑guided optimisation, up‑to‑date compilers, and simply benchmarking several codes/implementations and choosing the one that is fastest for the given system class. Because this changes nothing about the Hamiltonian, functional, basis or numerical approximations, the results are bit‑for‑bit the same physics, yet factors of 2–10× in time‑to‑solution are routine, and the gains multiply with every algorithmic or hardware acceleration strategy.

A route not used before is to **cut the number of components/degrees of freedom carried by each Kohn–Sham state — i.e., simplify the spin and relativistic structure of the Hamiltonian.** A fully four‑component Dirac(–Kohn–Sham) or noncollinear two‑component spinor calculation costs roughly 4–8× (in matrix dimension, and up to ~64× in the cubic diagonalization step) more than a one‑component treatment, and a spin‑polarized run costs twice a nonmagnetic one. So one should systematically "fold down" this structure: replace the 4‑component Dirac Hamiltonian by an exactly or approximately decoupled 2‑component one (X2C, ZORA, Douglas–Kroll–Hess, or relativistic effective core potentials that bury the small‑component/core physics in a pretabulated potential), then further to a **scalar‑relativistic, spin‑free** Hamiltonian with spin–orbit added only *a posteriori* in a small perturbative or state‑interaction step over a handful of low‑lying states rather than variationally in every SCF cycle. Likewise, run non‑spin‑polarized where magnetism is demonstrably absent; for collinear magnets exploit the fact that the two spin channels decouple into two independent, smaller eigenproblems that can be solved on separate node groups; and for noncollinear magnetism use the **generalized Bloch theorem** so that a spin spiral of arbitrary wavevector q is treated in the chemical unit cell instead of a large magnetic supercell (with symmetry‑constrained or fixed‑moment/constrained‑DFT initializations to avoid the many wasted SCF cycles and metastable magnetic solutions that plague magnetic systems). Because the neglected couplings are small and can be restored perturbatively where they matter (heavy elements, magnetic anisotropy, spin–orbit splittings), the accuracy for total energies, geometries and thermochemistry is essentially preserved, while the matrix dimension, the number of bands, and the SCF iteration count all shrink — typically giving factors of 2–10, and it stacks with every other acceleration strategy.

A route not used before is to **rewrite the whole DFT code as a differentiable, batched, just‑in‑time‑compiled program and differentiate *through* the self‑consistent solution with automatic differentiation (AD).** If the Kohn–Sham solver is expressed in a framework such as JAX/PyTorch/Enzyme, one can (i) JIT‑compile and fuse the kernels (grids, FFTs/stencils, XC quadrature, integral builds) into single optimized GPU/TPU kernels, (ii) use `vmap`‑style vectorization to run whole *batches* of systems, k‑points, spins, perturbations or trial geometries simultaneously as large tensor operations that saturate the hardware instead of many small serial calls, and (iii) obtain **every** derivative essentially for free by reverse‑mode differentiation combined with the implicit‑function theorem applied to the SCF fixed point (so one does *not* backpropagate through the 20–50 SCF iterations — a single extra linear solve of the same size as one SCF step suffices, and the same trick handles differentiation through the eigensolver and the geometry optimizer). The payoff is that the cost of a gradient becomes independent of the number of parameters differentiated against: forces, stresses, response and derivative properties, and — crucially — gradients with respect to *non‑structural* inputs such as pseudopotential/basis parameters, exchange–correlation functional coefficients (enabling functional and ML‑functional training by direct end‑to‑end fitting to observables rather than by expensive finite differences), continuous composition/nuclear charges, and external fields all come out of one backward pass. This converts screening and design campaigns, force‑field/functional parameterization and constraint (inverse‑design) problems — which conventionally require thousands of independent, finite‑difference DFT runs — into smooth gradient‑based optimizations needing a handful of solves, while the JIT/batched execution alone typically gives an order‑of‑magnitude wall‑clock gain. Because AD returns the exact analytic derivatives of the same Kohn–Sham equations, no physical approximation is introduced, and the approach stacks with every other acceleration strategy.

A route not yet used is to **stay on the cheapest rung of Jacob's ladder and buy back the missing physics with corrective terms whose evaluation costs essentially nothing.** Rather than paying for a hybrid, meta‑GGA, nonlocal‑vdW, RPA or DMFT treatment, run an ordinary (semi)local LDA/GGA calculation — whose Kohn–Sham matrix build is a simple pointwise quadrature and whose SCF cost per iteration is the smallest of any functional — and repair its known systematic failures with local, parameter‑level add‑ons evaluated once per cycle at negligible cost: an on‑site Hubbard **+U** (and inter‑site **+V**, or +J for Hund's physics) to remove self‑interaction/delocalization error in transition‑metal oxides, rare earths and defects, giving band gaps, magnetic moments and redox energetics close to hybrid or DMFT quality for ~1 % of the cost; Koopmans‑compliant, self‑interaction‑correction, DFT‑1/2 or scissor/GW‑derived level corrections for gaps and level alignment; constrained‑DFT terms to enforce the right charge/spin localization; and simple analytic pair‑wise corrections for the remaining weak interactions. Crucially, the empirical character can be removed without extra cost by computing the parameters *ab initio* once — U and V from linear response/DFPT or constrained RPA on a small primitive cell — and then transferring them across the whole chemical family, temperatures, cell sizes and MD trajectory, so a single cheap linear‑response run replaces thousands of expensive hybrid or correlated evaluations. Because these are diagonal, short‑ranged corrections to the potential and total energy (with analytic forces and stresses), they leave the solver, basis, grids and scaling untouched, add well under 1 % to the runtime, avoid the 10–100× penalty of exact exchange and the k‑mesh/empty‑state burden of nonlocal correlation, and therefore stack with every other acceleration strategy while often *improving* agreement with experiment for strongly correlated systems where plain GGA fails.

A route not used before is to **exploit a *dual (mixed) representation* of the Kohn–Sham problem — keep the orbitals in one basis and the density/potentials in another, and move between them with fast transforms.** This is the "Gaussian‑and‑plane‑waves" (GPW/GAPW, as in CP2K's Quickstep) and augmented‑basis (APW+lo/LAPW, mixed‑basis pseudopotential) idea: expand the Kohn–Sham orbitals in a small, strictly local, atom‑centred Gaussian/numeric basis, so the Hamiltonian and overlap matrices are tiny, sparse and built from *analytic* two‑centre integrals with distance screening; but collocate the resulting density onto a plane‑wave/multigrid real‑space mesh, where the Hartree potential is obtained by a single FFT‑based Poisson solve in O(N log N) with no four‑centre electron‑repulsion integrals at all, and the exchange–correlation potential is evaluated pointwise; then integrate the potential back against the Gaussians to complete the matrix build. Each representation is used only for what it is good at — compactness and analyticity for the wavefunctions, diagonality and fast convolution for electrostatics — so one escapes both the N⁴ integral bottleneck of pure Gaussian codes and the millions of basis functions of pure plane‑wave codes. Additional structure is handled by hierarchical multigrids (sharp Gaussians mapped onto fine meshes, diffuse ones onto coarse meshes, so the collocation cost is nearly independent of basis exponent range) and by atom‑centred augmentation spheres (GAPW/PAW/APW+lo) that carry the hard nuclear‑cusp part analytically, letting the smooth mesh stay coarse even in all‑electron calculations. Because it is only a change of representation of the same functional and Hamiltonian — with accuracy controlled by the basis, the mesh cutoff and the augmentation radius — it introduces no new physical approximation, routinely gives one to two orders of magnitude speed‑up for condensed‑phase systems of hundreds to thousands of atoms (making ab initio MD in liquids and biomolecules practical), and stacks with every other acceleration strategy.

A route not yet used is **dimensional/structural reduction through non‑crystallographic "objective" (helical and cyclic) boundary conditions — i.e., Cyclix/helical DFT.** Many technologically important systems are periodic not under translations but under *screw* and *rotational* operations: single‑ and multi‑walled nanotubes of arbitrary chirality, nanowires, nanoribbons, nanocoils, DNA‑ and protein‑like helices, and, crucially, systems under *torsion, bending or twist*. Treating these in a conventional orthogonal‑cell code forces one to build a huge translational supercell (a chiral nanotube may need hundreds to thousands of atoms, plus thick vacuum padding in two directions) and then solve an O(N³) problem on it. Instead, one can formulate the Kohn–Sham equations directly in helical/cylindrical coordinates and impose the *objective* symmetry group generated by a screw operation (translation by Δz combined with rotation by α) and a cyclic rotation of order 𝔪, so that the orbitals obey a generalized Bloch theorem ψ(𝒮r) = e^{i(η ν + 2πμ/𝔪)}ψ(r). The fundamental domain then contains only the two or three symmetry‑irreducible atoms of the structure, and the "k‑points" become the pair of conjugate helical/cyclic quantum numbers (η, μ), which are perfectly independent and embarrassingly parallel. Everything else follows: the Poisson equation and the kinetic operator are discretized on a cylindrical/helical finite‑difference or spectral grid (with a radial coordinate that naturally truncates the vacuum instead of padding it), the electrostatics are solved with true open boundary conditions in the radial direction so no artificial image interactions arise, and integration/Brillouin‑zone sampling is reduced by the full order of the symmetry group (often 10²–10³×). Since the cost scales as the cube of the *symmetry‑reduced* cell, this converts a many‑thousand‑atom supercell calculation into a few‑atom one — routinely three to five orders of magnitude cheaper — and it uniquely makes accessible whole classes of deformations (continuous twist, uniform torsional/bending strain, chirality scans, moiré‑like relative rotations) that are strictly incommensurate and hence *impossible* in a translational supercell. Because the symmetry is exact for the idealized structure, the results are numerically identical to the corresponding infinite supercell calculation — no new physical approximation is introduced — and the scheme stacks with pseudopotentials, GPU acceleration, iterative/spectrum‑slicing eigensolvers and any other strategy.

A route not used before is **spatial coarse‑graining of the *nuclear and field degrees of freedom* themselves — quasi‑continuum / multiscale "coarse‑grained DFT" (QC‑DFT, MacroDFT).** Many important DFT problems (dislocations, crack tips, point defects, grain boundaries, indentation, solute–defect interaction) are *local* in their chemistry but *long‑ranged* in their elastic/electrostatic fields, so a brute‑force supercell must contain millions of atoms merely to accommodate the slowly varying strain field far from the core. Instead, keep full atomistic Kohn–Sham resolution only in a small "core" region, and in the far field replace the individual atoms by a **finite‑element interpolation of the displacement field**: only a sparse set of representative atoms sits at the element nodes, the positions of all remaining atoms are slaved to the (smooth, nearly uniform) interpolated deformation, and their energy contribution is estimated by **cluster/quadrature summation rules** — computing small periodic "unit cells under local strain" at a handful of quadrature points and multiplying by the number of atoms they represent — rather than by an explicit calculation. The same coarse‑graining is applied to the *fields*: the electron density, effective potential and the electrostatic (Poisson) solution are represented on an adaptive real‑space/finite‑element mesh that is atomically fine only near the defect and progressively coarser outward, with the far field either interpolated from a bulk/periodic reference density or matched to a continuum elastic/multipole solution, so no vacuum or buffer padding and no artificial periodic images are needed. Corrections that restore accuracy — non‑local "ghost force" removal, boundary/Dirichlet coupling to linear or nonlinear continuum elasticity, and cheap perturbative (Harris‑type) energy corrections in the transition zone — are inexpensive and systematically refinable by simply enriching the mesh.

Because the number of degrees of freedom then grows like the *logarithm* (or a small fractional power) of the physical system size instead of linearly with the atom count, systems containing 10⁶–10⁹ atoms of material can be represented with only 10²–10⁴ atoms actually solved quantum‑mechanically — a three‑ to six‑order‑of‑magnitude reduction in cost — while the region where the electronic structure genuinely matters is treated at full Kohn–Sham accuracy with no change to the functional, pseudopotentials or solver, so the scheme stacks with every other acceleration strategy.

A route not used before is to **inject randomization into the *linear algebra and the big sums* of a conventional (still fully deterministic-orbital) DFT code — i.e., randomized/sketching numerical algorithms and Monte‑Carlo sub‑sampling of the expensive summations.** Almost every costly step of a Kohn–Sham calculation is either a low‑rank‑compressible operator or a huge sum over indices whose terms are highly redundant, and both are ideal targets for randomized methods. Concretely: (i) build subspaces and compress operators with **randomized range finders / randomized SVD / interpolative decompositions** — sketch the Hamiltonian or the occupied subspace with a few random Gaussian or fast Johnson–Lindenstrauss (subsampled FFT/Hadamard) test vectors, run one or two power/Chebyshev-filter passes, and orthogonalize only the resulting thin matrix, which yields the occupied invariant subspace and the density matrix at a cost of a handful of matrix–vector products instead of a full O(N³) diagonalization, with rigorous probabilistic error bounds; (ii) compress the density‑fitting/ERI tensor, the exchange operator, the polarizability and the pair‑product (ISDF) grids by **randomized pivoted QR / column–row (CUR) selection**, which picks the O(R) genuinely important auxiliary functions or grid points automatically instead of using a fixed, over‑complete auxiliary basis; (iii) use **stochastic trace/diagonal estimators (Hutchinson, Hutch++, XTrace)** for the traces, density-of-states, entropies and Fermi‑level searches that would otherwise need every eigenvalue; (iv) apply **"sketch‑and‑solve"/randomized preconditioning and randomized least squares** inside the SCF mixing (Anderson/DIIS histories are strongly rank‑deficient and can be sketched), and randomized rank‑revealing updates of the density matrix between MD steps; and (v) **sub‑sample the quadratures stochastically during the early SCF cycles** — random batches of XC grid points, k‑points, or orbital pairs — treating the resulting noisy gradient like stochastic‑gradient optimization, then switch to full deterministic sums only for the last cycles and the final energy/forces, so the exact answer is recovered while most iterations cost a fraction of a full one. Crucially, the randomness here is only a *computational* device: the physics, functional, basis and boundary conditions are untouched, the error is controlled by a single knob (the number of random samples/sketch size) and can be measured on the fly, and a cheap deterministic "clean‑up" step (a residual‑based refinement, or one exact iteration at the end) removes the statistical bias entirely. Because randomized kernels reduce to large dense matrix–matrix products with almost no synchronization, they map perfectly onto GPUs and scale nearly ideally in parallel, typically giving one to two orders of magnitude reduction in the diagonalization, integral‑compression and quadrature costs — and they stack with every other acceleration strategy.

A route not yet used is to **exploit the reality and structure of the fields, and to trim the "empty space" and the number of states, so that each operation moves half (or less) of the data.** Concretely: (i) whenever the calculation is Γ‑point only (large supercells, molecules, liquids, biomolecular and amorphous systems), impose time‑reversal symmetry so the Kohn–Sham orbitals can be taken **real**, storing only half of the plane‑wave coefficients (c(−G) = c*(G)) and doing real arithmetic instead of complex — this halves memory and cuts the FLOPs of the FFTs, the subspace overlaps and the orthogonalization by roughly 2–4×; likewise the density and potential are always real, so all grid transforms should be real‑to‑complex/complex‑to‑real (Hermitian‑packed) rather than full complex FFTs, and the same Hermitian packing applies to the structure factors and to the ±G pairs in the Hartree and local‑pseudopotential terms; (ii) eliminate the wasted degrees of freedom in vacuum by using **truncated/tailored Coulomb kernels** (spherical, wire or slab cutoffs, Martyna–Tuckerman or Poisson solvers with open boundary conditions) so that isolated molecules, wires, 2‑D layers, charged systems and surface slabs need only a thin vacuum buffer instead of 10–20 Å of padding — since cost scales with the FFT box volume this alone can give several‑fold savings and simultaneously removes spurious image interactions (with the analogous Gygi–Baldereschi/Ewald singularity corrections and optimized Ewald splitting parameter to accelerate the long‑range lattice sums); and (iii) carry only the states you actually need — the occupied bands plus a minimal, adaptively chosen buffer of empty bands set by the smearing width (rather than a fixed generous number), drop the empty‑state manifold entirely where the method permits, and use a non‑orthogonal/compact representation so the O(N_band²·N_grid) orthogonalization and subspace‑rotation work shrinks quadratically with the band count.

All three are exact bookkeeping/boundary‑condition choices — the Hamiltonian, functional, pseudopotentials and solver are untouched and the results are numerically identical (indeed *more* correct for charged and low‑dimensional systems, where periodic images are removed) — yet together they routinely cut memory and wall time by factors of 2–10, and they multiply with every other acceleration strategy.

A route not used before is to **make each application of the Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian intrinsically cheap by recasting all of its operators into *separable, analytic, short‑ranged* form.** The dominant inner‑loop cost of any iterative solver is the repeated product H·ψ, and much of that cost comes from operators that are formally dense or long‑ranged. Three concrete transformations remove this:

1. **Separable (Kleinman–Bylander) nonlocal pseudopotentials.** A semilocal ionic pseudopotential Σ_ℓ |ℓ⟩ v_ℓ(r) ⟨ℓ| acts as a *dense* matrix in the basis, costing O(N_basis²) per band per atom. Rewriting it in fully separable form, V_NL = Σ_i |β_i⟩ D_ij ⟨β_j| with only a handful of projectors β_i per atom (Kleinman–Bylander, and the analytic Gaussian‑form Hartwigsen–Goedecker–Hutter or ONCV multi‑projector variants, with ghost‑state checks), reduces the operation to a few inner products and rank‑one updates — O(N_basis × N_proj) — i.e. one to two orders of magnitude cheaper, and it converts the projector overlaps into small, GEMM‑shaped batched matrix products that map ideally onto GPUs.

2. **Real‑space (rather than reciprocal‑space) projection of those projectors.** Because β_i is strictly confined to a small sphere around each nucleus, evaluating ⟨β_i|ψ⟩ on the real‑space grid touches only the few hundred grid points inside that sphere, so the nonlocal term becomes strictly **O(N) with N atoms** and requires only nearest‑neighbour (halo) communication, instead of O(N_atoms × N_PW) global reciprocal‑space sums with all‑to‑all reductions. The same locality lets the local potential, the augmentation/PAW charges and the compensation multipoles be applied pointwise on the grid.

3. **Analytic, closed‑form representations everywhere else.** Choose pseudopotentials, projectors, atomic‑orbital basis functions and compensation charges as sums of Gaussians/polynomials so that the local potential, structure factors, core charges and their derivatives (forces and stresses) are given by *analytic* dual‑space formulas rather than by numerical radial integrals interpolated on tables, eliminating both the interpolation error and the table lookups; combine with erf/erfc splitting so the singular 1/r part is handled analytically and only a smooth remainder is put on the grid.

Because these are exact algebraic re‑expressions (or, for KB separability, a controlled construction validated against the original semilocal potential), the physics, functional, basis and boundary conditions are unchanged and the results are essentially identical — yet the cost of every Hamiltonian–vector product, and hence of the entire SCF and of every force/stress evaluation, falls by roughly an order of magnitude while simultaneously improving parallel scalability, and the gain multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

Use a **cheap surrogate Hamiltonian as a nonlinear "coarse level" that preconditions the expensive DFT solve** — i.e., multilevel/cross‑fidelity preconditioning and continuation of the Kohn–Sham problem.

Concretely, pair the full calculation with a much cheaper model of the *same* system — a tight‑binding/DFTB or minimal‑basis Hamiltonian, a coarse‑grid/low‑cutoff version of the same DFT problem, or a linearized model of the dielectric response — and use it not to replace the answer but to *drive* the expensive one. The cheap model is solved essentially for free at every step and supplies: (i) the nonlinear preconditioner for the self‑consistency fixed point, so that instead of mixing the raw density residual one applies the inverse of the cheap model's response (its Jacobian/dielectric matrix), which captures charge sloshing, screening and long‑wavelength instabilities in metals and large or inhomogeneous cells almost exactly and collapses the number of costly SCF cycles from tens to a handful; (ii) the coarse‑grid correction in a full‑approximation‑storage (FAS) nonlinear‑multigrid V‑cycle over the SCF map, where the cheap/coarse level resolves the slowly converging long‑range components and the expensive fine level only has to smooth the short‑range residual; (iii) the search directions and subspace for the eigen/minimization problem, and the continuation path when a parameter is varied (geometry, strain, composition, field, temperature, U value, or a λ that morphs the cheap Hamiltonian into the exact one), so each new expensive solve starts already inside the convergence basin.

Because the cheap model only enters through the preconditioner/coarse correction — the residual that is driven to zero is always the exact Kohn–Sham one — the converged result is bit‑for‑bit the true DFT answer regardless of how crude the surrogate is; a poor surrogate merely means fewer saved iterations, never a wrong result. In practice this typically reduces the number of expensive Hamiltonian builds/diagonalizations by a factor of several to an order of magnitude (most dramatically for the hard cases: large metallic slabs, magnetic and strongly inhomogeneous systems, charged defects, where plain Pulay/Broyden mixing stagnates or diverges), it costs almost nothing to add, and it multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

A route not used before is to **treat numerical precision and memory traffic as tunable resources — "approximate computing" for DFT — rather than running everything in IEEE double precision.** Modern DFT is overwhelmingly *memory‑bandwidth and communication bound*, not FLOP bound: orbitals, integral/ERI tensors, density matrices, projectors and grid data are streamed repeatedly from memory across nodes, so halving the number of bits moved roughly halves the time of the dominant kernels. Concretely: (i) carry the bulk of the arithmetic in single, half (FP16/bfloat16), TF32 or even fixed‑point/integer‑quantized formats — Hamiltonian–vector products, FFTs, projector applications, subspace rotations, XC quadrature, integral evaluation and SCF mixing histories all tolerate low precision because they only need to produce a *search direction* or an intermediate iterate, not the final answer; (ii) restore full accuracy at the end by **iterative refinement / compute‑then‑correct**: compute the residual and a small correction step in double precision, so the converged density, energy, forces and stresses are numerically indistinguishable from an all‑double run (the same trick that makes mixed‑precision linear solvers and LU factorizations exact); (iii) make the precision *adaptive in time and in space* — very low precision in early SCF cycles, early geometry/MD steps, distant/loosely converged bands, small‑magnitude integrals and low‑density grid regions, tightening only near convergence and for the quantities (forces, gaps, energy differences) that are first order in the error; (iv) **compress the data itself**: store wavefunctions, density matrices and integral tensors in lossy but error‑bounded formats (ZFP/SZ floating‑point compression, low‑bit quantization with per‑block scaling, sparsity thresholding), compress MPI messages and checkpoint/restart files, or avoid storing altogether by *recomputing* cheap quantities on the fly (integral‑direct SCF, recompute‑instead‑of‑store) whenever arithmetic is cheaper than memory access; (v) exploit that reduced precision is exactly what AI‑oriented tensor/matrix units are built for, so the same kernels run 4–16× faster on modern GPUs/accelerators and the reduced footprint lets much larger systems fit in on‑device memory, eliminating slow host–device transfers and out‑of‑core I/O.

Because the low‑precision work only accelerates the *path* to the fixed point while the residual that is finally driven to zero (and the final energy/force evaluation) is computed at full precision, no physical approximation is introduced and the error is controlled by a single, measurable tolerance; in practice this yields 2–10× in wall time and memory across the whole code, and it multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

A route not used before is to **use the electronic temperature itself as an accelerator — i.e., run finite‑temperature (Mermin/ensemble) DFT with deliberately generous Fermi smearing and then anneal/extrapolate back to the ground state.**

The reason SCF cycles in metals, small‑gap semiconductors, magnetic systems and molecules with near‑degenerate frontier orbitals are so painful is that the occupations f(ε) are a step function: an infinitesimal change of the potential makes states cross the Fermi level, the density jumps discontinuously, "charge sloshing" sets in, and one needs an enormous k‑mesh to resolve the sharp Fermi surface. Replacing the step by a smooth occupation function of finite width σ (Fermi–Dirac, Gaussian, Methfessel–Paxton, Marzari–Vanderbilt cold smearing) and minimizing the *free* energy F = E − TS of the ensemble makes the whole map density → potential → density analytic and much better conditioned. The practical consequences are all speed‑ups: (i) the SCF converges in far fewer, more stable iterations, and simple mixing schemes stop diverging; (ii) the Brillouin‑zone integrals become smooth, so a coarse k‑mesh (often 2–5× fewer points in each direction) already gives converged energies and forces; (iii) crucially, the one‑particle density matrix ρ = f(H) decays in real space with a length that scales roughly as 1/√(T·gap‑less scale) — a *higher* electronic temperature means a *shorter*‑ranged density matrix, so truncation radii in linear‑scaling/sparse‑matrix, Fermi‑operator‑expansion, Chebyshev and stochastic methods can be much smaller, and fewer polynomial terms/moments are needed to represent the projector, which directly cuts the dominant cost of those methods; (iv) the smooth occupations also remove the need to converge individual near‑degenerate eigenvectors tightly, so loose eigensolver tolerances suffice, and metastable/spurious magnetic or charge‑ordered solutions are washed out instead of trapping the iteration.

Accuracy is preserved by treating T as a systematically controllable knob rather than a fudge: use an *annealing/continuation* strategy in which the first cycles (or the first geometry/MD steps) run at large σ and the width is progressively reduced, each stage starting from the previous converged density; then recover the T → 0 answer either exactly (the free energy and the entropy are variational, forces and stresses are the derivatives of F, so the finite‑T result is thermodynamically consistent), by the standard E₀ ≈ (E + F)/2 or Methfessel–Paxton/cold‑smearing extrapolation whose error is O(σ³–σ⁴) instead of O(σ²), or by a short final stage at small σ. And when the physical problem *is* at high temperature — warm dense matter, shock and plasma conditions, laser‑excited or liquid metals — this formulation is not an approximation at all but the correct physics, and it avoids the catastrophic growth in the number of thermally occupied bands that cripples conventional zero‑temperature codes.

Because only the occupation function (and the corresponding entropy term in the energy functional) is changed — not the functional, basis, pseudopotentials or solver — this typically cuts SCF iteration counts, k‑point counts and density‑matrix truncation costs by factors of several to an order of magnitude, and it multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**Attack the *model system itself*: solve the smallest chemically faithful problem instead of the "realistic" one.**

Because Kohn–Sham cost grows roughly as N³ (and memory as N²), the cheapest and most underused lever is to reduce the number of atoms and the dimensionality of the *scientific* model before any numerical trick is applied. In practice this means: (i) replace an extended periodic slab/solid by a finite **cluster or embedded cluster model** (or vice versa, replace a huge molecular assembly by a small periodic motif) whenever the property of interest is local — adsorption, defect chemistry, active-site catalysis, NMR/EPR parameters; (ii) **truncate the chemistry**: substitute bulky spectator ligands, protecting groups, alkyl chains or counter-ions by H/CH₃ or point charges, model a polymer or protein by its repeat unit or active-site pocket, use the parent rather than the substituted molecule for mechanism scans; (iii) **thin the model geometrically**: use the minimum converged slab thickness, minimal vacuum, minimal defect–defect separation and the smallest primitive cell consistent with the physics, and freeze/constrain the interior layers or rigid fragments so fewer ionic steps (and smaller Hessians) are needed; (iv) exploit **reduced dimensionality** — 1D radial solvers for atoms, 2D/1D-periodic solvers for layers and wires, and reduced‑dimensional (few collective coordinates, rigid‑scan) potential‑energy surfaces instead of full 3N‑dimensional exploration; (v) study **surrogate elements/compositions** (e.g., a 3d instead of a 5f analogue, a light instead of a heavy halide) when only trends are needed.

The key is to make this controlled rather than sloppy: perform **one** convergence study — a single calculation on the full, untruncated model (or a ladder of increasing model sizes) — to verify that the truncated model reproduces the target quantity within the desired tolerance, and rely on error cancellation by using the *same* truncated model on both sides of every energy difference. Since halving the number of atoms already gives roughly an eightfold speed‑up, and typical over‑built models contain 2–10× more atoms than the physics requires, this routinely buys one to three orders of magnitude, requires no change to the code, functional, basis or hardware, and multiplies with every algorithmic or computational acceleration strategy.

A route not used before is to **never run the fully converged, "brute‑force" calculation at all, but instead obtain the converged limit by *extrapolation* from a small ladder of deliberately cheap calculations, using the known asymptotic convergence laws of each numerical parameter.**

Every discretization knob in DFT converges with a known analytic tail: the total energy falls off with the plane‑wave cutoff roughly as E(E_cut) ≈ E_∞ + A·E_cut^(−3/2) (and the real‑space grid/finite‑element error as h^p for a p‑th‑order stencil or element), Gaussian basis‑set incompleteness behaves as X^(−3) in the cardinal number, Brillouin‑zone sampling errors decay smoothly (and often oscillate with a known form) with the k‑mesh density, and finite‑size errors in supercells for defects, liquids or correlated/vdW systems scale as 1/L, 1/L³ or 1/N with analytically known leading coefficients. Because the *cost* grows steeply with these same knobs (≈ E_cut^{3/2}–E_cut^{3} for the FFT box, N_k linearly for k‑points, N³ for the cell size), it is dramatically cheaper to run two or three inexpensive calculations on a sequence of coarse settings and perform a Richardson/Aitken‑style fit to the known power law than to run a single massively over‑converged one: the extrapolated answer typically matches the brute‑force limit to within meV/atom while costing a small fraction — often 5–100× less — and the spread of the fit simultaneously delivers an honest error bar.

The same idea generalizes across the whole calculation: dual/double grids with a coarse orbital cutoff and an extrapolated density‑grid correction; basis‑set superposition/incompleteness corrections (counterpoise, gCP, F12‑like or "basis‑set correction" functionals) that let a double‑ζ‑quality basis reproduce complete‑basis results; extrapolating the SCF fixed point itself (Aitken/vector extrapolation of the density sequence, or extrapolation of the converged density/wavefunctions along a geometry, strain, temperature or composition path so that each new point starts essentially converged); extrapolating smearing‑width dependence to T→0; and extrapolating trajectory‑length or ensemble averages with block/finite‑sampling scaling laws instead of running longer.

Since this is purely a numerical‑analysis device — the functional, basis type, pseudopotentials, solver and physics are untouched, and the extrapolant is the exact same quantity the expensive run would have produced — it introduces no new approximation, yields a quantifiable residual error, requires only cheap, mutually independent (embarrassingly parallel) runs, and multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**Exploit periodicity in extra (non‑spatial) dimensions by working in a "superspace"/Floquet representation, instead of building enormous approximant supercells or propagating long trajectories.**

Many expensive DFT problems are expensive only because a hidden periodicity is being represented by brute force in real space or real time:

- *Incommensurately modulated crystals, charge/spin‑density waves, misfit layer compounds, moiré bilayers and quasicrystals* are conventionally treated by constructing a commensurate "approximant" supercell containing hundreds to tens of thousands of atoms, at O(N³) cost. But such a structure is exactly periodic in a **(3+d)-dimensional superspace**: the atomic positions and the density are periodic functions of the ordinary lattice vectors *plus* d additional phase coordinates (the modulation phases / relative twist). Formulating the Kohn–Sham equations in this superspace (equivalently, expanding the orbitals, density and potential in the small set of modulation harmonics q, 2q, … and solving the coupled set of Bloch problems at k, k±q, …) lets one work with the few atoms of the *average* unit cell plus a handful of Fourier components, rather than with a giant approximant. The cost then grows with the number of harmonics actually needed (usually 2–5), not with the size of the commensurate cell, giving two to four orders of magnitude savings — and it removes the artificial strain/commensuration error that approximants introduce, since the true incommensurate ratio can be used exactly.

- The same trick applied to the **time** axis is Floquet‑DFT: for a system driven by a periodic field (laser dressing, AC bias, phonon pumping, Floquet engineering of topological states), one need not propagate the time‑dependent Kohn–Sham orbitals for thousands of optical cycles until a steady state emerges. Because the driven Hamiltonian satisfies H(t+T)=H(t), the solutions are Floquet states e^{−iεt}Σ_n e^{−inωt}φ_n(r); expanding in a modest number of harmonics n turns the whole dynamics into a *static*, block‑structured Hermitian eigenvalue problem for the quasi‑energies (and a self‑consistency condition on the time‑averaged density). One converged Floquet solve replaces an entire long real‑time run and directly delivers the steady‑state observables, quasi‑energy band structure, and high‑harmonic/nonlinear response, typically 10²–10³× cheaper.

More generally: whenever a degree of freedom (spatial modulation, twist, drive, spiral spin order, applied field oscillation) is periodic, transform to its conjugate Fourier index and truncate — the number of retained harmonics is a single, systematically convergible knob. Since this is an exact change of representation of the same Kohn–Sham problem, no new physical approximation is introduced, and it stacks with pseudopotentials, GPU acceleration, symmetry reduction and every other speed‑up.

**Skip both the self‑consistency loop and the full occupied manifold: build the charge density by "charge patching," then extract only the few states you actually care about with a folded‑spectrum (interior‑eigenvalue) solver.**

The key observation is that the self‑consistent charge density is *nearsighted and highly transferable*: the density around a given atom depends almost entirely on its local bonding motif. So one can run a handful of small, fully self‑consistent DFT calculations on prototype fragments (bulk unit cells, small molecules/clusters containing each distinct bonding motif, plus surface/passivation motifs), decompose the resulting converged densities into atom‑centred, environment‑labelled "patches," and then *assemble* the density of an arbitrarily large target system — a quantum dot, nanowire, alloy, defect supercell, strained or amorphous structure — simply by superposing the appropriate patches (with strain/bond‑length‑dependent interpolation of the motifs). This reproduces the true self‑consistent density to ~1 % and the resulting potential to a few meV, but costs essentially nothing and is strictly O(N), because no SCF cycle is ever run on the big system: the expensive nonlinear fixed‑point problem is replaced by a table lookup plus addition.

Having the potential, one then exploits the fact that almost no application needs *all* N/2 occupied orbitals — band‑edge states, optical gaps, dopant/defect levels, carrier wavefunctions, transport channels and quantum‑confinement effects involve only a few states near a chosen reference energy ε_ref. These can be targeted directly by a **folded‑spectrum method**: minimize ⟨ψ|(Ĥ − ε_ref)²|ψ⟩ (or use shift‑and‑invert/rational‑filter equivalents), which converts the interior eigenvalues of interest into the *lowest* eigenvalues of the folded operator, so a standard conjugate‑gradient/Davidson iteration converges to them without computing, storing, or orthogonalizing against the millions of lower‑lying occupied states. The cost of each state is then a fixed number of Ĥ·ψ products (FFTs or short stencils), independent of how many electrons the system contains, and the different target states are independent and embarrassingly parallel.

Together, charge patching plus folded‑spectrum diagonalization removes the two things that make large DFT calculations O(N³): the self‑consistency iteration and the orthogonalization over all occupied bands. The scaling becomes essentially linear (in practice, near‑constant per state), enabling electronic‑structure calculations on 10⁵–10⁶‑atom nanostructures — systems three to four orders of magnitude beyond conventional Kohn–Sham reach — while retaining near‑DFT accuracy for the levels of interest. Accuracy is systematically controllable: the patch library can be enlarged to cover more motifs and strain states, and one or two conventional SCF iterations can optionally be performed on the patched density as a correction. Since only the way the density is obtained and the way eigenstates are extracted change, the functional, pseudopotentials and basis are untouched, so this stacks with every other acceleration strategy.

**Use compressive sensing / sparse (L1) regression to reconstruct the high‑dimensional objects you actually want from a *sub‑Nyquist* number of DFT runs.**

Most DFT campaigns don't need one energy — they need a high‑dimensional function: an anharmonic force‑constant tensor (3rd/4th order), a full potential‑energy surface or dielectric/elastic response tensor, a cluster expansion over compositions and orderings, a band structure or spectral function. Brute force requires an exponentially or polynomially large set of displaced/decorated supercell calculations (hundreds to millions of DFT jobs). But these objects are *sparse* in a physically motivated basis: only a few symmetry‑allowed force constants, cluster interactions, or Fourier/wavelet components are non‑negligible. Compressive sensing exploits that: (i) expand the target quantity in a large, deliberately over‑complete symmetry‑adapted basis; (ii) run only a small number of *randomly chosen, information‑rich* DFT configurations (random thermal snapshots, random displacements, random alloy decorations) and collect the resulting energies and — crucially — the 3N force/stress components, each of which is an independent equation; (iii) solve the resulting strongly underdetermined linear system by L1/LASSO (or Bayesian‑compressive‑sensing / matching‑pursuit) minimization, which provably recovers the exact sparse solution when the sampling is incoherent, with cross‑validation supplying the regularization strength and an honest error estimate.

Because the number of required measurements scales like the *sparsity* times a log factor rather than the number of basis functions, this typically yields the full anharmonic/configurational model from tens of DFT snapshots instead of thousands of frozen‑phonon or ordered‑structure calculations — one to three orders of magnitude fewer self‑consistent solves — while automatically performing model selection (it discards irrelevant interactions rather than requiring you to guess a cutoff). The individual DFT snapshots are completely independent and hence embarrassingly parallel, no approximation is made to the underlying Kohn–Sham method (each data point is an exact DFT calculation), the recovered model can be systematically refined by adding a few more random samples, and the whole scheme stacks with any per‑calculation speed‑up.

**Reformulate the calculation around the *difference* density rather than the total density — i.e., use a neutral‑atom / screened‑potential decomposition and self‑consistency only on δρ.**

Write the electron density as a superposition of free‑atom densities plus a small remainder, ρ(r) = Σ_I ρ_I^at(|r−R_I|) + δρ(r), and correspondingly split the potential into (i) the *neutral‑atom potential* of each atom — the sum of its local pseudopotential/nuclear term and the Hartree potential of its own atomic density — plus (ii) the potential generated by δρ, plus (iii) the exchange–correlation term. The decisive point is that the long‑range 1/r tails cancel exactly inside the neutral‑atom potential: each atom's ionic charge is screened by its own electrons, so term (i) is strictly confined to a small sphere around each nucleus, and the notoriously slowly converging Ewald lattice sum, the local‑pseudopotential G→0 divergence and the compensating Hartree divergence all disappear analytically instead of being computed and cancelled numerically at every cycle (this is the SIESTA/OpenMX/FIREBALL "neutral‑atom potential" construction).

The practical speed‑ups follow immediately:

- **Short‑ranged, tabulated matrix elements.** Because the neutral‑atom and nonlocal projector potentials vanish beyond a few Å, all kinetic and potential matrix elements reduce to strictly *two‑ and three‑centre* integrals between confined atomic orbitals, which can be computed once on radial/angular Bessel–Fourier tables at the start of a run and thereafter obtained by spline interpolation and rotation as the atoms move. The Hamiltonian and overlap matrices become genuinely sparse with an O(N) build cost and negligible prefactor, and no four‑centre integrals, no global reciprocal‑space sums and no all‑to‑all communication are needed.

- **A tiny, easy Poisson problem.** Only δρ — a small, smooth, charge‑neutral, rapidly decaying field, typically 1–5 % of the total density and free of the sharp nuclear cusps — has to be put on the real‑space/FFT grid and fed to the Poisson solver. It therefore needs a far coarser mesh (or lower cutoff) for the same accuracy than the full density with its core peaks, and it admits open/multipole boundary conditions naturally.

- **Far fewer, better‑conditioned SCF cycles.** Self‑consistency is imposed on δρ rather than on ρ. Starting from δρ = 0 (Harris–Foulkes level) one is already close to the fixed point, the residual is small and short‑ranged, and mixing acts on a quantity with a much smaller dynamic range, so charge sloshing is suppressed and the iteration count drops. Better still, δρ can be represented compactly — by atomic multipoles, a small auxiliary/"charge‑density" fitting basis, or a few localized functions per atom — so the mixing/DIIS history and the self‑consistency variables number only a handful per atom instead of millions of grid points; forces and stresses likewise split into an analytic short‑ranged part plus a small δρ correction.

- **Trivial reuse between steps.** Since the atomic reference moves rigidly with the nuclei, in geometry optimization and molecular dynamics only the small δρ has to be propagated/extrapolated, making restarts essentially free.

Because this is an exact algebraic rearrangement of the same Kohn–Sham energy functional — the same functional, pseudopotentials, basis and boundary conditions, with accuracy controlled only by the orbital confinement radius and the δρ mesh — the converged answer is unchanged, yet the matrix construction, the electrostatics and the number of SCF iterations each become one to two orders of magnitude cheaper, and the gains multiply with every other acceleration strategy.

**Accelerate DFT by *linearizing the energy dependence of the basis and simplifying the shape of the potential* — i.e., the (TB‑)LMTO / LAPW / ASA family of augmented, minimal‑basis all‑electron methods.**

In augmented‑wave/multiple‑scattering formulations the natural basis functions are the exact partial‑wave solutions φ_ℓ(E,r) of the radial Schrödinger/Dirac equation inside each atomic sphere, but they depend on the energy E, so the secular problem is nonlinear and must be re‑solved at every trial energy. Andersen's linearization removes this entirely: expand the partial wave to first order about a fixed pivot energy E_ν, φ(E,r) ≈ φ(E_ν,r) + (E−E_ν)φ̇(E_ν,r), and match this augmentation smoothly to a smooth envelope function (plane wave → LAPW/APW+lo; Hankel/Neumann function → LMTO/NMTO; numerical orbital → ASW). The Kohn–Sham problem then becomes an *ordinary* generalized eigenvalue problem H c = ε S c that is diagonalized once per k‑point, with all radial integrals (the potential parameters, or "Slater–Koster‑like" matrix elements) tabulated once per SCF cycle. Because each basis function already contains the exact atomic wiggles and the nuclear cusp, the basis is *minimal and all‑electron simultaneously*: roughly 9–25 functions per atom (one per valence ℓm channel, plus a few local orbitals for semicore states) instead of thousands of plane waves — so the matrix dimension, memory, and the O(N³) diagonalization prefactor collapse by two to four orders of magnitude, without pseudopotentials and without any plane‑wave cutoff convergence study.

Further speed comes from *shape approximations to the potential and density*, applied only where they are physically justified: the muffin‑tin approximation (spherically symmetric potential inside spheres, constant in the interstitial) and, more aggressively, the atomic‑sphere approximation (ASA), in which space‑filling overlapping spheres eliminate the interstitial region altogether, so all integrals are one‑dimensional radial quadratures and the Madelung/electrostatic energy reduces to a small multipole sum. Truncating the spherical‑harmonic expansions of ρ and V at low ℓ_max, and screening the envelope functions into short‑ranged tight‑binding form (screened/TB‑LMTO), makes H and S sparse and nearly nearest‑neighbour, which both enables O(N) sparse/Green's‑function solvers and yields directly interpretable, transferable tight‑binding parameters that can be reused for large supercells, alloys and Monte Carlo without further DFT. For extreme conditions the same logic is pushed to its limit in *average‑atom* models: a single spherically symmetric atom in a neutral Wigner–Seitz cell with appropriate boundary conditions replaces the whole many‑atom simulation, giving equations of state, ionization balance, opacities and transport coefficients for warm/hot dense matter in seconds rather than in thousands of CPU‑hours of finite‑temperature Kohn–Sham MD.

The accuracy is systematically recoverable: full‑potential versions (FP‑LAPW/FP‑LMTO) restore the exact non‑spherical potential where needed, additional local orbitals and higher linearization orders (NMTO) widen the energy window over which the linearization is valid, and the pivot energies E_ν can be updated each SCF cycle. Since this changes only the *representation* of the same Kohn–Sham problem — the functional, self‑consistency and physics are untouched — it delivers one to three orders of magnitude in speed and memory (which is why it made all‑electron band‑structure calculations of complex magnetic and f‑electron solids routine), and it stacks with symmetry reduction, iterative eigensolvers, GPU acceleration and every other strategy.

**Exploit physics‑based correlations between quantities so that most numbers are *inferred* rather than computed — i.e., descriptor‑ and linear‑free‑energy‑relation‑based screening.**

In most applied campaigns (heterogeneous/electro‑catalysis, alloy and surface thermochemistry, molecular reaction networks) the expensive part is not one Kohn–Sham solve but the hundreds of intermediates, transition states, coverages and facets that must each be optimized. Empirically, however, these quantities are not independent: adsorption energies of whole families of species (CHx, OHx, NHx) are linearly related to those of one or two simple "descriptor" atoms (C, O, N); activation barriers correlate linearly with reaction energies (Brønsted–Evans–Polanyi relations); binding strengths correlate with cheap electronic descriptors (d‑band centre, generalized coordination number, work function, band filling, electronegativity/ionic radius); and molecular energies obey group‑additivity/bond‑increment and isodesmic relations. So one computes a *small* training set of full DFT points — a couple of descriptors per material, or the reference members of each family — fits the linear (or low‑order) relation once, and then predicts the entire potential‑energy landscape, microkinetic rate, volcano curve or thermochemical table for thousands of candidate materials and species analytically, at zero further DFT cost. Explicit DFT is then spent only on the handful of top candidates flagged by the model, on points where the relation is expected to break (to check and, if needed, extend the fit), and on the descriptor evaluation itself, which is a single small calculation per material.

Because the relations are grounded in bond‑order conservation/Hammond‑type arguments rather than in a black‑box fit, they extrapolate sensibly, need only a few data points per family, come with known scatter that can be quoted as an error bar, and systematically benefit from error cancellation (both sides of the correlation are computed with identical settings and functional). The result is typically a two‑ to four‑order‑of‑magnitude reduction in the number of self‑consistent solves and, crucially, elimination of the most expensive class of calculations altogether (NEB/transition‑state searches, coverage scans, full microkinetic parameterization). Nothing about the underlying Kohn–Sham method is changed — only how many times it is invoked — so this multiplies with every per‑calculation speed‑up.

**Exploit *approximate* symmetry and locality: cache and reuse results for repeated or unchanged atomic environments, instead of recomputing every site and every step from scratch.**

Exact space‑group symmetry is rarely present in the systems that are actually expensive (nanoparticles, amorphous solids, liquids, defect supercells, interfaces, biomolecules), but *near*‑equivalence is everywhere: the interior atoms of a nanoparticle are bulk‑like, most solvent molecules are far from the solute, most repeats of a defect supercell are pristine host, and in an MD or Monte‑Carlo run the overwhelming majority of atoms barely move between steps. One can therefore fingerprint every atom's local environment with a cheap descriptor (SOAP/ACE/coordination‑ and strain‑resolved motif labels), cluster the atoms into a small number of unique environment classes, solve the Kohn–Sham problem (or build the Hamiltonian/overlap blocks, the local density‑matrix block, the atomic multipoles and the local energy/force contributions) **once per class**, and simply copy the result to every site whose fingerprint matches within a tolerance — recomputing explicitly only the genuinely distinct sites (the surface, the defect core, the active site, the solvation shell). Because a system with 10⁴ atoms typically contains only 10–10² distinct environments, the number of quantum‑mechanical solves collapses by one to three orders of magnitude while the cost per solve is unchanged.

The same idea applied along the trajectory gives *incremental, localized* updates: when a few atoms move, only the density matrix, potential and matrix elements inside their nearsightedness/decay radius are dirty, so one recomputes and re‑self‑consistent‑izes only that spatial patch (with a boundary buffer), leaving the rest of the converged solution frozen and reusing the cached blocks — turning each MD/MC step from a global O(N³) solve into a local, constant‑cost update, and making single‑particle‑move Monte Carlo with DFT energies affordable.

The tolerance on the fingerprint match (and the size of the recomputed patch) is a single, systematically tightenable knob: shrinking it recovers the exact all‑distinct calculation, and the cached blocks can be refreshed periodically or spot‑checked against full evaluations to bound the error. Since the functional, basis, pseudopotentials and solver are untouched — only *how often* each piece of the problem is solved changes — this generalizes exact symmetry reduction to disordered systems, gives an honest error estimate, and multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

A route not used before is to **get excited‑state, spectroscopic and level‑alignment information from ordinary ground‑state‑like SCF runs with modified occupations — i.e., ΔSCF / Janak–Slater transition‑state (transition‑potential) methods — instead of from many‑body or linear‑response machinery.**
