Excitation energies, optical gaps, core‑level binding energies and X‑ray absorption/emission spectra are normally obtained from GW/BSE, TDDFT (Casida diagonalization over occupied–virtual pairs), or real‑time propagation — all of which need large numbers of empty states, dense k‑meshes, frequency loops and four‑index kernels, and typically cost 10–1000× a ground‑state calculation. But because the Kohn–Sham eigenvalue is the derivative of the total energy with respect to occupation (Janak's theorem), the same quantities can be extracted by simply *moving fractions of an electron* and re‑converging: (i) **ΔSCF** — converge the neutral system and the system with one electron promoted/removed/added (or a core hole created with a modified pseudopotential/all‑electron core hole) and take the total‑energy difference, which gives excitation, ionization, affinity and core‑level shifts including orbital relaxation and much of the self‑interaction error cancellation, at the price of two SCF runs; (ii) **Slater's transition state / transition potential** — converge *one* calculation with half (or a small fraction) an electron transferred, whereupon the eigenvalue difference already equals the excitation energy to third order in the occupation change, and the full XAS/NEXAFS or valence spectrum follows from the eigenvalues and dipole matrix elements of that single run; (iii) **constrained‑occupation / constrained‑DFT variants** (maximum‑overlap method, Δ‑self‑consistent charge‑transfer states, excited‑state geometry relaxation and forces) which give excited‑state structures, Stokes shifts and diabatic couplings — quantities that are extremely expensive in TDDFT and essentially unavailable in GW/BSE — from the same cheap machinery, with analytic forces.

The cost is therefore one to a few ordinary self‑consistent solves with the *same* functional, basis, pseudopotentials and solver, no empty‑state manifold, no frequency grid and no four‑index kernel — routinely two to three orders of magnitude cheaper than GW/BSE or Casida‑TDDFT — while accuracy is systematically checkable (compare against a small set of high‑level reference points, use fractional‑occupation/piecewise‑linearity or Koopmans‑type conditions, and rely on error cancellation since both states are computed with identical settings). Since only the occupation numbers imposed on the Kohn–Sham problem change, it stacks with every other acceleration strategy.

**Collapse the nested loops of a DFT calculation into a single, "inexactness‑aware" optimization instead of converging each inner loop tightly at every outer step.**

A standard run is three loops deep: an eigensolver (or density‑matrix solver) inside a self‑consistency loop, inside a geometry/cell‑relaxation (or MD/NEB) loop. Enormous effort is wasted converging the innermost problems to 10⁻¹⁰ while the outer iterate is still far from its solution — the electrons are polished to perfection at a geometry that will be thrown away in the next step. Instead, treat the whole thing as *one* coupled nonlinear system F(ψ, ρ, R, h) = 0 (Kohn–Sham stationarity + Hellmann–Feynman/Pulay forces + stress) and solve it with a **Jacobian‑free Newton–Krylov / simultaneous direct‑minimization scheme**: the electronic and ionic (and cell) degrees of freedom are updated together along a common descent/Newton direction, so the orbitals "ride along" with the moving nuclei and full self‑consistency is reached only once, at the final answer, rather than once per ionic step. Where a nested structure is retained, drive the inner tolerances with **inexact‑Newton forcing terms** (Eisenstat–Walker‑type rules): the eigen‑residual, SCF residual and integral/grid thresholds are set adaptively at each outer step to just the level at which the outer convergence rate is not degraded, tightening automatically as the outer residual shrinks, with a globalization (trust region/line search on a merit function, or a Lagrangian/penalty formulation with the idempotency and orthonormality constraints imposed only asymptotically) to guarantee robustness. The same logic applies to a transition‑state or constrained search — impose the constraint and optimize electrons, nuclei and Lagrange multipliers simultaneously rather than re‑converging the electrons for every trial structure — and to path/NEB images, which can be advanced concurrently at loose electronic tolerance and tightened only at the end.

Because the fixed point that is finally reached is exactly the fully converged Born–Oppenheimer solution — the inexactness affects only the *path*, never the answer, and is certified by the final residual — no physical approximation is introduced, yet the total number of Hamiltonian builds, diagonalizations and SCF cycles per optimized structure typically drops by a factor of 3–10 (the savings being largest precisely for the expensive cases: large relaxations, soft/floppy systems, cell optimizations and long reaction paths). It requires no new functional, basis, solver or hardware, and multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**Attack the most expensive *correlation* ingredients — the nonlocal van‑der‑Waals kernels and the RPA/ACFDT‑type correlation energy — by reformulating them as convolutions in imaginary time/frequency with interpolated kernels, so their cost collapses from O(N⁴–N⁶) to O(N log N)–O(N³).**

These "rung‑5" pieces are what make dispersion‑corrected and beyond‑semilocal DFT unaffordable, and each has an exact, purely mathematical restructuring:

1. **Nonlocal vdW functionals (vdW‑DF, VV10).** The correlation energy is a double real‑space integral ½∬ρ(r)Φ(q(r),q(r′),|r−r′|)ρ(r′), formally O(N_grid²) and prohibitive on fine meshes. Using the Román‑Pérez–Soler trick, interpolate Φ on a small fixed grid of ~20 q‑values with cubic splines, so the kernel becomes separable, Φ = Σ_{αβ} p_α(q(r)) Φ_{αβ}(|r−r′|) p_β(q(r′)). Each term is then a plain convolution evaluated by FFT in reciprocal space, and the total cost drops to a few tens of FFTs, i.e. O(N log N) — essentially the price of a GGA — with analytic potentials, forces and stresses obtained by differentiating the same splines.

2. **RPA/ACFDT and MP2‑like correlation.** Instead of summing over unoccupied states and looping over real frequencies, work in **imaginary time and imaginary frequency**: the polarizability χ⁰(r,r′,iτ) = G(r,r′,iτ)G(r′,r,−iτ) is a simple product of Green's functions in real space and imaginary time (the "space–time" method), so the formal N⁶ scaling of a sum‑over‑states/matrix formulation becomes N³ (or lower with sparsity). Move between τ and iω with optimized **minimax/Gauss quadrature grids** that need only 8–20 points for μHartree accuracy, because the integrands are smooth and exponentially decaying on the imaginary axis (unlike the pole‑riddled real axis). Eliminate empty states altogether by computing the response with **Sternheimer/Lanczos linear solves** projected onto the unoccupied space, which removes the slowly convergent virtual‑orbital summation and the associated basis‑extrapolation burden, and compress the resulting pair‑density objects with resolution‑of‑the‑identity/ISDF/Cholesky low‑rank factorizations plus stochastic trace estimation for the log‑determinant.

Because all of this is an exact rewriting of the same energy expression — the accuracy is controlled only by the interpolation grid, the number of quadrature points and the low‑rank threshold, all systematically convergible — one obtains dispersion‑ and RPA‑quality energetics at one to three orders of magnitude lower cost, making self‑consistent nonlocal correlation routine for hundreds of atoms; and since it changes only how the correlation term is evaluated, it multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**Use multi‑fidelity / multilevel Monte‑Carlo estimators with control variates, so that most of the sampling burden in a DFT study is carried by cheap fidelities and full DFT is needed for only a handful of "correction" samples.**

Almost every expensive DFT number is really a *high‑dimensional integral or average* — over the Brillouin zone, over quadrature points, over thermal/configurational disorder (alloy decorations, defect arrangements, MD snapshots, isotopologues), over compositions in a screening campaign, or over input uncertainties in a UQ study. Brute force evaluates that integral with N samples all at the highest fidelity, and the cost is N × (cost of one converged run). Instead, build a *hierarchy of fidelities* of the same quantity — level 0: an analytic/empirical or tight‑binding model, or DFT with a very coarse cutoff, sparse k‑mesh, small cell, cheap functional; level 1: intermediate settings; level L: the fully converged target — and write the desired expectation as a telescoping sum, E[Q_L] = E[Q_0] + Σ_ℓ E[Q_ℓ − Q_{ℓ−1}]. Because successive levels are *strongly correlated*, the difference terms have tiny variance, so they need only a few samples, while the many samples needed to beat down the statistical error are drawn at the almost‑free level 0. The optimal number of samples per level follows analytically from the measured variance‑to‑cost ratio of each level (or, in the control‑variate/ANOVA form, from the correlation coefficient between the cheap and expensive estimators, with the optimal weighting α = −Cov(Q_hi,Q_lo)/Var(Q_lo) determined on the fly from a small pilot run). One can equally use a cheap *surrogate* — a machine‑learned potential, DFTB, or an interpolated response model — purely as a control variate whose exact mean is known or cheaply computable.

The key properties are that (i) the estimator remains **unbiased with respect to the highest‑fidelity DFT**, no matter how crude the lower levels are — a bad low‑fidelity model only reduces the variance saving, it never corrupts the answer; (ii) it delivers a rigorous, reportable statistical **error bar** together with the mean; (iii) samples within a level are completely independent and hence embarrassingly parallel, with the cheap levels able to saturate idle nodes; and (iv) the same machinery applies unchanged to means, variances, sensitivities and rare‑event probabilities, and to adaptive refinement (add levels or samples where the variance‑times‑cost product says it pays). Typical variance reductions of 10²–10⁴ mean that a property which would require thousands of fully converged DFT runs is obtained from tens of them plus a swarm of cheap ones, at the same target accuracy — and since nothing about the functional, basis, solver or hardware changes, it multiplies with every per‑calculation speed‑up.

Accelerate the *solver itself* with machine learning, without ever giving up the exact Kohn–Sham answer: use trained models to supply near-converged starting points and learned iteration operators, so the SCF/eigensolver needs far fewer expensive cycles.

Concretely, train an (equivariant, geometry-conditioned) neural network on a database of previously converged calculations to predict, directly from the atomic positions and species, the *converged* electron density, density matrix, or Kohn–Sham/Fock matrix of a new system — and feed that prediction in as the initial guess instead of a superposition of atomic densities. Because the SCF error is quadratic in the density error, a guess that is 90–99 % correct typically cuts the number of self-consistency cycles by a factor of 2–10 (and removes many convergence failures in metals, magnets and charged/defective systems, where a poor guess causes charge sloshing or convergence to the wrong magnetic/electronic solution). The same idea can be pushed further: (i) learn the *mixing/update rule* itself ("learning to optimize" — a network that maps the history of density residuals to the next density, i.e., a data-driven replacement for Pulay/Broyden mixing, or a learned approximation of the inverse dielectric/Jacobian used as a nonlinear preconditioner); (ii) learn a *preconditioner or initial subspace* for the iterative eigensolver (predicting an approximate occupied subspace or Wannier-like guess to warm-start Davidson/LOBPCG/Chebyshev filtering, and predicting good filter bounds and adaptive thresholds); (iii) learn the *geometry-to-geometry transfer* so that in relaxations, MD and high-throughput scans each new configuration starts essentially converged; and (iv) let the model also predict good numerical settings (cutoff, k-mesh, smearing, U values, mixing parameters) so no run is over- or under-converged.

The crucial point is that the network only supplies the *starting point and the search direction*: the quantity finally driven to zero is the true Kohn–Sham residual, evaluated with the same functional, basis and pseudopotentials, so the converged energy, density and forces are numerically identical to a conventional run no matter how poor the prediction — a bad model merely saves fewer iterations, it can never introduce a wrong answer, and the achieved residual is a built-in, verifiable error check. The models are cheap to evaluate (milliseconds), are trained once on data that a group already generates as a by-product of its normal calculations, improve continuously as more runs are archived (and can be fine-tuned per system class or made into a transferable "foundation model" for initial guesses), and, since they change only *how many* iterations are taken rather than the physics, the resulting 3–10× wall-clock reduction multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**Exploit the block‑tridiagonal ("principal‑layer") structure that large, elongated or layered systems naturally have, and solve them by recursive Green's‑function / decimation algorithms instead of by global diagonalization or full matrix inversion.**

Nanowires, nanotubes, molecular junctions, stacked 2‑D heterostructures, superlattices, interfaces, slabs, long polymers/DNA and any system that is long in one direction all have Hamiltonians and overlap matrices that, in a localized basis (or with real‑space stencils/domain decomposition), couple only *neighbouring* slices of the structure. Ordering the basis functions layer by layer makes H and S **block‑tridiagonal**, and this structure can be used exactly:

- **Recursive Green's function / sweep algorithms.** The needed blocks of G(E) = (ES − H)⁻¹ — and hence the density matrix, local DOS, charge density, forces and transmission — are obtained by a forward and backward recursion over layers using only small block inversions of size (basis per layer). Because one never forms or inverts the full matrix, the cost is O(N_layers × n_layer³) instead of O(N³): **linear in the length of the device**, with an embarrassingly parallel loop over energies (and, on a complex contour or with Matsubara poles, over only a few tens of them). The same idea is the "selected inversion" principle: compute only the sparse blocks of the inverse that the density actually requires, never the dense inverse.
- **Decimation / renormalization (Lopez‑Sancho) for semi‑infinite leads and thick bulk regions.** Repeatedly eliminating alternate layers doubles the effective layer thickness each step, so a *semi‑infinite* electrode, substrate or bulk reservoir is summed to convergence in ~log₂ steps and enters the calculation as a small **self‑energy** matrix on the boundary of the scattering/active region. This removes the need for long supercells with thick "bulk‑like" padding and thick vacuum, gives true open boundary conditions (correct level broadening, no artificial quantization from periodic images, no fictitious charging of a finite slab), and lets one apply a bias or a gate potential self‑consistently (NEGF+DFT) — something a periodic supercell cannot do at all.
- **Practical consequences.** A junction that would need a 500–1000‑atom supercell to isolate the electrodes is reduced to a ~100‑atom central region plus tabulated lead self‑energies computed once; scaling in the transport direction becomes linear rather than cubic; memory drops from O(N²) to O(N·n_layer); and the layer recursions, energy points and k‖ points are all independent, so parallel efficiency is nearly perfect and maps well onto GPUs (many small dense block operations).

Accuracy is controlled by transparent, convergible knobs only — the layer/principal‑block size (chosen so that coupling beyond nearest layers is below threshold), the number of contour/energy points, and the decimation tolerance — while the functional, basis, pseudopotentials and self‑consistency are untouched. It is therefore an exact reorganization of the same Kohn–Sham problem that typically buys one to three orders of magnitude for quasi‑1‑D, layered, interface and transport problems, and it multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**Get many properties out of *one* DFT run by using fluctuation/correlation (linear‑response) formulas instead of performing a separate calculation for every perturbation.**

A large share of DFT cost in practice comes from the fact that each material property is obtained from its own dedicated set of runs: elastic constants from a grid of strained cells, dielectric/Born charges from finite‑field or field‑perturbed runs, thermal expansion from many volumes, IR/Raman spectra from displaced geometries plus polarizability calculations, thermal conductivity or diffusion from many separate non‑equilibrium simulations, heat capacity from finite‑difference of energies. But statistical mechanics says all of these are equilibrium *fluctuations* of quantities that a single ab‑initio molecular‑dynamics trajectory already produces as a by‑product. Thus, from **one** well‑equilibrated AIMD run at the target (T, P) one can extract simultaneously: elastic and compliance tensors from the strain–strain (or stress–stress, Parrinello–Rahman) fluctuations and the Born–Huang stress‑fluctuation formula; the heat capacity and thermal‑expansion coefficient from energy and energy–volume fluctuations; the static dielectric constant, Born effective charges and Raman/IR spectra from the autocorrelation functions of the Berry‑phase polarization and of the polarizability/dipole; thermal conductivity, viscosity, ionic conductivity and diffusion coefficients from Green–Kubo integrals of the heat‑flux, stress and current autocorrelations (or from the mean‑square displacement); phonon dispersions and their *anharmonic, temperature‑renormalized* linewidths from the velocity autocorrelation/dynamical‑structure factor or from fitting the fluctuating forces; free‑energy derivatives and defect/solute chemical potentials from the fluctuation of the relevant order parameters; and even the anharmonic force constants from the correlations of displacements and forces already stored at every step.

Because the same converged Kohn–Sham forces, stresses and polarizations are reused for all of these, the cost of the whole property suite is essentially the cost of one trajectory, replacing what would otherwise be dozens to hundreds of independent frozen‑phonon, finite‑strain, finite‑field or non‑equilibrium calculations — routinely one to two orders of magnitude fewer self‑consistent solves. It also automatically includes finite‑temperature anharmonic and entropic effects that a set of static 0 K calculations would miss, so the accuracy is often *better* than the brute‑force alternative; the only extra requirement is that the trajectory be long enough for the correlation functions to decay (a controllable, measurable statistical error bar, improvable by block averaging, multiple independent replicas run in parallel, or by fitting the tails to known analytic forms). Since it changes only *what one asks of an existing simulation* — not the functional, basis, pseudopotentials or solver — it stacks with every per‑calculation speed‑up.

Use **shifted, blocked and recycled Krylov‑subspace solvers**, so that the many linear systems a DFT calculation actually requires are solved *together* instead of one at a time.

Almost every expensive inner step of a modern Kohn–Sham code reduces to solving (H − zS)x = b for many different shifts z and many right‑hand sides b: Green's functions/resolvents at dozens of real or complex contour energies, Sternheimer/coupled‑perturbed response equations for every perturbation direction (each atomic displacement, strain component, electric field, frequency), the Poisson/Dyson solves, and the correction equations inside Davidson/Jacobi–Davidson eigensolvers. The key algebraic fact is that the Krylov space K_m(H, b) = span{b, Hb, H²b, …} is *invariant under shifts*: one single Krylov basis, built with one set of expensive Hamiltonian–vector products, yields the solution for **all** energies/frequencies simultaneously (shifted CG/GMRES/BiCG, shifted COCG, Lanczos continued‑fraction), so the cost of a whole spectrum or a whole complex‑energy contour is essentially that of one solve rather than one solve per point. Similarly, **block** Krylov methods treat all right‑hand sides (all bands, all perturbation directions, all k‑points in a group) as one tall matrix, converting memory‑bound BLAS‑2 mat‑vecs into BLAS‑3 GEMMs that run at near peak on GPUs while also converging in fewer iterations because the block space is richer; and **recycled/augmented Krylov** methods (GCRO‑DR, seed/deflated Krylov) keep the few dominant invariant‑subspace vectors from the previous solve and prepend them to the next one, so successive SCF cycles, successive MD/geometry steps, successive λ or U values, and successive perturbations each start with most of the slowly converging low‑frequency error already deflated — typically cutting iteration counts by 2–10× after the first solve.

Because this is exact linear algebra on the same Hamiltonian, with the only knob being the residual tolerance (which can be set loosely early and tightened near convergence), the converged density, energies, forces and response functions are numerically identical to those from independent solves; what disappears is the redundant re‑generation of nearly the same Krylov space hundreds of times. In practice this gives one to two orders of magnitude for spectra, transport, DFPT/response and contour‑integral (Green's‑function, finite‑temperature) calculations, improves parallel and GPU efficiency through blocking, and stacks with every other acceleration strategy.

**Trade exact forces for statistically corrected noisy forces in ab‑initio molecular dynamics: deliberately under‑converge (or entirely skip) the self‑consistency at each step and compensate the resulting noise/drift with a modified Langevin thermostat.**

In conventional Born–Oppenheimer MD one pays for 10–30 tightly converged SCF cycles per time step, because any residual electronic error shows up as a systematic, history‑dependent force error that heats or cools the system and destroys energy conservation. But this is over‑kill: only the *statistical* correctness of the sampled ensemble matters, not the exactness of each individual force. So one can (i) stop the SCF after a single (or very few) iteration(s) — or propagate the density/wavefunctions with an extended‑Lagrangian/predictor scheme and take just one corrector step — and (ii) treat the residual force error as a small stochastic perturbation, absorbing it in a Langevin equation of motion mv̈ = F_approx − γ_D v + ξ(t), where the intrinsic friction γ_D and the added white noise are tuned (from the measured variance of the force error, or self‑consistently by requiring the target temperature) so that the fluctuation–dissipation theorem is restored. The systematic drift is thereby cancelled and the trajectory samples the *correct* canonical distribution of the fully converged Born–Oppenheimer potential, even though no step is ever fully converged — this is the essence of "second‑generation Car–Parrinello"/Langevin‑corrected AIMD, and the same logic legitimizes other cheap sources of controlled noise (loose eigensolver tolerances, coarse grids, stochastic sampling of grid/k‑points, reduced precision).

Because static, structural and thermodynamic averages, radial distribution functions, free energies and diffusion coefficients depend only on the sampled distribution — and because the residual error is verifiable (compare a few snapshots against fully converged forces, monitor the force‑error variance, and shrink it by adding one more iteration) — accuracy is preserved with a single tunable knob, while the cost per MD step drops by roughly the number of SCF cycles avoided, typically an order of magnitude, and the time step and thermostat can be chosen to decorrelate the trajectory faster as well. Since the functional, basis, pseudopotentials and solver are untouched, this multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

Exploit **point‑group (site) symmetry to block‑diagonalize the Kohn–Sham matrices themselves**, not just to reduce the k‑point set. For any molecule, cluster, nanoparticle, adsorbate complex, defect supercell or crystal with a nontrivial little group at a given k, one can construct symmetry‑adapted linear combinations (SALCs) of the basis functions by applying the irreducible‑representation projection operators of the group. In that basis H and S are exactly block diagonal, one block per irrep (with degenerate partners identical, so only one partner needs solving). A single dense eigenproblem of dimension n therefore splits into ~n_irr independent problems of dimension ≈ n/g (g = order of the group): since diagonalization scales as n³, the work drops roughly by a factor g² (often 10–1000× for high‑symmetry systems such as fullerenes, icosahedral or octahedral clusters, and perovskite/zinc‑blende cells), memory drops by ~g, and the blocks are completely independent, so they can be distributed over separate nodes/GPUs with no communication and no global orthogonalization across blocks (states in different irreps are automatically orthogonal). The same group operations remove redundant work everywhere else in the cycle: only symmetry‑inequivalent atom pairs, shell pairs and integrals are computed and the rest are generated by rotation; the exchange–correlation quadrature and Poisson solve are done only over the irreducible wedge of the grid and the result symmetrized; only symmetry‑distinct displacements, strains, spin configurations and adsorption sites are ever calculated; and structure relaxations are carried out in symmetry‑adapted (irrep‑resolved) coordinates, which both shrinks the number of free parameters and prevents the optimizer from wandering into lower‑symmetry configurations. As a bonus, the irrep labels come out for free, letting one target only the symmetry sectors of physical interest (e.g., the totally symmetric ground state, or specific optically allowed channels) and follow states unambiguously along a path.

Because group theory is exact for the given geometry, the converged energies, densities and forces are numerically identical to a symmetry‑unaware calculation (with the caveat that one must verify the symmetric solution is the true ground state, e.g. by a final symmetry‑broken check for Jahn–Teller or magnetic instabilities), and the speed‑up multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**Treat a new system as a *low‑rank, localized perturbation of an already‑solved reference system* and update the solution algebraically (Dyson/Woodbury‑type updates) instead of running a new self‑consistent calculation.**

Most expensive campaigns consist of many systems that differ from a common parent only locally: a vacancy, interstitial, dopant or substitutional impurity in a bulk crystal; an adsorbate or step on a clean surface; a single mutated side chain or ligand; one displaced atom in an MD/Monte‑Carlo move; a single strained bond. Solving each of these as an independent, large supercell from scratch throws away the fact that the change in the Hamiltonian, ΔH = H − H₀, is confined to a handful of atoms and therefore has a *rank of only a few tens of basis functions*, while the pristine host H₀ has already been converged once (or can be taken from a database, in its small primitive cell).

Exploit that directly: keep the reference Green's function / density matrix / occupied subspace of the host, and obtain the perturbed one from the exact Dyson equation G = G₀ + G₀ ΔΣ G (equivalently, the Woodbury–Sherman–Morrison low‑rank inverse update, or a Löwdin/Feshbach downfolding onto the perturbed block). Because ΔH is sparse and low rank, this requires only inverting a small matrix of the size of the perturbed region plus a few reference blocks — cost independent of the size of the surrounding host — and it needs to be iterated to self‑consistency only inside the perturbation's screening/nearsightedness radius, with the far field held at its converged bulk values (plus analytic multipole/elastic matching to remove image and finite‑size errors). Total energies follow from Lloyd's‑formula/trace differences, forces from the perturbed block, and the same low‑rank machinery gives cheap *derivative* information for a whole family of related perturbations at once. Combinatorial studies (dopant series, alloy configurations, adsorbate coverages, defect charge states) then reduce to one host calculation plus one small update per candidate.

Accuracy is controlled by two transparent knobs — the size of the explicitly perturbed/re‑self‑consistent region and the rank/threshold of ΔH — and can be driven back to the exact supercell answer by enlarging them, or corrected by a single full SCF step on the updated density. Since the functional, basis, pseudopotentials and solver are untouched, this typically removes one to three orders of magnitude of redundant work in defect, alloy, catalysis and mutation studies, and it multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**A route not used before: curve the space instead of refining it — solve the Kohn–Sham equations in an adaptive curvilinear coordinate system.**

The cost of a plane‑wave/FFT calculation is set almost entirely by the number of Fourier components (or grid points), and that number is dictated by the *worst* place in the cell — the sharp cusp/oscillation region within ~0.3 Å of each nucleus (or of a hard first‑row/3d pseudopotential core). Everywhere else — in the bonds, the interstitial region and especially in vacuum — the orbitals are smooth and the same fine resolution is pure waste, yet a uniform Cartesian mesh forces you to pay for it over the whole volume.

The fix is to introduce a smooth, invertible coordinate map **r = 𝗿(u)** (with metric tensor g_ij = ∂r/∂u_i·∂r/∂u_j and Jacobian J) that *stretches* the region near each nucleus and *compresses* the smooth regions, and then to write the entire Kohn–Sham problem in the u‑coordinates: the kinetic operator becomes the Laplace–Beltrami operator (1/√g)∂_i(√g g^{ij}∂_j), the Hartree term a Poisson equation in the curved metric, the density and XC integrals acquire the Jacobian weight, and the orbitals are expanded in *ordinary plane waves of the curvilinear variable u*. Crucially, the mesh in u remains perfectly uniform and periodic, so all the machinery that makes plane‑wave DFT fast is preserved unchanged — O(N log N) FFTs, diagonal kinetic and Hartree operators in reciprocal space, pointwise XC evaluation, and the standard iterative eigensolvers — while the *effective* real‑space resolution is now concentrated where the physics is hard. The map itself is built as a superposition of smooth, spherically symmetric "bumps" centred on the atoms (adaptive‑coordinate/Gygi‑type schemes, or a Riemannian metric optimized variationally together with the orbitals), so it moves rigidly with the nuclei during relaxation or MD, which means there are no basis‑set (Pulay) forces from the deformation — only extra, analytic metric terms in the forces and stress.

The payoff: for a given accuracy the required cutoff/grid‑point count typically drops by factors of a few to an order of magnitude (the FFT box volume, memory, and the N_band²·N_grid orthogonalization/subspace work all shrink proportionally), which is exactly what makes hard elements (O, N, F, 3d transition metals) and even all‑electron/semicore treatments affordable in a plane‑wave code without resorting to ultrasoft/PAW softening; large regions of vacuum in slabs, wires and molecules can also be compressed to a handful of grid points instead of thousands. Accuracy is controlled by two transparent, systematically convergible knobs — the curvilinear cutoff and the strength/smoothness of the deformation — and in the limit of the identity map one recovers the standard calculation exactly. Since only the *coordinate representation* of the same Kohn–Sham functional changes (same functional, same pseudopotentials, same boundary conditions, same solver), no physical approximation is introduced, and the gain multiplies with every other acceleration strategy (GPU kernels, symmetry, iterative/Chebyshev eigensolvers, linear‑scaling density‑matrix methods).

**Exploit the local force theorem plus frozen‑potential/rigid‑band evaluation: converge the SCF once for a reference configuration, and obtain the energetics of many related configurations from a single *non‑self‑consistent* eigenvalue sum.**

Because the Kohn–Sham total energy is variational in the density, a small change of the system (a spin rotation, a magnetic ordering, a small atomic displacement or stacking fault, a change in doping, temperature or chemical potential) changes the Hartree and exchange–correlation "double‑counting" terms only at *second* order in δρ, while the first‑order change of the total energy is exactly the change in the sum of occupied one‑particle eigenvalues (band energy) evaluated with the **frozen** self‑consistent potential of the reference. So one pays for one converged SCF and then, for each new configuration, only for one cheap diagonalization — or, in a Green's‑function formulation, just a Lloyd's‑formula/integrated‑DOS trace on a complex contour, which is cheaper still.

Concretely this replaces whole families of expensive calculations: magnetic exchange couplings J_ij, spin‑spiral energies, Curie temperatures and magnetocrystalline anisotropy from infinitesimal spin rotations of one collinear reference (the Liechtenstein "magnetic force theorem") instead of hundreds of separately converged noncollinear supercells; surface, interface, stacking‑fault and adsorption energy differences from frozen‑potential band‑energy differences; and, in the rigid‑band spirit, all doping‑, carrier‑concentration‑ and temperature‑dependent properties (Fermi level, carrier density, Seebeck coefficient, electrical/thermal conductivity, Hall coefficient, optical response, alloy trends within a virtual‑crystal or frozen‑potential picture) obtained by simply moving the chemical potential and re‑occupying the *same* converged band structure — e.g. Boltzmann‑transport post‑processing of one SCF run instead of one charged/doped supercell calculation per composition.

The accuracy is controlled and checkable: the neglected term is quadratic in the density response, so it is small precisely for the "soft," weakly screened perturbations to which the method is applied, and it can be validated (or corrected) by re‑converging a handful of representative configurations fully self‑consistently, or by adding the first self‑consistency correction perturbatively. Since the functional, basis, pseudopotentials and solver are untouched — only *how many times self‑consistency must be reached* changes — this typically eliminates one to three orders of magnitude of redundant SCF work in magnetism, thermoelectrics, alloy and defect‑level studies, and it multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**Never run a calculation to completion when its outcome can already be *bounded* — i.e., use certified bounds, anytime evaluation and bandit-style resource allocation to terminate DFT runs early.**

Most DFT campaigns (screening candidate structures/compositions, ranking polymorphs, adsorption sites, magnetic or spin states, reaction pathways) only need an *inequality* — "is this candidate better than the current best?" — yet every candidate is run to full convergence at full accuracy, so almost all of the compute is spent proving in exquisite detail that a loser is a loser. Instead, exploit the fact that DFT supplies rigorous or near‑rigorous bounds *while it is still running*:

- The Kohn–Sham energy is **variational**, so every intermediate (non‑converged) density/orbital set already gives an upper bound to the converged total energy, while the Harris–Foulkes functional evaluated on the same iterate gives a complementary estimate that brackets it from the other side; the gap between the two, together with the SCF/eigen‑residual norms and Temple–Kato/Weinstein-type residual bounds on the eigenvalues, yields a computable interval [E⁻, E⁺] that shrinks monotonically with iteration count.
- Therefore, as soon as E⁻ of a candidate exceeds E⁺ of the current best by more than the tolerance of the decision (including a margin for the systematic error that cancels between the two, since both are run with identical settings), the run can be **killed on the spot** — typically after 2–5 SCF cycles on a coarse grid/k‑mesh instead of 30–50 tight ones, and often before geometry relaxation has even finished. The same logic applies to intermediate stages: coarse settings give a bound that prunes the candidate before the expensive fine stage is ever entered, giving a **branch‑and‑bound** search over structure/composition space rather than exhaustive enumeration.
- Allocate the remaining budget with **anytime / racing algorithms** (successive halving, Hyperband, upper‑confidence‑bound bandits): start *all* candidates at very cheap fidelity, keep only the top fraction whose bounds still overlap the leader, promote them to the next fidelity level, and repeat. Compute is then spent almost entirely on the few genuinely competitive candidates, and the wall‑clock cost grows like the log of the candidate count rather than linearly.
- The same "stop when the question is answered" criterion applies inside a single job: halt a relaxation once the forces are below the level that could change the ranking, halt an MD/free‑energy run once the confidence interval on the observable is narrower than the decision threshold (sequential hypothesis testing / SPRT on the running average), and abort obviously pathological runs (diverging mixing, wrong magnetic branch, exploded geometry) from early diagnostics instead of letting them consume their full wall‑time allocation.

Because the criterion is a *bound* on the same Kohn–Sham quantity — the functional, basis, pseudopotentials and solver are untouched, and any candidate that survives is eventually converged exactly as usual — the final scientific conclusion is provably identical to the exhaustive study, but with a certified error/decision guarantee attached. In practice, since typically fewer than 1 % of screened candidates matter and losers can be discarded after a small fraction of their full cost, this removes one to three orders of magnitude of wasted self‑consistent solves, requires only bookkeeping of bounds and a scheduler, and multiplies with every per‑calculation speed‑up.

**Attack the *multi‑parameter* convergence problem with a sparse‑grid / combination‑technique (multi‑index) strategy, instead of converging every numerical knob simultaneously in one expensive "fully converged" run.**

A production DFT result depends on several discretization parameters at once — plane‑wave cutoff (or grid spacing / basis cardinality), k‑mesh density, supercell size, smearing width, XC quadrature level, augmentation/projector accuracy, SCF tolerance. Standard practice converges each one separately and then runs a single calculation that is simultaneously fine in *all* of them, whose cost is the **tensor product** of the individual refinement levels (doubling the resolution in four independent knobs can mean a 10²–10⁴× more expensive job). But the error surface is, to leading order, *additive*: E(ℓ₁,…,ℓ_d) ≈ E_∞ + Σ_i a_i·h_i^{p_i} + (small mixed terms), i.e. the mixed derivatives with respect to two different knobs are tiny, because the cutoff error and the k‑sampling error (say) are almost independent of one another.

That structure is exactly what sparse grids exploit. Run only the *anisotropic* combinations that lie near the diagonal of the parameter lattice — fine cutoff with coarse k‑mesh, coarse cutoff with fine k‑mesh, fine cell with coarse everything, etc. — each of which is cheap, and form the target quantity as a signed linear combination (the Smolyak/combination‑technique weights, equivalently a multi‑dimensional Richardson/Archimedes‑like telescoping of first differences Δ₁Δ₂…). The mixed low‑order error terms cancel identically in the combination, so the result reproduces the fully refined tensor‑product calculation to within the (negligible) mixed remainder, while the cost collapses from O(N^d) to roughly O(N·log^{d−1}N) — typically one to two orders of magnitude fewer core‑hours for the same accuracy. Which indices to include can be chosen *adaptively and greedily*: measure the actual benefit‑to‑cost ratio of each candidate refinement direction from the first‑difference magnitudes already computed, and spend the next calculation only where the error‑reduction per CPU‑hour is largest (dimension‑adaptive sparse grids / multi‑index estimators). The same machinery extends beyond discretization knobs to any product space the study sweeps — volume × temperature × composition × field × trajectory length — and the individual runs are completely independent, hence embarrassingly parallel and ideal for filling idle nodes.

The scheme is self‑diagnosing: the size of the discarded mixed differences is *computed*, not assumed, so it doubles as a rigorous, reportable error bar, and adding one more index systematically drives it to zero. Because nothing about the Hamiltonian, functional, pseudopotentials, basis type or solver changes — only *which* combinations of numerical settings are ever executed — no physical approximation is introduced, and the savings multiply with every other acceleration strategy.

**Split the Kohn–Sham spectrum in *energy* and treat only the low‑lying part quantum‑mechanically, handing the high‑energy tail to a semiclassical (Thomas–Fermi/Wigner–Kirkwood) description.**

The number of orbitals that must be computed and orthogonalized is what kills DFT at finite/high electronic temperature (warm dense matter, shock physics, plasmas, laser‑heated matter, stellar/planetary interiors): the number of partially occupied bands grows roughly as T^{3/2}, so a calculation that needs 100 bands at 300 K needs 10⁴–10⁵ bands at tens of eV, and the O(N_band²N_grid) orthogonalization and O(N_band³) subspace work explode. But the physics of those high‑lying states is *nearly free‑electron*: above some cutoff energy E_c their wavefunctions are smooth, nodal‑dense plane‑wave‑like functions whose contribution to the density, entropy, pressure and free energy is given to excellent (and systematically improvable) accuracy by the semiclassical expansion of the Fermi operator — the Thomas–Fermi term plus ħ²‑order Wigner–Kirkwood/von Weizsäcker gradient corrections evaluated pointwise from the local potential, exactly the orbital‑free machinery that becomes *asymptotically exact* in the high‑energy limit.

So: diagonalize only the states with ε < E_c (occupied plus a modest thermal buffer) with the usual iterative solver, and add the tail contribution ρ_tail(r), S_tail, E_tail analytically from the local effective potential v_eff(r) and the chemical potential, with a smooth switching/matching function at E_c so that density, forces and stresses stay continuous and variational. The same idea applies at the *bottom* of the spectrum — tightly bound core/semicore states can be treated by frozen‑core or single‑site radial atomic solutions rather than by the global eigensolver — and it dovetails with spectral‑quadrature/Chebyshev and stochastic methods, where the semiclassical tail removes precisely the part of the spectrum that requires the highest polynomial degree or the most random vectors.

Accuracy is controlled by one transparent, convergible knob, E_c (push it up and the exact Kohn–Sham result is recovered; the error can be measured by raising it on a few snapshots), and no change is made to the functional, pseudopotentials, basis or boundary conditions. In practice this caps the band count at its low‑temperature value and makes the cost essentially *temperature‑independent*, giving one to three orders of magnitude for finite‑temperature simulations that are otherwise intractable — and it multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**Reformulate the electronic‑structure problem as a single constrained *optimization* on a matrix manifold and solve it with globally convergent second‑order methods, instead of iterating the SCF fixed point with diagonalization.**

Rather than repeatedly building H, diagonalizing it, and mixing densities — a fixed‑point iteration that has no convergence guarantee and that stagnates or oscillates ("charge sloshing", magnetic/metastable branch flipping) exactly in the expensive cases (metals, large or inhomogeneous cells, magnets, charged defects) — write the Kohn–Sham problem as the direct minimization of E[C] (or of the Mermin free energy with ensemble occupations) over the Grassmann/Stiefel manifold of orthonormal orbital coefficients, or equivalently over idempotent density matrices. Then apply modern Riemannian optimization: analytic gradients on the manifold, a **trust‑region or line‑search Newton/quasi‑Newton step** (Hessian‑vector products supplied matrix‑free, i.e. as a single extra Hamiltonian application — the same operator as the coupled‑perturbed/Sternheimer response), with the orthonormality constraint handled by curvilinear retractions or by an orthogonalization‑free "orbital‑transformation"/exponential parameterization so no Löwdin/Cholesky orthogonalization or dense diagonalization is ever performed, plus limited‑memory Riemannian BFGS updates and preconditioning by the (approximate) inverse kinetic‑plus‑dielectric operator.

The payoff is qualitative rather than incremental: (i) every step is guaranteed to *decrease* the energy, so the method cannot diverge and no empirical mixing parameters, damping factors or restart babysitting are needed — the failures that cost real users days of wall time simply disappear; (ii) near the solution convergence is quadratic, so the number of expensive Hamiltonian builds drops from tens to a handful; (iii) the dominant kernels become tall–skinny GEMMs and Hamiltonian–vector products, which are BLAS‑3, communication‑light and GPU‑friendly, and cost O(N·N_b²) with sparse/localized orbitals rather than O(N³) diagonalization; (iv) the same manifold machinery handles fractional occupations, constraints (constrained DFT, fixed spin/charge), and — crucially — allows the previous solution to be *recycled* as a warm start along a geometry relaxation, MD trajectory or parameter sweep, since the optimizer accepts any nearby point and simply descends from it; (v) because the target is a genuine objective function, one can attach a trust‑region radius and inexact‑step tolerances that automatically loosen far from the minimum and tighten near it.

Since the stationary point reached is exactly the Kohn–Sham/Mermin minimum — same functional, basis, pseudopotentials and boundary conditions, with the final gradient norm serving as a certified, reportable error — no physical approximation is introduced; only the *path* to the solution changes. In practice this yields factors of ~3–10 in Hamiltonian builds for well‑behaved systems and the difference between "converges" and "does not converge" for hard ones, and it multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

Recast the Kohn–Sham eigenvalue problem in **integral (Green's‑function) form and solve it in an adaptive multiwavelet multiresolution basis with a user‑specified precision** — the MADNESS/MRChem strategy.

Instead of iterating the differential operator (−½∇² + v_eff)ψ = εψ — whose spectrum spans many orders of magnitude, which is what makes the eigensolver ill‑conditioned, forces preconditioners, and demands a uniformly fine grid everywhere — rewrite each orbital equation using the bound‑state Helmholtz kernel: ψᵢ = −2 Ĝ_{μᵢ} [v_eff ψᵢ], with μᵢ = √(−2εᵢ) and Ĝ_μ = (−∇² + μ²)⁻¹. The differential operator disappears; what remains is a *smoothing* convolution, so the iteration is intrinsically well conditioned, needs no preconditioner or level shifting, and converges in a handful of self‑consistent updates (accelerated by KAIN/Anderson on the orbitals themselves).

The convolution is made cheap by two devices: (i) the kernel is expanded as a **short sum of separable Gaussians** (Beylkin‑type sinc quadrature), so a 3‑D convolution becomes a few 1‑D applications; and (ii) all functions live in an **adaptive multiwavelet (discontinuous Legendre/wavelet) tree**, refined locally only where the wavelet coefficients exceed a threshold ε — deep near the nuclear cusps, extremely coarse in bonding regions and vacuum, and refined *independently for every orbital and every operator*, since core, valence and diffuse states need very different resolutions. Because the multiwavelet basis is orthonormal and has vanishing moments, both the functions and the non‑standard form of the operators are provably sparse, so each application is O(N) with rigorous, a‑priori error control.

The practical payoff: ε is a single knob that gives a *guaranteed* error bound on the density, energy and forces (no basis‑set incompleteness, no BSSE, no cutoff/grid convergence studies, no Pulay forces since the basis is adaptive and complete); arbitrary boundary conditions (isolated, charged, periodic) come free from the choice of kernel; all‑electron calculations are affordable because refinement is local to the cusps rather than global; and the same separated‑kernel machinery delivers the Poisson solve (1/r kernel) and exact exchange at the same cost structure. It is an exact reformulation of the same Kohn–Sham problem, so it introduces no new physical approximation, and it stacks with GPU, symmetry, pseudopotential and linear‑scaling strategies.

**Flip the self‑consistency problem into its dual — optimize the *effective potential* in a compact auxiliary basis instead of iterating the density.**

Standard SCF searches for a fixed point in the space of the density (millions of grid points / a full density matrix), a nonlinear map with no descent property, which is why it stalls, sloshes, or diverges for metals, magnets and large inhomogeneous cells. But by Hohenberg–Kohn/Lieb duality the Kohn–Sham ground state is equivalently the stationary point of a *concave* functional of the local effective potential v(r) (the Legendre transform of the universal functional; the same structure that underlies optimized‑effective‑potential and Wu–Yang‑type inversion algorithms). Working in this dual, potential space has three concrete payoffs:

1. **Drastically fewer unknowns.** The self‑consistent potential is smooth and short‑ranged, so it can be expanded in a small auxiliary basis — a few tens of atom‑centred Gaussians/multipoles per atom, or a truncated set of long‑wavelength Fourier components — typically 10²–10³ coefficients for a system whose density needs 10⁶–10⁸ grid values. The fixed‑point/Newton problem is then small enough that the *exact* Jacobian (the static dielectric/response matrix, obtained once by cheap Sternheimer solves in that same small basis) can be built and inverted explicitly, giving true quadratic Newton convergence instead of the empirical Pulay/Broyden guesswork.

2. **Guaranteed, monotone convergence.** Because the dual objective is concave (and the primal energy convex‑like in the corresponding variable), one can wrap the iteration in a trust‑region/line‑search framework (trust‑region SCF, potential mixing with a merit function) in which every step provably improves the objective, so convergence no longer depends on hand‑tuned mixing parameters and hard cases stop failing outright — often the difference between a job that converges in 8 steps and one that never converges at all.

3. **Better conditioning and reuse.** Long‑wavelength charge sloshing appears in the potential representation as a single, well‑characterized soft mode that the small explicit Jacobian handles exactly (no Kerker fudge factor); and because the potential coefficients are few, smooth, and transferable, they can be stored, extrapolated along geometry/MD/composition paths, or regressed against structure, so each new calculation starts essentially self‑consistent.

The residual finally driven to zero is the exact Kohn–Sham stationarity condition, evaluated with the same functional, basis and pseudopotentials — the auxiliary expansion controls only the *search directions* (and can be enlarged, or the final step taken in the full space, to remove any bias) — so the converged energy, density and forces are unchanged while the number of expensive Hamiltonian builds/diagonalizations typically drops by a factor of several to an order of magnitude, and the gain multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**Replace the grid/basis itself with a compact, self‑adapting neural‑network parameterization of the Kohn–Sham problem and solve it by direct variational (gradient‑based) energy minimization.** Instead of expanding the orbitals/density in millions of plane waves or grid points, represent them by a small neural network (or a network‑generated set of basis functions/orbital coefficients) whose inputs are the spatial coordinate and the atomic environment: ψ_i(r) = NN_θ(r; {R_I, Z_I}), with the ansatz built to satisfy the required symmetries (rotational/translational equivariance, periodicity through Fourier features, nuclear‑cusp factors, orthonormality imposed by an explicit Gram–Schmidt/Cholesky layer or a penalty). The total energy functional is then evaluated by Monte‑Carlo or quadrature sampling of the integrals and minimized directly with respect to the network weights θ using stochastic gradients (Adam, natural‑gradient/KFAC), with automatic differentiation supplying all derivatives — so the self‑consistency loop, the dense diagonalization and the fixed uniform mesh all disappear, replaced by one smooth optimization.

The advantages are (i) *adaptivity for free*: the network concentrates its representational capacity near nuclei, bonds and interfaces and spends essentially nothing on vacuum, so a few 10⁴–10⁵ parameters can replace 10⁷–10⁹ grid values, with no cutoff‑convergence study, no basis‑set superposition error and no Pulay forces; (ii) *mesh‑free and boundary‑condition‑free*: isolated, charged, low‑dimensional or aperiodic systems need no supercell padding; (iii) *hardware fit*: everything is dense tensor algebra and sampling, which runs at near peak on GPUs/TPUs and batches trivially over many systems, k‑points or geometries; and, most importantly, (iv) *amortization by pretraining/transfer*: a network trained on one geometry (or on a family of molecules/materials) already encodes the solution manifold, so for a new configuration only a few fine‑tuning steps are needed rather than a full solve — the cost of the *n*-th calculation in a relaxation, MD trajectory or screening campaign falls far below the cost of the first, and in the limit the network becomes a differentiable "solution emulator" whose predictions can still be certified.

Accuracy remains controllable and verifiable because the object being minimized is the exact Kohn–Sham energy functional evaluated on the network's own density: the variational principle means any converged network gives a rigorous upper bound, the residual/gradient norm is a computable error measure, and enlarging the network (or performing one conventional SCF/eigen‑refinement step on the network's density as a clean‑up) systematically recovers the standard result. Since only the *discretization and the optimization path* change — the functional, pseudopotentials and physics are untouched — this stacks with every other acceleration strategy.

**Solve the Kohn–Sham/Poisson equations with domain‑decomposition (Schur‑complement / substructuring) algorithms, so the big linear systems are broken into many small, independent, cacheable local problems coupled only through a tiny interface problem.**

Partition the simulation cell into overlapping or non‑overlapping spatial subdomains (or, in a localized basis, into groups of atom‑centred functions). Order the unknowns as "subdomain interior" plus "interface/skeleton," and eliminate the interiors exactly by local factorizations: each subdomain's interior block is factorized (or its local Dirichlet‑to‑Neumann/Poincaré–Steklov map is built) completely independently of every other subdomain, with no communication at all, and the whole problem is condensed onto the Schur complement defined only on the interfaces — a system perhaps 10–100× smaller than the original. That small interface system is then solved iteratively with a scalable substructuring preconditioner (additive/restricted Schwarz, BDDC/FETI‑DP, or a coarse‑grid correction that carries the long‑wavelength/global information and keeps the iteration count independent of the number of subdomains). The same machinery applies to every expensive linear operation in the code: the Hartree/Poisson solve and the electrostatics with arbitrary boundary conditions, the shift‑and‑invert or correction equations inside the eigensolver, the resolvents needed for Green's‑function/contour methods, and the response (Sternheimer/DFPT) solves.

Why this is a speed‑up rather than just a rearrangement: (i) **the expensive work becomes embarrassingly parallel and communication‑light** — only thin interface data are exchanged, replacing the all‑to‑all traffic of global 3‑D FFTs and global orthogonalization that caps strong scaling of conventional codes at a few thousand cores; (ii) **local factorizations are reusable** — during geometry optimization, molecular dynamics, Monte‑Carlo moves, defect/adsorbate scans or parameter sweeps, only the few subdomains containing moved atoms are "dirty," so their factorizations are recomputed while all the others are simply reused, turning a global solve into a local update; (iii) **each subdomain problem is small and dense enough to be cache‑ and GPU‑friendly** (batched small factorizations/GEMMs instead of memory‑bound global operations), and different subdomains can even be discretized differently (finer mesh, higher‑order elements, or a richer basis only where the chemistry is hard) since they communicate only through interface conditions; (iv) the decomposition naturally supports **heterogeneous boundary conditions and non‑matching regions** (vacuum, continuum solvent, elastic far field), which lets cheap models be attached at the subdomain boundaries.

Accuracy is untouched: with exact interior elimination the Schur‑complement solution is the *same* solution as the global solve, and the only knobs are the interface iteration tolerance, the overlap width, and the coarse‑space size — all systematically convergible and certified by the final residual. Because the functional, basis, pseudopotentials, grids and physics are unchanged and only the *linear‑algebra data flow* is reorganized, this typically buys an order of magnitude in time‑to‑solution and parallel efficiency on large machines, and it multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**Use k·p perturbation theory to eliminate most of the explicit k‑point (and empty‑state) work.** Because the periodic parts of the Bloch functions at neighbouring wavevectors are related analytically — H(k+q) = H(k) + (ħ/m)q·(p + …) + ħ²q²/2m — one only has to solve the Kohn–Sham equations self‑consistently on a very coarse mesh of "anchor" k‑points, and then generate the Hamiltonian, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, velocities and momentum/dipole matrix elements at *arbitrarily many* nearby k‑points by diagonalizing a tiny k·p matrix built in the small subspace of bands already computed at the anchor (the required p‑matrix elements come out of the same run, so no extra SCF, no localization/Wannierization step and no new integrals are needed).

The consequences are immediate speed‑ups: Brillouin‑zone integrals that need an ultradense mesh (Fermi surfaces, densities of states, optical/dielectric response, Berry curvature and topological invariants, carrier concentrations, Seebeck and transport coefficients, electron–phonon and impurity scattering rates, band‑gap and effective‑mass extraction) are evaluated on a 10²–10⁴ times denser mesh at essentially zero additional cost, since each extra k‑point costs one small dense diagonalization of dimension equal to the handful of retained bands rather than a full iterative solve over millions of plane waves. The same expansion also supplies effective masses, Luttinger and Kane parameters and g‑factors analytically instead of by finite differences over several converged runs, and it yields compact multiband k·p envelope‑function Hamiltonians that then describe quantum wells, nanostructures, heterojunctions, strain and magnetic‑field (Landau‑level) problems containing millions of atoms — systems where a direct supercell DFT calculation is impossible — while remaining parameterized entirely by the single bulk DFT run. Strain, alloying and small perturbations enter through deformation potentials obtained from the same expansion, so composition and strain sweeps need no new self‑consistent calculations.

Accuracy is governed by two transparent, systematically convergible knobs — the number of bands kept in the k·p subspace and the anchor‑point spacing (i.e. the maximum |q| over which the expansion is used, with second‑ or higher‑order/Löwdin‑folded terms for remote bands) — and the exact result is recovered by densifying the anchors. Since the functional, pseudopotentials, basis, solver and self‑consistency are untouched, this is an exact reorganization of how band‑structure information is obtained, and it multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**Enforce exact physical constraints, symmetries and sum rules as a post‑processing "correction" on deliberately under‑converged data, instead of brute‑force converging every calculation until those constraints are satisfied automatically.**

Much of the expense in a DFT study comes from pushing cutoffs, k‑ or q‑meshes, supercell sizes, quadrature grids and SCF tolerances to the point where quantities that are *exactly known on physical grounds* come out right by themselves. But those quantities need not be computed at all — they can be imposed. Concretely: symmetrize the computed density, forces, stress, force‑constant and dielectric tensors with the full space/point group of the structure (this removes the random, symmetry‑breaking part of the numerical noise, which is typically the dominant error, and is equivalent to averaging over many independent samples for free); impose the **acoustic sum rule** and rotational/translational invariance on interatomic force constants and the **charge‑neutrality sum rule** on Born effective charges, so phonon dispersions computed on a coarse q‑mesh with loose thresholds no longer show spurious imaginary acoustic branches near Γ; enforce **Kramers–Kronig** relations and the **f‑sum rule** on optical/dielectric spectra so only the imaginary part must be computed, on a modest frequency grid, and the real part and normalization follow analytically; use the **virial/Hellmann–Feynman and Pulay identities** to cross‑check and correct stresses and forces obtained in a small basis; use **charge neutrality, Friedel and Luttinger sum rules, Janak's theorem, piecewise‑linearity/Koopmans conditions and known exact asymptotic limits** (uniform‑gas, high‑density, long‑range 1/r behaviour of the potential) to fix chemical potentials, level alignments and long‑range tails that would otherwise require huge cells or very dense meshes; and constrain fitted models (cluster expansions, force‑constant fits, tight‑binding downfoldings) to obey the crystal symmetry and the known analytic limits, which drastically reduces the number of free parameters and hence the number of DFT data points needed to determine them.

Practically, this is implemented as a small constrained least‑squares/projection step: take the cheap, noisy DFT output, project it onto the manifold of tensors/spectra that satisfy all the exact constraints (the closest symmetric, sum‑rule‑obeying object), and use that as the result. The correction costs microseconds, but because the enforced constraints are precisely the ones that converge most slowly with cutoff, mesh and cell size, the residual error after projection typically corresponds to a calculation several times more expensive — routinely allowing 2–10× coarser numerical settings (and an order of magnitude fewer displaced/perturbed configurations in phonon, elastic and response studies) for the same final accuracy. The size of the violation *before* projection is itself a free, honest error diagnostic that tells you how converged you actually are. Since the functional, basis, pseudopotentials and solver are untouched — only exactly true physical information is added — no approximation is introduced, and the savings multiply with every other acceleration strategy.

**Design the *ingredients* of the calculation for numerical conditioning and smoothness — not just for physical accuracy — so that the same answer is reached with much coarser settings and far fewer, better‑behaved iterations.**

Most of the cost of a DFT run is dictated not by the physics but by how badly conditioned and how "rough" the discrete problem is: a functional whose energy density is stiff or non‑analytic forces a very dense exchange–correlation quadrature and makes the SCF oscillate; a basis containing near‑linearly‑dependent diffuse or over‑complete functions produces an overlap matrix with a condition number of 10⁸–10¹² that destroys eigensolver and mixing convergence (and can even give spurious energies in reduced precision); sharp potentials and cusped densities force high cutoffs everywhere. All of these are *choices*, and they can be re‑engineered once, offline, at no cost to the physics:

- **Regularized, numerically smooth functionals.** Replace stiff meta‑GGAs and other forms with mathematically regularized versions of the same physics (e.g. r²SCAN in place of SCAN, smoothly damped dispersion kernels, regularized kinetic‑energy‑density and iso‑orbital indicators, bounded enhancement factors). These remove the pathological grid sensitivity and the SCF oscillations/false minima that otherwise demand ultra‑fine radial/angular grids and dozens of extra cycles, typically cutting grid sizes several‑fold and iteration counts by factors of 2–5 while reproducing the parent functional's accuracy essentially exactly.
- **Well‑conditioned basis sets.** Prune or re‑contract near‑degenerate primitives, use canonical/Löwdin orthogonalization with an eigenvalue threshold, geometric/even‑tempered and confinement‑regularized numeric atomic orbitals, and orthogonalized or "optimized‑norm" projector sets — so the overlap and Hamiltonian matrices are well conditioned. Krylov/Davidson/LOBPCG iteration counts scale roughly with √(condition number), so this alone can halve or quarter the eigensolver work and lets aggressive mixed/reduced‑precision arithmetic be used safely.
- **Smooth potentials and smooth reference densities.** Generate pseudopotentials, projectors, compensation charges and pseudo‑core densities under an explicit *smoothness* (low‑cutoff) objective rather than only a transferability one; smear or regularize the nuclear/ionic singularity analytically; use confinement radii and cutoffs chosen so that no field on the grid has spectral content beyond the mesh's resolution. The FFT box/grid‑point count falls with the required cutoff, and forces/stresses become smooth functions of geometry, so geometry optimizers and MD integrators converge in fewer steps and tolerate larger time steps.
- **Smooth, consistent quadrature and interpolation.** Use grids and interpolation schemes whose weights vary smoothly with atomic positions (smooth Becke partitioning, smoothly switched pruning, spline‑continuous tabulated radial functions) so that the potential‑energy surface has no numerical noise or discontinuities; noise‑free forces are what allow loose convergence thresholds and large optimizer/MD steps to be used without breaking down.

Because none of this changes the functional's physical content, the Hamiltonian, the boundary conditions or the solver — the converged energies, densities and forces agree with the "brute‑force" reference to within the tolerance one chooses — it is essentially free accuracy‑preserving speed: coarser grids and cutoffs, fewer SCF cycles, fewer eigensolver iterations, larger ionic steps, and robustness in low precision, routinely worth an aggregate factor of several to an order of magnitude. And since it acts on the inputs rather than on the algorithm or hardware, it multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**Attack data movement and synchronization rather than arithmetic: reformulate the DFT kernels as "communication‑avoiding," latency‑tolerant algorithms that provably minimize the number of messages and global reductions.**

On modern machines a floating‑point operation is essentially free while moving a word across the memory hierarchy or the network costs 10²–10⁴× more, and the true scaling wall in DFT is the *synchronization* built into its standard algorithms: classical Gram–Schmidt/Löwdin orthogonalization and subspace projections issue one global all‑reduce per band; Krylov/Davidson/LOBPCG issue one or two global dot‑product reductions per iteration; distributed 3‑D FFTs issue full all‑to‑all transposes twice per Hamiltonian application; dense eigensolvers broadcast panels at every step. Each of these is a latency‑bound barrier at which every rank waits for the slowest one, so beyond a few thousand cores the machine idles no matter how fast the local kernels are.

The fix is to rewrite these steps in forms that attain the known communication lower bounds:

- **Orthogonalization without per‑vector reductions** — replace modified Gram–Schmidt by TSQR ("tall‑skinny QR" via a reduction tree), CholeskyQR2, or block/Cholesky orthonormalization of the whole band block at once, so all bands are orthogonalized with *one* reduction of a small Gram matrix instead of N_band sequential ones, in pure BLAS‑3 form (with a second pass or shifted‑Cholesky to restore stability at high condition number).
- **s‑step / pipelined Krylov and Chebyshev filtering** — compute s matrix–vector products (a "matrix powers kernel" using ghost‑zone halos of width s) *before* any inner products, then perform all s reductions in a single fused all‑reduce; use pipelined/non‑blocking CG–GMRES variants in which the reduction is overlapped with the next Hamiltonian application, so latency is hidden rather than paid.
- **Communication‑optimal dense linear algebra** — 2.5D/3D matrix multiplication and Cholesky/eigensolves that replicate data to trade extra memory for asymptotically less bandwidth; two‑stage tridiagonalization; block‑cyclic layouts and process grids chosen to minimize the surface‑to‑volume ratio of each panel exchange.
- **Avoiding the all‑to‑all** — pencil/slab decompositions and batched FFTs that transpose only along one axis, "FFT‑avoiding" formulations that keep the nonlocal projectors and local potential entirely in real space with nearest‑neighbour halo exchange only, and mapping the remaining transposes onto the topology of the interconnect.
- **Asynchrony as a design principle** — task‑based, dependency‑driven runtimes (StarPU/Legion/OpenMP tasks) with no global barriers: bands, k‑points, spins, subdomains and grid blocks proceed independently, communication is one‑sided/non‑blocking and overlapped with computation, and load imbalance is absorbed by work stealing instead of by everyone waiting; algorithms are chosen in *asynchronous* variants (asynchronous Jacobi/Schwarz smoothers, relaxed/inexact reductions) that tolerate stragglers, faults and heterogeneous nodes.

Because all of these are exact algebraic reorganizations of the identical operations — the same Hamiltonian, functional, basis, pseudopotentials, grids and convergence criteria, with only the *order and grouping* of the arithmetic and the placement of the data changed (and stability guarded by re‑orthogonalization or a second Cholesky pass) — the converged density, energy, forces and stresses are numerically the same to within round‑off. What changes is that the calculation stops being latency‑bound: strong scaling extends from thousands to hundreds of thousands of cores/GPUs, typically giving several‑fold to an order‑of‑magnitude reduction in time‑to‑solution for large systems, and the gain multiplies with every physical, algorithmic or hardware acceleration strategy.

**Split the Kohn–Sham operator into "cheap" and "expensive" pieces and update them at different rates — a nested, multi‑rate (dual‑level) SCF with operator freezing.**

In practice the Hamiltonian is not a monolith: a semilocal (LDA/GGA) part plus the Hartree term is cheap to rebuild, while a few specific ingredients dominate the cost per cycle — exact/Fock exchange in hybrids, the nonlocal van der Waals kernel, meta‑GGA kinetic‑energy‑density terms, PAW/augmentation and multipole reconstructions, the +U/DFT+DMFT self‑energy, the fine XC quadrature, implicit‑solvent (Poisson–Boltzmann) response, and spin–orbit/relativistic couplings. Because these expensive terms are smooth, weakly varying functionals of the density, they change far more slowly along the SCF trajectory (and along an MD or relaxation trajectory) than the density itself does.

So: build the expensive operator **once**, freeze it, and then run a full inner self‑consistency loop in which only the cheap terms are rebuilt each iteration, converging the inexpensive sub‑problem tightly at essentially the cost of a GGA calculation; then refresh the expensive operator with the new density and repeat. Typically only 3–6 outer refreshes are needed instead of 20–50 expensive builds — a nearly one‑order‑of‑magnitude reduction for hybrids, nonlocal‑correlation functionals and solvated/correlated systems. The same operator‑splitting logic generalizes: freeze the exchange operator or the solvent reaction field over several MD steps and correct it perturbatively; do early outer cycles on a coarse XC/augmentation grid and only the last on the fine one; treat the difference (expensive − cheap) operator as a slowly varying correction that can be extrapolated (ASPC/Anderson‑style) from previous outer iterations rather than recomputed.

Convergence is safeguarded because the outer loop is itself a fixed‑point iteration on the *exact* Kohn–Sham residual (it can be wrapped in DIIS/Anderson acceleration on the outer variable, with the inner loop acting as a very good nonlinear preconditioner). Crucially, the converged solution is the true, fully self‑consistent result of the full functional — freezing affects only the intermediate iterates, never the fixed point — so no physical approximation is introduced, the final residual certifies the answer, and the savings multiply with every other acceleration strategy.

**Stop re‑diagonalizing at every SCF cycle: after the first few iterations, update the orbitals *perturbatively* instead of solving the eigenproblem again ("pseudo‑diagonalization" / incremental subspace rotation).**

Once the SCF is roughly converged, the Kohn–Sham matrix expressed in the *previous* cycle's molecular‑orbital basis is already nearly block‑diagonal: the occupied–occupied and virtual–virtual blocks are essentially diagonal, and only the small occupied–virtual coupling block F_ov remains. Since the total energy depends only on the occupied *subspace*, not on the individual canonical eigenvectors or eigenvalues, one does not need a new eigen‑decomposition at all — it suffices to annihilate F_ov. This can be done by (i) a first‑order/second‑order perturbative rotation, θ_ia ≈ F_ia/(ε_a − ε_i), applied as an exponential/Cayley (unitary) transformation C ← C·exp(−Θ) that keeps orthonormality exactly and is a simple tall–skinny GEMM; or (ii) Stewart‑style pseudo‑diagonalization, i.e. a few sweeps of 2×2 Jacobi rotations restricted to occupied–virtual pairs, with pairs whose |F_ia| lies below a threshold skipped entirely (their number collapses as convergence is approached). Because only the N_occ×N_virt block is touched — and, near convergence, only a small screened fraction of it — the cost per cycle drops from a full O(N³) dense diagonalization (or a full Davidson/LOBPCG restart) to a fraction of it, typically a 4–10× reduction of the diagonalization time, which is often the single largest term in medium‑sized Gaussian‑basis and localized‑orbital DFT runs.

The same "reuse the previous solution and correct it" logic extends naturally in three directions: the converged orbital subspace of the previous *geometry/MD/parameter* step is carried over and only perturbatively rotated for the new Hamiltonian (so each successive point in a relaxation, trajectory, or λ/U/strain sweep needs almost no eigenwork); the virtual space can be truncated to a small energy window in the rotation, since only low‑lying virtuals contribute appreciably to θ; and the deflated/frozen part of the spectrum (deep core‑like states, well‑separated bands) can be locked and excluded from the update altogether.

Accuracy is untouched and self‑certifying: a full, exact diagonalization is performed for the first few cycles and once more at the end (and whenever the residual ‖F_ov‖ or the loss of orthonormality exceeds a set tolerance), so the converged density, energy, eigenvalues and forces are those of the standard calculation — the perturbative updates change only the *path* to the fixed point, never the fixed point itself. Since the functional, basis, pseudopotentials, grids and solver framework are all unchanged, this is essentially free wall‑clock time and multiplies with every other acceleration strategy.

**Let the code choose its own algorithm and settings: automatic, hardware‑ and system‑aware solver selection plus runtime auto‑tuning.**

For any given Kohn–Sham problem there are many mathematically equivalent ways to get the density matrix — dense ScaLAPACK/ELPA diagonalization, iterative subspace methods (Davidson/LOBPCG/Chebyshev filtering), spectrum‑slicing/contour solvers, pole expansion with selected inversion (PEXSI), sparse density‑matrix purification, or orbital‑transformation direct minimization — and the fastest one depends strongly on the *regime*: number of atoms and basis functions, sparsity and band gap, metallic vs. insulating, number of k‑points and spins, memory per node, and the balance of CPU/GPU throughput, memory bandwidth and interconnect latency on the specific machine. Users almost never sit at the optimum, because they pick one solver (usually dense diagonalization) and one hard‑coded parallel layout and keep it for every system and every SCF cycle, so calculations routinely run 3–30× slower than the same code is capable of.
