- **Buildable now:** event‑driven timing ASICs, beam chopping/blanking at GHz rates, and multi‑GB/s streaming electronics all exist; the engineering task is the timing jitter budget, the ~TB/s data pipeline and matching the chopper duty cycle to acceptable beam current.

The result is a microscope in which every electron that passes through the specimen contributes simultaneously to structure, chemistry and dynamics — pushing the instrument to the information‑theoretic limit set by radiation damage rather than by detector choice.

**Add an integrated ultrafast module that turns the microscope into an attosecond‑resolution "movie camera": a laser‑driven optical/THz pulse compressor and streaking cavity built into the column, combined with an in‑column pump laser and event‑timestamping detector.**

How it works: a femtosecond laser photoemits (or gates) electron bunches at the gun; these are then compressed and *phase‑locked* to the optical cycle by microwave/THz or free‑space laser fields in a resonant cavity just above the specimen (inverse‑FEL / photon‑induced near‑field electron microscopy interaction), producing attosecond‑scale electron pulse trains with attosecond timing jitter relative to a synchronised pump pulse illuminating the sample. A second streaking cavity below the specimen maps arrival time onto transverse position on the detector, so each electron's interaction time is read out directly.

Why this is the improvement worth making:
- **It closes the last missing dimension.** Modern instruments already resolve single atoms in space and single bonds in energy, but their time resolution is set by detector frame rates (~µs–ms) or, in ultrafast TEM, by ~100 fs–ps electron pulses. Attosecond–femtosecond gating would let one watch charge transfer, plasmon and polariton dynamics, phonon propagation, bond breaking, magnetic switching and phase‑transition nucleation *as they happen*, at atomic spatial resolution.
- **Timing metrology instead of averaging.** Streak‑based per‑electron time stamping removes the need for perfectly reproducible pump–probe averaging, tolerating jitter and drift and allowing single‑shot or few‑electron‑per‑pulse operation that avoids space‑charge broadening.
- **Dose benefit.** Because the sample is interrogated only during the femtosecond window of interest, the beam is off for essentially the whole duty cycle — dynamics are captured without continuous irradiation damage.
- **Buildable now:** photoemission guns, THz/IR compression cavities, PINEM interactions and event‑driven timing ASICs are all demonstrated separately; the task is engineering them into one aberration‑corrected column with a common optical clock.

**Rebuild the specimen area as an extreme‑high‑vacuum (XHV), contamination‑free environment with an integrated in‑vacuo sample‑preparation and transfer suite.**

Concretely: replace the conventional ~10⁻⁷–10⁻⁸ mbar column with an all‑metal‑sealed, bakeable, cryo‑ and NEG/ion‑pumped stage region reaching <10⁻¹¹ mbar, surround the specimen with a liquid‑helium‑cooled cryo‑shroud (an anti‑contamination "cold trap" at 4 K that cryopumps residual hydrocarbons and water onto itself rather than onto the sample), and connect the column via a UHV load‑lock/transfer line to attached preparation chambers (plasma/UV cleaning, ion milling, annealing, cleaving, MBE/evaporation, gas dosing) plus a UHV suitcase port.

Why this is the improvement worth making:

- **Carbon contamination, not optics, is what actually ruins many atomic‑resolution experiments.** Beam‑induced deposition of cracked hydrocarbons builds up within seconds on the very spot being imaged, blurring lattice images, corrupting EELS/EDS quantification, and making long ptychographic, tomographic or spectrum‑image acquisitions impossible. XHV plus a 4 K shroud essentially eliminates the mobile hydrocarbon supply.

- **It makes surfaces and 2D materials honest.** At 10⁻⁷ mbar a clean surface is covered by an adsorbate monolayer in about a second, so today's "atomic‑resolution surface imaging" is really imaging an unknown adlayer, and 2D materials, catalyst facets, battery interfaces and reactive intermetallics oxidise between preparation and insertion. XHV extends the clean‑surface lifetime to hours and lets genuine, atomically clean surface structure, adsorption sites and single‑atom catalysts be resolved and chemically identified.

- **It rescues dose‑limited and in‑situ work.** Removing contamination growth recovers information currently lost to specimen degradation during low‑dose acquisitions, and it means a residual‑gas background low enough that deliberately dosed gases in in‑situ reaction experiments are the only species present — real, quantitative gas–solid chemistry rather than a hydrocarbon‑polluted approximation.

- **Buildable now:** XHV technology, cryo‑shrouds, UHV transfer suitcases and attached prep chambers are standard in surface science (STM/ARPES) and in field‑ion/atom‑probe instruments; the engineering task is bakeout compatibility of the lenses and detectors, and vibration‑isolating the cryopumps from the column.

The result is a microscope in which what you image after an hour is still the specimen you put in — shifting the limit from the vacuum and its contamination chemistry back to the intrinsic physics of the material.

**Build a cryogenic super‑resolution fluorescence microscope directly into the electron microscope column, so the same specimen can be imaged optically and electron‑optically without ever being moved (true in‑situ correlative light–electron microscopy).**

Concretely: mount a high‑NA cryogenic objective (or a fibre/ solid‑immersion optic threaded through the pole‑piece gap) that views the grid at the eucentric position, with laser excitation, single‑molecule‑localisation/STED‑class resolution at liquid‑nitrogen or liquid‑helium temperature, and an optical path shared with the electron beam via a mirrored or perforated in‑column element.

Why this is the improvement worth making:

- **It solves the "needle in a haystack" problem.** In cryo‑EM and cryo‑tomography most of the effort (and most of the wasted dose) goes into finding the rare cell, organelle, protein complex or defect worth imaging. Fluorescent labels localised in situ to ~10–20 nm would point the electron beam straight at the target, raising useful data yield by orders of magnitude and making low‑abundance and *in‑cellulo* structural biology routine.

- **Perfect registration, no transfer damage.** Today's cryo‑CLEM requires physically shuttling the grid between two instruments, which costs hours, introduces ice contamination and devitrification, and leaves 100 nm–1 µm registration errors. Doing it in one column gives nanometre correlation accuracy and eliminates the most damaging handling step.

- **Adds chemical/functional identity that electrons cannot provide.** Fluorescence reports on molecular species, conformational state (FRET), redox and pH, and photoactivation state — information invisible in an electron image — while the same optics enable cathodoluminescence detection, photo‑excitation of the specimen for opto‑electronic and photocatalytic in‑situ experiments, and optical control of labelled molecules during acquisition.

- **Buildable now:** cryo‑stage light microscopes, in‑column mirror optics (already used for cathodoluminescence and for laser‑driven guns), and cryogenic single‑molecule localisation are all demonstrated separately; the engineering task is fitting a high‑NA, low‑drift, vacuum‑ and field‑compatible objective into the pole‑piece gap and suppressing beam‑induced luminescence background.

The result is a microscope that knows *what* it is looking at before it spends the specimen's limited electron dose on it.

**Add spin to the electron microscope: build a spin‑polarized illumination source together with a spin‑analyzing detector, so the instrument measures not just where electrons go and how much energy they lose, but their spin state.**

Concretely: replace/supplement the gun with a strained‑superlattice GaAs photocathode pumped by circularly polarized laser light (>90 % spin polarization, with fast helicity switching via a Pockels cell), transport the polarization through the column with a Wien‑filter spin rotator so the spin direction can be set arbitrarily relative to the specimen, and place a compact spin polarimeter (Mott scattering, exchange‑scattering VLEED, or a spin‑filter crystal) after the EELS spectrometer so scattered and energy‑loss electrons can be spin‑resolved.

Why this is the improvement worth making:

- **Magnetism becomes a direct, local observable.** Today magnetic information in TEM/STEM is obtained only indirectly, from the Lorentz deflection or Aharonov–Bohm phase of the *integrated* induction (Lorentz microscopy, DPC, holography) — which is weak, requires field‑free objective operation, and cannot distinguish antiferromagnetic or compensated order at all. Spin‑polarized illumination gives contrast from the exchange interaction itself, i.e. from the atomic‑scale spin arrangement, allowing antiferromagnets, spin spirals, skyrmion cores, domain walls and interfacial spin canting to be imaged at near‑atomic resolution.

- **Spin‑resolved spectroscopy.** Analysing the spin of the transmitted beam turns EELS into a spin‑ and momentum‑resolved probe: magnon dispersions, spin‑split band structures, exchange splittings and spin‑dependent excitations could be mapped with nanometre spatial resolution — combining what is now split between neutron scattering, spin‑ARPES and SP‑STM into a single transmission instrument.

- **Helicity modulation kills systematic error.** Because the laser helicity (and hence the beam polarization) can be flipped at kHz rates while everything else in the column stays fixed, the magnetic signal is recovered as a lock‑in difference between helicities, immune to drift, contamination and charging — the noise sources that currently swamp weak magnetic phase signals.

- **Buildable now:** high‑polarization GaAs photocathodes, Wien spin rotators and efficient VLEED/exchange spin filters are mature in accelerator physics and spin‑ARPES; SEM with polarization analysis (SEMPA) already exists. The engineering task is maintaining the ultra‑high vacuum and cathode lifetime needed for negative‑electron‑affinity photocathodes in a TEM column, preserving brightness/coherence, and improving the low figure of merit of spin detectors (multichannel imaging spin filters would give the required efficiency).

The payoff is an electron microscope whose contrast mechanisms extend beyond charge and chemistry to the spin degree of freedom — atomic‑resolution magnetic imaging of the materials (antiferromagnetic spintronics, 2D magnets, multiferroics) that current instruments are essentially blind to.

**Turn the specimen holder into a universal, atomically‑thin "lab‑on‑a‑chip": a standardized MEMS *operando* platform with graphene‑windowed nano‑cells and on‑chip sensing/feedback.**

Concretely: a single silicon‑nitride/MEMS chip that clamps into the pole‑piece gap and combines (i) nanofluidic and gas channels sealed by bilayer‑graphene windows only ~1 nm thick (instead of the 20–50 nm SiN windows and micron‑thick liquid layers used today), (ii) integrated micro‑heaters, four‑probe electrical and electrochemical contacts (working/counter/reference electrodes), mechanical straining actuators, micro‑coils for local magnetic fields and a waveguide/fibre for optical excitation, and (iii) on‑chip thermometry, pressure/flow, current and displacement sensors read out in closed loop so the *actual* local conditions are measured, not inferred, and drift is actively nulled at the chip level.

Why this is the improvement worth making:

- **The environment, not the optics, now limits in‑situ science.** Aberration‑corrected columns resolve single atoms, but as soon as gas or liquid is admitted, thick windows and fluid layers scatter and blur the beam, destroying resolution and EELS quantification. Atomically thin graphene windows are nearly transparent and electrically conductive (suppressing charging and radiolysis), so catalysis, corrosion, battery cycling and electrodeposition can be watched at true atomic resolution *under realistic pressures and potentials* rather than in dried, post‑mortem samples.

- **Quantitative, reproducible conditions.** Today's in‑situ results are hard to compare because temperature, potential and local flow are poorly known. On‑chip calibrated sensors plus feedback control make experiments quantitative and reproducible across laboratories, and allow multiple stimuli (heat + bias + gas + light) to be applied and swept simultaneously with the microscope’s image/spectrum stream as one synchronized dataset.

- **Better mechanics and dose economy.** A rigid, low‑mass MEMS chip has far less thermal drift and backlash than a bulky heating/straining rod, enabling long low‑dose acquisitions, tomography and ptychography during a reaction; conductive graphene windows also carry away charge and heat, reducing beam damage.

- **Buildable now:** MEMS heating/biasing chips, graphene‑sealed liquid cells and closed‑cycle microfluidics have each been demonstrated; the task is integrating them into one standardized, multi‑stimulus, sensor‑instrumented chip format with a common electrical/fluidic interface and control software.

The result is a microscope that images materials *while they work*, at the same resolution it achieves on a dry, static specimen — closing the gap between microscopy and real device/reaction conditions.

**Eliminate the "missing wedge": replace the conventional ±70° tilt holder with a true 360°, on‑axis rotation stage designed around needle‑shaped (rod/pillar) specimens.**

Concretely: a cryo‑compatible cartridge that grips a ~100–300 nm diameter pillar (FIB‑milled, or a cryo‑jet‑frozen sample in a fine capillary/needle mount) on the optic axis, with a piezo‑driven rotary bearing giving continuous, backlash‑free full rotation at nanometre eucentric accuracy, combined with a wide pole‑piece gap and a small‑diameter holder tip so nothing shadows the beam or the EDS/EELS detectors at any angle.

Why this is the improvement worth making:

- **Isotropic 3D resolution.** Today's slab specimens can only be tilted to ~±60–70° before the projected thickness explodes and the holder shadows the beam, leaving a missing wedge that elongates and distorts every tomogram by a factor of 2–3 in the beam direction and creates fan artefacts. Full 360° rotation of a needle gives complete Fourier‑space coverage and truly isotropic reconstructions — atomic‑resolution tomography of nanoparticles, defects, dislocation networks and interfaces, and artefact‑free cryo‑electron tomography of cellular volumes.

- **Constant, minimal path length = better dose economy.** A cylindrical specimen presents the same thickness at every angle, so no tilt wastes dose on 3–5× thicker projections, multiple/inelastic scattering stays low and quantitative (EELS/EDS tomography becomes genuinely quantitative rather than absorption‑biased), and the total dose needed for a complete tilt series drops substantially — critical for beam‑sensitive and biological material.

- **Enables continuous‑rotation, "on‑the‑fly" acquisition.** With a stable on‑axis bearing the specimen can rotate continuously while an event‑driven detector streams data, removing the stop‑settle‑track‑focus overhead that dominates tilt‑series time, and allowing 4D (time‑resolved) tomography of in‑situ processes.

- **Buildable now:** needle/pillar geometry is routine in atom‑probe tomography and FIB preparation, cryo‑rotation stages and piezo rotary bearings exist, and 360° tomography has been demonstrated in prototype holders; the engineering task is nanometre‑level eucentric stability of the bearing at cryogenic temperature and a robust workflow for mounting frozen‑hydrated samples in needle form.

The result is a microscope whose 3D information is limited by the specimen's radiation tolerance rather than by the geometry of its own holder.

**Build a full chromatic‑aberration (Cc) corrector into the column and optimise the whole instrument for *low‑voltage* operation (~20–80 kV) rather than 200–300 kV.**

Concretely: add an electrostatic–magnetic quadrupole–octupole (or mirror‑type) corrector that cancels both Cs and Cc simultaneously, together with a high‑transmission monochromator and low‑voltage‑optimised detectors/spectrometer optics, so sub‑ångström resolution is retained at accelerating voltages far below today's standard.

Why this is the improvement worth making:

- **It removes knock‑on damage, the dominant destruction mechanism for the most interesting samples.** Graphene, TMDs, MOFs, zeolites, organics and single‑atom catalysts have displacement thresholds around 30–80 kV; dropping below them means atoms are no longer sputtered out of the lattice, so structures can be imaged and spectroscopically analysed for minutes instead of seconds.

- **Chromatic blur, not spherical aberration, is what stops low‑kV imaging today.** At 30–60 kV the relative energy spread and the larger interaction time make Cc the resolution limit; correcting it recovers deep sub‑ångström performance at voltages where existing Cs‑only correctors give only nanometre‑scale detail.

- **Bigger signal per electron.** Elastic and inelastic cross‑sections rise steeply as energy falls, so each low‑energy electron produces far more image contrast and a far stronger EELS core‑loss signal — better information per unit dose for thin, light‑element and beam‑sensitive specimens, and single‑atom chemical identification becomes routine.

- **Bonus: thick samples too.** The same Cc corrector removes the chromatic blur caused by energy loss inside thick specimens (cryo‑sections, whole cells, device cross‑sections), improving resolution and depth of information in tomography, and it enables large‑energy‑window energy‑filtered imaging without loss of resolution.

- **Buildable now:** Cc/Cs correctors have been demonstrated (e.g., in TEAM/SALVE‑class instruments); the task is making them stable, routinely alignable and commercially available as part of a fully low‑voltage‑optimised column.

The result is a microscope whose resolution is set by the specimen's radiation tolerance at an energy where the specimen actually survives, rather than by the historical compromise of running at high voltage to beat aberrations.

**Build a true electron Mach–Zehnder interferometer into the column** — replace the single Möllenstedt biprism used for off‑axis holography with a set of nanofabricated (or laser‑standing‑wave) coherent electron beam splitters and recombiners that physically separate the illumination into a "sample" arm and a well‑separated, undisturbed "reference" arm, then recombine them on the detector.

Why this is the improvement worth making:

- **Quantitative phase everywhere, not just near an edge.** Conventional off‑axis holography needs a vacuum reference wave overlapping the field of view, so it only works within a micron or so of the specimen edge and cannot phase‑image the interior of a cell, a device cross‑section or a thick film. A physically separated reference arm removes that geometric restriction, giving absolute, drift‑referenced phase maps of arbitrary regions — electrostatic potentials, dopant profiles, charge accumulation at working interfaces, magnetic induction inside continuous films.

- **Common‑mode noise rejection.** With both arms sharing the same lenses, power supplies and mechanical path, lens ripple, stray AC fields and drift cancel in the interference signal, pushing phase sensitivity toward the shot‑noise (and ultimately Heisenberg) limit — micro‑radian phase precision, enough to see single‑charge states, individual dopant atoms and weak magnetic textures.

- **The reference arm can be actively used.** Modulating the reference path (phase stepping, energy offset, path‑length delay) enables lock‑in phase detection, energy‑resolved interferometry, and pump–probe path‑delay measurements; blocking one arm turns the same optic into an interaction‑free / quantum‑nondemolition measurement that extracts phase information with a fraction of the electrons hitting the specimen — a direct dose saving for beam‑sensitive material.

- **Buildable now:** coherent electron beam splitting has been demonstrated with nanofabricated gratings, magnetic biprism arrays and laser standing waves; the engineering task is stabilising the two arms to a fraction of the de Broglie wavelength and preserving coherence through the recombiner.

The result is a microscope that measures the electron *wavefunction* interferometrically with an independent reference, making phase — and hence fields, potentials and magnetism inside real specimens — a routinely quantitative, noise‑immune observable.

**Introduce "photonic" electron optics: use intense, structured light fields (ponderomotive laser lenses) as active optical elements in the column, in place of — or alongside — the static magnetic pole‑piece lenses and multipole correctors.**

How: a high‑power, high‑repetition‑rate laser (e.g., an enhancement cavity or fibre‑amplifier system) is brought into the column and shaped (with a spatial light modulator into Laguerre‑Gaussian, Bessel or toroidal "doughnut" intensity distributions) so that its ponderomotive potential acts on the passing electrons. Because the ponderomotive force always pushes electrons toward low intensity, a hollow, radially increasing light shell focuses the beam, and the profile can be sculpted essentially arbitrarily.

Why this is the improvement worth making:

- **It sidesteps Scherzer's theorem.** Static, round, charge‑free magnetic lenses are *forced* to have positive spherical and chromatic aberration; that is why correctors are complex, expensive and unstable. A light field is not bound by that constraint — it can be given intrinsically negative or zero Cs, or any prescribed higher‑order term, simply by reprogramming the laser mode, replacing a rack of multipole hardware and its dozens of drifting power supplies with a software‑defined optic.

- **Femtosecond switching and gating.** The "lens" exists only while the pulse is present, so it doubles as an ultrafast shutter, a pulse compressor, and a beam blanker with no electrostatic plates or deflector settling time — enabling stroboscopic imaging, precise dose gating (the beam is off between pulses, so beam‑sensitive specimens receive only the electrons actually used) and jitter‑free synchronisation with pump lasers.

- **No hysteresis, no stray field, no pole piece.** The optical element has zero magnetic remanence and perfect day‑to‑day reproducibility, and it needs no iron around the specimen — freeing an enormous sample space for in‑situ cells, large tilt ranges and near‑4π detectors, and leaving the specimen in a genuinely field‑free environment (essential for magnetic and Lorentz imaging, and for superconducting or skyrmion‑hosting materials that today must be studied with the objective lens switched off at ruinous cost in resolution).

- **Programmable, aberration‑free reshaping on demand.** The same optic can be re‑tuned between imaging and diffraction, high‑ and low‑magnification, or converted into a phase element or beam splitter within microseconds, and it can be updated in closed loop from live diffraction data.

- **Buildable now:** ponderomotive deflection, laser‑induced electron phase modulation (PINEM), optical mirrors/gratings for electrons and cavity‑enhanced high‑average‑power lasers have all been demonstrated separately; the engineering task is sustaining the required intensity (~10¹²–10¹⁴ W/cm² in a cavity) at high duty cycle inside a vacuum column and synchronising it with a pulsed source.

The result is an electron microscope whose optics are reconfigurable light, not fixed iron — removing the fundamental aberration limit, the hysteresis and stray fields of magnetic lenses, and the pole‑piece constraint on specimen space in one stroke.

**Add time‑correlated electron–photon coincidence detection: couple a high‑collection‑efficiency in‑column light collector (parabolic mirror/waveguide) feeding superconducting‑nanowire single‑photon detectors to an event‑driven, time‑stamping EELS detector, so every energy‑loss electron can be correlated in time (ps resolution) with the photon its excitation emits.**

Why this would improve the state of the art:

- **Background‑free, single‑quantum spectroscopy.** Today's EELS spectra sit on a huge tail from the zero‑loss peak and bulk plasmons, which buries weak signals (single defect emitters, excitons, band‑edge states, phonon polaritons). Accepting only electrons that arrive in coincidence with a detected photon suppresses uncorrelated background by orders of magnitude, giving effectively background‑free, few‑meV loss spectra at atomic spatial resolution.

- **It separates what electrons alone cannot.** Coincidence gating distinguishes radiative from non‑radiative decay channels, coherent (transition/Cherenkov) radiation from incoherent luminescence, and lets one measure quantum yields, excited‑state lifetimes and photon statistics (g⁽²⁾, bunching/antibunching) of a *single* nanoscale emitter — turning the microscope into a nanoscale quantum‑optics bench that can certify single‑photon sources, colour centres and qubit candidates in situ.

- **More information per electron, i.e. per unit damage.** Because each detected coincidence carries far more information than a raw count, useful spectra can be built at doses where conventional CL or EELS is hopeless, which matters for beam‑sensitive semiconductors, perovskites, organics and 2D materials. The photon channel also acts as a herald: post‑selection recovers signal that would otherwise require long, damaging exposures.

- **New contrast and correlation dimensions.** Combining photon arrival time with electron energy and probe position yields (x, y, ΔE, ΔE_photon, Δt) datasets: nanoscale lifetime mapping, energy‑transfer pathways between neighbouring emitters, and pump–probe photon‑heralded dynamics — all intrinsically registered to the atomic‑resolution image.

- **Buildable now:** efficient in‑column CL mirrors, SNSPDs with <50 ps jitter, and Timepix‑class time‑stamping electron detectors all exist; the engineering task is threading high‑NA light collection through the pole‑piece gap, keeping the SNSPD cryostat vibration‑isolated, and matching the beam current to the low electron flux (< ~10⁷ e/s) needed for unambiguous coincidences.

The result is a microscope in which each electron's excitation is followed all the way to its emitted photon, exposing optical, excitonic and quantum‑optical properties of individual nanostructures that current instruments can only infer from ensemble averages.

**Give the microscope an atom‑counting mass spectrometer: build a compact time‑of‑flight mass/isotope analyser into the specimen chamber of a STEM, so that atoms removed from the specimen (by controlled field evaporation from a needle tip, by a focused laser/ion pulse, or by the beam itself) are captured, mass‑analysed and correlated in real time with the atomic‑resolution image of the very site they came from.**

Concretely: mount needle‑shaped specimens on a high‑voltage, pulsed (laser‑ or voltage‑pulsed) cryo‑cartridge on the optic axis; place a segmented, position‑sensitive, time‑stamping delay‑line detector on the opposite side (or in a side port with a reflectron) at wide solid angle; interleave imaging frames with evaporation pulses, so the microscope alternately *sees* the surface layer with sub‑ångström resolution and then *weighs* the atoms that layer contained — an "image‑then‑identify" loop, layer by layer.

Why this is the improvement worth making:

- **It supplies the one thing electron optics fundamentally cannot: isotopic and hydrogen/lithium sensitivity.** EELS and EDS cannot distinguish ¹²C from ¹³C, ⁶Li from ⁷Li, or H from D, and are extremely weak for H, He and Li. Mass spectrometry identifies every ion unambiguously by m/z, with equal sensitivity for light and heavy elements and ppm‑level trace detection — enabling isotope‑labelled tracer studies of diffusion, corrosion, catalysis, battery cycling and biological uptake at the atomic scale, plus direct imaging of hydrogen embrittlement sites and Li in electrodes.

- **It converts damage into data.** Sputtered/evaporated atoms are currently a pure loss (the specimen degrades and the ejected material is discarded). Collecting and analysing them means the dose already spent on the sample yields chemical information, dramatically improving information per unit damage.

- **It solves atom‑probe tomography's blind spot.** Atom probe gives 3D chemistry with near‑single‑atom sensitivity but no direct crystallographic image, so reconstructions suffer from unknown trajectory aberrations and ~nm positional error. Simultaneous STEM imaging/diffraction of the same tip provides the true lattice, tip shape and defect structure as a geometric constraint, turning the reconstruction from a model‑dependent estimate into a metrologically accurate, lattice‑registered 3D chemical map.

- **Buildable now:** pulsed‑laser atom probes, cryo needle preparation by FIB, delay‑line position‑sensitive TOF detectors and event‑driven electron detectors are all mature; the engineering task is fitting the high‑voltage tip and TOF flight path into the pole‑piece region without spoiling the electron optics or vacuum, and synchronising evaporation pulses with imaging frames.

The result is a microscope that not only resolves where every atom sits, but tells you exactly *which isotope of which element* each of those atoms is.

**Fix the specimen support and freezing step: give cryo‑EM a standardized "active grid" — an atomically thin, conductive, chemically functionalized graphene support combined with on‑instrument, spray‑and‑jet vitrification that traps particles before they ever reach an air–water interface.**

Concretely: replace holey amorphous‑carbon/ice grids with single‑ or bilayer‑graphene (or ultrathin doped‑carbon/graphene‑oxide) films whose surface is patterned with affinity chemistry (Ni‑NTA, streptavidin, nanobody or DNA‑origami arrays) so target complexes are captured in a controlled surface density and, if desired, a controlled orientation; plunge/jet‑freeze the sample in tens of milliseconds within a device docked to the microscope's loading port, so the specimen never sits at a liquid surface or warms during transfer.

Why this is the improvement worth making:

- **The grid, not the microscope, is now the limiting factor.** Modern columns already deliver near‑perfect optics, near‑ideal detectors and 1.2 Å reconstructions on favourable samples; the vast majority of failed projects fail at sample preparation — particles denature at the air–water interface, adopt preferred orientations, aggregate in thick or uneven ice, or are simply lost to the grid bars. Milliseconds‑fast vitrification onto an affinity surface removes the dominant destruction and orientation‑bias mechanism.

- **Better signal per electron.** A ~0.3 nm graphene film adds essentially no background scattering compared with 5–20 nm carbon or thick vitreous ice, so contrast and achievable resolution rise at the same dose; it is also electrically and thermally conductive, suppressing charging‑induced beam‑induced motion and image‑degrading specimen movement in the first, most informative frames.

- **It unlocks the hard targets.** Small (<50 kDa), scarce, fragile, membrane and *in‑cellulo* complexes — where the ensemble of particles per grid square is tiny — become tractable because nearly every molecule is intact, well‑distributed, correctly oriented and in thin ice, raising usable particle yield by orders of magnitude and cutting screening time from days to minutes.

- **Buildable now:** graphene transfer, plasma/UV functionalization, affinity monolayers and millisecond spray‑jet freezing devices have each been demonstrated; the task is turning them into a reproducible, mass‑manufactured, quality‑controlled grid format with an integrated, contamination‑free load‑lock so preparation and imaging become one automated workflow.

The result is an instrument whose achievable structure is limited by the molecule's intrinsic dynamics and radiation tolerance, not by what happens to it in the seconds before it is frozen.

**Push the accelerating voltage up rather than down: build a compact, aberration‑corrected MeV‑class (~1–3 MV) STEM optimised for thick specimens.**

Concretely: use a shielded, RF‑ or DC‑accelerated 1–3 MV column with a high‑brightness gun, superconducting/permanent‑magnet high‑field lenses scaled for relativistic electrons, and radiation‑hard, high‑stopping‑power detectors (thick‑sensor hybrid‑pixel arrays) plus a high‑dispersion spectrometer matched to MeV energies.

Why this is the improvement worth making:

- **It breaks the thickness barrier.** At 200–300 kV the useful specimen thickness is ~300–500 nm; multiple and inelastic scattering then destroy contrast and resolution. At MeV energies the elastic mean free path grows several‑fold and the inelastic‑to‑elastic ratio falls, so whole eukaryotic cells, tissue sections, complete device stacks, thick battery/catalyst layers and mm‑scale connectomics volumes can be imaged in projection at nanometre resolution without sectioning them into ribbons.

- **Better information per unit damage for thick samples.** Because a larger fraction of transmitted electrons scatter elastically only once, more of the dose deposited contributes usable phase/Z‑contrast signal instead of blurring background — the effective dose efficiency for thick cryo specimens improves rather than degrades.

- **Cleaner tomography.** Reduced beam broadening and chromatic blur through the specimen mean tilt series of thick slabs stay in focus and stay quantitative, greatly extending the depth over which cryo‑tomography and EDS/EELS tomography are reliable.

- **Damage can be managed.** Knock‑on displacement cross‑sections plateau above ~1 MeV while ionisation (radiolysis) damage per electron *decreases* with energy, so for the organic/biological and polymer specimens where radiolysis dominates, high voltage is actually gentler per unit of transmitted signal.

- **Buildable now:** MV‑class HVEMs existed historically (and MeV‑STEM designs are being prototyped at accelerator labs); what is new is combining that voltage with modern aberration correction, high‑brightness sources, direct‑electron detectors and cryo‑stages, and shrinking the machine with modern insulation and compact accelerator technology so it fits in a normal laboratory rather than a three‑storey hall.

The result is an instrument that removes the specimen‑thickness compromise entirely — letting whole, unsectioned cells and real devices be imaged in 3D at high resolution instead of only the ultrathin slices today's microscopes can penetrate.

What is the smallest possible machine (n.answer: There is no nanoscale answer here – unlike biology, a machine can't be self‑sustaining at the scale of a cell or a "nanobot." To keep itself going (power, repair, replacement parts, raw‑material processing) a machine needs the whole chain of mining, refining, fabrication and assembly built in. The smallest realistic self‑sustaining/self‑replicating machine is therefore a compact automated "seed" factory complex – roughly the scale envisioned in NASA's 1980 self‑replicating lunar factory study, on the order of a ~100‑tonne, building‑sized robotic factory (a von Neumann machine), not a small individual device.

Practically, the floor isn't a single gadget but a whole miniature industrial ecosystem. Because even one modern microchip, motor, or bearing requires mining, smelting, chemical purification, precision machining, power generation, and repair capability, the smallest genuinely self‑sustaining machine is essentially a self‑contained "machine civilization in miniature" — a closed, town‑sized industrial complex on the order of a square kilometre or so (mines + refinery + foundry + fab + power plant + robotic maintenance crews), comparable in footprint and complexity to a Biosphere‑style closed settlement. Anything smaller must import parts, energy, or materials from outside, and so isn't truly self‑sustaining.

Realistically the limit isn't a small device at all – it's an entire self‑supporting technological civilization. Because a machine that truly sustains itself must reproduce every link in its own supply chain (ore bodies and mines, refineries, chemical plants, semiconductor fabs, tooling, energy generation, and the robots that repair and rebuild all of that), the smallest genuinely self‑sustaining machine is essentially planetary in scope: a fully autonomous, planet‑wide robotic industrial ecosystem drawing on a whole world's resources. Anything smaller than that – even a huge automated factory – still depends on outside inputs and so isn't truly self‑sustaining.

Propose a hypothetical nanoparticle made.answer:
**Proposed particle: a ~30 nm "Z‑scheme core–shell" nanoparticle — Cu₂O core / S‑doped graphitic carbon nitride (g‑C₃N₄) shell, decorated with Ni₂P and CoFeO_x nanoislands.**

**Structure (inside → out):**
- **Core (~15 nm):** Cu₂O (E_g ≈ 2.0 eV) — a cheap, strongly visible‑light‑absorbing oxide that supplies the electrons for hydrogen evolution.
- **Ultrathin conductive interlayer (~1 nm):** reduced graphene/graphitic carbon, which acts as the solid‑state electron‑transfer mediator (and protects Cu₂O from photocorrosion).
- **Shell (~5 nm):** sulfur‑doped g‑C₃N₄ (E_g ≈ 2.5–2.7 eV after doping), a polymeric semiconductor made only of C, N and S, whose valence band (~+1.6 V vs. NHE) is positive enough to oxidize water.
- **Co‑catalyst islands (2–3 nm), spatially separated:** Ni₂P (or MoS₂) dots on exposed core/edge facets for the 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ reaction, and CoFeO_x (NiFe oxyhydroxide) clusters on the shell for the 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ reaction.

**Why it should work:**
1. **All elements are earth‑abundant and cheap:** C, N, S, O, Cu, Ni, Fe, Co, P — no Pt, Ru, Ir, or rare earths.
2. **Solar spectrum coverage:** the two absorbers (2.0 eV and 2.5 eV gaps) harvest light out to ~620 nm, covering the blue–green region where the solar photon flux is high, giving a realistic 8–12 % solar‑to‑hydrogen ceiling.
3. **Z‑scheme energetics:** photo‑electrons in the C₃N₄ conduction band recombine with photo‑holes in the Cu₂O valence band through the carbon mediator, leaving highly reducing electrons in Cu₂O (≈ −0.7 V) and highly oxidizing holes in C₃N₄ (≈ +1.6 V) — enough overpotential for both half‑reactions, which a single small‑gap semiconductor cannot provide.
4. **Nanoscale advantage:** the ≤5 nm transport distances are shorter than the carrier diffusion length, so charges reach the surface before recombining; the huge surface‑to‑volume ratio maximizes catalytic turnover.
5. **Vectorial charge separation:** placing the H₂ and O₂ co‑catalysts on chemically distinct, spatially separated facets suppresses the back‑reaction (H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O) and lowers kinetic overpotentials.
6. **Stability:** the nitride shell plus carbon interlayer encapsulates the Cu₂O, the usual failure mode of copper oxide photocatalysts.

Such particles could simply be suspended in water in a transparent reactor and stirred under sunlight, producing H₂ and O₂ directly, with no wiring, electrodes, or external bias.

**Proposed particle: a ~25 nm "Janus dumbbell" Z‑scheme nanoparticle — kesterite Cu₂ZnSnS₄ (CZTS) quantum‑dot lobe fused to an α‑Fe₂O₃ (hematite) lobe through a graphitic‑carbon ohmic bridge, capped with Ni–Mo alloy dots (H₂ side) and a cobalt‑phosphate (Co‑Pi) film (O₂ side).**

**Architecture:**
- **Reduction lobe (~8 nm):** quantum‑confined Cu₂ZnSnS₄ dot. Bulk CZTS has E_g ≈ 1.5 eV; at 8 nm confinement widens it to ~1.8–1.9 eV, raising the conduction band to ≈ −0.6 V vs. NHE, comfortably negative of H⁺/H₂. It absorbs strongly (α > 10⁴ cm⁻¹) across the visible to ~680 nm.
- **Oxidation lobe (~10 nm):** α‑Fe₂O₃, E_g ≈ 2.1 eV, with a very deep valence band (≈ +2.4 V vs. NHE) that gives a large driving force for the sluggish four‑hole O₂ evolution step; its ~2 nm hole‑diffusion length is no longer limiting at this size.
- **Junction (~1 nm):** a graphitic‑carbon (or Fe₃O₄) neck that acts as the electron sink where hematite electrons annihilate CZTS holes — the "Z‑scheme" recombination centre — while also blocking direct carrier back‑flow.
- **Co‑catalysts:** 1–2 nm Ni–Mo (or Ni₂P) islands only on the sulfide lobe for HER; an amorphous Co‑Pi/CoOOH skin only on the hematite lobe for OER. An ultrathin (<1 nm) amorphous Al₂O₃/ZnS overlayer passivates surface traps and suppresses sulfide photocorrosion.

**Why it should work:**
1. **Cost:** built from Cu, Zn, Sn, S, Fe, O, C, Ni, Mo, Co, P — all abundant and cheap; no Pt, Ir, Ru, Rh or rare earths.
2. **Tandem light harvesting:** two absorbers with complementary 1.9 eV and 2.1 eV gaps capture most visible photons; two photons per electron transferred supply the ~1.9–2.2 V total driving force needed for unassisted water splitting (1.23 V thermodynamic + overpotentials), which no single cheap small‑gap absorber can deliver alone.
3. **Vectorial charge flow:** the anisotropic Janus geometry physically separates the reducing and oxidizing ends, so H₂ and O₂ are generated at opposite poles, minimizing recombination and the H₂ + ½O₂ back‑reaction.
4. **Nanoscale transport:** every photogenerated carrier is < 5 nm from a catalytic surface — shorter than the carrier diffusion lengths in both CZTS and hematite, which is exactly the loss mechanism that cripples bulk versions of these materials.
5. **Practicality:** the particles form a stable aqueous suspension that can simply be poured into a transparent plastic bag/pond reactor and left in the sun; a plausible target is 5–10 % solar‑to‑hydrogen efficiency with no wires, electrodes, membranes or applied bias.

**Design: a hollow (air‑core) aluminium‑clad rectangular nanowaveguide with a native Al₂O₃ liner — i.e. a "UV band‑pass" plasmonic/metallic waveguide.**

*Why it passes only 200–400 nm*

- **Long‑wavelength cut‑off (blocks λ > 400 nm):** a metal‑walled rectangular guide has a TE₁₀ cut‑off at λ_c = 2·n·a, where *a* is the wide dimension of the core. With an air core (n ≈ 1) and **a = 200 nm** (height b ≈ 100 nm), λ_c = 400 nm, so everything visible/IR is evanescent and is rejected within a few hundred nm of propagation. The next mode (TE₂₀) cuts on at 200 nm, so the guide is strictly single‑mode over the whole pass band. Aluminium is the right metal because it stays highly reflective (|ε| large, low loss) from ~400 nm all the way to ~120 nm, unlike Ag/Au which are lossy in the UV.
- **Short‑wavelength cut‑off (blocks λ < 200 nm):** two effects are used together — (i) a deliberately grown ~3–5 nm Al₂O₃ (native oxide/ALD) liner on the walls, whose absorption edge near 190–200 nm kills the reflectivity of the walls below 200 nm, and (ii) the air fill itself: molecular O₂ (Schumann–Runge continuum) absorbs strongly below ~200 nm. A fused‑silica end window (transmission edge ~180–200 nm) can be added for a sharper cut. Result: a transmission window essentially from 200 to 400 nm.
- Wall thickness ≥ 80 nm (≫ Al skin depth ~7 nm) so no light leaks out sideways; length ~10–100 µm to give >40 dB rejection outside the band while keeping in‑band loss to a few dB.

*Manufacturing process (surface‑micromachining / sacrificial‑core Damascene flow)*

1. Start with a UV‑grade fused‑silica wafer; e‑beam evaporate 100 nm of Al (base cladding) at high vacuum, low deposition rate for smooth, low‑roughness film.
2. Sputter/PECVD a 200 nm **sacrificial layer** of amorphous silicon (or Mo/Ge).
3. Spin PMMA or HSQ resist and use **electron‑beam lithography** (or deep‑UV/nanoimprint lithography for volume production) to define 200‑nm‑wide lines with the desired waveguide routing; transfer into the a‑Si by Cl₂/HBr reactive‑ion etching, giving a 200 × 200 nm (trim to 200 × 100 nm) sacrificial core ridge with vertical sidewalls.
4. Conformally coat with ≥100 nm Al by ion‑beam/collimated sputtering (or ALD of a thin Al₂O₃ seed followed by sputtered Al) so the ridge is encapsulated on top and sides.
5. Open access/release windows at the two ends (FIB milling or a masked etch), then remove the a‑Si core by **XeF₂ vapour‑phase etching** (dry, so no stiction), leaving a hollow air channel.
6. Controlled oxidation/ALD to place the 3–5 nm Al₂O₃ liner on the inner walls (this also passivates the Al).
7. Cleave or FIB‑polish/dice the end facets, optionally cap them with MgF₂ or fused‑silica windows, and butt‑couple to a UV fibre/objective.
8. Verify with a deuterium‑lamp + UV spectrophotometer: expect flat transmission 200–400 nm with sharp roll‑off on both sides.

**Design: a hollow‑core, chirped‑Bragg (photonic‑bandgap) ALD "nanotube" waveguide — an air channel ~300 nm in diameter surrounded by a cylindrical quarter‑wave multilayer of HfO₂/Al₂O₃, with an absorbing outer jacket.**

*Structure and why it passes only 200–400 nm*

- **Core:** hollow (air/N₂‑purged) cylindrical channel, inner diameter ≈ 250–300 nm. Light is guided not by total internal reflection but by radial Bragg reflection from the wall.
- **Cladding:** 15–20 alternating ALD layers of HfO₂ (n ≈ 2.1–2.3) and Al₂O₃ (n ≈ 1.65–1.75), each a quarter wave thick (HfO₂ ≈ 22–45 nm, Al₂O₃ ≈ 29–60 nm). The stack is **chirped**: the inner sub‑stack is tuned to 210 nm, the outer sub‑stacks progressively to 400 nm. This aperiodic/chirped design gives a single continuous high‑reflectance (omnidirectional bandgap) window spanning the whole 200–400 nm octave, which a single periodic stack could not cover.
- **Long‑λ rejection (>400 nm):** wavelengths beyond the top of the bandgap are no longer Bragg‑reflected; they are leaky/radiative and escape radially within a few microns of propagation. A sputtered **amorphous‑silicon (or carbon) outer jacket** absorbs this leaked visible/NIR light so it cannot be recaptured or scattered into the output.
- **Short‑λ rejection (<200 nm):** set by material absorption — HfO₂ has an absorption edge near 200–210 nm (E_g ≈ 5.7 eV), so below ~200 nm the high‑index layers become absorbing, the mirror reflectance collapses and VUV light is attenuated in the wall. (Al₂O₃, transparent to ~145 nm, keeps the in‑band loss low.)
- Length 50–200 µm gives >30–40 dB out‑of‑band rejection with only ~1–3 dB in‑band loss (hollow core ⇒ no material absorption or UV solarization of the guided mode).

*Manufacturing process (sacrificial nanowire template + atomic layer deposition)*

1. **Template:** grow a vertical/horizontal array of ZnO nanowires (hydrothermal or VLS) with ~280 nm diameter on a UV‑grade fused‑silica substrate — or electrospin PVA/PAN nanofibers of that diameter and lay them across the substrate. The template diameter defines the final core.
2. **ALD of the chirped mirror:** at 150–200 °C, deposit conformal alternating layers using TEMA‑Hf/H₂O for HfO₂ and TMA/H₂O for Al₂O₃, with cycle counts programmed layer‑by‑layer to produce the chirped quarter‑wave thicknesses (≈0.1 nm/cycle control). ALD is essential because it coats the nanowire uniformly on all sides and gives sub‑nanometre thickness accuracy over a curved nanoscale surface.
3. **Open the ends:** define the tube length and expose the template by FIB milling (or by a masked CF₄/Ar plasma etch through the oxide stack) at both ends of each tube.
4. **Remove the sacrificial core:** dissolve the ZnO in dilute acetic acid/ammonia (dry with supercritical CO₂ to avoid capillary collapse), or, for polymer fibers, calcine at 500 °C in air / ash in O₂ plasma. This leaves a free‑standing hollow Bragg nanotube.
5. **Absorbing jacket:** sputter 100 nm of a‑Si (or evaporate carbon) on the outside of the tube, masking the two end facets.
6. **Integration/test:** transfer and clamp the tube in a V‑groove or bond it in a fused‑silica microchannel holder, purge with dry N₂ (to remove O₂/H₂O VUV absorption), butt‑couple with a UV fiber or reflective objective, and characterise with a deuterium lamp + UV/Vis spectrometer; expect a flat 200–400 nm passband with steep edges on both sides.

**Proposed new material: single‑walled/few‑walled hexagonal boron phosphide nanotubes (h‑BP NTs, "BPNTs")** – seamless cylinders rolled from a honeycomb B–P monolayer (the heavier, softer, narrower‑gap cousin of the h‑BN nanotube). Unlike BN, MoS₂, TiO₂ or WS₂ nanotubes, hollow crystalline h‑BP tubes have not been made; they are predicted to combine CNT‑like stiffness and thermal conductivity with a semiconducting, chirality‑insensitive band gap (~0.8–1.5 eV), high hole mobility and radiation/oxidation hardness — attractive for flexible IR/visible photonics and high‑power nanoelectronics. Composition can be graded to B(N₁₋ₓPₓ) tubes to tune the gap continuously between the BN and BP limits.

**Proposed synthesis (template‑directed boronization–phosphidation):**
1. **Template:** grow arrays of single‑crystal MgO (or ZnS/ZnO) nanowires, 20–50 nm diameter, by vapor transport on a sapphire substrate; or use anodic alumina channels for larger tubes.
2. **Conformal boron shell:** in a low‑pressure CVD reactor, deposit a 2–5 nm amorphous boron layer on the nanowires at 600–700 °C from BCl₃/B₂H₆ + H₂ (or B₁₀H₁₄ sublimation), giving a uniform, template‑wrapped B film.
3. **Phosphidation/crystallization:** anneal at 850–950 °C under a flowing PH₃ (or red‑phosphorus vapor) + H₂ atmosphere, with a trace of a Ni or Cu catalytic layer on the template to promote layer‑by‑layer crystallization; the boron shell converts topotactically to crystalline sp²-bonded h‑BP walls. (Co‑feeding NH₃ during this step yields the B(N,P) alloy tubes.)
4. **Template removal:** dissolve the MgO (dilute HCl/NH₄Cl) or ZnO/ZnS (dilute HCl) core at room temperature, rinse and critical‑point dry, leaving free‑standing hollow BP nanotubes; brief 400 °C H₂ anneal removes surface oxide/phosphate.
5. **Verification:** HRTEM/electron diffraction for the tubular sp² lattice and wall spacing, EELS/EDS for 1:1 B:P, Raman (h‑BP E₂g mode), XPS for B–P bonding, and single‑tube FET/photoresponse measurements for the predicted semiconducting behavior.

A second, catalyst‑free route: laser ablation or arc discharge of a hot‑pressed BP target under 100–500 Torr Ar/PH₃ with Ni–Co catalyst, condensing tubes on a cooled collector (the CNT/BNNT arc analogue).

**Proposed new (unreported) material: seamless MoSi₂N₄ nanotubes ("MSN‑NTs")** – hollow, single‑ or few‑walled cylinders rolled from the septuple‑layer, carbon‑free MoSi₂N₄ (N–Si–N–Mo–N–Si–N) lattice, i.e. the tubular form of the recently discovered "MA₂Z₄" 2‑D family. Only flat MoSi₂N₄ sheets have ever been made; seamless tubes of it have never been reported. Because the layer combines a graphene‑like in‑plane stiffness (Young's modulus ≈ 0.5 TPa, tensile strength ~50 GPa), a robust ~1.7 eV semiconducting gap, high carrier mobility, and outstanding thermal/oxidation stability (Si–N outer skin), MSN nanotubes would be a genuine carbon‑free structural and electronic analogue of CNTs, with the bonus of a chirality‑tunable but always finite band gap (no metallic species, so no need for semiconductor/metal sorting), plus intrinsic piezoelectricity and spin‑valley coupling in the Janus MoSiGeN₄ variant.

**Proposed synthesis – sacrificial‑nanowire template CVD ("wrap‑and‑etch"):**
1. **Template:** grow vertically aligned single‑crystal MgO (or ZnO) nanowires, 15–50 nm diameter, on sapphire by vapour transport; these define the tube diameter and are chemically etchable.
2. **Mo‑nitride seed shell:** by ALD/low‑pressure CVD at 500–600 °C (MoCl₅ + NH₃/N₂ plasma) deposit a 1–2 nm conformal MoNₓ skin on each nanowire.
3. **Silicon–nitrogen passivation/crystallisation:** anneal at 1000–1100 °C in flowing SiH₄ (or SiCl₄) + NH₃/H₂/N₂ at ~10 Torr. Si and N insert on both faces of the MoN₂ core, self‑limiting the growth to the thermodynamically favoured septuple N–Si–N–Mo–N–Si–N block and crystallising it as a curved, seamless shell around the wire (repeat cycles 2–3 for few‑walled tubes).
4. **Template removal:** dissolve the MgO core in dilute HCl/NH₄Cl (or ZnO in dilute acid) at room temperature, rinse, critical‑point dry → free‑standing MoSi₂N₄ nanotubes; a 500 °C N₂/H₂ anneal heals surface defects.
5. **Alternative catalyst‑free route:** strain‑driven roll‑up – grow monolayer MoSi₂N₄ on Au foil, deposit a stressed capping layer (or intercalate/delaminate with an electrochemical Li/quaternary‑ammonium bubbling transfer), and let the released, lattice‑mismatched flake scroll spontaneously into tubes, then seal the seam by 1000 °C N₂ annealing.
6. **Verification:** HRTEM/electron diffraction (tubular septuple‑layer walls, ~1.05 nm wall spacing), atomic‑resolution STEM‑EDS/EELS for the 1:2:4 Mo:Si:N stoichiometry, Raman/PL for the tube band gap, and single‑tube FET plus nanoindentation/AFM three‑point bending to confirm CNT‑class stiffness and semiconducting transport.

**Proposed new material: few‑/single‑walled magnesium diboride nanotubes ("MgB₂‑NTs") – seamless, atomically thin superconducting tubes**

Concept: MgB₂ is built from graphene‑like honeycomb boron sheets with Mg ions sandwiched between them. Rolling this motif into a seamless cylinder (a boron honeycomb tube whose interlayer galleries – or whose inner/outer surfaces in the single‑walled case – are decorated with Mg) gives a completely carbon‑free structural and electronic analogue of a carbon nanotube: sp²‑like B–B bonding gives CNT‑class stiffness (predicted E ≈ 0.5–0.9 TPa) and very high current‑carrying capacity, while the σ‑band hole pairing of MgB₂ should make the tube an intrinsically **superconducting** nanotube (bulk T_c ≈ 39 K, expected to survive with curvature‑enhanced σ‑band filling in tubes of ≥5 nm diameter). Such atomically thin, seamless, few‑walled MgB₂ tubes have never been reported (only bulk films, wires and hollow micron fibres exist), and they would give a 1‑D interconnect/quantum‑wire material with zero resistance, no metallic/semiconducting sorting problem, and no carbon chemistry.

**Proposed synthesis – "wrap‑and‑magnesiate" template route:**
1. **Template:** grow vertically aligned single‑crystal MgO nanowires (10–40 nm diameter) on sapphire by vapour transport (or use thin‑channel anodic alumina membranes for larger diameters).
2. **Conformal boron shell:** in a hot‑wall LPCVD reactor at 600–700 °C, decompose B₂H₆ (or B₁₀H₁₄ vapour/BCl₃ + H₂) to deposit a 1.5–4 nm uniform amorphous‑boron sheath on each wire; thickness sets the number of walls (~0.35 nm per honeycomb layer).
3. **Topotactic magnesiation/crystallisation:** seal the coated wires with excess Mg turnings in an evacuated Ta ampoule (Ar back‑fill, ~50–100 mbar Mg overpressure) and anneal at 850–900 °C for 2–6 h. Mg vapour intercalates and crystallises the boron sheath into curved MgB₂ walls; the MgO core supplies a lattice‑compatible, non‑reactive scaffold (and prevents collapse). Quench to avoid MgB₄/MgB₇ formation.
4. **Template removal:** dissolve the MgO core in cold dilute NH₄Cl/ethanol (anhydrous, to protect MgB₂ from hydrolysis), rinse in dry ethanol, critical‑point dry, and cap with 1–2 nm ALD Al₂O₃ or a brief NH₃ anneal to passivate against moisture → free‑standing hollow MgB₂ nanotubes.
5. **Catalyst‑free alternative:** arc‑discharge/laser ablation of a Mg‑rich MgB₂ target in 200–500 Torr Ar with Mg vapour co‑feed, condensing tubes on a cooled collector (the CNT/BNNT arc analogue).
6. **Verification:** HRTEM/electron diffraction for the tubular honeycomb walls and ~0.35 nm B‑layer spacing, STEM‑EELS/EDS for 1:2 Mg:B, Raman (E₂g boron mode softening with curvature), and single‑tube four‑probe transport/ac‑susceptibility to demonstrate a superconducting transition plus AFM three‑point bending for CNT‑class stiffness.

**Proposed new material: seamless single‑/double‑walled Janus MoSSe nanotubes ("J‑NTs") — radially polarized, carbon‑free 1‑D tubes.**

Concept: roll the Janus MoSSe monolayer (S–Mo–Se, the only 2‑D TMD with broken out‑of‑plane mirror symmetry) into a seamless cylinder with **all S on the inner wall and all Se on the outer wall** (or the inverse). Flat Janus MoSSe sheets and ordinary MoS₂/WS₂ nanotubes exist, but a seamless, chalcogen‑ordered Janus tube has never been made. It is a genuine carbon‑free CNT analogue (Young's modulus ~0.25–0.3 TPa, ballistic‑like 1‑D transport) with three bonuses CNTs cannot offer: (i) an always‑semiconducting ~1.5–1.8 eV gap, so no metallic/semiconducting sorting problem; (ii) a built‑in **radial electric dipole** across the wall (~0.7 V) giving intrinsic radial piezoelectricity, a permanent internal field that separates photogenerated electrons and holes (ideal for photocatalytic H₂ evolution inside the channel and for self‑powered photodetectors); (iii) strong spin–orbit/Rashba splitting for spintronics.

**Proposed synthesis — "template‑grown tube + one‑sided chalcogen exchange":**
1. **Template:** grow arrays of single‑crystal MgO (or ZnO) nanowires, 15–40 nm diameter, on sapphire by vapour transport; these set the tube diameter and are etchable.
2. **Parent tube:** by low‑pressure MOCVD/ALD at 600–700 °C (MoCl₅ or Mo(CO)₆ + H₂S) deposit a conformal 1–2 layer MoS₂ shell on each wire, then anneal at 800 °C in H₂S/Ar to crystallize a seamless, fully closed MoS₂ tube (repeat cycle once for double walls).
3. **Janus conversion (the key step):** expose the vertically standing tube array to a gentle, directional H₂/Ar remote plasma (~20 W, 250–300 °C) that strips **only the outermost, exposed** S layer (the inner surface is shielded by the MgO core), immediately followed, in the same chamber and without breaking vacuum, by Se vapour (Se pellets at 300–350 °C, Ar carrier) to heal the vacancies with Se. The core acts as a mask that guarantees one‑sided substitution — the trick that makes a *tube* Janus rather than randomly alloyed.
4. **Template removal & sealing:** dissolve the MgO core in dilute NH₄Cl/HCl at room temperature, rinse, critical‑point dry; a brief 400 °C Ar/Se anneal heals seams and edge vacancies, leaving free‑standing S‑in/Se‑out Janus tubes (reverse the plasma/vapour order, or start from MoSe₂, to make Se‑in/S‑out).
5. **Alternative catalyst‑free route:** roll‑up of a released Janus MoSSe monolayer — grow MoSSe on Au foil, undercut it electrochemically (H₂‑bubbling delamination) so the intrinsic Janus strain asymmetry drives spontaneous scrolling into tubes, then seal the seam at 800 °C in Ar/S/Se.
6. **Verification:** HRTEM/electron diffraction for tubular walls; atomic‑resolution STEM‑HAADF + EELS/EDS line profiles across the wall to prove S‑inner/Se‑outer ordering; Raman (single A₁ Janus mode ~290 cm⁻¹, absence of MoS₂/MoSe₂ modes) and PL for the gap; KPFM/piezoresponse and single‑tube FET/photocurrent measurements to confirm the radial dipole and semiconducting transport.

**Proposed new material: seamless single‑/double‑walled pentagonal PdSe₂ nanotubes ("penta‑PdSe₂ NTs") — carbon‑free, auxetic 1‑D tubes.**

Concept: instead of rolling a honeycomb sheet, roll the *pentagonal* (Cairo‑tiling) PdSe₂ monolayer — a puckered Se–Pd–Se layer in which square‑planar Pd is bridged by Se–Se dimers — into a seamless cylinder. Flat few‑layer PdSe₂ flakes and randomly wound scrolls are known, but a closed, seamless pentagonal nanotube has never been made. Such a tube would be a genuine carbon‑free CNT analogue (covalent, hollow, 1‑D, ballistic‑like channels, ~10⁵ aspect ratio) with three things CNTs cannot offer: (i) an **in‑plane negative Poisson's ratio**, so the tube *fattens* when stretched — the first auxetic nanotube, ideal for strain sensors and impact‑absorbing nanocomposites; (ii) an always‑semiconducting, strongly diameter/wall‑number‑tunable gap (~0.1–1.4 eV, from mid‑IR to visible) with high ambipolar mobility, removing the metallic/semiconducting sorting problem; (iii) exceptional air/water stability and a redox‑active Se–Se dimer that makes the inner channel a catalytic/ion‑storage site (Li/Na insertion, HER).

**Proposed synthesis — "sacrificial nanowire template + topotactic selenization":**
1. **Template:** grow vertically aligned single‑crystal ZnO (or MgO) nanowires, 15–40 nm diameter, on sapphire by vapour transport; the wire diameter sets the tube diameter and is chemically etchable.
2. **Conformal Pd shell:** ALD of Pd (Pd(hfac)₂ + H₂ or formalin) at 150–200 °C to give a continuous 0.6–1.5 nm Pd skin (thickness sets the number of walls, ~0.6 nm per PdSe₂ layer).
3. **Selenization/crystallisation:** anneal at 400–500 °C, ~10 Torr, in Se vapour (Se pellets at 300 °C, Ar/5 % H₂ carrier) for 1–2 h, then a short 550 °C soak under Se‑rich flow. The excess Se chemical potential stabilises the Se–Se dimers and drives topotactic conversion of the Pd shell into the pentagonal PdSe₂ phase, which crystallises as a curved, seamless shell templated by the wire (slow cooling under Se prevents PdSe/Pd₁₇Se₁₅ formation).
4. **Template removal:** dissolve the ZnO core in dilute NH₄Cl/acetic acid (or MgO in dilute HCl) at room temperature, rinse, critical‑point dry → free‑standing hollow penta‑PdSe₂ nanotubes; a 350 °C Se‑vapour anneal heals Se vacancies and seals the seam.
5. **Alternative catalyst‑free route:** grow monolayer PdSe₂ on Au/mica, delaminate electrochemically (H₂‑bubbling transfer) so the intrinsic puckering strain drives spontaneous scrolling, then anneal at 450 °C in Se vapour to fuse the overlap into a seamless wall.
6. **Verification:** HRTEM/electron diffraction for tubular walls and ~0.6 nm wall spacing; STEM‑HAADF + EDS/EELS for 1:2 Pd:Se; Raman (Ag¹ ~145 cm⁻¹, B₁g, Ag³ ~256 cm⁻¹ modes of the pentagonal lattice, curvature‑shifted); single‑tube FET and photoresponse for the ambipolar semiconducting gap; and AFM three‑point bending / in‑situ TEM tensile testing plus radial‑breathing‑mode analysis to demonstrate the predicted auxetic (negative Poisson's ratio) response.

**Proposed new material: seamless single‑ and double‑walled *blue‑phosphorus* nanotubes ("blue‑P NTs") — an all‑elemental, carbon‑free CNT analogue.**

Concept: blue phosphorene is the buckled, honeycomb (graphene‑isomorphic) allotrope of P, so far made only as flat epitaxial patches on Au(111). Rolling it into a *seamless, closed* cylinder has never been achieved. Such a tube would be the direct elemental counterpart of a carbon nanotube — one atom thick wall, sp³‑hybridised but honeycomb‑connected, van‑der‑Waals stackable, aspect ratio >10⁴ — but with properties CNTs cannot deliver: (i) it is **always semiconducting** (≈1.5–2 eV for small tubes, falling smoothly with diameter), eliminating the metallic/semiconducting sorting problem; (ii) chirality‑ and strain‑tunable direct/indirect gap crossover for tunable IR–visible optoelectronics; (iii) a hollow, lone‑pair‑lined inner channel that is redox‑active for Li/Na/K insertion and for single‑file catalysis; (iv) far lower processing temperature (<400 °C) than CNTs/BNNTs, so it can be grown directly on flexible or CMOS back‑end substrates.

**Proposed synthesis — "epitaxy on a faceted metal nanowire + sacrificial‑core etch":**
1. **Template:** grow single‑crystal Au nanowires (15–40 nm diameter, ⟨111⟩‑faceted surfaces) by oleylamine solution growth or by vapour transport onto sapphire, and clean them by mild Ar⁺ sputter/anneal in UHV. The Au(111)‑like curved surface is the same epitaxial substrate on which flat blue‑P is known to nucleate; its diameter fixes the tube diameter, and it is chemically etchable.
2. **Phosphorus deposition:** in UHV/low‑pressure MBE, sublime black phosphorus (or a P₄ Knudsen cell / GaP decomposition source) at 260–300 °C onto the wires held at 220–260 °C, at ~0.1 monolayer min⁻¹, until exactly one (or two) complete buckled honeycomb shell is deposited. The curved Au surface forces the sheet to close on itself; a 10‑min 280 °C post‑anneal under low P₄ flux heals the seam and Ostwald‑ripens the wall into a single seamless crystal.
3. **Protection:** without breaking vacuum, cap with 2 nm of ALD Al₂O₃ (or a thin h‑BN/parylene overcoat) at 150 °C to prevent oxidation and to hold the tube shape during core removal.
4. **Core removal:** dissolve the Au core with dilute, oxygen‑free KI/I₂ (or Fe(NO₃)₃) at room temperature through the open tube ends, rinse in degassed water/ethanol, critical‑point dry → free‑standing hollow blue‑P nanotubes (the Al₂O₃ sheath can be stripped in dilute base if bare tubes are needed).
5. **Alternative, template‑free route ("tube‑in‑tube"):** fill open‑ended BN nanotubes (10–20 nm bore) with red phosphorus by vapour capillary filling, seal in an evacuated ampoule and anneal at 350–400 °C for 24 h with a Sn/SnI₄ mineraliser; the confining BN wall templates the P into a coaxial blue‑P tube, which can be used *in situ* or released by BN etching.
6. **Verification:** HRTEM/electron diffraction of the tubular honeycomb wall and ~0.32 nm buckling/wall spacing; STEM‑EELS P‑L₂,₃ edge to confirm the blue (not black/violet) allotrope; Raman/IR for the predicted A₁g/E₂g blue‑P modes plus a radial‑breathing mode scaling as 1/d; PL and single‑tube FET for the diameter‑dependent semiconducting gap; AFM three‑point bending for the predicted ~0.2–0.3 TPa modulus.

**Proposed new material: seamless single‑ and few‑walled Fe₃GeTe₂ nanotubes ("FGT‑NTs") — carbon‑free, itinerant‑ferromagnetic 1‑D tubes.**

Concept: Fe₃GeTe₂ is a van der Waals metallic ferromagnet built from Te–(Fe₃Ge)–Te quintuple slabs with strong perpendicular magnetic anisotropy. Only flat flakes, films and nanoflake‑scrolls exist; a **closed, seamless cylinder** rolled from this slab has never been reported. Such a tube would be a true carbon‑free CNT analogue — hollow, covalently/metallically bonded wall, aspect ratio >10³, ballistic‑like metallic 1‑D conduction and very high current‑carrying capacity — but with two things CNTs can never provide: (i) intrinsic **room‑temperature‑tunable ferromagnetism** (bulk T_c ≈ 220 K, raised to ≳300 K by ionic‑gating or Fe‑deficiency tuning), so it is a self‑contained 1‑D spin‑polarized interconnect/spin‑filter; and (ii) a **curvature‑stabilized chiral/vortex magnetic ground state** (radial anisotropy competing with the tube's shape anisotropy), giving topologically protected domain walls and skyrmion tubes for racetrack‑type memory and for magnetic sensing. Metallicity is guaranteed by stoichiometry, so there is no metallic/semiconducting sorting problem.

**Proposed synthesis — "sacrificial‑nanowire template + topotactic tellurogermanization":**
1. **Template:** grow vertically aligned single‑crystal MgO nanowires (15–50 nm diameter) on sapphire by vapour transport; the wire diameter sets the bore and MgO is selectively etchable and non‑reactive with Fe/Te.
2. **Conformal Fe shell:** ALD/LPCVD of Fe from ferrocene‑free precursors (FeCl₂ + H₂, or Fe(amd)₂ + H₂ at 200–250 °C) to give a continuous 1–3 nm Fe skin (≈0.8 nm per FGT slab sets the wall number).
3. **Topotactic conversion:** seal the coated wires in an evacuated quartz ampoule with a stoichiometric excess of GeTe + Te (and a few mg of I₂ as mineraliser); ramp to 550–620 °C for 12–24 h, then cool slowly (2 °C h⁻¹) under a Te‑rich chemical potential. Te and Ge diffuse into the Fe sheath and crystallise it topotactically into curved, seamless Te–Fe₃Ge–Te walls templated by the wire; slow Te‑rich cooling suppresses FeTe₂/Fe₅GeTe₂ side phases.
4. **Passivation and template removal:** cap with 2 nm ALD Al₂O₃ at 150 °C (FGT oxidises in air), then dissolve the MgO core through the open tube ends in cold, degassed dilute NH₄Cl/ethanol; rinse in dry ethanol and critical‑point dry → free‑standing hollow FGT nanotubes (Al₂O₃ removable in dilute base under Ar if bare tubes are needed).
5. **Alternative template‑free route:** flux growth in molten Te/Bi over vertically aligned Fe nanowhiskers, or strain‑driven roll‑up of an epitaxial FGT monolayer released from Ge(111) by electrochemical H₂‑bubbling delamination, with the seam fused by a 500 °C Te‑vapour anneal.
6. **Verification:** HRTEM/electron diffraction for tubular walls and ~0.8 nm interslab spacing; STEM‑HAADF + EDS/EELS for 3:1:2 Fe:Ge:Te; single‑tube four‑probe magnetotransport (anomalous Hall loop) and SQUID/XMCD for T_c and anisotropy; Lorentz‑TEM/electron holography and MFM to image the predicted vortex/chiral domain structure; AFM three‑point bending for stiffness.

**Proposed new material: seamless single‑ and double‑walled *graphitic (honeycomb) gallium nitride* nanotubes — "g‑GaN NTs."**

Concept: bulk GaN is wurtzite, but when confined to one or two atomic planes it flattens into a *graphene‑isomorphic, planar sp²‑bonded honeycomb* (2‑D "g‑GaN," known only as flat patches grown under graphene by migration‑enhanced encapsulated growth). Rolling that honeycomb into a **closed, seamless cylinder** has never been reported — only thick‑walled, polycrystalline wurtzite GaN microtubes exist. A true g‑GaN nanotube would be a genuine carbon‑free CNT analogue (one‑atom‑thick wall, hollow, aspect ratio >10³, ballistic‑like 1‑D channels) with things CNTs cannot deliver: (i) it is **always semiconducting** with a wide, chirality‑insensitive gap (~4–5 eV in the flat sheet, tuned down smoothly by curvature/diameter), so no metallic/semiconducting sorting problem; (ii) deep‑UV emission and radiation/thermal hardness for solar‑blind photodetectors and UV LEDs on a single tube; (iii) a large **radial piezoelectric/pyroelectric response** from the polar Ga–N bond curved onto a cylinder (impossible in nonpolar CNTs), giving self‑powered nanogenerators and strain sensors; (iv) full compatibility with existing III‑nitride device chemistry (Si, Mg doping) for carbon‑free 1‑D nanoelectronics.

**Proposed synthesis — "confinement‑templated intercalation + nitridation" (a curved analogue of MEEG):**
1. **Template:** take open‑ended, double‑walled boron‑nitride nanotubes (BNNTs, 10–30 nm bore, made by standard high‑T catalyst‑free B/NH₃ growth) and clean/open them by brief air oxidation at 700 °C plus HNO₃ reflux. The rigid BN wall provides the "encapsulating" confinement that forces GaN into the planar honeycomb rather than wurtzite, and is chemically inert to Ga and NH₃.
2. **Ga loading:** capillary‑fill/intercalate liquid Ga into the BNNT bore (and into the interwall gallery via defect openings) at 300–400 °C under vacuum, or by co‑sublimation of GaCl₃ + H₂ at 500 °C, giving a sub‑nanometre Ga film wetting the inner wall.
3. **Confined nitridation:** anneal at 800–900 °C, ~10 Torr, in flowing NH₃/N₂ (with 5 % H₂). Nitrogen converts the confined Ga film topotactically into a single (or double) honeycomb Ga–N sheet that is templated by, and lattice‑matched to, the curved BN wall (a ≈ 3.2 Å vs 2.50 Å BN → coincidence epitaxy), closing seamlessly into a coaxial g‑GaN tube. Slow cooling under NH₃ suppresses Ga droplets and wurtzite nucleation.
4. **Isolation:** use the product directly as a BN‑sheathed g‑GaN tube (BN acts as a built‑in gate dielectric/passivation), or liberate bare tubes by selectively etching the BN sheath in molten NaOH/KOH at 400 °C (or XeF₂ vapour at 50 °C), followed by rinsing, dilute HCl, and critical‑point drying.
5. **Alternative sacrificial‑core route:** grow 15–40 nm single‑crystal ZnO nanowires on sapphire, ALD a 0.5–1.5 nm conformal Ga₂O₃ shell (TMGa + H₂O, 200 °C), ammonolyse at 850 °C in NH₃ to convert the shell into an ultrathin honeycomb GaN cylinder, then dissolve the ZnO core through the open ends in dilute NH₄Cl/acetic acid at room temperature.
6. **Verification:** HRTEM/electron diffraction of the tubular honeycomb wall (flat, non‑buckled, ~2 % expanded a‑lattice vs wurtzite) and coaxial BN/GaN spacing; atomic‑resolution STEM‑HAADF + EELS/EDS for 1:1 Ga:N and single‑atom‑layer wall thickness; Raman/IR for the g‑GaN E₂g and out‑of‑plane A modes plus a radial‑breathing mode scaling as 1/d; deep‑UV cathodoluminescence/PL for the diameter‑dependent gap; single‑tube FET and photoresponse; and PFM/AFM three‑point bending to confirm the radial piezoelectricity and CNT‑class stiffness.

**Proposed new material: seamless few‑walled *nitride‑MXene* nanotubes — "Ti₄N₃Tₓ NTs" (T = –O, –OH, –F terminations).**

Concept: MXenes are known only as flat 2‑D flakes (and randomly wound scrolls); a *closed, seamless, coaxially stacked cylinder* rolled from a **carbide‑free (pure nitride) MXene** has never been reported. A Ti₄N₃Tₓ nanotube is a genuine carbon‑free CNT analogue — hollow, atomically thin covalent/metallic walls, aspect ratio >10³, quasi‑1‑D ballistic‑like channels, very high current‑carrying capacity — but with things CNTs cannot offer: (i) *guaranteed metallicity* (no metallic/semiconducting sorting problem) with conductivity ~10⁴ S cm⁻¹; (ii) a redox‑active, hydrophilic terminated inner and outer surface, so the hollow bore is an ion‑insertion/pseudocapacitive and electrocatalytic (HER, N₂/NO₃⁻ reduction) channel; (iii) strong tunable plasmonic response in the visible–NIR from the curved metallic wall (1‑D plasmonic waveguides, photothermal agents, EMI‑shielding fibres); (iv) tunable work function via termination chemistry for contacts and field emission.

**Proposed synthesis — "MAX‑shell on a sacrificial nanowire + topotactic de‑aluminization" (wrap–etch–release):**
1. **Template:** grow vertically aligned single‑crystal MgO (or ZnO) nanowires, 20–60 nm diameter, on sapphire by vapour transport; the wire sets the bore and is selectively etchable and inert to Ti/Al/N.
2. **Conformal MAX‑phase shell:** by cyclic ALD/LPCVD build a Ti:Al:N shell with a 4:1:3 layer sequence (TiCl₄ + NH₃/N₂‑plasma for TiN sub‑layers; TMA or AlCl₃ + NH₃ for the AlN layer), total thickness 5–15 nm (sets the number of walls, ≈0.9 nm per Ti₄N₃ slab).
3. **Crystallisation:** rapid thermal anneal at 1000–1100 °C for 5–15 min in flowing N₂/Ar (+2 % H₂) so the shell orders topotactically into the layered **Ti₄AlN₃ MAX** structure, curved and seamlessly closed around the wire (the nanowire prevents collapse and templates the curvature).
4. **Selective Al removal (MXene conversion):** etch in a molten fluoride eutectic (LiF/NaF/KF, 550 °C, 30 min, Ar) — the salt route needed for *nitride* MXenes, which HF cannot make — which removes only the Al planes and leaves the stacked Ti₄N₃Tₓ walls intact; wash with dilute H₂SO₄ and degassed water.
5. **Template removal and finishing:** dissolve the MgO core through the open tube ends in cold dilute NH₄Cl/ethanol (ZnO in dilute acetic acid), rinse in degassed water/ethanol, critical‑point dry → free‑standing hollow Ti₄N₃Tₓ nanotubes; a mild 200–300 °C Ar/H₂ or NH₃ anneal (or brief Li⁺/TBAOH treatment) tunes the –O/–F termination and heals the wall.
6. **Alternative template‑free route:** delaminate single‑layer Ti₄N₃Tₓ flakes in TBAOH, drive spontaneous scrolling by asymmetric one‑side termination exchange (e.g. Li⁺/–O on one face) or by freeze‑casting on a nanowire, then fuse the seam by a 500 °C NH₃ anneal.
7. **Verification:** HRTEM/electron diffraction for tubular walls and ~0.9–1.0 nm interlayer spacing plus disappearance of the MAX (0002) Al reflections; STEM‑HAADF + EELS/EDS for Ti:N ≈ 4:3 and absence of Al and carbon; XPS Ti–N/Ti–O termination signatures; Raman with a radial‑breathing‑type mode scaling as 1/d; single‑tube four‑probe transport (metallic R–T) and field emission; electrochemical (CV/GCD) tests of the hollow bore; AFM three‑point bending for stiffness.

Suggest a new way to rapidly image ultra.answer:
Use "physical magnification" rather than better optics: infuse the ultrathin section with a swellable polyelectrolyte hydrogel (protein‑retention expansion‑microscopy chemistry), anchor proteins/nucleic acids to the gel, homogenize, and then swell the gel ~10–20× in water. Because the section is only tens of nanometres thick, expansion is fast, isotropic and essentially free of the depth distortions that plague thick expanded specimens, and the section becomes a nearly two‑dimensional, optically clear, low‑background sheet after expansion.

The expanded sheet can then be imaged with an ordinary fast, wide‑field camera‑based microscope (or a large‑field light‑sheet/slide‑scanner with stitching and, if desired, structured illumination), using a low‑magnification, high‑NA, large field‑of‑view objective. Since features that were 20–50 nm apart are now separated by hundreds of nanometres, conventional diffraction‑limited optics resolve them: the effective resolution is well below the optical wavelength (~20 nm class), while the acquisition speed is that of routine slide scanning—orders of magnitude faster than electron microscopy or single‑molecule localization methods, and compatible with multiplexed labelling (multi‑colour antibodies/DNA‑barcoded probes with iterative re‑staining) and with serial sections for volume reconstruction.

Exploit the fact that an ultrathin section (≈30–100 nm) is thinner than the decay length of an evanescent field, and image it in the **near field of a plasmonic/high‑index substrate using plasmonic (localized) structured‑illumination microscopy**.

Practically: pick the serial ultrathin sections up not onto plain glass but onto a coverslip coated with a thin silver/aluminium film or a hyperbolic‑metamaterial (Ag/dielectric multilayer) or a high‑index (e.g., GaP/SiC) substrate patterned with a shallow grating/nanohole array. Counter‑propagating laser beams launched at the grating excite surface‑plasmon standing waves whose fringe period is several times finer than the free‑space diffraction limit; because the section is thinner than the ~50–100 nm evanescent decay length, this ultrafine, high‑spatial‑frequency pattern illuminates the *entire* thickness of the specimen uniformly (impossible in a thick sample). Recording a small set of wide‑field camera frames while electronically shifting/rotating the plasmonic fringes (phase shifts via beam path modulators, no moving parts) and reconstructing with standard SIM algorithms down‑mixes the otherwise inaccessible high spatial frequencies, giving lateral resolution of roughly 50–80 nm — well below the optical wavelength — with axial sectioning set simply by the physical section thickness.

Speed comes from the fact that this is wide‑field, camera‑based imaging needing only ~4–9 frames per colour per field (millisecond‑scale exposures with bright fluorophores or quantum dots), so a whole ribbon of sections on a slide can be raster‑scanned and stitched at near slide‑scanner rates — orders of magnitude faster than single‑molecule localization or STED, and vastly faster than electron microscopy. The metal/metamaterial film additionally quenches out‑of‑plane background and enhances excitation, improving contrast; iterative elution/re‑staining of the same sections allows highly multiplexed molecular imaging, and imaging consecutive sections of the ribbon reconstructs sub‑diffraction 3‑D volumes (array‑tomography style).

**Massively parallel near‑field (nano‑aperture‑array) imaging of the section mounted directly on a "nano‑illumination chip."**

Instead of improving far‑field optics or expanding the specimen, exploit the fact that a 30–100 nm section is thinner than the near‑field decay length, so it can be imaged *in contact* with a nanostructured light source.
